Rudra and Rudrajaya, and likewise Āpa and Āpavatsaka.
On both sides of that ear-line, within the pairs of squares,
the preceptor [should place] Śarva, Guha, Aryaman, Jṛmbhaka, and Pilapicchikā.
One should worship Carakī, Vidārī, and Pūtanā in sequence;
one should worship these in the directions starting from the east, at the positions of the middle and the beginning and end of each.
The supreme teacher [should worship] the eight deities in groups of eight:
in order, Īśāna, Parjanya, Jayanta, Śakra, and Bhāskara.
Satya, Vṛṣa, and Antarikṣa are established in the eastern direction;
as are Agni, Pūṣan, Vitatha, and Yama, the guardian of the house. (32)
Gandharva, Bhṛṅgarāja, and Mṛga are situated in the southern direction;
then follow Nirṛti, Dauvārika, Sugrīva, and Varuṇa.
The Asuras Puṣpadanta and Śoṣa, as well as the two diseases, are situated in the western direction.
Vāyu, Nāga, Mukhya, Soma, Bhallāṭa,
the one named Argala, Aditi, and Aditi are situated in the direction of Kubera (the north).
In the *Mahākapilapañcarātra*, however, it is stated:
"For houses, palaces, wells, pavilions, and water [reservoirs], a *vāstu-maṇḍala* measuring eight cubits must be constructed; no other [size] is prescribed."
Īśānaśiva, however, has stated that Brahmins should worship in sixty-four squares, while kings and others should do so in eighty-one squares.
In the *Hayaśīrṣapañcarātra*, it is said: "An architectural site consisting of eighty-one squares is recommended for house-building."
A site consisting of sixty-four squares is recommended for palaces.
In the Mahākapilapañcarātra, however, it is stated:
"For a temple, [one uses] sixty-four [squares], and likewise for a house, eighty-one;
the Vāstu-cakra consists of eighty-one squares."
Śikhin, Parjanya, Jayanta.
Indra is the true Sun.
The wind is intensely pervasive in the intermediate space.
Diti, the waters, and the conquerors.
Indra is the true Sun.
The intense one is Pūṣan, the son of Savitṛ.
Aditi is Aditi; he is the calf.
Aryaman, Aryaman, Aryaman.
Savitṛ is false; he is false.
The serpent is Sumeru.
Brahmā, Brahmā, Brahmā.
Vivasvat was Bṛhatkṣetra;
Bṛhatkṣetra...
Soma, Soma, Sumeru.
Brahmā, Brahmā, Brahmā.
Vivasvat is Yama;
Yama is [the sun].
Bhallāṭa, Bhallāṭa, Sumeru.
Brahmā, Brahmā, Brahmā.
Vivasvān is a Gandharva;
[he] is a Gandharva.
Rājayakṣmā is the foremost of all [diseases].
Mitra,
Mitra, Mitra.
Indra is Bhṛṅgarāja;
Bhṛṅgarāja is Indra.
Ahi is Rudra, the witherer.
The Asura Varuṇa Puṣpadanta.
Sugrīva, Jaya, and Mṛga.
May disease,
evil, and wasting away not come to me.
The asura Varuṇa Puṣpadanta.
Sugrīva is the gatekeeper and father.
Thus it has been said. Regarding the term "Brahmā," [this refers to] when the four squares have been swept into a single form.
However, according to the system of eighty-one squares, Somaśambhu states: "In the center, Brahmā occupies nine squares; the remaining [squares] are known to be single [square] units."
The six-footed ones, beginning with Marīci, reside in the directions starting from the east in successive order.
Therein, one should also draw an eight-petaled lotus. As it is stated in the *Mahākapilapañcarātra*:
"In the center of the twenty-fifth square, one should worship Brahmā in due order.
And in the *Kādimata*: "In the very center, one should properly worship Brahmā, who is seated upon a lotus (*kamalāsana*)."
Golden-hued, four-faced, and distinguished by the study of the Vedas.
And the worship should be performed after filling the squares with the five powders. As it is stated in the *Gautamīya-tantra*:
"Having filled the squares of the aforementioned deities with the five [powders]..."
Then, one should offer oblations of milk-rice (pāyasa) to them with dust from those [sites].
The sixty-four-square Vāstu-cakra:
Śarva is in the Pilapicchikā, and Īśāna is in the [north-east].
Aditi,
Paryanya,
and Jayanta.
Śakra is the sun, the truth.
The bull is Agni in the intermediate space.
Aditi is Parjanya, she is Diti.
Jayanta, Śakra, and Bhāskara.
The true, bull-like Pūṣan.
Pūṣan is the bolt, the bolt.
The waters with their offspring, and Aryaman.
Aryaman is Savitṛ, the impeller.
Vitatha,
Vitatha,
Bhallāṭa.
Bhallāṭa, Mahīdhara, and Brahmā.
Brahmā, Vivasvat, and Gṛharakṣaka.
Soma is the guardian of the house; Soma is Soma.
The upholder of the earth is Brahmā;
[he is] Brahmā.
Vivasvat is the guardian of the house;
he is the guardian of the house.
Rudra is the foremost, the most eminent.
Rudrajaya is Mitra; Mitra is Rudrajaya.
Śakra, Indrajaya, and Gandharva.
Gandharva,
Nāga, Nāga.
Śoṣa,
Asura,
and Puṣpadanta.
Varuṇa is Sugrīva, the king of bees.
The doorkeeper is Bhṛṅgarāja;
he is the wind.
Disease, consumption, and the Asura.
Puṣpadanta, Varuṇa, and Sugrīva.
The doorkeeper is Mṛga,
Nirṛti.
One should worship Aryaman and Vidārī with sweet milk-rice (pāyasa) mixed with all [sweet substances];
or, for the sake of pacifying the humors (doṣas), the wise man should perform the worship with the respective materials appropriate to each.
In the *divyasārasvata* [mandala]: having cleared away nine squares in the center, one should fill them with white powder; furthermore, one should do so in the four directions surrounding it.
Having swept away the six squares, one should fill them with red powder;
and the remaining squares here should be arranged in their proper places.
"Then, in the center of those various [elements], one should thoroughly worship Brahmā.

Thus, the procedure for the worship of Brahmā is as follows: on the pericarp (karṇikā), [one worships] from the Tadmaṇḍūka up to the Supreme Reality (paratattva); on the filaments (kesara) and in the center, the nine pedestal-energies (pīṭhaśakti) beginning with Aṇimā and ending with Sarvasiddhi. Oṃ...

Having worshipped the central seat with the mantra, "Obeisance to the Yogapīṭha, whose lotus-seat manifests all knowledge and action," one should invoke Brahmā there as prescribed and worship Brahmā with the fivefold offerings (*pañcopacāra*) and so forth using the mantra, "Oṃ, obeisance to Brahmā. Thereafter, one should also worship the others as his retinue.
Regarding their meditation, it is stated in another tantra: "The forms of all the aforementioned deities are now described:
[Brahmā holds] a rosary and a sacrificial ladle in his right hands, and a staff and a water-pot in his left."
One should worship the eight-eyed one seated upon a lotus in the center;
all the gods, possessing four arms, are stationed within the body of Vāstu.
With palms joined in reverence, all of them— holding swords and shields in their hands—
gazed intently at Brahmā, facing his direction.
When they are situated in their respective places, it is described as "common" (sādhāraṇa).
Marīci is white in color, and Vivasvān is red in color.
Mitra resembles gold; Bhūdhara is black in color;
Savitṛ has the luster of blue; and Sāvitra has a smoky form.
Indra has the luster of the color of dawn, and Indrajaya is likewise white;
Rudra resembles a young sprout, and Rudrajaya is yellow.
Āpa is white as cow’s milk; Āpavatsa has the luster of a japā flower;
Īśāna is white as milk; Parjanya resembles collyrium.
Jayanta is like collyrium in appearance, and Mahendra possesses stainless luster;
Āditya is red in color, and Satyaka is variegated in hue.
Vṛṣa has the luster of the bandhūka flower; Antarikṣaka has the luster of a kunda flower; Agni has the brilliance of the rising sun; and Pūṣan resembles a red lotus.
35) Vitatha is like a rainbow, Vidyutvarṇa is the color of lightning, Gṛharakṣaka is like collyrium, Yama is like black aloe-wood, and Gandharva is like a ruby.
Bhṛṅgarāja is the color of a bumblebee, Mṛga resembles a cloud,
Nirṛti has the luster of fire, and Dauvārika is known to be yellow.

Sugrīva has the luster of a peacock's neck; Candrābha is like the moon; Puṣpadantaka has the appearance of crystal; Varuṇa has limbs with the brilliance of crystal; and the Asura is considered to have the luster of a bumblebee.
Consumption is like a blue lotus, and the disease is like sapphire;
wind is the color of a black cloud, and the serpent is like a conch shell or the moon.
Mukhya resembles a pearl, Bhallāṭa is like a white lotus,
Soma is like crystal, and Argala has the luster of a red lotus.
Diti is remembered as white as a jasmine flower or the moon, while Aditi is tawny;
Carakī resembles a conch shell, and Vidārī has the brilliance of fire.
Pūtanā resembles snow, Pilapicchikā has the luster of a cloud;
they carry a sword, a drinking vessel, a knife, and likewise a pair of shears.
Those assuming terrifying forms are proclaimed to be the Rākṣasīs;
white, red, yellow, and black are the Grahas beginning with Skanda.
Holding a vajra, a spear, a sword, and a noose, those with deformed faces are declared to be the terrifying grahas, beginning with Skanda.
Here, the specific offerings for the bali and the mantras for each deity are stated in the Mahākapilapañcarātra and the Gautamīyatantra:
"Combined with milk-rice, boiled rice, and parched grain, along with incense and flowers..."
O Brahman, accept this bali offering, joined with rice and other foods and adorned with black gram cakes; destroy the defects of the site.
O you who are called Āryaka, accept this cake of sugar and fragrant ingredients placed upon milk-rice; destroy all defects.
O Lord, accept this [offering] honored with sandalwood and the like, adorned with camphor and agallochum;
O Vivasvat, please destroy all defects.
O Lord, accept this pleasing oblation of milk-rice with jaggery, well-endowed with flowers and other offerings; O Friend, grant me peace.
O Lord of the Earth, accept this rice mixed with black gram and meat, combined with perfumes and milk; destroy every evil.
36) Having thus worshipped in the center, one should offer the bali-offering to Īśāna and the others.
By this [rule], even when the sequence begins with the southeast (āgneya) during worship, the sequence for the *bali* offering begins with the northeast (īśāna). It is stated elsewhere:
"The *bali* is generally described as revolving clockwise from the northeast;
however, there is indeed a distinction among all things regarding the determination of their positions."
In some places, however, worship is likewise prescribed:
"One should worship the deities in the corners beginning with the northeast according to the rule;
the wise one should worship those situated in the four corners starting from Īśāna. Thus it is said.
Likewise: "O Water, accept this pleasing offering consisting of milk mixed with sugar and adorned with flowers and other items; grant me peace."
O child, accept this offering of curd mixed with jaggery and well-conjoined with perfumes and other ingredients; dispel all obstacles here.
O Sāvitrī, accept these flowers, kuśa grass, and water scented with camphor and agallochum; grant me peace in this matter.
O Lord Sūrya, accept this offering of flour-cake with molasses, adorned with red perfumes and other ornaments; destroy all obstacles here.
O Lord Śakra, accept this cool food, as well as flowers accompanied by saffron and other offerings; take this *bali* offering, O vulture-eater, salutations be unto you!
O Indrajaya, accept this delightful offering of rice mixed with clarified butter and adorned with garments, perfumes, and other ornaments; homage be unto you!
O Lord Rudra, accept this pleasing offering of meat, both cooked and raw, combined with cloth, flowers, and other items; I bow down to you.
Accept this offering, consisting of meat cooked with ghee and combined with perfumes, flowers, and other ingredients; O Rudrajaya, grant me well-being.
O Vidārī, accept this red flower together with meat, accompanied by red garments and the like; destroy this obstacle of the Rākṣasa.
O Pūtanā, take this [child] joined with bile, blood, and bone, adorned with the scent of blood and the like; destroy this obstacle of the Rākṣasa.
O Śarva, accept this offering of black gram cooked with rice and ghee, combined with red perfumes and other substances; destroy the obstacles caused by the Rākṣasas.
O Skanda, accept this offering consisting of meat combined with flowers and other items, as well as black gram and cooked rice; ward off the obstructing spirits and demons.
Dog meat mixed with flour, accompanied by cooked meat and water— O Aryaman, accept this and destroy all obstacles!
O Jṛmbhaka, accept this offering of blood, meat, rice, fish, along with perfumes and flowers; destroy the obstacle of the Rākṣasa.
O Pilapiccha, accept this meat provided with goat’s ears, along with cloth, perfumes, and other offerings; destroy this obstacle of the Rākṣasa.
O Carakī, accept this meat prepared with ghee and endowed with garments, perfumes, and other offerings; destroy this obstacle of the Rākṣasa.
O Lord, accept this bali offering— consisting of cooked rice with ghee and unbroken grains, adorned with garments, perfumes, and other ornaments— which removes the defects of the site (vāstu).
O King of Clouds, accept this pleasing offering consisting of blue lotuses, milk-rice, and garments; homage be to you!
O son of Jiṣṇu, accept this five-cubit long, bright yellow banner adorned with flowers and other offerings; take this pleasing *bali* offering; salutations to you!
O King of Gods, accept this pleasing offering of cooked rice filled with clarified butter and adorned with the five jewels and other gems; homage be to you!
O Bhāskara, accept this pleasing bali-offering consisting of cooked food mixed with red flowers and accompanied by red perfumes and other offerings; salutations be unto you!
O Satya, accept this canopy, which has the luster of smoke-colored clouds, beautifully adorned with perfumes and other offerings, and joined with red; this oblation is for you—salutations to you!
But please accept this offering of black gram cooked with rice, honored with garments, perfumes, and other gifts;
O Bull, receive this oblation and destroy the defects of the site.
But accept this meat of the six flavors, well-prepared as an offering and so forth;
take this pleasing oblation, O Vyoman, and grant me peace.
O Seven-tongued One, accept this gold, flour-cake, and cloth along with perfumes and other offerings, accompanied by clarified butter; salutations be unto you!
O Lord Pūṣan, accept this pleasing offering of milk mixed with parched grain and combined with perfumes, flowers, and other ingredients; salutations be unto you!
Accept this offering of rice mixed with meat, accompanied by perfumes and garlands, and adorned with garments and other ornaments;
O Vitatha, take this bali and destroy the defects of the site!
O King Yama, accept this bali offering consisting of cooked rice mixed with fish and meat, adorned with perfumes, flowers, and other ornaments; grant me peace.
O Guardian of the House, accept this pleasing offering of cooked meat, rice, fresh butter, and ornaments such as garments; homage be to you!
O Gandharva, accept this offering combined with various fragrances and joined with red flowers and other items; destroy all defects.
But take this tongue of a bird placed upon a meal of black beans;
O Bhṛṅgarāja, accept this offering and grant me peace.
O God of the Deer, accept this pleasing bali-offering, consisting of barley, sesame, and ghee, combined with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings; homage be to you!
O King of Rākṣasas, accept this offering with pleasure—this sugar-sweetened portion adorned with cloth, perfumes, and other ornaments; homage be to you!
O Gatekeeper, accept this pleasing offering consisting of pieces of sandalwood and agalloch, along with garments, perfumes, and other items; homage be to you!
But this milk-rice, O Lord, mixed with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings—
O Sugrīva, accept this oblation and grant me peace.
O Lord of Water, accept this pleasing offering of milk adorned with barley and other grains presented upon the food; salutations be unto you.
O Puṣpadanta, accept this black-gram meal together with a bunch of kuśa grass and perfumes such as ghee; destroy the defects of the site.
O Lord of Asuras, accept this offering prepared with honey, ground with fragrant substances and the like; destroy all defects.
O Śoṣa, accept this offering consisting of ghee mixed with food and endowed with camphor and other ingredients; grant me complete peace.
O Lord, accept this offering of barley and rice, adorned with perfumes, flowers, and the like; O Disease, destroy all afflictions.
O Lord who has a deer for his vehicle, accept this pleasing offering of *maṇḍaka* cakes with clarified butter, adorned with various foods; salutations be unto you!
"O Lord of Pātāla, please accept this kṛśara-rice prepared with the scent of milk and other ingredients; dispel all obstacles here."
O Chief One, accept this offering consisting of coconut water, cooked rice, and yellow garments; destroy the defects of the site.
O Soma, accept this offering of milk-rice mixed with honey and accompanied by yellow flowers, and destroy all defects.
O Bhallāṭa, accept this pleasing oblation of cooked rice mixed with clarified butter and accompanied by fragrant flowers; homage be unto you!
O you named Argala, accept this pleasing offering of black gram cooked with clarified butter, adorned with perfumes, flowers, and other ornaments; salutations be unto you!
O Mother of the Daityas, accept this milk mixed with sugar and adorned with various offerings; destroy all defects.
O Mother of the Gods, accept this sweetmeat mixed with honey and endowed with garments, perfumes, and other offerings; accept this pleasing oblation; salutations be unto you!
May those deities who reside in heaven, the netherworld, and the mortal realm, and who are born of this site, accept this pleasing oblation; being satisfied, may they depart to their own abodes.
May the Mothers, the Bhūtas, the Vetālas, and whoever else desires a girl,
as well as the attendants of Viṣṇu, accept this sacrificial offering.
Having offered the bali-oblation to the ancestors and the guardians of the field according to one's desire,
one should worship with kuśa grass, flowers, and so forth, in the absence of the prescribed path.

In the *Prayogasāra*: "The offering to the quarters (*diśābali*), which consists of the remaining rites of the site-consecration, which bestows all protection and prosperity, and which grants satisfaction to the spirits (*bhūta*), is now described."
That which is intended for all beings, addressed by name to the assembly of the guardians of the directions,
and consists of worship ending with the ritual dismissal, should be known as the *diśābali*.
One should offer oblations (bali) in the various directions according to their respective order, using the substances of curd, water, turmeric, flowers, parched grain, flour, sesame seeds, and food.
Furthermore, it belongs to the gods, to the radiant ones, to the pretas, and even to the rākṣasas;
likewise, it belongs to the waters, to the vital breaths, and to the lunar mansions.
One should offer oblations to those aforementioned lords of the sciences (vidyās),
having uttered their names together with the words for their vehicles, as well as to their retinues and their powers (śaktis).
Then, having combined [the offerings] from all those to the side-elephants,
one should further cast the bali-offering in due order to the bhūtas by proceeding clockwise.
He is the remover of fear and suffering caused by elephants, piśācas, vetālas, and rākṣasas;
he who receives offerings from all directions and especially bestows the abundance of all prosperity.
At the laying of a foundation, the seizing of land, the planting of trees, when there is harm from spirits, at the entry into a new house,
and during an extensive peace-offering (śāntihoma), the offering to the quarters (diśāṃ bali) should be performed for the sake of success.
As for the mantra of dismissal (*visarjana*), it is stated in another tantra:
"May all the hosts of deities depart, taking with them this earthly worship, so that their desired objects may be accomplished, and for the sake of returning again."

The procedure here is as follows: having drawn the *vāstumaṇḍala* with colored powders and filled in the squares, one should fashion an eight-petalled lotus in the center according to the method to be described;
there, having meditated upon Brahmā in the manner stated, and having worshipped the respective deities in their respective squares, [one proceeds] in the eastern direction.

Having prepared either a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) or a leveled mound (sthaṇḍila), and having established the fire there according to the sequence to be described, one should invoke the deities beginning with Brahmā from the mandala into that place, and [offer] one hundred and eight oblations to Brahmā, and to the others...
Having offered ten oblations for each of the ten stages (*daśāhuti*) and performed the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*), one should again invite the deities into the mandala.

Having offered them the *bali* and the directional *bali* with the prescribed substances and mantras, and having worshipped them once more, one should dismiss them with the stated mantra. Then, one should give the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to the preceptor (*ācārya*).
The disciple should prostrate before him.
Thus ends the ritual procedure for the Vāstu-sacrifice.
Now follows the means for determining the directions, such as the east and so forth, for the purpose of constructing the pavilion.
In the *Tantrarāja*: "The preceptor, having ascertained the directions by the movement of the sun, should perform the rites;
for where the cardinal points are not correctly known due to irregularities in the site."
Having fixed a gnomon there, one should ascertain the location of the direction of Indra (the east).
Listen as I explain, according to the rule, how the directions are to be fully known by means of its movement.
Having fashioned a circle on a perfectly level ground by means of rotation,
one should place a twelve-finger-long gnomon at its central point.
When the two circles formed by the succession of the shadows of the tip have been drawn in the east and west,
one should likewise mark points on both sides of that [central] point for the forenoon and afternoon.
Having again formed two circles with their own equal circumferences,
[one should place] the one situated in the south and the one situated in the north at the center produced by their mutual contact.
And at the two junctions, one should lay down the thread between the eastern and western lines;
then, using the tips of those [threads], one should determine the directions starting from the east, with the southern and northern threads.

41) Regarding the essence of the ritual action: having made the ground level there, one should fashion a circular mandala measuring one cubit in diameter and twelve finger-breadths in height, using a gnomon (śaṅku) made of khadira wood.
If such wood is not available, the wise man should install a sacrificial tree there;
that spot which his shadow touches is considered the middle point between them.
One should extend the thread crosswise; the middle [threads] are known as south-north.
From the extension of four threads, the other four corners are formed.
Thus has the thorough knowledge of the directions been clearly explained;
having understood this, the wise practitioner should properly construct the pavilions and other structures.
The pavilion (maṇḍapa), moreover, is of three kinds, distinguished as superior, inferior, and middling. As it is stated in the *Pratiṣṭhāsārasaṃgraha*:
"This [smallest] is twelve cubits; from that point, it increases successively by two [cubits] each time."
Somaśambhu also states:
"The pavilion may be twelve cubits or ten cubits; the remaining auspicious pavilions are formed by increasing the size by two cubits each."
Also in the *Mahākapilapañcarātra*:
"Starting from twelve cubits and increasing by two in succession,
one should thus prepare the sacrificial pavilion after performing the purification of the ground."
It should be nine cubits, five cubits, or three cubits, according to one's inclination.

By the statement from the *Gautamīya Tantra*, namely "nine cubits" and "five cubits," as well as by "fourteen cubits," "nine cubits," and "three cubits," the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*) is said to be twelve cubits [in size]. Likewise: "It is considered to be five, seven, or nine cubits; this is another opinion."

Thus it is also stated in the Śāradā-tilaka: by the phrase "with five and seven," a pavilion of twelve cubits is described; by "with five and nine," one of fourteen cubits; and by "with seven and nine," one of sixteen cubits. Likewise—
"One should then construct a pavilion with a smooth altar measuring only two arms of seven *acalas*.

Thus it is stated in the *Kramadīpikā*. Here, "seven *acalas*" refers to two arms; therefore, the meaning is that it measures fourteen cubits (*hasta*s). For if taken literally [as seven cubits], it would be impossible for the eight sacrificial pits, the altar, the officiating priests, their movements, and so forth to fit.
As for that which states:
"For the purpose of the ritual procedures such as the fire-oblation and consecration of kings, one should construct a pavilion measuring nine cubits in both width and length."

This statement from the *Tantrarāja* refers to a pavilion (*maṇḍapa*) intended for rites other than initiation (*dīkṣā*), because it is stated in the same manner in the first half [of the verse]. In the *Siddhāntaśekhara*, it is said: "The site of the pavilion is declared to be one hundred and twelve finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) in height."
In the *Mahākapilapañcarātra*, however, it is stated:
"The height shall be one cubit, perfectly level and very beautiful.
(42) In the *Śāradā*: "It is joined with sixteen pillars, four of which are situated in the middle."
Eight cubits in height, twelve [images] should be installed on all sides.
Measuring five cubits, they should be without holes, straight, and auspicious;
the best among those who know the tantras should bury one-fifth of them into the earth.
One should cover its exterior on all sides with coconut leaves.

Regarding the phrase "eight cubits": this refers specifically to the sixteen-cubit pavilion (*maṇḍapa*), according to the statement in the *Pañcarātra*: "The pillars should be half the height of the pavilion and provided with four finials (*cūḍā*). The installation of the pillars, whether in the center or on the outside, follows the sequence starting from the southeast (*āgneya*).
The commencement of the work—
namely, the raising of pillars, the laying of stones, the fixing of pins for the application of measuring lines,
and the excavation and preparation of pits— is performed when the fire is in its proper domain.
Thus it is stated. In the *Siddhāntaśekhara*: "In the center there should be four pillars, and in their midst a pedestal (*vedikā*) is prescribed.
In another tantra: "Having placed pillars in the form of the Vedas at the corners of the pedestal (*vedikā*)."
In the Pañcarātra: "One should make the pillars firm, straight, and uniform, fashioned from heartwood."
In the *Kriyāsāra*: "For the work of pillars, one may use a sacrificial tree, bamboo, or the *kramuka* tree;
or other pure trees may be used, but not trees of any other kind."
In the work of constructing pillars, a house-post that is dry by itself, crooked, ancient,
and produced from inauspicious soil must be abandoned.
The measurement of twelve pillars for the middle and lowest types [of temples] should be calculated by means of the rule of three proportions (*tryairāśika*).
"One should place a fifth part upon the ground; this is the rule common to all," according to the statement in the *Vāstuśāstra*.

Furthermore, according to the statement in the *Siddhāntaśekhara*, "The excavation for all [pillars] is declared by Śiva to be one-fifth [of the height]," the digging for all the pillars of the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*) is indeed by one-fifth [of their height]. The phrase "with coconut leaves," etc., is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*).
"The pavilions, beginning with Vijaya, should be covered with excellent mats," according to the statement in the Vāstuśāstra. In the Mantramuktāvalī:
"One should construct four doors in the cardinal directions, [measuring] one-fifth [of the width]."
In the *Pañcarātra*: "In the smallest [mandala], it should be two cubits, increasing by four finger-breadths."
One should install the captivating door between the middle and the upper [sections].
What does "here" refer to? One should construct four archways (toraṇa) at the gates outside the pavilion.

As it has been said: "Outside the gates of the pavilion, according to the measurement of the altar and following the sequence of the directions, one should install archways made of Plakṣa, Udumbara, Aśvattha, and Vaṭa wood."
Somaśambhu states: "The archways (toraṇas) are made respectively from Plakṣa, Udumbara, Aśvattha, and Vaṭa trees."
They should be arranged starting from the east, or else with the beginning and end reversed;
however, if they cannot all be obtained, one should place even a single one of them in all directions.
In the Siddhāntaśekhara: "If a pure tree is not available, there should be only one;
in its absence, the śamī tree, or the heartwood of the jambu and khadira, or the tāla tree is prescribed for the archway (toraṇa)."
In the *Mahākapilapañcarātra*:
"The gods are stationed in the form of archways within the sacrificial pavilion,
for the purpose of destroying obstacles and for the protection of the sacrifice."
One should plant a nyagrodha tree in the east, an udumbara in the south,
a pippala in the west, and a plakṣa in the north.
The very beautiful [image] in the east, consecrated with the Ṛgveda and other [Vedas],
and that called Subhadra in the south, [is consecrated] with the mantra "iṣe tvā."
One should place the one called Sukarman in the west with the Sāmaveda and so forth, using the mantra "śanno devī"; and one should place Suhotra in the north.
In the Śāradā [Tantra]: "At the gates, there should be arches (toraṇas) made from milk-bearing trees;
their pillar-height is traditionally recorded as seven cubits each."

Its circumference is said to be ten finger-breadths (aṅgulas) in measure; the measurement of the horizontal beam (phalaka) should be half the measurement of the pillar. One should fashion the spikes (śūla) in the middle of the archway (toraṇa) with a measurement of one cubit (hasta).
"By seven cubits" refers to the case of the best pavilion (*maṇḍapa*). As it is stated in the *Vāstuśāstra*:
"They [the pillars] are five cubits in measurement, two cubits in width;
by an increase of six *aṅgulas* and so forth, they become seven cubits in the best [pavilion]."
Regarding "six finger-breadths, etc.": by this, the ground space between the two *toraṇa* pillars in the lowest pavilion (*maṇḍapa*) is two cubits;
in the middle one, it is two cubits plus six finger-breadths; and in the highest one, it is two cubits plus twelve finger-breadths.
By this distinction of pavilions, the measurement of the horizontal planks is also stated for the lowest and highest ones.
By stating that the height is five or seven cubits, it follows that for the middle [class], a height of six cubits is prescribed. In the *Piṅgalāmata*:
"The door-frames should be marked with tridents at their own tops."
The central shaft should indeed be straight, while it is slightly curved at the two sides.
44) That is declared to be both; one should then plant three *aṅgulas* [of wood].
In the *Kriyāsāra*: "Having thus constructed the archway (*toraṇa*), one should place three tridents (*śūla*) upon its summit."
The length of the trident (śūla) is nine finger-breadths (aṅgula), and its width is one-fourth of that;
for the remaining parts, the increase is two finger-breadths, and the insertion (veśa) increases by one finger-breadth.
And this arrangement of the trident is found in the Śaiva and Śākta traditions. However, there is a specific distinction in the Vaiṣṇava *Vāstuśāstra*:

"On the head [of the structure], one should place the conch, discus, mace, and lotus with a measurement of twelve parts, according to the sequence starting from the east, made from their own respective woods."

In the Śāradā [Tantra] it is said: "One should tie banners in the various directions that possess a splendor equal to that of the world-protectors (lokapālas), and one should adorn the pavilion with canopies, garlands of darbha grass, and other such ornaments."
In the *Pratiṣṭhāsārasaṃgraha*: "The banners are recorded as being five cubits in length and colored yellow, red, and so forth;
they are considered to be joined with staffs made of bamboo, measuring ten cubits."
With banners five or ten cubits long; elsewhere it is also said:
"The banners should be made five cubits, or alternatively two cubits;
the staff should be ten cubits, and one should place them in the eight directions."
In the *Hayaśīrṣapañcarātra*: "O Brahmin, in a pavilion devoid of a banner, all acts such as worship, fire-offerings (*homa*), and recitation (*japa*) performed by the wise would be in vain."
Just as a field belonging to its owner perishes without a protector,
so too a temple would utterly perish without its banner.
The cruel attendants of Viṣṇu, such as the Kūṣmāṇḍas and others who are remembered [in tradition],
seize the offerings and the like if they see the deity unprotected.
But having seen the banners of the God in the pavilion, blazing with the splendor of fire,
they all perished like darkness dispelled by the rays of the sun.
In the *Siddhāntaśekhara*: "Abounding with garlands of mango sprouts, adorned with canopies, covered with variegated cloths, and embellished with pillars shaped like scales."
With fruitful plantain trunks, betel nuts, and coconuts;
with various kinds of fruits and edible foods, as well as mirrors and chowries.
One should decorate the pavilion, making it radiant with jewels and flowers.
In the *Hayaśīrṣapañcarātra*: "One should adorn the pillars with mirrors, chowries, bells, and cloths."
With water-pots, jars, and likewise with basins and stones provided with stands.
In that regard, one water-pot (kalaśa) should be placed at each archway (toraṇa); two at each side of every door;
and one at each corner. As it has been said: "One should place within those [archways] pots provided with perfumes, flowers, and garments."
On those archways, one should certainly worship Dhruva, Vākpati, and Vighneśa;
and in the pitchers located at the corners of the pavilion, these [deities] should be worshipped in sequence.
Amṛta, Durjaya, Siddhārtha, and likewise Maṅgala— these,
along with Śakra and the others, are to be worshipped in the pitchers at the door with their respective excellent mantras.
Elsewhere it is also said: "In the pavilion, one should place two jars at each door, filled with filtered water and adorned with mango sprouts."
In the *Śāradā-tilaka*: "Then, on a field measuring one-third of that [area], one should prepare a square altar (*vedi*) one cubit (*aratni*) in height for the sake of the mandala."
Elsewhere also: "Then one should determine the thread for the pavilion as threefold;
by its middle portion, the altar is established in order starting from the east."
In the Siddhāntaśekhara as well: "Having divided the pavilion into nine parts, an altar is prescribed for the central part;
it should be one cubit (aratni) in height, or one hand (hasta) in elevation."
From those four [finger-breadths] comes a fist; three times that is a span (vitasti);
two of those is a cubit (aratni), and from two of those, O Śivā, comes a hand (hasta).
For it is stated in the *Tantrarāja*: "Thus, the words *aratni* and *hasta* are declared to be synonyms.
And in that same work: "Therein, from one-third of that [measurement], one should construct an altar (*vedī*) in the center, raised by the measure of one cubit (*kara*). [End of] Mantra...
In the Muktāvalī as well: "A wise person desiring success should construct an altar resembling a mirror, made either of bricks or clay, and one cubit high by the measure of a king's hand."
In the *Kriyāsāra* as well: "Having divided the mandala into three parts, the middle part shall be the altar (*vedikā*);
its height should be one cubit, and it should be square and level."
Likewise: "One that is crooked on the sides, moist in the middle, rough, and unpleasant to look at;
or one that is deficient or excessive in measure—that destroys the work of the artisan."

The defect arising from the improper construction of the pavilion (maṇḍapa) is stated in the *Kriyāsāra*: "If a pavilion is constructed with unmentioned materials, or if it is crooked in shape, or if it exceeds or falls short of the prescribed measurements, it causes the destruction of the ritual."
This beautiful pavilion, well-constructed with the means prescribed by the verbal roots, equal in measure,
and pleasing to the mind, brings auspiciousness to the performer of the rite.
Thus ends the description of the pavilion (maṇḍapa).

46) Now, regarding the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas), the Śāradā [Tantra] states: "In the previously described pavilion, the wise man [should divide the area] outside the altar (vedikā) into three parts."
Having divided the field, one should designate the eastern and other directions within the central portion.
In the eight directions, there are sacrificial pits (kuṇḍa) of beautiful form in sequence:
square, yoni-shaped, crescent-moon, triangular, and perfectly circular.
These [fire-pits] are hexagonal and lotus-shaped, as well as octagonal by name;
the preceptor’s pit should be in the middle, between the lords of Gaurī and Mahendra.
In the Siddhāntaśekhara: "Between Purandara and Īśa, [the site] is either circular or square; that is prescribed for the preceptor."
In the *Kriyāsāra*: "The central area for the Bull and the Lord [Śiva] may be circular or square.
Furthermore, regarding the square sacrificial pit (*caturasrakuṇḍa*), the *Tantrarāja* states: "Having stretched a cord from east to west, one should mark the center of it."
Having done that, afterwards, at a measurement of twelve finger-breadths from the front, [he should proceed].
Having thoroughly wiped that area as well, one should establish a pair of marks; using the measurement of the east-west marks, one should hang [the cord] from those two very points.
Having made a *haṃsapada* mark to the south and north, one should then stretch a thread between those two and erase them according to the stated measurement.
Then, taking hold of those tips according to the measurement of the central mark, one should form the *haṃsapada* (swan’s footprint); from there, one should cast out the squares.
The fourfold [altar] should be a square and perfectly even;
within that, I shall describe to you the other sacrificial pits according to their measurements.
In the *Gautamīya-tantra*: "Having extended a cord one cubit in length from east to west, one should clearly form a pair of fish at its two ends."
Having divided that cord into two parts, one should drop it from south to north.
One should then form a pair of fish-marks at its two ends so that they are clearly defined.
One should then drop four cords in the four directions according to that same measurement.
It should be quadrangular, consisting of four compartments, and exceedingly beautiful.
One should draw two diagonal lines; by means of that measurement, one should mark out a square sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) endowed with all the required characteristics.
47) Likewise: "By this [measurement], the best of mantra-knowers should produce all the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas).
In the *Śāradā*: "Those who know the tantras understand a cubit (hasta) to be twenty-four finger-breadths (aṅgulas) long, measured by the middle joint of the right hand of the performer."
The measurement finger (mānāṅgula) is declared to be the length of the middle [finger];
the mānāṅgula is declared to be fashioned from eight barley grains.

Here, according to the stated method—"one should multiply [the side] by half the square root of the area"—the area of a one-cubit (*hasta*) pit is five hundred and seventy-six finger-breadths (*aṅgula*);
for two cubits and so forth, it is double that, and so on. This is calculated by means of the diagonal cord (*karṇasūtra*) of a one-cubit pit.
The central cord of a two-cubit pit is thus [calculated]; by means of that ear-cord, the central cord of a four-cubit pit is to be understood. The same applies hereafter.
As it is stated in the Gautamīya-tantra:
"One should excavate a pit measuring two cubits according to the measurement of the ear-ornament (karṇasūtra).
In all pits everywhere, one should increase [the size] according to this rule.
In reality, having doubled or tripled the area of one cubit and so forth, one should determine its square root.

The measurement of the central cord for a sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) of two cubits, three cubits, and so forth, should be understood [accordingly]. One should dig it with that respective measurement multiplied in due order;
this is because of the statement in the *Jñānārṇava*: "In the case of ignorance regarding the multiplication..."

The measurement of the central cord for sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍa*) of two cubits and so forth should be understood from the words of authoritative masters (*abhiyukta*). As it is said: From one hand (*hasta*) up to ten, the measurements in finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) are: four, three, three, four, three, and five; then six, four, and four. (This corresponds to 24, 36, 48, 60, 72, 84, 96, 108, 120, and 132 *aṅgulas*.)

The completed [figures] are: oceans (4), arrows (5), Viyas (2), and Yavas (1) in the left hand; half (1/2), pairs (2), groups (3), six (6), elephants (8), limbs (6), Viyas (2), and Yavas (1); and six mountains (7) diminished by the eye (2) and sages (7) and a Yava (1).
And thus, the width (vyāsa) of one cubit is twenty-four finger-breadths (aṅgula);
that of two cubits is thirty-four; that of three cubits is forty-one finger-breadths and five barley-corns (yava);
that of four cubits is forty-eight finger-breadths; and that of [five] cubits is fifty-three finger-breadths and six barley-corns.
For five cubits: fifty-three *aṅgulas* and seven *yavas*; for six cubits: fifty-eight *aṅgulas* and four *yavas*; for seven cubits: sixty-three *aṅgulas* and seven *yavas*; for eight cubits:
sixty-seven *aṅgulas* and seventy-two *aṅgulas*; for nine cubits: seventy-two *aṅgulas*.

For a ten-hand (daśahasta) [square] pit, the measurement is seventy-five finger-breadths (aṅgula) and seven barley-corns (yava). However, pits of two hands and so forth are mentioned here incidentally as they are useful for ritual applications, since in initiation (dīkṣā), only the one-hand pit is utilized. Thus ends the description of the square pit (caturasrakuṇḍa).
48) Now, regarding the characteristics of the *yonikuṇḍa*, the *Tantrarāja* states: Having expanded the *brahmasūtra* by one-fifth of the length of the *tandhya*,
[one should mark] a pair of squares from the east to the west, from the middle of the two compartments.
O Dear One, one should rotate [the cord] according to the measurement of those corners, reaching as far as the western tip,
the northern tip, and likewise the southern tip.
By supporting the two tips of the transverse line in the middle of that [square] in such a way,
two lines should extend as far as the Brahma-line (the vertical axis). O auspicious one, this is the Yoni-kunda, which exists in four forms, each possessing both natures.
Thus ends the description of the *yonikuṇḍa*.
Now, the description of the *ardhacandrakuṇḍa* is as follows:
In a square field (*catuṣkoṇe kṣetre*), having established a line (*guṇa*) at the center of one-fifth part (*jinalavaka*).
Leaving aside one and a half units below and the same amount above,

the wise man should reduce the upper portion by a sixteenth part; he should then draw a circle with that measurement as its diameter, and from that, the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) is formed as a crescent moon.
In this regard as well, the statements of the Tantrikas yield inconsistent results concerning the area of the sacrificial pit (*kṣetraphala*).
This concludes the description of the crescent-shaped pit (*ardhacandrakuṇḍa*);
now follows the description of the triangular pit (*trikoṇakuṇḍa*).

In the middle portion of the field, which is devoted to the share of the Jina, the wise man should increase the *śroṇi* (hips) by three *śara-lavas* each; then, at the front, by the eighth and ninth parts of the Jina, and finally with ten [parts], the pit (*kuṇḍa*) is formed here by applying three lines for each of the three triangles.

Thus, even according to the direction of the learned, there is an absence of equilateral symmetry. Therefore, having established a middle plumb-line of thirty-two finger-breadths and a ground of thirty-six finger-breadths, one should construct a triangular sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) by laying down three lines; by that means, both equilateral symmetry and the fullness of the area are achieved.
This is to be understood.
Thus ends the description of the triangular sacrificial pit (trikoṇakuṇḍa); now follows the description of the circular sacrificial pit (vṛttakuṇḍa).

In the central sūtra-field divided into sixteen parts, in the portion of the field increased in front, there is a single [unit]; then, by rotating from the internal marks, there shall be the maṇḍala and the kuṇḍa.
Other statements, however, have been disregarded as being inconsistent with the results regarding the area of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*).
Thus ends the description of the circular pit (49).
Now follows the description of the hexagonal pit.
In the *Kriyāsāra*: "Having divided the site into eight parts, one should place two parts on each of the two outer sides;
by this measurement, one should lay it out equally from the center."
There are four other corners and two on each of the two sides;
one should lay down six lines upon them, and that shall be the six-cornered sacrificial pit (ṣaṭkoṇakuṇḍa).
In the *Siddhāntaśekhara*: "When a square has been established as even, one should add an eighth part of the field on the outside;
from that location, one should join [the lines] at the two ends of the central thread."
Having placed a rotating mechanism with a thread of the same measure as the interior of the womb both inside and outside the womb, it comes into being through its rotation.

Then, two pairs of fish-marks should be placed externally on the north and south sides. Subsequently, in the outer portion of the Pisces (mīna) sign, and then in the pair of fish-marks within the Pisces, one should lay down six lines in succession; that is declared to be the hexagonal sacrificial pit (ṣaṭkoṇa-kuṇḍa).
Thus ends the description of the hexagonal sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).
Now follows the description of the lotus-shaped sacrificial pit:
in a lotus-shaped pit, one should divide the central line into twenty-four parts.
One should rotate the circle of the pericarp with a measurement equal to one and a half times the radius of the circle.
The filaments (keśara) are on a circle with a radius equal to half the measure of a circle divided into six parts;
the space between the petals (patramadhyabhūḥ) is on a circle with a radius equal to half the measure of a circle divided into nine parts.
From the twelve-part arc of the semicircle, the arc above the petal is prescribed;
having made the semicircle of the tips of the petals with fifteen parts.
By rotating [the compass] through sixty-four parts minus five— one part being sixty-fourths—
one should fashion the tips of the petals from the edges of the leaves starting from the ends of the lines.

Other statements, however, have been disregarded as they yield results inconsistent with the field [of practice]. In this regard, the pericarp (karṇikā) should be made three finger-breadths high and six finger-breadths in diameter. As it is stated in the Kāmika:
"Thereafter, one should fashion its height according to the measure of half the [diameter of the] pericarp."
Thus ends the description of the lotus-shaped sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).
Now follows the description of the eight-cornered sacrificial pit:
in an eight-sided pit, one should divide the central line into twenty-four parts.
It is circular, increased by one-thirtieth part, and further augmented by an increase of one part.
In the center of that, by drawing eight lines in the directions, one obtains an equal octagon.
(50) As for other statements, they have been disregarded because their calculated areas are inconsistent and they prescribe unequal lines.
Such is the characteristic of the eight-cornered sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*).
However, one who is unable to construct a pit of this size should, in all cases, construct square pits or circular pits.

The sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) may be square or circular in shape; these are praised according to the secret tradition (āmnāya). Furthermore, based on the statement of Somaśambhu, "They are always either circular or square," the middle option is the system of five pits (pañcakuṇḍīpakṣa), while the system of making a single pit (ekakuṇḍakaraṇapakṣa) is the lowest. [Then] nine or five...

"Or it should be made as a single [consecration] endowed with the proper characteristics," according to the secret teaching of the Āgamas. Its placement is also stated in that very same source: "In the ritual arrangement of five sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas), the fifth shall be in the northeast.
And in the Jñānaratnāvalī: "The [pits] in the directions are square (vedāsra) and [triangular], while the fifth is within the domain of Īśa (the northeast)."

In the Nāradīya [Tantra], however, it is said: "In that ritual where a set of four sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) is prescribed, they are respectively a square, a half-moon, a circle, and one resembling a lotus."
The wise one should construct four sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) in the directions beginning with the east;
O twice-born one, he should cause a fifth pit to be made in the region of the northeast.
Thus it has been stated. Regarding the position [of the fire] when there is a single pit (*ekakuṇḍa*), the Teachers have said:
"Alternatively, one should construct a single square pit in the northern direction.
But Somaśambhu says: "Or the wise man should cause a single [pit] to be made in the direction of Śiva (the north) or in the west."
Thus it has been said. And this sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) should be made either square or circular. As it is stated in the *Kriyāsāra*:
"The sacrificial pit may be square or even circular, for the worship of immobile deities, the worship of mobile deities, daily rites, and the act of oblation."

Also in the Piṅgalāmata: "A circular pit (kuṇḍa) measuring one cubit, provided with a girdle, a neck, and a navel, is considered auspicious for daily rites, initiation, pacification, and nourishment."
Now, regarding the excavation for the autumnal [rite]: the depth of the pit is said to be equal to the width of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*).
This is also stated in the *Prayogasāra* and the *Divyasārasvata*:
Having first drawn a square divided into four compartments with threads as before, one should dig a pit in its center, measuring one cubit in depth and length.
In the *Gaṇeśvaravimarśinī*:
"It should be twenty-four finger-breadths in length and provided with a corresponding excavation.
As for that which is stated in the *Mohaśūra* by Vyāsa: "One should dig a pit one cubit deep, both horizontally and vertically, together with a girdle (*mekhalā*)."

In the *Viśvakarmīya*, it is stated that "the excavation (*khāta*) is said to be one *tithi* (fifteen) finger-breadths deep," while in the *Prathama-tantra* it is said, "the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) is twenty-four finger-breadths across, together with the girdle (*mekhalā*) above;
the measurement of the pit's excavation shall be together with the girdle above."

Furthermore, it is stated in the *Siddhāntaśekhara* that this [prescribed size] pertains to very small fire-offerings (*svalpatarahoma*) and to offerings made with delicate flowers by those who are indolent; this is how it should be understood. In the *Gautamīya*:
"Then the mantrin should dig the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) according to the injunctions of the scriptures."
Having carefully abandoned the body of the serpent, he proceeded toward the region of its head.
If struck on the head, death occurs; if struck on the hump, there is the destruction of the body; if on the tail, the arising of suffering; but on the chest, it is the accomplishment of all goals.

The determination of the Nāga’s head and other parts is stated in another Tantra: "He indeed always lies on his left side according to the measurement of the site (vāstu). After three months, having turned over upon the ground, the Siddhas call him the Vāstunāga."
In the months beginning with Bhādrapada, that Nāga has his head toward the north; in the three months beginning with Mārgaśīrṣa, his head is toward the south;
indeed, at the start of Phālguna, his head is toward the west; and in the months beginning with Jyeṣṭha, that Nāga has his head toward the north.
Now, regarding the measurement of the neck, it is stated in the Mahākapilapañcarātra: "The neck is indeed proclaimed to be one twenty-fourth part."
The neck outside the pit is one finger-breadth; this is the rule for all fire-pits (kuṇḍas).

One should fashion the *maṅgala* as the twenty-fourth part. Now, regarding the girdle (*mekhalā*) according to the *Piṅgalāmata*: leaving aside one finger-breadth from the excavation, the placement of the girdles occurs.
In the Śāradā [Tantra]: "Whatever is the form of the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas), such also is that of the girdles (mekhalās)."
In the Vāyavīya-saṃhitā:
"There may be three girdles, or two, or even one.
In the Kriyāsāra: "A sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) provided with a navel and a yoni, and possessing three girdles, is the most excellent."
The pit should have two ridges in its middle, while the lower part should have a single ridge.
In the *Somaśambhu*: "The sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) for a Brāhmaṇa has three ridges (*mekhalā*); for a Kṣatriya, two ridges;
and for a Vaiśya, one ridge.
In that same work: "The twenty-fourth part of the pits is designated as a finger-breadth (*aṅgula*)."
By means of this [measurement], the girdle, the neck, and the navel are to be divided.
In the Mahākapilapañcarātra:
"The first [line] is known as six parts of a kuṇṭha, the second as eight parts,
and the third should be twelve parts."
52) In the *Yoginīhṛdaya*: "O Goddess, hear from me concerning the girdle, especially regarding the hands and other [limbs].
Measured by portions of six, nine, and twelve [units], these auspicious [girdles] should be kept secret."
In another tantra: "Whichever girdle is first, that is declared to be the [first] ground.
Here, "first" (pūrva) should be understood as starting from the outside. In the *Kriyāsāra*, the height of the principal girdle is stated here to be nine finger-breadths (*aṅgula*).
The height of the outer girdle surrounding that is traditionally recorded as five finger-breadths.
The height of the outermost girdle is two finger-breadths;
its width, consisting of three girdles, is respectively four, three, and two finger-breadths.
Here, the statement regarding height is made with reference to the foundational ground. In the *Lakṣaṇasaṃgraha*:
"The first [pedestal] is two finger-breadths in length and nine finger-breadths in height;
the middle one is three finger-breadths on the outside; but the third is four finger-breadths."

As for that which is stated: "The girdles (mekhalās), endowed with the qualities preceded by sattva, rising respectively twelve, eight, and four finger-breadths in height, and extending four finger-breadths in width on all sides, are considered to bestow all perfections."

Thus it has been stated by the teachers; that [statement] refers specifically to the particular results [of each girdle]. For this very reason: "In that case, the first girdle is twelve finger-breadths wide, and its height on all sides is four finger-breadths."
And above that, there should be a parapet (vapra) four finger-breadths high,
and it should be properly extended all around by eight finger-breadths.
Furthermore, above that, a third embankment (vapra) should be constructed;
it should be four finger-breadths wide and likewise elevated.
The Vasiṣṭha-saṃhitā also states the same:
"When Vyāsa is divided into twenty-four parts, three [parts] are the width of the four and three eyes;
the girdle outside the neck is considered to have a height of nine, six, and three parts respectively on all sides."

Some have stated that these [three altars] are equal in height to their width; however, another has prescribed that the height of the first is one-twelfth of its width, while for the other two, it is one-fourth, respectively.

Thus it was stated by the followers of Vājapeyin; however, that should be disregarded due to a lack of authoritative evidence. In the work of Gautama, the characteristics of the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) are described as follows: "The first girdle is said to be sāttvika, the second is remembered as rājasa, and the third is to be known as tāmasa."
Regarding the view that there are five girdles (*mekhalā*), their measurement is stated in the *Lakṣaṇasaṃgraha*:
"Five girdles indeed should be made with [widths] of six, five, four, three, and two [units].
Also, in the *Siddhāntaśekhara*:
There should be five girdles, measuring six, five, four, three, and two [units] respectively.
Regarding the view of two girdles (*mekhalā*), another Tantra states: "The two girdles are considered to be [respectively] one-sixth and one-eighth [of the width].
Regarding the view of a single girdle, the *Piṅgalāmata* states:
One girdle is considered to have a height and width of six finger-breadths.
Also, in the *Mahākapila-pañcarātra*:
"Or else, one girdle is prescribed with a width equal to one-fourth [of the base]."
In the *Prathama-tantra* as well: "Outside the neck [of the pit], a single girdle (*mekhalā*) six finger-breadths wide should be made.
Also in the *Siddhānta-śekhara*: "One should make a single girdle for the sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍas*) measuring six finger-breadths."
Now, regarding the characteristic of the *yoni*, the *Śāradā* states: "The *yoni* of these [lines] is in front of the *hotṛ*, above, like a leaf of the *aśvattha* tree.
In the *Somaśambhu*: "Above those [lines], there should be a *yoni*, shaped like an *aśvattha* leaf in the middle."
In the *Svāyambhuva*: "The sacrificial pits (kuṇḍa) situated in the east, southeast, and south are said to have their openings facing north;
the remaining ones are recorded as facing east, arranged according to what is aesthetically pleasing."
Also in the *Trailokyasāra*:
"The [fire] located in the south is for the southeast; the one located in the water is for the northwest.
For the ninth pit as well, the *yoni* is situated on the southern petal."
In the Svāyambhuva [Tantra]: "The girdle is in the middle; the yoni is half the width of the pit and two-thirds [of that];
it should be made with a rim and neck the size of a thumb, shaped like a leaf of the Aśvattha tree."
Also in the Siddhāntaśekhara: "The womb (yoni) is [measured] by long solar parvas; it is eight finger-breadths in width, and its height is two finger-breadths."

Also in the *Prayogasāra*: "One should fashion the vulva (yoni) in the middle, occupying three parts [of the altar], twelve finger-breadths in length, twelve parts high, and slightly set within the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*)."
And thus: "The *yoni* of sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍas*) measuring one, two, or three *muṣṭis* [in area] is said to possess a length, width, and height of six, four, and two *aṅgulas* respectively."
Thus says the *Śāradāvacana*:
"Its length is six finger-breadths and its width four finger-breadths.
And Rāghavabhaṭṭa maintains that the statement from the *Kriyāsāra* refers to the position of having only a single girdle (*ekamekhala*). However, in reality:

The phrase "six, four, and two finger-breadths" applies cumulatively to the length and other dimensions. As it is stated in the *Pañcarātra*: "One should fashion the vulva (*yoni*) with a height of twelve finger-breadths and a length equal to that. Also elsewhere: "The vulva should be equal in height and length, or it may be ten finger-breadths."
This is also stated in the *Vasiṣṭha-saṃhitā* regarding the position where the girdle is thick. However, in the *Nāradīya*:
"The width of the *yoni* is one-third of the pit (*kuṇḍa*), and its height is one finger-breadth;
it should be half the length of the pit, and thus its height is one finger-breadth."
It has been stated in the *Tryailokyasāra* as well: "The *yoni* is one solar digit (*sūryāṅgula*) in length, reduced by one-third in width,
and it is one digit high."
In the *Piṅgalāmata* as well: "The width of the *yoni* is eight fingers, and its height is measured at one finger.
Its width of eight fingers is at the base; it is said to be like a leaf of the *aśvattha* tree because it narrows toward the tip. In the *Tryailokyasāra*: "Likewise, it enters within..."
It is considered to be joined with two jars and resembling the leaves of the Aśvattha tree.
In the Vāyavīya-saṃhitā it is also stated:
"One should fashion the girdle at the middle, or on the west or the south;
it should be beautiful in the middle, slightly depressed, and tapering gradually toward the ends."

[The yoni] faces the *kuṇḍa* at its front, with its girdle (*mekhalā*) slightly released [from the base]. In the *Śāradā*: "One should make the tip of the yoni one finger-breadth wide and slightly downward-facing.
Here, by means of one part, a rim (*nemi*) should also be made all around the top of the yoni, characterized by width and height. This has been stated:

By Rāmavājapeyin: The pit (kuṇḍa) is as long as the diameter of its width and as wide as one-third of that; it is as high as one-fourth of the width, and it is surrounded on all sides by a circumference of the same measure.
It enters into the interior of the pit with its own tip of the same dimension.
It is beautiful with two downward-turning petals and has the shape of an aśvattha leaf.

"Antarvilā" means that it has a cavity inside, just as a hollow (vila) exists for the purpose of holding ghee; thus, the meaning is "possessing a cavity. "Adhovṛttā" means that its lower portion consists of two half-circles joined together in the shape of a jar (kumbha).
Now, regarding the stalk (*nāla*) in the *Śāradā*: "Starting from the base (*sthala*), the stalk should extend into the center of the womb (*yoni*) with a perforation.
Also in the *Pañcarātra*: "Starting from the base, the stalk should be outside the girdle (*mekhalā*) and possess a chamber (*sabha*)."
But in the *Prayogasāra* it is said: "To the west of the vulva, the stalk (*nāla*) is four finger-breadths in length;
its width is desired to be three, two, and one finger-breadth respectively, tapering toward the top.
The outer girdle (*bāhyamekhalā*) has a height and width of four finger-breadths.

The traditional teaching is that an altar (vedi) should be constructed at the base of the stalk, square and aligned with the cardinal points. Now, regarding the characteristics of the navel (nābhi), the *Śāradā-tantra* states: "One should fashion within the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍa) a navel resembling a lotus."
Alternatively, its measurement is declared to be in accordance with each respective fire-pit (kuṇḍa).

In sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) measuring one muṣṭi, one aratni, or one hasta, the navel should be two, three, or four finger-breadths (aṅgulas) in height and width; in other [larger] pits, one should increase these dimensions accordingly.
The noble-minded [author], following the sequence of two *yavas*, [measures] the navel separately.
However, by Rāmavājapeyin, a single characteristic applicable to all sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍa*) has been stated:
"The wise man should conceive that the height of the pit is one-twelfth of its diameter, and twice that [height] should be the width."
In the *Śāradā*: "This was stated from a gross perspective because the difference is slight.

In the *Śāradā*: "In a yoni-shaped sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), one should avoid the yoni; in a lotus-shaped pit, one should avoid the navel. In the *Śāradā*: "One may perform the daily (*nitya*), occasional (*naimittika*), and optional (*kāmya*) rites either in a sacrificial pit or upon a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*)."
It is square on all sides and possesses a height of one finger-breadth.

On the lunar seat (candrapīṭha), a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) one cubit in measure should be fashioned from sand and other materials; it is triangular and square, and one span (vitasti) in height. The first embankment (vapra) is declared to be two finger-breadths (aṅgula) in height.
Furthermore, above the level of the rampart (vapra), it should be joined with a height of two finger-breadths;
the width of all [the elements] therein is stated by the wise to be two finger-breadths.
Regarding the increase in the *homa*, it is stated in that very same [text]: "The sacrificial ground (*sthaṇḍila*) should likewise be twice the size plus a half-cubit.
Now, the characteristics of the *sruk* [ladle] are described in the *Śāradā*: "One should fashion the *sruk* for the sacrifice according to the method that will be explained."
The Guru [should take] one of the following: śrīparṇī, śiṃśapā, or a milky-sap tree.
Having taken [the area], one should divide it by thirty-six to the extent of a cubit;
with twenty parts there shall be the staff (daṇḍa), and with eight of those [parts] there shall be the altar (vedi).
The neck is measured by one part; the mouth is measured by seven parts;
and the width of the neck is proclaimed to be three parts.
56) One should fashion the mouth portion so that its tip is level with the throat,
measuring one *kaniṣṭhā* finger-breadth for the purpose of allowing the clarified butter to flow out.
In the center of the altar, the pericarp (karṇikā) should be fashioned with one part;
outside of it, one should construct a pit (avaṭa) on all sides using one part.
Its pit should be circular with three parts, and outside [that] by one-eighth part;
with one part, one should arrange petals all around.
The girdle (mekhalā) and the sacrificial mouth-altar (mukhavedi) should be equal [in measure], while the rim (nemi) is half that measure.
At the base and tip of the staff (daṇḍa), there should be two bulbous ornaments (kumbha) measuring three and four finger-breadths respectively.
The pair of *gaṇḍīs* should consist of eight parts; this is declared to be the *anāha* of the staff.
The back portion of the altar (*vedī*) should be six parts and shaped like a tortoise.
One should draw the face of a swan, or a female swan, or a boar;
the characteristic of the sacrificial ladle (sruva) is said to be on the back part of its face.
*Śrīparṇī* is *gāmbhārī*. The "milk-bearing trees" (*kṣīraśākhinaḥ*) are the *aśvattha*, *udumbara*, *vaṭa*, and *plakṣa*.
In the *Phetkārītantra*: "One may have [the image] made from *kāraskara*, *āmalakī*, *palāśa*, or *khadira*; or likewise from gold, silver, copper, or even iron."
In the Vāyavīya Saṃhitā:
"The *sruk* and *sruva* ladles should be made of metal; those of bell-metal, iron, or lead are not to be used.
Alternatively, they may be made of sacrificial wood (*yajñadāru*), as approved by craftsmen for the practitioners of Tantra."
Or [the ladles] may be made from the leaves of a sacred tree (*brahmavṛkṣa*) or the like, provided they are without holes, elevated in the middle, and made of iron;
here, the injunctions and prohibitions pertain respectively to cruel and gentle rites. As it is stated in another Tantra:
"The *sruk* and *sruva* ladles should be made entirely of gold for gentle rites."
These two, made of iron, should be used in rites such as the immobilization of others.
Elsewhere it is also stated: "In the absence of that [wood], the oblation is offered with two leaves of the *palāśa* tree.
Also in the *Vasiṣṭha-saṃhitā*:
"The *sruk* and *sruva* ladles are considered to be made from flawless and beautiful *palāśa* leaves."
Or one should perform the oblation in a small leaf of the aśvattha tree during the rite of homa.

"One cubit" (*hastamātra*) means "one arm's length" (*bāhumātra*). This is according to the statement in the *Agastyasaṃhitā*: "One should indeed fashion the *sruk* ladle for the purpose of oblation with the measurement of an arm. Thus, the *sruk* should be thirty-six finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) long.

And because of the statement in the *Phetkāriṇī*: "By a third part of the altar" means by one-third of the altar, and not by three parts, for that would result in a contradiction regarding the position of the altar-pads. Here, there is no digging out of the petals, as there is a lack of authoritative evidence. This is stated specifically with reference to the *sruva* ladle in the *Mantramuktāvalī*:
The wise one should create a passage below the throat for the flow of clarified butter,
and he should perform the piercing at the mouth with a red-hot iron rod.
In the *Vasiṣṭha-saṃhitā*: "The hollow at the neck should extend as far as the little finger.
Now, regarding the characteristics of the *sruva* ladle, the *Śāradā-tantra* states: "One should fashion the *sruva* from twenty-four parts of the *sruk* ladle."
Its measurement by the staff (daṇḍa) is proclaimed to be twenty-two parts.
The head of that [sacrificial post] measures four parts and should be smeared with ghee;
one should bury it two parts deep in the mud in the shape of a deer's footprint.
The *gaṇḍī* should be at the base and tip of the handle and adorned with a bracelet;
thus is the rule for the *sruva* explained.
*Gaṇḍī* means a jar. One should fashion two very beautiful jars at the base and the tip.
From the *Mantramuktāvalī*:
"Now, regarding the offering of sprouts (*aṅkurārpaṇa*), the *Śāradā* states: 'Seven days prior to the day of initiation, according to the prescribed rule...'"
One should perform the rite of sowing the germinating seeds (aṅkurārpaṇa) for the attainment of all auspiciousness.
In the Siddhāntaśekhara:
"During consecration, initiation, ritual bathing, and likewise during festivals; for the purpose of purification, for peace, at marriage, and at the binding of the sacred thread."
In all auspicious rites, one should perform the rite of sowing the seeds (aṅkurārpaṇa) on the ninth or seventh day prior to the day of the consecration.
The offering of the seed-ling (aṅkurārpaṇa) may take place on the fifth day, the third day, or immediately.
Also, in the *Mahākapilapañcarātra*:
"Having caused the proclamation of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be made by means of Brahmins, the Preceptor (deśika), together with the Brahmins..."
On that very day, one should plant the sprout of auspiciousness.
Either on the seventh or the ninth day prior to the sacrificial rite;

as it is stated in another tantra: "On the auspicious seventh or ninth day before the day of the recommended sacrifice, or on the fifth day at a favorable moment, one should perform the ritual for the auspicious sprouts."

Elsewhere it is also stated: "Even before the seventh day from the purification of the self, once the preceptor has been purified, having made the formal resolve (saṅkalpa) and observed a fast, the auspicious rite of sowing the germinating seeds (aṅkurāropaṇa) should be performed. (58)
One should perform the Nāndīmukha Śrāddha on the preceding day and the Svastivācana;
one should indeed carry out this according to the procedure prescribed in one's own Gṛhya-sūtra.
In the *Saṃhitā* as well: "In all cases, one should perform at the very outset the *abhyudaya-śrāddha*, which is like the production of a sprout for a rite of an auspicious nature."
In the Śāradā-tilaka: "On the northern side of the pavilion, one should construct a secret hall extending from east to west; then, within that hall, the wise man should fashion the mandala."
And this [mandala] should be known as having one gate on the south. Likewise:
"One should lay down five lines measuring five cubits each, extending from east to west; the distance between them shall be twelve finger-breadths."
In the same manner, one should lay down eleven threads from south to north;
forty squares are thus produced there, which one should then erase.
By means of rows, four paths are formed at the ends on both sides of the four corners;
two paths remain, and here three sets of four squares are left over.
Also in the *Prayogasāra*:
"Having stretched out the cord, one should snap it so that it extends from south to north;
then one should lay down two [lines] on each side, measuring five cubits."
In the same manner, according to the previously stated measurement, one should subsequently lay down eleven threads in sequence, twelve finger-breadths apart each, running equally from east to west.

Upon those lines, one should drop [the measurements] at intervals equal to the distance between the previous threads. As stated in the *Śāradā*: "The wise man should color those squares with white, yellow, red, and black powders; then, he should fill the pathways with dark-colored powder."

In the *Prapañcasāra*, however, the sequence of coloring is also stated as follows: "Yellow, red, white, and black, beginning with fire (Agni) and ending with Śarva, for each quarter. In the *Śāradātilaka*:
"They say that there are three kinds of vessels for the rites of offering sprouts (*aṅkurārpaṇa*)."
The *pālikās*, the five-faced [liṅgas], and the shallow bowls (*śarāvas*) are likewise arranged in four stages respectively.
Those consisting of Hari, Brahmā, and Śiva have been declared by the knowers of all Tantras;
their height should be inferred as sixteen, twelve, and eight [parts] respectively.
Having gradually wound auspicious threads around those [spots] measured in finger-breadths,
the preceptor washes them and places rice grains upon those locations.
59) One should place [the vessels] upon bunches of fragrant *darbha* grass, starting from the west.
In the *Mahākapila-pañcarātra*, it is stated:
"The width of the mouth of the *pālikā* vessel is said to be sixteen finger-breadths (*aṅgula*)."
It may be the throat-passage, or it should be eight finger-breadths in width.
The width of the footstool is declared to be six aṅgulas;
its height is four aṅgulas, and the joint between them should be one aṅgula.
From the junction of those [parts], however, there arises the "I-not-I" (nāhaṃ), as well as the half of the footstool;
thus the five-faced ghaṭikā becomes the granter of all desires.
They say that the five faces indeed have a width of four finger-breadths;
four are in the four directions and one is above, according to the rule.
The width of the *ghaṭikā* is said to be twelve finger-breadths;
some teachers, however, state it to be sixteen finger-breadths.
The mouth of the earthenware bowl (śarāva) is said to be twelve finger-breadths in width;
its base at the bottom is stated to be four finger-breadths in width.
Elsewhere also: "In this case, there should be a five-faced water-clock (*ghaṭikā*) measuring one *tāla* in width and equal in its breadth and height;
it should have four faces toward the cardinal directions and one face in the center, with its parts symmetrically arranged."
The shallow bowl (śarāva) should have a mouth as wide as a palm tree leaf, with its height measuring half of its breadth;
its handle should have a circumference of four finger-breadths, and its neck should be raised, excluding the opening.
These should be made of gold, silver, copper, or clay, provided they are fresh and unblemished.
In the *Prayogasāra*: "One should place the vessels upon them, individually in the four [corners] from the southeast (vahni) to the northeast (īśāna)."
In the *Sārasvata-mata*, it is stated: "One should worship Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva in those vessels that have been mentioned.
Also in the *Siddhānta-śekhara*: "One should worship Rudra in earthen bowls with sandalwood and flowers."
Likewise, one should place Viṣṇu in the *pālikās* and Brahmā in the *ghaṭikās*.
In the *Śāradā*: "One should fill those vessels with dried cow-dung, sand, and earth.
In the *Prayogasāra*: "And one should fill the vessels from above with earth, sand, and dried cow-dung. Regarding the specific details concerning the earth, there is this in the *Siddhāntaśekhara*:
Having worshipped the spade with perfumes and other offerings on another day,
the preceptor and others— some mounted on chariots and others likewise on elephants—
proceed to the bank of a pond, a river, or a flower grove.
There, having swept a pure portion of the ground with *darbha* grass while reciting the *astra-mantra*,
and having sprinkled it with *arghya* water while recollecting the respective mantras;
Having invoked the Earth with the *hṛdaya* mantra, one should worship her with perfumes and flowers;
then, having dug the earth with a spade while reciting the weapon mantra, [one takes] the soil.
Having taken [the earth] with the Vāmadeva mantra, one should fill a bronze vessel;
having cleansed the clay with the Hṛdaya mantra and covered it with a cloth, one should hold it.
Then, having circumambulated the city or the dwelling with the sounds of all auspicious instruments, the preceptor should lead [the disciple] to the pavilion.

A wise person should perform this rite during the daytime, not at night. As stated in the *Śāradā*: "The knower of the Tantra, having washed the seeds with milk using the seed-syllable of nectar (*sudhā-bīja*), should consecrate them with the root mantra preceded by the five sounds."
Preceded by auspicious customs and the benedictory words of the twice-born,
the preceptor, with a restrained mind, should pour [the offerings] into those vessels.
In the *Sārasvata-mata*, however, it is stated:
"Having washed those seeds with water and then with milk in succession";
thus, washing first with water is prescribed. In the *Siddhānta-śekhara*:
Facing either the east or the north,
one should sow all the seeds, beginning with the primary seed, into the *pālikās* and other vessels in their proper sequence.
Soma is the lord of seeds; therefore, one should perform the offering at night.
Regarding the phrase "by the principal seed": it means by that [mantra] which has the seed-syllable (*bījākṣara*) as its primary element at the beginning. According to the *Sārasvata-mata*:
Since he is radiant at night due to the seed-syllables and the deities,
the preceptor should therefore sow the seeds only during the night.
In the Śāradā [Tantra]: "Rice, śyāmāka, āḍhakī, mung beans, sesame, niṣpāva, mustard, kulattha, kaṅgu, and māṣa—these are the seeds for the rite of germination."
In the *sārasvata* [oblation], one worships Skanda; in *priyaṅgu* or *niṣpāva*, Vāyu and Agni; in *kulatthaka*, Nirṛti; in *mudga*, Soma; and in sesame seeds, Vaivasvata.

One should worship Prajāpati when the seed is rice (*śālī*), Ananta when it is mustard (*sarṣapa*), Indra when it is black (*śyāma*), and Varuṇa during the month, O Daughter of the Mountain. According to the *Siddhāntaśekhara*: "One should worship Soma daily until the day of the consecration (*adhivāsa*)."
When the day of the formal acceptance has arrived, the preceptor should cause the Soma to be dismissed.
In the *Prayogasāra*: "Salutations again and again to Tryambaka, to Śarva, to Śaṅkara, and to Śiva; to the eternal one who is the foremost of all worlds."
Having scattered [the seeds] with this mantra, one should rain down water mixed with turmeric powder upon them, and sprinkle them with water every day.
