In the Śāradā-tantra: Having sprinkled [the image] with turmeric water and covered it with cloths, the preceptor should offer the bali-oblation for the three types of vessels in the directions, starting from the east.
With [mantras] beginning with *praṇava* (Oṃ) and ending with *namaḥ*, using the names of the Lords of Night (*rātrīśa*) during the night;

the plural number in the word "cloths" (*vastraiḥ*) refers to the number three according to the principle of the *kapiñjala-nyāya*. Consequently, it results that one should cover each of the four [deities] with a single cloth. Likewise—
The spirits, the ancestors, the yakṣas, the nāgas, Brahmā, Śiva,
and Hari are declared to be the deities of the seven nights.
For the *bhūtas*, parched grain (*lāja*), sesame seeds, turmeric, curd, and barley flour are prescribed; for the *pitṛs*, rice accompanied by sesame seeds is proclaimed;
and for the *yakṣas*, *karambha* and parched grain, combined with coconut water, are offered.
He gave powdered parched grain to the Nāgas and lotus-seeds to Brahmā.

The food for Śarva and Viṣṇu should consist of rice with cakes; for [Śiva] it should be rice with jaggery, and for Viṣṇu, milk-rice during the Navarātra period. And for Viṣṇu, there should be rice mixed with sesame (kṛśara), if the bali offering is prescribed in sequence throughout the Navarātra. Thus it has been stated by the Teachers. And this applies to the first two days.
The object of awakening. Regarding the offering of the *bali*: in the five-day fortnight, it begins with the *yakṣas*, and in the three-day fortnight, it begins with Brahmā.
As stated in the *Śāradā*: "Then one should duly offer the *bali* even to the world-protectors (*lokeśvara*)."
According to the *Sārasvata-mata*: "One who is not [the authorized person] should never look at the fully grown sprouts;
only the teacher himself, or his disciple by his command, may enter."
In the *Siddhāntaśekhara*:
"For the sake of the prosperity of the patron, one should examine the sprouts;
they should be properly grown upward, tender, and white."
Those that are smoke-colored, incomplete, or likewise directed horizontally [are inauspicious].
One should avoid those that are dark, crooked, and inauspicious;
a dark sprout portends incomplete birth and famine.
If it moves horizontally, there will be disease; if it is crooked, there will be fear of enemies.
When an inauspicious sprout has arisen, one should perform a pacifying homa;
the preceptor, together with those who bear the [divine] forms, should offer oblations with the root mantra.
One should perform [the rite] with the Aghora weapon or the Astra weapon a hundred or even a thousand times.

According to the Sārasvata-mata: one should indicate the auspicious or inauspicious results for the practitioner by the sprouts that have grown. If the sprouts are dark or black, there is loss of wealth; if they grow horizontally, there is disease; and if they are swaying, [there is danger].
If the lines are crooked, there is suffering; if they are poorly formed, death; if they are bent, diseases; and if they are curved, loss of one's position, country, and desired objects.
The section concerning the ritual of offering the seed-syllable (aṅkurārpaṇa) is completed.
Thus ends the second wave in the *Tārābhaktisudhārṇava* composed by the Great Mahopādhyāya, the illustrious Ṭhakkura Narasiṃha. || 2 ||
The Third Wave. Now, regarding initiation (*dīkṣā*), the *Śāradā* states: "It is declared to be fourfold, according to the distinctions of *kriyāvatī* and so forth."
She is endowed with action, composed of the qualities (varṇa), consisting of the creative arts (kalā), and also consisting of penetration (vedha).
These [mantras], which bring about prosperity, are described in this tantra in their proper sequence.
The preceptor, having bathed according to the rules and performed his morning rites, [should proceed].

Adorned and observing silence, he should proceed to the sacrificial pavilion for the sake of the sacrifice. As stated in the *Gautamīya*: "The disciple, having bathed, well-attired, and equipped with all the necessary materials..."
One should choose a preceptor with devotion, honoring him with garments, ornaments, and decorations.
One should perform the Nāndīmukha Śrāddha and satisfy the Brāhmaṇas;
one should gratify one's own preceptor with gifts such as cows, gold, and garments.
Just as one who is contented, gracious, and a granter of boons bestows [the mantra], so should one choose the officiating priests (ṛtvij) there—ten, five, or two.
In the *Yāmala*: "Then, having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), the disciple, with his senses subdued..."
For the sake of destroying sins committed from birth, one should offer gold with sesame seeds.

In the Śāradā-tilaka, beginning with the section on the Guru: "Having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) according to the rules and having prepared the general offering (sāmānyārghya) there,
one should sprinkle the door with water consecrated by the weapon-mantra (astra-mantra) and perform the worship of the door."

The procedures for bathing, the twilight rites (*sandhyā*), libations (*tarpaṇa*), the worship of the door, and so forth, will be explained in the section on daily worship (*nityārcana-taraṅga*). Likewise:
"Touching slightly with his left hand the branch [of the door], the Guru should cross the threshold;
contracting his limbs, he should enter within with his right foot."
One should worship Vāstveśa and Brahmā in the south-western direction;
one should then sprinkle the sacrificial pavilion with the five products of the cow and with water for the arghya offering.
One should perform the purification of that area up to the crossroads by means of inspection and other rites;
inspection is performed with the root mantra, while sprinkling is considered to be done with the weapon mantra.
With that very [mantra], one should perform the striking; sprinkling with the armor-mantra (*varma*) is prescribed.
The wise one should fumigate the interior with sandalwood, agallochum, and camphor.

64) One should scatter there offerings (vikirān) over which the mantra of the arrow has been recited seven times; these are parched grain, sandalwood, white mustard seeds, ashes, sprouts of dūrvā grass, and unbroken rice.
Those known as the Vikiras have been commanded to destroy the mass of all obstacles.
One should sweep them with a handful of darbha grass consecrated by the recitation of the Astra mantra,
and one should prepare a seat for the Vardhanī vessel in the direction of Īśa (the northeast).
But in the *Somaśambhu*, it is said:
"The scattered offerings (*vikirān*) should be either pure parched grains (*lājān*) or [other materials] consecrated seven times with the Weapon-mantra (*astra*),
sprinkled with water from the Weapon-mantra, and veiled with the Armor-mantra (*kavaca*)."
Having fashioned [the weapons] out of darbha grass thirty-six finger-breadths in length, they take the form of various implements that ward off the flood of obstacles.

"O best of beings, restrain the fist with the Śivāstra mantra recited seven times. Thus it is said. In the *Śāradā*: "Having caused the Brahmins to recite the *puṣpāhva* [mantra] and having satisfied them, one should draw one of the prescribed mandalas upon the altar."

The *maṇḍala* refers to the *Sarvatobhadra* and others. Regarding the *Sarvatobhadra-maṇḍala*, as described in the *Śāradā*: "In a square divided into four compartments and provided with diagonal lines (*karṇasūtra*), one should draw four diagonal lines across all four compartments."
One should cause it to fall in such a way that fish remain here and there at intervals.
The practitioner should place two [lines] extending from east to west and two extending from south to north.
One should drop four equal threads across those fish-marks;
as before, one should drop diagonal threads (karṇasūtra) in the corner squares.
The mantra-practitioner should cast the lines there according to that same procedure, up to two hundred and fifty-six squares.
In the center, one should draw a lotus with excellent characteristics using thirty-six squares;
outside, there should be a pedestal (pīṭha) consisting of one row, and a pathway (vīthikā) consisting of two rows.

The practitioner of mantra should fashion the primary and secondary ornaments of the gateways according to the remaining [parts] by means of the procedure prescribed in the scriptures; thereafter, he should draw a lotus.
Having set aside one-twelfth part of the lotus-field on the outside, the wise one should divide its center into three equal parts by means of three circles.
The first [circle] should be the location of the pericarp; the second, that of the filaments;
the third, that of the petals; and the tip of each petal is said to be by the aforementioned proportion.
65) Having placed half-moons all around the tips of the filaments according to the prescribed rule, the wise one should measure the space between the outer and inner [circles].
Having drawn the lines for the joints, one should drop the threads there;
and with the same measurement as that of the tips of the petals, one should draw the circle.
In the interval between those, the wise one should draw the tips of the petals all around with the outer hand, on both sides of the central line.
One should arrange the filaments in pairs at the bases of the petals;
this is declared by those who know the tantras to be the common lotus design.
One should sweep three squares for the purpose of the pedestal at the corners of the platform;
with the remaining squares, the wise man should fashion the limbs of the pedestal.
One should sweep the squares arranged in rows without breaking their alignment;
then, one should fashion doors in the cardinal directions using two or four squares.
Then, there should be three and one squares for the *śobhās* on both sides of the door;
immediately thereafter, the *upaśobhās* should consist of one and three squares.
With the remaining six squares, one should form the four corners;
one should then color that enchanting maṇḍala with five colors.
Yellow is from turmeric powder; white is derived from rice;
red is from safflower powder; and black is produced from burnt husks.

It is stated that the five-colored [pigment] produced from leaves such as those of the *vilva* tree is black (*śyāma*). Elsewhere, another red variety is mentioned: "Likewise, copper dust combined with alkali is called red."
Thus it is said. Regarding another type of *śyāmā*, the *Prayogasāra* states: "The dust arising from the petals of the *śyāmā* is declared [to be used] in one's own rites.
There is a specific distinction in other tantras:
If one who is capable should desire fierce accomplishment, he should adorn the mandalas here with gems of those respective colors— using pearls, topazes, rubies, sapphires, and green gems.
In the *Mahākapilapañcarātra*, however, its necessity is stated as follows: "Earth is to be known as yellow; water is proclaimed to be white;
fire indeed has the color red; and wind is proclaimed to be grey."
O Great Sage, the fifth [element], space, is black in color;
Rudra is the presiding deity of the white [color], and Brahmā is the presiding deity of the red.
O sinless one, Viṣṇu is remembered as the presiding deity of the yellow [color], and Acyuta of the black;
the serpent is declared by me to be the presiding deity of the dark-blue.
White [sandalwood] destroys the affliction caused by the planets; red [destroys] that arising from the assembly of cruel beings;
black [destroys] the prowess of all asuras; and blue likewise [destroys] that pertaining to Vaināyaka.
It destroys the piśāca and rākṣasa [obstacles] and removes the green dust;
therefore, it is especially used in fire-offerings (homa), consecrations (abhiṣeka), and sacrifices (yāga).
With those [colours], one should draw the maṇḍala which brings satisfaction to the deities.
In the *Śāradā*: "The boundary lines, one finger in height and width, are white and auspicious;
the pericarp is yellow, and the filaments are reddish."
The practitioner of mantras should color the petals with white pigment and their joints with black; alternatively, the pericarp may be yellow.
The filaments should be yellowish-red, and the petals should also be reddish;
the joints should be black in color, and [the pericarp] should be either yellow or black.
One should color the interiors of the pedestals; the feet should have a reddish glow, and its limbs, as well as those in the four pathways, should be white.
One should draw wish-fulfilling creepers endowed with leaves, flowers, and fruits,
variegated with various kinds of colors and enchanting to the sight of all.
But in the Gautamīya [Tantra]: "Outside of that, one should fashion four beautiful wish-fulfilling trees (kalpaśākhin), graceful, with blossoms in full bloom, and adorned with fruits and sprouts."
"They were adorned with flowers born both of water and land,
and their branches were occupied by swans, cranes, *kāraṇḍava* ducks, parrots, bees, cuckoos, peacocks, ruddy geese, and other birds," so it is said.
In the Śāradā-tantra: "The doors are white in color; the ornaments (śobhā) are said to be red;
the secondary ornaments (upaśobhā) are yellow in color; and the corners are black."
One should draw three lines on the outside, white, red, and black in sequence;
this is known as the Sarvatobhadra mandala, which is common to all.
In the *Vasiṣṭha-saṃhitā*, however, there is this specific instruction:
"Yellow [should be offered] in the east, white in the west and likewise in the north;
red in the south, black, and pale-red (pāṭala) situated in the southeast."
67) In the southwest [the deity] is blue in color, while in the northwest it is smoke-colored;
in the northeast it is designated as fair (gaura); this is the sequence for the eight petals.

Then, having sat upon the seat and performed the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*), the placement of the alphabet (*mātṛkānyāsa*), the internal sacrifice (*antaryāga*), the preparation of the water for the offering (*arghya*), and so forth,
[he should worship] from the foundational power (*ādhāraśakti*) up to the seat-mantra (*pīṭhamantra*) upon the lotus of the *sarvatobhadra* maṇḍala.
Having performed worship, one should establish the water-jar (kalaśa); this is the procedure common to all tantras. As stated in the Śāradā-tilaka:

"The jar, fashioned from gold or other precious materials, with its interior washed by water consecrated with the weapon-mantra (astra), fumigated with sandalwood, agallochum, and camphor, and possessing a beautiful form..."
Its body is encircled by a triple-stranded thread, leaving no gap;
it is worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, and provided with a tuft of grass and unbroken grains of rice.
The practitioner of mantra, uttering the syllable *tāra* (Om), should place [the vessel] whose interior contains the nine gems.
In another tantra: "In all sacrifices, one should wrap it with a braid of twenty-seven blades of *darbha* grass, adorned with knots; that is proclaimed as the *kūrca*."

In the *Śāradā-tilaka*: "The knower of the ritual procedure, having conceived the unity of the pitcher and the pedestal, [should bathe them] with a decoction of milky trees or with that produced from the bark of the *palāśa* tree."
Or with waters from sacred fords, well-scented with camphor, fragrance, and flowers,
one should perform the ritual according to the rules by identifying oneself [with the deity] through the *mātṛkā* in reverse order.
In the same manner, one should fill the conch with the root-mantra of Japan, perceiving it as the deity;
within the conch filled with decoction water, one should place the eight fragrant substances (gandhāṣṭaka) which bestow desired boons.
Having stirred [the vessel], one should worship within it, having invoked all the *kalās*:
first the ten *kalās* of Fire, then the twelve of the Twelve-fold Self.
Having recited the sixteen digits of the moon in reverse order, followed by fifty digits, the knower of mantras should likewise recite the root mantra in reverse.
With a concentrated mind, meditating upon the deity of the mantra,
the wise practitioner should perform the rite of *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* (the installation of vital breath) in each respective instance.
One should pour the decoction, which consists of one-sixteenth part and is situated in a conch shell, into the pitcher;
[and add] sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, *coraka*, saffron, and yellow pigment (*rocanā*).

"Jaṭā, māṃsī, and kapi—these are known as the eight fragrances of Śakti. Regarding "gold and so forth": by the word "and so forth," silver and other metals are included. *Coro* is commonly known as *bhaṭa* (uraga); *kapi* is commonly known as *geḍhīmana*. [As stated] in the *Mahākapila-pañcarātra*:
A beautiful vessel made of gold, silver, copper, or even one made of clay that is free from defects, and smeared with sandalwood paste. (68)
As for the measurement of the pitcher (kalaśa): its width is fifty finger-breadths and its height sixteen finger-breadths;
the measurement of the pitchers' mouths, moreover, should be eight finger-breadths.
Thus it is declared in another Tantra. Also in the Vāyavīya Saṃhitā:

"Whether made of gold, silver, copper, or even clay, [the vessel] should be strewn with fragrant scents, flowers, and unbroken grains (akṣata), and honored with blades of kuśa grass and sprouts of dūrvā."
It is encircled at the neck with a white thread and covered with a pair of new garments.
Regarding the cord, there is a specific detail in another tantra: "With a triple-folded cord made from thread spun by a maiden, which serves as armor..."
One should encircle it evenly on all sides with that which consists of the three qualities.

In the *Śāradā*: "Afterwards, the Guru [should worship] with the tender sprouts of the *aśvattha*, *panasa*, and *cūta* trees, bound together with *indravallī*, with the thought that they are celestial trees (*suradruma*)."
Having covered the mouth of the pitcher with this cup containing fruit and unbroken rice,
one should duly place it there with the thought that it is the fruit of the wish-fulfilling trees.
Then, one should wrap the jar with a pair of stainless linen cloths;
having worshipped the form with the root mantra, [one should place it] upon this branch of the wish-fulfilling trees.
Having invoked [the deity], the practitioner of mantra (mantrī) should worship the deity of the mantra within that [liṅga].
Likewise, one should worship the limbs (aṅgas) and the enclosures (āvaraṇas), ending with the world-protectors (lokapālas).
In the case of the initiation for the five abodes (pañcāyatana-dīkṣā), having established five jars (kalaśas), one should invoke the respective deities.

One should perform the worship. According to the statement in the *Prapañcasāra*, "In this manner, one may worship with a single jar according to the prescribed rite, or with many jars. Regarding that, the sequence for the installation of the deities is stated in the *Jñānamālā*:
"When, however, one worships Śaṅkara in the center, one should worship Śrīpati in the northeast."
Likewise, one should place the Haṃsa in the south-east and the son of Pārvatī in the south-west.
And Bhavānī, who is affectionate toward her devotees, should always be worshipped in the northwest;
however, when Govinda is in the center, one should worship Śaṅkara in the northeast.
The practitioner, being composed, should worship Gaṇanātha in the southeast, Tapanas in the southwest, and Ambikā in the northwest.

When [the sun] is at the meridian, one should worship the Thousand-rayed One (Sahasrāṃśu) in the center, the Lord of Pārvatī (Pārvatīpati) in the northeast, the Single-tusked One (Ekadanta) in the southeast, and Acyuta in the southwest.
One should worship the Goddess in the northwest, who is the sole ground for worldly enjoyment and liberation;
however, when Bhavānī is in the center, one should worship Mādhava in the northeast.
The preceptor should worship Pārvatīnātha in the southeast, Gaṇanāyaka in the southwest,
and Pradyotana in the northwest.
When one should worship Heramba in the center, Acyuta in the northeast,
Pañcavaktra in the southeast, and Jagadambikā in the southwest.
The practitioner, free from sloth, should indeed worship the Sun (Dyumaṇi) in the northwest;
for deities who have been displaced from their proper places bestow sorrow, suffering, and fear,
and the king as well as the practitioner perishes when situated within that [disordered] mandala.

In another Tantra: "When Śambhu is in the center, Hari, Naha, Hara, Bhū, and Devī are established; when Harī is in the center, Śaṅkara, Bhāsya, Nāgasutā, Ravi, Hara, Gaṇeśa, Ajā, and Ambikā are established; when Devī is in the center, Viṣṇu, Hara, Ekadanta, Ravi, Lambodara, Aja, Īśvara, [Gaṇeśa, and Ambikā are established]."
Those [planets] situated in the portion of Śaṅkara are declared to be *ryena*s; when they are separated [from that portion], however, they are the givers of loss.
The sequence of worship is stated in another tantra: "Having offered a handful of flowers to the Principal Deity, the worship of Gaṇeśa and the others should take place.
If Gaṇeśa himself is the Principal Deity, then it should follow the sequence of Sūrya."
In the Cāmuṇḍā Tantra: "For Śyāmā, Bhairavī, Tārā, and Chinnamastā,
as well as for Mañjughoṣa and Raudra, the five-limbed [nyāsa] is not prescribed by the wise."

The five-limbed sacrifice (pañcāṅgayāga) consists of the form of the initiation into the five currents (pañcāyana-dīkṣā). As stated in the Śāradā-tilaka: "Having prepared a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) on the south and having placed the fire there, the wise man, having consecrated it according to rule, should perform the Vaiśvadeva rite."
There, having worshipped the deity whose form has been described with perfumes and other offerings,
the knower of mantras, having offered oblations with the *tāra* (oṃ), the *vyāhṛtis*, and the root mantra;

Having offered twenty-five oblations of milk-rice mixed with clarified butter while reciting the *vyāhṛti* mantras, one should again worship [the deity] with perfumes and other offerings. Having joined that [deity] to the form situated upon the pedestal, one should dismiss the fire.
With the remaining sacrificial oblation, one should scatter the bali offering all around.
[One should offer] to the attendants of the deity [substances] accompanied by fragrance, flowers, and unbroken rice (*akṣata*).

Regarding this, the author of the *Kaumudī* maintains that by the term *vaiśvadeva*, only the daily fire-oblation (*nityahoma*) is intended, because it is etymologically derived from its connection with "all the gods" (*sarvadeva*). However, others hold that this is indeed distinct from the daily oblation, because of the scriptural injunction regarding the consecration of the fire (*vahnisaṃskāra*).

Rites such as the establishment of the sacred fire (*agnyādhāna*) and so forth do not exist in the daily oblation (*nityahoma*), because the *Vasiṣṭha-saṃhitā* prohibits the consecration of the fire (*vahnisaṃskāra*) in the daily oblation. And after this oblation, [the rite is performed] in the common (*laukika*) fire—
Then, O Goddess, having sprinkled [the area], one should perform the daily fire-oblation (nityahoma).
O Mistress of the Gods, one should offer five oblations in sequence with the root mantra.
One should know that the nature of the five oblations consists of prāṇa, apāna, vyāna, udāna, and samāna.
"Six oblations [are offered] in the six limbs; this is declared to be the daily homa (*nityahoma*).

Thus say Rāghavabhaṭṭa that the daily homa mentioned in the *Jñānārṇava* should be performed. That is not correct, because nowhere in this [text] or in other tantras is the Vaiśvadeva mentioned as a separate ritual act.
"In the daily (nitya), occasional (naimittika), and optional (kāmya) rites, this is remembered as having the fire as its mouth.

Since the *Agastyasaṃhitā* thus prescribes the consecration of the fire even for the daily oblation (*nityahoma*), the truth is that for the daily oblation there is indeed an option between the two sequences mentioned in the *Śāradā-jñānārṇava*. In the *Śāradā*:
Having recited the root mantra one thousand times with undistracted mind,
he should offer that recitation to the deity for the sake of attaining all prosperity.
Then, in the northeast direction, which has been previously prepared by the preceptor,
there should be a water-pot filled with water and provided with gold, cloth, and other such items.
Having established her upon that [seat], one should worship the deity of the weapon (astradevatā), who is seated on a lion, bearing a sword and a shield,
possessing a terrible form, and facing west.

Having worshipped with the *calāsana* and taken that [image], the Guru should again protect it by sprinkling water from the mouth of the vessel while reciting the names of the World-Protectors (*lokapāla*).
Having caused the command of the deity to be heard, having turned around clockwise,
and having recited the weapon-mantra (astramantra), he should establish [the deity] as before.
Having worshipped the Astra-mantra there once more with perfumes and other offerings while seated on a firm seat,
one should then cook the *caru* oblation with cow’s milk in the consecrated fire.
In a new vessel made of copper or another material, which has been cleansed with the Astra-mantra,
one should place rice grains produced from the Śāli variety, consecrated by the recitation of the Mūla-mantra.
Having poured fifteen handfuls [of water] and recited the Astra-mantra,
one should wash the mouth of the vessel and cover it with the Kavaca-mantra.
Facing the east, the preeminent teacher should cook the sacrificial porridge (caru) with the root mantra.
Afterwards, he should bring down that vessel with the root mantra and lower it [into the fire] with the armor mantra (kavaca).
Then, the Guru, according to the prescribed rule, [should place it] upon the maṇḍala strewn with kuśa grass over which the weapon mantra has been recited.
Having divided that into three parts, one should set aside one portion for the deity;
another, the preceptor should offer into the fire, and the remaining portion he should consume himself.

Then, having performed the ritual rinsing (*ācamana*), he should eat together with his disciple. Regarding the term "consecrated" (*saṃskṛta*): this consecration takes place in the *ācārya*-pit alone, because it is an action to be performed by the *ācārya*.
As it is stated in the *Prayogasāra*: "Having sprinkled the pit with the weapon-mantra (*astra-mantra*) and having placed the sacrificial fire therein..."
Then, one should duly worship the deity Sannidhānādika.

"Having performed the pouring of rice grains, one should cook the *caru* in that milk. "One should offer another [oblation] into the fire"—the remainder [of the sentence] is "the teacher (*ācārya*) and the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*). As for the sequence of that [rite], it is stated right there, after describing the purification of the fire to be performed by the teacher in the teacher's sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*):
Then, in other consecrated fire-pits (kuṇḍas) according to the prescribed rite,
the preceptor (ācārya), being composed, should attend to the fire in the eastern and other directions;
and the officiating priests (ṛtvijas) [should worship] the deity together with the limbs (aṅgas) and enclosures (āvaraṇas) by means of perfumes, flowers, and so forth.
Having worshipped the deity mentioned in the Tantra twenty-five times.
"They should offer oblations with clarified butter using the root mantra, and likewise with clarified butter and *caru*.

Thus it is stated. The purification of the other sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍa*), however, is performed by the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*). Regarding the phrase "by the disciple," there is a specific detail here mentioned in the *Somaśambhu*: "One should take a third portion of the *caru*, measured as three mouthfuls."
Or it may be the measure of eight mouthfuls, free from contact with the teeth.
Having placed [the food] in a cup made of *pālāśa* wood for one who has been initiated, and in a leaf-cup of *pippala* for one who is eating,
the practitioner of mantras should cause them to eat with the *hṛdaya-mantra* and cause them to rinse their mouths with pure waters.

In the *Śāradā-tilaka*: "Having brought the disciple who has sipped water and performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa, the preceptor [should place] a staff made from a milk-tree or similar wood, measuring the height of a palm tree, over which the *hṛdaya-mantra* has been recited."
Then he should give a tooth-stick to the disciple who is humble in spirit;
having carefully cleansed his teeth and washed that stick, he should discard it.

In the *Nārāyaṇīya*: "A tooth-stick produced from a milky tree or similar source, consecrated by reciting the *hṛdaya-mantra*, should be used to clean the teeth; having cut it [to the proper length] and rinsed it, one should cast it upon the ground."
In the directions starting from the east, including the zenith and nadir, its falling upon the tip [of the shadow] results, in sequence:
growth, suffering, death, wealth, loss, peace, illness, and money.

The increase of happiness is supreme suffering; these are the fruits it proclaims. Also, in the *Vāyavīya-saṃhitā*: "If that discarded tooth-stick is seen by the Guru, whether its tip points east, north, west, or northeast, it is auspicious; otherwise, it is inauspicious."
When that inauspicious aspect is present, the preceptor, for the sake of pacifying its defect,
should perform one hundred or fifty oblations, or half of that again, with the root mantra.
In another tantra: "Now, in this case, a tooth-stick measuring twelve finger-breadths should be given from a mango tree; it should be chewed by the tips of the teeth."
One should cast the upper face there into that mandala and raise the pedestal;
if the auspicious fall occurs in the directions of the West, North, Rudra (North-East), and Indra (East), it is favorable, otherwise it is inauspicious.
One should offer one hundred oblations with the Astra-mantra to destroy ill omens.

As stated in the *Śāradā*: "Having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) according to rule and having protected him by binding his topknot (śikhā), the Guru, together with him, [should place him] upon a bed of Darbha grass on the altar."

He should sleep on that [bed] for that night; this is declared to be the consecration (adhivāsa). In the Nārāyaṇīya: "Furthermore, having caused that disciple—who has sipped water (ācānta) and is protected by the tying of the topknot (śikhābandha)—to sit upon the altar, the Guru should sleep together with him on a bed of darbha grass."
In the *Piṅgalāmata*: "Having resorted to the *māṇava* dream [state], one should cause them to sleep with their heads toward the east.
Also in the *Somaśambhu*: "The householders, protected by the Weapon-mantra, should be placed on beds of *darbha* grass with their heads toward the east."
With his heart, [he saw] the ascetics upon a bed of pure ashes, with their heads toward the south.
In the Vāyavīyasaṃhitā:
On the right side of the deity, the pure disciple should be made to dwell upon a bed of Darbha grass spread over a new cloth covering.
Having consecrated it with mantras and meditating upon Śiva, he should sleep at night with his head toward the east;
then the Guru, having tied the thread around the disciple's crest-lock, [binds] that crest-lock with his own crest-lock.
Having wrapped it with a new cloth and covered it with armor,
one should draw three lines all around with ashes mixed with sesame and mustard seeds.
Having performed the rite with those [mantras] consecrated by the weapon-mantra (astra), one should offer oblations (bali) to the lords of the directions outside of that.
As stated in the *Mahākapilapañcarātra*:
"Having performed the worship of the Guru’s feet, fasting and with senses subdued..."
Having gone to a bed of darbha grass at night, one should report whatever dream is seen.

In the Yoginītantra: "When the divine [power] has arisen far away while one is awake, having restrained these mantras three times with self-restraint, eating only what is obtained, and lying on the right side, one should examine the dream according to the instruction."
73) O Blessed One, Lord of the gods of gods, wielder of the trident, whose vehicle is the bull,
O Eternal One, declare to me, while I am asleep, what is auspicious and what is inauspicious.
Thus, having slept upon a bed strewn with kusha grass with a disciplined mind,
he beholds at the end of the night a dream, whether auspicious or inauspicious.
In the Piṅgalāmata: "The Tāra (Om), followed by 'hili' twice, then 'śūlapāṇaye', and ending with 'dviṭha' (svāhā)—this is declared by Śambhu to be the mantra of Svapnamānava."
Salutation to the unborn, the three-eyed, the tawny-hued, the Great Soul;
salutation to the left-handed one, whose form is the universe, the Lord of dreams.
"O Maheśvara, tell me the truth in my dreams regarding all matters without exception; by your grace, I shall bring about the accomplishment of every undertaking."

In the *Mantratantraprakāśa*: "Oṃ! Salutation to Viṣṇu, the all-pervading Lord, the source of all worlds, the universe itself, whose form is the universe, and the sovereign of dreams. This mantra for the Dream-Man (Svapnamānava) has been declared by Nārada and others."

In the Nāradīya [Purāṇa]: "O Lord, you who are the very nature of the Supreme Brahman, moving within as the sustainer of the universe, reveal to me in a dream the course of my auspicious and inauspicious destiny."
Having uttered this, one should pay homage while kneeling upon the ground;
being pleased and restrained in speech, one should lie down upon it and contemplate the desired object.
Now, regarding auspicious dreams, it is stated in the Yoginītantra: "His vision is of three kinds:

that which is according to reality, that which is not according to reality, and that which is not born of [ordinary] causes—the vision of those who are established in their own state and are self-restrained."
That which is according to reality and that which is not according to reality arise from an unsteady state and from physical disorder;
mental [dreaming] is said to have results that accord with reality.

According to the established doctrine of the Āgama: in the first [case], digestion occurs after a year; in the second, after half a year; in the third, after a quarter of a year; and in the fourth watch of the night, there is immediate digestion—this being what is observed regarding those who have attained emission (visarga).
Likewise: "In the case of a cruel [dream], it is inferior; in one that is not seen, it is middling;
but in the case of the most excellent, one indeed beholds the God who is one's own desired object and the source of all."
The Guru, with a face radiant with grace, is like the stainless orb of the moon;
he is the Gaṅgā, the Bhāgīrathī, the Sun, the possessor of the Liṅga, and the Lord of the Vedas.
One should recognize a favorable dream-vision there as an indication of success.
In the *Nāradapañcarātra*: "The acquisition of land, being wounded, crossing the ocean, the worship of fire, performing a *homa* when the fire is blazing, and likewise victory in battle."
[The gift of] swans, cuckoos, and peacocks, as well as the mounting of a chariot.
In the *Mahākapila-pañcarātra*: "A maiden, an umbrella, a chariot, a lamp, a palace, a lotus, and a river..."
An elephant, a bull, a garland, the ocean, and a fruit-bearing tree.
Having seen a mountain, a sacrificial horse, raw meat, liquor, spirits, and all such things as these, one shall attain success.
When one sees a woman in dreams while performing rites for the fulfillment of desires,
one should know that there will be success in accordance with that dream-vision.
Crossing rivers and the ocean, traveling through the sky,
as well as the rising of the sun and the blazing of the sacrificial fire.
The sight of the orbs of the moon, eclipses, constellations, and stars;
or the climbing of a palace tower, or even the very summit of a mansion.
Mounting upon elephants, horses, bulls, and lions; climbing trees and mountain peaks; traveling in celestial chariots; and beholding those who have perfected the mantras.
Having seen such things as these, a man shall attain success;
likewise, in a dream, the drinking of liquor and the eating of raw meat [are auspicious].
Anointing with worms and excrement, being sprinkled with blood,
eating curd-rice, and anointing oneself with white garments.
Seeing a lion throne, a chariot, a vehicle, a banner, a royal consecration, jewels, ornaments, and the like in a dream, one becomes joyful.
In the *Nāradapañcarātra*: "The Guru, the Deity, the twice-born, a maiden, cows, elephants, horses, and the lion;
a mirror, a conch, kettledrums, stringed instruments, and yellow pigment."
The chewing of betel, as well as saluting while holding curd,
cooked food, raw meat, liquor, women, wine, and spirits;
An umbrella, a vehicle, white clothing, as well as other white sandalwood,
garlands, pearls, necklaces, and the full, rising moon.
The sun with its fierce rays, the river, and the great ocean;
the tree in full bloom, the rice crop, yellow pigment, saffron, and honey.
Parched grain, white mustard seeds, seed-grain, a new vessel, and milk-rice;
then the preceptor, having approached, [recites] the Gāyatrī conjoined with the excellent [mantra].
75) All dreams are said to be auspicious, bestowing the fruits of both spiritual accomplishment and liberation.
In the Nāradīya [Purāṇa]: "The seizing of women, likewise approaching those who should not be approached, being bitten by the white serpent, and being bound with chains and the like."
Weeping, beating, running about, and striking the limbs [are punishments for stealing] earth,
iron, tin, bronze, or even lead from a contemptible person.
The acquisition of a mineral, as well as flowers, both fruit and jewels,
a fan, and fanning the fire by oneself or by another.
The wise have described these and other such auspicious [dreams].
Now, regarding inauspicious dreams, it is said in the *Nāradapañcarātra*: "Those others which are the opposite of these and cause distress to the mind..."
For those dreams are censured, loathed by the world, and bring about inauspicious results.
In the *Mahākapilapañcarātra*: "A *cāṇḍāla*, a young camel, a crow, a pit, an empty place, an inauspicious thing,
a man smeared with oil, a naked person, and a dry, thorny tree."
Upon seeing the ground-level of a palace, a man may contract a disease.

Kapila states: "And having seen an evil dream, one shall attain success through a fire-oblation (homa). In the Piṅgalāmata: "If it is auspicious, his [result] will be auspicious; if inauspicious, he should offer a hundred oblations."
"By means of the Astra [mantra]," thus the learned one [should perform] the rite for the preliminary consecration of the disciple in due order.

In the *Nāradapañcarātra*: "O Sage, having seen [the toothbrush twig], one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) prescribed for the toothbrush twig, or with clarified butter alone, using the Siṃha-mantra for the sake of pacification."
In the *Nibandha*: "Oṃ, obeisance to the Great Lion whose weapons are diamond-claws and fangs, hūṃ phaṭ!"—this is the mantra of the Great Lion. Likewise:
"Or a hundred, a thousand, or eight [repetitions], or according to one's capacity, O twice-born."
And with their names enclosed by the weapon-mantra (astra) and accompanied by "svāhā," [one should offer oblations].

The mantra for the weapon-siṃha (astra-siṃha) consists of the words "jahi jahi" (slay, slay), ending with the name [of the target]. There is an option between these two mantras. In the Nāradīya [Tantra] it is said:
"The eating of cooked meat, and the cutting off of the ears, nose, and so forth..."
Anointing with red fragrant substances, or even anointing with mud.
An encircling by a black serpent, and an encircling with a red garland.
Embracing wicked women, laughing, and likewise dancing;
the acts of seeing or mounting donkeys, camels, and buffaloes;
being thrown down, entering [a house], anointing with oil, and likewise traveling toward the southern direction.
76) Vomiting of blood and so forth, the acquisition of those very things,
the breaking of limbs, sleep, and the vision of Yama’s messengers.
The appearance of portents celestial, terrestrial, and atmospheric;
the reviling of kings, cows, preceptors, and Brahmins; and the consumption of poison.
The wise know that beholding fearsome serpents, sexual intercourse with a man, and other such acts as these are censurable.
To counteract that, the preceptor should recite the mantra a thousand times;
he should likewise offer a thousand oblations of sesame seeds and proclaim a rite of pacification.
Now, regarding the reporting of the dream,

it is said in that very same [text]: "The disciple, pure and having sipped water (ācānta), with flowers in his hand, should joyfully bow his head to the most excellent Guru and report the dream to him."
If one should suddenly see a marvel that brings joy, whether in a dream or before one's very eyes, it must not be told to anyone except the Guru.

In the *Mahākapilapañcarātra*: "Having performed the worship of the Guru’s feet, fasting and with senses subdued, one should go to a bed of *darbha* grass at night; having seen a dream, one should report it."

In this context, the procedure for fasting is intended for examining dreams occurring at another time, because the consumption of milk-rice (*pāyasa*) as prescribed for initiation is mandatory. As stated in the *Piṅgalāmata*:
"Alternatively, one should perform the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsa*) immediately according to the rule."
In the *Mantratantraprakāśa*: "A wise practitioner should perform the rite of initiation (*dīkṣākarma*) in exactly two days;
or there may be immediate consecration (*sadyo'dhivāsana*) if it occurs on a single day.
Now, the purifications of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍasaṃskāra*).

Now, the consecration of the fire used for the *ukta-homa* is described. Among these, first is the consecration of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), as stated in the *Śāradā-tilaka*: "There are eighteen consecrations for the sacrificial pits prescribed in the Tantras.
Inspection with the root mantra and sprinkling with the *śara* [mantra] are considered [the first two]."
Striking with that same [mantra] is prescribed, sprinkling with darbha grass while reciting the armor-mantra (varma),
digging and lifting up with the weapon-mantra (astra), and filling with the heart-mantra (hṛd).
Leveling is performed with the Astra-mantra, and sprinkling is considered to be done with the Varma-mantra.
Crushing is performed with the Heti-mantra, and cleansing with the Varma-mantra.
Thereafter follows the application of ointment and the fashioning of artistic forms.
Thereafter, the triple-threading [of the rosary] and worship with the heart-mantra are prescribed.

77) One should perform the vajrīkaraṇa with the Astra-mantra, the drawing of lines with auspicious kuśa grass using the Hṛdaya-mantra, and the construction of the protective enclosure at the crossroads using the Kavaca-mantra.
In the sacrifice, one should consecrate the sacrificial pits with these aforementioned consecrations;
or else, one should consecrate them with the four [rites] beginning with inspection (vīkṣaṇa).
What is meant by "the visualization of the form of desire" (*kāmarūpakalpana*)? It means the contemplation of the digits (*kalā*) of the Moon, Sun, and Fire within the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*).
As for the "cutting of the blades," it is stated in the *Nāradapañcarātra*:
"Then, with the tips of *darbha* grass not yet severed, which have been consecrated with the Weapon-mantra (*astramantra*)."
One should adorn the entire Kuṇḍamittigaṇa with armor.

Thus, the consecration of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) known as akṣapāṭa has been described. It has been stated that if these consecrations are not performed at the time of constructing the pit, they must still be performed once it has been completed, for the sake of the unseen merit (adṛṣṭārtha). This is said in the Nāradapañcarātra:

"If, however, at the time of commencing the construction of the pit (kuṇḍa), the consecrations have not been performed, then all of them must indeed be performed in their proper sequence once it is completed.
Thus [it is said] in the Śāradā-tantra: "One should draw three lines each, facing east and north, with the heart-mantra (hṛdaya)."
Regarding the sequence of drawing here, it is stated in the *Sautrāmaṇitantra*:
"One should draw [the lines] facing east, extending upward and ending in the north, beginning from the south;
one should draw [the lines] facing west, extending toward the north and ending in the east, beginning from the west."
Having written three sets of three [lines] in this manner, one should sprinkle them with the Vāgbhava mantra.
In the *Śāradā*: "The deities for those lines pointing eastward are remembered as Mukunda, Īśa, and Purandara."
Of the lines with their tips pointing northward, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and the Moon [are the presiding deities].
Alternatively, one should draw a triangle surrounded by a hexagon there.
As it is said in the *Yāmala*: "O Goddess, one should draw a triangle surrounded by a hexagon.
And in the *Śāradā*: "Having sprinkled all [the components] with the *Tāra* mantra, one should then worship the *yogapīṭha*."

In this context, there is an option between the Vāgbhava and the Tāra [syllables]. Regarding "the seat of yoga" (yogapīṭha): the meaning is from the Foundation Power (ādhāraśakti) up to the end of the seat-mantra (pīṭhamantra). Herein: Jayā by name, then Vijayā, Ajitā, and Aparājitā.
Nityā, Vilāsinī, Dogdhrī, Aghorā, Maṅgalā—the nine [Mātṛkās].
Thus end the powers of the *pīṭhas*. "Hrīṃ, obeisance to the self of the Yoga-pīṭha of Vāgīśvarī and Vāgīśvara"—this is the *pīṭha-mantra*.
As it is said in another Tantra: "Obeisance to the self of the Yoga-pīṭha of Vāgīśvarī and Vāgīśvara."
This is the seat-mantra (pīṭhamantra) beginning with *hrīṃ*; having invoked [the deity] into this, one should worship her.
In the *Śāradā*: "Vāgīśvarī, who has bathed after her menses, resembling a blue lotus.
(78) In the *Gaṇeśvaravimarśinī*: "One should [worship] Vāgīśī with the seed-syllable of Śakti, and Vāgīśa with the mantra of the one to be accomplished (*sādhya*)."
The word "should worship" is to be supplied as the ellipsis. However, in the Rudrayāmala:
"Then, the two mantras ending in 'namaḥ' are declared for Śiva and Śakti;
having worshipped with these three times each, one should prostrate with this mantra."
I bow to Vāgīśvarī, who has bathed after her menses and is adorned with all ornaments,
united with Vāgīśvara, for the sake of attaining the perfection of writing.

Thus it has been said. However, in the Vaiṣṇava tradition, Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa are to be worshipped in the place of Vāgīśvarī and Vāgīśvara; as stated in the Tattvasārasaṃhitā: "There, one should worship Lakṣmī, who is in her menses, together with the Lord Nārāyaṇa."
One should contemplate the fire produced there by means of the village rite (grāmyadharma).

And here: "Vibhūti (sovereignty), unnati (elevation), kānti (splendor), sṛṣṭi (creation), kīrti (fame), sannati (humility), puṣṭi (nourishment), utkṛṣṭi (excellence), and ṛddhi (prosperity)—these are declared to be the nine powers."
Thus end the powers of the *pīṭha*. Because of the statement, "having offered the seat beginning with the seed-syllable," the *pīṭha-mantra* is:

*Śrīṃ, namaḥ to the essence of the yoga-seat of Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa*. Regarding the *Śrīvidyā*, however, in the *Jñānārṇava*: "Kāmeśvarī, full of desire and joined with her season [of menses], is in the center of the *kuṇḍa*..."
Having propitiated and fully worshipped [the deity], one should cause the fire to enter its interior.

In the *Śāradā-tilaka*: "Having brought fire produced from a sun-crystal or the like, or that which has come from the house of a Vedic scholar (*śrotriya*), into a vessel, one should discard the portion belonging to the flesh-eaters."

According to Gautama: One should fetch fire produced from stone, or that produced from a fire-drill, or that found in the house of Vedic scholars (śrotriya), or that which is maintained in the forest.
If [the guest] arrives by chance and is unfit for the sacrificial rite,

or if he is a Brāhmaṇa who maintains no sacred fires (niragni), the gift received from him yields only half the merit. If the gift is obtained from a Kṣatriya, the consumer of the oblation (Agni) bestows a fourth part of the fruit.
If performed by a Vaiśya or a Śūdra, that rite of burnt offering (homa) becomes fruitless.

In the Uḍḍīśatantra: "Whether it be produced from the house of a Vedic scholar, or born from a sun-crystal, or even produced from a fire-drill, it should be cast into a vessel made of gold or other precious materials."
The practitioner, using a copper vessel or similar, should bring it while it is covered;
or else, once it has been brought, he should place it upon a bronze dish.

Atri also says: "When a beautiful vessel such as a copper bowl has been covered with another vessel, one should perform the bringing forward of the fire (agnipraṇayana), or even in a similar earthenware cup."

But in the *Smṛtisāra*: "One should not perform the bringing forward of the fire (*agnipraṇayana*) in a broken bowl, a cracked vessel, a potsherd, or even a firebrand; it brings about the fear of loss of health."

Thus, the prohibition of using a shallow dish (śarāva) should be understood to apply when vessels made of copper or other such materials are available. Regarding the specific procedure for discarding the portion belonging to the flesh-eaters (kravyāda), another Tantra states: "Having established the fire with the Astra-mantra and having covered it with the Kavaca-mantra..."
O beloved, one should cast away the portion belonging to the flesh-eaters toward the southwest using the Astra-mantra.
Also in the *Mantramuktāvalī*:
"Having brought [the portion] to the southwest with the Astra-mantra, the wise one should discard the portion belonging to the flesh-eaters (kravyāda);
he should establish the portion belonging to the deity in front with the Mūla-mantra."
In the Uḍḍīśa, however, it is stated: "One should discard the portion belonging to the flesh-eaters (kravyāda) in the southwest using the Kūrca and Astra mantras.
In the Gaṇeśvara as well: "One should discard the portion belonging to the flesh-eaters with the root mantra ending in *hūṃ* and *phaṭ*."
In the *Kriyāsāra*: "He who eats raw meat in places such as cremation grounds is called Vahni; his name is Kravyāda. One should avoid [offering] anything to this consumer of corpses."

In the Śāradā-tilaka: "The preceptor should purify that [thread] according to the rule by means of the rites of inspection and so forth, while meditating on the unification of the terrestrial element with the fire of the lunar orb through its own grandeur."
Likewise, one should unite the consciousness with the fire-seed syllable within the sacrificial fire.

In the *Sārasaṃgraha*: "Having diligently invoked the light in the form of a lamp-flame, one should effect the unification of the earthly element with the digestive fire (*jāṭhara*) and the lunar fire (*vaidyuta*)."
Then, having recollected [the mantra] consisting of the seed-syllable of fire (raṃ), one should unite his consciousness with it.
The "Vaindava" fire is situated between the eyebrows. As stated in the Uḍḍīśa:
"Like the analogy of a lamp from another lamp, it flashes forth, facing in all directions."
Then, one who knows the mantra should worship by means of the armor-mantra through the path of the breath.

In the Śāradā-tilaka: "The practitioner, having consecrated [the water] with the Tāra mantra, rendered it nectar by means of the Dhenu-mudrā, protected it subsequently with the Astra mantra, and veiled it with the Tanutra mantra."
Having circumambulated it three times while it is being worshipped, the preceptor then performs a circumambulation around the pit, preceded by the utterance of the *tāra* mantra.
With his knees touching the ground, he should place this fire facing himself into the womb of the Goddess, perceiving it as the seed-syllable of Śiva.
In the Uḍḍīśa: "Having placed the knees on the ground, [one should utter] the Kūrca-bīja, Vahni (Ra), and Caitanya (Ca), ending with 'ṅe namaḥ'; by means of this, one should raise the pure [deity]."
With the thought that it is the seed-syllable of Śiva, one should cast the fire into her womb.
As stated in the *Tripurāsārasamuccaya*: "The mantra-knower should place this [fire] in the womb facing his own mouth, and afterwards [place] the fire with the root-mantra."

Thus it has been stated. Regarding the phrase "by means of the consciousness of the Śiva-bīja," this refers to the Śaiva and Śākta traditions. However, in the Vaiṣṇava and other systems, it should be understood as "by means of the consciousness of the Viṣṇu-bīja" and so forth. Furthermore, in the Vāyavīya-saṃhitā it is said:
"Having uttered the fire-bīja, one should install the fire upon the seat."
Likewise, it should be done through the path of the womb or directly facing oneself.
"By the path of the *yoni*, that is, through the opening of the *yoni* established above the girdle (*mekhalā*). In the *Śāradā*:
'Afterwards, the preceptor should offer water for sipping (*ācamana*) and so forth to the God and the Goddess;
then he should kindle that fire with this mantra.'"
Having uttered "cit piṅgala hana daha paca yugmāni," this mantra previously mentioned is completed with "sarvajña ājñāpaya svāhā."

In the Rudrayāmala, however: "O Goddess, with the mantra *hrīṃ hrīṃ*, followed by two instances of *jvala* and then two instances of *prajvalat*, and finally *huṃ phaṭ svāhā*, the wise man should kindle the fire."
Thus it has been said. However, the kindling [of the fire] must be done with the mouth alone. As it has been stated:
"Those who have offered oblations should offer sacrifices using their hands, winnowing baskets, ladles, and so forth;
they should not blow upon the fire, nor should they do so with fans and the like."
"One should blow upon the fire with the mouth alone, for it was born from the mouth;
however, that which says 'one does not blow upon the fire with the mouth' applies to worldly [fire]."
Thus it is said. Here, Jvālinī refers to that which has been described as the ritual of *homakarma*. In the *Yāmala*:
"Then, having risen and properly joined his palms, the wise one should say:
'I bow to the blazing fire, the Jātavedas, the consumer of oblations.'"
One should worship the fire according to the rules with this mantra— [the fire] which is golden-hued, stainless, kindled, and facing in all directions.
In the *Uḍḍīśa*: "Having silently cast into the fire a fuel-stick the size of a span, saturated with ghee at both its root and tip, one should install the deity upon the tongue [of the fire].
In the *Śāradā*: "One should install the tongues of the fire-eater within one's own body by means of mantras."
In the penis, anus, head, mouth, nose, and eyes, everywhere.
The letters from 'sa' to 'ya', joined with the fire (ra), the moon (i),
and the lord of stars (m), along with the bindu, are declared by the teachers of the seventeen [tongues] to be the mantras of the tongues.

The tongues are said to be of three kinds according to the distinction of qualities (*guṇa*) in ritual acts: Hiraṇyā, Gaganā, and Raktā; another is considered Suprabhā, Bahurūpā, and Atiraktā—these are the *sāttvika* ones for sacrificial rites. (81)

*Vahni* is the letter *ra*; *ira* is the letter *ya*; *arghīśa* is the long *ū*. Here, in the case of the sattvic tongue, the sequence of *bahurūpā* and *atiraktā* follows the order of the seed-syllables (*bīja*) and not the order of the ritual placement (*nyāsa*), because *bahurūpā* is to be placed upon all limbs. As it has been said:
In another tantra: "One should sequentially place that exceedingly red [syllable] on the penis, anus, head, mouth, nose, and eyes, and the multiformed one on all the limbs."
Thus say Rāghavabhaṭṭa. In reality, however: Hiraṇyā, Gaganā, Raktā, Kṛṣṇā, Suprabhā, Bahurūpā, O Maheśānī, and likewise Atiraktā.

Immediately after this, O Goddess: "One should place each [syllable] on the linga, then on the anus, the head, the mouth, the nose, and likewise the eyes; thereafter, one should place them on the entire body."
According to the words of the Vīracūḍāmaṇi:
"Then the practitioner of mantra should place the tongue of the Fire-god upon his own body,
in sequence, upon the penis, the anus, the head, the mouth, the nose, and the eyes."
And on all the limbs, tongues are said to be of three kinds:
golden, sky-colored, red, and the radiant black.
"Multiform, extremely red, and [having] seven tongues—these are the Sāttvika [tongues].
According to this statement from the *Mantratantraprakāśa*, it is most appropriate to perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the extremely red [tongue] upon all the limbs.
Furthermore, if the statement written by Rāghavabhaṭṭa is authoritative, then there is indeed an option (*vikalpa*); such is the truth.
In the *Śāradā*: "Padmarāgā, Suvarṇā, another called Bhadralohitā;
after Lohitā comes Śvetā, Dhūminī, and Karālikā."
The tongues of fire prescribed for rites performed for desired objects are:
Viśvamūrti, Sphuliṅginī, Dhūmravarṇā, and Manojavā.
Lohitā, Karālā, and Kālī are said to belong to Tamas;
these seven are employed by practitioners of mantra in cruel rites.
The tongues of those of auspicious seed— immortals, ancestors, gandharvas, yakṣas, nāgas, and piśācas— shall be equal in luster to their respective names.
The Rākṣasas are the presiding deities (adhidevatā) of the seven tongues.
The mention of presiding deities is for the purpose of ritual placement (nyāsa) and worship in the respective locations of those tongues,
so that the various tasks of the gods and others may be accomplished.
82) Or, one should perform oblations; those deities will grant the desired accomplishment.

According to this statement from the *Prapañcasāra*, in the case of performing oblations (*homa*) with various substances upon their respective tongues, it is for the purpose of those [tongues] being offered.
In the *Kriyāsāra*: "The seer (*ṛṣi*) of this is Bhṛgu, the metre (*chandas*) is Gāyatrī, and Agni is the deity (*devatā*)."
The seed-syllable is "raṃ" and the power is "svāhā"; one should assign the seers and other [limbs] as before.
In the *Śāradā-tilaka*: "One should assign the mantras of the limbs of Fire to the body by the method already described:
Sahasrārcis, Svastipūrṇa, Uttiṣṭhapuruṣa, and again..."
"Dhūmavyāpin, Saptajihva, and Dhanurdhara"—
these are declared to be the six-limbed mantras, joined respectively with their seed-syllables (jātis).
The preceptor should assign the eight forms of Jātavedas upon his own body,
[placing them] on the head, the shoulders, the sides, the groins, the hips, and the sides of the hips and shoulders.
One should assign [the mantras] by way of circumambulation, or they are recited according to their sequence:
Jātavedas, Saptajihva, and the one named Havyavāhana.
Another is known as Aśvodaraja, while another is called Vaiśyānara;
Kaumāratejas would be Viśvamukha, who is remembered as Devamukha.
The forms of Fire (Vahni-mūrtis) consist of the words beginning with "Tārāgnaye" and ending with "Namaḥ.
Having prepared the seat for Agni, one should contemplate his form.

The seat (āsana) is the pedestal (pīṭha); the word "on the body" is to be understood as the ellipsis. Therein, having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) starting from the foundational power (ādhāraśakti) up to the fire-mandala (vahnimaṇḍala), one should place the powers of the pedestal (pīṭhaśaktis) upon the filaments and in the center; and right there, one should also place the pedestal with the mantra: *raṃ, obeisance to the yoga-pedestal of fire*.
It is stated in that very same work: "One should worship within one's own mandala the nine powers of the lords of the seats (pīṭheśa):
the Yellow, the White, the Red, the Black, the Smoky, the Intense (tīvrā), and the Sparkling (sphuliṅginī)."
"Rucirā and Jvālinī are declared to be the nine powers (śaktis) of Fire.
Having offered a seat with its own seed-syllable (bīja), one should fashion the form (mūrti) by means of the root-mantra (mūla). Likewise:
"One should meditate on the desired Śakti, who is the color of hibiscus, holding a svastika and the gesture of fearlessness (abhaya) aloft with her long arms."
One should meditate upon Fire, adorned with golden ornaments, seated upon a lotus, possessing three eyes, and wearing a crown of matted locks;
this intermediate meditation is described in the Rudrayāmala:
[He is] resembling the bandhūka flower, with the luster of well-refined gold.
Seated upon a lotus for the sake of the patron, and adorned with two faces.
The god, composed of the seven meters, seated upon his celestial chariot,
with three necks and three lotus-feet, is the destroyer of the offerings to gods and ancestors.
Adorned with the four horns of the Brahman, Adhvaryu, Udgātṛ, and Hotṛ priests, it consists of the Pāñcarātra, the Pāśupata, the Kāpila, and the Mahā-mata systems. (83)
The Buddhist and the Vedic [traditions] are its six tawny eyes;
the meaning of the Vedas is its four ears, and the sound of the Śrauta scriptures is its voice.

having then made the formal resolve (saṅkalpa), one should perform the optional fire-sacrifice (kāmyahoma)."

Having uttered the root mantra ending with *svāhā*, and saying "to the deity, this [is offered]," one should offer oblations into the kindled fire; the number [of oblations] should be performed all around.
In the *Śāradā*: "The practitioner of mantra should offer oblations into its mouth twenty-five times with clarified butter using the root mantra; this is indeed the unification of the faces."
In the Śaiva Āgama: "Thus, within the desired face, there is the inclusion of all faces and their unification;
or else, one should contemplate the measurement of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) as being like that of the desired face."
The faces are to be internalized; their unification with that [central face] is considered the intended meaning. One should contemplate the identity of the fire, the deity, and oneself.
With the root mantra, one should offer eleven oblations of clarified butter.
This junction of the channels has been taught by those who know the scriptures;
one should offer oblations to the principal limbs and the enclosures in their proper sequence.
The most excellent of teachers should offer each oblation properly with clarified butter; at the end, ten oblations should be offered with the root mantra. As it is said in the *Tripurāsāra*:
"One should offer one oblation for each member of the retinue, and ten oblations for the Goddess."
Thus is the procedure for the consecration (*adhivāsa*).
Now, regarding the daily duties, the *Śāradā* states: "Having risen in the morning, they should again perform oblations with sesame seeds mixed with clarified butter."
Or, with substances prescribed by the ritual manuals, one should perform [the rite] separately one thousand and eight times.
"They should offer oblations" means the preceptor and the officiating priests. In this context, sesame seeds and other materials are to be offered with either the *sruva* ladle or by hand.
As it is stated in the *Vāyavīyasaṃhitā*:
"Ghee is offered with the *sruva*, the remaining materials with the *sruc* held in the hand, or otherwise by hand."
In that case, it should be offered with the divine or the ṛṣi-designated tīrtha; so it is said.
93) In the *Mahākapilapañcarātra*: "One should not offer oblations when the fire is not yet ignited, nor even when it is in its middle stage and not yet fully kindled.
Oblations should be offered into the blazing, licking fire for the sake of the accomplishment of ritual action."
Also in the *Ahvṛcapariśiṣṭa*:
"If one who is the patron of the sacrifice should offer oblations into a smoky fire with his face turned downwards, he shall become blind; such is the Vedic revelation regarding having a good son."
In the *Chandogapariśiṣṭa* it is also said:
"The man who offers oblations into a fire that lacks flames or one whose embers are extinguished is born with weak digestion, prone to disease, and impoverished."
In the *Tripurāsāra*: "From an oblation in the ear of the fire, there is affliction by disease; in the eye, blindness; in the nose, mental distress;
and on the head, the loss of one's wealth. Therefore, a wise man should always perform the oblation within the mouth [of the fire]."
In another Tantra: "Where there is wood, there is the ear; where there is smoke, there is the nose;
where there is a small flame, there is the eye; and where there are embers, there is the head."
Where the blazing flame is, that is the tongue of Jātavedas.
Elsewhere it is said: "The fire with smoke should be known as the head, and the smokeless fire as the eyes;
the flickering, thin flame is the ear, and that which is attached to the wood is the nose."
Where the fire blazes like pure crystal,
that should be known as the mouth, measuring four finger-breadths in size.
In the *Vanadurgākalpa*: "Where there is wood, there is the ear; where there is smoke, that is the nose;
where there is a small flame, that is the eye; and where there is ash, that is the head."
Wherever the fire blazes, there the tongue is proclaimed to be.
In the *Śāradā-tantra*: "The preceptor should meditate upon Vaiśvānara as standing during fuel-wood oblations;
as reclining during clarified-butter oblations; and as seated during all other matters."
Likewise: "The auspicious color of Suvarṇaretas is proclaimed to resemble gold, vermilion, the morning sun, saffron, and honey."
The sound of fire that resembles the roar of a kettledrum, a rain-cloud, or a lordly elephant brings auspiciousness;
likewise, a scent resembling the nagakesara, campaka, punnaga, patala, or yudhika flowers is auspicious.
The auspicious fragrance of fire is described by those learned in the Tantras as being like that of the lotus, the blue water-lily, the white water-lily, clarified butter, and guggulu resin.
Cocks whose crests move clockwise, are free from trembling, and resemble umbrellas in appearance bestow auspiciousness upon the sacrificer,
and especially upon his kingdom.
94) Smoke as white as a jasmine flower or a conch shell is declared to bring auspiciousness from fire;
smoke that is black, having the color of a black path, shall destroy the sacrificer.
A white [halo] portends the swift destruction of the kingdom; a sound resembling the cry of a crow or similar to the braying of a donkey, or like the roar of fire, brings about total ruin.
If the fire emits a foul odor, it will bring about suffering;
if the flame becomes broken or flickering, it portends death and the total loss of wealth.
Smoke resembling the wing of a parrot or having a luster like that of a pigeon portends the eventual loss of horses and cattle.
In the event of such defects, the preceptor should offer twenty-five oblations of clarified butter with the root mantra as an act of expiation.

In the *Tripurāsāra*, however, it is said: "In these cases of defects, the king of practitioners should perform a propitiatory rite (*śāntika*) by offering one hundred and eight oblations of clarified butter with the Astra-mantra, and then perform the worship of the *cakra*. In the *Śāradā*: "Then, [the teacher should initiate] the disciple who has washed his teeth and face, who has bathed, and who is composed in mind."
Having made [the disciple] drink the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), one should bring him into the vicinity of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).

In the *Prayogasāra*: "Having drunk the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) as prescribed and having sipped water according to the rule, one should then cause [the disciple] to enter the place of sacrifice by the southern door."

In the *Śāradā*: "Having beheld that consciousness within the heart-lotus with divine vision, the Guru, having united it with his own self, should perform the purification of the paths (*adhva-viśodhana*)."
In another tantra: "Having taken that consciousness situated in the heart, which has the form of a shimmering star, one should establish it within one's own heart by means of the goad mudrā."
In the *Ṣaḍanvayamahāratna*: "Purification (*śodhana*) is the contemplation of the unity of the cause of the principles (*tattvas*);
it is the contemplation of the oneness of consciousness within that [purification] of the phonemes (*varṇas*), the primary elements (*kalās*), and so forth."

Now, regarding the purification of the paths (*adhva-śodhana*), it is stated in the *Śāradā*: "The triad consisting of the path of the creative energies (*kalādhvā*), the path of the principles (*tattvādhvā*), and the path of the worlds (*bhuvanādhvā*);
and the other triad consisting of the path of the phonemes (*varṇādhvā*), the path of the words (*padādhvā*), and the path of the mantras (*mantrādhvā*)."
In the *Vāyavīyasaṃhitā*: "Here, three paths are declared as 'word' (śabda) and three as 'meaning' (artha).
In another Tantra: "The path of mantra, the path of word, and the path of phoneme constitute the threefold [division] by way of word;
the path of worlds, the path of principles, and the path of phases constitute the threefold [division] by way of meaning."

In this [text], however, the statement follows the order of withdrawal (*saṃhāra-krama*); it should be understood that in the *Śāradā*, it follows the order of emanation (*sṛṣṭi-krama*). In the *Śāradā*: "The five levels beginning with Nivṛtti are proclaimed as the path of the levels (*kalādhvan*)."
95) The path of reality (tattvādhvan) is divided in many ways according to the differences between the various original scriptures:
there are thirty-six Śaiva principles (tattvas), whereas the Vaiṣṇava principles are thirty-two.
The twenty-four principles are friendly toward primordial nature (prakṛti);
furthermore, ten principles are said to belong to the three-footed Self (puruṣa), and seven to the other.
The Śaiva principles are now stated: Śiva, Śakti, Sadāśiva, Īśvara, and Vidyā; these five indeed constitute the pure [principles].
Māyā, Kāla, Niyati, Kalā, Vidyā, Smṛti, Rāga, and Puruṣa— these seven are both pure and impure. Then there are Prakṛti, Buddhi, Ahaṃkāra, Manas, and the organs of knowledge.
The organs of action, the subtle elements, and the five gross elements—
these twenty-four, O Teacher, are declared in the Āgama to be impure.
Here, the division of the Śaiva principles (*tattva*) is also demonstrated.

Regarding the term "pure" (*śuddha*): purity consists in being free from the three impurities (*mala*), namely the *āṇava*, *kārmaṇa*, and *māyīya*. Among these, the *āṇava* is the non-recognition of oneself as Sadāśiva; the *kārmaṇa* is... [text fragment ends].
The notion "I am possessed of merit and demerit" is what is called the illusory ego-sense (*māyīya-ahaṃkāra*), which is the cognition of the self within the ego-principle and so forth.
Regarding the terms "pure" and "impure": they are "pure" insofar as they are causes and are free from the three impurities (*mala*);
they are "impure" insofar as they are effects and are joined with those [impurities]. This is the meaning.

Likewise: the individual soul (jīva), the vital breaths (prāṇa), the intellect (dhī), the mind (citta), the organs of knowledge and action, the subtle elements (tanmātra), the five gross elements (bhūta), the heart-lotus, and the triad of luminaries.
Vāsudeva and the others—these are the principles (tattvas) of the wielder of the Śārṅga bow:
the five gross elements, the subtle elements, the sense organs, and likewise the mind.
The wise know that pride, intellect, and the primary matter (pradhāna) are the [five] Maitrāṇīs;
following these are the five kalās beginning with Nivṛtti, and then again the Bindu and the Kalā.
The wise know that Nāda is Śakti, ever prior, and Śiva is Prakṛti;
subsequently, Śiva is Ātma-vidyā, while Vidyā is Śiva himself.
All reality and the principles (tattvas) have been declared as belonging to the threefold nature;
this indeed is called the path of principles (tattvādhvan) by those who know the various Āgamas.

The wise have designated the "path of the worlds" (*bhuvanādhvā*) as the fourteen worlds. This is because of the statement in the *Gautamīya Tantra*: "The path of the worlds is said to be the fourteen worlds.
However, in the *Vāyavīyasaṃhitā*—

"The path of worlds (bhuvanādhvan) is proclaimed as extending from the Foundation (ādhāra) up to the Beyond-mind (unmanī). Thus it has been said. (96) Likewise, the wise declare the "path of phonemes" (varṇādhvan) to consist of the letters beginning with 'a' and ending with 'kṣa'.
The "path of words" (padādhvan) is the lion of phonemes, while the "path of mantras" (mantrādhvan) consists of the multitudes of mantras.
In the Vāyavīya-saṃhitā, however, it is stated:
"The path of words (padādhvan), consisting of a collection of words divided into many varieties,
exists as the constituent parts of great mantras and subordinate mantras."
That path consists of five parts by virtue of its primary constituents.
It is also stated in the *Gautamīya*: "The path of words (*padādhvan*) is a collection of words. Regarding "masses of mantras":
this refers to the collection of Vedic and Tantric mantras—the path of mantras (*mantrādhvan*) is the mass of mantras, for they [are such].
"Vaidika and Tāntrika [practices]," according to the statement of Gautama. And in the Śāradā:
"The best of gurus should purify these six paths in their proper order."
One should also remember the feet, the navel, the forehead, and the head of the child.

Then, touching him according to the rule with the *kūrca* grass-bundle, the Guru should perform the oblation in the preceptor’s fire-pit (*ācāryakuṇḍa*) using purified sesame seeds saturated with clarified butter (*ājya*).
"I purify this path; Svāhā!"—with these words, one should offer eight oblations individually for each path, beginning with the syllable *TĀRĀ*, and thereby lead them to dissolution in due order.
The supreme teacher, beholding that infant with his divine vision, should cause those [elements] merged within Śiva to arise from Śiva by way of the path of emanation.
One should then project that consciousness, which resides within oneself, into the disciple.
As stated in the *Kulārṇava*: "For Śūdras and those born of mixed castes, purification of the path (*adhva-śuddhi*) is not prescribed;
one should effect their liberation from sin by means of offering water for the feet and other such rites."
In the *Śāradā-tilaka*: "The preceptor, having offered the *pūrṇāhuti* with the *sruc* ladle while reciting the root mantra...
In the *Vāyavīya-saṃhitā*:
"Then, having filled the *sruc* ladle with the clarified butter remaining from the *homa*..."
Having placed a flower before it, [he should offer] that [libation] with the sruva spoon turned downwards.
Having covered [the fire] with the sixfold ritual materials and risen with the root mantra joined with the añjali gesture,
one should offer a continuous stream of oblations, measured by a barley-corn, ending with the syllable *vauṣaṭ*.

In the *Hayaśīrṣapañcarātra*: "Having offered oblations with clarified butter, one should offer three full oblations (*pūrṇāhuti*) with the sacrificial ladle (*sruk*), using the mantra ending in 'vauṣaṭ'... [as stated].
In the *Nāradapañcarātra*: "In the absence of clarified butter, however, one should fill [the vessel] with whatever substance is used for the oblation."
One should place ghee upon that, and above that, saffron and other substances.
(97) In the *Tūrṇayāga*, having uttered the root mantra ending in *namaḥ* while beginning with the left foot,
the practitioner of mantra should then offer the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) with the thought that it is supreme nectar.
In this context, he offers one oblation each to the chosen deity (iṣṭadevatā) and the presiding deities (varaṇadevatā). As stated in the *Gautamīya Tantra*:
"Having taken up the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles and filled them with clarified butter, and having again placed the sacrificial materials therein, he should then place them at his navel."
One should again offer the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) with the mantra "brahmārpaṇam.

Whatever has been done previously by me—through the authority of my vital breaths, intellect, body, and duties, and during the states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep—whether by mind, speech, action, the two hands, the two feet, the belly, or the generative organ; whatever was remembered, spoken, or performed...
"Whatever has been spoken and whatever has been performed, may all that be an offering unto Brahman, svāhā!
This is the mantra for the offering unto Brahman, prescribed for the rite of *brahmārpaṇa*.
Having thus performed the procedure for the oblation (*homa*), [one should worship] the deities residing in the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) and the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*).
The Guru should also bring the guardians of the directions (dikpāla-devatās) and the deities of the aṅkurārpaṇa rite; he should then contemplate the oneness of Kṛṣṇa within the water-pot (kalaśa).
"Kṛṣṇa," [is said] with reference to the subject at hand. In the *Śāradā*:

"The Guru, having dismissed the deity along with the limbs (*aṅga*) and the enclosures (*āvaraṇa*) into the water-pot (*kumbha*), should again offer oblations with the *vyāhṛtis* to the tongues and other parts of the Fire."
Having offered each oblation individually and sprinkled water upon himself,
he should unite the fire with his own self, along with the enclosing sticks and the surrounding grass mats.
The practitioner of mantras should burn these [substances] during occasional rites (*naimittika*), but he should not burn them during daily rites (*nitya*).

This is because of the scriptural injunction: "One should conclude the fire-oblation (*homa*) with the *vyāhṛtis* and the *mahāvyāhṛtis*, preceded by the *mahāvyāhṛtis*. As for the procedure for that, it is stated in the *Gautamīya*:
Then, one who knows the ritual procedure should offer the *pūrṇāhuti* with water as well, [reciting]:
"Oṃ bhūr! To Agni, to the Earth, and to the Great One, svāhā!"
"Bhuvaḥ! To Vāyu and to the great intermediate space, Svāhā! Then:
Svaḥ! To the Moon, to the quarters, and to the lunar mansions, Svāhā!"

Oṃ bhūr-bhuvaḥ-svaḥ, to the Moon, to the constellations, and to the quarters, and to the Great One, svāhā! Having thus joined the purifier (the fire), the method for doing so is stated in the *Gaṇeśvaravimarśinī*:
"O Vahni, O you of great power, accomplisher of all rites!"
Even when another task has arisen, show me your respectful attention.
Having thus offered prayer with this mantra, one should also cause the fire to be extinguished.
(98) In the *Śāradā*: "One should bind the eyes of the disciple with a cloth using the eye-mantra (*netramantra*).
In the *Mahākapilapañcarātra*, it is stated: "Having bound the eyes with a new white cloth... and so forth.
In the *Piṅgalāmata*: "One should bind his eyes with a cloth over the eyes using the Netra-mantra.

In the *Nārāyaṇīya*: "One should bind [him] with the Netra-mantra and so forth. In the *Śāradā*: "Having taken that disciple by the hand, one should lead him from the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) to the mandala."
