Having again filled his joined palms with flowers according to the prescribed rite, he—
One should cast [the flowers] into the jar while reciting the root mantra for the pleasure of the deity.
In the *Nārāyaṇīya*: "Having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) upon the body of the disciple, one should lead him around [the jar] clockwise;
having brought him to the western door, one should cause him to cast a handful of flowers."
In the *Piṅgalāmata*: "Having filled his joined palms with flowers, he should offer them upon the seat of yoga (*yogapīṭha*).
A fall of the flower toward the west, north, the direction of Rudra (north-east), or Indra (east) is auspicious; otherwise, it is inauspicious."

Then, having repeatedly withdrawn and re-emitted [the self] through the sequence of the sacrifice of the self, the teacher should perform the ritual placements (nyāsa) on the body of the disciple as prescribed by their respective mantras.

The sacrifice of the self (*ātmayāga*) is the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*). In the *Prayogasāra*: "One should cause the elements, beginning with earth, which reside within the body, to dissolve according to their constituent qualities (*guṇāṃśa*), by means of the yoga of the process of withdrawal (*saṃhārakrama*)."
Then, one should contemplate the body according to the very order of emanation.
As stated in the *Mantratantraprakāśa*: "Seated upon a divine seat, one should withdraw its physical form;
one should dissolve the earth, which is conjoined with the sense of smell and other qualities, into water," and so forth.

In the *Śāradā*: "Having worshipped the chosen deity residing in the water-pot with the fivefold offerings, one should perform the ritual of sakalīkṛti for her according to the method taught in the Tantras."
Immediately following this, the teachers have described the petition for boons from the presence of the deity:
"O Goddess, abode of compassion, refuge of all presences;
O Mother, affectionate toward those who seek shelter, bestow Your grace upon this child."
O Goddess of the gods, O Sovereign, show compassion toward this wretched one who is bound by the fetters beginning with the *āṇava*, you who are the vessel of mercy.
"Let him be nourished even by the enjoyments of this world and the next;
let his entire devotion be offered to Him who is the refuge of the partless (niṣkala).
Thus it is said in the *Prayogasāra*: "Now, when the knower of mantras has projected his form in the northeastern direction..."
On the square altar of the pedestal, with the tips of darbha grass in hand.

99) One should consecrate one's own disciple who follows the reality of the Self. In the *Somaśambhu*: "In a bathing pavilion constructed in the northeast direction from the sacrificial hall, one should fashion an altar two cubits in length and eight finger-breadths in height."

Having placed a seat made of *śrīparṇī* wood and other materials there, and having seated the disciple— who is bowed before him— facing east upon that seat, one should worship him after performing the ritual of personification (*sakalīkaraṇa*).
In that very same [text]: "For bathing, one should face north; for liberation, face east; and for enjoyment, face east as before.

Also elsewhere: "Having established the mandala in the direction of Īśa (the northeast), one should seat those seeking liberation facing north, and for the sake of enjoyment, seat the disciples there facing east."
In the *Śāradā-tantra*: "While the five musical instruments resound, the Guru, together with the benedictions of the Brahmins,
having duly lifted the pitcher and placed the celestial trees situated at its opening upon the head of the disciple, should mentally recite the Mātṛkā."
The knower of the Self should sprinkle him with water consecrated by the root mantra.
Having joined the *mātṛkā*— that is, the reverse *mātṛkā* (*vilomamātṛkā*)—

to the head of the disciple while reciting it, [one should do so] "with the letters beginning with *kṣa* and ending with *ra*, filled with the principles (*tattvas*), and preceded by the mantra repeated three times," according to the statement in the *Dīpikā*. Thus, one should join [it] to the disciple's head while muttering the reverse *mātṛkā*.
Having likewise recited the root mantra, one should perform the consecration of the deity.
And because of the statement of Gautama: "Likewise,
having taken up again the *vardhanī* vessel, which has been worshipped and is of the nature of a weapon,
one should immediately sprinkle [the disciple] with its well-prepared waters for the sake of protection."
With the remaining water, the Guru should cause the disciple to sip;
then, the knower of the Self, having performed the ritual integration (sakalīkaraṇa) upon him, regards him as identical with the deity.
Having risen and put on two clean garments,
and having sipped water and become silent, the disciple should sit in the presence of the teacher.
The supreme teacher, perceiving the oneness of those two, should worship the deity who has been transferred into the disciple with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings.

Then one should impart the knowledge to that disciplined person, preceded by the offering of water. In the *Vasiṣṭha-saṃhitā*: "Then, having placed his own hand upon the disciple's head, he should mutter [the mantra] a hundred times, or even one hundred and eight times; he should impart it preceded by the offering of water."
In the *Gautamīya*: "Having diligently deposited the network of nyāsas upon his body, the Guru, with a full mind, should whisper the mantra three times into his right ear."

100) In the *Kulāmṛta*: "One should recite the Vidyā three times into the ear, even for one who lacks knowledge. And in the *Dīpikā*: "Then the Guru should duly speak the priceless and excellent mantra, complete with its seer (*ṛṣi*) and other attributes, three times into the right ear."
Elsewhere as well: "One should recite the Vidyā three times into the right ear with a single utterance.
This is the rule for the twice-born; for women and Śūdras, it is from the left.
In another Tantra: "May it yield equal fruit for us both"—thus one should declare.
With a serene countenance, that bull among sages [spoke] to that disciple.
"The Guru should contemplate the Vidyā, consisting of light, as departing from himself;
the disciple should contemplate it as having arrived, bowing especially with the words, 'I am prostrate.
Thus [it is said]. In the Gautamīya: Having recited the mantras of Gaṇeśa and the others, the Guru should proclaim the rules (samayas)."
The bestowal of mantras such as that of Gaṇeśa occurs in the case of initiation into the Pañcāyatana system.
As stated in the Dakṣiṇāmūrtisaṃhitā:
"Having properly worshipped [the deity] near the Cakrarāja, the preceptor..."
One should fashion a beautiful name joined with the first syllable.
Having thus united oneself with the gurus among men,
one should then properly remember all the gurus preceded by a full prostration.
Having written the vidyā upon the ground, one should worship it properly with flowers and other offerings;
then, O beloved, one should show the vidyā to the disciple after it has been recited a hundred times.
If there is great devotion in the disciple who is prostrate,
then one should mutter the supreme mantra into his right ear with a single utterance.
In the *Tantrarāja*: "A disciple endowed with the aforementioned characteristics and adorned by proper conduct, purified for many days by means of the five- and six-peaked vidyās."
Having consecrated him with water-pots and seated him within the Śrīcakra,
one should contemplate the Cakra in the center, at the base, the heart, and the head.
Having invoked [the deity] from one's own heart, established [her], and worshipped her together with the ritual placement (nyāsa),
one whose mind is full and who is identical with the Goddess should recite the Vidyā three times into the ear.
One should joyfully contemplate the identity of the deity, the guru, the mantra, and one's own self as the single reality;
standing before them, one should recite the mantra a hundred times and reside in their presence for three days.
If that mobile power does not reach the Guru, there is no doubt;
therefore, one should dwell near him, performing worship, prostrations, and so forth.
In the Gautamīya: "One should dwell with devotion for three days in the presence of the Guru for the sake of accomplishment;
otherwise, there is no doubt that the splendor residing in that [disciple] will go to the Guru."

101) In the *Mantratantraprakāśa*: "A mantra that has not been received from a preceptor, or one that has been received but for which the ritual fee (*dakṣiṇā*) has not been given, will not attain accomplishment even if it is recited constantly."

Having given to the guru a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) consisting of either one's entire property or half of it, while avoiding any stinginess regarding wealth, the reception of the mantra is then considered appropriate.
In another tantra: "If one cannot give abundant cattle, land, gold, houses, fields, and so forth, then half of that, or half of that again, or even a tenth part of it."
One should give food, clothing, and so forth without distress, according to one’s wealth.
In the *Brahmasaṃhitā* it is said: "O Nārada, that which is performed without a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) is certainly in vain. Give me a lute as my fee, along with a rosary and a water-pot."
Therefore, O great sage, receive the mantra according to the prescribed rule;
for an action performed devoid of the proper rite never bestows success.

In the Gautamīya: One intent on devotion should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the guru, either half of one's wealth, or half of that, or whatever one can afford according to one's capacity and with devotion.
One should not practice stinginess regarding wealth, for such a deed brings about misfortune;
one should then present cows, land, gold, clothing, and so forth to the preceptor.
One should give garments and ornaments, as well as desired food according to one's inclination and ability, to the son of the guru, his wife, and his disciple.
One should give sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) to the officiating priests, accompanied by garments and ornaments.

As stated in the *Brahmasaṃhitā*: "Having performed the purification of the *praṇītā* vessel, one should give the fee for the Brahman priest according to one's own means, free from greed and delusion."
Then, having dismissed Brahmā, one should feed the Brāhmaṇas;
being consecrated by the words of blessing from the learned, one shall become happy.
Then, having consumed the remnant of the oblation (hutaśeṣa) in a quantity the size of a hen's egg,
which has been consecrated with the Gāyatrī mantra—
thus it is said in the Vāyavīyasaṃhitā.
One should present the pavilion, along with the sacrificial implements, to the preceptor.
In the *Nārāyaṇīya* and the *Mahākapila-pañcarātra*:
"Having imparted the mantra, the instructor should indeed recite it a thousand times for his own spiritual accomplishment."
Elsewhere it is also stated: "One should recite [the mantra] one thousand and eight times in order to avoid the loss of one's own power.
In the *Kulāmṛta*: "One should instruct the disciple, who has prostrated like a staff, in all the rules of conduct.
In another Tantra: "Bathing, the twilight rituals (*sandhyā*), right conduct, as well as the obligatory and the optional [rites]."
The teacher should also explain to the disciple the various modes of attaining success through mantras.

The conduct regarding the observances (*samayācāra*) will now be explained. On the day of initiation (*dīkṣā*), fasting is prohibited. As it is said in the *Yoginītantra*: "If a teacher, having imparted the mantra, should practice fasting, he becomes a worm in the hell of Great Darkness; it is not otherwise."
When the mantra-practitioner, having bestowed initiation, observes a fast,
the deity always becomes enraged and, having uttered a curse, departs for his own city.
Now, regarding the specific procedure for the Vīradīkṣā: there,

having performed the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi), the placement of the Mātṛkās (mātṛkānyāsa), the sixfold placement (ṣoḍhānyāsa), and so forth, upon both his own body and the body of the Śakti, the Guru shall perform the installation of the water-pot (kalaśa) and the installation of the Śrīpātra and other vessels.
Having produced and consecrated the substances arising from the *kuṇḍa* and *goḷa* according to the sequence of the *dūtī-yāga*,

and having performed the consecration even of fish, meat, and so forth, one worships the deities according to the sequence of the *vīra-pūjā* to be described; then, at the time of imparting the mantra to the disciple—
O Maheśānī, O Kuleśvarī, having placed the vessel in the hand of the disciple—
this being the *vīrapātra* as described in the *Vīracūḍāmaṇi*:
"Drink this pure nectar, the medicine for existence."
This cause for the total severance of the bonds of the individual soul was proclaimed by Bhairava.

Thus, with the mantra spoken in the *Kulārṇava*, the teacher should place [the substance] in the hand of the disciple. The disciple, likewise with this same mantra, having recited "I drink" (*pibāmi*) in place of "let it be drunk" (*pīyatām*), should drink with the mantra to be mentioned later, beginning with "The oblation of dharma and adharma is kindled... Then the teacher should impart the mantra. Regarding that:

In the *Yāmala*: Having written this [mantra] together with its seer (*ṛṣi*) and other [limbs], and having placed it within the ground, one should worship it thoroughly with flowers and other offerings, and then show it to the disciple.
If there is great affection for the disciple, then the Guru should speak it into his ear;
even more so if the disciple is an object of the Guru's exceeding love.
Then the most excellent guru should indeed give it to her with a mouthful of water;
even if the disciple is free from conceptual constructs, he should receive it with a joyful mind.
In the absence of that, there would be no accomplishment and one would incur the curse of the deity.
As stated in the Dakṣiṇāmūrtisaṃhitā:
"One should sprinkle the auspicious [object] three times with sprouts placed within the water-pot."
When he has been consecrated, then he becomes the foremost of teachers.
When joined with the reality of the mouthful (gaṇḍūṣa-tattva), then this person is worthy of the worship of Śiva;
otherwise, O Pārvatī, there can be no accomplishment for one who possesses conceptual construction (savikalpa). 103)
If a doubt arises in the disciple regarding the offering of the mouthful of water (gaṇḍūṣa), he shall have no accomplishment anywhere; even Śrīvidyā turns her face away from him.
The remainder is the same as the initiation for animal sacrifice (*paśu-dīkṣā*). Now, regarding the specific details of the *tārā-dīkṣā*, the *Nīlatantra* states:
"One should perform one thousand and eight oblations with *vilva* leaves;
or else, one should perform one hundred and eight, or even twenty-eight."
One should offer milk-rice (pāyasa), rice mixed with sesame (kṛsara), sweetmeats (modaka), and candied sugar;
having presented the sacrificial offering (bali) consisting of goat meat and the most excellent meat of the monitor lizard (godhā),
one should diligently offer plantain flowers and the śāla fish.
Then, having offered barley-milk and rice mixed with honey,
one should gratify one's own guru with gifts such as cows, land, gold, and clothing.
In the Cāmuṇḍā Tantra:
"In all the secondary sciences (upavidyās), in the accomplishment of the six rites (ṣatkarma) and so forth,
there is no requirement for initiation here, nor is there the worship of the limbs (aṅgas) and other such [auxiliaries]."

Secondary sciences (*upavidyā*) include *yakṣiṇī* and so forth; they are the mantras for accomplishing the six rites (*ṣatkarma*) and the like, such as the specific mantras used for subjugation (*vaśya*) and other purposes in the application of the *Kālikā-mantra*. Now, [it may be asked]:
"O beautiful one, by whomsoever a mantra written in a book is recited..."
Success does not arise for him; rather, there is only loss at every step.
All rites performed under the guidance of the preceptor bestow the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
for it is certain that all rites not instructed by the preceptor are fruitless.
If it is asked, "How can this be so, given various statements such as these?"—it is not so;

for even though initiation preceded by the selection of a *kuṇḍa*, a pavilion, and a preceptor (*ācārya*), as well as the *homa* sacrifice and other rites, is prohibited, the prohibition does not extend to the oral instruction (*upadeśa*). As stated in another Tantra:
When the moon or sun is eclipsed, at a sacred ford (tīrtha), in a field of accomplishment (siddhikṣetra), or in a temple of Śiva—
the mere recitation of the mantra is called "instruction" (upadeśa).

Because, by such statements as these, even instruction [by a teacher] is prescribed. Nor should it be argued that knowledge of the mantra derived even from a book produces success, on the basis of the statement: "Having learned the mantra either from the scripture or from the mouth of the guru, one should accomplish it."

In this regard, because the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) for both [the ritual and the mantra] is prescribed by the scripture, the term "mantra" is construed with the word "should accomplish" (*prasādhayet*).
Thus ends the rule for initiation involving ritual action (*kriyāvatī-dīkṣā-vidhi*).

104) Now, regarding initiation consisting of phonemes (*varṇamayī-dīkṣā*): if one is unable to perform this, any one of the initiations beginning with that consisting of phonemes should be administered. Among these, initiation consisting of phonemes is as described in the *Śāradā*:
Now I shall describe the initiation consisting of phonemes (varṇa), as known from the Āgamas.
Phonemes consist of the Puruṣa and Prakṛti; the body is likewise of that same nature.
Therefore, the preceptor should project the phonemes upon the body of the disciple;
he should then withdraw those phonemes, joined with their respective locations, in reverse order.

Then, by his own command, through the deity-state and according to the prescribed rite, the supreme teacher causes this disciple— whose constituent principles have dissolved— to become possessed of a divine body.
Having united that consciousness with the Supreme Self, the supreme guru should then bring forth those phonemes from it and install them once more within the body of the disciple.
One should duly apply consciousness according to the sequence of emanation;
thus the child arises, possessing the nature of the deity and consisting of supreme bliss.
This initiation consisting of the phonemes (varṇa), which bestows consciousness, has been described.
Thus concludes the procedure for initiation consisting of the phonemes (*varṇamayī dīkṣā*).
Now, regarding the *kalāvatī* [initiation] in that very same context: "Thereafter, the *kalāvatī* initiation is described according to the rule."
The five kalās, beginning with Nivṛtti, are the powers from which the elements arise.
Therefore, having visualized them within the body composed of the elements, one should pierce those [channels] of the disciple;
Nivṛtti is situated starting from the soles up to the knees.
The *pratiṣṭhā* [kalā] abides pervading from the knees up to the navel;
the *vidyā* [kalā] extends from the navel to the throat, and beyond that is the *śānti* [kalā].
Pervading from the throat up to the forehead, and from there up to the crown of the head, the Śāntyatītā level is to be known; thus is described the pervasion of the Kalās.
By means of the yoga of the process of withdrawal, the wise Guru, having joined [the disciple] from one station to another,
should pierce those [channels] by command up to the level of Śiva.
This is declared to be the initiation of the *kalā*, which bestows a divine state of being.
Thus ends the ritual procedure for the initiation of Kalāvatī.

Now, regarding the initiation consisting of piercing (*vedha*) in that very same context: "Thereafter, I shall describe the initiation consisting of piercing, which liberates one from transmigratory existence."
One should meditate within the body of the disciple, at the four-petalled mūlādhāra.
105) In the center of the triangle, which is stainless and expanded by the threefold radiance,
[one should meditate on her] endowed with three coils and possessing a splendor equal to ten million flashes of lightning.
Having swiftly pierced the six cakras, one reaches the Goddess who consists of Śiva and Śakti, whose form is pure consciousness alone, the subtle and most subtle Power.
As she proceeds through the central path toward the divine Supreme Śiva,
one should withdraw the phonemes situated in the petals from *va* to *sa* into the Lotus-Seated One.
Having joined that [consciousness] within the Svādhiṣṭhāna, which consists of a six-petalled lotus endowed with the letters from va to la, the Guru should pierce it by means of the Command (ājñā).
The Guru should dissolve those phonemes into Viṣṇu, and then join him into the navel-lotus,
which has ten petals and is enriched with the phonemes from *ḍa* to *pha*.
The Guru should withdraw those phonemes into Rudra, and then, having joined him into the heart-lotus—
which is enriched by the twelve solar phonemes from *ka* to *ṭha*— he should unite him with Īśvara.
One should withdraw those phonemes into this [heart], and then again join them to that [lotus] in the throat, which is rich in vowels and possesses sixteen petals, by once more applying the vowels.
Having withdrawn them into Sadāśiva, the Guru then joins him once more within the two-petaled [lotus] between the eyebrows, which is white and marked with the syllables *ha* and *kṣa*.
The Guru should dissolve those two vowels into the Bindu, join that [Bindu] into the Kalā,
then join that [Kalā] into the Nāda, and subsequently join the Nāda into the end of the Nāda (nādānta).
Having joined that [power] into Unmanī and then into the interior of Viṣṇu’s mouth,
the best of teachers should join it again into the mouth of the Guru.
Together with his own self, he should pierce the power into the supreme Śiva;
then, by the command of the Guru, the disciple—his bonds severed—shall fall to the earth.
Having attained divine awakening, he finds everything at that very moment;
he becomes Śiva manifest—there is no need for deliberation on this point.
This initiation consisting of piercing (vedha) has been described as bestowing pure consciousness.
Thus ends the procedure for the initiation consisting of piercing;
now follow the varieties of the individual (āṇava) initiation.

In the *Ṣaḍanvayamahāratna*, it is recited by the learned who are experts in the scriptures: "The initiation pertaining to Āṇava is manifold, while that pertaining to Śakti and Śambhu is, moreover, only one."
Having stated that the *āṇavī* [power] is manifold, its divisions are now described:
it is the *smārtī*, the *mānasikī*, the *yaugī*, the *cākṣuṣī*, and likewise the *spārśanī*. (106)
The consecration (abhiṣecikī) is of four kinds: vocal, mantra-based, sacrificial (hotrī), and scriptural (śāstrī).
Now, regarding the traditional (smārtī) initiation: the Guru, having remembered the disciple who resides in a foreign land, [severs] the three bonds (pāśatraya) in succession.
By means of the procedure for the dissolution and enjoyment of the latent impressions, [the soul] is properly united with the supreme Śiva;
this is called the "Smārta initiation" (smārtī dīkṣā).
Now, as for mental initiation (mānasī dīkṣā):
having perceived one who is seated in his presence and pure in mind,
that which liberates from the three impurities by means of specific methods is indeed mental initiation.

Then, having entered the body of the disciple according to the sequence prescribed for yoga, the yogin takes hold of that disciple's self and performs the act of union with his own self; this is the initiation of yoga.
That is declared to be the initiation of yoga (yogadīkṣā), which destroys the three impurities.
Now, the initiation of the eye consists of gazing with eyes moistened by compassion, having resolved: "I am Śiva."
That visual initiation (*cākṣuṣī dīkṣā*) destroys all sins.
Now, as for the initiation by touch (*sparśadīkṣā*),
the Guru, having himself become Supreme Śiva, with a mind free from doubt—
One should touch the head of the disciple with the hand of Śiva while reciting the mantra;
that is called the initiation by touch (sparśadīkṣā), which effects the manifestation of Śiva.
Alternatively, the vocal initiation consists of the guru, with due reverence, visualizing his own mouth as the mouth of the disciple,
and [transmitting] divine mantras and so forth into the disciple by means of the application of the guru’s mouth.
Together with the placement of mudrās and so forth, one should perform this, for it is indeed the vocal initiation (vācikī-dīkṣā).
Now follows the mantra initiation (māntrī-dīkṣā),
and likewise the supreme initiation (parā-dīkṣā), wherein the body is conjoined with the placement of mantras.

Having oneself become the embodiment of the mantra, one should respectfully bestow the mantra along with its ritual procedure upon the disciple; that is the Mantra-initiation, which destroys impurities.

107) Now, regarding the Hotrī initiation known as the "Hand of Śiva": one should fashion a mandala with perfumes upon one's own right hand. One should worship the Lord there according to the prescribed rite; in this manner, it becomes the "Hand of Śiva."
The meaning is: "in the manner taught by Somaśambhu.

Having deposited the fire into either the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) or upon the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) according to the prescribed rule, one should proceed through each path (*adhvan*) in due order, following the sequence of the yoga of dissolution (*layayoga*).
One should perform oblations for the sake of purification into the very levels of mantra, varṇa, kalā, tattva, pada, and viṣṭapa; this is declared to be the initiation of the Hotṛ priest.

Now, when the teacher bestows the scripture along with the three Vedas upon a disciple who is worthy of initiation, devoted, and intent on service and worship, that is called "scriptural initiation" (śāstrī-dīkṣā).
Now, regarding the consecratory initiation (abhiṣecikī-dīkṣā):
having reverently worshipped Śiva and the consort of Śiva in the ritual pitcher (kumbha),
that initiation becomes consecratory through the consecration from the Śiva-pitcher.

"By means of the sequence of *layayoga*" means by means of the sequence of the initiation of piercing (*vedhadīkṣā*), in the form of the withdrawal of the deities of the phonemes presiding over the *mūlādhāra*.
Now follows the full consecration (*pūrṇābhiṣeka*).
In the *Sārasaṃgraha*: "I shall describe the full consecration (*pūrṇābhiṣeka*), which brings auspiciousness to practitioners;
without which consecration, a practitioner cannot attain the state of perfect awakening."
He does not attain the status of a teacher nor the desired higher state;
therefore, the guru, having instructed his beloved disciple, should perform the consecration.
Having fashioned a vast and exceedingly beautiful wheel within the pavilion,
one should place a jar filled with a khārī measure of water in the center of the wheel.
There, upon other petals, various water-pots provided with cloth and gold should be placed; having invoked the chosen deity there, one should worship it.
Having worshipped the deities of the limbs and the surrounding retinue both in the center and at the extremities,
one should perform the consecration for the disciple under his birth asterism, as previously described, with those [deities].
In the *Triśaktiratna*: "Having worshipped with various offerings, one should perform a thousand oblations in a pure fire."
The Guru should consecrate the disciple and himself bestow a name upon him;
this is known as the Full Consecration (pūrṇābhiṣeka), which confers the status of an Ācārya.

108) In the *Sārasaṃgraha*: "This is the full consecration (*pūrṇābhiṣeka*), which grants the desired accomplishments of the practitioner. Regarding the definition of a *khārī*, the *Skandapurāṇa* states:
"Two *palas* make a *prasṛti*; a *kuḍava* is considered to be double that [i.e., two *prasṛtis*]."
Four *kuḍavas* make one *prastha*, and an *āḍhaka* consists of four times that amount.
Four guṇas make one droṇa; two of those are known as a kumbha.
Eight of those kumbhas make a khārī.
And this full initiation (pūrṇābhiṣeka) is essential for the Kaulikas;
for if a Kaulika dies while deprived of the full initiation, [he suffers].
"He attains the state of a *piśāca* until the dissolution of all beings (*yāvadābhūtasaṃplavam*)," according to the statement in the *Kulārṇava*. [Such a one is] a *kaulika* hero.
Thus is the *pūrṇābhiṣeka*.
Now, regarding the procedure for the purification of mantras,
it is stated in the *Tantraśekhara*: "Those mantras which are proclaimed to be defiled by defects such as being 'cut' (chinnā) and so forth do not yield fruit, even when constantly practiced."
Therefore, listen as we describe the purificatory rites for the destruction of those defects:
the practitioner, having divided the triangle into seven equal parts, [should proceed].
One should likewise proceed from the northeast corner and similarly from the southeast corner;
thus, there shall be forty-nine yonis there on all sides.
The practitioner of mantra should write the letters in sequence from Īśāna to Varuṇa;
having worshipped the Goddess here, he should then extract the mantras.
This is called "generating" (janana), and it is also termed "kindling" (dīpana).
Having encased [the mantra] with the *hasa* mantra, one should recite the mantra one thousand times.
This is declared to be the "illumination" (dīpana); now the "awakening" (bodhana) is described.
One should recite the mantra encased within the armor-syllable (vam) joined with the letter 'ra'.
This awakening is prescribed to be performed five thousand times;
the wise practitioner should recite the mantra encapsulated by the *astra* [mantra] one thousand times.
This is declared to be the striking; now the consecration (abhiṣeka) is described:
the mantra-practitioner should recite the mantra over the water one thousand times using the syllables *vāk*, *haṃsa*, and *praṇava*.
Reciting this mantra, one should consecrate the mantra with auspicious waters;
meanwhile, it should be encapsulated by the mantra "sroṃ" at the beginning and ending with "vaṣaṭ."
109) One should recite this mantra a thousand times for the purpose of purification;
the wise one should recite the mantra enclosed within the *svadhā* and *śikhā* [syllables] a thousand times.
This is declared to be the "living" (jīvana) libation with water mixed with milk and clarified butter;
it is known as the "satisfying" (tarpaṇa) libation, while the mantra is encapsulated by Māyā.
Recited five thousand times, that is called concealment (*gopana*).
However, in the *Gautamīya*, it says: "In the case of the Śakti-mantra, with honey; and in the Vaiṣṇava, with water mixed with moon-juice (*soma*)."
In the Śaiva tradition, the satiation with clarified butter has been correctly prescribed by the masters of mantra.

Likewise: "One should recite the mantra encapsulated between the white *candra* (the letter *sa*) and the *anugraha* (the letter *i*), which is the moon (*u*). This is declared as *āpyāyana* (nourishment) by those learned in the science of mantra.
The ten consecrations (saṃskāras) for mantras have been declared there as enjoined; however,
the ten consecrations described in other ways in the *Śāradātilaka* and other texts should be investigated in those very sources.
Now, the procedure for abandoning hostile mantras:
next, the procedure for the abandonment of mantras that yield undesirable results is stated. In the Tantra:
"Now, the procedure for the complete abandonment of hostile mantras is clearly explained."
The term "inauspicious" (arī) is an elliptical expression (upalakṣaṇa) to be understood as "yielding undesirable results. Likewise:
"Having become pure and composed, on an auspicious day, the preceptor should commence the excellent rite for the destruction of all suffering."
There, first, in a beautiful hall, the wise one should place the water-pot upon the mandala according to the sequence of the initiation rite, and fill it with auspicious waters.

Having performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa and worshipped [the deity], one should worship the surrounding deities (āvaraṇas). Thus, having worshipped the deity of the mantra along with its attendants, the twice-born practitioner of mantra should offer oblations of clarified butter, even from a cow, using the mantra in reverse order.
The wise person should likewise satisfy the Lord with one thousand and eight, or one hundred and eight [offerings],
using the mantra "brahmārpaṇam" at the end.
Then, one should offer the bali-oblation to the deities with milk-rice as prescribed,
in the intermediate directions and the cardinal directions, using the supreme mantras that will be described hereafter.
Come, O Indra, Lord of the Suras, Śatamanyu, Lord of Śacī!
Salutations to you; accept this offering of flowers, incense, and other oblations.
Come, O Lord of splendors, O bearer of oblations, O bestower of boons!
Accept this well-worshiped offering of flowers, incense, and other gifts.
110) O King of Pretas, come hither, you who possess a luster like that of crushed collyrium! Having accepted this offered oblation, be well-pleased and become a granter of boons.
Salutations to you, O Lord of the Rakshasas, Nirṛti; you have come here.
Accept this offering, worship, and other gifts presented by me with devotion.
Come, O Guardian of the Western Quarter, Lord of the Waters; salutations to you!
Accepting this worship offered with devotion, may you attain satisfaction.
O Wind, Lord of Life, come here with your retinue;
accept with respect this offering presented by me according to the prescribed rite.
May Kubera and the Lord of the Stars, the two best of gods, come here;
may they, being pleased by flowers, incense, and other offerings, become granters of boons to me.
O Lord, O Blessed One, you alone are the sovereign power that is the refuge of all sciences;
worshipped with flowers, incense, and other offerings, be pleased for the sake of our prosperity.
Come, O Lord of all worlds, O Brahmā; accept this worship and turn back all my obstacles. Homage be to you!
Come, O bestower of boons, unmanifest Viṣṇu, leader of the universe;
worshipped with supreme devotion, may you be the giver of happiness to me.
Then, one should worship the deity of the mantra along with his retinue using flowers, lamps, and offerings, employing the mantra in reverse order. Thereafter,
the wise practitioner should offer a prayer to the worshipped deity of the mantra.
Without considering what was favorable, I, with my fickle intellect, [acted].
O Lord, by that very nature of the mantra which has been received and honored,
dispel entirely the agitation of my mind.
May evil be warded off, and may there be eternal well-being;
may your purifying devotion alone extend auspiciousness to me.
Having thus offered this prayer, one should write the mantra in reverse order upon a leaf and worship it with *amalaka*, camphor, and sandalwood.
Having placed it upon the water-pot with supreme devotion,
the wise man should then bind that leaf to his own head.
One should bathe with the auspicious waters contained in the consecrated pitcher, which are permeated by mantras;
then, having restrained oneself, one should fill the pitcher again with other water.
111) Having placed the mantra-leaf within it,
one should then worship that pitcher on the bank of a river or in another pure body of water.
Then one should cast [the mantra] into the Brahmins and feed them according to one's capacity;
for one who has performed the rite in this manner, the afflictions arising from the enemy's mantras shall cease.
They perish indeed, there is no doubt; gradually, clarity of mind arises, and that family, becoming exceedingly prosperous, prospers in due course.
Thus ends the third wave in the *Tārābhaktisudhārṇava* composed by the Great Professor, the illustrious Ṭhakkura Narasiṃha.
The Fourth Wave: Now, regarding devotion to the Guru, it is said in the *Kulārṇava*: [Devotion is due] toward Nārāyaṇa, Mahādeva, one's mother and father, and the king.
O Goddess, one should act toward one's own guru in such a way that devotion arises.
Likewise: A disciple residing in the same village should prostrate to the guru at the three junctions of the day;
even one residing a *krośa* away should bow to the guru every day.
A disciple who travels half a *yojana* should prostrate on the five festival days (*parvan*),
starting from one *yojana* up to twelve *yojanas*.
Having traveled for as many months as there are *yojanas* [between him and the teacher], he should bow to the guru;
when the disciple is situated very far away, he should go only when there is a desire [to do so].
One should not approach a king, a deity, or a teacher with empty hands;
one should offer fruits, flowers, garments, and so forth, according to one's ability.
Likewise: "One should not perform penance in the presence of the Guru, nor bathe for one's own personal satisfaction;
one should not give orders to the Guru, nor address him with the word 'you'."
Likewise: "Having become a disciple, one should never, at any time, engage in lending or borrowing money, nor in the buying or selling of goods, together with one's gurus."
O Ambikā, he who worships another while the Guru is present goes to a terrible hell; that worship becomes fruitless.
If there is a desire for a particular object on the part of the guru, one should not experience it oneself;
however, if there is a necessity, one may experience it only by his command.
O beloved, he who takes even a very small amount of a guru’s property that was not given to him enters the womb of a beast and is devoured by carnivorous creatures.
One who covets the property of a guru and is eager to have sexual intercourse with the guru’s wife becomes fallen;
of this there is no doubt, and no atonement exists for such an act.
He who obstructs the position of the guru, the tradition, or its dharma, is to be expelled by the gurus; that sinner is to be punished and pierced [with arrows].
Upon seeing the sandals, seat, garment, vehicle, umbrella, or fly-whisk of the Guru, one should prostrate; one must not employ them for one's own enjoyment.
113) Regarding tasks both mentioned and unmentioned, one should not allow indifference toward what is pleasing;
whatever the guru says, whether it be good or bad, that should be carried out without hesitation.
Even after committing a hundred murders of Brahmins, one should fulfill the command of the Guru;
O Goddess, one must not sit upon a seat in the presence of the deity or the Guru.
Whether one is distinguished by birth, learning, or wealth, upon seeing the Guru from afar,
one should joyfully perform a single prostration like a staff and circumambulate him three times.
Likewise: "But when there is a connection between the Guru and his own Guru, O Dear One, one should salute the *praguru* (the higher teacher);
then one should bow to the Guru, and that [higher teacher] shall not disregard the Guru's command."

In the presence of the preceptor’s preceptor, the disciple should bow mentally to his own guru. One should never abandon the venerable guru; rather, O beloved, one should proceed only when commanded by him.
When the guru is seated below, one should never stand above him;
one should not walk in front of them, nor stand when the guru has risen.

"He should remain standing"— the word "seated" is understood as the ellipsis. Wherever there may be censure of the venerable Guru, one should cover one's own ears and immediately depart from that place to a distance, so as not to hear it.
Afterwards, one should recite the name of the Guru; that is the remedy for hearing [the teaching].
One should not show contempt toward the Guru’s friends, well-wishers, female servants, male servants, and so forth.
The Guru’s consort and his eldest son are equal to the Guru;
the younger sons are like one's own self, and the protectors of the lineage are like one's own children.
The word "ascetic practice" (*tapacaryā*) is to be understood as the remainder [of the sentence].
Now, regarding the conduct of the observance (*samayācāra*), the *Bhairavatantra* states: "In the Great Cīna tradition alone, Tārā bestows results swiftly."
And by the very sequence known as the Gandharva, the fifth [state] is indeed difficult to attain.
By the very method of Mahānīla, Kālikā bestows the fruit;
likewise, by the very method of Mahācīna, the rite of Chinnamastā is prescribed.
In the Kālītantra: "By the very method of Mahācīna, Tārā bestows the fruit of swift success."

Mahācīna is a specific region abounding in Buddhists. Its procedure is stated in the *Sārasaṃgraha*: "Bathing and so forth, mental purification, worship, and libations—all these are auspicious; no inauspicious time exists anywhere."
114) There is no distinction between day and night, nor between twilight and the night;
one should always worship the Goddess, even while unwashed and after having eaten.
At midnight, one should cause an offering to be presented with the mantra in a pure place;
one must never harbor hatred toward women, and especially should women be honored.
Having placed a large conch shell at the place of recitation, one should perform the recitation while moving above it;
even while approaching, touching, or looking at a woman, or wherever else one may be, provided one is not uncircumcised.
Eating betel-leaf and other auspicious substances according to his desire,
as well as fish, meat, honey, milk, vegetables, and sugarcane products.
Having offered all substances with devotion and having partaken [of them], one should perform the recitation;
here there is no restriction regarding direction or place, nor any restriction regarding posture and so forth.
There is no restriction regarding time for recitation, nor for worship and the like, nor even for the offerings;
here, in the practice of the Great Mantra, it is said that one may follow one's own will.
In that state, neither unrighteousness arises nor does righteousness arise;
here, conduct according to one's own will is prescribed, and one should proceed with a joyful mind.
Considering his purpose accomplished and having satisfied his own mind,
one should know that whatever practice is prescribed for a particular mantra, such is the dharma therein.
By that [means], one becomes one who has accomplished the goal— whether it be heaven or even liberation.
In the Svacchandabhairavatantra, rituals such as purification and the like, as enjoined by the Smṛti scriptures, are not to be performed.
One [application] on the penis, three on the anus, and so forth, as they have been proclaimed.
Those [practices] should not be performed by the best of practitioners if they desire long life.
In the *Yāmala*: "Now I shall proclaim the conduct (*ācāra*) by means of which one partakes of the nectar of immortality;
[the practitioner] should be devoted to the welfare of all beings and a protector of the rules of conduct (*samayācāra*)."
One who has abandoned impermanent actions and is intent upon eternal practice,
offering all actions to the Supreme Deity.

The word "syāt" (might be) is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence]. Regarding the phrase "impermanent action," and so forth: one who desires liberation should not perform any action out of desire.

Being devoted to obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) duties, and contemplating, "By the propitiation of the mantra alone, my welfare shall come to pass," one should dedicate the performed action to the deity; such is the meaning of the entire passage.
Devotion to the worship of another mantra, the veneration of another mantra,
the reviling of a woman of the *kula* or a hero (*vīra*), and the theft of their substances.
115) A wise person should always avoid anger and physical assault toward women;
for the entire world consists of women, and one should oneself likewise become so.

One who strives with a disciplined mind should contemplate all things— the drinkable, the chewable, the suckable, the edible, and the lickable— as well as the home, happiness, and the form of young women.
Upon seeing a young woman of noble birth, one should offer salutation with a concentrated mind,
provided that such a sight of a noble family occurs through the power of one's fortune.
At that very time, one should perform mental worship of them—
whether they be young girls, those intoxicated with youth, or likewise beautiful old women.
Or, having paid homage to one who is contemptible or greatly wicked, one should meditate upon them;
likewise, one should contemplate their blows, their abuse, their crookedness, and their unpleasantness.
Under no circumstances should this be done otherwise, for it would obstruct success.
Women are the gods; women are the life-breaths; women alone are the ornament.
One should always remain attached to women, even if it means being attached to one's own wife;
for flowers gathered by their hands and water offered by their hands [are the proper offerings].
One should offer food prepared by his own hand to the deities;
even for a hundred offenses, one should not strike a woman, even with a flower.
A wise person should not enumerate faults, but should manifest only virtues.
In the Rudrayāmala: "O Goddess, if by chance one sees a woman sleeping, a guru sleeping, an elder sleeping, or naked persons, the wise man should perform the Śrīcakra."
The term "asleep" is an elliptical expression; it means that one should not look upon these [initiates] while they are naked due to a lack of attention.
In the *Kulārṇava*: "O Goddess of the Gods, one should not give the sandals of the venerable Guru, the mudrā, the root-mantra, or the sandals to anyone other than a disciple."
O Dear One, the lineage tradition, the oral transmission, the mantra, the tantra, and so forth—
all of these become fruitful only when obtained from the mouth of the Guru, and not otherwise.
O Pārvatī, one should practice the Kula scriptures as if they were one's own wife;
one should avoid all Paśu scriptures as if they were another's wife.
Just as milk placed in a dog’s hide is not to be drunk by the best of the twice-born,
so too the breath blown from the mouth of a beast is not to be heard by the Kaulikas.
Likewise: raw meat, a jar of liquor, an intoxicated elephant, a perfected ascetic, a mango tree, an aśoka tree, and young maidens eager for play.
116) Upon seeing a solitary tree, a cemetery, a gathering of women, or a woman dressed in red garments, one should pay homage with devotion.
The gurus, the powers (śaktis), the sons, the elder and younger brothers, the family preceptors, the scriptures of the Kula system, the Kula substances, and the Kaulikas.
O Yogī, [I see] those who incite, those who indicate, as well as those who speak,
those who show, teachers, enlighteners, and yogīs, yoginīs, and perfected beings (siddhapuruṣas).
One should not criticize, loathe, laugh at, or insult girls, young maidens, naked women, those who are insane, or those with exposed breasts.
One should not speak untruth or anything unpleasant to any member of a Kulayogin family;
nor should one call a Kulayogini "ugly" or "black."
One should not look at a woman who has fallen from her status, one who is naked, one who is insane, or one whose breasts are exposed;
one should not consort with a woman during the day, nor should one gaze upon her private parts.
Whatever woman there may be in the world, she is born from the maternal lineage;
the family yoginīs become enraged by the transgression against women.
In the Rudrayāmala: "One who drinks a substance that has not been consecrated, engages in sexual intercourse by force, or kills an animal with one's own hand, shall go to the Raurava hell."
In the Kulārṇava: "A Kaula should avoid these five: performing penance, falling from a cliff, renunciation, observing ascetic vows, and undertaking pilgrimages."
Killing a hero, drinking intoxicants in vain, stealing the property of a hero,
sexual intercourse with the wife of a hero, and association with those who commit these acts— this is the fifth [grave sin].
What is called a "mahāpātaka" (great sin) in the Kula lineage of the Kaulikas has a distinct expiation prescribed in the Tantras; likewise, the observance of vows is also [different].
Visiting sacred fords (*tīrthayātrā*) is according to the Smārta method, because visiting the *pīṭhas* is ordained in the Tantras.

And approaching the wife of a hero is not forbidden if it is with the consent of her husband. O Goddess of the Gods, the merit of one who gives his sister, daughter, or wife to a kula-yogin who is intoxicated with honey-wine cannot be calculated.
Thus, from the words of the *Kulārṇava*:
"One who regards the Guru as a mere human being, the mantra as a mere string of syllables,
and the icons as mere stone shall go to hell."
When both previous faults are present, this abandonment of both results in an even greater fault:
"O Dear One, whatever action one performs while possessed by doubts—such as austerity, worship, and so forth—even if it involves excrement, urine, or food leavings—all of that becomes impure. (117)
Likewise: "Desiring to enter the abode of the Guru, with a tranquil mind and great devotion, [he should offer] a fan, sandals, an umbrella, clothing, a vehicle, and so forth."
Having discarded betel, collyrium, and [ostentatious] dress, she should enter slowly;
[she should perform] the washing of the feet, bathing, anointing with oil, and the cleaning of the teeth.
Urine, spitting, shaving, lying down, indulgence with women,
the vīrāsana posture, harsh speech, excessive laughter, and wringing the limbs.
O beloved, [one should avoid] loosening the hair, wearing a turban, wearing a bodice, as well as nakedness, stretching out the feet, debate, quarreling, and finding fault.
O Ambikā, [these include] the breaking of limbs and members, the clapping and shaking of hands,
gambling, and the fighting of cocks, rams, and so forth.

One should not practice [prohibited acts] in the presence of the Guru, a Yoginī, a Great Siddha, a Pīṭha, a Kṣetra, an Āśrama, and so forth; for by practicing out of delusion, one incurs the curse of the deity.
In the Kali age— O Īśāna, how can one who is my devotee become a Kaulika without wandering at night and worshipping the Śakti at night?
In the *Kulāmṛtadīpikā*:
"One should never look upon the naked Śakti except at the time of worship;
indeed, she should not be approached by practitioners except at the time of worship."
And this practice must always be kept secret. For it is said in the Kulārṇava:
"The Vedas, Śāstras, and Purāṇas are as public as courtesans;
but this Śāmbhavī Vidyā is as secret as a woman of noble family."
The deities favor those who maintain the well-guarded Kaulika conduct;
they grant the fulfillment of desires, but destroy [the practitioner] through disclosure.
In the *Kūlacūḍāmaṇi*: "O lady of virtuous vows, the practice of the Kula known as the Right-hand path has been told to you;
it must not be spoken of to anyone if one desires one's own welfare."
The flower of the family, the substance of the family, the worship of the family, the recitation of the family,
the Guru who is the lord of the family, the rosary of the family, and that which is both family and non-family.
One should never reveal the family-circle (kulacakra) or the family-meditation (kuladhyāna);
from revealing them, there would be a loss of accomplishment (siddhi), and from revealing them, there would be bondage and the like.
From disclosure there would be loss of strength; from disclosure there is injury to the gods;
(118) from disclosure there may be the attainment of death; therefore, it should never be disclosed.
O Maheśānī, if anyone should enter here at the time of worship, [the rite is disrupted].
One should indeed display the Vaiṣṇava mudrā and perform the Nyāsa of Viṣṇu according to the hymn.
At times there may be a loss of limbs, yet never a manifestation;
furthermore, no worship should be performed, nor ever a manifestation.
Internally Śākta, externally Śaiva, and in the assembly considered Vaiṣṇava—
heroes assuming various forms wander upon the surface of the earth.
In the *Phetkāriṇītantra*, in the *Śrītārākalpa*:
"One should always conceal this mantra as well as the guru;
by that, the vidyā becomes powerful, but it becomes powerless through disclosure."
In the Tantra: One should not sit on the great riverbank, nor sleep in the midst of darkness;
one should not revile the circle of Yoginīs, nor should one revile the fair-eyed woman.
One should perform the ash-bath (bhasmasnāna) and likewise gaze [upon the deity] with devotion;
one should worship the yantra, which is marked with vajra-flowers, using vajra-flowers.
Especially at the time of worship, one should not remember the name of Hari;
setting aside other perfumes, one should use sandalwood and red sandalwood.
One should worship with red flowers and also worship with bilva leaves;
one should not worship with tulasī, mālatī, dhātrī, or maruvaka.
O Goddess of the Gods, even without the *śakti*, recitation, fire-offerings, libations,
meditation, worship, and all such practices lead only to the obstruction of spiritual accomplishment (*siddhi*).
O Maheśānī, when one watch of the night has passed, one should set aside other substances and perform the worship of the Vīras using substances such as Ṣaṣṭhī flowers.
One should not observe a fast, nor perform any other vow;
having constructed a pavilion according to the rules, with blue banners and a blue archway.
O Goddess, one should construct a triangular sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) marked with the *nāgaśūla*.
Now, regarding the dispositions (*bhāva*),
in the *Bhāvacūḍāmaṇi*, the Goddess said:
O Mahādeva, the state of the Hero (vīrabhāva) is described; listen, O Bhairava!
Having made the mind free from dualities, one whose body is the form of the Kāmakalā within the heart [should practice].
119) Indeed, worship performed at night is always the most excellent and is endowed with its proper cause;
for, having established one's own lineage, one assumes the form of Bhairava oneself.
And having performed the extensive placement (*nyāsa*) upon its limbs of the *kula* in the form of Bhairavī,
as well as the entire placement consisting of the nine wombs (*navayoni*).
"Consisting of nine wombs" refers to the Śrīvidyā. In the midst of a cushion of flowers,
strewn with heaps of blossoms and filled with various perfumes, one should [place] the Yantra with the Kula-substance.
Having written [the mantra], one should worship it if able, preceded by the ritual installation of a water-pot (ghaṭasthāpana);
on one's left side is a hexagon, and in its center is the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra).
Having inscribed [the mantra] there, one should place a pitcher— either made of gold,
silver, copper, or even earth— as long as it is devoid of base metals;
this pitcher, perfumed with fragrant scents, shall serve as the support for the water-jar (kalaśa).
One should completely fill the causal substance according to the distinctions of the Brahmins and others.

"According to the distinction of Brāhmaṇas and so forth" means that milk, clarified butter, honey, and wine are to be filled [into the vessels] by the Brāhmaṇas and the other castes respectively. And thus, even for a Brāhmaṇa hero, milk alone is the substance in the place of the *hetu* (cause); but for others, even that is not permitted.
One should meditate upon the object of awakening;
having first drawn the yantra there, whatever originates from one's own lineage,
and having visualized one's chosen deity therein, one should recite the mantra one hundred and eight times.
Then, having displayed the source of the cow (dhenu-yoni), one should contemplate that which has issued forth;
indeed, seeing the nectar thus obtained, the hosts of yoginīs dance.
All the Bhairavas dance, and the Mothers dance as well;
all the gods, beginning with Indra, dance, longing for the honeyed wine.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Maheśa, and the others dance, intent on joy;
having divided the vessel of nectar into three parts, one portion is given to the Guru.
Having given one [portion] as a nest for the family, and with one [portion] performing the libation to the deities,
he drinks the essence of the clan, adorned with various garments and ornaments.
If the Guru is not personally present, then one should offer [the offering] into water;
having become one whose nature is bliss, one should worship the Supreme Goddess.
One should worship each [deity] with the respective ritual procedure and with the corresponding effort;
then, having performed the dismissal (visarjana), one should finally unite [the deity] within one's own lineage.
120) By drinking the nectar of that orb, I partake of immortality;
from tasting the essence of that cakora bird, great joy arises within me.
Merely by grasping that fruit, he descends from the peak of Mount Meru;
by the mere act of embracing the creeper, his body becomes washed with nectar.
When the root-yoga has been performed there, one should recite eight thousand [times];
and in both daily recitation and fire-offering, wherever no specific number has been prescribed.
In this regard, the following enumeration is prescribed: one should take one thousand and eight offerings of sacrificial substances purified with water and then perform the libation (tarpaṇa).
Having performed the libation (tarpaṇa), O Lord, one should follow [the deity] in circumambulation;
then, having praised and prostrated, one should gratify [the deity] with the hymn prescribed in the Kalpa.
Thus, O God, the Vīra-kula is enchanting and worthy of worship by the gods;
O Bhairava, wherever a hero exists, that land or even that family belongs to it.
There shall be no fear of pestilence there, nor any fear of kings and the like;
it shall always be auspicious, bringing an increase of wealth and sons.
O Mahādeva, at the foot of a tree, the mantra of Svapnaprabodhinī certainly makes Lakṣmī firmly established there.
It must be applied with diligent effort so that no obstacle arises;
it is not suitable for another hero, even with the grasping of deities.
It is not lost by the Yoginīs, nor is one stained by sin,
when one goes to the cremation ground on any day, even on a Tuesday.
The fruit of worship performed there shall equal that of seven days;
when the fourteenth day has passed, the fruit of worship for an entire fortnight shall be attained there.
One who does not proceed with noble conduct in this state is undoubtedly like a mere beast;
he is solely intent on the thought, "There is no god superior to this one."
Through intoxication, one who enjoys the ritual substances becomes devoted to the Kula;
when the practitioner falls into agitation, my own agitation arises.
Therefore, through diligent effort, one becomes a supreme hero, endowed with enjoyments and happy;
through enjoyment one attains liberation, and through enjoyment one achieves the Kula practice.
Without a cause and without tasting [the object], Maheśvara is possessed by agitation;
there is neither worship nor contact with me, neither meditation nor reflection.
121) Therefore, having eaten and drunk, one should worship the Supreme Goddess;
herein there is no fault of transgression, nor is there any other ornament of fault.
Whatever one speaks, sleeps, does,
or worships— all that, having meditated upon as being of the nature of the Kula, one should dwell in happiness.
Alone in a secluded place— whether in a cremation ground, on a mountain, in a forest,
in an empty house, or on a riverbank— one should wander joyfully, free from attachments.
For heroes, the time for recitation is praised as being at all times;
it should be performed in any place and on any sacred seat—of this there is no doubt.
If a Brahmin should become fallen, yet remains devoted to the duties of his lineage,
then he must perform the propitiation of the lineage according to this prescribed method.
The Brahmin is indeed a hero.
But in the interior of the other flower is the charming seat of the lineage (kulasthāna),
which is the mouth of all the gods and consists of the essence of the great art of desire (mahākāmakalā).
In the *hayāri* flower, Lord Sadāśiva himself is ever present;
taking a small amount of that [flower] and sandalwood within the flower—
Having offered a red flower and meditated upon oneself as having the nature of Śiva,
one should unite [the offering] with the power of Śiva (Śiva-śakti) and contemplate their oneness with the intellect.
Having reflected for a moment and worshipped the Supreme Goddess right there,
he recited that very mantra which is the substance known as the *kuṇḍa*, most difficult to obtain.
O Bhairava, where the Aparājita flower, the Javā flower,
the red and white Karavīra, and the Droṇa flower are found;
There, by means of the Goddess, one should constantly worship me in that yantra;
and when a hibiscus flower is offered, one shall obtain the fruit of silk garments.
Sins such as the killing of a Brahmin are certainly destroyed in an instant;
however, O Maheśvara, it is impossible to describe the greatness of Aparā.
The rite of heroic accomplishment (vīrasādhana) must be performed by heroic men;
it may be performed even by divine beings, but not by those who are bound [by worldly ties] (paśus) or by the vulgar.
It is certain that even the work of a commoner is better than that of a beast;
for that which was previously declared as untrue regarding the practice of mantras and conventions does not exist.
The hero of great power should prepare collyrium, pills, and so forth;
there is no difference between the divine and the heroic, yet that which constitutes their distinction is now described.
The Śānta (peaceful) hero is calm, disciplined, sweet, and endowed with artistic grace;
the Divya (divine) hero is generally like a god; and the Vīra (heroic) hero possesses an exalted mind.
Whether adorned with magnificent ornaments or smeared with sandalwood paste,
whether concealing his outward appearance or abandoned— O Kulabhairava!
Whether smeared with red sandalwood paste or possessed of great wealth, if one is non-Vaiṣṇava,
he shall always remain delighted and nourished by insults as well as by worship.
Whether one is intent on censuring the gods, or intent on the worship of this or that [deity],
or intent on worship while devoid of it— one who stands firm in the Kula and Akula doctrine [is liberated].
Endowed with his own true nature, he should move about on earth like a god;
at the end of his lineage, the preliminary practice (puraścaryā) must be performed at night and not otherwise.
O God, just as there can be no discourse on the Vedas for a twice-born man devoid of Vedic knowledge,
so too, O Goddess, devotion to you cannot flourish without devotion to Viṣṇu.
Just as liberation without the knowledge of Śakti leads only to ridicule,
so too there is no entitlement whatsoever to the Tantra without a Guru.

Just as a woman deprived of her husband is excluded from all ritual activities, so too am I excluded from the worship of the gods and from the performance of my spiritual practice when devoid of a kinsman.
"One who belongs to the Kaula tradition is not qualified [if lacking discipline]; therefore, be devoted to the inner state (bhāva). How can one whose family is undisciplined be my worshipper?
Therefore, one must act with such effort that one becomes endowed with discipline."
In the Kula scripture, there is no qualification whatsoever based on existence or non-existence;
therefore, a practitioner who is purified of existence becomes a Kaulika.
Thus ends the sequence of the heroic state (vīrabhāva).
Now, regarding the animal state (paśubhāva),
the Goddess said in the *Bhāvacūḍāmaṇi*:
I shall explain the state of the sacrificial animal (paśubhāva); listen with a concentrated mind, my child.
Having received the knowledge of the animal according to the prescribed rule, one should be devoted to that state.
First, for the sake of preliminary service, one should diligently practice purification;
one should not eat fish, nor should one even mentally recall women.
One should not covet the wealth of others, nor should one set one's mind upon enjoyments;
[one should practice] on the shore of the ocean, on a mountain, in a forest, or in a temple of the gods.
At the root of a bilva tree, in a secluded place, or in a beautiful and holy field,
one should not allow a Śūdra to see [the ritual], and one should diligently abandon all crookedness.
The deity of auspicious complexion should be meditated upon by those who are well-composed;
one should perform the worship of the deity at the three junctions of the day and practice recitation at the three junctions of the day.
At night, one should never touch the mantra or the rosary;
nor should one recite the mantra after eating, but remain observant of silence in all ritual acts.
The best of practitioners should never approach a woman during the time of the lunar festivals;
having personally brought flowers, incense, and water, he should perform worship.

One should completely avoid sexual intercourse, talk about it, and social gatherings concerning it; furthermore, one should not approach a woman with passion except during her fertile period. One should have faith in listening to the Purāṇas and be devoted to the meaning of the Vedas and Vedānta.
O Supreme Lord, a wise man should not consume betel leaf at night.
Whatever has been commanded by the Guru, all that one should perform with diligence;
likewise, O Bhairava, one’s own birth-flower and the causal substance.
Having touched [such a person] or likewise smelled them, one is purified by the five products of the cow (pañcagavya). One who is devoted to the Goddess should not accept red garments.
O auspicious one, praised by heroes, in the Viṣṇu-tantras one should perform only their prescribed practice;
one should not engage in conversation concerning the deeds of heroes.
One who is devoted to dharma should perform the daily śrāddha, the śrāddha at Gayā, the twilight worship (saṃdhyāvandana),
bathing at sacred fords (tīrtha), and visiting the sites of the sacred seats (pīṭha).
O God Bhairava, the animal (paśu) is of two kinds, including the former;
its authority lies in worship, never in the state of being a guru.
The former has no authority regarding worship or coming and going to the sacred site;
indeed, the former must be excluded from his own country by all those worthy of the Kaula tradition.
One should practice the vision of the Kula by means of the mere initial vision;
O Lord, it is better to commit sins such as the killing of a Brahmin than [to fail in this], for truth is supreme.
The vision of the past alone is the truth here; I tell you the truth.
O Lord of Gods, that Self of mine is also the All-pervading One, O Master.
Nevertheless, a doubt arises within me at every step;
it would be better to abandon one's family, and better still to suffer harm from one's own kin.
It is better to suffer the ruin of one's own family than to destroy one's own lineage;
it is better to protect one's own family through body, mind, and speech.
One should not form an attachment to a beast, for it causes the destruction of one's own path;
in the Kula scripture, two things are considered the gravest sins that lead to the ruin of the lineage.
O Lord of the Kula, there is great infamy within one's own family and union with another’s [family]; even greater than that, O Great Sinful One, arises from association with the uninitiated (paśu).
O God, through the manifestation of that state as the state of the bound (paśu) over three births, it becomes the state of the hero (vīra); from that, the divine state (daiva) arises.
A hero is born from destiny, and from a hero, destiny is born;
in every respect, O Lord of the Family, these two states should not be made manifest.
In the divine and the heroic [rasas], there is no doubt; they are designated as "equivalence" (sāmya). But since *bhāva* is a mental state (*mānasa-dharma*), how indeed could it be verbal (*śābda*)?
Therefore, the actual state of being cannot be described; only a mere indication has been given.
Just as the sweetness of a sugarcane stalk is known by its taste, O Lord, so too is the nature of existence contemplated by the mind.
Thus ends the fourth wave in the *Tārābhaktisudhārṇava* composed by the Great Professor, the illustrious Ṭhakkura Narasiṃha.
The Fifth Wave:
Now, regarding the daily ritual (*nityavidhi*), it is stated in the *Kulacūḍāmaṇi*: "The practitioner, having risen in the morning and having bowed to the *kula*-tree..."
Having meditated upon the Kula from the base (mūlādhāra) up to the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra), one should remember the Guru.
The family trees according to the Rudrayāmala:
the Śleṣmātaka, Karañja, Nimba, Aśvattha, Kadambaka, Bilva, Vaṭa, Śāla, Tāla, Śākhoṭa, and likewise the Kharjūra.
"The family trees have been fully described.
In reality, however, those who know the secret maintain that the "family tree" is the excellent woman (*varāṅganā*). In the *Vīracūḍāmaṇi*:
"The practitioner, having risen in the morning, should remember his guru with reverence."
Having meditated upon Mahācīnaguru, one should then [meditate upon] the lineage of the Gurus beginning with Vyāsa.

Having worshipped with the five offerings according to the sequence of heroic substances, I salute the Hero, the treasury of compassion— he who wears blue garments, is anointed with blue unguents, whose body is adorned with conch shells and other ornaments, who is joyful and two-eyed, and whose left lap-seat is occupied by his blue Śakti.
Having meditated upon the supreme deity, the beautiful blue one, in the heart—
dwarfish, blue, large-eyed, and adorned with the five mudrās.
Holding a skull and a chopper in her hands, bearing a sword and a blue lotus,
with a mass of matted hair adorned by a garland of snakes, and possessing full, elevated breasts.
Having thus meditated upon the Great Goddess, who is full of fresh youth and whose eyes roll with intoxication, the practitioner shall become omniscient.
The wise practitioner should perform the ritual visualization (saṅkalpa) of the Great Vidyā known as Vīrahaṃsa.
Out of a desire for the welfare of mantra-practitioners, I shall now describe the practice known as Haṃsa.
By the mere knowledge of whom one becomes omniscient on earth,
that Blessed Lady in the form of the *haṃsa* the living soul chants at all times.
By the mere remembrance of this, a person becomes liberated while living;
its seer is declared to be Haṃsa, and its deity is Parahaṃsa.
The meter is unmanifest Gāyatrī; the application is the bestowing of success in yoga.
In the Surendra-saṃhitā: "The seer is Haṃsa preceded by Vyakta; Gāyatrī is said to be the meter.
The deity is the Supreme Āditya; Haṃsa is said to be the seed-syllable (bīja). (126)
"Aḥ" is the Śakti, "Kīlaka" is "So'ham," and the Praṇava is indeed the Tattva;
thus is the Udātta accent proclaimed as the mantra of this [mantra].
This application is for the sake of liberation; thus a person should always act.
In the *Vīracūḍāmaṇi*: "O Goddess, the heart belongs to the nature of the Sun; likewise, the head belongs to the nature of the Moon.
The *śikhā* is the stainless light, and the others are without appearance."
Having placed the Unmanifest (Avyakta) upon the two eyes, one should also cast Ananta upon the weapon (astra) with the syllable *phaṭ*.
Having thus performed the rite of placement (*nyāsa*), one should offer it to Gaṇeśa and the others.
In the Surendra-saṃhitā: "The individual soul always chants the Blessed One who is of the nature of the Haṃsa;
with the syllable *ha*, it goes out, and with the syllable *sa*, it enters again."
By the mere awakening to this, a person becomes liberated while living.
By the power of prāṇāyāma, one indeed becomes liberated while living.
A living being should recite daily twenty-one thousand six hundred times the supreme mantra consisting of the bliss of Brahman.
Its arising is the commencement; its death is the offering.
Without [formal] recitation, there is constant recitation at all times.
When the recitation has been thus completed, one should offer it to Gaṇeśa and the others.
In the *Vīracūḍāmaṇi*: "Six hundred for Gaṇeśa, six thousand for Prajāpati, six thousand for Gadāpāṇi, and six thousand for Pinākin."
One thousand [offerings] to oneself, one thousand to the Supreme Self (Paramātman), and one thousand to the Guru; this is the ritual resolve (saṅkalpa) according to the rules.
One should offer six hundred oblations to the red-colored Gaṇeśa at the four-petalled mūlādhāra, which is joined with the Vādi-veda.
The Svādhiṣṭhāna [cakra] has the luster of coral, is six-cornered, and consists of the six vowels;
joined with Sāvitrī, one should offer it to Brahmā.
I salute Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa, who possess the splendor of a mass of lightning; the petal consists of the ten syllables beginning with *ḍa*, and one should offer six thousand [oblations].
And upon the twelve petals beginning with *ka*, which possess the luster of great sapphire, I bow to Umā and Maheśvara; one should offer six thousand [oblations].
One should place the vowels upon a pure smoke-leaf and a leaf of *kalā*;
I bow to that which consists of the power of vital breath (*prāṇaśakti*), and one should offer a thousand [oblations].
One should employ the auspicious letters *ha* and *kṣa* in the command (*ājñā*) and the lightning-flash (*vidyudābhā*).
And one should offer a thousand [oblations] into the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) and the Supreme Power (*parāśakti*).
One should meditate upon the Guru, who is blue in nature and resplendent with the luster of camphor, within a thousand-petaled lotus, and one should offer a thousand [prostrations].
O Goddess whose girdle is the ocean, whose breasts are the mountain ranges, O Consort of Viṣṇu, salutations be unto you; forgive my touch of your feet.
O Goddess, one should maintain the practice according to the measure of one's own breath;
one should perform bodily purification and the like, and carry out the bath of ashes.
Seated in the vīrāsana posture, smeared with heroic ashes,
and meditating upon the Hero, O Great Goddess, the wise one should recite the vīramālā mantra.
One should offer one thousand and eight [oblations] into the left hand;

this is the ash of heroes (vīrabhasma), the ash of the cremation ground (śmaśānabhasma). Because of the mention of "the left hand," it appears that this is the recitation of the root mantra (mūlamantra). However, in the Viśuddheśvara [Tantra], it says:
"Having performed the recitation (*japa*) according to one's capacity and having offered praise, one should satisfy Śivā.
Thus it is said. Prior to this, the recitation of the Guru-mantra has also been mentioned elsewhere. As it is stated in the *Tattvacintāmaṇi*:
"Alternatively, one should extract the Vāgbhava, Māyā, and Lakṣmī-bījas."
Hasakhaphreṃ, as well as the one named Ānandabhairava, [is] Sahakhaphreṃ.
The wise practitioner should remember the name of the Guru, the name of the Śakti, and the Śrīpādukā; he should then recite [the mantra] ten times, seven times, or even three times.
"Afterwards, one should offer the recitation (*japa*) into the right hand of the venerable Guru. Thus [it is said].
In the *Vīracūḍāmaṇi*: "O fair lady, one should perform the cleansing of the teeth with 'vajra-flower' (*vajrapuṣpa*).
Vajra-flower refers to menstrual blood or a hibiscus flower (*javākusuma*). And this is the cleansing of the teeth.

This should be performed immediately after the purification of the body, for it is seen as such elsewhere: "O Maheśānī, the wise one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) and touch the Śakti along with her limbs."
One should perform gestures of amorous expression and the like, and carry out the ritual of bathing.
The smearing with the ashes of a hero (*vīrabhasma*) and so forth pertains exclusively to the heroic practitioner (*vīrasādhaka*). Furthermore, this morning rite (*prātaḥkṛtya*) is essential.
As it is stated in the *Yāmala*: "He who worships the Goddess with devotion without having performed the morning rite..."
And his worship is fruitless, like a ritual performed without purity.
Now, as for bathing, it is threefold, distinguished as physical (audaka), verbal (māntra), and mental (mānasa). Among these, the physical is first described because of its primary importance.

128) In the *Nāradapañcarātra*: "Having taken earth with a *śaṅku* consecrated by the *astra-mantra*, one who is pure should bathe after having empowered it with the *astra-mantra* according to the ritual for entering the water."
Therein, first one should wash the water-vessel with the water of the weapon-mantra;
then, having divided the clay into two parts, one should take one portion from there.
Having carefully placed cow-dung, darbha grass, and consecrated sesame seeds,
one should diligently set aside the first portion for the worldly host.
Having first performed the impurity-bath (*malasnāna*), one should then perform the ritual bath (*vidhisnāna*).
In the *Kūlacūḍāmaṇi*: "Now, O child, I shall describe to you the bath that brings happiness to the Kula;
my various playful forms are black, red, and yellow."
In that regard, whatever family a disciple belongs to, he should contemplate that very form;
having sipped water with the *kula*-darbha grass, he should hold the *kula*-flower together with the darbha.
Then, taking a vessel of good lineage along with darbha grass, sesame seeds,
and water, one should perform a bath for the pleasure of the family deity.
Having formed this resolve, he should place the *kulacakra* in the water,
having brought forth the *kulamudrā* from the *kulasura* with the *kuśa* grass.
Having brought the family-tirthas right there,
one who is of the nature of the lineage should drink that water three times and perform the sprinkling of the body three times.
Regarding the lineage (kula) to which one belongs when initiated by a preceptor, the *Kuladarbha* is described in the *Rudrayāmala*:
"Three types of darbha grass are prescribed: those made of gold, silver, and kuśa.
Among these, two are intended for the Śākta tradition, while three are considered appropriate for others."
Gold and silver alone are declared to be effective for the performance of rites such as recitation (japa) and worship;
however, wild kuśa grass is not considered true kuśa.
Elsewhere it is also said: "Silver should be held with the index finger, and gold should be held with the ring finger;
this alone is declared to be *kuśa*, not the *darbha* grass grown in the forest."
In the *Yāmala*: "Without *dūrvā* grass, there is never any worship of the Goddess here at all.
Therefore, one should take the auspicious *dūrvā*, which embodies all flowers.
Having placed a sprout of *dūrvā* in one's hand, one should perform the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*) according to the prescribed rule."

*Kulapuṣpa* refers to the *javā* flower and others. *Kulapātra* refers to a vessel made of gold or similar materials. *Kuladeva* refers to one’s chosen deity (*iṣṭadevatā*). *Kulacakra* is the triangular wheel (*trikoṇacakra*). Regarding the method of drawing it, the *Mālinītantra* states:
