"One should draw the triangle with the root mantra, while reciting the *haṃsaka* [mantra] dedicated to Savitṛ."
129) O Goddess, being composed in mind, one should draw [the diagram] precisely according to the clockwise sequence.

Regarding the phrase "by the root seed-syllable": in another mantra, namely the Sāvitra or solar mantra, [one recites] the "Haṃsaka" mantra, *haṃsaḥ*. And as for the Aṅkuśa-mudrā: "Having formed a right fist, then the index finger takes the form of a hook;
this great mudrā called Aṅkuśa is capable of attracting the three worlds."

Thus it is stated in the Tantra. Furthermore, the mantra for the invocation of the sacred waters (*tīrthāvāhana*) is found in the *Śrīkramasaṃhitā*: "O Gaṅgā, Yamunā, Godāvarī, Sarasvatī, Narmadā, Sindhu, and Kāverī! Grant your presence in these waters."

The drinking of water is threefold, consisting solely of the form of *ācamana* (ritual sipping). That is performed with the root mantra (*mūlamantra*). Sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) is also performed with that same mantra.
As it is said in the *Triśaktiratna*: "Having sipped water three times with the root mantra and the gesture known as the 'water-pot' (*kumbhamudrā*)."
The wise one should sprinkle his head three times with water purified by the mantra.
And this mudrā is described in the Tantra:
"Having inserted the right thumb into the left thumb with both hands,
forming a single fist with some space between the fingers— this is the mudrā known as the 'Jar' (kumbha)."

In the Gandharva Tantra: Having recited the root mantra, the foremost of practitioners should pour water upon his head with the *kumbha* mudrā three times, and thereafter perform the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*).
Then, by means of the principles (tattvas) of Ātman, Vidyā, and Śiva, one should proceed to the sacrificial hall.
Regarding the phrase "by means of the principles of Ātman, Vidyā, and Śiva": "By the principle of Ātman, I purify the gross body, svāhā!
By the principle of Vidyā, I purify the subtle body, svāhā! By the principle of Śiva, [I purify] the supreme body..."
The meaning is that one should take three handfuls of water with the three mantras ending in "śodhayāmi svāhā. In the *Nīlatantra*:
"Having thus submerged oneself three times with the *vidyā*, one should likewise sip water (*ācamana*) with [the same] water.
In the *Vasiṣṭhasaṃhitā*: "Having first performed the Vedic bath, one should then perform the Tantric [bath]."
Having performed the six-limbed assignment upon the body, preceded by breath control (prāṇāyāma).
Having drawn the sacred water from the orb of the glorious sun by means of the *aṅkuśa* mudrā,
one should bathe it with the syllable *vaṃ* and veil it with the *kavaca* mantra.
Having protected [the site] with the root weapon-mantra, one should consecrate it eleven times;
thereafter, one should perform self-protection by sprinkling water empowered by the weapon-mantra.
Having immersed oneself there, one should meditate upon the glorious deity (Śrīdeva) and recite the mantra according to one's capacity.
Having emerged, and having formed the *kumbha-mudrā*, one should sprinkle water upon one's own head.
In the Tripurārṇava: "Having performed the Vedic bath, one should then perform the Tantric one;
having taken earth with the Astra-mantra and having sprinkled it [with water] by means of that [mantra]."
130) Having purified [the body] with the *śikhā* mantra, one should consecrate it with the root mantra;
then, having smeared the body from the crown of the head down to the feet with that [substance].
Having bound the *sammukhīkaraṇī* mudrā and restrained the vital breath (*prāṇa*),
one should submerge oneself and then rise silently while standing in water reaching up to the navel.
Having performed three breath-controls (prāṇāyāma) with the root mantra, the knower of mantras,
having performed the six-limbed assignment (ṣaḍaṅga-nyāsa), should visualize a sacred bathing place (tīrtha) before him.
Then, the knower of mantras, having pierced the solar orb— the sacred ford— located there with the *ghṛṇi* mantra and the *aṅkuśa* mudrā, should pray to that tīrtha.
O Dear One, one should invoke the sacred waters (tīrtha) using the invocation mantra for the tīrtha,
having joined it with the root mantra within the prepared tīrtha-maṇḍala.
Having invoked the power of the sacred ford (tīrtha-śakti) right there from the solar orb,
and having meditated upon it and worshipped it with its specific mantra, one should consecrate it with the Gaṅgā-mantra.
O beloved, listen to these two mantras for this auspicious [rite] to be performed seven times:
the syllable *ja* situated in water (the letter *ya*), joined with the six long vowels of space (*ū*), differentiated by the vowels, and accompanied by the bindu.
O Dear One, the mantra of the Tīrtha-Śakti is said to consist of twenty-one syllables: *sarvānandamaye tīrthe śakte ehyehi yugam dviṭhaḥ*.
One should utter "Tāraṃ namo bhagavati ambe," and then "ambike," "ambālike," "mahāmālini ehy ehi bhagavati."
One should utter the seed-syllable of Māyāśrī at the root-basin of all holy fords without exception;
then [the mantra] "O Gaṅgā seated upon the matted locks of Śiva, O Mother Gaṅgā," ending with the Dviṭha (svāhā).
This Gaṅgā-vidyā has been declared with fifty-three syllables;
it should be stirred together with Bhuvaneśī and rendered nectarine by means of the atom of Sudhā.
Then, having veiled [the deity] with the Kavaca mantra and protected it with the Astra mantra,
the knower of mantras should [worship] the deity there with the root mantra, together with the limbs (aṅgas) and the enclosures (āvaraṇas).
Having invoked [the deity] into the water and meditated upon it, and having visualized the sacred bathing-place (tīrtha) as emerging from his two feet,
one should remember the root mantra and bathe in the water three times.
Having emerged, one should sprinkle [water] with the root mantra using the *kaṃ* (water) jar mudrā;
then, having sipped water according to the rule, one should afterwards offer libations with the root mantra.
Having emerged from the water three times with the goddess, and having put on two clean garments washed [in the stream],
one should then apply the tilaka and perform the twilight devotion (sandhyā).
131) "One should pray thus": "O Ravi, all the sacred fords within the belly of the cosmic egg have been touched by your rays;
by that truth, O Lord of Gods, O Maker of Day, grant me a sacred ford."
The meaning is "by this [mantra]"; "by the mantra for the invocation of the Tīrtha" means by the mantra beginning with *gaṅge ca*. Regarding "having meditated":
[one should meditate on her] as consisting entirely of bliss, the destroyer of all sins, possessing the luster of the moon, three-eyed, and holding a noose and a goad in her two raised left hands.

Within, I worship the two golden jars filled with nectar, the excellent rosary of pearls, and the power of the sacred fords (Tīrtha-Śakti) together with the Gaṅgā, Sindhu, and other preeminent rivers.
In this manner: when these methods are not mutually exclusive, they are to be combined; when they are mutually exclusive, there is an option.
Furthermore, some say that the method described in the *Tripurārṇava* pertains specifically to the Traipura [tradition].
Now, the ritual bath of mantras (*māntrasnāna*).
In the *Nāradapañcarātra*, beginning with "Now hear the auspicious mantra," it says:
"O Durgā, that which must be done in the absence of water at a time when one is self-controlled,
for the sake of swift success in traveling or in great undertakings, [should be performed] by one who is untiring."
O best of Brahmins, O sage, when you had thus reached the night portion,
you washed your feet and sipped water with water drawn up from a vessel.
Having purified the site and the ten directions as before, one should then sit down;
having placed the *astra* mantra on the palms of the hands, one should then perform the ritual placements (*nyāsa*) in their proper order.
One should indeed perform [the rite] beginning with the root mantra by means of the entire collection of mantras;
for [a bath] consisting of mere water, devoid of ritual consecration, is insufficient.
Whatever fruit is obtained by one who has completed his vows at sacred fords such as Prabhāsa,
it should be known that the fruit of the mantra-bath is ten times greater than that, according to certain authorities.

"In the absence of water" (*toyābhāve*) means when there is no water suitable for a ritual bath. "The weapon-mantra" (*astram*), etc.: having placed the weapon-mantra of one's own *vidyā* upon the two hands, one should perform the entire network of placements (*nyāsajāla*) as prescribed in one's own *tantra*, preceded by the placement of the mantra; this is the meaning. Regarding the word "merely" (*kevalāt*): here, "bathing" consists solely of the form of the *nyāsa*. However, in another *tantra* it is said:
One should wash the hands from the wrist downwards, the feet from the ankle downwards, and then the face; this constitutes the five-limbed bath (pañcāṅga-snāna), which bestows purity.

Now, regarding the mental bath (*mānasasnāna*) in the Śaiva Āgama: "One should perform the mental bath with the mind and the root-mantra (*mūlamantra*), preceded by breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), which is prescribed for all occasions."
In all respects and in all branches of knowledge:
132) In the *Nāradapañcarātra*—I shall now describe the bath of meditation (*dhyānasnāna*), which is superior even to the other two.
One should contemplate the Lord, the lotus-eyed one, who resides in the sky and whose form is the mantra.
One should contemplate the stream born from the water of his feet falling upon one's own head,
entering one's own body through the subtle aperture.
By means of that [water], one should wash away all this impurity residing in the body;
at that very moment, the practitioner becomes free from passion (viraja) and resembles a crystal.
This excellent bath is considered to be a hundred times more meritorious than a bath performed with mantras.
The mention of "Puṇḍarīkākṣa" (the Lotus-eyed One) is an illustration; the intended meaning is that one should remember whichever deity is one's own chosen deity.
Regarding the phrase "by both": it is said to be superior by means of both because it yields its fruit with little effort. Not... [text ends]

Therefore, it should be understood that this [physical bath] is secondary (*pradhāna*). However, because this *vidyā* is to be practiced according to the sequence of the Mahīcīna [tradition], here the mental bath (*mānasasnāna*) alone is primary. Having risen from that, one should put on two garments. As it is said in the *Kulacūḍāmaṇi*:
Having risen and put on two garments of noble lineage,
and having certainly applied the sectarian mark (tilaka) of the noble form, one should complete the rite.

Regarding the term *kulavastra*, here the word *kula* denotes "excellent red. By *kula* is meant the root mantra (*mūlamantra*). The *tilaka* in the form of the *kula* is the hero’s *tilaka* (*vīratilaka*) as stated in the *Matsyasūkta*: "The wise man should constantly apply the triple mark (*tripuṇḍra*) with earth from cremation grounds."

In the *Nāradapañcarātra*: "Then, having put on a well-washed pair of garments that do not cause perspiration—or, in their absence, a single lower garment (*śāṭī*) together with a meditation-band (*yogapaṭṭaka*)."
And one should never be clad in only a single garment;

for one seeking liberation, according to the *Svatantra-tantra*, should wear two red garments, while one seeking enjoyment should wear two white garments. Having thus dressed, the wise man should then enter the sacrificial ground.
In the *Yāmala*: "One should wear two bright garments and a sectarian mark (*tilaka*) according to the distinction of caste.

Regarding the phrase "according to the distinction of caste": "The vertical mark (*ūrdhvapuṇḍra*) belongs to the Brāhmaṇa; the triple mark (*tripuṇḍraka*) to the Kṣatriya; the half-moon (*ardhacandra*) to the Vaiśyas; and the circular shape to the Śūdra."
The meaning is: "according to the sequence taught in the Nāradapañcarātra. In the *Samayātantra*:
"One should make a tilaka with ashes or three puṇḍraka marks with [sacred] earth.
In the *Bhairavītantra*: "The tilaka [should be made] with red sandalwood paste or with gopīcandana."
One should inscribe the weapon-mantra of the Goddess on the forehead, and then the seed-syllable *tāra* in the heart.
The practitioner, the best among men, should cause the *śakti* to enter the center.

In the *Bhairavītantra*: "Having sipped water for purification (*ācamana*), facing the east, and having sat down, the knower of mantras, being composed, should then perform the Vedic and Tantric twilight devotions (*sandhyā*)."

133) In the Śaiva Āgama: Having performed three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma), the knower of mantras should perform the ritual placement of the limbs (aṅganyāsa) upon the body with the root mantra, preceded by the ritual placement on the hands (karanyāsa).
Having rendered the water in front of him nectar-like by means of the *dhenumudrā*,
the practitioner should consecrate it seven times with the root mantra.
One should sprinkle [the disciple] three times on the head with each syllable of the Mātṛkā, from *a* to *kṣa*, accompanied by the bindu, using kuśa grass or the root mantra.
In the *Kumārīkalpa*: having first extracted the *praṇava* (oṃ), [the mantra is] "maṇidharaṇī vajriṇi," followed by two *rakṣas*, and then "hūṃ phaṭ svāhā."
With this very mantra, the wise one should perform protection;
having sipped water again and performed the six-limbed placement (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*), the knower of mantras [should proceed].
Taking water in the left hand,
one should perform a sevenfold sprinkling with the falling drops of water while reciting the mantra over the head.
Holding the remaining water in his right hand, the knower of mantras [visualizes] the accumulated mass of sins washed away within the body of Kṛṣṇa by means of the iḍā [nāḍī].
The practitioner of mantra, having visualized that water— which has been expelled through the right nostril— as being black in color and the very form of sin, should [discard it] with his right hand.

One should throw [the water] onto a vajra-stone in front [of oneself] while reciting the Astra-mantra; the experts in reality maintain that this constitutes the protection in the form of binding the topknot (śikhābandhana). In the *Yāmala*:
"Having performed the six-limbed ritual placement (ṣaḍaṅga-nyāsa), one should then take water in the left hand."
Having taken it with the right hand, one should then form the hollowed-cup gesture (saṃpuṭa).
Furthermore, having consecrated [the materials] three times with the seed-syllables of Śiva (H), Vāyu (Y), Water (V), Earth (L), and Fire (R),
and seven times with the root-mantra using the *tattva-mudrā*.
The foremost of practitioners should place that water upon his head and set the remainder on his right side,
thereby washing away the sins residing within his body.
One should apply a tilaka with the root mantra; for this indeed is the Kaulika twilight rite, O beautiful lady of the Kula, as it has been taught concerning the disciple belonging to the Kula.
The seed-syllable of Śiva is the letter *ha*; the seed-syllable of air is the letter *ya*; the seed-syllable of water is the letter *va*; the seed-syllable of earth is the letter *la*;

and the seed-syllable of fire is the letter *ra*. These constitute the seed-syllables when accompanied by the *anusvāra*. Having encased the left hand, which holds water, within the right hand, one should consecrate the water three times with these seed-syllables.
The *tattvamudrā* is formed by the union of the ring finger and the thumb; likewise, the meaning is that one should sprinkle the water held in the hand seven times upon the head with the root mantra.
(134) In this regard, the alternative options (*vikalpa*) found in the *Kumārīkalpa* and the *Yāmala* are to be determined according to the lineage of the gurus (*gurukrama*).
In the *Vīracūḍāmaṇi*:
Having uttered "viyadvahni" (the sky and fire), [one utters] Nārāyaṇa with the bindu;
having uttered the seed-syllable of Māyā, [one utters] the sky conjoined with fire.
One should first utter "Haṃsa," adorned with the left ear and joined with the half-moon (the nasal bindu), followed by the seed-syllable of the solar orb. Then,
having uttered the word "Tārāyai," one should cast the añjali at the end of the heart-mantra.
Then one should recite the Gāyatrī. As it is stated in the Śaiva Āgama:
"Or else, one should offer three *arghya* oblations with the Gāyatrī or with the root-mantra;
then, one should satisfy Śiva, who resides within the mandala, by pouring water into his mouth with the root-mantra."
Then, having recited the Gāyatrī twenty-eight times— here,
"Gāyatrī" refers to the Gāyatrī of one’s own chosen deity— the Tārā-Gāyatrī is stated in the *Kālikārṇava*: "Aiṃ, O Blessed One, Ekajaṭā, we know [thee]," and then the word *vidmahe*.
We meditate upon her with her formidable fangs; may that Tārā inspire us.
In the Mālinītantra: "O Dear One, we know Mahogrā; we meditate upon Tārā.
May that Goddess [grant] us [the fruit of our] prayers; may She who inspires our intellects impel us."
In the *Vīracūḍāmaṇi*: "The wise one should mutter the Gāyatrī eight or ten times, having first uttered the Vāgbhava [seed-syllable]: 'We know her who is Ekajaṭā...'"
Having uttered "Devī" and "strīm," one should say "we meditate upon Nīlasarasvatī"; then, having uttered "Hṛllekhā," one should say "may Tārā inspire us."
Having recited [the mantra], one should perform the offering of dedication (samarpaṇa) into the left hand of the deity.
Regarding the visualization of Gāyatrī, it is stated in the Tantra:
"One should meditate on her as resembling the rising sun, with her hands enriched by a book."
One should meditate upon Brāhmī, wearing a black antelope skin, against a sky filled with stars.
At midday— one should meditate on the Goddess of dark complexion, with four arms, her hands shining with the conch and discus,
holding a mace and a lotus, and taking refuge in the orb of the sun.
In the evening, the wise man should meditate upon the boon-granting goddess Gāyatrī—
white-complexioned, clad in white garments, seated upon a bull-throne, three-eyed,
and holding a boon-granting gesture, a noose, a trident, and a human skull.
In the Gautamīya: "Or, due to incapacity, the mantra-practitioner may perform a condensed twilight ritual;
having meditated upon Kṛṣṇa at evening, morning, and midday, he should recite the mantra."
135) Thus, the three junctions (sandhyās) have been proclaimed as bestowing success upon those engaged in ritual action (karmis).

"Kṛṣṇa" is an elliptical designation; the meaning is "one's own chosen deity. Regarding this very point, it is said in the Āgama: "The omission of the sandhyā must not be performed, for such indeed is the command of Śambhu."
One who is initiated but devoid of the twilight devotions does not enjoy the fruit of initiation.
If one has missed the twilight prayer (sandhyā), then at the next twilight, having performed the ritual of the preceding twilight,
one should diligently perform the ritual of the subsequent twilight.
In the *Gautamīya*: "If the twilight [prayer] has been omitted, one should mutter the *gāyatrī* ten times.
However, in the *Tantrarāja*, it is stated: "In the event of the omission of bathing, twilight prayer, or worship, one should mutter [the mantra] one hundred and eight times.
Now, the libation (*tarpaṇa*).
In the *Kūlacūḍāmaṇi*: "One should satisfy the gods, the sages, and the ancestors with the water of the lineage (*kulavāri*).
Having meditated again upon those whose nature is the lineage, one should satisfy them by merging into the lineage."

With the water of the lineage—that is, with the water consisting of the invoked lineage-virility—one should dissolve and invoke the divine stream, the stream of the Siddhas, and the human stream, who are of the nature of the lineage, into the *pūjācakra* of the lineage. Likewise:
"And to the god Bhairava, who causes the descent (*āveśa*) of Bhairava..."
Having first uttered the mantra, that which is called Bhairava should be bestowed.

The grammatical connection is that [this] is the mantra called Bhairava. And that Anandabhairava mantra will be explained. Prior to the libation to the three currents (oghatriya), as stated in the Yamala: "At the beginning of the libation, one should employ [the mantra]: 'May Brahman-Bhairava be satisfied.'"

The mention of the ancestors (pitṛs) by way of Bhairava during the libation (tarpaṇa) pertains specifically to the subject of the *vīra*. However, for the *paśu*, the *Mālinītantra* states: "Having turned toward the southern direction and then taken up a blade of *moṭaka* grass, one should perform this libation while saying, 'May the ancestors be satisfied.'"

In the Śaiva Āgama: "Having meditated upon the Lord and having worshipped him properly in the water with the root mantra, one should then perform the libation (tarpaṇa) one hundred and eight times with the root mantra."
One should satisfy [the deities] ten times by half of that amount, or by half of that again;
thereafter, one should satisfy the deities of the limbs and the surrounding enclosures in their proper order.
Likewise, with each handful [of offerings], preceded by the root mantra,
one should then worship the Lord of Gods together with his limbs and retinue.
One should meditate upon oneself as being identical with that [deity] within one’s own heart, which is connected to the mouth.
In the *Yāmala*: "Having meditated on the King of Yantras in the water and having placed the Goddess there—preceded by the gods, sages, and ancestors, and accompanied by her weapons and retinue..."
136) Whether in the forest or at home, the wise one should satisfy the Goddess;
having satisfied the lineage of Gurus, he should also satisfy Vaṭuka and the others.
Having gratified the Root Goddess, one should gratify her retinue;
likewise, one should gratify the gatekeepers and the deities of the limbs and so forth.
Then, [he should worship] Śeṣikā and Sundarī in the west, the supreme Guru in the northeast,
Parāpara in the southeast, and Parameṣṭhin in the southwest.
One should satisfy the lineage of gurus from the northwest (Vāyavya) up to the northeast (Īśa),
and one should satisfy the limbs in their respective locations and the Goddess in the center.
Regarding Tārā, however, there is a specific rule in the Mālinītantra:
"Facing the northern direction, one should offer libations to the Goddess alone, using water from a sacred ford, sesame seeds, a medicinal paste, milk, and unbroken grains."

By the word "only" (*mātra*), it is indicated that the satisfaction of the retinue is performed with water alone. The method for the satisfaction of the chosen deity (*iṣṭadevatā*) is stated in the *Nīlatantra*:
"At the end of the root mantra, saying 'I satisfy' (*tarpayāmi*), followed by 'svāhā', is considered the manner of satisfaction."
Having thus performed the threefold libation, the destruction of evil occurs.

Before the word "tarpayāmi" (I satiate), the name of the deity in the accusative case should be joined, because an action requires an object (*karman*), and because this is seen to be the case everywhere.
At the end of the root mantra, having uttered "Tāriṇīm," one says: "I satiate Agnivallabhā."

This is also because of the statement in the *Mālinītantra*: "The libation (*tarpaṇa*) for the chosen deity is appropriate there [in the same place] as the application of the root-mantra. However, this refers to others besides the Vaiṣṇavas; for in the *Gautamīya-vaiṣṇava* it is said:
"First, having uttered the mantra, one should also say 'Śrī Kṛṣṇa'."
Having uttered the word "pada" (foot/step), a person should offer libations ending with "namaḥ."
But in other cases, the word "tarpayāmi" (I satiate) should be joined at the end of the mantra with one's own names in the accusative case;
such is considered the mantra for the rite of libation (tarpaṇa).

Thus, the primary method of satiation is by repeating [the rite] one hundred and eight times; this is the first position. Since it is said that "the destruction of sins shall occur," it is determined that this [rite] is both obligatory (*nitya*) and optional (*kāmya*). When one is unable to perform the satiation of each individual limb (*aṅga*), retinue (*parivāra*), vehicle (*vāhana*), and weapon (*āyudha*), [one should instead say]: "I satiate such-and-such deity, together with his limbs, retinue, vehicles, and weapons."

The traditionalists maintain that one should satisfy the deity itself with "svāhā" in this manner according to one's capacity. Thereafter, one should offer the *arghya* (water-offering) to the Sun. This is stated in the *Yāmala*: "One should present the *arghya* three times, saying 'To Mārtaṇḍa Bhairava'."

The phrase "to Mārtaṇḍabhairava" is an elliptical expression [for the full mantra]. That mantra, however, is: *hrīṃ haṃsaḥ, to Mārtaṇḍabhairava, together with the Power of Radiance (*prakāśaśakti*), this *argha* offering, svāhā*.
(137) In the *Tantrarājottara*: "Having recollected the god Bhairava, known as Mārtaṇḍa, the Lord of Umā..."
O Goddess, [one should do so] with the root mantra or else with the mantra of the Sun.
Having extracted the seed-syllable of Māyā, one should then take "so'ham" in reverse order;
this is Mārtaṇḍabhairava, ending in the letter Ṅa and conjoined with the power of Light (prakāśa-śakti).
"The mantra of the Sun is thus proclaimed.
In the *Nandikeśvara-saṃhitā*:
"Standing, one should offer three handfuls of water to the Lord of Day."
As long as the arghya offering is not presented to the Sun-god,
one should not worship Viṣṇu, Śaṅkara, or the Queen of the Gods.
Then one should offer the *arghya* to the Goddess residing within the solar disc (*sūryamaṇḍala*). As it is stated in the *Nīlatantra*:
"Having placed *kuśa* grass, *iḍara* flowers, *kulapuṣpa*, *kuśa*-water, and unbroken grains (*akṣata*) in a copper vessel, one should present the *arghya*."

At the end of the root mantra, the formula "svāhā" is prescribed as follows: "to her who abides in the mandala from the word 'rising sun' (udyadāditya), and who consists of the consciousness of Śiva. This is remembered as that mantra.

*Kuśīta* is red sandalwood; *kulapuṣpa* is seasonal (flower). Here, according to the statement "having performed the Tantric bath by the very procedure prescribed [for the Kālī-tattva]," this very *sandhyā* is indeed *kaulikī*.
For it is stated in the *Brahmayāmala*: "It has been taught with reference to a disciple belonging to the *kula*."
The ritual action of one performing Kaulika rites is not called Vaidika;
the ritual action of one performing Vaidika rites is not called Kaulika.

Based on this statement from the *Rudrayāmala*, and because the *Atharvaveda* states that "action [is] indeed the form of the womb" (*yonirūpam eva karma*), the Kaulikas claim that Vedic rites such as bathing, the twilight prayers (*sandhyā*), and libations (*tarpaṇa*) need not be performed. That is not so; for having first performed the Vedic bath, one should then perform the Tantric one—such is the injunction of the *Vasiṣṭha-saṃhitā*.

Furthermore, because there is a contradiction between the statement in the *Tripurārṇava*, "Then one should perform the Vedic bath and subsequently the Tantric [bath]," and the statement in another Tantra, "Having performed the Vedic and Tantric *saṃdhyā* rites, one should perform the libation (*tarpaṇa*"), the meaning of those statements is interpreted otherwise. To explain: in the phrase "by that very [method]" (*uktenaiva*), the particle *eva* (only/very) is displaced from its position.

The word "only" (eva) connects with the phrase "having performed. In the expression "this very twilight," the particle *eva* signifies that there is no other ritual procedure (*kalpāntara*) belonging to the Tantric tradition.
The statement from the *Rudrayāmala*, as well as the statement from the *Atharva* [Veda], regarding "one who performs the Kaulika [rite]," is as follows:

This [objection] amounts to nothing, for it merely prohibits the simultaneous performance of both sets of subsidiary rites (itikartavyatā) as established by the principle that "the ritual act is one and the same across all recensional branches" (*sarvaśākhāpratyayam ekaṃ karma*).
Now, as for worship (*pūjā*):
And that [sacrifice] is threefold, distinguished as superior, middling, and inferior. Thus it is said in the *Phetkāriṇītantra*:
"Endowed with the Śaktis, the Mūrtis, and the Lokapālas, the sacrifice performed according to the sequence of the *pīṭha*-yantras is the superior *nityayāga*."
Accompanied by the entire *pīṭha* alone, without an external enclosure,
and endowed with fire-rites, oblations, and ornaments.
The sacrifice preceded by mantras is the daily sacrifice; that is the middling one.
Likewise, the worship of each respective deity accompanied by the purification of the ritual substances [is also middling].
Having set aside various kinds of garments, ornaments, and objects,
and being devoid of fire-rituals according to the requirements of time and place.

Worship accompanied by ritual services (*upacāra*) and material offerings (*dravya*) is considered the inferior form (*adhamam*). In this regard, the practice depends upon one’s capacity. As stated in the *Tattvasārasaṃhitā*:
"Worship is traditionally held to be of two kinds: with remains of offerings (*sanirmālya*) and without remains of offerings (*anirmālya*)."
With divine substances born of the mind, such as perfumes, flowers, garlands, and the like.
The worship of which yields divine enjoyments and liberation, and for which there is no discarded floral offering (*nirmālya*),
is performed with charming sacrificial substances produced from villages, forests, and other such places.
Whatever worship is properly performed by devotees with offerings including flower garlands,
those flowers, as soon as they are born, are naturally already smelled [by the deity].
And by the five great elements, as well as by the sun and the moon,
by living beings such as bees and others, and even by flowers— of this there is no doubt.
Therefore, it is called *nirmālya*.
In this matter, the ascetics (*yatis*) have the right of authority from the very beginning. Agastya says:
"The worship of Manu is of two kinds: external and internal."
It is said that for renunciants (nyāsins) there is only one name, while for others they know both.
The yogi should worship with flowers grown in the wilderness;
in the case of harming flowers for the sake of Śiva, that shall not be considered an act of violence.
Thus says the *Śivarahasya*, referring to those whose senses are unsubdued:
"A wandering mendicant, by means of knowledge alone and without [the performance of] fire-offerings, gifts, and so forth, becomes liberated from all the demons of suffering; it is not otherwise."
O lotus-faced one, both the detached wandering mendicant and the detached householder sink into the Kumbhīpāka hell.
If virtuous women and householders were to act in this manner every day,
they would not turn back from saṃsāra due to the fault of transgressing the injunctions.

Thus, according to the statement in the *Agastyasaṃhitā*. In the *Padmapurāṇa*: "In the remembrance, the glorification, and likewise the mental worship of Viṣṇu, there is always the entitlement for all, even for those who have committed great sins."
O moon-faced one, a householder does not attain auspiciousness in this world or the next through mere knowledge alone,
without [the performance of] gifts, fire-offerings, and other such rites.
If a householder should give gifts and so forth, yet fail to offer oblations,
who would perform this daily according to this prescribed rite?
"O lady, one who practices the life of celibacy has no authority to give;
for even to all his gurus, who indeed would give what is desired?"
The fruit obtained from a flower merely smelled is small, not like that which comes from the mind;
therefore, because it is unavoidable and because otherwise there would be no means [to achieve it].
For those whose intellect is not small and who are free from sloth, the ritual may be performed with external flowers.
In the *Tattvasārasaṃhitā* it is said:
"In the *Pañcarātra* and other Tantras, worship is declared to be fivefold."
And these [five] consist of approaching [the teacher], receiving instruction, sacrificing, studying, and practicing yoga.
In that context, what is called "approaching" (abhigamana) is described by the ministers as the ritual preparation of the temple of the deity, such as sweeping and smearing it with cow dung.
The *upādāna* (material cause) would be the union for the means of worshipping the deity;
from that, there would further arise the worship (*ijyā*) with perfumes, flowers, and so forth,
as well as the worship of the pedestal (*pīṭha-pūjā*) and the worship of the deity along with his limbs and retinue.
Recitation is the chanting of the mantra preceded by the contemplation of its meaning;
the thorough reflection upon that scripture is remembered by practitioners as *svādhyāya*.
The contemplation of the identity between the Guru, the Deity, and one's own Self is called Yoga.
It consists of Sālokya (residing in the same realm), Sārūpya (having the same form), Sāmīpya (proximity), and that which is named Sārṣṭi (sharing the same power).
They know that the fruits of these five [observances] are, in order, even union (*sāyujya*).
Regarding those, first the locations are stated in the *Phetkāriṇī*:
"In a solitary linga, in a cremation ground, in an empty house, and at a crossroads."
Established therein, the yogi should accomplish the Vidyā, the Mistress of the Three Worlds.

Regarding the *ekaliṅga*, it is stated in that very same [text]: "Where one does not perceive another *liṅga* within a radius of five *krośas*, that is declared to be an *ekaliṅga*; there, the highest accomplishment (*siddhi*) is attained. (140)
The cremation ground and other such places are described in the *Triśaktiratna*: "That place where the lifeless are burned, crowded with the stakes of corpses,
and surrounded by vultures, jackals, crows, and others greedy for flesh."
That place is known as a cremation ground, frequented by hosts of piśācas,
filled with the nests of crows and other birds, and abounding in human skins, umbrellas, and the like.
That which is abandoned from afar by the citizens, which causes distress to those who dwell there,
and which is overgrown with weeds upon its mansions— such a place is called an empty house.
Where the meeting of four roads occurs simultaneously,
that is called a crossroads (catuṣpatha), which bestows desired objects during the night.
Each preceding one among these is praised as superior, while each subsequent one is inferior.
As stated in the *Kumāritantra*: "In Kāmarūpa, Pūrṇagiri, the divine Oḍḍānaka, Vārāṇasī, Lauhitya, and in the waters of the Karatoyā river."
In Āryāvarta, at Prayāga, and likewise in Brahmāvarta, worship yields infinite fruit; thus it is everywhere, whether in water or on land.
In the absence of that [image], [one should worship] in a sacred house marked with vermilion and other substances,
and adorned with a sword, trident, mace, scimitar, chowrie, fan, and so forth.
It was crowded with canopies and banners, well-perfumed with black agallochum incense,
and beautifully adorned by throngs of courtesans who were young women intoxicated with wine.
In a house filled with the sound of conchs and bells and resplendent with rows of lamps— in such a place, the worship of Kālikā is most beautiful.
The procedure for assuming any form at will and so forth yields the fruit of the [three] qualities. In the Rudrayāmala:
"In a solitary liṅga, in a cremation ground, in an empty house, at a crossroads, upon a corpse, on a funeral pyre, or at the root of a kula-tree."
One should worship the Vidyā with excellent substances— specifically with *yonipuṣpa* flowers, or in the vulva itself, or in a vulva-shaped yantra— using hibiscus, fire, and vermilion.

A person should recite [the mantra] six thousand times at each junction of the day (saṃdhyā), accompanied by offerings of fish and meat, incense, lamps, and various kinds of food oblations (naivedya).
By the excellence of this great vidyā, it grants accomplishment through mere recitation;
established therein, the yogi shall achieve the vidyā that liberates from the three worlds.

141) In the dialogue between Hara and Gaurī: "She should be worshipped with effort in an empty house, at a crossroads, in a temple of Śiva, at the root of a bilva tree, and always in the kula-maṇḍala."
In the *Vīratantra* it is also said: "Every time is auspicious; no inauspicious time exists anywhere. There is no distinction between day and night, or between twilight and the dead of night.
And in the *Phetkāriṇī*: "If all [rites] such as the offering of oblations (*bali*) and worship are performed at night..."
That becomes inexhaustible through the grace of the goddess Tārā.

Now, regarding the five purifications (*pañcaśuddhi*) in the *Kulārṇava*: "The purification of the self, the place, the vessel, the substance, and fifthly, the purification of the deity— O Goddess, as long as these are not performed, there is truly no worship of the deity."
The purification of the self and so forth will be explained later.
[The ground] has been made like the surface of a mirror by means of sweeping, smearing, and other such acts;
it is adorned with canopies, incense, lamps, and the like, and graced by extended banners.
The painting with powders of five colors is called the purification of the site;
thereafter, the best of practitioners, contemplating the mantra within his heart, [proceeds].
With his mind not turned outward, the yogi should then enter the sacrificial ground.
According to the *Kumārīkalpa*: "The knower of mantras, having brought water with the mantra *tāra-vajrodake hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*, should then purify the seat on his right."

"On the left" means in the direction of the left. Likewise: "Having first extracted the Praṇava and likewise the seed-syllable of Lañjā (Hrīṃ), then [the word] 'viśuddha', followed by 'sarvapāpāni śamaya'."
At the end of "aśeṣa," there should be the word "vikalpam"; remove that which follows it.
O Dear One, the mantra for washing the feet consists of the *kūrca* seed-syllable (*hūm*).
The *vedādya* (the beginning of the Vedas), as well as *māyā* and *svāhā*, are considered the mantra for sipping water (*ācamana*).
In the *Tārārahasyavṛtti*, a reversal of the order of the mantras for washing the feet and sipping water is stated;
furthermore, in the first mantra, the word *dharmagātrī* is placed after the letter *su* and before the word *viśuddha*.

Immediately after the *kūrca* seed-syllable, it is stated: *phaṭ svāhā*. The tradition follows exactly this. In the *Pheravīya*, having performed the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*) twice and tied the topknot (*śikhā*), one then performs the purification of the ground with the mantra: *maṇidhari vajriṇi śikhariṇi sarvavaśaṅkariṇī huṃ phaṭ svāhā*.
The binding of the topknot (*śikhābandhana*) is taught in the *Matsyasūkta*. The purification of the ground will be explained below.
In the *Bhairavatantra*: "Having sipped [water] with the three variations of *Tārā*, one should wash the hand with *Māyā*."
142) Having wiped the lips twice with "strīṃ hūṃ," one should wash the hands with "phaṭ" syllables.
By touching the mouth, nose, eyes, ears, navel, chest, head,
and arms with Vairocana and the other [deities], one is liberated from all sins.
Having sipped water (ācamana) and become Bhairava, one beholds her within a year through various forms of Tārā—namely, in the forms of Ekajaṭā, Nīla, and Sarasvatī. As stated in the *Uttara-tantra*:
"Having sipped water, attained purity, and being well-bathed, [one should proceed] to the worship of the deity."
Standing outside the altar of worship at a distance of four cubits, one should [visualize] with the mind.
If at home, standing at the doorway, one should bow the head to the guru and mentally salute one's chosen deity as well as the guardians of the directions.
Whatever sin was previously accumulated, whether on that day or on another, shall not be destroyed by expiatory rites; one should indeed remember that sin with the mind.
To remove that evil, one should recite these two verses:
"O Goddess, my mind, which was natural, has become overcome by sin."
Extract that evil from my mind: *hūṃ phaṭ* and homage to you!
The sun, the moon, Yama, Time, and the five great elements—
These nine are the witnesses here of one's auspicious and inauspicious karma;
then, [one should recite] "Hūṃ Phaṭ" toward the sides, above, and below.
Then, looking at oneself with a gaze of wrath, one should become well-disposed.
When this act of expelling sin has first been performed in this manner,
whatever sin is most firm remains far away.
By performing worship in the past, one returns once more to one's own station;
furthermore, whatever sin may be very slight, it goes to destruction.
For one who has abandoned all evil during worship, whatever is desired shall be attained in an instant.

In the *Svatantrottaratantra*: "Having driven away all the hosts of obstacles situated on the earth and in the sky with unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*) mixed with white mustard seeds and sesame seeds, one should sit upon the seat."
In the *Yāmala*: "The practitioner should perform the expulsion of spirits with this mantra;
once it has been performed on the site for the worship of the deity, the spirits depart to a distance."
While those beings remain there, the greedy ones constantly plunder the food offering and the mandala, and the deities do not accept them.
Oṃ! May those beings depart who reside upon the earth;
may those beings who create obstacles perish by the command of Śiva.
In the Bhairavatantra: "Then, having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), one should prepare the general offering (sāmānyārghya).
Thereafter, one should fashion a mandala consisting of a circle, a triangle, and the form of the earth."
Having worshipped the supporting power (ādhāraśakti), one should place the vessel upon it;
having purified the vessel with the weapon-mantra (astra-mantra), one should fill it with the heart-mantra (hṛdaya-mantra).
Having invoked the sacred ford (tīrtha), one should deposit it with the syllable Om (praṇava) and offer perfumes and other articles;
one should indeed display the cow-mudrā (dhenumudrā)—this is considered the procedure for the general arghya offering.
O Goddess of gods, one should worship the deities of the gateway with the general offering (sāmānyārghya)—
namely Gaṇeśa, Kṣetrapāla, Vaṭuka, and Yoginī, as well as Gaṅgā, Yamunā, Lakṣmī, and Vāṇī— and then enter.
In the Tantra: [one should worship] Gaṇeśa preceded by the seed-syllable *gāṃ*, likewise Vaṭuka preceded by *vāṃ*, Kṣetrapāla preceded by *kṣāṃ*, and likewise Yoginī preceded by *yāṃ*.
In the upper, left, right, and lower directions respectively;

"upper" and so forth refers to the threshold according to the context. Thus, they worship Gāṃ Gaṅgā, Yāṃ Yamunā, Śrīṃ Lakṣmī, and Aiṃ Sarasvatī. Likewise, [they place] dūrvā grass and other items all around the house.
One should meditate upon the obstacles as being scattered and driven away. Its mantra is as follows:
*kumārīke*, first uttering *paṇavam*, then *sarvavighnān*, followed by the two words *utsāraya*, then *hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*.
With this very mantra, the wise one should dispel obstacles;
having first uttered the Praṇava, followed immediately by "rakṣa rakṣa" (protect, protect).
One should purify the ground with the mantra *hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*.

According to the Tantrikas, purification consists of sprinkling water. This purification of the ground was previously mentioned in the *Pheravī* [Tantra] as being for the purpose of dispelling obstacles. Likewise—
Then, one should first extract the Praṇava (Oṃ) for the Pavitra-vajra and other rites;
after that, [the syllables] Rakṣa twice, followed by Hūṃ Phaṭ Svāhā.
And with this very mantra, one should perform the consecration of the ground.
Now, the procedure for the seat is stated in the *Svatantratantra*: "Having drawn a triangle on the ground, one performs the worship of the Support-Energy (*ādhāraśakti*) and so forth.
Merupṛṣṭha is declared to be the seer (*ṛṣi*), and Sutala is said to be the meter (*chanda*)."
O Goddess, the Tortoise is the deity here for the placement of the seat;
its application (viniyoga) is declared to be for one who, having assumed the seat, should recite [the mantra].
144) O Earth, by you the worlds are supported; O Goddess, you are supported by Viṣṇu.
And you, O auspicious one, support me; make this seat pure.
Having thus taken hold [of them], O Goddess of Gods, one should cast those *kuśa* grasses right there.
Regarding the word "those *kuśas*": this is a restatement of what is obtained from the alternative view that is about to be described. Likewise:
"Having uttered the seed-syllable of *māyā*, then [the mantra] 'to the Support-Power (*ādhāra-śakti*)'..."
Having inscribed the lotus-seat (kamalāsana), one should worship it with the mantra ending in "namo".
"Namontam" means that one should join the word "kamalāsanapada" (the word for the lotus-seated one) ending in the dative case with the word of salutation (*namaḥ*).
In the *Mantracūḍāmaṇi*: "There, one should worship the seat made of clay as the pedestal (*pīṭha*) with the pedestal-mantra:
*Oṃ aiṃ klīṃ kāmapīṭhāya*. This is said to end with 'hṛdayāya' (to the heart)."
There, having assumed the heroic posture (vīrāsana), the practitioner should then purify himself.
As stated in the *Uttaratantra*: "Then, one should sit upon that excellent seat with the self-mantra (*ātman-mantra*)."

Whatever defect of the seat there may be—such as being poorly crafted by an unskilled artisan—is destroyed if it remains unknown; however, if one sits upon it while reciting the mantra, [the defect is neutralized].
The practitioner should know that the first syllable of his own name, joined with the letter *sa* (for Soma) and the letter *ma* (for Āmiṣa),
is his personal mantra (*ātman-mantra*).
The half-moon is the essence of Soma. In the *Yāmala*:
"There, one should protect oneself by means of the application of a rampart of fire;
one should indeed mentally visualize a rampart all around with the seed-syllable of fire."
At the end of the syllable ĀḤ, with "Surekhe" and then "Vajrarekhe," one should utter "HŪṂ PHAṬ SVĀHĀ" over the mandala upon the corpse-seat.
Regarding the specific posture, the *Matsyasūkta* states: "Seated upon a soft woolen blanket, or on other soft materials,
or seated upon a grass mat (*viṣṭara*), one should accomplish the highest perfection."

Having obtained the skin of a black antelope, a leopard's skin, or likewise a hairless woolen blanket (kambala), from one fallen in battle or killed while still hairless, or having obtained it six months after death, either on a funeral pyre or near it; ||| 10.54 ||
And one should prepare a yellow or white-colored seat.

The mention of the "six-month-elapsed foot" is a reiteration of the soft woolen blanket for the sake of showing extreme reverence; its placement at the end follows from the context. As it is also stated in the *Śrīkrama*:
"From after six months until ten months, as before."
145) A child who has fallen from the womb and died before the eighth month is called a *bāla*; one who dies thereafter is a *śava* (corpse).

That which was described as "a child" (*bāla*) by the final [verse] is stated in the *Matsyasūkta* by means of the term "tender" (*mṛdu*). In the *Tantra*: "A male who has undergone the tonsure ceremony but whose initiation (*upanayana*) has not yet occurred—if he dies in his fifth year, they know him alone to be 'tender' (*komala*)."
Up until the age of five, one is a "child without the tonsure" (*bālamacūḍaka*).
In this context, the neuter gender is used according to Tantric convention. As stated in the *Vīratantra*:
"In the absence of a corpse, one should imagine a seat in the form of a corpse."
With fifty [strings] one becomes Brahmā, but with half of that, a *viṣṭara*.
In the *Kālītantra*: "In the absence of a corpse, one should prepare a seat in the form of a corpse.
Because of the statement "in the absence of a corpse," there is not even a seat of *kuśa* grass as a secondary substitute for the corpse of a bound soul (*paśu*).
This is because eligibility for a secondary substitute belongs only to one who has eligibility for the primary rite. In the *Svatantratantra*:
A renunciant or a celibate student may sit upon a blanket, or on one that is red or black, or even upon a tiger skin; however, he should sit upon a black skin.
A tiger skin leads to all accomplishments; the skin of a deer brings the accomplishment of knowledge;
a cloth seat removes disease, while one made of cane increases affection.
Silk is said to bestow nourishment, while a woolen blanket grants all accomplishments;
it may be white or black, but a red blanket is especially meritorious.
A seat made of monkey skin that is soft and supple, whether it has fallen on a battlefield or was killed by a living creature, is prescribed.
Or one may fashion from the skin of a woman who has miscarried, or from the skin born of a womb, an image in the form of that very body; O Śivā, then perform the worship.
Or one should prepare a seat with cloth dyed with the blood of a seasonal animal;
or a throne fashioned from the wood of a cremation ground, or born of sacrificial timber.
A householder who has not received initiation should never enter [the sacred area] wearing the skin of a black antelope;
likewise: [the seat should be] one or two cubits in length and four finger-breadths in height.
The wise practitioner should perform the installation and worship on a pure seat.
However, some maintain that in the *Svatantra* and other tantras, the procedure for the woolen blanket (*kambala*) and so forth is not independent;
rather, it serves as a covering for the *vīrāsana*, because the *vīrāsana* is mandatory. As it has been said:
In the Kālītantra: "O Goddess, that man who recites the mantra of Kālikā without the corpse-seat (mṛtāsana) should be known as a denizen of hell for as long as the dissolution of all beings."

146) In reality, this [practice] is supreme for heroes (*vīra*). Here, regarding the corpse-seats (*śavāsana*), there is an optional choice (*vaikalpika*). A wooden seat (*kāṣṭhāsana*) is prescribed for others [than heroes], while it is prohibited [for them]. In the *Brahmayāmala*:
"Grass, sprouts, wood, stone, and likewise clay..."
A bamboo seat, a cloth, or the bare ground alone as a seat.

O Goddess, one should thus avoid these eight kinds of seats. Regarding the rule for cloth seats in rites performed for specific desires, the Vārāhītantra states: "Facing north, one should sit upon a soft seat."
Success is swift with a woolen blanket; liberation is attained with a tiger skin.
In a deer-skin seat there is prosperity; with a yellow garment, there is subjugation;
on a wooden seat there would be the destruction of accomplishment; and on the bare ground, the destruction of one's lineage.

If the leaf is made of bark, one becomes poor; if even of grass, one’s prosperity is destroyed. Liberation is attained with a mat of *kuśa* grass, while the *śrīparṇī* wood is praised for [attaining] fortune.
In the absence of mango and bilva trees, even on a *picumarda* tree,
or on an *āmra*, *nimba*, or *kadamba* tree, sitting [there] causes total destruction.
The mango and the hog-plum;
the jackfruit, the *kiṃśuka*, and the *vakula* have had their splendor destroyed.
In the *Kumārikalpa*: "One should sit in the *vīrāsana* posture after having worshipped the seat itself."
Having sat there according to the prescribed rite and having eaten the substance along with its causal ingredients.
The *vīrāsana* is described in the *Gorakṣasaṃhitā*:
"Then, having placed one foot upon one thigh, he remains seated.
In the *Yāmala*: "At night he should perform [the practice] facing north; during the day, facing east or north."
A wise person should always perform the worship of Śiva while facing north.

In the *Phetkāriṇī*: "One seeking knowledge, being composed, should perform everything while seated in the lotus posture (padmāsana), facing either east or north, according to the sequence to be described."
One desiring prosperity should stand facing west here with the svastika diagram.
In the *Kālikā-purāṇa*: "Among the divisions of the directions, the northern direction is the giver of pleasure to Śiva;
therefore, seated facing that [direction], one should always worship Caṇḍikā."

In this regard, the inclusion of the "cause" (hetu) is also stated in the Bhāvacūḍāmaṇi: "O Maheśvara, having experienced [the state] without the cause, one who is possessed by agitation shall perform neither worship nor the ritual seat, nor meditation, nor contemplation."
Therefore, having eaten and drunk, one should worship the Supreme Goddess.
Also, in the *Kulārṇava*: "O Dear One, without the consecration of the ritual substance (*dravya-adhivāsa*), one should neither meditate nor recite mantras.
O Great Goddess, for those who do so [without it], there is suffering at every step."
Without liquor there is no mantra, and without mantra there is no liquor;
since they are mutually contradictory, how can worship be performed?
Having ascertained the removal of those doubts from the mouth of the Guru, one should worship [the deity],
adorned with visualization, sprinkling, meditation, mantra, and mudrā.
The substance should be fit for satiation and a cause for the gratification of the deity. Inspection is performed with the divine gaze; sprinkling with water consecrated by the root mantra;
meditation upon it as nectar; the mantra is recited eight times; and the mudrā is that called the "cow" (dhenu).
The experts of the tradition [state]: "This is an elliptical indication; it should be understood that all the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) to be mentioned hereafter are also to be performed.

This practice is carried out because of the continued existence of the remnants from the worship of the previous day. Here, *tarpaṇa* (satiating) means drinking. However, this refers to those other than Brahmins, because for a Brahmin, the taking up of such [liquor] is prohibited.
Now, [one might object]: "Brahmins should always drink it; Kṣatriyas, upon the arrival of battle;
Vaiśyas, when employing wealth; but Śūdras never at all"—so it is stated in the *Kulārṇava*.
Furthermore, in the *Samayācāra*, it says: "In the Sautrāmaṇī sacrifice and in the Kulācāra, a Brahmin may drink liquor."
In the Kṛta age, the Goddess was worshipped by the four castes in succession with milk, clarified butter, honey, and flour-offerings; in the Tretā age, she was worshipped with ghee by all classes.
If it is argued that since it is stated in the *Yāmala*—“In the Dvāpara age, [the Goddess] was worshipped with honey of all varieties;
in the Kali age, the Goddess is to be worshipped with *āsava* liquors alone”—how can there be no qualification for a Brāhmaṇa? It is replied: Brāhmaṇas are [like] kings...
"The others [should worship] with meat, milk, clarified butter, honey, and fermented liquor," as stated in the *Laghustava*;

"Indeed, there are different substances according to the distinction of the sequence of castes (*varṇa*)," as stated in the *Jñānārṇava*; and "A Brāhmaṇa should worship Śivā with a purely *sāttvika* substance."
Having stated the classification of intoxicants (āsava), [the text continues]: "In this manner, even a Kṣatriya should never offer liquor made from flour (paiṣṭikī).
Coconut water should be offered in a vessel of bell-metal (kāṃsya), and likewise cow's milk and honey in a vessel of copper."
The gift [of a cow] belongs to the Kṣatriya and the Vaiśya, but never to a twice-born Brāhmaṇa;
for by the mere act of giving it away in this manner, the Brāhmaṇa would become short-lived.
In the *Mahākālasaṃhitā*: "The Brāhmaṇas should be gratified with milk, those born of the royal lineage with ghee, the Vaiśyas with honey, and those of the Śūdra caste with *āsava* liquors.
And in the *Bhairavītantra*: "Where the offering and worship of wine is specifically prescribed as mandatory..."
"A Brāhmaṇa should prepare honey and wine in copper vessels. (148) Thus it is stated in the *Kulacūḍāmaṇi*: "By giving liquor, a Brāhmaṇa falls from his very status as a Brāhmaṇa;
by giving the blood from his own body, he incurs the sin of self-slaughter."
In the *Haṃsamāheśvaratantra*, within the section on the characteristics of the Kali age (*kalidharma-prakaraṇa*) in the *Gṛhyapariśiṣṭa*,
the teacher Ahinātha has stated that the taking of *surā* (liquor) is prohibited in the *Sautrāmaṇī* sacrifice;
furthermore, regarding the phrase "it should always be drunk by Brāhmaṇas," this is due to the elision (*praśleṣa*) of the letter *a* [to form *na peyam*].
Now, regarding breath control (prāṇāyāma): whatever action is performed without breath control is fruitless.
Therefore, those who seek auspicious results should practice breath control with great effort.

In the Tantra: "The wise practitioner should perform three breath-controls (prāṇāyāmas) using either the root-mantra, the syllable Om (praṇava), or the seed-syllable of the mantra, according to the prescribed rule."
Likewise: "One should fill the breath with sixteen [counts] and perform *kumbhaka* with four times that;
one should exhale with half of the *kumbhaka*, or if unable, with a fourth of it."
Elsewhere also: "In the event of inability to do that, the restraint of breath (prāṇasaṃyama) should be performed with the fourth [vowels];
without prāṇāyāma, there is no fitness for worship and other rites."
In the *Viśuddheśvara*: "One should perform three breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*) with the Vidyā immediately thereafter. In the *Samayāṅgamātṛkā*:
"One should fill the air through the *iḍā* [nāḍī] once with the root-vidyā."
O fair-faced one, one should perform the retention of breath (kumbhaka) in the central channel for a duration equal to the number of Vedas.
One should exhale through the path of Piṅgalā according to the sequence of the number of eyes (two),
again and again in that same order, so that it occurs three times.
In the Kumārītantra: "Then, having carefully brought a sixteen-year-old woman—one who is youthful, intoxicated with passion, well-attired, and possessing a beautiful smile—"
The wise man should place on his left that woman who always delights in him, who is full of longing, whose forehead is marked with vermilion, and who is affectionate toward the practitioner.
The term "left" (*vāma*) is an elliptical expression; it should also be understood as meaning "above the worshipped yantra," as stated in the *Vīracūḍāmaṇi*.

(149) In the *Samayācāra*: "Having placed the hand on the left shoulder and having placed one's own body upon its lap, worship should be performed according to the rule with an attitude free from laziness."
One should perform the ritual rotation— the consecration of the water for sipping, the flowers, and so forth,
as well as the mantra for tying the knot and the purification of body, speech, and mind.

In this context, the ritual action itself is designated by means of its mantra. The mantra for sipping water (ācamana) has already been written above. And the mantra for the consecration of the flower is found in the Kumārī-kalpa:
"For the consecration of the flower, one should first utter the Praṇava."
The word "śatābhiṣeka" [is used], and after that, "śatābhīti."
The word "sekha" is proclaimed, followed by "hūṃ phaṭ svāhā";
then the Praṇava, Puṣpaketu, and likewise Rājārhata.
Puṣpe puṣpe mahāpuṣpe supuṣpe puṣpasambhave | puṣpacayāvarkīṇe ca hūṃ phaṭ svāhā tataḥ param ||
With this mantra, one should perform the purification of the flower for the Goddess;
then, according to the tradition, one should tie a knot in the hem of the upper garment with scattering materials while reciting the *śikhābandhana* mantra as prescribed for the *saṃdhyāvandana*.
The mantra for purifying the body and so forth is stated in the Kumārītantra: "Having first extracted the Praṇava (Oṃ), and immediately after that,
Hūṃ Phaṭ Svāhā— this is declared to be the mantra for the purification of body, speech, and mind."

*Rakṣa rakṣa hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*—this mantra should be used for self-protection. Next, one should perform the purification of the hands (*karaśuddhi*). The method for this is stated in the *Uttaratantra*:
"Having formed the hollow of the joined palms, [one should recite] on the left and right sides..."
Having bowed to the Guru, Gaṇeśa, and one's own chosen deity (iṣṭadevatā) before them;
Taking garlands, perfumes, and flowers smeared with sandalwood, the practitioner who knows the mantras should properly rub his hands together and make them fragrant.
Having taken it in the left hand, churned it, and smelled it again,
one should discard it from afar toward the northeast using the mantra that will be described hereafter.
The mantra is as follows: "May all those who harm me, the assailants, go to dissolution;
may death, disease, fear, and afflictions fall upon the head of the enemy.
And the renunciation is performed with the *nārācamudrā*. The practitioner of mantra should cast the flower to the north with the *nārācamudrā*.

From the *Sārasaṃgraha*: In the *Uttaratantro*, it is stated that for the purpose of cleansing the hands, the practitioner should take a flower with his fingertip while reciting the Viṣṇu-mantra, in order to rub [it]. (150)
One should crush the flower with both hands using the *prāsāda* mantra;
one should wipe it clean with the *kāmabīja* mantra and then smell it again with the *brāhma* mantra.
One should perform the renunciation with a cheerful mind, especially toward the northeast;
having wiped [the vessel] with the left hand, one should smell it with the left hand.
One should cast this flower held in the palm of the hand toward the northeast;
when this is done, there shall be incomparable purification of the two palms.
The wise know that the fingertips become pure by grasping flowers;
the two palms become purified by being rubbed with the ointment.
From the wiping away [of the hand], the back of the hand [is purified]; from the nose, the tip of the nose is supreme. The sacred fords (tīrthas) come together at the tip of the nose and the hand.
Therefore, O Bhairava, these rites should be performed with effort;
at the beginning, [the letter] is colored by the Moon (u) and joined with the Void (śūnya).
This Vaiṣṇava mantra is considered to be joined with the end of Rudra at the top.
The letter *ha* is near the end; at the beginning, on the head, is the moon—the anusvāra as a half-moon. The end of Rudra is the long vowel *u*; by that, [the syllable] becomes *hūṃ*.
It is also endowed with the color of Vāsudeva, beginning with the final letter.
The *prāsāda* mantra is said to be joined with the crest-bindu of Śambhu.
The letter *ha* is at the end and at the beginning; Vāsudeva is the letter *o*. From that, there is a euphonic combination (*sandhi*), resulting in *hau*.
The crest-bindu of Śambhu is the half-moon (*ardhacandra*).
The seed-syllable of desire (kāma-bīja) should be known as Vāsudeva [the letter A] with the lunar drop (bindu);
the consonants are the first and the last, preceded by the final labial letter.
The first and the last of the two [consonant groups], followed by a consonant and the syllable Om—
this is declared to be the seed-syllable of Brahmā, which destroys all sins.
"It is to be understood from another tantra"—this is the remainder [of the sentence]. He extracts the seed-syllable of Brahmā:
Vāsudeva is the syllable *o*; Indu is the half-moon (*ardhacandra*); Bindu is the anusvāra; thus, *oṃ*. The first of the dentals is the letter *ta*;
a consonant devoid of a vowel. The final dental phoneme is *sa*; that which has this as its initial part is *sat*.
After the *praṇava* (Oṃ), at the end of the *praṇava*, there are two [syllables], the first and the last, which are two *takāra*s. Regarding that, he states the distinction:
"the second *takāra* comes after. A consonant is devoid of vowel. Thus, "Oṃ tatsat" is produced.
Having completed the purification of the hands (*karaśuddhi*), one should then perform the three claps (*tālatraya*).
151) The preceptor should also perform the binding of the directions, both above and below, with the root mantra.
The splendor generated by that [mantra] shall provide protection on all sides.
In the *Nīlatantra*: "If a person reciting my mantra does not know the *kullukā*, he will meet his death or become insane."
The mantra of Tāriṇīkullukā, excluding the kullukā,
should never be recited by a wise man for the sake of the twice-born.
And by wearing the *kullukā* upon one's head, one obtains the fruit of all sacrifices;
there is no other deliberation on this matter anywhere—this is the consensus of Virūpākṣa.
For men who have excluded the *kullukā*, there may be attendance at a sacrifice;
however, my worship is always in vain, and likewise my sacrifice.
The *kullukā* of the Tārā mantra is the supreme three-syllable mantra;
for Mahogrā, worship is always performed with the *kullukā* as the supreme element in the rite of worship.
And whenever one performs the practice of hymns, mantras, vows, and so forth,
if she is not performed [as the presiding deity], all of that becomes fruitless.
In the Matsyasūkta: "That lowest of men who mutters the six-syllabled supreme Brahman, as well as the mantra of Tāriṇī Caṇḍikā devoid of its *kulluka*..."
That stealer of the Veda,
together with his ancestors, is cooked in the most terrible Kumbhīpāka hell, which is filled with blood.
The knower of mantras should always recognize the *kullukā* in the six-syllabled mantra;
he should bear it upon the region of his head, for it bestows all desires.
By wearing the *kullukā* upon one's head, one obtains the fruit of all sacrifices;
its authority is universal, according to the consensus of Virūpākṣa.
If men perform a sacrifice while excluding the Kulluka, their attendance at the sacrifice shall be in vain;
all those sacrifices will become fruitless, and they shall go to hell.
Those who recite the Tārīṇī mantra without knowing the goddess Kullukā undergo the destruction of their lineage and go to hell.
The worship of the Goddess (devīpūjā) is always in vain, as is the sacrifice to the Goddess (devīyāga).

Furthermore, the Kullukā-mantra has already been stated in the section on the extraction of mantras (mantroddhāra-prakaraṇa). Therefore, having written the Kullukā-mantra in the form of the three-syllabled Nīlasarasvatī and placed it upon one's head, one should perform the daily worship (nityārcana).
"One should perform [it]"—this is the meaning established by the context. However, in the *Brahmasaṃhitā*: "The *tāriṇī* is declared to be the *kullukā*, which always bestows all accomplishments.
O Sage, listen with a one-pointed mind as I shall explain its extraction. (152)
Having first uttered the Praṇava, likewise the pair of words "Padme," then the word "Mahāpadme," and finally the auspicious word "Padmāvati."
"Māye svāhā"—this mantra consists of seventeen syllables;
it is declared to be a protector, O supreme practitioner, at all times.
Likewise: "Alternatively, the three-syllabled mantra may become the *kullukā-tāriṇī*.
Having performed worship without the *kullukā*, one would go to a miserable state at the end."

"Devī-pūjā is always fruitless"—from such various statements, it is understood that this [worship] is for the sake of the ritual (*kratvartha*). The statement "one would obtain the fruit of all sacrifices" is an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*).
In reality, however, according to the principle of the section on "separateness of connection" (*saṃyogapṛthaktvādhikaraṇa*), by the rule "one offers with curd" (*dadhnā juhoti*)...

By the statement "with curd for one desiring sensory power" (*dadhnendriyakāmasya*), both its status as being for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvarthatva*) and its status as being for the sake of the person (*puruṣārthatva*) are understood;
likewise, it should be noted that here too there is a dual purpose.
As stated in the *Tantracūḍāmaṇi*: "He who, having mastered the knowledge of mantras, worships Vāsudeva..."
One correctly attains that fruit and shall go to union with Hari.
Vāsudeva, Hara, Brahmā, Tāriṇī, and Prakṛti are always one form;
they should always be meditated upon as a single form, and they always abide as a single form.
Likewise, in the *Phetkāriṇī*:
"One whose nails, teeth, hands, and feet are perfectly pure, who is joyful-minded regarding the faults of others, who observes silence,
who is devoted to the lotus-feet of Hari and Hara, shall possess long life and become an abode of Sarasvatī."
By such statements as these, it is understood that the worship of Hari is an ancillary part (*aṅga*) following the retention of the *kullukā-vidyā*.
In the *Ekavīrākalpa*, within the section on preliminary rites (*puraścaraṇa*), it is stated:
"At the time of reciting the mantra, one should always carefully avoid one's wife."
One should avoid the Vaishnava ritual manual; one should avoid even a leaf of Tulasī.

Likewise, in the dialogue between Hara and Gaurī, following the narration of the Thousand-Name Stotra: "Whatever names of the primary enemy exist here, those alone should be taken as appropriate for the ritual; never any others."

By such statements as these, it is determined that [the omission] causes a deficiency in the worship and other rites. Therefore, an option (vikalpa) is determined, just like the injunctions "one takes the ṣoḍaśin cup in the Atirātra" and "one does not take the ṣoḍaśin cup in the Atirātra. Just as in the case of taking the ṣoḍaśin cup in the Atirātra, one postulates an abundance of fruit for that alternative, so it is here as well.

For if the result were already established, it would follow that [the mantra] lacks authority, being characterized by non-performance; therefore, the statement that "one obtains that fruit correctly" is consistent. In reality, however, because of the scriptural injunction *mantrakāle* (at the time of the mantra) and because of its co-occurrence with the wife's speech...

The worship [of the deity] results only in the deficiency of the *puraścaraṇa* (preliminary rite), and not in the deficiency of the daily (*nitya*) worship; for that would contradict the statement in the *Tantracūḍāmaṇi*. Likewise, since it is mentioned in the section on hymns (*stotra*), it should be inferred that the recitation of the deity’s name and so forth is merely an ancillary part (*aṅga*) of the recitation. Therefore—

The prohibition regarding *puraścaraṇa* and other such rites applies to one who is already engaged in daily worship (*nityapūjā*), because otherwise there would be the logical fallacy of prohibiting something that is not applicable. Nor is this prohibition of worship— pertaining to the case of the *pañcāyatana-dīkṣā*— restricted solely to daily worship.
This must be stated [as an objection]: because it contradicts the *Tantracūḍāmaṇi*, and because here there is a prohibition of initiation (*dīkṣā*) into the five-deity system (*pañcāyatana*).
For this very reason, the prohibition of worshipping that [system], even though it was not previously applicable, is intended as a censure of the qualified practitioner (*adhikārin*).
Thus, the argument that it is like the phrase "those who speak non-sacrificial dialects" (*ayajñīyavaibhāṣāḥ*) is refuted.

Furthermore, by the statement "one should avoid the Vaiṣṇava ritual" (*kalpa*), there is no prohibition of the worship itself, but rather of the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) of that ritual. Thus, the meaning is that one should avoid worshipping the Goddess according to the procedure prescribed for the Viṣṇu-mantra. Therefore...

Having raised the doubt that the worship of one mantra is impossible due to the ritual requirements (*itikartavyatā*) of another mantra, it is stated in that very same [text]: "One should avoid the *tulasī* leaf. Thus, the very act of worship with *tulasī* leaves and so forth is the meaning of the injunction regarding that [worship]; and since that [worship] is not impossible, the prohibition against it can be effectively made.

This is the intended meaning. Thus, worship of Hari is an auxiliary (aṅga) both at the time of daily worship and at the time of occasional worship, such as *puraścaraṇa* and the like. It follows that in its absence, there is an absence of the fruit of the Goddess’s worship. And so, with the words "Those names... and so forth, at the time of reciting the hymn for the purpose of avoiding the fault of sexual intercourse when it is not an occasion for it—
Even the name of Hari should not be uttered during [the forbidden times], much less that of another.

Regarding the possibility of obtaining [the required water] and so forth, and when the secondary alternative (*anukalpa*) of sipping water (*ācamana*) or the recitation of Viṣṇu’s name presents itself, one should employ only those [alternatives] which have been specifically set forth here in this context as applicable to the occasion, and no others. And thus:
Regarding the statement "one should not utter the name of Hari," even here, based on the maxim *vedo vā*,
there is a prohibition against uttering the name of Hari that is not included within a hymn (*stotra*). Alternatively, since a mere explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) would otherwise be purposeless,
if one were to entertain the possibility of [uttering] the Name, one should not even take a leaf of *tulasī* which has become the locus of Hari’s ownership.
The meaning is that one should neither accept nor even touch [it].

Alternatively, there are three types of practitioners (*sādhaka*)—the *divya*, the *vīra*, and the *paśu*. Among them, from the perspective of the *paśu*, the statements in the *Tantracūḍāmaṇi* and other texts establish that [the worship] is an ancillary part of the worship of Hari. From the perspective of the *vīra*...
The secret of the established doctrine (*siddhāntarahasya*) is that passages from the *Ekavīrākalpa* and other texts which prohibit the worship of Hari are to be applied [as exceptions].

Now, regarding the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*), it is stated in the *Bhairavatantra*: "Having placed both hands upon the lap, [one should contemplate] the letter Bha (bhṛgu), joined with the sky (v) and the bindu."
By means of the mantra "sargavān," [one should contemplate] the reality (satattva) joined with Kuṇḍalinī.

Then, having pierced the vital wheels (cakras) and joined the red power of consciousness (citkalā) to the auspicious lotus situated at the head, one should recite slowly while meditating on it at the navel.

Then, having dried his body with the wind expelled through the *vāmanāsikā* (the left nostril) and having burned away his sins with the blazing fire, he [proceeded] by means of the *dakṣā* (the right).
One should recite the seed-syllable of the bride, which has a yellow luster and the form of wind;
meditating on it in the heart while reciting, one should fill it with the breath drawn in through the right nostril.
One should blow the ashes out through the left nostril;
[one should visualize] the syllable HŪṂ, radiant as the full moon, upon the lunar disc on the forehead.
Having become afraid of this recitation, he shall then cast down the nectar;
having caused that bone to be flooded, he should thereafter produce a body.

Thus, by means of the mantra, having sequentially brought the principles (tattvas), the individual soul (jīva), and Kuṇḍalinī to their respective places, I have withdrawn that which consists of Tāriṇī.

In the Vārāhītantra: "The Tantrika should join the vital breath (prāṇa), which has risen from the mūlādhāra, with the Supreme Self (paramātman) at the station of Puṣkara by means of the Haṃsa [mantra] through the path of Brahman (brahmamārga)."
In the Rudrayāmala: One should perform the withdrawal of the phonemes (varṇasaṃhāraka), consisting of the letters from *kṣa* down to *a*.
Having withdrawn them in reverse order, one should unite them with the Supreme Self.
Thereafter, he who would recite the five elements within the Supreme Self should,
according to the method of the sequence of withdrawal in the *Svatantra*, extract the five principles.

The five principles (*pañcatattva*) are the five elements (*pañcabhūtāni*). The method for their extraction is stated in the *Jñānonnayana*: "One should contemplate the place of earth as a yellow square with a thunderbolt (*vajra*), joined with the syllable *laṃ*, extending from the feet to the knees."
One should meditate upon the element of water as being white in color, marked with a lotus, resembling the crescent moon from the knees up to the navel, and joined with its own seed-syllable.
From the navel up to the throat is a red-colored triangle;
together with a svastika and joined with its own seed-syllable, it is the mandala of Fire.
One should contemplate the mandala of wind as black, extending from the throat to the center of the brows;
it is hexagonal, joined with six dots, and should be meditated upon with the seed-syllable.
One should meditate on the space between the eyebrows and the aperture of Brahma as a circular region marked with a banner,
smoke-colored, and joined with its own seed-syllable.
Having meditated thus, one should then dissolve those elements:
earth into water, that [water] into fire, fire into air, and air into space.
Having thus dissolved space into space, and then that space into primordial nature (prakṛti),
one dissolves that power of illusion (māyā-śakti), which is of the nature of the lower Brahman, into the Supreme Self (parātman).
Having thus dissolved the entire manifold of the body and so forth into the Supreme Self,
one should remain for some moments in the form of the Supreme Brahman.
Then [he saw] that evil, resembling a man, accumulated through beginningless existence,
with the murder of a Brahmin as its head and the theft of gold as its two arms.
The heart is joined with the drinking of liquor, and the two hips with violating the Guru’s bed;
the pair of feet consists of association with such persons, while the major and minor limbs are the various types of sin.
One should meditate on Kṛṣṇa to the right, with body hair standing erect due to minor transgressions, with red beard and eyes, and holding a sword and shield at his waist.
In another tantra: One should visualize [the deity] holding a sword and a shield, the size of a thumb, black in color, and facing downwards, within the right side of the belly.

In the *Vīratantra*: "Then one should perform the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*) through the application of the syllables of one's own mantra. In the *Pheravī*: "Having meditated on the *māyā* (the syllable *hrīṃ*) of red color at the navel, one should then contemplate the subtle body consisting of sin as being burnt by the fire produced from it."

One should visualize the syllable *trīṃ* in the heart, yellow in appearance; then, having caused the ashes to be blown away by the wind arising from it, one should contemplate [the syllable] on the forehead.
Having realized that the bone has been drenched by the nectar arising from that *kūrca* which resembles the color of snow, one should contemplate oneself therein.
It is completely free from all suffering, stainless, and of the nature of the deity;
