it is within the water that pervades the universe, upon the pericarp of a white lotus.
In the Rudrayāmala, in the section on the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*) pertaining to Tārā:
"One should fill the body with the mantra by means of the seed-syllable of air (*yaṃ*) through the *iḍā* [nāḍī], using the sixteen vowel-letters. Thus it is said.
There is an option between these two; however, the traditional path is indeed the former one. As stated in the *Yāmala*:
"Then the practitioner, with a steady mind, should perform the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*), having placed his own two hands face upwards upon his own lap."
In the mūlādhāra, one should contemplate Kulakuṇḍalī, whose nature is the root-vidyā,
coiled like a sleeping serpent, and consisting of three and a half coils.
Like a parrot in a wild rice field, she was slender, the embodiment of all sciences,
resembling ten million flashes of lightning, and encircling the self-manifested linga.
Having meditated upon her with the Haṃsa-mantra, or again with the Praṇava,
or with the Kūrca-bīja, O Goddess, the Guru should contemplate her firmly.

156) Having brought about the unification of those two— the individual self (jīvātman) and the supreme self (paramātman)— one should contemplate the supreme void, wherein the earthly element has dissolved into the waters.
One should contemplate water as being made black by fire, having the form of fire;
or one should meditate on fire as being extinguished by air, having the form of air.
The wind is drawn in by space, and space indeed dissolves into the mind;
the mind is under the control of the ego, while the ego is drawn in by the Great Principle (Mahat).
Then, by its very nature, the Great Principle (mahattattva) should unite with Prakṛti;
it is eternal, consisting of light, and having the nature of the knowledge of Brahman.
She is absolute, solitary, peaceful, devoid of qualities, and of the nature of the Supreme Self;
she is this supreme light and the ultimate state free from all affliction.
The supreme state, whose nature is emptiness, resides in the center of the thousand-petaled lotus.
Likewise: "One should contemplate the syllable *yaṃ*, smoke-colored wind, in the region of the navel;
by that alone, one should dry up the *liṅga* and the body with sixteen measures (*mātrā*)."
Having performed the retention (*kumbhaka*) for sixty-four measures consisting of the *karma* [breath],
one should practice exhalation (*recana*) through the right [nostril] for thirty-two measures, or again by means of that [left].
One should contemplate the red-colored seed-syllable of fire at the base of the penis;
one should burn the body with that linga, which consists of the seat of impurities.
According to the sequence previously described,
the preceptor should likewise exhale through the left nostril by means of that same count.
Having visualized the syllable *vaṃ*, the seed-mantra of Varuṇa, within the hour-glass-shaped vessel (*ghaṭikā*),
one should produce nectar from that thousand-petaled lotus.
Having performed the practices of inhalation (pūraka) and so forth, one should flood [the body] down to the soles of the feet;
one should then visualize the syllable *laṃ*, the seed-syllable of Earth, at the root of the anus.
By that very same sequential method, the wise one should inundate with his intellect the supreme Śāmbhava body, which is entirely liberated from both sin and merit.
Immediately thereafter, one should accomplish [the rite] by that very same path of completion;
with the *so'ham* mantra, one should bring the life-force (*jīva*) into the lotus of the heart.

Furthermore, one should bring that goddess Kuṇḍalinī back to the mūlādhāra. As stated in the Phetkāriṇī-tantra: "The wise man, having extracted with the *praṇava* the Liṅga—which resides in the heart of the task and is consciousness, the witness of all—from the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*) to the outside."
157) Having encased [the body] with that very [mantra], one should hold it above the head;
thus the body, both external and internal, becomes devoid of consciousness.
Having meditated upon the seed-syllable *yaṃ*, smoke-colored, situated in the center of the circle of wind located in the middle of the navel-center, one should purify by means of it.
Then, by means of the seed-syllable *raṃ*, which has the form of fire and is situated within a circle of fire, one should burn [the body] away;
thereafter, it becomes a heap of ashes in the shape of the body.
One should meditate upon the mandala of Varuṇa, situated between the eyebrows or in the heart;
it is shaped like a half-moon and marked with two lotuses and two footprints.
Then, in that manner, one should flood [the area] which has the form of Manu;
having placed the earthly seed-syllable, one should contemplate the golden mandala.

Having divided [the self] into two parts by means of the Praṇava, one should then contemplate the Self there in the form of pure consciousness, and subsequently in the form of the deity of the mantra.
Having described the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi) in the form of breath control (prāṇāyāma), the Uḍḍīśa [Tantra] states:
"Alternatively, having united the Goddess Kuṇḍalinī with the five elements and so forth within the Supreme Self, one should contemplate the identity of those two."

"Through the yoga of meditation, one should contemplate 'I am He, I am He' with the mind. This refers to those who are incapable [of the more elaborate process]. This very sequence is also stated in the *Śāradā-tantra*. In the *Nīla-tantra*:
"Having thus performed the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi), one should contemplate the entire universe as void (*śūnya*)."
The Self is stainless, devoid of qualities, pure, and identical with Tāriṇī.
Then, one should meditate on a red lotus in the intermediate space arising from the syllable Ā; furthermore, above that, one should meditate on a white lotus arising from the syllable ṬAṄ;
and above that, one should again meditate on the syllable DHŪṄ, which resembles the color blue.
Then, with the seed-syllable *hūṃ*, one should meditate upon a scythe adorned with that seed-syllable,
and the body of the Supreme Self situated above that scythe.

Māyā, whose essence is the Word-Brahman (Śabdabrahman), the Mother (Mātṛkā), the Supreme Nature (Parā Prakṛti), was born; from the Mother of the World, space (Ākāśa) arose, and from space, wind (Anila).
From the wind fire arose; from fire, water; and from that, the earth.
From these very elements, he fashioned for himself a body in the form of radiant energy.
One should contemplate that [the deity] has arisen as fit for the propitiation of the divinity.

As stated in the *Vasiṣṭhasaṃhitā*: "Having thus meditated with the mantra 'So'ham' upon that primordial [deity] who is realized at the end of the *nāda*, one should place the portion of the individual soul (*jīvakalā*) from the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*) into the heart. (158)
In the Tantra: "Then the preceptor should project the individual soul (jīva) with the Prāṇamantra.
In the Śāradā: "Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva are declared by those who know the Tantras to be the sages (munayaḥ)."
The meters of the Ṛgveda and Yajurveda have been described by those expert in prosody; now [the meter] of the Sāmaveda is stated.
The deity is said to be the power (śakti) whose nature is consciousness and whose essence is the vital breath (prāṇa).
The heart is said to be [represented] by the guttural class (ka-varga) and by the elements beginning with space (viyat).
Immediately after that, the head is uttered with the letters beginning with *ca* and the word *śabda*;
the topknot (*śikhā*) is proclaimed with the letters beginning with *ṭa* and the sense organs (*jñānendriya*).
The armor is proclaimed by means of the organs of action, beginning with the *ta*-group;
the eye is declared by means of the organs of speech and so forth, beginning with the *pa*-group.
The weapon (astra) of this [deity] is said to be joined with *buddhi* and so forth, along with *yā* and so forth;
the limb-mantras (*aṅgamantra*) of the same class are declared to end in *ātmane*.
One should place the seed-syllable of the noose (pāśa) from the navel down to the feet;
thereafter, one should place the seed-syllable of power (śakti) from the heart down to the navel.
The wise practitioner should place the goad from the crown of the head down to the heart;
then, he should place the seven [vowels] beginning with *ya* in sequence upon the elements within the heart.
Then, the knower of the ritual should place the two syllables of the color of the *haṃsa* separately upon the *prāṇa* and the *jīva*;
with this entire [mantra], he should perform the pervasive placement (*vyāpaka*).
In the *Vīracūḍāmaṇi*, however, the six-limbed placement (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) and other rites are described differently, as follows:
"Between *a* and *ā* is the *ka*-group; between *i* and *ī* is the *ca*-group;
between *u* and *ū* is the *ṭa*-group; and between *e* and *ai* is the *ta*-group."

O Maheśānī, one should perform the placement (nyāsa) of the labial class (pavarga) between *o* and *au*, and the palatal class (yavarga) in the middle of the remaining vowels, as the six limbs beginning with the heart.
Likewise: "Having thus performed the rite of assignment (nyāsa), one should then perform the assignment of the phonemes (varṇanyāsa).
Nārāyaṇa is said to be in the navel, while Māyā is in the middle of the belly."
Having placed the fat on the left shoulder, one should place the marrow and bone in the hands;
one should indeed place the semen on the right foot and space on the left.
O Great Goddess, one should project the Wrathful One from the head down to the feet. Nārāyaṇa says: "Āṃ" is the syllable. In the Śāradā:
"Then one should contemplate the Goddess, who has become the life-force and consists of the universe."

I bow to the goddess who is red in hue, possessing three eyes, and seated in the center of a boat upon a red ocean; she holds in her lotus-like hands a noose, a goad, a sword, a sugarcane bow, arrows, a trident, and a skull-cup.
Then, touching the heart with the lelihāna-mudrā to be described hereafter, one should mutter the prāṇa-mantra.
As for the mantra, it is stated in that very same source:
"At the end of the three-syllabled form beginning with *pāśa*, there should then be the word *amuṣya*."
In this [body], the vital breaths are the breaths in succession, and likewise the individual soul (jīva) is situated here.
May all the senses of this person become [one with] the state of that [deity];
likewise, may the states of speech, mind, eyes, ears, nose, and vital breath [be attained].
"Having come here afterwards, may they remain happily for a long time—thus the two *ṭha*s. This is declared to be the life-force mantra (*prāṇamanu*), which bestows life upon all living beings."
In this context, the name of the deity should be substituted in place of the word *amuṣya*. As it is stated in the Rudrayāmala:
"Whatever form the word *amuka* takes when seen in a mantra, one should employ that specific form of the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*) in that position."

In the *Vasiṣṭha-saṃhitā*: "Then, for the sake of accomplishing the sixteen purificatory rites (*saṃskāras*) beginning with birth, one should perform sixteen repetitions of the *praṇava* and meditate upon the Supreme Power (*parā śakti*)."
Now, regarding the *mātṛkā-nyāsa*, the *Phetkāriṇī-tantra* states: "Mantras become mute without the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the letters;
therefore, for the sake of the successful accomplishment of all mantras, one should first perform the placement of the letters."
In another tantra: "One should fill the breath through the *iḍā* with the vowels and retain it (*kumbhaya*) with the consonants;
then one should exhale through the *piṅgalā* with the sibilants (*ūṣman*) beginning with *ya*."

In the same manner, there should be filling, retention, and then exhalation of the breath through the *iḍā*; thereafter, the triad of filling and the other two [retention and exhalation] should again be performed through both nostrils.

Having performed three breath-control exercises (*prāṇāyāma*), one should thereafter perform the pervasive visualization (*vyāpaka*). [One should contemplate] from the soles of the feet to the crown of the head with the letters beginning with *a* and ending with *kṣa*. In the *Śāradā*: "Brahmā is declared to be the seer (*ṛṣi*), and Gāyatrī is said to be the meter (*chandas*)."
Sarasvatī is proclaimed as the deity by the most excellent of teachers.
The six limbs, joined with the [six] seed-syllables (jāti), should be applied by the teachers in sequence using the six phonemes contained within the non-neuter short and long vowels.
Her face, arms, palms, waist, and chest are adorned with the fifty letters of the alphabet; she wears a radiant crown bound with a crescent moon, possesses full and lofty breasts,
and holds in her lotus-like hands a mudrā, a rosary, a jar brimming with nectar, and a book.
I take refuge in the Goddess of Speech, who bears a pure radiance and possesses three eyes.

In the *Mantratantraprakāśa*: "O Pārvatī, having first projected [the letters] within upon the six supports (*ṣaḍādhāra*), one should project those from the letter 'a' to 'kṣa' externally upon the gross body."
Dakṣiṇāmūrti: One should properly place the vowels upon the lotus of sixteen petals at the throat;
one should place their respective letters on the twelve-petaled lotus at the heart, and place them on the ten-petaled lotus at the navel.
O Goddess, one should place ten syllables at the root of the *liṅga* in the six-petalled [lotus], and likewise four syllables in the four-petalled *ādhāra*. Then, one should assign them.

One should place the internal *mātṛkā* between the eyebrows on two petals as *ha* and *kṣa*. However, in the *Gautamīya-vaiṣṇava*, it is proclaimed that the internal placement consists of pronouncing each letter individually from the *mūlādhāra* up to the head, ending with the word "namas."
Likewise: "One should place the internal Mātṛkā within the four-petalled Mūlādhāra;
and in the six-petalled Svādhiṣṭhāna, which has the form of lightning and the luster of fire, endowed with the six letters ba, bha, ma, ya, ra, and la, O lady of excellent vows."
In Maṇipūra, which has ten petals and resembles a dark blue cloud,
there are the letters from Ḍa to Pha, each adorned with a nasal drop (bindu) upon its head.
In the unstruck (anāhata) twelve-spoked [cakra], resembling the luster of a coral sprout,
joined with the letters from Ka to Tha, which gladdens the heart of the Yoginīs.
In the pure sixteen-petaled [lotus], smoke-colored and adorned with the vowels,
and in the Ājñā-cakra, moon-like and two-petaled, marked by the letters ha, kṣa, and la.
In the thousand-spoked [cakra], resembling gold and adorned with the colors of all [the elements].
In the three lines beginning with 'a', adorned with the three syllables 'ha-la-kṣa',
one should place the supreme bindu in their midst, which consists of creation, maintenance, and dissolution.
Thus, with a concentrated mind, one should meditate; this is the internal nyāsa.
One should meditate upon Viṣṇu, whose nature is consciousness, from the base (mūla) up to the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra).
One should install the *mātṛkā* while satisfying it with streams of nectar dripping from the drops,
pronouncing each individual syllable from the *mūlādhāra* up to the end of the eyebrows.

The placement ending with "namas" is proclaimed as the internal (āntara) placement. The internal Mātṛkā placement should be performed by means of the mind alone, according to the statement in the *Mantratantraprakāśa*: "One should place these [syllables] with flowers, or with the hand excluding the thumb (anāmaya), or even mentally. Here, "anāmaya" means with the hand excluding the thumb (*sāṅguṣṭha*).

161) "The ritual placement (*nyāsa*) with the thumb and the ring finger is accepted everywhere," according to the statement in the *Padyavāhinī*. In this regard, the established rule is as follows: [the placement] upon the form of the deity is performed with flowers; upon one's own body with the *anāmikā* (ring finger); and within the *mūlādhāra* and other centers by means of the mind (*manas*). And this—

Because other mudrās are prescribed therein for cases distinct from the assignment of the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅganyāsa) beginning with the ṛṣi, and so forth, as well as the external mātṛkā; as stated in the Kulārṇava:
"O Kuleśvarī, ascetics and forest-dwellers should perform [the ritual] ending with the withdrawal (saṃhāra)."
For householders, renunciation (nyāsa) occurs at the end of their stay; for those in the [other] stages of life (varṇin), it occurs at the end of their creation.
In the Tantra: "Having performed the internal placement of the Mātṛkā, one should then perform its external placement.
Now, the locations for the placement of the Mātṛkā according to the Gautamīya: "On the forehead, the face, the circle [of the head], the eyes, the ears, the nose, and the two cheeks..."
On the lips, teeth, head, face, and on the joints and tips of the arms and feet.
On the two sides, at the back, at the navel, in the abdomen, in the heart, and on the shoulder;
then on the hump, the shoulder, and starting from the heart, on the pair of hands and feet.
One should place the letters of the Mātṛkā in sequence upon the belly and the face;
they are known to consist of skin, blood, flesh, fat, bone, marrow, and semen.
One should assign the letters beginning with *ya* and *ha*, preceded by the knowledge of the Self and the Supreme,
as follows: in the *Vīracūḍāmaṇi* it is said— on the head, the mouth, likewise the eye, the two ears, the nostrils, the cheek, the lip, the tooth, the tip of the tongue, and the region of the throat.
One should place the *kādi* group on the right hand and the *cavarga* on the left hand;
one should place the *ṭavarga* on the right foot and the *tavarga* on the left.
In the belly, the back, the navel, and the abdomen are the five beginning with the feet;
skin, blood, flesh, fat, bone, marrow, and semen are the constituents (dhātus).
Then one should perform the placement (nyāsa) of the letters beginning with 'ya' in sequence for both the individual soul (jīvātman) and the supreme soul (paramātman):
one should place them on the heart, the right shoulder, the hump, and from the left shoulder.
The best of practitioners should perform the placement [of mantras] starting from the hands and feet up to the head, and then from the head down to the feet.
Thus it has been said. Therefore, there is an option between these two. In the *Kulāvatāra*: "The placement of the fifty syllables is proclaimed in sequence;
[the mantra] begins with *Oṃ* and ends with *Namaḥ*, or else it includes the nasal bindu or is devoid of the bindu."
The arrangement of the fifty phonemes has been taught in sequence by the wise;
now that secret, consisting of both [the vowels and consonants] along with the visarga, is being told.
162) Bestowing wealth when joined with a nasal bindu, and devoid of the bindu at the beginning of a mantra;
bestowing sons when accompanied by a visarga, and bestowing devotion when possessed of both.

The seed-syllable of Māyā-Lakṣmī, or alternatively that beginning with Vāgbhava, or again that beginning with the three seed-syllables, or that beginning with Ramā— these should be installed by the most excellent practitioners.
Now, regarding the placement (nyāsa) of creation and so forth,
in the *Vīracūḍāmaṇi*: "O Maheśānī, one should perform the triad of Mātṛkās— creation, dissolution, and maintenance—
and especially perform the placement as prescribed in the Kalpa."
In the Kulāvatāra: "From creation comes the procreation of sons and the nourishment [of the lineage]; from maintenance comes its protection;
from withdrawal comes the removal of defects; therefore, one should practice this triad."
In the *Śāradā*: "Having meditated upon the Goddess according to the rule, one should place [the letters] endowed with the *sarga* (visarga) through the process of emanation (*sṛṣṭi*);
one should place this same [series] joined with the nasal dot (*bindu*) through the process of withdrawal (*saṃhṛti*) in reverse order."
The wise one should know the previously mentioned [deities], beginning with the Ṛṣis, together with their limbs;
the auspicious Goddess Vāgvallabhā is to be meditated upon upon a seat composed of syllables.

Bow down to the Mistress of Colors (Varṇeśvarī), who holds in her hands a rosary of beads, a young deer, a prominent chisel, and sacred knowledge; who has three eyes, wears the crescent moon upon her crest, is ruddy in hue, dwells within a lotus,
and is bent by the weight of her breasts.
Having placed the letters beginning with Ḍa, starting from the vicinity of the Sargabindu, according to the path of maintenance (sthiti).
In the *Phetkāriṇītantra*, it is stated:

"The placement [of the letters] begins from the abdomen and is considered to abide up to the heart. And since this is taught according to the method of the internal *mātṛkā*, there is in effect no difference whatsoever.
In the *Triśaktiratna*: "Having divided the mantra and the script according to the threefold classification beginning with 'a', one should first assign the *ka*-group, and after that, the *a*-group."
One should then place the *tavarga* (the dental class of consonants); this is proclaimed as the "Station" (*sthiti*).
Likewise, one should place [the letters] beginning with *ya*, starting from *ta* and ending with *ma*, according to their respective positions; or rather, this is declared to be the "Station."

Starting from *bha* and ending with *kṣa*, and beginning with *a* and ending with the last [consonant], one should assign them to the previously mentioned locations; or else, this may be the arrangement.
In the *Śāradā*: "The wise one should know the seers (*ṛṣi*) and so forth previously mentioned, together with their limbs;
here, he should meditate upon the Mistress of the Letters (*Varṇeśvarī*) accompanied by her beloved."

[She] has the luster of vermilion, is adorned with immeasurable ornaments, and possesses three eyes; she holds a book, a rosary, a young deer, and a boon-granting gesture; and [I salute] the Blessed Lady as well, who stands by her side and has a golden body.
One should meditate [on her] holding a book and a rosary of beads in her lotus-like hands.

163) Now, regarding the *mātṛkā-nyāsa*, it is taught in another tantra: One should place [the letters] on the forehead with the middle fingers of both ring fingers; and one should likewise place the index, middle, and ring fingers upon the circle of the face and the two eyes.
The best of practitioners should join the index and ring fingers and place them [on the shoulders];
having placed the thumbs on the ears, he should place the little fingers and thumbs on the nostrils.
Placing the middle fingers on the two cheeks, one should place the middle fingers on the two lips;
placing the ring fingers on the teeth, one should place the middle finger on the crown of the head.

The ring finger and the middle finger should be placed on the mouth; the little finger, the ring finger, and the middle finger on the hand and the two sides; and likewise, they should be placed on the back.
The practitioner should place all of them with the thumbs at the region of the navel and in the belly;
likewise, he should place them all at the heart, on the two shoulders, and at the crown of the head.
The palms [are placed] on the heart, the front of the hands, the feet, the belly, and the mouth;
these are proclaimed as the Mātṛkā-mudrās in their proper sequence.
If one performs the ritual placement (nyāsa) without knowing [the procedure], that placement shall be fruitless.

Regarding this, some [hold] that because of the statement in the *Tantracūḍāmaṇi*, "O Goddess, one should perform the placement preceded by the sixfold placement (ṣoḍhānyāsa)," the sixfold placement is prescribed at the very beginning.
One should perform only the *aṅganyāsa* and *karanyāsa* right here;
the wise person should practice what is prescribed for this [mantra] in this [rite], and should not apply anything else.
Furthermore, based on the statement of the *Phetkāriṇī*, some claim that there is no *mātṛkā-nyāsa*. That is not so—for it is said:
"Mantras become mute without the placement (*nyāsa*) of the letters;
therefore, for the sake of the accomplishment of all mantras, one should first perform the placement of the letters."
Thus, from the *Phetkāriṇī Tantra*:
"One should perform the triad of Mātṛkās as creation, maintenance, and withdrawal;
O Great Goddess, one should especially perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) as prescribed in the *Kalpa*."
And because of the statement in the *Vīracūḍāmaṇi* concerning the section on Tārā: "Therefore, at the outset, the Mātṛkā itself must be deposited.
As for the precedence of the sixfold deposition (*ṣoḍhānyāsa*), that is possible only in relation to other depositions";
this statement from the *Tantracūḍāmaṇi* serves as the decisive authority.
Now, regarding the sixfold deposition (*ṣoḍhānyāsa*), it is stated in the *Tantracuḍāmaṇi*: "I shall proclaim the sixfold [mantra] of Tārā, which is hidden in all tantras,
which pacifies all obstacles, and destroys all sins."
164) She who pacifies great poverty, bestows all prosperity,
grants all desires, is eternal, and confers universal sovereignty.
To a disciple who is endowed with devotion, humble, high-souled, generous,
of noble birth, and devoted to pure conduct;
O Goddess of gods, having prepared it in this manner, one should reveal it to the practitioner;
otherwise, there will be a loss of accomplishment—such is the command issued by Śambhu.
The first assignment is with the Rudras, the second is considered to be with the planets,
the third should be with the world-protectors, and the fourth with the power of Śiva.
The fifth [position] is formed by Tārā and the others; the sixth is said to be by means of the Pīṭhas.
Now, regarding the Rudra-nyāsa:
the Rudras are proclaimed to be fifty-one.
With the letters of the Mātṛkā joined with the Bindu, preceded by the three-syllable seed-mantra.
O Goddess, the wise one should install them in sequence with the mantras *ṅenta*, *ina*, and *monta*.
This three-syllabled *Tāriṇī* is proclaimed as the destroyer of the bonds of worldly existence.
She is blue in color, possesses three eyes, and is seated upon a corpse;
she wears various ornaments and is adorned with Akṣobhya (or a crescent moon) upon her crown.
Having thus meditated upon Tāriṇī for a long time with a concentrated mind, [one should know] "she is accompanied by one. And these [deities] are mentioned in the *Śāradā*:
"Śrīkaṇṭha, Ananta, Sūkṣma, Trimūrti, and Amareśvara."
Arghīśa, Bhārabhūtīśa, Tithīśa, Sthāṇuka, and Hara.
Jhiṇṭīśa, Bhautika, Sadyojāta, Anugraheśvara,
Akrūra, and Mahāsena are the sixteen forms of the vowels.
Afterwards come Krodhīśa, Caṇḍeśa, Pañcāntaka, and Śivottama;
then Ekarudra, Kūrma, Ekanetra, and Caturānana.
Ajeśa, Sarvasomeśa, as well as Lāṅgalin and Dāruka;
Ardhanārīśvara, Umākānta, Aṣāḍhin, and Daṇḍin.
There are those known as Adri, Mina, and Meṣa; likewise Lohitāśva and Śikhin;
Chagalaṇḍa and Dviraṇḍeśa; and those named Mahākāla and Bālin.
Likewise, there are those known as Bhujaṅgeśa, Pinākīśa, and Khaḍgīśa;
as well as Śvetabhṛgvīśa, Nakuli, Śiva, and Saṃvarttaka.
165) "These Rudras are remembered as being red in color, holding tridents and skull-cups.

Regarding the phrase "endowed with the *bindu*," and so forth: by that [rule], the applications are such as *hrīṃ trīṃ hūṃ aṃ śrīkaṇṭheśāya namaḥ*, *hrīṃ trīṃ hūṃ āṃ ananteśāya namaḥ*, and so on. However, some [hold]...
They perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) of these [deities] together with the powers (śaktis) such as Pūrṇodarī and others. Regarding these powers, the Śāradā states:
"Pūrṇodarī, Virajā, and after that Śālmalī;
Lolākṣī, Vartulākṣī, and Dīrghaghoṇā are proclaimed."
Sudīrghamukhī and Gomukhī, likewise Dīrghajihvā,
Kuṇḍodarī and Ūrdhvakeśī, as well as Vikṛtamukhī.
Then Jvālāmukhī is to be known, followed by Ulkāmukhī; Suśrīmukhī and Vidyāmukhī—these are the powers of the vowels.
Mahākālī and Sarasvatī are endowed with all supernatural powers;
Gaurī is the knowledge of the three worlds, and beyond that is the power of the mantra.
Ātmaśakti, Bhūtamātā, and likewise Lambodarī are considered [the powers]; furthermore, Drāviṇī, Nāgarī, Khecarī, and Mañjarī.
Rūpiṇī, Vīriṇī, Kākodaryā, Pūtanā,
Bhadrakālī, Śaṅkhinī, and Garjinī are likewise the Yoginīs.
Kālarātri, Kubjinī, Kapardinī, and Vajriṇī; Jayā, Sumukheśvarī, Revatī, and likewise Mādhavī.
The western direction is said to belong to Varuṇa, while the northwestern direction is the destroyer of Rākṣasas;
thereafter follows Sahajā Lakṣmī, who is all-pervasive and endowed with Māyā.
These goddesses are seated upon the lap-throne of Rudra, their bodies crimson with vermilion;
the lotuses of their hands are adorned with red lotuses and skull-cups.
Thus ends the Rudra-nyāsa.
Now follows the Graha-nyāsa:
one should place the red Sun in the heart with the vowels preceded by the three-syllable mantra.
One should place the white Soma, along with the *ya*-group of consonants, in the middle of the eyebrows.
One should place Maṅgala, who is red, in the three eyes with the *ka*-group;
one should place Budha, who is dark-complexioned, in the circle of the heart with the *ca*-group.

One should place Bṛhaspati, yellow in color, at the pit of the throat with the *ṭa*-group [of consonants]; one should place Bhārgava, pale white in color, in the region of the throat with the *ta*-group [of consonants].
166) One should place Saturn, blue in color, at the region of the navel with the *pa*-group;
then one should place Rāhu, smoke-colored, in the mouth with the *śa*-group.
O fair-faced one, [one should place] two *lakṣas* at the region of the anus for the smoke-colored Ketu;
all [of these deities] assume forms at will and are adorned with every ornament.
Thus ends the placement of the *grahas*.
Now follows the placement of the world-protectors (*lokapāla*):
Indra, Agni, Yama, Rakṣas, Varuṇa, Pavana, and Vibhu.
One should [worship] Īśāna on the crown of one's head and in the eight directions in due order.
One should place Ananta below and Brahmā at the region of the head;
[this is done] with the eight groups of consonants preceded by the three-syllable [mantras] consisting of short and long vowels.

"Short," and so forth. Thus: *hrīṃ trīṃ hūṃ aṃ iṃ uṃ ṛṃ ḷṃ eṃ oṃ aṃ indrāya namaḥ* on the forehead in the east; *hrīṃ trīṃ hūṃ āṃ īṃ ūṃ ṝṃ ḹṃ aiṃ auṃ aḥ agnaye namaḥ* in the southeast, above the right ear. The eight groups [of consonants] are *ka-ca-ṭa-ta-pa-ya-śa-la*. Thus.
The placement of the world-protectors (*lokapālanyāsa*); now, the placement of Śiva and Śakti (*śivaśaktinyāsa*):
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva.
Beyond that, O Goddess, Paraśiva is proclaimed as the six Śivas.
One should place Brahmā together with Ḍākinī at the mūlādhāra;
in all instances, he is joined with the three syllables and the consonants from *va* to *sa*, accompanied by the bindu.
In the wheel called Svādhiṣṭhāna, one should likewise place Ākiṇī together with Viṣṇu,
and having assigned the letters from va to la, [one places them] in the Maṇipūraka at the navel.

One should install Rudra together with the letters from Ḍa to Pha, as well as Lākinī; and in the Anāhata [cakra], one should install Īśvara together with the letters from Ka to Tha, as well as Kākinī.
Then, having placed Sadāśiva and Śākinī, together with the sixteen vowels, in the great cakra called Viśuddha, as before.
O Goddess of the gods, one should place the Supreme Śiva, whose form is Brahman, accompanied by Hākinī and endowed with the syllables *ha* and *kṣa*, in the Ājñā-cakra.
Thus ends the Nyāsa of Śiva and Śakti.
Now follows the Nyāsa of Tārā and others:
Tārā, Ugrā, Mahogrā, Vajrā, Kālī, and Sarasvatī.
Kāmeśvarī and Cāmuṇḍā—these eight are considered to be Tāriṇīs.
167) Having first uttered the three-syllable mantra everywhere, one should proceed in sequence, adorned with a pair of vowels, a consonant class, and the bindu.
The deities beginning with Tārā, ending with Namo, preceded by meditation,
should be placed in the aperture of Brahmā, the forehead, the space between the eyebrows, and the cavity of the throat.
One should place [the mantras] in the heart, the region of the navel, the linga, and the foundation (ādhāra).
The applications begin with: *hrīṃ trīṃ hūṃ aṃ āṃ kaṃ khaṃ gaṃ ghaṃ ṅaṃ tārāyai namaḥ*, and so forth.
Thus ends the placement of Tārā and others; now follows the placement of the sacred seats (pīṭhanyāsa):
Kāmarūpa at the mūlādhāra, and Jālandhara in the heart.
On the forehead is the place called Pūrṇagiri, and Uḍḍiyāna is above that.
Vārāṇasī is between the eyebrows, and she shines as the three eyes;
Māyāvatī is on the circumference of the face, and then Madhupurī is at the throat.
One should designate Ayodhyā at the navel region and Kāñcī at the waist;
these ten are known as the principal pīṭhas in their respective order.
One should perform the placement (nyāsa) in sequence with the eight groups [of consonants], both short and long, ending with the word "namaḥ.
This is the Pīṭha-nyāsa;
thus concludes the Mahāṣoḍhā-nyāsa as taught in the Tantracūḍāmaṇi.
Now, the sixfold placement (ṣoḍhā-nyāsa) of Tārā as taught in the Nīlatantra:

In the Nīlatantra it is said— "O lady of excellent hips, having interspersed the Mātṛkā with the mantra, one should perform the placement six times in both direct and reverse order; this is proclaimed as the sixfold placement of Tārā."
But when merely the ritual placement (nyāsa) is performed, all sin is destroyed;
he becomes worshipful to the Yoginīs, for he is a god and not a mere human.
O Great Goddess, he whom those who have assumed their sixfold forms bow down to shall immediately become short-lived; the deity trembles with fear.
In the worlds, there is no one more worthy of worship than he, who is radiant with his father and mother at the head.

Six times [he performs] the sequence of creation, maintenance, and withdrawal; by him [is performed] the sequence of creation, maintenance, and withdrawal, or withdrawal, maintenance, and creation—so say some. Others, however, [state it as] withdrawal, creation, and maintenance, and again...

They say it is exactly so; however, since in reality only the direct (krama) and reverse (utkrama) orders are established by verbal authority, one should place the letters from *a* to *kṣa* and from *kṣa* to *a*, interspersed with the mantra, three times each.
It is my conviction that in this way the sixfold placement (*ṣoḍhānyāsa*) is accomplished. Thus [it is said].
The Sixfold Placement (Ṣoḍhānyāsa) of Tārā as taught in the Nīlatantra (168).
Now follows the Sixfold Placement of Tārā as taught in the Rudrayāmala.
In the Rudrayāmala: "Listen, O Goddess; I shall proclaim this secret Ṣoḍhā, O beloved."
This [instruction] for the protection of the minister's body must not be disclosed anywhere.
O Pārvatī, one should place the Praṇava enclosed by the letters of the Mātṛkā in the locus of the Mātṛkā; likewise, one should place each letter enclosed by that very [Praṇava] in that same place.
O Goddess, the seed-syllable of Māyā should likewise be deposited with effort;
and in the same way, one who is well-composed should deposit the seed-syllable of Badhū.
O Goddess, the seed-syllable of the *kūrca* mantra should likewise be deposited in its entirety;
and having likewise deposited the *astra* mantra, one should thereafter deposit everything completely.
O Goddess, this secret sixfold [practice] must never be disclosed;
meditation, worship, and recitation must certainly be performed daily.

Here, "aṃ oṃ aṃ oṃ aṃ oṃ namaḥ" is for the forehead; this is the first placement (*nyāsa*). "aṃ hrīṃ aṃ hrīṃ aṃ hrīṃ namaḥ" is for the forehead; this is the second sequence. "aṃ trīṃ aṃ trīṃ aṃ trīṃ namaḥ" is the third sequence. "aṃ hūṃ aṃ hūṃ aṃ hūṃ," and so forth, is the fourth. [The fifth is] "aṃ phaṭ."
"Aṃ Phaṭ, Aṃ Phaṭ, Namaḥ," and so forth, is for the fifth [stage]. "A Oṃ Hrīṃ Trīṃ Hūṃ Phaṭ, Aṃ Oṃ Hrīṃ Trīṃ Hūṃ Phaṭ, Aṃ Oṃ Hrīṃ Trīṃ Hūṃ Phaṭ, Namaḥ," and so forth, is the sequence for the sixth.
Thus concludes the Tārā-Ṣoḍhā-nyāsa as taught in the Rudrayāmala.
The sixteen-fold placement (*ṣoḍhānyāsa*) taught in the *Vīratantra* will be explained in the section on Kālī.

Now, regarding the placement of the stars (*tārakānyāsa*), the *Vīratantra* states: "One should perform the placement according to the sequence beginning with 'A' and the sequence beginning with Rohiṇī."
And one should join the principles in reverse order, connecting each remainder with the subsequent remainder.
Having performed the great Nyāsa beginning with Rohiṇī,
the wise and excellent man certainly becomes beyond grief in this creation, like the son of Rohiṇī.
His speech in the narrative becomes composed of both prose and verse;
he certainly becomes an expounder of scriptures never before seen or heard.
If one recites the mantra of Tāriṇī without having performed the *tārakā-nyāsa*,
then even if it is recited ten million times, the mantra will not grant accomplishment.

In this regard, the ritual application according to the tradition is as follows: *Aṃ kaṃ*, salutation to the one whose nature is the principle of space (*ākāśatattva*), in the form of Rohiṇī, on the head; *Āṃ khaṃ*, salutation to the one whose nature is the principle of air (*vāyutattva*), in the form of Mṛgaśiras, on the face; *Iṃ gaṃ*, salutation to the one whose nature is the principle of fire (*tejastattva*), in the form of Ārdrā, on the heart; *Īṃ ghaṃ*.
Oṃ! *Namaḥ* to the one whose essence is the water-tattva, who has the form of Punarvasu; [this is] for the secret place.

169) *Uṃ ūṃ*, *namaḥ* to the one whose essence is the earth-tattva, who has the form of Puṣya; [this is] for the two feet. *Ūṃ caṃ*, *namaḥ* to the one whose essence is the nose-tattva, who has the form of Aśleṣā; [this is] for the two nostrils. *Ṛṃ chaṃ*...

Salutation to the one whose essence is the principle of taste (*rasanatattva*) and who has the form of Maghā; [salutation] upon the tongue. *Ṛṃ jaṃ*: Salutation to the one whose essence is the principle of sight (*cakṣustattva*) and who has the form of Pūrvaphalgunī; [salutation] upon the two eyes. *Ḷṃ jhaṃ*: Salutation to the one whose essence is the principle of touch (*tvaktattva*) and who has the form of Uttaraphalgunī; [salutation] upon all the limbs. *Ḹṃ ñaṃ*...

Oṃ *Eṃ* *Ṭaṃ*, salutation to her whose essence is the principle of hearing (*śrotra-tattva*) and who has the form of the hand; [this is] for the two ears. Oṃ *Aiṃ* *Ṭhaṃ*, salutation to her whose essence is the principle of smell (*gandha-tattva*) and who has the form of Citrā; [this is] for the two nostrils. Oṃ *Aiṃ* *Ṭhaṃ*, salutation to her whose essence is the principle of taste (*rasa-tattva*) and who has the form of Svātī; [this is] for the tongue. Oṃ *Ḍaṃ*, [salutation] to her whose essence is the principle of form (*rūpa-tattva*).

*Namaḥ* to Viśākhā, who is the form of *rūpa*, to the eyes. *Oṃ ḍhaṃ*, *namaḥ* to Svātī, who is the essence of the *rasa*-tattva, to all the limbs. *Aṃ ṇaṃ*, *namaḥ* to Jyeṣṭhā, who is the essence of the *śabda*-tattva, to the two ears. *Aḥ taṃ*, [to her] who is the essence of the *upastha*-tattva...

*Oṃ* *mū* *ā* *rū* *ā* *yai* *namaḥ* to the one whose form is the root, at the *liṅga*. *Am* *tham* to the one whose nature is the principle (*tattva*) of the anus and whose form is Pūrvāṣāḍhā, *namaḥ* to the secret place (*guhya*). *Ām* *dam* to the one whose nature is the principle of the feet and whose form is Uttarāṣāḍhā, *namaḥ* to the two feet. *Im* *dham* to the one whose nature is the principle of the hands...

*Oṃ śraṃ vaṃ*, salutation to the one whose form is Śravaṇā, who consists of the principle of hearing; *namas* to the hands. *Īṃ naṃ*, salutation to the one whose essence is the principle of speech (*vāk-tattva*), who has Dhaniṣṭhā as her form; *namas* to the mouth. *Uṃ paṃ*, salutation to the one whose essence is the principle of bliss (*ānanda-tattva*), who has Śatabhiṣaj as her form; *namas* to the *liṅga*. *Ūṃ phaṃ*, [salutation] to the one whose essence is the principle of emission (*visarga-tattva*).

Salutation to her whose form is Pūrvabhādrapadā, at the secret place. Ṛṃ vaṃ, salutation to her whose nature is the principle of motion (gatitattva) and whose form is Uttarabhādrapadā, at the feet. Ṛṃ bhaṃ, salutation to her whose nature is the principle of grasping (ādānatattva) and whose form is Revatī, at the hands. Ḷṃ maṃ, [salutation] to her whose nature is the principle of speech (vacanatattva) and whose form is Aśvinī...

*Namo mukhe* (Salutation to the face). One should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) from the navel down to the feet with: *Ḷṃ eṃ aiṃ oṃ yaṃ raṃ laṃ vaṃ*, [salutation] to the one whose essence is the lower principles (*adhastattva*), who has the form of the lunar mansion Bharaṇī. One should perform the placement from the navel upwards with: *Auṃ aṃ aḥ śaṃ ṣaṃ saṃ haṃ laṃ kṣaṃ*, [salutation] to the one whose essence is the upper principles (*ūrdhvatattva*), who has the form of the lunar mansion Kṛttikā.
One should perform the placement up to the head.
This is the Tārakā-nyāsa.
Now follows the Ṛṣyādi-nyāsa.
In the Tantra: "When [the mantra] is recited without the placement (vinyāsa) of the seer, the meter, and the deity, even if it has been mastered, its fruit will be insignificant."
In the *Mantracūḍāmaṇi*: Akṣobhya is the seer (*ṛṣi*) of this [mantra], the *bṛhatī* is declared to be its meter (*chandas*), and the goddess Nīlasarasvatī is concealed within the three worlds.
The seed-syllable *hūṃ* is the weapon (*astra*) and the power (*śakti*), which bestows the fruits of the four aims of life.
Their ritual placement (*nyāsa*) is performed upon the head, face, heart, genitals, feet, and all limbs. As it is stated in the Tantra:
"The placement of the Seer (*ṛṣi*) is on the region of the head, while the Metre (*chandas*) is on the lotus of the mouth."
The deity is in the heart, and the seed-syllable is in the secret region.
One should place the *śakti* on the two feet and the *kīlaka* on all the limbs.
In the *Yoginītantra*: "O Goddess, one should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) of the seer (*ṛṣi*) and the others, ending with the heart in the dative case.
The fourth case is the dative; "heart" means *namaḥ*.

170) In the *Sārasaṃgraha*: "For the placement (*nyāsa*) of the seers (*ṛṣi*), meters (*chandas*), and deities (*devatā*), the fingers—excluding the thumbs—are prescribed; one should then perform the placement up to the Power (*śakti*).
The placement of the seed-syllables (*bīja*) and the powers (*śakti*) is likewise. The placement of the pins (*kīlaka*) is performed with both hands spread apart over all the limbs.
Thus it has been said:
"The foremost of practitioners [should perform] the ritual pinning (kīlaka) upon all limbs with the two hands placed apart.
Now follows the ritual assignment (nyāsa) of the hands and the limbs.

In the *Phetkāriṇī*: "Then, the placement [of mantras] on the hands and limbs is performed with the first seed-syllable preceded by the six long vowels. Regarding the specific procedure for the hand-placement (*karanyāsa*), it is stated in that same work:
'Starting from the thumb and ending with the little finger, and likewise again...'"
The ritual placement (nyāsa) known as "origination" is its reverse, which is "dissolution."

Beginning from the base of the middle fingers of both hands, one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) up to the tips of the index fingers; this is known as the "Establishment" (*sthiti*), which brings about the arising of the Name.
In the *Siddhasārasvata*: having uttered [the mantra] "She whose form is the entirety of speech," one should say "Salutation to the Heart" (*hṛdayāya namaḥ*).
And "Akhaṇḍavāgrūpiṇīm" is for the head; "Vahnivallabhā" [is the next].
Having uttered "Brahmavāgrūpiṇī," one should also say "Śikhāyai Vaṣaṭ";
having uttered "Viṣṇuvāgrūpiṇī," one should pronounce "Kavacāya Huṃ."
One should also say "to the three eyes, vauṣaṭ" for the one whose form is the speech of Rudra;
then, having said "whose form is all speech," one should remember "to the weapon, phaṭ."
One should join those [mantras] with the six long vowels at the end of the seed-syllable;
as stated in the *Tantracūḍāmaṇi*: "At the end of the seed-syllable, 'Ekajaṭāyai' is proclaimed as the heart;
likewise, 'Tāriṇyai' is for the head, and similarly, 'Vajrodake' is for the crest-lock."
The armor is assigned to Ugrajaṭā and likewise to Mahāparisara;
similarly, the eye-weapon and the missile-weapon are proclaimed for Piṅgograikajaṭā.
Thus it has been said. Therefore, the statement from the *Phetkāriṇī* is intended as an illustration for other sections.
There is an option between the two methods taught in the *Siddhasārasvatatantracūḍāmaṇi*.
The ritual placement of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) taught in the *Siddhasārasvata* applies to Nīlasarasvatī.
They also state that the method for the six-limbed placement (ṣaḍaṅganyāsa) as taught in the *Tantracūḍāmaṇi* applies to both Tāra and Ekajaṭā.
In the Tantra: "The wise one should place [the mantras] on the heart with the middle, ring, and index fingers;
and he should perform the placement on the head with the middle and index fingers."

One should place [the seed-syllables] on the crest-lock with the thumb, on the armor with ten fingers, and on the eyes with three; the weapon-mantra should be placed three times, moving upwards from the top.
The limb-mudrās (aṅgamudrā) are also taught by means of the middle and index fingers;
the meaning is that one should perform the triple clapping (tālatraya) with the middle and index fingers in an upward sequence.
(171) Regarding mantras whose limbs are not explicitly stated, [the procedure applies] either word by word or even syllable by syllable.
One should [worship] one's own limbs with the root mantra itself, or with the entire [mantra].

Now, regarding the pervasive placement (*vyāpakanyāsa*), the *Bhairavatantra* states: "One should pervade [the body] fivefold, or ninefold, or likewise sevenfold by means of the root mantra"—the word "one should pervade" is understood as the remainder [of the sentence]. In the *Svatantratantra* as well:
O Dear One, one should perform the pervasive placement (*vyāpakanyāsa*) nine times using the root mantra.

Herein, there is no placement of the Yoga-pīṭha, because it is not seen mentioned anywhere in the *Tārātantra*, and because of the statement: "The wise man should not transfer anything else. If the attainment of that [placement] is desired by means of the extension (*atideśa*) from the *Kālītantra*, [then it may be done].
Then, its placement (nyāsa) should be understood according to the sequence of the worship of the sacred seat (pīṭha-pūjā) that will be described hereafter.

In the Kumārī-tantra: "Thereupon, one should assume the attire of a woman, with the forehead marked by vermilion (sindūra), enriched with ornaments radiant with erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra), and the mouth filled with betel."
In this manner, one should likewise cause the entire [ritual], beginning with the attire and including the woman, to be performed.

By the word "etcetera" (ādi), the rites from the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi) up to the pervasion (vyāpaka), as well as the ritual placements (nyāsa) and so forth mentioned in the fifth yoga, are indicated.
As stated in the *Kulārṇava*: "O Dear One, he who recites the mantra while shielded by the armor of ritual placement (nyāsakavaca)..."
Seeing him, the obstacles flee, just as elephants do upon seeing a lion.
That fool who recites the mantra without having performed the web of nyāsa will be afflicted by all obstacles, like a young deer by tigers.
In the *Svatantra-tantra*: "Having thus disposed the body [of the mandala], one should draw the King of Wheels (cakrarāja) upon gold, silver, copper, stone, or on eight kinds of metals."
The Svayambhū flower, rocanā and agaru derived from the kuṇḍa and gola, saffron, musk, and sandalwood produced in Malaya; these constitute the Kula.
This fragrance has been fully described as always dear to Caṇḍikā;
with this combination of fragrances, one should draw the yoni-cakra.
In this context, the choice of fragrant substances is optional. As stated in the *Kumārītantra*:
"One should draw this [diagram] upon copper smeared with *kuṇḍa* and *golaka*.
And in the *Rudrayāmala*: "Then the yogi should prepare the yantra with saffron and vermilion."
In one made of gold, silver, copper, crystal, or likewise of wood;
The Goddess should be worshipped by the best of men according to the prescribed rite.
A yantra in the form of stable lines drawn on crystal and similar materials is also highly recommended; for this very reason, it is stated in the *Sārasaṃgraha*:
"In copper, [the worship] lasts for twelve years, but in crystal and other such materials, it is always effective."
172) Among those, however, that which is made of crystal bestows all accomplishments.
In another tantra: "O Dear One, for as long as one lives [the practice is done] with gold; with silver for twenty-two years;
with copper for twelve years; and beyond that, on birch bark."
In the Rudrayāmala: "Having made [the gift] one tola, two tolas, three tolas, or four tolas—or according to one's own desire—a man incurs sin.
Likewise: it is said that [the merit] is multiplied a hundred thousand times in copper and becomes ten millionfold in silver."

A yantra on gold yields infinite fruit; what need is there for me to tell you of its effect on gems and the like? O beloved, whether it be fashioned from coral, ruby, sapphire, cat’s-eye, crystal, or even emerald— The result is the same. It grants all desires and bestows liberation upon those who possess it. One will certainly obtain wealth, sons, as well as wives and fame;
and likewise, by means of a finger-measure from the Jewel-Ocean, one obtains gold and silver.
The same proportions as for copper apply to ruby and the other gems, according to one's desire.
In the Gaurīyāmala: "The wheel indeed possesses a fourfold nature, and its arrays (prastāra) are as follows:
the earth-array, the tortoise-array, the lotus-array, and likewise the Meru-array."
The arrangement of the earth, consisting of the conjunction of horizontal lines, has been described by me.
The *kūrmapadmaka* grid with upward-pointing lines has been described by me.
In the *Sautrāmaṇitantra*: "If the lines are straight, there will be prosperity; if the lines are curved, there is poverty.
In the *Kulārṇava*: "Due to the beauty of the image, especially because of the worship, and through the faith of the practitioner, the presence of the deity occurs."
Having rotated [the diagram], one should draw an eight-petaled lotus with a pericarp radiant with a triangle.
Having placed the *māyā* (hrlṃ) on the eastern petal, one should place the second seed-syllable on the southern [petal].
Likewise, one should then write two *phaṭ* syllables in the north and the west;
having written the seed-syllable in the center, one should perform the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*).
"Bhūtaśuddhi" means the purification of the five "ma" syllables; this is because the word *bhūta* signifies the number five.
Otherwise, there would be a contradiction with the statement: "Having thus disposed [the syllables] upon the body, one should draw the King of Wheels."
Some, however, maintain that there is indeed an option regarding the sequence of the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*) and the drawing of the yantra.
In the *Vīratantra*: "One should draw a hexagon and an eight-petaled lotus with its proper characteristics.
In the *Phetkāriṇītantra*: "A beautiful eight-petaled lotus with a yoni [in the center], made from cow dung."
The city of the earth (bhūpura), enriched with eight vajras, is the yantra consisting of Ekajaṭā.

173) The "Fortress of the Earth" (bhūpura) has also been described as superior. Thus, there is an option between the six-cornered and three-cornered [mandalas]; however, the view of the Vīracūḍāmaṇi will be stated [later] that it is indeed a combination.
In the Nīlatantra: "In the moon of the sky, the pericarp consists of the letters of the tongue (rasanārṇa); its filaments flash with pairs of vowels."

This supreme yantra of the Blue-Body Lord (Nīlatanu), which bestows the attainment of all goals, is described as having petals radiant with the syllables of the groups (vargas) in full bloom, encircled by the abode of the Earth (the square), and beautified by the corners of the directions shining with the excellent colors of the Moon and the Lord of the Stars (the lotus).
Here, because of the mention of "the blue-bodied one" (*nīlataṅoḥ*), worship in this yantra is for a practitioner of the three-syllable mantra;
however, for a practitioner of the four-syllable or five-syllable mantras, it is in the yantra described in the *Phetkāriṇī* and other texts.
Some also say that the *dhāraṇā-yantra* has been described by the verse beginning with "in the moon of the sky" (*vyomendau*).
In the Matsyasūkta: "In the case of an unmentioned ritual procedure, one should draw a lotus with eight petals, having a hexagonal pericarp, circular, and adorned with four doors."
In the *Tantra*: "Āḥ, O beautiful line, O adamantine line, hūṃ phaṭ, and [to] Vahnivallabhā.
With this mantra, one should draw a charming lotus petal.
In the *Kumārītantra*: "Joined with self-arisen flowers (*svayambhūpuṣpa*) and smeared with saffron-red [pigment]."
And on a pure seat, unseen by common folk, one should place [the vessel] in front.
In the Dakṣiṇāmūrtisaṃhitā: "O Goddess, O lady of excellent complexion, one should install the Cakra on a cloth produced from Śrīkhaṇḍa, Raktaśrīkhaṇḍa, or Śrīparṇī, and not elsewhere."
In the Kulārṇava it is said: "O Goddess, when she is worshipped in the yantra, she becomes propitiated instantly, because it restrains all sufferings arising from defects such as lust and anger."
They call this a "yantra," for within it the deity is truly gratified,
O beloved, just as the body is for the soul or as oil is for a lamp.
Likewise, the yantra is established for all the gods;
therefore, having drawn the yantra and meditated upon the auspicious dwelling and enclosure, [one should proceed].
Having first learned this from the mouth of the Guru, O Dear One, one should perform the worship according to the prescribed rite.
Likewise: "The practitioner should never mark the yantra at night;
if it is marked through negligence, he shall incur the curse of the deity."

In the *Siddheśvarītantra*: "O Goddess, O Sovereign of the Gods, having established [the deity] before him on an auspicious seat, the practitioner should offer a handful of flowers there with the root mantra. In the *Yoginītantra*: "There, one should scatter a handful of flowers with the root mantra of the Yoginī."
One should make it non-empty with flowers; one should designate an empty [space] as an obstacle.

The root mantra of the Yoginī, as stated in the Bhairava Tantra: "O Dear One, [the syllables are] the short vowel, the witness (S), fear (BHA), the white one (I), the Lord (BHA), Madana (GA), the crane (VA), their consecration (Ū),
and likewise having uttered Bhṛgu (M), Kālī (Ā), and Marut (HA)."

One should cast a handful of flowers upon the yantra with the mantra "Kūrcāstra-vahnibhāryā" (the weapon-mantra of the tuft, the wife of fire). *Bhaya* is the letter *bha*. *Sākṣi* is joined with the short vowel *i*. *Śveta* is the retroflex *ṣa*. *Bhagavān* is joined with the vowel *e*. *Madana* is the letter *ka*. *Vaka* [is the letter *va*].

The letter *śa* is palatal (*tālavya*). Its consecration (*tābhiṣeka*) is its own form. *Bhṛgu* is the dental *sa*. *Kālī* is the letter *ma*. *Marut* is the letter *ya*. *Kūrca* is the syllable *hūṃ*. *Astra* is *phaṭ*. *Vahnibhāryā* is *svāhā*.
In the *Kumārītantra*:
Then one should perform the ritual placement of the seats (pīṭhanyāsa), beginning with the foundational power (ādhāraśakti),
followed by primordial nature (prakṛti), the tortoise (kamaṭha), Śeṣa, and the earth (pṛthvī).
The ocean of nectar, the island of jewels, the palace of the wish-fulfilling gem,
as well as the cremation ground and the Pārijāta tree, and at its base, the jeweled altar.
Upon that jewel, the best of practitioners should place a pedestal,
and in the four directions, sages, deities, corpses, and severed heads.
One should place Dharma and the others, as well as Adharma and the others, upon the four limbs and members;
likewise, O Maheśvarī, one should place the lotus in the heart, and within that lotus, the Sun and Moon.
Having likewise deposited Vaiśvānara, as well as the qualities of sattva, rajas, and tamas,
and the Self itself, one should deposit the Śaktis within the heart-lotus.

Regarding this, they say that the inclusion of the term "nyāsa" (ritual placement) in the instruction "one should then perform the pīṭhanyāsa" is intended according to the *Kālikākrama*, because the *Kumārītantra* belongs to that tradition; and its utility here lies in the sequence for the external worship of the pīṭhas. As for the phrase "dharma and so forth," by that [it is meant] in the four corners.

The meaning is that one should worship in the four directions *dharmajñānavairāgyaiścaryāṇi* (virtue, knowledge, dispassion, and sovereignty), and *adharmājñānāvairāgyānaiścaryāṇi* (non-virtue, ignorance, non-dispassion, and non-sovereignty). The *śaktīḥ* are the *pīṭhaśaktīs*.
As stated in the *Tārārṇava*:
Within the hexagon is a lotus, and again, two earth-mandalas;
in their center, one should worship the vehicle of the Goddess, which is indeed a corpse.
Having visualized a cremation ground there, one should imagine a wish-fulfilling tree (kalpadruma) therein;
at its root is a jeweled pedestal adorned with various gems.
Richly adorned with various ornaments and graced by sages and gods,
it was surrounded on all sides by auspicious female spirits (śivās) who delighted in flesh and bones;
and in the four directions were headless corpses, decorated with funeral pyre embers and bones.

175) On the filaments (keśara), the powers of the pedestal (pīṭhaśakti) are to be worshipped. And these are stated in the *Siddhasārasvata*: "Lakṣmī, Sarasvatī, Rati, Prīti, as well as Kīrti, Śānti, Puṣṭi, and Tuṣṭi—these are the eight powers."
In the *Sārasaṃgraha*: "Then one should worship the power of the seat (pīṭhaśakti) on all the filaments;
holding the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, one should worship the seat with the seat-mantra."
In the Vīracūḍāmaṇi, however, it is stated: "One should worship the nine Śaktis according to the ritual for the Pīṭha-Śaktis:
Rati, Prīti, Priyā, Kānti, Kāminī, and Kāmamālinī."
The nine Śaktis are Kandarpadalinī, Durgā, and Bhāvinī;
having uttered the mantra "viyat-bhṛgu" (ha-kāra) conjoined with the digit of the Bindu.
The mantra ending with "mahāpreta-padam" and concluding with "hṛdayānta" is the *manu*.
The *manu* is the *pīṭha-manu*. In the *Kumārītantra*, the *pīṭha-mantra* as stated in another tantra is as follows:
having first uttered the *vāgbhava* [syllable], immediately thereafter [utter] "parāyai".
To Aparā, to Parāparā; after this, the syllable Hsau is to be uttered.
"Sadāśiva-mahāpretaṅenta-padmāsana," as well as "Namaḥ"— this is declared to be the mantra for the seat-consecration (pīṭhanyāsa).
Although the *Kumārikā-tantra* has Kālī as its primary focus, they say that by extension (*atideśa*), it applies here as well.
In the *Vasiṣṭha-saṃhitā*:
"Then the learned twice-born man should cause the ritual application of the *saptacchada* tree to be performed."
Having encased it with the syllable *hrīṃ* and endowed it with the syllable *oṃ*.
Every day, at the beginning of worship and other rites, a Brahmin should recite the mantra seven times;
by this procedure, there is protection for the power of the mantra.
All things have become goddesses, as have the supreme practitioners;
indeed, the god Bhairava himself is eager for the splendor of the mantra.
All [the powers] carry away one's splendors, except for the protection afforded by the *saptacchada* tree.
Now, regarding the purification of the mantra, it is said in the *Kulārṇava*: "Having strung together the syllables of the root mantra with the letters of the *mātṛkā*..."
By repeating this twice, both in direct and reverse order, this purification of the mantra is accomplished.

Now, regarding the purification of substances, it is stated in the Kulārṇava: "Having consecrated the articles of worship with the root mantra and the water from the weapon-mantra according to the rule, one should display the cow-mudrā; this is proclaimed as the purification of substances."

176) Now, regarding the specific purification (*viśeṣa-śuddhi*), it is stated in the *Kulārṇava*: "The purification of the power of the Kula-substances shall be explained hereafter. Om! Viṣṇu is praised for his heroic might;
like a terrifying beast that roams and dwells in the mountains, he in whose three wide strides all things abide."

One should purify the meat with the mantra "bhuvanāni viśvā. According to the injunction that one should employ the mantra "pratad viṣṇuḥ" for the purification of meat, [one should recite]: "Oṃ, we worship Tryambaka, the fragrant, the increaser of prosperity; may I be liberated from death like a cucumber from its stem, but not from immortality."

One should purify the fish with a mantra; for there is the scriptural injunction: "One should perform the purification of the fish with the mantra of Tryambaka. [The mantra is: *Oṃ tad viṣṇoḥ paramaṃ padaṃ sadā paśyanti sūrayaḥ | divīva cakṣurātatam | tadviprāso vipaṇyavo jāgṛvāṃsaḥ samindhate viṣṇoryat...*

One should purify the *mudrā* with the mantra "paramaṃ padam. According to the statement, "The mantrin should purify the *mudrā* which embodies the deity with the mantra 'tad viṣṇoḥ,' as well as with the *aṇu* [mantra] 'tad viprāsaḥ,'" one should perform the purification.
[The mantra is: "Oṃ, may Viṣṇu prepare the womb; may Tvaṣṭṛ fashion the forms; may Prajāpati pour [the seed]; may Dhātṛ [sustain it]."

"May she indeed bear a child; O Sinīvālī, grant a child; O Sarasvatī, grant a child! O divine Aśvins, you who wear lotus-garlands, bestow a child!"—with these two mantras, one should purify those born from a *kuṇḍa* or a *golaka*. Likewise, one should use the mantra "Viṣṇu [fashioned] the womb" and "Grant a child."
"A practitioner should employ [the substances] produced from the *kuṇḍa* and *golaka* for purification," according to this statement. In the Tantra:
"Having extracted the *tāra*, the *kūrca*, and the *astra*, joined with the three [syllables] beginning with Śiva and the *bindu*;
then the *vahnijāyā*, the *tāra*, the *māyā*, and the *śrībīja*, O beloved of amorous play."
The seed-syllable *tāra* (om), *māyā* (hrīṃ), *ramā* (śrīṃ), and the weapon (*phaṭ*), followed by the fire-born wife (*svāhā*) in a circle;
then "to you who arise from nectar" (*mṛtodbhavāyai*), and after that "O showerer of nectar" (*amṛtavarṣiṇi*).
O Beloved, [recite] the pair of *devīpada* joined with the mantra, which releases the curse;
recite the pair that flows nectar, the pair that makes it nectar.
One should perform the purification of semen (*śukraśuddhi*) with the mantra ending in the wife of fire (the *svāhā* suffix).
The letter *ma* is circular. In the Rudrayāmala it is said:
"The month is declared to be of three kinds: that which moves in water, that which moves in the sky, and that which moves on the earth.
Likewise: [the milk] produced from cows, humans, elephants, buffaloes, boars, goats, and deer.
The "Eightfold Great Meat" (mahāmāṃsāṣṭaka) is proclaimed as that which brings pleasure to the deities.
In the *Kulārṇava*: "Fish is said to be of three kinds—superior, inferior, and middling.
O Goddess, the superior kind is of three types: the *kṣāla*, the *pāṭhāna*, and the *rohit*."
That which is well-prepared, free from thorns, seasoned with oil, and endowed with a sweet flavor,
which indeed brings delight to the Goddess, is declared to be of middling quality.
The superior ones declare all those [other types] to be minor and inferior. 177) Likewise: "This [sweetmeat] made of rice flour is auspicious, circular in shape, resembling the orb of the moon;
it is beautiful, well-cooked, captivating, and filled with sugar and other ingredients."
And at the time of worship for the goddesses, this is proclaimed as the mudrā.

However, in another tantra it is said: "O Goddess, the mudrā is declared to be roasted chickpeas and the like; whatever roasted grain and so forth may be prepared, one should employ it as something to be chewed."
"His designation is 'the Mudrā,' which increases great joy. Thus it is said.
And in the *Muṇḍamālā*: "The *kuṇḍa* produced from union with a virtuous woman bestows supreme prosperity;
the *gola* produced from union with a widow bestows accomplishment (*siddhi*) upon the earth."
In the Kulārṇava: "O Goddess, if one performs recitation, sacrifice, austerity, or a vow without the substances of the Kula, that becomes fruitless, like an oblation poured into ashes."
Now, regarding the secondary alternative (anukalpa), it is stated in that same work: "In the absence of liquor, however, one should satisfy [the deity] by dissolving a pill in water;
or else, with buttermilk mixed with jaggery, or with a vessel of honey."

Or one may perform this rite with sour gruel (sauvīra); one must not omit it. The method for preparing the pill (vaṭikā) is stated in that very same place: "Wine, meat, and Vijayā, well-mixed with the eight fragrant substances (aṣṭagandha)."
Having worshipped it and formed it into a pill, the wise one should take hold of it.
The phrase "one should prepare a vessel of honey" is to be supplied as the conclusion of the preceding statement. *Sauvīra* is fermented gruel (*kāñjika*).
In the *Kumārītantra*: "One may pour coconut water or honey into a vessel of bell-metal or copper;
likewise, cow's milk placed in a copper vessel is equal to liquor, with the exception of clarified butter."
In the *Samayācāra*: "Buttermilk, milk, jaggery, honey, liquor, clarified butter, sesame, sugar, oil, marrow, and sugarcane juice—these are remembered as the ten types of substances.
Regarding the secondary alternative (*anukalpa*) therein:
In the absence of meat, however, one should take garlic, ginger, or dry ginger and worship the Goddess; otherwise, it shall be fruitless.
Likewise: "O Great Goddess, salt, fresh piyāla, wheat with māṣa as the fifth, and garlic are prescribed as substitutes for meat."
In the *Bhāvacūḍāmaṇi*, the fifth alternative is stated:
"If a Brahmin should be terrified [of worldly life] and devoted to the worship of his lineage (*kula*),
then he should perform that which arises from the lineage according to this procedure."
178) But in Aparāpuṣpagarbha is the charming Kulasthāna;
O God, in Hayārikusuma, Sadāśiva himself is ever present.
Having placed a small amount of sandalwood in the center of that,
or having offered a red flower in the midst of the flowers, one should meditate upon oneself as being of the nature of Śiva.
One should unite them while contemplating with the intellect that oneness of Śiva and Śakti;
having meditated for a moment right there, one should then contemplate the Supreme Goddess.

Having recited [the mantra], one should offer that very substance called *kuṇḍa*, which is extremely difficult to obtain—namely, fresh menstrual blood (*ārtava*). Alternatively, if menstrual blood is unavailable, one may use a red flower. "In the midst of flowers" means in the midst of *karavīra* flowers. *Candana* refers to white sandalwood. As stated in the *Bhairavītantra*:
In the absence of *svayambhū* flowers, one should cast red sandalwood (*raktacandana*).
It should be understood that all of this refers exclusively to the *vīra*.
Now, the ritual of subduing (*sādana*).
In the *Kulacūḍāmaṇi*: "Various kinds of flowers and various fragrances,
scented with camphor, nutmeg, incense, and the like, as well as perfumed cloth, betel-leaf, the materials to be offered, and whatever incense, lamps, and so forth [there may be]."
Adorned with all varieties of ornaments, the Lord of the Kaulikas should then install [the image],
having sprinkled it with water consecrated by the recitation of the root mantra.
One should place everything on one's right side and set the *arghya* offering on the left. One should hold the materials belonging to the deity's lineage (*kuladravya*) to the west of the deity.
As stated in the *Kālikāpurāṇa*: "One should place the wine behind [the deity], and other drinks likewise behind."
The syllable *tu* also signifies "and. Thus:
"After washing the hands, one should place the vessel behind;
one should arrange auspicious lamps, ignited with ghee and other substances, all around."
One should offer all flowers with a mind imbued with devotion, especially those of the *oḍra* flower mixed with the *vajra* flower.
Regarding the varieties of flowers, the *Matsyasūkta* states:
"One should worship with fragrant white and red flowers,
with *bilva* and *maruvaka* and other auspicious blossoms, provided they are free from *tulasī*."
In the *Yāmala*: "The gods are pleased by flowers; the gods are established within flowers. Moreover, what is the use of saying much more? The description of the flower is merely a brief indication."
179) The supreme light, residing within the flower, is propitiated by the flower alone.
The flower is the means for achieving the three goals of life (trivarga) and bestows nourishment, prosperity, heaven, and liberation.
Brahmā dwells at the root of the flower, while Keśava resides in its center.
Mahādeva is at the tip of the flower, and all the gods reside upon the petals;
therefore, a person endowed with devotion should always worship the gods with flowers.
She should always be worshipped with devotion by men, for she bestows results swiftly;
[with offerings] such as the *vajra* flower and others. In the *Muṇḍamālā*:
"One should likewise offer flowers that are red, black, and white."
O beloved, [offer] white flowers, hibiscus flowers, and likewise oleanders.
Tagara, mālatī, jasmine, sevantī, and likewise yūthikā;
dhustūra, aśoka, vakula, and the white and black aparājitā.
Vakapuṣpa, bilvapatra, campaka, nāgakeśara, mallikā, jhiṇṭikā, kāñcī, and whatever is proclaimed as red [flowers] [are suitable].
O Pārvatī, she becomes especially pleased on the eighth lunar day by arka flowers, barbara, bandhūka, and priyaṃvadā.
All the deities are satisfied by a red lotus flower;
whether they be black or white, Kālikā becomes a granter of boons.
The supreme Dhūmāvatī is satisfied with the dhattūra flower from the cremation ground alone,
while the goddess Pārvatī is satisfied with various kinds of wild flowers.
Pārvatī is pleased by the flower of the *āmalakī*, and even more so by its leaf;
on the eighth and fourteenth lunar days, one should worship her with various kinds of flowers.
In a cremation ground, or during the remainder of the night on a Saturday or Tuesday, at night;
[this refers to] the procedure for *mālatī* [flowers] when there is another deity [involved], because of the prohibition here. For instance, it is said in the *Haragaurī-saṃvāda*:
"One should avoid *mālatī* flowers; one should avoid *tulasī* leaves."
In the *Triśaktiratna*: "One should worship with *vajrapuṣpa* flowers mixed together for the sake of attaining accomplishment (*siddhi*).
In the absence of *vajrapuṣpa*, one shall obtain accomplishment through its recollection."
One of clear intellect should offer flowers, with the exception of *tulasī* and *mālatī*.
As stated in the *Kālikā Purāṇa*: "The *kokanada*, the lotus (*padma*), the *javā*, and the *bandhūka* flower..."
Among all species of flowers, the red flower is preeminent.
180) In the *Kriyāsāra*: "For the goddesses, the *arka* and *mandāra* flowers; for Āditya, likewise the *tagara*;
and for Gaṇeśa and Sūrya, the red flower (*raktapuṣpa*) is most beloved."
Likewise: "One should not worship the Goddess with *vakula* flowers, nor should one offer unripe fruit;
having ascertained that it is pure, one may even discard fruit that is only slightly ripened."
One should not worship Viṣṇu with unbroken grains (akṣata), nor Vināyaka with Tulasī;
one should not worship Caṇḍī with Dūrvā grass, nor Vināyaka with Bilva leaves.
The *unmatta* and *markapuṣpa* should always be avoided by the wise when offering to Viṣṇu;
for Śiva, the *kunda*, *madantī*, *yūthī*, *bandhuka*, and *ketaka*.
In the Gautamīya [Tantra]: "One should never take red sandalwood or red flowers;
one should not worship the Son of Devakī with bilva leaves or those flowers."
One should not worship Viṣṇu with flowers, leaves, or fruits that are dried,
brought after bathing [the deity], stale, begged for, or black in color.

One should avoid *bṛhatī* flowers that have blossomed on their own and fallen to the ground by themselves; one should especially avoid those that are scentless. Furthermore, one should never worship with flowers that have fewer than three petals.
One should avoid the *kusuma* flower as well as the *pāṭalī* and the *śirīṣa*. One should avoid flowers that have fallen to the ground, with the exception of the *śephālī* and the *vakula*.
An intelligent person should not offer [the image] to Śivā when it has been carried away wrapped in cloths;
likewise, it should be abandoned along with the Kālikās, except for the Campaka and Padmaka.
O Hari, one should avoid the red hibiscus at the three junctions of the day, as well as the two types of jasmine, the ketaki, saffron, the white water-lily, and the red oleander.
In the case of the bilva, the khadira, as well as the dhātrī fruit,
the tamāla, and the lotus, there is no fault if they are cut or broken.
In the *Puṣpamālā*: "Guñjā, parājitā, unmatta, along with varāhakrāntā and this āmrātaka flower—these flowers are forbidden in the worship of the Sun."
Tagara, kaṇṭakārikā, mandāra, arka, dhustūra, śālmalī, kāñcana, and arjuna are forbidden when the sun is in [the sign of] Leo.
The Vibhītaka flower is prohibited for the worship of Viṣṇu;
likewise, the Śirīṣa and the white Pundraka are both prohibited and prescribed for Viṣṇu.
In the worship of Narasiṃha, the two types of *ketakī* are forbidden.
(181) However, for Śiva, the flowers of the *śirīṣa*, *bandhūka*, *vibhītaka*, *madantika*, *ketakī*, *puṇḍraka*, *karañja*, *sarja*, the *indramahīruha* tree, and the *kunda* are recommended.
Flowers that have been washed in water, those that have withered on their own, and those that have dissolved upon the ground—
these they say are ineffective for the ritual of worshiping all the gods.
For the worship of other goddesses besides Durgā, the Mandāra and Arka flowers are highly recommended.
However, in the *Matsyasūkta*, the following are prohibited for Mahālakṣmī: the *tulasī*, the *jhiṇṭikā*, and likewise the *kāñcana*.
In the chapter on flowers: One should not worship the Sun with *kunda* flowers, nor Vināyaka with *tulasī*;
one should never worship Kamalā with lotuses, nor Śaṅkha with water from a conch-shell.
A flower requested [from someone] is fruitless, and one purchased for a price is also fruitless;
however, there is no such thing as "stale-ness" regarding Tulasī, Agastya, and Bilva flowers.
Even for a lotus, there is no state of being stale after six months;
yet one should avoid a flower that has become stale, and one should avoid water that has become stale.
The water of the Gaṅgā is not to be rejected, nor is a leaf of Tulasī.
As stated in the Kālītantra: "With various offerings and oblations, with various beautiful flowers, with Apāmārga leaves, and with auspicious Bhṛṅgas—all provided they are free from Tulasī."

She should always be worshipped with devotion by men for the swift attainment of results [with the words] "excepting Tulasī"; this refers specifically to the divine hero (divyavīra). However, as stated in the *Kaulāvalī*:
"Worship devoid of Tulasī shall never bear fruit."
But that [worship] occurs in the state of the sacrificial animal (paśubhāva). Even there, there is a specific distinction:
worship performed for Bhairava, Sundarī, Kālī, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Vivasvat, when devoid of Tulasī, shall become fruitful.
In the *Yāmala* as well: "Upon smelling the fragrance of *tulasī*, the beautiful goddess becomes enraged.
In the *Kriyāsāra*: "Worship of all the deities should always be performed with all flowers, whether prescribed or prohibited; here, the yoga of devotion is the essential cause."

The worship of the Goddess is always praised, whether performed with aquatic or terrestrial flowers, whether they are prescribed or forbidden, provided the mind is filled with devotion. As stated in the *Mālinītantra*: "O Supreme Goddess, one should worship even with leaves in the absence of flowers."
If leaves are not available, one should worship with those produced from trees, shrubs, and the like;
if even those growing on that ground are unavailable, one should worship with their fruit.
Or else, with unbroken grains (akṣata) or water; and in the absence of these, with mustard seeds. 182)
In the absence of these as well, one should perform mental worship.
In the Rudrayāmala: "One should worship the Vidyā with one's own substances, such as saffron, fire, and vermilion.
Likewise: "The blood known as 'Vedana' is declared to be red."
O Maheśānī, the oḍra flower is said to be the flower of the yoni.
Regarding the threefold nature of the *vajrapuṣpa* (diamond-flower), it is stated in the *Muṇḍamālā*:
"That which is unmarried up to sixteen years of age is the best, granting all accomplishments (*siddhi*).
That which has been married by force is middling, increasing worldly enjoyment (*bhoga*)."
O Goddess, by the power of the *rajoyoga*, another [substance] arises on earth that bestows inferior pleasure; the *svayambhūkusuma* is thus born in three forms.
[This refers to] one who is unmarried and has not been enjoyed [sexually]; [it refers to] one who is married and has been enjoyed.
Now, regarding the installation of the water-jar (*kalaśa*), in the *Bhāvacūḍāmaṇi*: "On one's left side is a hexagon; in its center is the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*)."
Having inscribed [the mantras] there, one should place a pitcher— either made of gold,
silver, copper, or even of earth, provided it is free from base metal— as a support for the *kalaśa*; this pitcher should be scented with fragrant perfumes.
And the support (ādhāra) is described in the Kulārṇava:
"They say the support is of three kinds: having six parts or four parts;
or else, O Goddess, one should make it circular and beautiful."
Likewise: "Without a support (ādhāra), there is indeed a fall; the deities are not pleased.
Therefore, O Mistress of the Kula, one should fashion the support according to the rule."
In the Tantra: "The width of the jars shall be fifty finger-breadths, their height sixteen finger-breadths, and the opening at the mouth shall be eight finger-breadths."
Likewise, having introduced the jar:
"O Maheśānī, it is wrapped in a red cloth, adorned with a red garland,
and placed on the left side within the square mandala."
There, O auspicious one of beautiful countenance, he should establish [the deity] in the goddess’s pit,
in the mandala, in the jar, in the ritual substance, and in the orbs of fire, sun, and moon.
