The word "should worship" is to be supplied as the ellipsis. The term "quadrangular" (*caturasra*) is an indicator for the mandala as previously described.
In the Tantra: "Having drawn two yonis, one should enclose the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*) within them;
having surrounded it with a circle, one should then surround it with a quadrangle. (183)
Having sprinkled it with *arghya* water and established the yantra there,
one should worship the fire-mandala therein as pervaded by the ten *kalās*.
Having washed it with the *hetimantra* and adorned it with red garlands,
one should place the flask there, made of gold or other such materials according to the distinction of one's means.
The practitioner of mantra should worship the solar disc here, conjoined with the twelve digits (kalās),
and should complete it with the pure root mantra as the cause.
In this rite, one should worship the lunar disc pervaded by sixteen digits;
one should protect it with the weapon-mantra and veil it with that same mantra.
The practitioner should gaze with the root mantra, sprinkle [the object] with that same [mantra],
worship it thoroughly with perfumes and other offerings, and contemplate it as being of the nature of the deity.
The mantra practitioner should worship the triad of images with three portions of the *tāra*.

Regarding "with portions of the *tāra*": this means with the letters *a*, *u*, and *m*. This is the sequence: "Oṃ, *maṃ*, salutation to the fire-maṇḍala consisting of ten digits" at the base (*ādhāra*). "Aṃ, [salutation] to that which consists of twelve digits... [and so forth].

One should worship with "Oṃ, salutation to the solar disc" upon the water-pot (kalaśa), and with "Uṃ, salutation to the lunar disc consisting of sixteen digits" upon the substance (dravya), because such is seen in the case of the *arghya* and other offerings. This is the purification of the substance (*dravya-śuddhi*).
Then one should purify the substance. As stated in the *Kalāmṛtadīpikā*:

"Having first seen and bowed to the Water-element (Vāruṇī) Kalā in its form, and having offered a flower with the *Tāra* [syllable], one should sprinkle it with water empowered by the *astra* mantra."
Having offered unbroken grains with the Nārāca weapon, one should protect them with the Mūla-weapon.
Having liberated it from the curse of Śukra, one should purify it with the Pavamāna mantra;
one should dry it with the Vāyu mantra and subsequently burn it with fire.
Above, the practitioner of mantra should visualize the sun and the solar orb,
O Goddess of gods, while reciting the solar mantra and mentally recollecting Vāruṇī.
One should contemplate a stream of nectar falling from the sun,
while reciting the seed-syllable of Soma, ending with the letter *Ha* and accompanied by the crescent moon, which consists of pure ambrosia.
The practitioner should fill the vessel with the prescribed *dhenumudrā* and recite the *amṛta-mantra* seven times while forming the *kūrmamudrā*.
Then, having taken the *amṛta* and perfumed it with camphor and other substances,
one should raise it slightly, pour it into another vessel, and cast fire into it.
O Goddess of the gods, one should display the *yonimudrā* by means of the principle of knowledge (*vidyātattva*).
Thereafter, one should contemplate the Goddess there as consisting of all beings;
having brought her into oneness with oneself, one should unite her with the Great Self.
Thereafter, one should contemplate oneself as consisting of all beings—that is, as having the form of the deity. The solar mantra is *haṃsa*. *Amāmayīm* means consisting of nectar (*amṛta*).
The lunar seed-syllable is *sa*. That which ends with *ha* is the letter *ha*; joined with the half-moon, it is *ha*. Thus, it becomes *so'ham*.
Siddham. The Amṛta-kūrmamudrā will now be described. One should cast [the substance] into the fire. Regarding "in the nectar situated in another vessel":
by means of the mantra "By the principle of knowledge (vidyātattva), I purify the subtle body, svāhā," one acts through the principle of knowledge.
The meaning is that, as before, one should raise Kuṇḍalinī, unite her with Śiva, and meditate upon oneself as consisting of all beings (*sarvabhūtamaya*).
The mantras for the release from the seed’s curse have been stated.
In the Kumārītantra: "Listen further, O Goddess of gods, to how no loss occurs in rites such as those of the Kula; hear those mantras, O beloved."
The Supreme Brahman alone is eternal, consisting of both the gross and the subtle;
by means of that, I destroy for you the sin of killing a Brahmin, which has arisen from a mere flash of thought.
O Goddess, born from the solar disc, arisen from the abode of Varuṇa,
composed of the seed-syllable *amā*, may [this person] be released from the curse of Śukra.
If the Praṇava is the seed of the gods and consists of the bliss of Brahman,
by that truth, O Goddess, may it dispel the sin of killing a Brahmin.
Having thus consecrated the auspicious food with the recitation of mantras alone, one should indeed present it as an offering (naivedya) to Caṇḍikā; she shall then take it into her own stomach.
Another method for liberation from the curse is stated in the *Tārārṇava*:
"O fair-faced one, having first extracted the *praṇava*, then the seed-syllable of the Moon (*candrabīja*),
joined with the six long vowels and endowed with the *bindu*, *nāda*, and *kalā*."
Then, one should offer salutations to the goddess Surā, the liberator from Śukra’s curse,
and recite the mantra twelve times for the sake of release from Śukra’s curse.
In the commentary (vṛtti), however: "Salutations to you, O Goddess Amṛtā, who were liberated from the curse of Śukra, and who are differentiated by the six long vowels [from *veda* to *varuṇa*]."

"One should recite the mantra twelve times for the sake of liberation from Śukra’s curse"—thus it has been stated. Therefore, there is an option (*vikalpa*) between these two methods of liberation from Śukra’s curse, because a combination (*samuccaya*) is impossible when two [methods] have equal purpose and are equally capable [of achieving that end]. Following that: *oṃ vāṃ vīṃ vūṃ vaiṃ vauṃ*.
The liberation from the curse of Brahmā is performed by reciting either "Obeisance to Sudhādevī, who has been liberated from the curse of Brahmā" ten times,
or by reciting "hrīṃ śrīṃ krāṃ krīṃ krūṃ kraiṃ krauṃ kraḥ sure kṛṣṇaśāpaṃ mocaya amṛtaṃ srāvaya srāvaya svāhā" ten times.

By reciting [the mantra] twelve times, one shall effect liberation from the curse of Kṛṣṇa. As it has been said: "The seed-syllable of Varuṇa, preceded by the Vedas (Om), conjoined with the six long vowels, followed by 'to the Goddess Sudhā who is liberated from the curse of Brahmā, obeisance'."
One should recite the mantra ten times for liberation from the curse of Brahmā;
[the mantra consists of] Māyā (Hrīṃ), Śrī (Śrīṃ), and Aṅkuśa (Kroṃ), differentiated by the six long vowels.
After the end of the form of *surekṣṇa*, release the curse (*śāpa*);
thereafter, [utter] the pair that distills nectar (*amṛta*), and after that, the wife of Fire (*vahnijāyā*).
By means of this mantra, the practitioner shall release [himself] from the curse of Kṛṣṇa:
"Pavamāna is supreme bliss; Pavamāna is the supreme essence."
"Pavamāna, the purifier; by that I purify you.
Having thus recited the Pavamāna mantra and stirred [the substance], one should perform the meditation upon Bhairava and Bhairavī in the midst of the substance.
As it has been said:
In the *Tārārṇava*: "The God has eighteen arms, five faces, and three eyes; he resembles ten million suns and is as cool as ten million moons."
Seated in the midst of an ocean of nectar, resting upon the Brahma-lotus,
mounted upon his bull, blue-throated, and adorned with all ornaments.
The god holds a skull-cup and a khaṭvāṅga staff, sounds a bell and a ḍamaru drum,
wields a noose and a goad, and carries a mace and a club.
Holding a sword, a shield, a battle-axe, a mallet, a trident, and a staff, and bearing a lance and a severed head, with hands granting boons and fearlessness.
The best of practitioners should meditate upon Lohita, the Lord of the Gods of gods.
Having thus visualized him, he should worship with three handfuls of flowers while reciting his own mantra. Thereafter, he should meditate upon Ānandabhairavī.

In that very place: "And one should meditate upon the goddess Surā, possessing the luster of ten million times ten thousand moons, white as snow, kunda flowers, and the moon, with five faces and three eyes."
Endowed with eighteen arms, intent on bestowing all bliss,
smiling, large-eyed, and facing the God of gods.
Alternatively, one should worship Ardhanārīśvara, the Lord of the gods of gods.
Having meditated thus, one should perform the worship with one's own mantra.
The two mantras are stated in the Tantra as follows: "Śiva and Candra [ending] with Mātṛkā, and likewise Mala, Va, and Vahni."
And the wind, filled through the left ear, is the Bindu and the Nāda.
Having uttered this seed-syllable, as well as Ānandabhairava ending in *ṅ*,
one should properly write the first seed-syllable conjoined with the crest-mantra (*śikhāmantra*).
Having abandoned this initial *candra*, one should place [the letter] in the ear and join the left eye;
then for the goddess Surā, *voṣaṭ*, and for Yamānandabhairavī.
One should worship those two with this pair of mantras preceded by meditation:
Śiva is the letter *ha*; Candra is the letter *sa*; the end of the Mātṛkā is the letter *kṣa*, whose nature is impurity (*malava*);
Vahni is the letter *ra*; Vāyu is the letter *ya*; and the left ear is the letter *ū*. These two [letters] should be joined, ending with the letter *ṅ*.
The fourth case ending [is applied]. The *śikhā-mantra* is "vaṣaṭ. He states the *bhairavī-mantra*: "the first seed-syllable," and so forth.

An inversion of the first two letters should be performed. Having removed the vowel *ū* from the final syllable, the vowel *ī* (the "left eye") should be joined. The meaning is that this is the *ānandabhairavī-mantra*.
Joined with *māyā* at the beginning, and joined with fire (*ra*) and the moon (*i*) in the middle;
at the end, there is the void of supreme space (*paramākāśaśūnya*) for the Supreme Mistress (*paramasvāminī*).
"O Vāhinī, at the end of the lunar steps, O consumer of sun and fire!
Enter the vessel, enter, svāhā!"—one should recite this mantra ten times.
"Vāṅmāyākamalāprānte ānandeśvari vidmahe, sudhādevyai dhīmahi, tanno 'rdhanārīśvarī pracodayāt."

The wise one should recite the Gāyatrī ten times with the mantra "pracodayāt. Then, in the *Svatantra*, it is said: "O Dear One, one should then contemplate the substance as nectar, marked by the letter 'ra'; it is adorned with the three syllables 'ha', 'la', and 'kṣa' arranged in three rows beginning with 'a', 'ka', and 'tha'."

Within the previously mentioned *yonimudrā*, one should contemplate the nectar (*amṛta*) arising from the union of Śiva and Śakti; one should meditate on the substance as nectar and recite the *Amṛtā* mantra eight times.
But this is the reason, O Goddess, why it is frequented by the hosts of gods;
for this very reason, its name is "Sudhā" (the Nectar) throughout the three worlds.

Because of that lack of fragrance, Kaulika Keśava did not worship the supreme goddess Caṇḍikā, Kālikā, or Śivā. In the triangle beginning with "A," one should place the sixteen vowels in the left row.

Having written the sixteen letters beginning with *ka* in the bottom row, the sixteen letters beginning with *tha* in the right row, and *halakṣa* in the middle, one should raise Kuṇḍalinī according to the previously mentioned procedure, unite her with Śiva, and [receive] the stream of nectar flowing from that through the left nostril.

The meaning is that, having visualized [the substance] fallen into the midst of the materials, one should meditate upon the substance as consisting of nectar. The mantra for nectar is stated in the Kulārṇava:
Vāgbhava is the purifier, the earth, endowed with nourishment and the bindu;
and Sthiti is the purifier, adorned with grace and the half-moon.
The syllable *sthirā* joined with *arghīśa* (ha) and the moon (i), followed by *śveta* (sa) conjoined with two dots (bindu);
then one should utter the word *amṛte*, and after that, *amṛtodbhave*.
Then, having uttered "Amṛteśvari," followed by "Amṛtavarṣiṇi," and the pair "Amṛtaṃ śrāvaya," ending with the *dviṭha* (svāhā), this [mantra] effects the purification of substances.
The mantra known as Amṛta is said to consist of thirty-five syllables.

Vāgbhava is the syllable *aikāra* (ai). Pāvana is the syllable *pakāra* (pa). Bhūmi is the syllable *lakāra* (la). Puṣṭi is the syllable *ūkāra* (ū). Bindu is the anusvāra (*m*). By this, *aiṃ plūṃ* is established. Sthiti is the syllable *sakāra* (sa). Pāvana is the syllable *repha* (ra).

*Anugraha* is the letter *au*. *Ardhendu* is the nasal *anusvāra* [joined with] the half-moon. By this, *srauṃ* is established. *Sthira* is the letter *ja*. *Arghīśa* is the letter *ū*. *Indu* is the nasal *anusvāra*. Thus, *jūṃ* is established. *Śveta* is the letter *sa*. *Binduyuga* is the *visarga*. Thus, *saḥ* is established. *Dviṭha* is *svāhā*.

The rest is easy to understand. Its recitation is eightfold, according to the written statement. In the *Kulāmṛta*, this recitation is said to be performed prior to the rising of Kuṇḍalinī; therefore, it should be practiced here in accordance with the authentic tradition. In the *Tantra*:

May the Blessed Lady protect her devotees— she who, mounting a blue horse, proceeds ahead, enriched with playful garments, ornaments, garlands, and ointments; she who conceals the worlds with the veil of sleep and is equipped with a sword.
Having meditated thus, the supreme practitioner should recite the two vidyās;
at the end of both Māyā and Lakṣmī, he should say "namo bhagavati."
O Maheśvarī, at the end of the *svarūpa* [mantra], [add] "sarvapaśujana," then the pair of manas and cakṣus, followed by the word "tiraskaraṇam" and the two *ṭha*s.
Then [he should worship] Lañjākāmeśvarī, who likewise repels others;
then Vāṇī with the mantra *glauṃ*, and [the deity] who repels all people.
"Vāgvādinī" (the speaker of speech) and "the progenitor of the entire host of bound souls" constitute the transcendence of the functions of mind,
sight, hearing, taste, and smell.
One should recite the mantra consisting of two *kuru*s, three *ṭha*s, along with the *visarga* at the head;
above that, one should recite one's own root-mantra and the syllable *va* (Varuṇa) seven times.
By this procedure, one should perform the purification of substances.
In the *Bhāvacūḍāmaṇi*, purification is stated by another method as follows:
"One should fill the jar with the causal substance," and so on.
188) Having first drawn the yantra there, whatever originates from one's own *kula*,

and having meditated upon one's chosen deity (*iṣṭadevatā*) therein, one should recite [the mantra] one hundred and eight times. Then, having visualized the *dhenu* and *yoni* [mudrās], one should contemplate that [yantra] as being eight finger-breadths wide.
Seeing that the nectar has indeed been obtained, the hosts of yoginīs dance;
all the Bhairavas dance, and the hosts of Bhairavīs dance.

"Whatever arises from one's family" means whatever kind of *yantra* belongs to which deity. As for the *dhenu* and *yoni* mudrās: the little fingers and ring fingers are again joined and pressed against each other, facing one another.
Likewise, the Dhenu-mudrā, formed with the index and middle fingers, bestows nectar.
The middle fingers should be bent and placed upon the index fingers;
likewise, the ring fingers and the little fingers should be positioned in the same manner.

"Joining all [the fingers] together in one place and pressing them with the thumbs is declared to be the Yoni-mudrā, the mother of the origin of the three worlds. Thus it is stated in the Tantra. Now follows the placement of the vessel (pātra-sthāpana).

In the *Samayācāra*: "Then, having prepared the general *arghya* with milk, the best of practitioners, having sprinkled the mandala with that water, should then place the vessels. They place the general *arghya* even before the setting out of the articles of worship. And the procedure for that is as follows:"
It is written in that very tantra:
"Between the practitioner and the object of practice, there should be thirty-six finger-breadths;
twelve finger-breadths above, and likewise one finger-breadth in the lower part."
The wise one should place it there, situated in the middle of twelve finger-breadths (dvādaśāṅgula).
Likewise, [one should consider] the finger-breadth as twelve finger-breadths. Furthermore: "Having abandoned two and twelve, for the sake of the deity, one should abandon the twelfth."
One should place the arghya offering there, situated in the middle of twelve finger-breadths.
In the *Kumārīkalpa*: "Then, O beautiful goddess, the mantra-practitioner should place the *arghya* vessel to his left.
In the *Triśaktiratna*: "To the right side of the *kalaśa*, having drawn a triangle combined with a circle, a hexagon, and a square, [one should place it] from the middle of that area."
And one should likewise paint a Gandharva with a shimmering crescent moon.
One should worship the sacred seats (pīṭhas), such as Oḍḍiyāna and Pūrṇagiri, in the four directions;
and in the hexagon, one should worship the Śakti with the limb-mantras (aṅgamantras) according to the threefold division of the root-mantra (mūlamantra).
Having worshipped Ādhāraśakti as before, one should also worship the Yantric [deity].
One should place therein a vessel made of a large conch, coconut shell, gold, silver,
copper, or even mother-of-pearl.
"Vilasat" refers to the *gandharva* syllable *mī*. Regarding *o*, *jā*, *pū*, *kā*, and so forth—these are Oḍḍiyāna, Jālandhara, Pūrṇagiri, and Kāmarūpa;

their worship is performed, according to tradition, upon the lines of the square (*caturasra*) starting from one's own front and proceeding clockwise. In the worship of the limbs (*aṅga-pūjana*), the word "namas" (salutation) alone should be appended at the end of all those mantras, and not [any other].

A different category [of mantra]. This is because it is seen as such in the worship of the enclosures (*āvaraṇapūjā*) in passages beginning with "with the limb-mantras ending in *namaḥ*. In the triangle of Śakti, worship is performed according to the three divisions of the root [mantra], that is, by means of the three sections of the root [mantra].
The Support-Energy (*ādhāraśakti*) is the vowel *ī*; the Pivot (*yantrikā*) is the vowel *ā*. And the worship of these is as follows:
The worship of the fire consisting of ten digits is indeed [the core]. The distinction regarding the vessels is also stated in the *Kulārṇava*:
"Made of gold, silver, stone, tortoise-shell, skull, gourd, or clay; or originating from coconut, conch, pearl-oyster, copper, or mother-of-pearl."
The auspicious vessel, produced from the tree of merit, is well-stirred; "well-stirred" means made circular. In the *Mahāhāravatantra*:
"The skull of Viśvāmitra is indeed the most excellent among all vessels."
Likewise: "Upon seeing a coconut vessel, sins such as the killing of a Brahmin, as well as the betrayal of trust—all of these indeed perish."
O Maheśānī, he who gives gifts of ten million maidens and likewise performs hundreds of fire-offerings when the sun is eclipsed by Rāhu;
The fruit of that [offering] is multiplied ten millionfold by means of a coconut vessel for the arghya;
in the absence of such a vessel, one should worship using another vessel.
Likewise: "O highly fortunate one, the human skull (narapātra) is to be known as the most excellent of the excellent;
O Goddess, that called the coconut (nārikela) is to be known as the middling of the excellent."
O lady of beautiful hips, the jewel-vessel should be known as the most excellent ritual implement.
Having worshipped the vessel according to the *Triśaktiratna*— [regarding it as] a minor vow— the practitioner of mantra, having honored it as before, should fill the conch with the ritual substance.
He should write the letters in reverse order from Japan, radiant with the root mantra.
Having worshipped there as before, one should draw a circle and within it a hexagon;
then, from the center of the circle, one should draw a triangle consisting of three lines starting from 'A', 'Ka', and 'Tha'.
Then, one should worship the triangle with three segments of the root mantra;
in the hexagon, one should worship the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga), and thereafter, one should meditate upon it as consisting of the holy waters (tīrtha).
Having meditated upon Ānandabhairava and worshipped him according to the prescribed rite,
one should worship the five jewels and cast in the substances of the Kula.

190) One should perform [the remaining rites] as before; this is known as the procedure for the *arghya*. "Ānandabhairava" is an elliptical designation (upalakṣaṇa), meaning that Ānandabhairavī is also to be worshipped because of the invocation of the couple (*yugala*).
Furthermore, the worship of the five jewels (*pañcaratna*) is performed with the substances contained within the *arghya* vessel: *glūṃ gaganaratnāya namaḥ*, *slūṃ*...

One should perform [the worship] in the center and in the four directions starting from one's own front with the following: "Obeisance to the Jewel of Heaven, *plūṃ*; obeisance to the Jewel of the Netherworld, *mlūṃ*; obeisance to the Jewel of Mortals, *nlūṃ*; obeisance to the Jewel of Nagas, *nlūṃ*.
The ritual substances (*kuladravya*) are those produced in the womb and so forth. In the *Kumārīkalpa*:
The wise practitioner should carefully place the materials for the *arghya* offering into the *arghya* vessel,
as well as substances produced from the *kuṇḍa* and *goḷa*, and likewise the *svayaṃbhū* flower.
"No unrighteousness exists, O fair-browed one, in the accomplishment of a great mantra.

In the *Sārasaṃgraha*: "One should draw a triangle surrounded by a circle and encircled by a square on the ground smeared with fragrance, at the tip of the left [hand], using the *matsyamudrā* gesture."
Having worshipped with perfumes and offered the *arghya* water to the deity, one should worship the limbs [of the deity] at the corners and in front of the square with the *namo’ṇu* mantra.
Having worshipped the weapon-mantra in the various directions, one should place the conch-stand;
and having washed the conch-stand with the root-mantra, one establishes it.
Likewise, one should extract the syllable *kā* with its nasal bindu, followed by *bhujaṅgeśāya*,
then *maṇḍalāya*, and similarly *adharmapradāyai*.

Having uttered "Obeisance to the one whose self consists of ten digits," one should worship with perfumes and other offerings. The passage beginning with "the triangle" describes an alternative method for constructing the wheel (*cakra*). In that very [method], the worship of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) is performed within the squares and corners. Thus, in these two systems, the practice should be carried out according to the instruction of one's own guru.
And the Matsyamudrā is described in the Tantra: "One should place the palm of the left hand upon the back of the right hand;
one should move the two thumbs—this is the Matsyamudrā, which has the form of a fish."
*Kāla* is the letter *ma*; the *bindu* is the anusvāra; the *bhujaṅgeśa* is the letter *ra*. Likewise, it is joined with the *bindu*.

Here, the fire-energies (*vahnikalā*) should also be worshipped individually, as is seen elsewhere. Thus: having washed the conch with the weapon-mantra (*astra*), one should place it there and worship it.
The *arghamāna* measure, however, is one *prādeśa* in length and four *aṅgulas* in height.
Having declared "this is the arghya vessel," one should say with the mantra "I place [it]," and then say "to the solar orb" twelve times.
Having uttered the word "pada" for the self of the kalās, and the heart-mantra for the arghya vessel,
one should worship the conch with this [mantra] and then worship the kalās of the Sun.

In another tantra: "The practitioner, having washed the auspicious great conch upon the base with the seed-syllable of Wrath and the seed-syllable of the Weapon, should then place it there while reciting [the mantra] for the woman."
Śivā, endowed with the three long vowels, accompanied by Kālī, Brahmā, and Ramā;
the Lord of Śacī [Indra] with a long vowel, Vāyu, the Heart [Hṛ], and the last part of Manmatha [Na].
Tāriṇī is again as before, endowed with the three long vowels;
Śiva is endowed with the three long vowels, and from the word Līlā it is as before.
The final syllable of *māyā* (hrīṃ), joined with the moon of the left ear (*śaṃ*),
followed by *sarvakāmaḥ*, *kālarātriḥ*, and then the long *lā* from the word *lāya*.
To the support of all, to all, to the source of all, from everywhere;
then to that which consists of the purity of all, and from the state of all the Asuras.
"O you whose splendor is red as blood, O auspicious one, O vessel for the gods!
Come, O Goddess!"—this mantra, ending with "to the skull," is considered [the mantra].
One should worship Mahāśaṅkha with these four mantras:

with the two seed-syllables of Krodha and Astra, namely *hūṃ* and *phaṭ*; with *strīṃ* as the essential form; with *hrīṃ* for Śivā; with the three long vowels *ā*, *ī*, and *ū*; with *kālī* as the essential form; and [the mantra of] Brahmā.
The letter *ka* is the syllable *ka*. *Ramā* is the letter *pa*. "Endowed with *āyu*" means joined with the long vowel *ā*. "Endowed with the long [vowel]" means joined with the long vowel *ā*.
*Śacīpati* is the letter *la*. *Vāyu* is the letter *ya*. "Heart" is *namaḥ*; by that, the first mantra is: *hrāṃ hrīṃ hrūṃ kālīkapālāya namaḥ*. The last of the "Manmathas" is the syllable *strīṃ*.

The three long vowels are the forms *ā*, *ī*, and *ū*. *Tāriṇī* is the essential nature (*svarūpa*). Again, as before, [one says] "salutation to the skull" (*kapālāya namaḥ*). Thus, *strāṃ strīṃ strūṃ tāriṇīkapālāya namaḥ* is the second mantra. *Śiva* is the letter *ha*. It is endowed with the three long vowels, joined with *ā*, *ī*, and *ū*. From the word *līlā*...

After the two syllables *lī* and *la*, as before, one says *kapālāya namaḥ*. Thus, *hāṃ hīṃ hūṃ līlākapālāya namaḥ* is the third mantra. *Māyā* is the syllable *hrīṃ*. The final letter of the arrows is the seed-syllable *sa*. *Śambhu* is the letter *ha*. It is joined with the moon of the left ear, that is, joined with the vowel *ū* and the *anusvāra*.

*Sarve* is the essential form (*svarūpa*). *Kāma* is the letter *ka*. *Kālarātri* is the letter *pa*. *Dīrghā* is that which is joined with the vowel *ā*. *Lāyā* is the essential form. *Kānti* is the vowel *ā*. *Kṣut* is the letter *ya*. By that [is formed] *hrīṃ saḥ hūṃ*, [addressed] to the All-Skull, the Support of All, the All, the Source of All, and that which consists of the Purity of All.
"Salutation to the one who is crimson with the blood of all asuras, to the white one, to the vessel of the gods, to the skull-cup of the Goddess"—
this is the fourth mantra. Therein, the practitioner of mantra should worship the mandala of the fiercely radiant one.
The practitioner, knowing the ritual procedure, should fill [the vessel] with the root mantra, perceiving it as nectar.
Having scattered perfumes, flowers, and unbroken grains (akṣata), the mantra-practitioner should again display the three-part gesture (trikhaṇḍā) and worship the mandala of the Moon of Nectar there.

The third root [mantra] of Bhairavī is radiant with the seed-syllable of Krodha; it consists of the vowel *tāra* (Oṃ), the power *śakti* (Hrīṃ), and the power *ameśakti* (Hūṃ), adorned with the nasal *anusvāra*.
With this mantra, the practitioner of mantras should contemplate the water eight times.
*Śakti* is the syllable *E*.
Having infused the nectar with the *śakti*, he should display the *śaṅkhayoni* mudrā.
In a beautiful central chamber, within an eight-petaled lotus and a hexagon, [is the seat].
Having reflected upon the Mistress of the Kula in the manner that will be described,
the knower of mantras should worship her with ritual offerings using the root mantra.
By joining the thumb and the ring finger, one should satisfy Tāriṇī;
by joining the index finger and the thumb, by joining the middle finger and the thumb,
by joining the ring finger and the thumb, and by joining the little finger and the thumb.
One should satisfy that deity, who is the essence of the Vedas, with the root mantra.
Likewise, it is said elsewhere:
"Then, reciting the Mātṛkā up to the end of the root [mantra], one should [satisfy her] with waters consisting of nectar."
The worshipper should fill it with the reverse order [of the letters] using this mantra.
Having said, "I fill the argha vessel," one should then fill it completely;
then [one should utter] the two syllables *karṇa* (ka) and *candra* (ca), joined with the nasal drop (*bindu*), followed by the word *kāmada*.
Then, at the end of the sixteen [fingers], having worshipped with scents and flowers while reciting "Obeisance to the Self whose essence is the word *kalā*," one should worship the sixteen *kalās*.

The letter *ka* is Karna; the letter *ca* is the half-moon (*ardhacandra*); the dot (*bindu*) is the anusvāra. Thus, [the syllable] is *u*. The Kalās have been described in the *Kulārṇava*: "Dhūmrārcis, Ūṣmā, Jvalinī, Jvālinī, Visphuliṅginī, Suśrī, Svarūpā, Kapilā, and also Havyavahā and Kavyavahā."
The ten digits (kalās) arising from the letters beginning with *ya* belong to Agni; they bestow righteousness (*dharma*) and are Tapinī, Tāpinī, Dhūmrā, Marīci, Jvālinī, and Ruci.
Suṣumṇā, Bhogadā, Viśvā, Bodhinī, Dhāriṇī, Kṣamā,
Kamā, Ādyā, Vasudā, and Saurā— these twelve, ending with Ṭha and Ḍa, are proclaimed.
Amṛtā, Mānadā, Pūṣā, Tuṣṭi, Puṣṭi, Rati,
Dhṛti, Śaśinī, Candrakānti, Jyotsnā, Śrī, Prīti, and Aṅgadā.
O Mistress of the Kula, these sixteen digits born from the vowels— Pūrṇā, Pūrṇāmṛtā, and the others— are said to be gentle and bestowers of desires.
193) Regarding the phrase "arising from the letters beginning with *ya*": having first placed the ten letters beginning with *ya* together with the *bindu*, one places the fire-energies (*agnikalā*).

Having first placed the letters from *ka* to *ṭha*, from *bha* to *ḍha*, and the letters in reverse order, all joined with the *bindu*, one places the sun-energies (*sūryakalā*). And having first placed the sixteen vowels beginning with *a*, joined with the *bindu*, one places the moon-energies (*candrakalā*).
The meaning is that they are worthy of worship.

Likewise, in the *Merutantra*: "As before, having invoked the sacred site (*tīrtha*) there with the *tīrtha-mantra*, and having joined [it] with the *netra-mantra* and placed the flower with the *śikhā-mantra*..."
Having displayed the Gālinī mudrā and, by means of the mudrā known as Dhenus,
having duly rendered [the offering] nectarine with the seed-syllable of Sudhā, the practitioner—
Having meditated upon his chosen deity there and performed the ritual integration of the limbs (*sakalīkaraṇa*),
the practitioner should protect the ten directions with the placement of the limbs (*aṅganyāsa*) and the weapon-mantra (*astra*).
Having gazed [at the vessel] with the Netra-mantra, having stabilized it with the mudrā known as the conch (śaṅkha),
and then having ignited it with the mudrā known as the cow (dhenu).
There, one should worship the chosen deity with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings;
having fully worshipped the six limbs, one should consecrate [the offering] with the root mantra.
Then, one should cause the *argha* offering to be presented eight times with the Matsya-mudrā;
in rites of sorcery (*ābhicārika*), one should recite the mantra in reverse order.
Thus, the specific rule regarding the recitation of the root mantra has been stated in the *Karmopadeśinī*. Likewise:

"One should pour a little of that water contained in the conch into the water of the pitcher, as before, with the *aṅkuśa-mudrā* and the *tīrtha-mantra*, beginning with 'O Gaṅgā,' and so forth, having thus united them."
The *tīrthas*. The *gālinī-mudrā* is described in the *Mantratantraprakāśa*:
"The little fingers and thumbs of the two hands are joined with one another;
the index, middle, and ring fingers are held together, unbent."

This is declared to be the Gālinī mudrā, moved above the conch (śaṅkha). The seed-syllable of nectar is *vam*. The grammatical connection is that one should perform the ritual of the limbs (*sakalīkṛtya*) by means of the assignment of the limbs (*aṅganyāsa*). The meaning is that having struck the three claps (*tāla*), one should bind [the mudrā] with snapping fingers (*choṭikā*). The Śaṅkha mudrā is described in the Tantra as follows:
Having placed the thumb within the left fist with the fingers straight,
one should touch [the thumb] with the thumb of the right hand.
This is declared by the knowers of mantra to be the unsurpassed Śaṅkhamudrā.
In the *Triśaktiratna*: "One should arrange the series of vessels according to the procedure prescribed for the jar.
The sequence of installation is also stated in the Tantra:
One should place all the vessels between the *śrīpātra* and the jar;
the *gurupātra* at the end of the jar, and the *bhāgapātra* at the end of that.
At its end is the vessel for the Śaktis, and near that is the vessel for the Yoginīs;
at its end is the vessel for the Vīras, and near that is the vessel for the bali offering.
One should arrange the vessels for water for the feet (pādya) and water for sipping (ācamanīya) in their proper order.
Nine vessels are considered best, seven are middling, and three are lowest; one should never employ only a single vessel.
In the Merutantra: "One should consecrate each vessel eight times with the root mantra and display the dhenu-mudrā."
The word *anta* signifies proximity. The mention of "water for the feet" (*pādya*) and "water for sipping" (*ācamanīya*) is illustrative;

the vessels for the *arghya*, the bath-water (*snānīya*), the honey-mixture (*madhuparka*), and the water for sipping again should be placed right here. Regarding this, when there is an inability [to do so], it is stated in the *Triśaktiratna*:
Alternatively, there may be a water-pot (*kalaśa*), a conch (*śaṅkha*), and three vessels for the *śakti*.
In this first procedure, the vessels for the foot-water (*pādya*) and so forth should be established because they are required for worship. As stated in the *Navaratneśvara*:
"One may prepare two vessels in the absence [of more], but one should not perform the rite with fewer."
One should not use a single alms-bowl, even if it were Maheśvara himself.
The mantras turn away, and misfortunes arise at every step;
in this world there is poverty, and after death one falls into the state of a beast.
And one should fill the vessels for the water for the feet and so forth with water alone.
The traditionalists [state]: This sequence is for the *vīra-kalpa*. However, in the *paśu-kalpa*, one should place the *prokṣaṇī* vessel on one's right and fill it with water;
having taken a small amount of *arghya* water, one should add it to the water in the *prokṣaṇī* vessel.
Then the wise one should place the common vessel (sādhāraka-pātra) in front;
beside it, the offering of water for the feet (pādya), and beside that, the offering of the respectful oblation (arghya).
One should place the water for sipping (ācamanīya) at its side, honey and sugar-candy to its left,
and then place the water for sipping again and the water for bathing in that sequence.
This is the sequence. The substances for the water for the feet (*pādya*) and so forth are described in the *Phetkāriṇī*:
"One should prepare *uśīra* and *rocanā* in the vessel for the water for the feet, as well as the tips of *kuśa* grass, unbroken rice (*akṣata*), sesame, *vrīhi* rice, and barley."
One should cast clarified butter, white mustard seeds, and flowers into the vessel for the *arghya*;
likewise, jasmine, camphor, *kakkola*, *bahumūla*, and *tamālaka*.
Having ground it according to the rule, one should pour it into the water for rinsing the mouth (ācamanīya),
likewise adding honey, sugar, clarified butter, curd, and milk.
Having prepared the madhuparka, one should offer it beginning with the curd;

then the bath-water consisting of pure, fragrant water. For it is stated in the *Puraścaraṇacandrikā*: "One should cause the bath to be performed with fragrant waters. Again, the water for sipping (ācamanīya) is offered in the same manner as the previous sipping. (*Triśaktiratna*)
Having drawn out a drop from the conch of nectar with flowers and other offerings,
one should place it into all the vessels and contemplate everything as divine.
Now, regarding the libation (*tarpaṇa*) in the Tantra: having thus arranged the vessels, one should perform the libation with that very [liquid].
In this context, even before the libation to the Guru, they offer libations to Bhairava and Bhairavī with the left hand using the *tattva-mudrā*.
That method is stated in the *Tattvārṇava* after describing the previously mentioned meditation:
"Having meditated thus, the wise practitioner should offer libations upon the head to both of them.
"Both of them" refers to the two Bhairavas. Having joined one's own name to the end of those two previously mentioned mantras, [he should perform the libation].
The conclusion is that "he should satisfy those two.

In the *Triśaktiratna*: "In the aperture of his own crown (*brahmarandhra*), the wise practitioner of mantra, using the vessel of the Guru and the substance [of offering], should satisfy the three lineages (*oghatraya*) with the mudrā known as *tattva*."
Having especially gratified one's own gurus three times or once,
[one should meditate on the Goddess] surrounded by her retinue within the lotus of one's own heart.
One should also satisfy the Mistress of the Kula with the nectar from the Goddess’s vessel.

The *tattvamudrā* is employed for the libation by joining the ring finger and the thumb. Thus it is said in the *Jñānārṇava*: "Furthermore, one should offer libations three times with the *tattvamudrā*."
"This is declared to be the *tattvamudrā* by means of the thumb and the ring finger.

As for that which is stated: "The *tattvamudrā* is proclaimed [to be formed] by the union of the index finger and the thumb"—that is prescribed for meditation (*dhyāna*) and so forth, other than for the libation (*tarpaṇa*). And the triple current (*oghattraya*) belongs to Tārā.
In the *Bhāvacūḍāmaṇi* it is said:
"Now I shall describe the gurus of Tārā, who bestow both seen and unseen fruits:
Ūrdhvakeśa, Vyomakeśa, Nīlakaṇṭha, and Vṛṣadhvaja."
"O child, the divine currents bestow accomplishments; now hear from me the true nature of the lineages of the Siddhas:
Vasiṣṭha, Kūrmanātha, Mīnanātha, and Maheśvara."
Now Harinātha shall speak of the multitudes of men and the true gurus:
Tārāvatī, Bhānumatī, Jayā, Vidyā, and Mahoddeśvarī.
Sukhānanda, Parānanda, Pārijāta, Kuleśvara, Virūpākṣa, and Keravī— thus has the Tāriṇī-kula been described.
The gurus, ending with the word Ānandanātha, bestow all accomplishments; even women, in the form of gurus, are proclaimed to end with the word Devī.
One's own gurus, supreme gurus, higher-lower gurus, and supreme-abiding gurus.
In the *Kulacūḍāmaṇi*: "In ignorance regarding the names of the gurus, one should indeed worship the triad of gurus, or the quartet; beyond that, no restriction should be made."
In the Bhāvanirṇaya: "O Goddess, in the beginning, everywhere the giver of mantra is the supreme Guru;
for you are indeed the Parāpara-guru, and I am the Parameṣṭhi."
The intention is that the Parameṣṭhin Guru, as the "higher-than-higher" (parāpara), should be meditated upon in his form as you, and thus satisfied.
He states the fourfold [classification]: "The Guru, the Paramaguru, and likewise the Parāparaguru..."
Parameṣṭhin and Guru are indeed declared to be your gurus.

The traditionalists maintain that one should offer libations by first pronouncing the worldly name of the gurus preceded by "Śrī," then appending the titles "Guru," "Paramaguru," and so forth, and finally saying, "I satisfy the sandals of [Name]. The vessel for the Goddess is indeed the special arghya vessel; with its contents, one should [satisfy] the [deity] along with the limbs.

The meaning is that one should perform the libation (tarpaṇa) in this manner: "I offer libation to the venerable [Name] Goddess, together with her retinue, her weapons, and her vehicle. Alternatively, they perform the libation with the nectar from the vessel of enjoyment prior to the invocation.
As stated in the *Samayācāra*: "Having taken pure substance, one performs the libation with the *tattvamudrā*."
Having taken up the purification between the thumb and the forefinger on the left side.
The wise practitioner should satisfy the Goddess with both the left and the right hand.
Regarding the expression "with both the left and the right," some maintain that this indicates an optional choice (vaikalpika) between the two hands for the act of satisfying the Goddess.
Others, however, hold that one should take up the water for purification with the left hand and satisfy the Goddess with the right hand using the *tattvamudrā*.

"Between the thumb and the index finger": they say that this is merely for the purpose of grasping purity, because the *tattvamudrā* has already been described in another way in the context of libation (*tarpaṇa*). Now, the purification of the principles (*tattvaśuddhi*).

Then one should perform the purification of the principles (*tattvaśuddhi*). Regarding this, the scripture says: *Oṃ, may my prāṇa, apāna, vyāna, udāna, and samāna be purified; may I become light, stainless, and free from evil, svāhā*. *Oṃ, may my earth, water, fire, air, and ether be purified; may I become light,* and so forth. *Oṃ, [may my] prakṛti-*

"May my ego-sense, intellect, mind, and ears be purified," and so forth. "Oṃ, may my skin, eyes, tongue, nose, and speech be purified," and so forth. "Oṃ, may my hands, feet, anus, genitals, and sounds be purified," and so forth. "Oṃ, may my touch, form, taste, smell, and space be purified..."

197) "May they be purified," and so forth. Reciting the seven mantras beginning with "Oṃ, may my self consisting of wind, fire, water, and earth be purified," one should touch all the limbs seven times with both hands; this is the purification of the elements (*tattvaśuddhi*).
Now, regarding the offering of the *bali*:
one should then offer the *bali* to Vaṭuka and the others. For it is said in the *Kulārṇava*:
"O Kuleśvarī, as long as one has not offered [the *bali*] to Vaṭuka, so long [the rite] is not complete."
All the deities are satisfied by both its recollection and its sacrifice.
Therefore, one should worship Vaṭuka and the others with perfumes, flowers, wine, and meat;
by means of the specific application of their respective mantras, one shall obtain the favor of the deities.
O Mistress of the Family, whatever collection of substances has been brought for the purpose of worship or as a means of enjoyment,
let it be given with devotion to the Lords of the Field (Kṣetreśas).
The term "Vaṭuka" is an elliptical expression; it means "among Vaṭuka and the others. As stated in the Jñānārṇava:
"O Dear One, having prepared mandalas in the northeast, southeast, southwest, and northwest corners as before, one should then worship them as previously described."
As before, one should offer the bali-oblation for the sake of all prosperity,
O Maheśānī, to Vaṭuka, to the Yoginīs, and to Vallabha.
One should offer the bali-oblation to Gaṇeśa and Kṣetrapāla as before. However, according to the Samayācāra:
one should give the offering to Vaṭuka in the south and the bali to the Yoginīs in the north.
One should offer the bali to the spirits in the east, and to the guardian of the field (kṣetrapāla) in the west.
Likewise: "The offering for Vaṭuka is prescribed with the thumb and ring finger;
one should present the offering for the Yoginīs using the little finger and the thumb."
One should offer the bali-offering to the Kṣetrapāla with the thumb and forefinger;
O Dear One, the bali-offering to the Bhūtas is said to be made with all the fingers.
In the *Jñānārṇava*: "Likewise, place the middle finger of the clenched fist like a staff;
this is the Great Elephant-Tusk Mudrā, which is used for the offering to Gaṇeśa."
The mantras, however, are found in the Jñānārṇava itself: "Ehyehi devīputra, [then] vaṭuka, [then] nātha;
[then] kapila, [then] jaṭābhārabhāsvara, [and finally] trinetra."
And Jvālāmukha, at the very end: "Destroy, destroy the obstacles!
Accept the bali offering together with all ritual services! [This consists of] two words. 198)
The mantra of Vaṭuka is declared to be joined with the wife of Vahni (the fire-goddess, Svāhā).
O Goddess, one should offer the oblation to Vaṭuka with this mantra.

Whether above the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) or in heaven, in the expanse of the sky, on the surface of the earth, in the partless realm, in the netherworld (pātāla), in fire, or in water and wind— wherever situated,
or having taken her place in sacred fields (kṣetra), seats (pīṭha), and secondary seats (upapīṭha)— [she is worshipped] with flowers, incense, and other offerings.
May the goddesses, who are equal to the lords of the gods, always protect us with their auspicious power through this rite of bali-offerings.
At the end of this, O Maheśānī, one should write the seed-syllable *yāṃ*, followed by *yoginī*, then *bhyaḥ svāhā*; at the end of all these syllables, one should write the word *yoginī*.
Having written the armor (*kavaca*) and the weapon (*astra*) mantras, one should again write the *vahnijāyā* (the consort of fire, *svāhā*).
O Goddess, with this mantra, one should offer the oblation (*bali*) to the Yoginīs.

Likewise—one should again write the syllable *kṣa* conjoined with the six long vowels; according to tradition, a bindu is placed upon the *kṣa*. Furthermore, one should write the term for the field (*kṣetrapada*) and the protectors, incense, lamps, and so forth.
Having drawn the bali-offering together with [the deity], one should then say: "Take, take! (gṛhṇa gṛhṇa).
O beautiful one, this is the mantra of Kṣetrapāla, joined with the wife of Vahni (the fire-goddess, Svāhā).
O Goddess, with this mantra one should offer the bali-oblation to the Kṣetrapāla;
having written the three syllables *gāṃ*, *gīṃ*, and *gūṃ*, one should utter "Gaṇapati" ending in the suffix *-ṅe*.
At the end of *vara*, at the end of *varada*, and at the end of *sarva*, one should write the word *jana*;
having said "bring [him] under my control" (*me vaśaṃ cānaya*), one writes the two words "accept the offering" (*baliṃ gṛhṇa*).
The mantra of Gaṇeśa, joined with the wife of Vahni (the *svāhā* ending), should be used to offer the *bali*.
In the *Jñānārṇava*: "Then, one should place it upon a mandala prepared on the left side;
there, one should worship the base (*ādhāra*) and the vessel filled with food and water."
Having consulted with [the preceptor] regarding the cause, one should offer the bali-oblation to all beings three times with the sixteen-syllable mantra, O Goddess praised by heroes.
Then, O Bhuvaneśānī, [one should utter] *tāram*, the word for all obstacles (*sarvavighnapadam*),
then *kṛdbhyaḥ* and *sarvabhūtebhyaḥ*, the syllable *hūṃ*, and the beloved of fire (*vahnivallabhām*).
One should offer the *bali* while reciting [the mantra] with the mudrā known as *tattva*.

This has been stated in accordance with the oral tradition (*sampradāya*). In reality, however, the offering of *bali* to Vaṭuka and the others is more appropriate using the mantras taught in the *Vīracūḍāmaṇi*, which will be mentioned in the section on *puraścaraṇa*.
Because that alone is unique in this context.
199) Now, regarding the invocation (*āvāhana*), it is stated in the *Kumārīkalpa*: "Then [one should visualize her] flashing within the heart-lotus, having the form of lightning..."
Having led it through the path of the Suṣumṇā to the location of the head, O Maheśvarī.
O Goddess, the wise knower of mantras, using the wind-seed syllable through the left nostril and with the mantra beginning with "Deveśī," should invoke [the deity] into the wheel and other locations.
Having first meditated upon the *kāmakalā*, one should thereafter meditate upon the Goddess.
The mantra for the Mistress of Gods (*deveśī*) is as follows: "O Mistress of Gods, who are easily accessible through devotion, accompanied by Your retinue;
remain steadfast for as long as I worship You."
Thus [it is said]. From the *cakra*, that is, from the lotus situated on the head; as stated in the *Svatantra-tantra*:
"Then, having invoked Kālikā through meditation upon the *kāmakalā*, one should place the flower in the center of the *cakra* by means of the mudrā called the tortoise (*kūrma*)."
The *kūrmamudrā* is described in the Tantra: "One should join the index finger of the left hand with the little finger of the right,
and likewise place the thumb of the left hand upon the right index finger."
One should raise the right thumb and join the middle and other fingers of the left hand to the back of the right hand.
Then, with the left hand using the *pitṛ-tīrtha* (the space between the thumb and forefinger), one should likewise place [the water] upon the middle and ring fingers;
subsequently, one should perform this with the right hand, facing downwards.
One should make the right mandala equal to the back of a tortoise;
such a "tortoise-hand" bestows all accomplishments.
Regarding the meditation on the *kāmakalā* in the *Tantracūḍāmaṇi*:
"The face has the form of a *bindu*; below that is a pair of breasts;
and below that is [the letter] with the *parārdha*, together with the adorned circle."
This meditation on the Kāmakalā is to be kept strictly secret by the most excellent practitioners.
This secret must be understood from the mouth of one's own guru.
Now, the meditation:
In the Gandharva Tantra: Having visualized a cremation ground there, one should imagine a wish-fulfilling tree (kalpadruma) therein;
at its root, a jeweled pedestal adorned with various gems.
On all sides, there were jackals rejoicing at the abundance of flesh and bone; in the four directions lay corpses, skulls, funeral pyres, charcoal, and bones as ornaments.
In the midst of that, one should meditate upon the Goddess according to the yoga of meditation as described:
"In the *Nīlatantra*— [one should visualize her] with feet in the *pratyālīḍha* posture, terrible, adorned with a garland of severed heads,
dwarfish, pot-bellied, fearsome, and draped at her waist in a tiger skin."
Endowed with fresh youth, adorned with the five mudrās,
four-armed, with a lolling tongue, most terrifying, and bestowing boons.

One should meditate on her holding a sword and a knife in her right hands, and a severed head and a blue lotus in her left; she has one fierce, tawny matted lock, and her crown is adorned by Akṣobhya.
Adorned with three eyes shaped like the orb of the rising sun,
she stands amidst the blazing cremation ground, her face terrifying with protruding fangs;
her countenance is filled with passionate intensity, and she is decorated with ornaments of bone.
She is situated upon a white lotus within the waters that pervade the universe.
In the *Mantracūḍāmaṇi*: "Above that, in the house, [one should meditate on] the Goddess—dwarfish, with the luster of a sapphire, pot-bellied, her hips covered by a tiger skin."
She possessed a mass of full and elevated breasts, with round red eyes;
her tongue lolled out, she was most terrifying, and she blazed with millions of fangs.
She wears a radiant garland of blue lotuses, her hair is tied in a topknot, and she is terrifying;
she is adorned with a white bone-plate and beautified by five skulls.
She has an earring made of a red serpent upon her forehead,
and she is most brilliantly radiant with a necklace fashioned from a magnificent, exceedingly white great serpent.
She has an elephant with skin as dark as a blade of durva grass serving as her sacred thread;
she is four-armed, and with one fist, she is tearing apart pieces of raw red flesh.
She is adorned with a mass of matted hair and a rosary of beads;
she is graced by a sharp-edged sword held aloft in her right hand, and she is the roaring heroine.
Below that, one should visualize the supreme goddess adorned with a seed-vessel and a small knife;
she is beautiful, naked, and possesses a red stalk on her upper left side.
She holds a blue lotus, and beneath it a skull-cup;
she holds that which is endowed with the dullness of the worlds, resembling a jasmine flower.
Her arms were quickly adorned with armlets fashioned from a multitude of smoky-colored nāgas,
and her hands shone with bracelets made of golden-hued nāgas.
201) [She is] the one whose pure and stainless seat was fashioned by the white-complexioned Mahādeva;
likewise, she is of a nature that contracts her feet out of fear of constraint.
She stands with her left foot mounted upon the two feet of a corpse, gazing upward with great intensity;
she possesses three eyes and a waist-band adorned with a serpent as white as a jasmine flower.
Her sprout-like anklets were made of blood-red serpents,
and she was adorned with blood-red ornaments consisting of freshly severed heads from which blood was still dripping.
The Supreme Goddess is adorned with a great garland of fifty [heads], whose hair is interwoven with one another and whose lotus feet hang down.
Seated in the midst of a blazing funeral pyre, with a leopard skin as her upper garment,
her matted locks bound by the Akṣobhya nāga, she bestows boons.
Having thus become the Great Goddess—both oneself and the sacrificial substance—one should inform Mahādeva: "I am a scholar, a great poet."
In the Tāropaniṣad: [He meditates on] the Guru, whose body is a mandala of contradictory meanings of sentences, who has the luster of a fresh cloud, a protruding belly, and is exceedingly short;
she stands in the bloom of youth, with a tiger skin beneath her and hair reaching down to her head.
Having seized Anaṅga, she stands upon a corpse, her middle encircled by a half-āliḍha posture;
her complexion is faded, she is adorned with a garland of human heads, and her three reddish eyes are the transformations of the Triple Veda.
She is resplendent with a single matted lock of hair tawny like honey, adorned with ornaments of severed white bones that inspire awe;
she is decorated with great serpents representing the multitude of the eight great supernatural powers, and she grants fearlessness to the worlds with her loud, boisterous laughter.
Ananta was in her matted locks, Takṣaka in her ears, and the great serpent Padma served as a necklace upon her heart;
likewise, Karkoṭaka formed her sacred thread, and the divine Vāsuki was her beautiful girdle.
It is said that Śaṅkhapāla is considered the bracelet (kaṅkaṇa); Padma bears the beauty of the anklet (nūpura) upon his feet;
the Kulika serpent is considered the armlet (aṅgada) on his arms; and his state is established as being adorned with a great garland of half-serpents (bhujaṅga).

The serpent species here consist of all the following color-types: white, red, pale-white, dark-blue, as well as white and pale-yellow; thus have they been described by the sages who sat upon the blazing funeral pyre.

She always holds with her own arms, which arise from her own prowess, a skull and a curved knife entwined by fierce matted hair, a garland of blue lotuses together with their stalks, and a sword drawn from its scabbard on the right side.
One should meditate upon her, resplendent with the five mudrās that perceive the non-duality of all things and wearing a garland of blue lotuses;
one should contemplate her as the bestower of poetic genius and recite the mantra of Tāriṇī for the sake of one's heart's desire.

Also in the *Phetkāriṇītantra*: "The most excellent one, arisen from the seed-syllable HŪṂ, stands in the pratyālīḍha posture with her foot placed upon the heart of a corpse; she possesses a terrible loud laugh and holds in her hands a sword, a blue lotus, a flaying knife, and a skull-cup;
she is short of stature, her vast matted locks are dark and tawny, and she is encircled by fierce serpents. (202)
Having deposited her own dullness into the skull-bowl, Ugratārā herself destroys the three worlds.
The definition of *pratyālīḍha* is given in the *Saṅgītaratnākara*: "In that posture where the left leg is bent with the thigh lowered first toward the inside,
and the right foot is extended five *tālas* in front."
One should know that both [the hands] are in the *asra* (spear) position; however, when accompanied by the deity, it is *ālīḍha*.
By reversing the limbs of the *ālīḍha* posture, it is called *pratyālīḍha*.
A *tāla* is a *vitasti* (span), for it is stated in that very same source: "A *vitasti* is the measure of a *tāla*. *Asrau* means crooked.
Regarding the phrase "adorned with Akṣobhya on the crown," here *Akṣobhya* refers to a *nāga*.
This is because of the statement in the *Bhāvacūḍāmaṇi*: "Akṣobhya, who possesses a triple form, assumes the shape of a *nāga* upon the head of the Goddess."
In the *Brahmasaṃhitā*:
"Now I shall describe the meditation upon Tāriṇī, which bestows all perfections—
[meditating on her] as standing in the midst of a funeral pyre blazing with a mass of flaming fire, well-nourished and of short stature."
Standing with her right foot pressing upon the throat of the corpse, she presses down his foot with her left foot.
With a large, hanging belly, cloud-colored, and beautiful with the expanse of her high, full breasts;
flushed with the glow of the *javā* flower, three-eyed, and with a face terrifying due to a protruding tongue and fangs.
Her limbs are draped in a leopard skin; her face is graced with a smile; and in the midst of her mass of matted hair rests a blue lotus.
Upon the region of her head, amidst her matted locks, shines the form of Akṣobhya, emerging from the center like a shimmering golden serpent.
She wore a human garland of fifty severed heads, freshly cut and dripping blood as they were bound together by their hair;
she bore a multitude of fifty severed heads upon her stainless limbs.
She holds a great sword in her right hand, which grasps a heap of large quantities of blood and flesh;
and in her left arm, she holds a slightly quivering blue lotus with its red stalk trembling.
Holding a sharp knife aloft in her right hand and a skull-cup in her left—
[the cup] filled to the brim with the dullness of worldly existence that binds the universe— she shatters it with the flashing edge of the knife she wields.
She wears upon her forehead a formidable skull-ornament adorned with a variegated garland of bones and marked by five [sindūra dots];
her high mass of matted hair is crowned by a thick snake, and she shines with earrings formed from a serpent of intense red hue.
Delightful with the beauty of shimmering, lovely armlets upon her great-bodied nāga-form, throbbing with rays of smoke-like light;
she shines brilliantly with a golden-hued nāga-bracelet, radiant and charming with a gleaming white nāga.
Upon her body she wears a beautiful sacrificial thread fashioned by Nāgas dark as dūrvā grass blades, and she also bears a sacred,
lovely waist-string perfectly made by a Nāga white as a kunda flower.
I have long contemplated her, who is adorned with a circular ornament made of great coral and set upon her two feet— she of such beautiful form, immeasurable, faultless, boundless, and full of grace.
I bow to her whose feet are colored by the luster of the crowns of the hosts of gods, who removes all defects from those who prostrate before her, and who bestows desired boons;
through her grace, people obtain this entire world that has come into being and rejoice perfectly.
Whoever should always recite this hymn with a single-minded heart, the world will surely come under his control;
he shall have neither poverty nor sin, nor shall he possess a wicked mind, and he shall likewise attain liberation, as well as virtue and desire.
Now, regarding the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* in the Tantra: invocation (*āvāhana*), installation (*sthāpana*), making [the deity] present (*sannidhāpana*),
as well as what is called confinement (*sannirodhana*) and likewise facing [the deity] (*sammukhīkaraṇa*).
Having performed the stabilization of the vital breath (prāṇasthāpana) with their respective mudrās, one should proceed;
the characteristics of these are stated in the *Lakṣaṇasaṃgraha*:
"Having formed a hollowed-añjali gesture with both hands, [at] the root-joint of the ring fingers..."
One should place the two thumbs [within]; this is considered the *mudrā* for invocation (*āvāhanī*).
When this [mudrā] is indeed turned face-downward, it is called Sthāpanī;
when there is the joining of two fists with the thumbs raised, it is Sannidhāpanī.
When the thumbs are inserted within [the palms], that same mudrā is considered *sarodhinī*;
with both fists turned upward, it becomes the *saṃmukhīkaraṇa* mudrā.
A fist formed with the left hand, with the index finger extended and pointing downward,
is the *avaguṇṭhana* mudrā when it is rotated all around.
The placement (*nyāsa*) of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) upon the limbs of the deity constitutes the act of "making complete" (*sakalīkṛti*).
The "rendering nectar-like" (*amṛtīkaraṇa*) is performed with the *dhenumudrā*; that has been described. [As for that mudrā:
the thumbs are interlaced and the other fingers are extended.
This Great Seal is joy, O beloved, in the act of bringing [the object] to its ultimate state.
One should employ these mudrās in the rite of summoning the deity.
Regarding these first five mudrās, they say in sequence: "Come here! Stay here! Be present here! Be firmly established here! Be face-to-face here!"
In the Uḍḍīśa: "Therefore, in the worship of the deity who is already fully present, the act of invocation (āvāhana) is said here to be the respectful bringing about of her presence before one."
For this very reason, simply by displaying the *āvāhana-mudrā* (the gesture of invocation),
the wise have declared that the placement of the Lord within the yantra is accomplished;
indeed, having accepted the worship being offered, He bestows grace and other benefits.

204) That which possesses the capacity to perform [these functions] is called its "presence" (sānnidhya). For the presence of the All-pervading Lord extends as far as the completion of the ritual section (karmakāṇḍa).
That cessation has been taught by those who know the mantras as the abode of bliss, the reality characterized by existence, consciousness, and bliss, out of devotion for men.
In this rite of veiling (avaguṇṭhana), the entire [deity] should be meditated upon as pervading [the practitioner];
having performed the ritual of making [the self] complete (sakalīkaraṇa) with these mantras, one should then attain oneness.
One should effect the immortalization of the limbs together with the possessor of the limbs;
forgiveness of their transgressions should be understood as the supreme act of honoring them.

Regarding the offenses of [conceiving] Brahman, which is unlimited, as being limited by means of gestures such as invocation (*āvāhana*): these are the offenses consisting in the notion that [Brahman] has the nature of being delimited. Other gestures (*mudrā*) are described in the *Bhairavatantra*, following the statement "adorned with the five gestures," as: the Yoni, the Bhūtinī, and the one called Bījā.
Daityadhūminī and Lelihānā— these are proclaimed as the five well-guarded mudrās.
Their seed-syllables (bījas) are found in that very place:
the wise know them to be, in order, the Yoni, Māyā, the Cow, the Daughter-in-law, and the Kūrca.
I shall now describe their characteristics and seed-syllables in sequence.
The *yoni* is *ai*; *māyā* is *hrīṃ*; the *adharā* follows immediately after that; the *dhenu* is *vaṃ*; the *vadhū* is *strīṃ*;
and the *kūrca* is *hūṃ*. Likewise: [these are placed] respectively on the index finger, the ring finger, the middle finger, and the little finger.
And one should join the two hands at the base of the little fingers.
Having placed the tip of the thumb [within], it is proclaimed as the Great Yoni (mahāyoni).
One should display this mudrā facing downwards, preceded by the seed-syllable.
But in this [mudrā], O Goddess, having brought down the two index fingers behind and then placing them upon the thumbs,
it is proclaimed as the Bhūtinī mudrā.
Also in another tantra: "Having formed the yoni-mudrā, make the two middle fingers curved;
place them upon the tips of the two thumbs—this mudrā is considered to be Bhūtinī."
In the Bhairavatantra: Having crossed the hands and touched the pair of thumbs and index fingers, one should simultaneously and evenly form the manner of the half-moon shape.
Drawing the little finger downward, one should join it with the middle fingers;
O Goddess, this mudrā is called Bījā, whose nature is knowledge.
Having turned the two hands over and drawn the middle fingers with the little fingers,
one should place the pair of ring fingers below and the pair of index fingers separately [on top].
205) Having tightly bound them together with the tips of the thumbs and ring fingers interlocked,
this mudrā called Dhūmaketu for the Daityas has been taught, O beloved.
Having opened wide the mouth, one should move the tongue downward;
with a pair of fists placed at the sides, this is celebrated as the *lelihānā* (licking) mudrā.
Then, one should perform the consecration of the vital breath (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*) using the previously mentioned *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* mantra and the *lelihā* mudrā.
As for the *lelihā* mudrā: one should bring the index, middle, and ring fingers together, pointing them downward.
Having made the ring finger straight, one should place the extended little finger upon the ring finger.
This mudrā, named lelihā, is proclaimed for the placement of the vital breath (jīvanyāsa).
Next, one should perform the purification of the deity (devaśuddhi). As it is said in the Kulārṇava:
Having established the deity upon the pedestal and performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa,
the practitioner [should worship] with the root mantra, the Dīpinī, the Mālinī, and with water for the arghya offering.
The wise one should sprinkle [the deity] three times; O Dear One, this is the purification of the deity (*devaśuddhi*).

The installation (*pratiṣṭhā*) and the ritual of integration (*sakalīkaraṇa*) have already been explained. Furthermore, it is established by reasoning that the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) here is performed with the root mantra (*mūla-mantra*) alone.
Since the *Dīpinī* and *Mālinī* consist of the *Parā-prāsāda* mantra, their application belongs specifically to the Upper Tradition (*ūrdhvāmnāya*).
In the Kulārṇava:
"Having performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa, having kindled its vital breaths and the senses, and having established [the deity], one should worship the Lord; otherwise, it shall be fruitless."
In the *Triśaktiratna*: "One should indeed satisfy the Goddess as before with the nectar of the Goddess’s procession.
In the *Phetkāriṇī*: "Having invoked and established [the deity], and having meditated upon her, one should then worship her.
In the *Sārasaṃgraha*: "Having displayed the mudrās according to rule, one should worship her with the ritual services (*upacāra*)."
The mudrās are those such as the *āvāhanī* (invoking) and others. The ritual services (*upacāras*) are described in the *Mantramuktāvalī*:

"Water for the feet (*pādya*), the respectful offering (*arghya*), water for sipping (*ācamanīya*), bathing, clothing, ornaments, perfume, flowers, incense, lamps, food offerings (*naivedya*), and further water for sipping."
One should employ betel, worship, hymns of praise, libations, and prostration;
these are the sixteen services to be performed during the ritual worship.
Then, having offered water for the feet (pādya), the respectful offering (argha), and likewise water for sipping (ācamanīyaka),
as well as the honey-mixture (madhuparka) and another sipping, he should then offer fragrance and flowers.
Incense, lamps, and food offerings are considered the ten-fold service (daśopacāraka).
Worship consisting of items from fragrance up to food offerings is known as the five-fold service (pañcopacārikā).
In the *Prapañcasāra*: "Worship is said to be threefold; one should resort to one of these.
It is threefold according to the distinction of sixteen, ten, and five types of offerings. (206)
In the Kuloḍḍīśa: "Among all the ritual offerings (upacāras), whatever may be difficult to obtain, one should mentally visualize all of that and arrange it by means of scattering flowers."
In each instance, one should offer water at intervals between the ritual services (*upacāra*). Now, the procedure for the ritual services is written down; in the *Sārasaṃgraha*:
On the left side of the deity, one should offer a seat with the root mantra.
A sixfold seat is prescribed— made of flowers, wood, cloth, leather, silk (kauśa), or metal— which brings pleasure to the deity.

The *pauṣpa* [seat] is one fashioned from fragrant flowers. The *dārumaya* [seat] is one made of wood, either carved from thorny wood or fashioned from sandalwood and the like. The *vāstra* [seat] is one made of cotton, silk, wool, blankets, and so forth. The *kauśa* [seat] is a mat (*viṣṭara*) consisting of twenty-seven layers of grass.

Thus it is stated in the *Ḍāmara*: "A seat (*viṣṭara*) consisting of twenty-seven blades of *darbha* grass, adorned with a knot at the tip, is proclaimed as the defining characteristic for all sacrifices.
"Metallic" (*taijasam*) means fashioned from gold and the like, excluding iron, lead, and so forth. "Leather" (*carmam*) refers to the skin of deer, tigers, and the like.
One should perform the welcoming rite by displaying the *svāgata* (welcome) mudrā and uttering, "Welcome, O Śrī Amukadevī!
As stated in the *Kālīkalpa*: "The knower of mantras should offer water for the feet (*pādya*) at her feet with the mantra ending in *namaḥ*."
In the *Śāradā*: "This [offering] is declared to be with water from *śyāmāka*, *dūrvā*, lotus, and *viṣṇukrāntā*.
In the *Kālīkalpa*: "O Goddess of gods, one should offer the *arghya* above the head with the mantra *svāhā*."
In the Śāradā-tantra: "With perfumes, flowers, unbroken rice, barley, tips of kuśa grass, sesame seeds, and mustard, along with dūrvā grass—this is declared to be the arghya for all the gods."

In the *Kālīkalpa*: "The sipping of water (*ācamana*) and the honey-mixture (*madhuparka*) should indeed be offered into the mouth with the *svadhā* mantra. In the *Śāradā*: "One who knows the mantras should offer the water for sipping into the mouth with the *svadhā* mantra, combined with nutmeg (*jātī*), cloves (*lavaṅga*), and kakkola."
With the *svadhā* mantra and the seed-syllable *vaṃ*. As it is stated in the *Svatantra*:
"The preceptor should place the *madhuparka* in the mouth with the water-mantra.
Likewise: "Then, with the *svadhā* syllable, he should offer the *madhuparka* into the lotus of the mouth."
This [mixture] of clarified butter mixed with curd and honey is declared by the wise.
In the Kuloḍḍīśa: "Having prepared a madhuparka consisting of honey, sugar, clarified butter, curd, and milk, one should offer it according to the prescribed rite."
207) Honey is superior in every respect; curd, ghee, and sugar are equal [in quantity];
but milk is said to be the least of all in the *madhuparka*.
In the *Śāradā*: "With that very mantra, one should perform the offering of water for sipping (*ācamanīyaka*).
Regarding the second sipping of water, the *Kālīkalpa* states:
"One should offer the bath and the fragrance with the *hṛdaya-mantra*, and the flowers with 'vauṣaṭ'."
Then, saying "I offer," one should give everything, O Maheśvarī.
And in the *Yāmala*: "With the seed-syllable of Varuṇa, one should offer the honey-mixture (*madhuparka*) into the lotus of the mouth;
with that same mantra, one should perform the water for sipping (*ācamanīyaka*) using water."
One should cause the bathing to be performed with scented water and have [the deity] clothed in two garments;
one should offer a divine sacred thread as well as necklaces and other ornaments.
The fragrance should be offered with sandalwood, camphor, and black aguru;

and a garment of fine *dukūla* silk should be given, according to the statement in the *Puraścaraṇacandrikā*: "Having given two fine pieces of *dukūla* silk. Even there, for one who has the means, red cloth is recommended. Red...

This is according to the *Yāmala* statement: "Of power, the sun, and obstacles... In the *Mantratantraprakāśa*: "From [a rosary] defiled by oil and the like, disease arises; from one with holes, there will be affliction;
from an old one, poverty for the practitioner; and from a dirty one, a lack of luster."
In the *Sārasaṃgraha*: "Having offered the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*), one should then present the ornaments;
in worship and other rites, one should employ the name of the deity preceded by the word 'Ṅ' (the vocative case) and ending with 'namaḥ'."
These may be of various kinds according to the distinctions of crowns and so forth;
they should be understood by the wise according to the distinctions of female and male.
The meaning is that the sacred thread (yajñopavīta) should be given to the male deity. Regarding perfumes, they are described in the *Puraścaraṇacandrikā*:
"Sandalwood produced in Malaya, unadulterated and very cooling."
Auspicious camphor, agallochum, and musk, ground with cool water.
"Kṣodita" means ground or rubbed. According to another tantra, saffron and red sandalwood are also recommended:
"In the Tārārṇava, this 'eight-fragrance' (aṣṭagandha), consisting of gorocanā, kapikā, kuṅkuma, māṃsī, tagara, candana, and cora, bestows pleasure upon Tārā."

*Kapirbālā* is a type of plant; *goṭhimana* is a certain [plant]; *cora* is *śaṭhī*; *tagaru* is a specific kind of fragrance. The flowers prescribed here have been mentioned in the section on the procurement [of materials]. The rules regarding flowers are found in the *Puraścaraṇacandrikā*:
Not offered to another, flawless, pure, meritorious, fresh, and auspicious;
endowed with the sandalwood of virtuous qualities, it is enchanting with various fragrances.
In the *Jñānārṇava*: "O Goddess, one should not worship with flowers that have been stale, even if they are made of gold;
O Supreme Goddess, one should not worship with flowers that have become impure or are leftover from a meal."
"By 'remnants' (ucchiṣṭa) is meant those left over from the worship of other deities. In the Jñānamālā it is said:
'A leaf, or a flower, or a fruit should not be offered face-down;
that is declared to be a source of suffering. It should be offered exactly as it was produced.'"
Likewise: "The offering with the face turned downwards is not desired in the rite of the handful of flowers (puṣpāñjali);
however, in the act of giving the añjali, being face-downward is not a fault. This is the meaning. In the Tantra:
"One should present the flower to the wheel (cakra) with the thumb and the index finger."
The procedure for incense is found in the *Puraścaraṇacandrikā*:
"In this manner, one should prepare the incense in an auspicious vessel made of copper, bell-metal, or similar materials, having two feet, a curved stem, and adorned with lotuses."
With incense smoke arising from resinous substances such as guggulu and agallochum, cast upon glowing charcoal, and with fragrant materials that have been brought forth.
"Resin" refers to *sarjarasa* and the like. In the *Prapañcasāra* and the *Tantralīlāvatī*:
"With *jaṭāmāṃsī*, *guggulu*, as well as sandalwood and *aguru*; combined with *candana*, *rajani*, honey, and *kuṅkuma*..."
O Maheśvarī, one should offer incense mixed with clarified butter to the Goddess,
using guggulu, aguru, uśīra, sugar, ghee, honey, and sandalwood.
One should burn incense from below using pieces of heartwood cast into glowing coals.
As stated in the *Kuloḍḍīśa*: "Guggulu, Sarala wood, resinous wood, leaves from the Malaya mountains, hrīvera, aguru, kuṣṭha, jaggery, sarjarasa, and ghanasāra."
Harītakī, nakha, lākṣā, jaṭāmāṃsī, and śailaja—
these sixteen ingredients are known as the incense for rites dedicated to the gods and the ancestors.
Alternatively, [one may offer] guggulu along with aguru, camphor, and sandalwood,
as well as honey, clarified butter, jaṭāmāṃsī, śailaja, and saffron.
This incense, dear to Pārvatī, should be prepared by mixing these [ingredients].
In the Tantra: "Honey, musta, ghee, fragrance, guggulu, agallochum, śailaja, sarala, śihlaka, and siddhārtha—this ten-ingredient incense (daśāṅga-dhūpa) is prescribed."
Guggulu, agallochum, and sandalwood mixed with sugar, clarified butter, and honey—
this six-ingredient incense is always dear to all the gods.

In the Śaiva Āgama: Having sprinkled the incense vessel with the Astra-mantra and worshipped it with the Hṛdaya-mantra, one should burn guggulu while sounding the bell that has been consecrated with the Astra-mantra. (209)
The term *guggulu* is indicative of all substances prescribed for incense. In the Tantra it is said:
"Then, having worshipped the incense, lamps, and so forth with the Astra-mantra, one should offer them.
O Goddess, the wise practitioner should offer incense just as he did the perfume."
"So be it. This means with the middle finger and the thumb. The procedure for the lamp is stated in the *Kuloḍḍīśa*:
"The first is a ghee lamp, followed by one produced from sesame oil, mustard oil, resin from fruits, or one arising from lotuses."
The seven lamps are proclaimed to be those made from curd and those made from food;
the wick should be made from lotus fibers or from darbha grass fibers.
The wick used for the purposes of a lamp is always remembered as being of five kinds: made from nettle, from bādarī fiber, or produced from a tuft of cotton.
A lamp-vessel made of bell-metal, copper, iron, clay,
coconut shell, or even from the king of grass (palmyra) is recommended.
In this manner, one should prepare a lamp for the purpose of delighting the eyes;
however, until the conclusion of the sacrifice, one should arrange the lamp with its flame facing downwards.
In the Kālikā Purāṇa: "He whose heat is obtained from a lamp even at a distance of four finger-breadths is not declared here to be a mere lamp; he is remembered as the 'flood-fire' (oghavahni)."
Likewise— one should never give hemp, cotton, cloth, or even that which is worn out or soiled, nor anything already used, for the purpose of making a wick.
One must never extinguish a lamp prepared for the sake of the deities;
the thief of the lamp shall become blind, and the one who extinguishes it shall become one-eyed.
In the *Puraścaraṇacandrikā*: "Having lit lamps with a wick containing camphor and using either clarified butter or sesame oil, one should display them on high, fragrant and radiant."
Likewise: "And a lamp, like incense, in a vessel fashioned in the shape of a lotus, with each petal illuminated by a wick soaked in cow's ghee."
In this case, there is an option between cow’s ghee, oil, and so forth, but not a combination.
One should not offer oily substances such as ghee and the like after mixing them together;
by offering mixed oil, one goes to the Tāmisra hell.
Thus it is stated in the *Kālikāpurāṇa*.
In the *Tūrṇāyāga*: "One should show the lamp, which has the appearance of a whirling pigeon, to the eyes and other [senses].
(210) A lamp with ghee on the right and one with sesame oil on the left."
