The white wick should be on the right, while the red wick is on the left.
As stated in the Kālikā Purāṇa: "A lamp should be offered upon chests, but never upon the ground;
for although the earth is all-enduring, she cannot endure these two things."
A man who strikes with his foot upon what should not be struck, or likewise scorches a lamp,
thereby causing distress to the earth, should extinguish that lamp.
He surely attains the hell of burning sin; of this there is no doubt.
In the Tantra it is said: "O Goddess of gods, having held the lamp with the tip of the thumb, one should offer it;
likewise, one should perform the raising [of the lamp] with the Gāyatrī and the root-mantra."
Regarding this, collyrium is also mentioned in the Tantra: "Sauvīra, Jāmbala, Tuttha, Mayūraśrīkara, Darvikā,
and Meghanīla— these are the six types of collyrium."
The flowing variety is sauvīra, as well as jāmbala and prastara;
the mayūraśrīkara is a gem, while the meghanīla is fiery (taijasa).
Having rubbed and immersed these on a stone slab or one made of metal,
O son, one should offer them to all the gods and the goddesses as well.
The collyrium that is produced by means of ghee, oil, and other substances in copper or similar vessels using the flame of a lamp is proclaimed as *darvikā*.
A widow should not apply collyrium for the sake of the supreme Mahāmāyā;
furthermore, the practitioner should not apply eye-ointment using an earthen vessel.
The offering (naivedya) is described in the *Svatantrotantra*:
"One should repeatedly present to the Goddess as an offering food cooked in a hot oven, food cooked in oil, milk-pudding mixed with ghee, and whatever is pleasing to the mind."
In the Matsyasūkta: One should offer milk-rice (pāyasa) and rice mixed with sesame (kṛśara), combined with sugar and jaggery;
therefore, one should cause those [offerings] mixed with clarified butter, curd, and honey to be presented.
The knower of mantras should diligently offer the śāla fish, the pāṭhīna fish, the excellent flesh of the monitor lizard, and food combined with honey.
The *śālamatsya* is well known as the *mahāśāla*. In the *Muṇḍamālā*:
"One should offer the *śālamatsya*, the *pāṭhīna*, the *śakula*, the *gaḍaka*, as well as the *madgura*, the *celliśa*, and even the flesh of the buffalo."
O beautiful lady, [one should offer] the flesh of birds, various kinds of raw meat,
the black goat known as *mahāmāṃsa*,
as well as the lizard, the doe, aquatic fish-flesh, and the flesh of the *gaṇḍakī* crocodile.
Various milks with diverse seasonings, and many other condiments.
In the Kumārītantra: "Listen to me regarding other food offerings for practitioners:
betel-leaf with camphor, and coconut with sugar."
Milk-rice with ghee, ginger with jaggery,
sesame seeds with rice, and curd with sugar.
The citron, the jackfruit, and likewise the āmrātaka fruit;
the plantain, the tamarind, and the excellent śrīphala fruit;
as well as the karañja, the bakula, the palmyra palm, and the date palm.
And other fruits that are fragrant and delicious.
In the Rudrayāmala: "And in vessels made of fire-essence (taijasa), such as those of gold, silver, copper, stone, or even again on a lotus leaf."
Or the wise one should prepare the food offering (naivedya) even on a plate made of sacrificial wood;
but in the absence of all these, O Maheśī, it may be fashioned by his own hand.
Whatever is appropriate, having placed it in the *arghya* vessel, one should present it.

As stated in the *Sārasaṃgraha*: "Having placed [the vessel] upon a stand in a golden vessel within the mandala, and having set it down in a square [area], one should consecrate it according to the path of the scriptures."
Having sprinkled it with the weapon-mantra and protected it with the wheel-mudrās,
one should purify it with the wind-seed-syllable and burn it with the fire-seed-syllable.
Touching it with the tip of the right hand, one should consecrate it with the *sudhā* seed-syllable;
then, having rendered it all nectar, one should do so again with the root mantra.
Touching it with both hands, one should consecrate it eight times according to the prescribed rite;
then, having displayed the *dhenumudrā*, one should worship it with perfumes and flowers.
In the Tantra: "O Goddess, one should present the food offering with the mudrā called Tattva;
having offered betel-leaf with the root mantra, the practitioner [should do so] with that same mudrā."
With that root mantra and with the *tattva-mudrā*. In the *Yāmala*: "One should offer all the ritual implements and so forth at the end of the root mantra.
If one is unable [to do so physically], one should offer them mentally; one must not omit this sequence."
One should offer a handful of water according to the ritual rules and display the five mudrās;
then one should again offer a handful of water after having presented the finest betel.
It was blended with cardamom, cloves, camphor, nutmeg, and other ingredients,
and made fragrant by portions of tamāla leaves, camphor, and betel nut.

In the *Mālinītantra*: "One should join [the word] 'namas' at the end of all offerings preceded by the first case ending. In the *Nīlatantra*: "Having made everything consist of mantra, one should offer it to the deity.
Also in the *Phetkāriṇī*: "Having invoked and established [the deity], and having meditated, one should indeed establish [the offering] thereafter."
The practitioner should recite: "O Śrīmad-Ekajaṭā, accept this vajra-flower," together with the root mantra ending in *agnipriyā* (svāhā) and accompanied by the *satārā* (oṃ).

*Tāra* is the syllable *oṃ*. Its connection [to the deity] is established by tradition from the very beginning. Furthermore, this mantra should be recited without modification in the worship of all deities, such as Tārā and others, because they are all introduced [in the ritual procedure]. By means of this mantra, having offered the special *arghya* water, all the ritual services (*upacāras*) [are completed].
They are to be presented according to the scriptures. As it is stated in the *Svatantra*:
"The Great Goddess does not accept that which is offered by others, even if it has been prepared with hundreds of rituals, if it is poured from vessels other than those containing the *argha* water."
In the *Yāmala*: "One should present perfumes, flowers, and ornaments in the front portion;
one should offer lamps to the right or in front, but not to the left."
The incense should likewise be on the left or in front, but not on the right;
the food offering (naivedya) should be on the right, the left, or in front, but never behind.
In the Yoginītantra: "Scent, flowers, incense, lamps, and food offerings, as well as whatever is given—clothing, ornaments, gold, and so forth [to each deity]."
Having uttered their respective deity-mantras and performed the sprinkling and worship,
one should release them with the root mantra and offer [the oblation] by means of each individual name.
In the *Gautamīya*: "You are the underlayer of nectar, svāhā!"—with this, one should offer water.
In the *Dīpikā*: Displaying with the left hand the *grāsamudrā*, which resembles a full-blown blue lotus, one should display the [mudrās] of *prāṇa* and the others with the right hand.
In this first mudrā, one should touch the little finger and the ring finger with the tips of one's own thumbs;
likewise, the other [mudrās] consist of the index and middle fingers, and the middle and ring fingers.
The ring finger, the index finger, and the middle finger; likewise, the fourth [finger] together with the little finger;
and the fifth should be likewise—these are declared to be the mudrās of Prāṇa and the others, joined with their respective mantras.

The mantras, however, are "Oṃ prāṇāya svāhā" and so forth. As it is stated in the *Candrikā*: "Prāṇa, apāna, samāna, udāna, and vyāna, preceded by the syllable 'Tāra' (Oṃ), joined with the dative case-ending and the word 'agnivadhū' (the consort of fire)—these are remembered as the prāṇa-mantras."

Then, having given water for drinking and having visualized that the deity is satisfied, one should give the counter-rinse (pratyapośāna) with the mantra: "Thou art the covering of nectar; svāhā! As it is stated in the *Gautamīya*:
"Having reflected for a moment, the wise man should then offer a mouthful of water."
With this mantra, "Thou art the covering of nectar; svāhā!"—by means of this [mantra].
In the *Dīpikā*: "Gargling, cleaning the teeth, sipping water, wiping the mouth and hands, anointing with unguents, perfumes for the mouth, garlands, and ornaments."
Having also offered betel leaf, honor him with excellent instrumental music, dance, and song, making him fully satisfied as before.
Then, having offered the *argha* along with its retinue using perfumes and other offerings, and having respectfully formed a handful of flowers (*kusumāñjali*),
one should praise him, bow with the head, and offer oneself at the base of his lotus feet with water held in cupped palms.

Now, regarding the summary of the characteristics of the ritual gestures (*upacāramudrā*): "The lotus gesture (*padmamudrā*) should be used for the seat; it consists of both hands facing downwards. This same gesture, with the hands facing upwards again, is used when inquiring about one's welfare."
The *svāgata* (welcome) gesture is the *argha* mudrā, while the *añjali* is said to be the [offering] mudrā;
that same [mudrā], through the joining of the ring finger and the thumb, is called the *pādya* mudrā.
The wise practitioner, having placed the right hand face upwards with the palm hollowed out,
should keep the four fingers— excluding the little finger— joined together and raised.
O fair-faced one, this same mudrā with the palm facing downwards is declared for the ritual sipping of water (ācamana);
when the thumb is touched [to the other fingers], it becomes the mudrā for the offering of honey-mixture (madhuparka).
O Supreme Goddess, this mudrā of bathing is said to be a fist formed with the right hand facing downwards, with the little finger extended.
Having placed the right hand palm upwards, one should then touch its middle finger with the thumb; this is proclaimed as the mudrā of clothing.
This same [mudrā], when touching the ring finger, is known as the *bhūṣaṇa* (ornament) mudrā;
indeed, when touching the little finger, it is the mudrā of the sacred thread (*upavīta*).
One should touch the tip of the little finger with the tip of the thumb; this is the *mudrā* for the fragrance.
In another tantra it is said: "O Pārvatī, the practitioner should offer pure fragrance with the tips of the middle, ring, and thumb fingers, while reciting the root mantra."

One should offer the flower upon the yantra with the thumb and the index finger. Likewise: "O Supreme Goddess, having turned the hand face-downward, one should join the tip of the thumb to the tip of the index finger; this is the mudrā known as Puṣpā."
O Maheśvarī, one should touch the tip of the index finger with the tip of the thumb;
this is declared to be the incense mudrā (dhūpamudrā), which brings pleasure to all the gods.
O worshiper of the gods, one should touch the tip of the middle finger with the tip of the thumb;
this is declared to be the *dīpamudrā*, auspicious and beloved by all the deities.
O Goddess, the preceptor should touch the tip of the ring finger with the tip of the middle finger;
this is declared to be the *naivedya-mudrā*, which brings satisfaction to the deity.
Now, regarding the worship of the retinue (*āvaraṇapūjā*), it is stated in the *Somabhujagāvalī*: "Then, the wise practitioner should offer libations three times with the root mantra;
having received permission from the Great Goddess, he should worship the members of her retinue."
The first ritual procedure is performed with the six limbs; the second is with the gurus;
the third should be with the retinue; and the fourth is with the world-protectors.
Thus, the fifth [stage] is declared by means of the weapons; such is the general sequence.
In the *Yāmala*: "Thereafter, one should worship the deities of the limbs with water for the feet (*pādya*) and so forth.
In the *Mālinītantra*: "Now, omniscience, contentment, and that which is designated as primordial awakening (*anādibodha*)."
Independence is another [aspect] which is eternal and possesses unimpaired power;
these are indeed proclaimed by name as the six-limbed deities.
In the Tantra: "One should worship the six limbs upon the body and the filaments of the lotus.
Regarding the sequence of worship on the filaments, it is stated in the *Jñānārṇava*:
"The worship of the limbs is performed in the directions of Agni, Īśa, Asura, Vāyu, and the center."
In the Somabhujagāvalī: "Having worshipped the heart in the southeast, one should worship the head in the northeast;
the tuft (śikhā) is to be worshipped in the southwest, and one should worship the armor (kavaca) in the northwest."

Having worshipped the Eye (Netra) in front, one should then worship the Weapon (Astra) in the directions. In the *Tantra*: "One should worship the lineage of Gurus from the northwest (Vāyavya) up to the northeast (Īśa). The lineage of Gurus is the collection of the Divine Current (*divyaugha*), the Siddha Current (*siddhaugha*), and the Human Current (*mānavaugha*), as previously stated.
And one's own three gurus. In the *Mālinītantra*: "O child, if one performs worship without first worshipping the guru, then at that time of fault, O child, one should perform the Kula-worship."
Wherever there is a deficiency or a lack of quality, it is rectified by the worship of the Kula.
In the *Vīracūḍāmaṇi*: "Having invoked her, one should worship her along with the limbs and the enclosures (āvaraṇas).
O Maheśānī, one should also worship the Triśakti in the center of the Bindu."
Thereafter, one should worship the couple Rati and Prīti, who are dear and radiant, as well as the flower-arrowed god holding his bow, and the four-faced Gāyatrī.
One should meditate upon the final Sāvitrī and worship Viṣṇu as the deity;
having invoked Vāgīśvarī, one should worship Rudra in union.
O Goddess of the gods, one should worship the Guru Akṣobhya in the form of a row;
thereafter, one should worship the knife and worship the charcoal from the funeral pyre.

O Goddess, having performed the placement of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga-nyāsa*), one should worship in the hexagon and offer libations; one should extract the mantra ending with *dviṭha* (svāhā), preceded by the *praṇava*, the first letter [of the name], and the word for that name,
followed by "accept the vajra-flower" (*vajrapuṣpaṃ pratīccha*).
And I shall proclaim the names, in their respective places, according to the proper order.
In the Vīra Tantra: "Then, outside [the central circle], the eight Yoginīs should be worshipped at the bases of the petals:
Mahākālī, Rudrāṇī, Ugrā, and likewise Bhīmā."

Ghorā, Bhrāmarī, Mahārātri as the seventh, and Bhairavī is declared as the eighth; one should worship those Yoginīs. In the *Yāmala*: "One should worship [them] on the petals in the four directions of the Goddess, starting from the east in due order."
In the east is the one named Vairocana, and in the north is Asitābha.
One should worship the one named Padmanābha in the west and Śaṅkhapāṇḍava in the south;
thereafter, one should worship them in the intermediate directions, starting from the southeast corner in due order.
The practitioner shall everywhere employ the name accompanied by the vocative case— whether it be *nāmaka*, *māmaka*, *pāṇḍara*, or *tāraka*.
In the *Vimalātantra*: "When a mantra cannot be obtained, the seed-syllable (*bīja*) consisting of the first letter of one's own name is proclaimed [as the substitute].
In the *Yāmala*: "And on the tips of the petals, O Maheśānī, one should worship Brāhmī and the others."
And one should worship Padmāntaka and the others in sequence at the four gates:
Padmāntaka, Yamāntaka, and Vighnāntaka thereafter.
Having fully worshipped Narakāntaka, one should worship the guardians of the directions;
then, having worshipped the Sun in the center, one should [worship] the lineage of gurus to the north.
One should worship the Buddha first, and then worship the Goddess again;
the wise one should offer three handfuls of flowers and recite the mantra according to the respective number.
In the independent square, one should worship the world-protectors (lokapālas) and their weapons outside of that;
however, there is a specific rule in the *Matsyasūkta*:
"The goddesses beginning with Kāmeśvarī are to be worshipped in the triangle within the fire-mandala."
"Kāmeśvarī, Dikkaravāsinī, and Caṇḍanāyikā"—thus it is said.
Then, one should cast three handfuls of flowers with the root mantra (mūlamantra).
Taking red flowers, one should recite the Kullukā mantra over one's head.
Thus it has been said. One should also worship Akṣobhya upon the crown of the Goddess, because of the statement: "One should worship Akṣobhya on the crown.
And this they perform prior to the worship of the surrounding deities (*āvaraṇa-pūjā*). Now follows the determination of the directions at the beginning of the worship.

In all these cases, the deity who defines the directions is primary; therefore, the worship of the lineage of gurus is accomplished starting from the left rear corner of the Goddess and extending to the front left corner.
The wise declare that the direction between the worshipper and the object of worship is the East.
That which is south shall be the south, and that which is north shall be the north.
According to the statement in the *Mānasollāsa*:
"In rites such as worship and fire-offerings (*homa*), one should know that the directions— east and so forth— are ten spaces facing the sacrificer, with the gods facing the [sacrificer]."

And because of the statement in the *Sārasaṃgraha*: "Thus, the dark-hued one is likewise in the north," and so forth, even in such cases, the left-hand portion of the Goddess is said to be situated precisely in the well-known southern direction. Therefore, the order of worship proceeds by counter-clockwise rotation (*vāmāvarta*). However, the tradition (*sampradāya*) here follows the well-known sequence starting from the east and so on.
The worship of the deities beginning with Brāhmī, however, proceeds starting from the petal in front of the Goddess and continuing strictly clockwise,
since no specific direction has been stated. Now, as for the worship of the enclosures (āvaraṇa-pūjā), one should designate the east as being in front.
Then follows the worship of the retinues, proceeding clockwise.
This is also because of the statement in the *Nṛsiṃhakalpa*. The same should be understood for what follows as well. However, this must be noted:

prior to the invocation of the deity, the worship of Dharma and the others in the southeast corner and the worship of the pedestal-shaktis (*pīṭhaśakti*) on the eight filaments starting from the east should be understood according to the visualization of facing forward and being oriented toward the east.
Because the object of worship has not been invoked, there is at that time no distinction between the worshipper and the worshipped.
O Goddess, when one should extract the *cakra* facing the northern direction, then the northern direction is to be understood as the eastern direction; of this there is no doubt.
O Goddess of gods, when the practitioner facing west raises the wheel, then the northeast is the southeast; of this there is no doubt.
217) At that time, the western direction should be known as the eastern direction, without a doubt;
the northwest corner will then become the southeast, and the northeast will become the southwest.
When the practitioner, facing the southern direction, extracts the wheel,
then the eastern direction becomes the southwest (rakṣas), and the southeast corner becomes the northeast (vahni).
This is because the statement from the *Jñānārṇava* cannot be explained otherwise.

Facing the western direction and so forth pertains specifically to optional (*kāmya*) worship; for in the case of daily (*nitya*) worship, only two directions are prescribed by such passages as, "facing east, or else facing the direction of the Giver of Wealth (the north)," and so on. However, some [hold that...]
They worship Indra and the others according to their natural directions [such as east]. The authority for this should be considered.

Now, regarding the visualization of the deities of the enclosure (*āvaraṇadevatā*), the *Śāradātilaka* states: "In the northeast corner [is Indra], holding a shining staff, a water-pot, a rosary, and displaying the gesture of fearlessness."
The practitioner of mantra should worship Gāyatrī and likewise Brahmā as well.
In the southwest corner, one should worship Sāvitrī, who holds a conch, a discus, a mace, and a lotus, and is dressed in yellow garments, as well as Viṣṇu, who is likewise adorned.
In the northwestern corner, one should worship the pure Sarasvatī, who holds a battle-axe, a rosary, and the gesture of fearlessness, and likewise Rudra, characterized by those same attributes.
Here, by the words "the northeast corner" and so forth, there is a designation of the directions—east and so on—for the deities themselves.
The visualization of those possessing the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) is precisely therein:
[they are] with rays that are white as frost, crystal, dark, blue, black, and ruddy.
The principal female forms hold the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.

Therefore, the deities of the limbs (aṅgadevatās) should be meditated upon by the wise in that very same sequence as the "principal bodies" (pradhānatanavaḥ). Rāghavabhaṭṭa states that this is an alternative meditation. Since no specific distinction is mentioned, the meditation on Mahākāla and the others at the base of the petals is to be performed like that of the root deity.
The meditation on Vairocana and others is described in another tantra:
"Vairocana has two arms and holds a staff and a spear;
he is yellow, seated upon a bull, possesses three eyes, and is affectionate toward his devotees."
[One should meditate on] the god Śaṅkha, who has three heads, is dark-complexioned yet golden-hued,
holds a book and displays the gestures of fearlessness and granting boons, is stainless, and has a rabbit as his vehicle.
"Śaṅkha with three heads"—the rest is black. Regarding "book," etc.: one should understand that he has four arms because he holds a single book with both hands; the same applies hereafter.
Padmanābha has the face of an elephant, holds a book, and displays the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
And [he saw] the auspicious god, three-eyed and the bestower of boons, holding a noose.
218) White, three-eyed, bestowing boons, and holding a book and the gesture of fearlessness— this is my [form], visualized as joined with the god Valaya.
[He saw] Kṛṣṇā, with a formidable face, naked and in the prime of youth;
[he saw] Godhikā mounted upon a lizard, and Tārakā mounted upon a peacock.
One should meditate upon Pāṇḍarā, who is white, endowed with four arms,
red in complexion, pot-bellied, and seated upon five corpses.
The hand-meditation for all of my [deities] is as follows:
having first uttered the seed-syllable, one should worship the dark-green Tārā;
then, O Śāṅkarī, on the lotus petals starting from the east, one should worship with the respective seed-syllables.
One should worship with each verse beginning with the *dhruvaka* and ending with *namaḥ*.
Now, regarding the meditation (*dhyāna*) on Brāhmī and the others, it is stated in the *Śāradā*: "The staff, the water-pot, and then the rosary, and finally the gesture of fearlessness."
Bearing a golden luster, the Brahmi goddess shines with a radiant black antelope skin.
Carrying a trident, an axe, a small drum, and a human skull,
the auspicious Māheśvarī, white as snow, should be meditated upon.
Holding a goad, a staff, a khaṭvāṅga, and a noose in her hands,
Kaumārī resembles a bandhūka flower and bestows boons.
Holding a discus, a bell, a skull-cup, and a conch in her hands,
the goddess Vaiṣṇavī— dark as a tamāla tree and radiant with grace— is to be meditated upon.
Vārāhī, possessing the complexion of a dark cloud at the end of time, should be meditated upon as holding a pestle, a sword, a shield, and a plough with her four hands.
Holding a hook, a javelin, lightning, and a thunderbolt in her hands,
Indrāṇī, who resembles a sapphire, should be meditated upon as the bestower of all prosperity.
Cāmuṇḍā, whose body is red, should be meditated upon as holding a trident, a sword, a human head, and a skull-cup in her hands, adorned with a garland of severed heads.
Holding a rosary of beads, a citron, a skull, and a lotus in her hands,
Mahālakṣmī is described as being golden-hued.

Some, however, say that here only the group of eight beginning with Brāhmī and Nārāyaṇī—mentioned in the section on Kālī—is to be worshipped, because it is said that "as Kālī is, so is Tārā. Their visualization will be described in that very same place. 219) Now, the visualization of Indra and the others.
In the *Tūrṇāyāga*: "Having thus properly worshipped the enclosure (*āvaraṇa*), the best of mantra-knowers should finally worship the world-protectors (*lokapāla*) and their weapons in due order."
[One should meditate on] Indra, the lord of the gods, yellow in color, holding a thunderbolt in his hand, accompanied by his vehicle;
and Agni, the lord of splendor, red in color, holding a spear in his hand, and beautifully adorned.
One should worship Yama, the lord of the pretas, who is black and holds a staff in his hand;
and Nirṛti, the lord of the rākṣasas, who is very smoky-colored and holds a sword in his hand.
One should worship Varuṇa, the lord of aquatic creatures, who has a noose in his hand and very radiant limbs;
and Vāyu, the lord of the vital breaths, who is smoke-colored and whose hand is enriched with a goad.
One should worship Kubera, the lord of the yakṣas, who is white in color and holds a mace;
likewise, one should worship Īśāna, the lord of knowledge, who is transparent and holds a trident.
One should worship Ananta, the lord of the Nāgas, who is fair-complexioned and holds a discus;
one should worship Vidhātṛ, the lord of the worlds, who is red and holds a lotus in his hand.
Likewise, Airāvata, the ram, the buffalo, the dead man,
the crocodile, the deer (and the horse), the goat, the bull, the chariot, and the swan.
The wise know the vehicles of Indra and the other world-protectors;
one should worship the yellow thunderbolt, the white spear, and the black staff.
One should meditate upon the sword as resembling the sky and the noose as being like lightning.
One should worship the goad, which is red in color, and the mace, which is white in color.
Thereafter, the practitioner of mantra should worship a trident of blue color;
then he should worship a wheel with the luster of a jasmine flower and a red lotus.
One should worship the weapons of the world-protectors (lokapālas) in this sequence.

Although other mantras for the worship of the six limbs, beginning with the heart, as well as for Indra and the others, are mentioned in other tantras, those are intended for the worship of the retinues of different deities. And here—
"Accept the vajra-flower, HŪṂ PHAṬ SVĀHĀ"—
with this mantra, one should worship all the retinue members at the end.
According to such statements from the *Vīratantra* and other sources, the worship of the entire retinue is performed with the mantra beginning "vajrapuṣpa" and so forth.
Following the worship of Indra and the others, the mudrās of the world-protectors (*lokapāla*) should be displayed. As it is stated in that Tantra:
"With the bases of the hands well joined, all the fingers are extended."
This is the mudrā of the Lords of the World; one should display it during their worship.
220) In the *Tūrṇāyāga*: "O you who are compassionate toward those who have come for refuge, grant me the accomplishment of my desired goal!
With devotion, I offer to you this worship of the first enclosure (*prathamāvaraṇa*)."
Thus one should offer a handful of flowers and prostrate with great devotion;
indeed, one should offer each successive enclosure by its respective name.

In the *Svatantra*: "Then again, having worshipped the Root Goddess with mudrās, libations, and offerings, and having performed the recitation (*japa*), one should thereafter perform the dismissal (*visarjana*)."

The *mudrā* is called the *yoni*. The method of worship has been stated in the *Tūrṇāyāga*: "Again, having recited the root mantra together with its limbs (*aṅga*) and its attendants (*parivāra*), and having uttered the name of the Goddess ending in the dative case, [one should say] 'to Vārā'."

The practitioner should worship [the deity] three times with the mantra "Namaḥ" using perfumes, flowers, and other offerings. Now, regarding the offering of the bali-oblation, the *Triśaktiratna* states: "In the left portion, there should be a triangle, a circle, and a square."
Having prepared [the site] with red garlands and other offerings, one should worship according to the prescribed ritual.
One should present an offering to the Goddess with the mantra to be recited hereafter:
having pronounced "Dhruvam" and "Lajjām," one should utter "Ekajaṭām" ending in the feminine nominative singular suffix.
Likewise, for the sake of the great lord of yakṣas, one should offer the presented bali;
then, [recite] "grahṇa-grahṇāpaya" twice and "sarvapada" after me.
One should utter the pair "śāntiṃ kuru," and after that, the supreme vidyā;
having drawn [the mantra] from the end of the pair, one should speak the pair "truṭa chindhi."
This is declared to be the *bali-mantra*, ending with the word "brīḍā-vahni-vadhū-prāntā.
It should be offered using either water from the *bali* vessel or the special *arghya* water. In the *Narasiṃha Purāṇa*:
"One should perform the fire-oblations, the sacrificial offerings, and the *bali*s with the measure of a fresh *āmalaka* fruit."
The ritual procedure for the goat-offering and other oblations shall be described hereafter. First, having recited the *kulluka* mantra, the *tārā* mantras are to be recited.
As it is stated in the *Triśaktiratna*: "Without having recited the *kulluka* mantra and without remembering Hari, the Lord of Śrī..."
Whoever mutters the Tāriṇī mantra shall sink into hell.
Having recited the *kulluka* mantra one hundred and eight times, the wise practitioner should thereafter recite the *Tāriṇī* mantra; otherwise, one shall not attain success.
Having held the *kulluka* in his hand, he should worship the Great Goddess;
or else, having placed it upon his head, he should worship it and also recite its mantra.
In the *Brahmasaṃhitā*: "If one abandons the mantra of Akṣobhya and recites the mantra of the goddess Tārā, there will be a loss of accomplishment for him, and he shall go to the Raurava hell."
Likewise: "O Brahmin, the mantra of Akṣobhya is the armor, the most excellent essence;
it is a supreme secret and a great meditation, the best among all meditations."
First I shall proclaim the *mantra*, and after that the meditation (*dhyāna*);
thereafter, I shall relate the armor (*kavaca*) in due order.
Having extracted the unsurpassed [seed-syllable] devoid of conceptual proliferation (prapañca),
the great mantra begins with *akṣobhya* and ends with *svāhā*, preceded by *ramā*.
The letter *a* is the unsurpassed; the letter *ma* is the fifth, [representing] *papañca*. By that, there is the *bindu*.
He is himself proclaimed as the *ṛṣi*, and the *virāṭ* is declared to be the *chandas*. Akṣobhya is proclaimed as the deity, possessing three forms and assuming the shape of a serpent.
Its application, moreover, is invariably restricted to the four aims of human life.
Now I shall describe the meditation (dhyāna) which bestows all prosperity:
[one should meditate upon the Lord] who resembles a thousand suns, who assumes the auspicious form of a serpent,
whose face is like ten million flashes of lightning, and whose eyes shine with the brilliance of fire.
It is endowed with three and a half crescents and is situated at the tip of the crest of matted hair.
Endowed with great beauty, saluted by gods and asuras,
possessing a luster like the sun and lightning, [he was seated] upon the crest of a great jewel.
"This form of great body is well-worshipped even by the gods.
Śiva said:
"The seers of this armor (kavaca) are Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra; the meter is Virāṭ; the deity is Akṣobhya; [the seed-syllable is] Śrīṃ."

*Bīja* is *svāhā*, and *śakti* is for the sake of *dharma*, *artha*, *kāma*, and *mokṣa*; this is the application (*viniyoga*) in recitation. May *Śrīṃ* as the seed-syllable protect my head, and may the primordial seed-syllable protect my forehead. May the syllable *A* protect my throat, and may the syllable *Kṣo* protect my heart.
May the syllable *bha* protect my navel, may the syllable *ya* protect the private region;
may the power of the mantra protect all my limbs, and may the seed-syllable protect my two eyes.
May Akṣobhya always protect both arms with all his manifestations;
may Brahmā protect the two feet, and Viṣṇu protect the two knees.
May Mūlādhāra protect my head, and may Vṛṣa protect me at Svādhiṣṭhāna;
may the consort of Śiva always protect me at Maṇipūra.
May the ten deities beginning with Indra protect my unstruck lotus;
may the Sun constantly provide protection for me at the Viśuddha-cakra.
May Maheśvara always protect the most beautiful wheel of command;
may Brahmā and Śukra protect me, and may Bhairavī protect my navel.
And in the lineage of gurus beginning with Divya, Akṣobhya is mentioned everywhere;
thus, being pure, one should recite the armor-mantra according to this sequential procedure.
Whoever recites this daily at the three junctions of the day, endowed with faith and devotion, shall experience no loss of accomplishment; of this there is no doubt.
Now, regarding the procedure for the rosary (*mālā*):

for the recitation of this mantra, a secret rosary (*rahasyamālā*) is the primary and most highly recommended for the hero (*vīra*). For it is said in the *Triśaktiratna*: "When Tāriṇī is recited with a secret rosary, she bestows accomplishment (*siddhi*)."
Therefore, one who desires accomplishment should fashion a rosary with that [thread].
A rosary made of great conch shells, fashioned from fifty gems, is declared to be the secret rosary; it should be concealed with great effort.
The bone situated between the ear and the corner of the eye is proclaimed as the *mahāśaṅkha*;
in its absence, it may indeed be made from any other part [of the body].
The *mahāśaṅkha* is the bone of a human head; and those learned in the tradition maintain that it must be unburnt. In the *Yāmala*:
"In the midst of a fierce battle, the practitioner of the *Mahāvidyās* should indeed have a circular garland fashioned from the severed heads of men, elephants, horses, and camels."
In the absence of those, a crystal rosary (sphāṭikī) should be used, for it grants success in all matters.
In the *Muṇḍamālā*: "One should move the rosary held at the thumb from the tip of the middle finger. Being impure, one should not touch it, nor should one allow it to fall from the hand."
In the *Triśaktiratna*: "Alternatively, the wise one should perform recitation with a rosary consisting of the *mātṛkā* [vowels].
Having uttered each individual letter, he should recite it separated by the [next] letter."
The wise practitioner alone should then bring together the letter ending in *l* and the one ending in *m*; for the practitioner must never overstep the letter *kṣa*, which is indeed the form of Meru.

Also in the *Muṇḍamālā*: "O Supreme Goddess, by means of the garland of letters arranged in both direct and reverse order, ending with the letter *la* according to the sequence of the initial letters."
One should never overstep the letter *kṣa*, which has the form of Mount Meru;
for a rosary that is devoid of Meru, or one in which Meru is overstepped, [is ineffective].
But if it were impure in this case, that garland would be fruitless.
That which is the variegated *brahmanāḍī*, appearing like twenty threads,
should be meditated upon as strung together by it, bestowing the fruits of all desires.
At the beginning of the hundred and eight recitations, one should first utter the neuter [seed-syllable].
The four phonemes ṛ, ṝ, ḷ, and ḹ are declared to be neuter;
or else, there is also an octad of classes according to the sequence of their desired distinctions.
The eight groups [of consonants] are: *a, ka, ca, ṭa, ta, pa, ya, śa*.

When the recitation of one hundred and eight [times] is to be performed, one should first utter the four neuter vowels (*klība*) and at the conclusion of the reverse order, one should likewise recite those four in reverse; this is one method. Through both direct and reverse orders, there are fifty [recitations].
The meaning is that there is another method: having pronounced the [first] letter, one should then pronounce the letters of the remaining eight groups.
As stated in the *Yāmala*: "Having pronounced the letter together with the bindu, the wise man should thereafter recite the mantra."
Having visualized Mount Meru, one should perform the recitation; one must not overstep it.
The meaning is that one should utter the syllable *kṣaṃ* alone as the pure Meru, but one should not utter any mantra after it. Likewise, in the *Kulamūlāvatāra* and the *Sārasaṃgraha*:
"And having visualized the letters from *a* to *kṣa*, which reside within the Brahma-nāḍī..."
Having joined the vowel *arṇa* with the nasal drop (*bindu*), the wise one should mutter this most excellent mantra.
Having joined [the letters] beginning with 'a' and likewise those beginning with 'ka' in their proper sequence,
one should then conceive the Mistress of the World (Jagadīśvarī) there, with the letter 'kṣa' as the Meru.
Then the script shall consist of a rosary numbering fifty beads;
by means of this, the recitation of all mantras accomplishes every purpose.
Likewise: "The fifty beads of the rosary consist of the letters from *a* to *kṣa*;
the letter *kṣa* is situated at the position of Meru, [beginning] from *la* in reverse order."
Through the division into eight groups, there are one hundred and eight [mantras];
each mantra, separated by one [syllable], bestows fruit according to its respective deity.
When recited with each individual syllable of the mantra joined by a string of letters arranged in both direct (anuloma) and reverse (viloma) order, they grant swift accomplishment;
this applies even to hostile mantras of men, let alone other mantras.
Therefore, the application of the term "garland" (*mālā*) elsewhere is figurative. Likewise:
"Liberation [is achieved] by twenty-five; the accumulation of wealth by thirty;
all worldly goals by twenty-seven; and the rite of sorcery (*abhicārika*) by fifteen."
Success in ritual action (*karmasiddhi*) occurs with fifty [recitations], and likewise with those increased by four;
while a recitation common to all purposes consists of twenty-seven [recitations].
224) In the *Mantratantraprakāśa*: "Recitation performed by counting on the fingers is said to have a single-fold merit;
one should know that it is eight-fold when using lines, and a hundred-fold when using [rosary] beads."
In that regard, while performing the counting of recitations (japa) with the fingers, one should count using all the fingers including the thumb;
an action performed without the thumb shall be fruitless.
One should always perform the recitation of the mantra by means of the finger-joints.
Thus it is stated in another Tantra: "The two joints of the ring finger [and the others] in the order beginning with the little finger.
And likewise: "Having made the middle joint of the ring finger the *meru*, one must not overstep it."
If a practitioner recites [the mantra] here at the tips of the index finger and the middle finger, four things will perish for him: life-span, knowledge, fame, and wealth.
Likewise: "Beginning from the base of the ring finger and proceeding in a clockwise direction as far as the base of the middle finger, one should recite [the mantra] over the eight joints."
One should not cross over Meru, making the joint between the ring finger and the middle finger its center.
This rule applies to the recitation (*japa*) of one hundred and eight repetitions of the *Bhinnashakti* mantra of Tripurasundarī.
However, for the recitation of a hundred mantras, the process is performed ten times, beginning from the middle of the ring finger and ending at the base of the index finger.
The mere recitation (japa) is what must be understood. In another tantra:
"Beginning from the base of the ring finger and proceeding in a clockwise direction up to the base of the index finger, one should perform the recitation upon the nine joints."
One should take the three middle fingers as the object of grasping, and likewise the root of the ring finger;
making the ring and middle fingers together as the single *meru*, one must not overstep it.

And this [practice] is performed by repeating [the mantra] twelve times, with the ultimate goal being one hundred and eight recitations. Regarding the *saundarya* [mudrā], it is stated in the *Yāmala*: "O Maheśvarī, [place] two joints each of the ring finger and the middle finger at the root and the tip [of the thumb], and three joints of the little finger and the index finger."
O Goddess, one should perform the auspicious double circumambulation of Meru using both the ring finger and the middle finger, and thus recite the mantra of Tripurasundarī in a clockwise sequence.
In the Vaiṣṇava tradition and others, however, it is stated in the Sanatkumārasaṃhitā:
"Beginning from the ring finger and the middle finger,
and starting from the little finger up to the base of the index finger, one should perform the recitation over the ten joints."
Likewise: "One should never separate the fingers during the time of recitation;
by the separation of the fingers, the recitation flows away through the gaps."
One should not skip any count nor contract the palm;
one should always perform the recitation with the hands, but never that which is for the sake of specific desires.
225) One may even perform the optional rite (*kāmya*) with [any material] in hand if a garland is not available.
"Is not available" means it has not been prescribed. For this very reason, it is said in the *Kulāmṛta*:
"When the Goddess, whose nature is purity, is present, then that is the worship of the seat of the mind (*manaḥ-pīṭha*)."
I have already explained this to you specifically, along with the fire sacrifice.
Recitation performed with a rosary made of beads or with the mind is called mental recitation;
O Goddess of the gods, it bestows liberation as well as the fulfillment of desires.
When the supreme Goddess Kula-kuṇḍalinī, whose form is consciousness, is present,
then worship is to be understood as taking place in the yantra, and it is prescribed in the sacrificial fire-pit (homakuṇḍa).
O Great Goddess, recitation performed with a rosary made of beads such as gems, or even with a string of seeds, is whispered (upāṃśu), and it bestows swift accomplishment.
When the Goddess, in the form of the *yoni*, is worshipped within the *yonimaṇḍala*,
there, O Mistress of the Gods, the fire-oblation (*homa*) is performed through sexual union according to the prescribed rite.
"O Maheśānī, the recitation (japa) should likewise be performed with a rosary made of conch shells," so it is said in the *Kulamūlāvatāra*:
"Beads produced from conch shells are declared to be bestowers of fortune."
Those made of crystal bestow liberation, while those made of lotus seeds increase nourishment.
The meritorious Rudrākṣas bestow enjoyment and liberation, granting all spiritual accomplishments;
those originating from the Putrajīva tree grant the prosperity and success of sons, cattle, and grain.
Gems originating from coral bestow wealth, good fortune, and subjugation;
pearls are said to grant liberation as well as all forms of prosperity.
Those made of *kuśa* grass remove sin and grant desires; those made of gold and silver likewise do so.
As stated in the *Śāradātilaka*: "A rosary of Rudrākṣa beads brings about one's heart's desires through recitation (*japa*);
a rosary fashioned from lotus seeds is considered a destroyer of enemies."
A rosary made of knots of *kuśa* grass destroys all sins;
one fashioned from *putrajīva* fruits brings about the attainment of sons.
A rosary fashioned from precious gems, when used for recitation, grants one's desires;
a garland crafted from golden beads bestows all longed-for objects.
A garland fashioned from sprouts bestows abundant wealth;
a crystal garland grants good fortune; and one fashioned from pearls confers prosperity.
One fashioned from conch shells and gems brings about imperishable fame;
a garland constructed from all of these together leads to the liberation of men.

By this [it is meant]: "If one should perform the recitation with *indrākṣa* beads, or likewise with *rudrākṣa* or crystal beads, nothing else should be inserted in between, such as *putrajīva* and so forth."
If, however, one should employ another [bead] in the rosary during the rite of recitation,
that "Beloved" [rosary] will grant neither his desires nor liberation.
And in another birth, O Goddess, everyone becomes one who has mastered the Vedānta;
thereafter, there is the acquisition of friends even among Caṇḍālas of sinful deeds.
Thus, the statement from the *Uttaratantra* should be understood as referring to the addition of something distinct from all [the aforementioned materials]. Nārada says:
"A Brahmin should recite with a knot of *kuśa* grass; a Kṣatriya with gold and gems;
a Vaiśya with *putrajīva* seeds; and everyone may also use lotus seeds."
In the Tantra: "A wise person should fashion a rosary from these—beads produced from the *tālamalaka* tree and those made from *tulasī* wood—for the Vaiṣṇava mantra."

For Gopāla, the white lotus-seed rosary is recommended, according to the words of Gautama: "With a concentrated mind, [one should perform recitation] with a rosary of white lotus seeds. In the *Nāradapañcarātra* it is said:
"They say that the counting of the recitation should be done with lotus seeds, which increase devotion."

Since the *Varāha-purāṇa* states, "Having first [honored] the Blessed One... and with rudrākṣas it is excellent," the rudrākṣa rosary is praised even for Vaiṣṇavas. However, the chanting of *śakti-mantras* during the day with a rudrākṣa rosary is prohibited. As it has been said:
In the Yoginītantra: "O Dear One, he who recites a Śakti mantra during the day using rudrākṣa beads falls into misfortune; his recitation is fruitless."

Thus it is stated in the Bhairavī-vidyā. In the Vārāhī-tantra: "One should make a rosary of gold, gems, crystal, or fashioned from conch-shell, or indeed of coral; one should avoid the *putrajīva* seeds."
One should use lotus seeds, and especially rudrākṣas and indrākṣas.
Now, regarding the time for the consecration of the rosary, the Yoginītantra states: "On the twelfth lunar day, the Vaiṣṇava rosary should be prepared by the most excellent practitioners."
By those who know the mantras, [the offering] should be performed with effort using the Viṣṇu-mantra during the divine portion;
that is, during the divine portion in the forenoon. Likewise: "The [offering] for the Śaktis should also be performed according to the rule after eating at night."
And on the eighth, the ninth, and likewise on the fourteenth day.
O Goddess of the gods, one should likewise perform [the rite] for Śiva on the thirteenth day.
Now, regarding the consecration of the rosary (*mālā-saṃskāra*), the *Yoginītantra* states: "A rosary made from silk thread is always pleasing to the Goddess."
A Vaiṣṇava garland may indeed be made of cotton threads or even of lotus fibers.
A garland of Śiva is praised even when made of wool or bark;
however, a specific distinction regarding cotton thread is stated in the dialogue between Umā and Maheśvara:
"That woman who has living children, who is beautiful, and who is dear to her husband..."
With that spun thread, she fashioned a garland that brings auspiciousness.
It is fashioned from threads of silk, fine cloth, and cotton;
it may be made of gold and silver, or even of gold alone, which brings auspiciousness.
This auspicious garland, strung by the Guru himself with thread spun by a maiden,
has been formed into a circle and takes the form of a cow’s tail.
One should by all means avoid a yellow thread made from village cotton,
or one produced from *caitra* cotton, during the act of tying the knots.
In the Yoginītantra: "Then, having tripled the threefold thread made by a virtuous woman of a noble brahmin family and free from knots, one should wash it."
One should wash it with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), according to the statement: "And one should wash with the five products of the cow. In the *Tantra* it is said:
"Cow urine, cow dung, milk, curd, clarified butter, and water infused with *kuśa* grass—this is declared to be the *pañcagavya*, which destroys even the greatest sins."

Regarding the measurement of the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), it is stated in the *Gautamīya*: "The portion of milk should be one *pala*, and the cow urine is likewise desired to be that much;
the clarified butter (*ghṛta*) should be one *pala*, and the cow dung (*gomaya*) two *tolakas*."
The curd should be the measure of one handful; this is known as the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
Alternatively, it is said that the portions of the five products of the cow should be equal.
Having first observed a single meal, the practitioner, having performed his daily rites and being pure, should himself string the beads according to the prescribed number,
being a knower of mantras.
Having carefully gathered seeds according to one's desire and availability,
they should be uniform in appearance and neither too thick nor too thin.
Those [vessels] which are not defiled by insects and the like, being neither old nor new,
should be washed individually with the five products of the cow.
First, on the preceding day, it should be understood that [the thread] must be distinct from Śakti.
(228) Upon a base fashioned in the shape of a lotus with nine fresh leaves of the *aśvattha* tree,
one should place the gems, having washed them there with scented water, upon the thread.
Having placed the *tāra*, the *śakti*, and the *mātṛkās* upon the thread and the beads,
one should worship them and offer oblations of clarified butter according to one's ability.
Likewise: "Taking each jewel one by one, one should join them there to the thread."
But in another tantra: "The wise one, muttering each individual letter of the Mātṛkā preceded by the Tāra-mantra, should take the gems and string them together with a thread, one after another."
Having thus formed the *brahmagranthi* and having tied the *meru* together with the knots,
one should first string the rosary and then commence the consecration (*saṃskāra*).
In the *Gautamīya-yāmala* it is said: "O Supreme Goddess, having prepared the rosary in this manner, one should indeed purify it;
one should fashion a lotus-shape using nine leaves of the *aśvattha* tree."
In the midst of that, one should place the rosary while reciting the Mātṛkā and the root mantra;
one should wash it with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and pure water using the Sadyojāta mantra.
In the *Tantra*: "The mantra-practitioner should consecrate each [bead] individually with the fifth mantra once, one after another. In the *Gautamīya*, concerning the entire rosary as a whole:
"One should consecrate it with the fifth mantra itself, provided it is not fewer than one hundred [recitations]. Thus it is stated.
O Mālā, O Mālā, O Mahāmālā, you who embody the nature of all reality!
The fourfold aims of human life are entrusted to you; therefore, grant me spiritual accomplishment.
Having performed the preliminary rites beginning with the seed-syllable of Māyā, one should worship with red flowers;
one should consecrate them with the root mantra, following the sequence of both direct and reverse order.
In the same way, one who knows the reality of mantras should recite with the letters of the *mātṛkā*.
In the *Yoginītantra*: "Then one should perform the rite of fire-offering (*homakarma*) for the sake of attaining identity with the deity;
having offered one hundred and eight oblations, one should pour the residual clarified butter (*sampātājya*) [into the vessel]."
If one is unable to engage in the fire-sacrifice (homa), one should perform double the number of recitations (japa).
O Rosary (mālā), you are considered the bestower of all accomplishments for all people.
"By that truth, O Mother, grant me success; salutations to you!
Having spoken thus and performed worship, the householder should then protect [the vessel] with great care.
In the Śaiva Āgama: "It should be made like a cow’s tail, with a single neck and provided with a handle."
In the *Uttaratanttra*: "A single Meru, arising from the gross [form], should be given there for all;
one should place it in sequence because it has the form of a serpent."
229) One should fashion each seed-syllable according to the rule, provided with a *brahmagranthi*;
or else, it may be without a knot, provided with a firm cord.
By repeating three times through the middle, and then half-repeating from the end,
a knot that winds clockwise is called a *brahmagranthi*.
Regarding the specific characteristics of the rudrākṣa, it is stated in the Kālottara:
Skanda said:
"O God of gods, Mahādeva, Lord of creation, preservation, and dissolution!"
O Maheśvara, how indeed should one fashion a rosary for recitation from rudrākṣa beads?
"And how, O Lord, should the consecration (saṃskāra) be performed, and what is its fruit?
Īśvara said:
"Listen, O Ṣaṇmukha, I shall explain how it is performed with rudrākṣas."
By means of the prescribed method for the rosary, it bestows the perfection of recitation.
They should be made with one face, two faces, four faces, five faces, or six faces; however, one should avoid mixing them together.
One should place the mouth upon the mouth and join the tail with the tail;
this, measured by the size of an emblic myrobalan fruit, is declared to be the best.
It should not be made with a size equal to a jujube seed for the middle or lowest [initiations];
it should be woven with nine or three threads, touching [the fingers] evenly.
Its upper face, named Meru, should be made; one must not step over it.
One should wash it with the Sadyojāta mantra and rub it with the Vāmadeva mantra.
Then one should fumigate it with the Ghora mantra and smear it with the Tatpuruṣa mantra;
one should consecrate each part a hundred times with the fifth mantra itself.
One should likewise consecrate Meru with the fifth [syllable] and the Ghoramantra;
having displayed the eight mudrās, one should worship each one in succession.
Having strung it with five [threads] and worshipped it according to the previous rules and as prescribed,
this consecration of rudrākṣas is declared, as enjoined by the Śruti.
In other cases, the procedure prescribed in the Tantras should be performed by the practitioners of Guha;
the remainder [of the instruction] is that one should wash [the image] with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
One should wash it with the five products of the cow while reciting the Sadyojāta mantra, and with pure water.
Because of this statement: "One should rub [the image] with the scents of sandalwood, agallochum, and so forth," and "One should smear it with sandalwood, saugandhika, musk, saffron, and so forth.
(230) The eight mudrās, beginning with āvāhanī, follow immediately, because worship is mentioned thereafter.

They say that this same consecration applies even to other gems and such materials. Another method is stated in the *Yoginītantra*: "The best of practitioners, having placed the rosary—strung with the aforementioned mantras upon the aforementioned trees—into a vessel smeared with perfumes and other substances..."
Having completed the worship beginning with the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi) and so forth, one should perform worship there;
having invoked Gaṇeśa, Sūrya, Viṣṇu, Īśa, and Durgā, one should worship them.
In the *Tantramālā*:
"Having sprinkled that rosary with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), one should consecrate it with the *hauṃ* mantra;
then, having lifted that rosary from there, one should place it in a golden vessel."
Then, having performed the rite of the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) in sequence with milk, curd, ghee, honey, sugar, and so forth, the wise practitioner should proceed with other types of incense.
Having established [the image] there in due order, one should bathe it with cool water;
thereafter, with sandalwood, fragrant flowers, musk, saffron, and so forth.
Having smeared her [with unguents], one should mutter the *hsauḥ* mantra one hundred and eight times;
upon her, one should worship the nine planets in a row and the guardians of the directions.
Then, having worshipped the Guru, one should take up the auspicious rosary.
In the Bhairavītantra it is said: "First, the wise man, being well-composed, should worship Lord Gaṇapati, Sūrya, Viṣṇu, Umāpati, and Durgā in relation to the rosary."
One should place the rosary in the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and consecrate it with the Prāsāda mantra;
then, having lifted the rosary, one should place it in a golden vessel.
Having established [the deity] with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) and cool water,
[one should worship] with fragrant sandalwood, musk, saffron, and so forth.
Then, having performed the consecration with this mantra,
the knower of mantras [should visualize] the vital breath mounted upon the individual soul (jīva) and adorned with the vowel Oṃ.
One should properly install the King of Mantras joined with the *bindu* and *nāda*.
Having worshipped the nine planets, one should then perform the worship of the guardians of the directions.
Thereafter, one should offer oblations according to one's capacity with sesame seeds mixed with clarified butter.
One should perform the placement [of the letters] one hundred and eight times. The letter *ha* is the vital breath (*prāṇa*); the letter *sa* is the individual soul (*jīva*).
In the *Kubjikātantra*: "First, one should worship the artisan with garments, perfumes, and ointments;
being well-pleased, he should fashion a pure rosary in the form of the phonemes."
231) A wise person should fashion a piercing rosary according to what is appropriate—

the supreme one, which consists of the forms of the fifty seed-syllables and possesses the nature of the phonemes. It should be made according to the measurement of the phonemes, and one should immerse it in the five products of the cow for three days.
Or else, on the fourth day, one should wash the thread with these mantras.

The excellent practitioner should string [the beads] with a thread of the same color while reciting the *hṛdayāṇu* (heart-mantra), or he may string them using gold and other such materials. Then, he should apply either the *brahmagranthi* (Brahma-knot) or the *nāgapāśa* (serpent-noose).
Intent on meditation, one should string the rosary with the armor mantra;
finally, at the end of all [the beads], one should place the *meru* bead joined by two threads.
The most excellent practitioner should string [the beads] together by means of the *tāra*-yoga and bind them;
having thus completed [the preparation], O Goddess of the Gods, he should perform the consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*).
Having drawn a mandala upon the sacrificial ground according to the sequence of the prescribed rules for each portion,
one should worship the chosen deity in due order and according to the proper method.
One should recite the mantra one thousand and eight times according to the prescribed rule,
and perform oblations with a tenth part of that number, using whatever is dear to whichever deity.
Then the wise one should place that garland in the center of the mandala;
having then applied the weapon-mantra (astramantra), he should contemplate it as a deity.

Having attained the state of non-differentiation, the best of practitioners should fashion a garland consisting of that very nature; then, according to the prescribed rule, he should offer the bali-oblation with curd-rice.
Having thus established the chosen deity within the garland,
the mantra-practitioner should worship the preceptor and the artisan according to the prescribed ritual.

One should not recite another mantra there if one desires success for oneself; [the mantras] beginning with the weapon (astra) are to be recited for the sake of the rosary. With those oblation-substances (bali).
Likewise, in the *Uttaratantra*:
One should fasten the thread firmly so that it does not slip during the recitation.
When the thread has worn out, one should join a new thread and recite the mantra one hundred times.
In the Śaiva Āgama: "When the rosary has been untied and re-strung as before, one should recite the mantra with undistracted mind once it has been consecrated."
In the Nāradīya [Purāṇa]: "If the rosary should fall to the ground while one is performing the recitation, the reciter should lift it up with the heart-mantra (hṛdaya)."
With the mantra "Namaḥ" [uttered] from the heart. In the Rudrayāmala (232):
One should not perform the count of *japa* with seeds, nor with hand-fingers, nor with grains, nor with flowers, nor with sandalwood, nor with clay.
Having mixed lac, kuśīda, vermilion, cow dung, and dried cow manure,
and having formed them into pills, one should perform the prescribed number of recitations.
In the *Nāradīya*: "Having placed [the rosary] on the ring finger of both hands, one performing the recitation (*japa*) should not tie the knot for counting."
If one performs [an act] that causes this [mantra] to flow away, one should recite it a hundred times for the sake of rectifying it.
Now follows the procedure for the consecration of the secret garland (rahasyamālā), established by tradition:
having empowered it seven times with the mantra *oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ klīṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*.

In a new vessel, one should deposit [the substances]. Then, having invoked the Blessed Lady together with her retinue by means of the mantras for invocation and so forth, and having worshipped her with the sixteen types of offerings (*ṣoḍaśopacāra*), one should repeat the root mantra while recollecting the third seed-syllable;
having rendered it nectar-like with the *dhenumudrā*, veiled it with the *kavaca* (armor) mantra, and covered it with the *mahāmudrā*.

Meditating upon that garland as having the form of the Goddess, one should perform the casting of drops. The mantras for this are: *oṃ hrīṃ svāhā*, *oṃ hūṃ svāhā*, *oṃ phaṭ svāhā*, *oṃ strīṃ svāhā*, *oṃ hrīṃ hūṃ svāhā*, *oṃ phaṭ svāhā*. With these, one should perform the casting of drops one hundred times.
Having offered incense and other offerings with musk, agallochum, and camphor, and having removed [the vessel] from the goblet, one should consecrate it with these mantras.
The mantra therein is: *oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ mahāvajriṇi mahāghorakarkaśamahāsthimaṇḍale praviśa sarvasiddhiṃ prayaccha | oṃ hūṃ hrīṃ hrīṃ svāhā mahākapālini*.
*Mahāghorarūpe svāhā*. *Oṃ hrīṃ hrīṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*.

Having worshipped with *dūrvā* grass and unbroken rice (*akṣata*), having performed the kindling with the seed-syllable of Kandarpa, having worshipped with the sixteen services (*ṣoḍaśopacāra*), having inflamed it with the *mātṛkā* mantra, and having encircled it with the syllable *hūṃ*.

One should offer the bali. It is as follows: Oṃ hrīṃ hrīṃ hūṃ oṃ hūṃ hūṃ oṃ hūṃ phaṭ hūṃ oṃ oṃ hūṃ svāhā. Oṃ hūṃ! O Great Yoginī, O Savior of the Three Worlds, dwell within the midst of this great garland of conch shells and bones; grant, grant all siddhis!

"Take, take, cause to take, cause to take the offerings of liquor and meat! Hrīṃ strīṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā! Having offered the *bali* with these aforementioned substances and having dismissed the Goddess, one should wear the rosary in a secluded place. Thus it is stated in the *Mantratantraprakāśa*:
Having performed the internal sacrifice with devotion one thousand and eight times,
that which one recites every day is known as the daily recitation (nitya-japa).
In the *Uttaratantro*: "The practitioner should never recite fewer than three hundred [mantras].
In the *Yoginītantra*: "Or, having recited one hundred and eight [times], he should place [the rosary] upon his head at the conclusion of the recitation:
'O Rosary, you are the giver of pleasure to all the gods; grant me auspiciousness!'"
"O auspicious lady, always grant me welfare, fame, and valor.
In the Śaiva Āgama: "One should recite [the mantra] one thousand and eight times, or half of that, or three hundred, or even one hundred and eight times daily, without indolence. (233)
And the recitation (japa) must be performed preceded by meditation (dhyāna). As it is stated in the Nīlatantra:
"I shall explain the meditation on the mantra, which bestows omniscience through recitation;
for, O Maheśānī, even a slayer of a Brahmin attains perfection through meditation on the mantra."
One should meditate upon Hṛllekhā at the mūlādhāra-cakra, possessing a radiance equal to ten million suns,
and the second [syllable], yellow in color, at the svādhiṣṭhāna.
At the navel, the practitioner of mantra [should visualize] the seed-syllable of Kūrca, possessing great luster and the hue of a rain cloud,
resembling the moon, and previously beheld by yogins.
One should meditate on the *kūrca* seed-syllable in the heart, possessing a radiance like the fire of time (*kālāgni*);
or else, one should meditate on the *kūrca* at the crown of the head, resembling the full moon and having the luster of nectar (*sudhā*).
One should visualize the tongue as blazing with masses of light from that [mantra];
one should visualize the entire Vidyā, resembling ten million suns and previously beheld by yogis, extending from the base to the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra).

Hṛllekhā is the seed-syllable of Māyā. It is also stated elsewhere: "Mantras that abide in their proper place grant boons, and those that abide in meditation bestow fruits; however, even if they are well-perfected, those devoid of the place of meditation become enemies."
In this very context, I shall describe that state without any doubt:
it is both with parts and without parts, subtle, and likewise both with and without parts.
Śiva has declared the sixfold mantra to be both differentiated by its parts (kalā) and transcendent of those parts;
know that the "with-parts" (sakala) resides in the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra), while that which is "without-parts" (niṣkala) is below it.
That which resides in the Bindu is differentiated by the Kalās, while that which transcends the Kalās is situated above it;
that very Kalā is Kuṇḍalinī, declared by Śiva to be the power of Nāda.
The mantras situated in these locations are proclaimed as "situated in their place. With minds composed, the mantras should be meditated upon within the Kuṇḍalinī by means of the mind.
Then, those established in meditation are said to contemplate her within the *bindu*.
Regarding the characteristics of *japa*, it is stated in the *Puraścaraṇacandrikā*:
"Japa is the repetition of syllables; I shall now describe its various types."
And recitation is said to be of two kinds: vocal as well as mental.
The first [type of recitation] is proclaimed to be twofold: whispered (upāṃśu) and loud (uccais).
The second is likewise to be known as twofold, through the distinction between the tongue and the mind.
One should recite the mantra with speech; that is called vocal recitation (vācika-japa).
One should recite the mantra softly, moving the lips only slightly.
That which is barely audible to the ear is known as whispered recitation (upāṃśu-japa);
that which is performed with the tongue alone is to be understood as vocal recitation (jihvā-japa).

When one recites a mantra with the mind alone, that is called mental recitation (mānasa-japa). It is superior to loud recitation by ten times; whispered recitation (upāṃśu) is ten times more effective than loud recitation.
Mental recitation is a thousand times more effective than recitation with the tongue,
provided one has placed the deity within the heart and made one's own heart steady.
Having bowed to Śiva and the other gurus, one should recite the mantra with a concentrated mind—
slowly and gradually, neither indistinctly nor too rapidly, and without delay.

Likewise: "One who wears a turban, one wearing a bodice, one who is naked, one with disheveled hair, one whose neck is covered, one whose hands are uncovered, one who is impure, or one who is talking—such a person should not mutter the mantra."
Having uncovered his hands, or even having covered them with his head;
or with a distracted mind, or angry, or bewildered, or filled with haste.

Neither while sitting, nor lying down, nor walking, nor standing up, nor on a street, nor in a place without a head (an open space), nor in a place shrouded in darkness, should one perform the recitation (*japa*).
The phrase "one should not recite" is to be supplied [to each clause]: whether one has one's feet covered by shoes, or is situated upon a vehicle or a bed;
likewise, upon seeing, speaking with, or hearing those who have fallen from their caste or those of the lowest castes.
Upon sneezing, the downward movement of wind, or yawning, one should cease the recitation.
Having risen and sipped water (ācamana), one should perform the six-limbed breath control (prāṇāyāma) at its edge;
then, having sipped water again, one should perform the remaining rites, or else the observation of the sun and other such acts.

The word "one should perform" (caret) is to be supplied as a grammatical ellipsis. In the *Kālītantra*: "The knower of mantras should offer the fruit of the recitation, consisting of radiant light, into the hand of the Goddess with the mantra: 'O You, the protector of that which is most secret among secrets.'"
The mantra is as follows: "O you who guard that which is more secret than the secret, accept this recitation performed by us;
O Great Goddess, Mother, may success be mine through your grace."

Thus it is established in another tantra. Having uttered this mantra and recited the verse on enjoyment (*bhogaśloka*), Somaśambhu states: "With the water of the *arghya* for the root mantra, one should offer [it] with the right hand into the excellent hand of Śambhu."

235) "To Śambhu" is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*). Whichever deity is present in a particular place, that deity should be understood as the recipient there. "In the hand of the boon-giver" (*varahaste*) means in the primary hand; by this, one should offer [the oblation] into the right hand of a male deity or the left hand of a female deity. Specifically, for goddesses, one should offer it into the left hand, while for gods, one should offer it into the right.
From the *Yāmala*: "In the Śaiva Āgama:
Having thus offered the recitation (*japa*), the practitioner, filled with devotion, should then properly praise [the deity] with hymns, preceded by the ringing of the bell."

The hymn (*stava*) is that declared in the *Brahmasaṃhitā* within the section on meditation (*dhyāna*). The armor (*kavaca*), known as the *Tryailokyavijaya*, will be described further on. As for the hymn of a thousand names (*sahasranāmastotra*), it is found in the *Rudrayāmala*:
"In the city of Kailāsa, [the sage addressed] the Lord, Mahādeva, Maheśvara..."
Bhavānī, out of affection, questioned the bestower of boons in private.
The Goddess said: O Īśāna, O Omniscient One, how do practitioners always obtain the supreme power? Tell me that, O Excellent Lord.
Īśvara said: O auspicious one, listen as I explain to you that by which people obtain [their goals] without worship, without meditation, without recitation, and without offerings.
I shall recount in its entirety the thousand names of Tārā;
listen, O Goddess, with constant devotion, for this is the supreme benefit for devotees.
O Goddess, listen as I describe to you that entire fruit which is obtained without the performance of ritual worship and without recitation.

Oṃ. For this *bhaktikulasarvasva-nāmastotra* of the venerable goddess Tārā, the deity is the venerable goddess Tārā; its application (*viniyoga*) is for the purpose of attaining all desires during recitation.
Tārā, Rātri, Mahārātri, Kālarātri, Kapālinī.
Kālikā, the bestower of desires, Māyā, Mahāmāyā, and Mahotsavā.
Delighting in great charity, adorned with sacrifices and sacrificial festivals,
moon-faced, with eyes like those of the *cakora* bird, she possessed beautiful eyes and lovely vision.
Three-eyed, with eyes like lotus petals, deer-eyed, and captivating;
Brāhmī, Nārāyaṇī, Jyotsnā, Cārukeśī, and Sulocanā.
Vārāhī, Vāruṇī, Vidyā, Mahāvidyā, Maheśvarī, Piṅgā, and Kuñcitakeśī, whose very form is the Great Sacrifice.
Gaurī, who has the color of a campaka flower, slender-limbed, worshipped on the riverbanks,
the embodiment of all bliss, and the savior from all perils.

Fortitude, intelligence, as well as Lakṣmī, faith, she who reclines upon the serpent,
Rukmiṇī, Jānakī, Durgā, Satyā, Satyavatī, and Rati.
Kāmākhyā, the giver of liberation and bliss, Nārasiṃhī, Sarasvatī,

Virūpā, Viśvarūpā, Mṛḍānī, the beloved of Mṛḍa,

The daughter of Bhagiratha, consisting of mind, intellect, and eternal bliss,
she who is forever dear to Hara, the daughter of the Mountain, the wife of Hara, the ascetic woman.

the bestower of great merit, the formidable one, and the destroyer of Madhu and Kaiṭabha.
Śaṅkhinī, Cakriṇī, Dhātrī, and she who holds a book in her hand;
Cāmuṇḍā, Capalā, Tuṅgā, Bhadrā, and the destroyer of the Daityas.
Śānti, Nidrā, Mahānidrā, Guhyanidrā, and Reṇukā;
Kaumārī, Kulajā, Kuntī, who is devoted to the Kaula vow.

she is Śivā, Śakti, Mahāśakti, Sāṅkarī, and the beloved of Śakti.

Śrīvidyā, Bhairavī, the auspicious one, Bhāratī, the destroyer of fear;
Tāpasī, the savior, the fierce one, the destroyer of the fierce Daityas.
The giver, devoted to charity, Kālī, Durgā, the destroyer of demons;
Padmā, Padmāvatī, the joyful, the contented, the nourished, and likewise Urvaśī.
Vajriṇī and Vajrahastā, as well as Nārāyaṇī and Śivā;
Khaṇḍinī and Khaḍgahastā, and she who bears a razor and a skull-bowl.
She is the celestial maiden honored by the gods, the daughter of Puloman;
she is blissful, the bestower of happiness, and the increaser of all well-being.

she is the most excellent, the giver of boons, speech, the knower, the giver of knowledge, and the stainless one.
Ugrakālī, Mahākālī, Bhadrakālī, and Dakṣiṇā;
born from the lineage of Bhṛgu, she is Bhārgavī, the beloved of Bhṛgu.

238) The beautiful woman wearing red garments is the mistress of the gods;
she is the supreme bestower of bliss, the eldest, and served by hosts of yoginīs.
Ambā, Jāmbavatī, Satyā, Satyabhāmā, Nagātmajā;
Raudrī, Raudrasvanā, Raudrā, and the destroyer of the fierce Daityas.
The maiden Kauśikī, the lore that destroys the Daitya Kāla;
the consort of Śambhu, devoted to Śambhu, the wife of Śambhu, Mahodarī.
She is the wife of Śiva, devoted to Śiva, the mother Ambikā;
likewise, she is the wife of Hara, devoted to Hara, the wife of Hara, and the wielder of the trident.
She is the beloved of Madanāntaka, the consort of Madanāntaka;
she is Girijā, the daughter of the mountain, and the beloved of Giriśa.
She is the past and the future, the nourisher, the purifier, and the protectress;
she is invisible, of unmanifest form, beloved, and the increaser of one's own desires.
The unfallen, the fallen, the life-breaths, the giver of life, the sovereign lady of Indra;
she who has arisen from the ocean, the supporter, and the firmly established one.
Udbhavā, Kṣobhaṇā, Kṣemā, Śrīgarbhā, Parameśvarī,
Karālā, Puṣṭadehā, Kāriṇī, and Kañjalocanā.
She is the refuge, the lotus-like one, the beloved, the increaser of stainless bliss;

She who is highly honored, the best of the gods, the eldest, the mistress of life, the steadfast;

She who removes the suffering of prostrate beings, the destroyer of the Daityas,
the Ḍākinī, the Śākinī, the virtuous one, and the bearer of the excellent Khaṭvāṅga staff.
Kaumudī, Kumudā, Kundā, Kaulikā, Kulajātmajā,
Garvitā, Guṇasampannā, Nagajā, and Khagavāhinī.

Jyeṣṭhā, Maghā, Puṣyā, Dhaniṣṭhā, and Pūrvaphālgunī;

Vīṇā, Vīṇāvatī, Vidya, Yaśodā, and Yaśasvinī;
