dispels fear yet bestows fear, and possesses a radiance equal to the web of the sun's rays.
Worshipful to the descendant of Bhṛgu, honored by Bhṛgu, and saluted by the son of Bharadvāja;
she who removes fear, yet is herself possessed of awe-inspiring power, beautiful as a cloud of terrifying form.
She who holds the power of illusion, who delights in pride, who is intent on honoring the mind;
she who bestows bliss upon Mādhava, who is like wine, and whose eyes are intoxicating—O Madirekṣaṇa!
Endowed with the quality of great energy, she is vast and most wonderful;
she is Madirā, whose delight is measured by joy, and who takes pleasure in immersion in wine.
Yaśodharī, Yaśovidyā, the increaser of the joy of fame;
white as camphor of glory, she is adorned by the river Yaśodā.
She is the sister of King Yama, who increases the bliss of the path of yoga;
she brings joy to the Yādavas and causes the joy of the Yādavas to flourish.
245) She who is pleased by sacrifice, who consists of sacrifice, who is adorned by the performance of sacrificial rites;
she who is dear to Rāma, who delights in Rāma, and who is intent upon pleasing Rāma.
She is the queen, the one worshipped in the royal palace, the sovereign of the kings of kings, the goddess Ramā;
she is the delightful woman, the source of pleasure, the beautiful one, and the bestower of bliss upon Rāma.
She is full as the moon at night, with eyes like red lotuses;
she is Lāṅgalī, satisfied by love, and fond of the affection of Lāṅgalī.
She is as crimson as lac, she is the woman, she is playfulness, she is Līlāvatī, she is absorption;
she is delighted by the virtues of the Lord of Laṅkā, and she is the bestower of boons upon the Lord of Laṅkā.
Delighting in cloves, she was adorned with a garland of clove blossoms;
the young wife of the Sun, she bore love for the Sun.
Variegated, straight, thornless, a refuge, the goddess Śrī, possessing the qualities of autumn,
she stands in the center of the six-cornered wheel, adorned with prosperity and the syllable Hrīḥ.
Kṣemā, Ambā, Tathājñā, Iḍā, and Īśvaravallabhā; Ugrākhyā, as well as Ūrṇā, Ṛkāra, and Ṛsvarodbhavā.
Established in the phoneme-cluster of the letter *ḷ*, adorned with the vowel *ḷ*;
established in the phoneme-cluster of the letter *e*, adorned with the vowel *e*.
Epyā, caiṣyā, and likewise coṣā, whose form consists of the syllable *au*;
aṃsā, who is like the woman of the letter *a*—she is well-guarded by all the Āgamas.
Whoever recites this hymn every day, endowed with devotion—
whether by day, by night, or at the time of twilight— that person is indeed Maheśvara.
By the mere recitation of this hymn, the King shall become a servant;
he shall be honored in all Āgamas, and Hara himself [shall be honored] in all Tantras.
Whether one recites or even listens to this in a shrine of Śiva, on a bed, in an empty house, or at a crossroads, that person is a yogi; of this there is no doubt.
O auspicious lady, those names of the Enemy of Mura which exist in this context should be meditated upon;
never any others.
One should not fail to utter the name of Hari, nor should one refrain from touching a leaf of tulasī;
one should never entertain thoughts of anything else, nor ever engage in the censure of others.
Whoever worships her with devotion using auspicious red flowers such as sindūra and karavīra, for that person nothing remains unattainable.
246) By the recitation of this hymn, one indeed brings about the paralysis of wind, the solidification of water, the immobilization of the sun’s movement, and even the cooling of fire.
It swiftly attracts women, forcibly crushes enemies,
bewilders even the wives of kings, and brings even the gods under one's control.
Whoever should always read or even listen with a single-pointed mind will be long-lived, happy, and eloquent; his speech shall bring all things under his control.
Whatever fruit is obtained by bathing at all sacred fords and by performing ancestral rites at Gayā,
that entire fruit belongs to him who recites this with one-pointed mind.
O Goddess, for those who have faith in propitiating you and those who are striving to accomplish it, their goal is everywhere fulfilled; their destination is the abode of your feet.
Standing amidst the creepers joined in season, one should strike with a staff;
having recited mantras and offered praise with devotion, one shall indeed go to the state of the Tārīkā.
Whoever worships on the eighth, the fourteenth, the ninth, on Saturday, at the time of a solar transit, on Tuesday, at night, or on the new moon day;
O Goddess of gods, having performed the rite for a year, the supernatural powers (siddhis) become subject to him;
and as for that woman whose sons have died, or that lady whose fetuses have perished—
And that woman whose husband has died, who is oppressed by the state of misfortune;
the barren woman, the woman who bears only one child, and the woman whose sons have died.
O Great Goddess, those who are destitute of wealth and grain, and those who are overwhelmed by disease and grief— by them this should be caused to be written on birch bark.
One should bind it on the left arm, and one shall possess all happiness;
likewise, even a man who is generally tormented by suffering [shall find relief].
In an assembly, in terrible calamity, in dispute, in danger from an enemy,
in a fourfold battle, or in every situation afflicted by misfortune;
O auspicious lady, by remembering her, [sins] go far away to their destruction;
she should be worshipped with diligence in an empty house or a temple of Śiva.
O Goddess, always at the foot of a bilva tree, within the kula-maṇḍala,
with devotees offering milk-rice mixed with sugar and liquor;
With appropriate offerings consisting of cakes and flour-mixtures,
and whatever substance has been presented as an offering, one should consume it with careful attention.
247) If that [offering] is not consumed out of delusion, the deities dance;
by this very procedure, he who worships the Supreme Goddess [attains success].
O Goddess, on the surface of the earth he is undoubtedly the Lord in person;
O auspicious one, by means of the great conch, all rites such as recitation and the like are accomplished.
I have described only the power of the Kulasarvasvaka;
it cannot be fully recounted even in hundreds of millions of years.
O Supreme Goddess, even I have spoken something out of impulsiveness;
it could not be fully told even in a thousand lifetimes.
It should be given to one of noble birth who is devoted to Tārā;
it must not be given to a devotee of another deity, and especially not to a Vaiṣṇava.
It should always be given to one of noble birth, of great aspirations, devoted to faith and reverence, a high-souled person whose virtues have been thoroughly tested.
It must not be given to one who is not a devotee, nor to one who delights in other paths.
O Goddess of the lords of gods, it is never to be disclosed; it is always to be kept secret in all scriptures.
O Goddess, it should always be recited at all times and in all circumstances.

The person who daily recites with devotion this hymn containing the family names shall become equal to the Lord of Wealth (Kubera) through heaps of riches, a master of speech through the power of knowledge,
Cupid incarnate in beauty, and like the cool-rayed moon in fame.
Only Śaṅkara is capable by virtue of his heroic power; no other is a lord of the earth.
Thus ends the hymn named *Kulasarvasva* of Tārā, from the *Śrīharagaurī-saṃvāda*. Now, one should perform the daily fire-oblation (*nityahoma*). This is stated in the *Jñānārṇava*:
O Supreme Goddess, having made the formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*), one should perform the rite of the daily fire-oblation (*nityahoma*).

The resolve is of this form: "For the propitiation of such-and-such a deity, I shall offer this many oblations. In the *Nīlatantra*: "I shall explain the daily fire-oblation by which one attains all goals."
Having properly performed the ritual service, one should offer the oblation as before.
Then the best of practitioners should remember the recitation (japa) and the libation (tarpaṇa); furthermore, the Brāhmaṇa should perform the bali offering, the Vaiśvadeva rite, and so forth.
Having brought the fire according to the prescribed rules, one should discard the portion belonging to the flesh-eaters (kravyāda).
Then, having uttered the mantra, [one should offer] either in the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) or on the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila).
Or, having spread fire upon the ground with the three *vyāhṛtis*,
one should offer three oblations and then perform the six-limbed (*ṣaḍaṅga*) oblation.
Then, having invoked the Goddess with the root mantra, having offered sixteen oblations,
and having praised and bowed to her, one should dismiss her into the lunar orb.

The tradition is that one should cast a single coal toward the southwest, saying, "Obeisance to the flesh-eaters (kravyāda)," reciting the formula, "The portion for the flesh-eaters, to Agni. In the *Sārasaṃgraha*:
"When the fire has been thus consecrated, the knower of mantras, having invoked the deity [into it]..."
Having performed worship with the root mantra, [he should offer] twenty-five oblations.
With honey and clarified butter as the oblation, or with sesame seeds, or with auspicious milk-rice,
or with rice mixed with sesame, or even with flowers alone.
One should offer one oblation for each of the deities of the limbs and the protective enclosures;
then, having dismissed the deity and the fire, one should proceed to the place of worship.
Having sat upon the seat, the practitioner of mantra (mantrī) should then offer the bali-oblation to the spirits (bhūtabali).

Thus, there is an option between twenty-five or sixteen oblations. Furthermore, the consecration of the fire (agnisaṃskāra) must be performed exactly as stated in the Nīlatantra and not otherwise. No ritual acts such as the formal establishment of the fire (agnyādhāna) and so forth are required for the daily homa.

According to the words of Vasiṣṭha: Now follows the ritual for the *ārātrika* (luminous waving of lamps), as stated in the *Jñānārṇava*: "Thereafter, one should perform the *ārātrika* for the sake of accomplishing all desires and aims."
In a vessel of gold, silver, or bronze—captivating the eyes of the world.
O fair-faced Śivā, one should draw an eight-petaled lotus with saffron;
having fashioned a sacrificial oblation (caru) in the form of the moon, [one should place it] upon the head in its center, O Auspicious One.
One lamp should be placed upon the pericarp, and lamps made of barley and wheat, combined with sugar and milk, upon the eight petals.
Then the mantra-practitioner, having consecrated with mantras those [vessels] which are adorned with the beauty of garlands, beautiful, and filled to the brim, thereafter [worships] Ratneśvarī.
Having worshipped with the root mantra, one should then perform the circumambulation;
lifting that vessel again and again up to the level of the head.
He should perform the *nīrājana* rite for the Great Goddess nine times;
during the *nīrājana* of the Great Goddess, he should display the *cakra-mudrā*.
The *Ratneśvarī-vidyā* is also taught in that very same place: "The best of mantra-knowers should write the Śrī-bīja and the Parā-bīja;
thereafter, he should write 'ga', 'sa', 'ma', 'pa', and 'la' in sequence, situated in the positions of Indra (the east)."
Joined with the left ear (the letter *v*) and endowed with the drop (*bindu*) and the sound (*nāda*),
these five seed-syllables, O beautiful one, are the five jewels.
This nine-syllabled mantra of Ratneśī follows the reverse order of the previous seed-syllables.

*Parā* is the *māyā*-seed syllable (*hrīṃ*). *Indra* is the letter *la*. The left ear is the vowel *ū*. The "previous seed" refers to the *śrī*-seed and the *parā*-seed. Thus: *śrīṃ hrīṃ glūṃ slūṃ mlūṃ plūṃ llūṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ*.
Thus Ratneśvarī is accomplished. The *cakramudrā* is described in the *Lakṣaṇasaṃgraha*:
"Having inverted the palms of the left and right hands, one should interlace the two thumbs between the little fingers and the ring fingers."
This is taught as the Cakramudrā, which always bestows all accomplishments.
Now,

regarding the circumambulation in the *Uttara-tantra*: "Both the followers of the Purāṇas and those of the Vedas should indeed perform circumambulation and prostration with the root mantra, which accomplishes the goals of dharma and artha."
In the *Yāmala*: "The bowing of Śakti is everywhere proclaimed to be triangular in form.
(Having gone from the south to the northwest direction, and from there to the northeast;
then having gone to the south—the salutation is like a triangle.)"
And the half-moon is said to be behind the head-ornament.
While performing the circumambulation of Śiva, the practitioner of mantra should follow the sequence of a half-moon;
indeed, by the sequence of right and left, he must not overstep the *somasūtra*.
Extending his right hand, with his head bowed low,
he should again show his right side and remain mentally inclined toward the right as well.
One should properly encircle the deity three times in a clockwise direction;
a single prostration with one hand or even a single circumambulation [is also sufficient].

An untimely visit to Viṣṇu destroys the merit accumulated in the past. Likewise: "One circumambulation at Caṇḍī, seven at the Sun, three at Vināyaka, four at Keśava, and half at Śiva [is prescribed]."

Now, as for prostration (*nati*), it may consist of either eight limbs (*aṣṭāṅga*) or five limbs (*pañcāṅga*). For it is said in the Tantra: "In the rites of worship, prostration with eight limbs or five limbs is approved."
With both hands, with both feet, with both knees, and likewise with the eyes.
250) It is said that [the prostration] has eight limbs through the head, the gaze, as well as speech, and the mind;
it is said to have five limbs through the hands, the knees, the head, the speech, and the intellect.
And regarding this, another variety of the bowing gesture (*nati*) is also stated in the Tantra:
"Facing forward, square, circular, and cow-faced—
these are said to be the five gestures (*mudrā*) for prostration."
In that context, the *sammukha-mudrā* consists of the palms joined at the ground with the heads [of the hands] touching.
The *caturasra-mudrā* consists of joining the head with the left palm placed face-up on the ground and the right hand placed across it with the fingers pointing downward.
The *vṛtta-mudrā* consists of two fists joined at the head with the thumbs pressed against the ground and not extended.

However, some say that the *vṛtta-mudrā* is formed by interlacing the fingers of both hands and placing the two thumbs crossed over one another. [Alternatively, it is formed by] the fingers spread out and pressed against the ground.
The *gomukhamudrā* consists of joining the head upon the two hands positioned in the form of a *saṃyuga*. The *yoni-mudrā* is well known, according to the traditional teachers. In the *Kulārṇava*:
"All [acts] such as worship, having been performed preceded by the mantras and the *puraścaraṇa*..."
From here on, one should offer [the oblation] to the deity with the first mantra.
The extraction of the mantra is stated in the *Sārasaṃgraha*: "First one should utter the word 'iti', then one should utter 'prāṇabuddhi';
[then] according to the authority of the functions of the body in the states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep."
One should utter the word "speech" (vāc) in all circumstances,
as well as through action— that is, by means of the two hands, the two feet, the mouth, and the belly.
Whatever word one speaks and whatever syllable one utters,
and whatever is said and whatever is done— may it all be an offering unto Brahman.
The supreme mantra for offering to Brahman is also declared to end with "svāhā.
Regarding the method of offering, it is stated in the Śaiva Āgama: having offered a small amount of the arghya water to the right of the deity...
O beloved, the wise one should offer the completed worship into his hand.

In this context, the offering is made into the left hand of the deities, according to the statement in the *Vīracūḍāmaṇi*: "One should offer [the oblation] into the left hand. Thereafter, one should dismiss the deity. This is stated in the *Haṃsaparameśvara-tantra*:
"Then, having formed the *saṃhāra-mudrā*, [one should visualize] Maheśvarī in the form of light."
Having meditated upon it, O Śivā, one should extract it with a flower through the path of the flowing breath.
Having caused it to enter the thousand-petaled lotus situated at the *dvādaśānta*,
and having rested there, one should bring that [vital energy] down through the central channel (*madhyamā-nāḍī*) into the lotus of the heart.

251) Having properly established [the deity] and worshipped thoroughly, one should meditate upon oneself as being identical with that [deity]. As for the *saṃhāramudrā*: having placed the hands joined at the backs, and having rotated them from between the fingers, one should then make the two index fingers straight.
"The mudrā designated as 'withdrawal' (saṃhāra) is prescribed for the rite of dismissal (visarjana);
thus it is stated in the Tantra. Thereafter, one should worship Nirmālyavāsinī. As it is said in the *Kulamūlāvatāra*:
"Having constructed a mandala in the northeast, devoid of gates and lotuses..."
Indeed, for the purpose of dismissal and for the worship of the bearer of the floral remains (nirmālya-dhāriṇī).

I offer you, by the command of Śrī Śiva, the remains of food and drink—such as items to be licked, sucked, eaten, and drunk—as well as flower garlands and unguents; I give you the remains of the offerings for your consumption.
Having thus offered the remainder of the food offering (naivedya) and bowed down, one should perform the dismissal;
the practitioner should wear the remains of the flowers (nirmālya) upon his head while reciting the root mantra.
O Dear One, having partaken of the water for the feet and the divine food offering (naivedya), one should distribute it among the devotees;
then, having eaten it oneself, one should dwell happily, absorbed in that [divinity].
Thus ends the fifth chapter, the ritual for the daily worship of Tārā, in the *Tārābhaktisudhārṇava* composed by the Great Professor, the Illustrious Ṭhakkura Narasiṃha. || 5 ||
Obtained by chance from another manuscript, the unprinted portion on the one hundred and forty-eighth leaf is now published here:
"For a Brāhmaṇa, there is always a prohibition; for a Kṣatriya, it applies at the time of battle, provided he is not incapacitated."

Because battle is impossible [for him]. For a Vaiśya, at the time of investing capital, otherwise there would be the consequence of having to give a hundred or more when only a twentieth part was required to be given due to deficiency. "Never by Śūdras" means it should always be drunk by them. Otherwise, it would contradict the statement: "All [liquors] are declared for the Śūdra, wherever that land may be."

Because this would result in a contradiction with the [preceding] statement. Likewise, in the passage "In every Kali age, the Goddess is to be worshipped with pure liquors (*āsava*) alone," the term "by all castes" (*sarvavarṇaiḥ*) is to be construed [with that]. It should be noted that the word *sarvavarṇa* here refers to those other than Brahmins.
Now: [the liquor] produced from milk-trees, or that which is derived from tree-bark (*vārkṣa*).
It should be known that liquor is produced from honey-flowers, and that which is produced from rice is *āsava*.

If it is argued that because the *Bhairavatantra* defines terms such as "milk" (*kṣīra*) as specific types of fermented liquor (*āsava*), it follows that even a Brahmin has the right to partake in them; here it appears that this statement [is intended] to explain how milk and the like can result in intoxication (*maireya*). Therefore, "tree-born" (*vārkṣa*) refers to that which is produced from a milk-tree (*kṣīravṛkṣa*).

The meaning is "distilled liquor" (maireya). The same applies in what follows as well; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of using terms such as "milk-tree" (kṣīravṛkṣa) in their reverse order, according to the maxim:
"One should not state the predicate without first stating the subject. Thus, [the term] is "rice-porridge produced from rice grains" (taṇḍulodbhava odanaḥ).

Therefore, for a Śūdra as well, only *āsava* (liquor) is to be placed in the position where rice (*odana*) would normally be; thus, according to that [text], the meaning is that separate rice should not be given by Brāhmaṇas and others, but rather *āsava*, because of the statement of Likhita: "Raw [food] for a Śūdra."

This is because of such Smṛti texts as: "Cooked food that has been cooked [and left over] is called *ucchiṣṭa* (remnant)," and so forth. Nor should it be argued that since the curse of Śukra pertains specifically to Brāhmaṇas, the injunction for its removal in the case of liquor (*surā*) is untenable;
for it is established by the scriptures that the right to that [removal] belongs to the Śūdra alone, and thus the injunction for the removal of Śukra’s curse [is appropriate].

Because its meaning is directly perceived. Furthermore, just as in cases such as "one worships the Gārhapatya fire with the Aindrī verse," where the direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) is stronger than the indicative mark (*liṅga*), so too is a direct prohibitive injunction— such as "having given wine to a Brāhmaṇa"— stronger than a prescriptive rule for giving *maireya* liquor that is merely inferred from the context of a rite for releasing a curse.

"Because the reasoning is the same. And thus, in the case of the sacrifice to the site (*vāstuyāga*) and so forth, the recitation of the mantra "surāprākāraka" is also for the sake of an unseen result (*adṛṣṭārtha*), just like the mantra "vajrapuṣpaṃ pratīccha svāhā" even when *vajrapuṣpa* flowers are absent.
It is also stated that for castes other than Brāhmaṇas, if *āsava* is unavailable, *vijaya* may be used as a substitute.
In the *Vijayākalpa*:
"Between consciousness (*saṃvit*) and bliss (*ānanda*), consciousness alone is more important;
therefore, the best of practitioners should employ consciousness here in worship and other rites."
And a great worship should be performed by those who are well-joyful.
Furthermore, she is fourfold— as Brāhmaṇī, Kṣatriyā, Vaiśyā, and Śūdrā—
distinguished by the colors white, red, yellow, and black.
O Consciousness, born of Brahman, daughter of Brahman, ever sinless!
And having given [this] to the Bhairavas, may you always be pure.
Oṃ, obeisance to Brāhmaṇī, svāhā; thus one should purify Brāhmaṇī.
O Goddess, beloved of the crest-jewels of the Siddhas, you who awaken those of inferior understanding!
O you who bring the king and the subjects under control, O destroyer of the throats of enemies!
*Oṃ*, salutation to the Kṣatriyā, *svāhā*! Thereafter, one should purify the Kṣatriyā.
O flame of the fire that illuminates the fuel of ignorance, O you whose form is knowledge,
grant me the arrival of bliss, joy, and perfect wisdom.
*Hrīṃ*, obeisance to Vaiśyā, *svāhā*; thereafter, one should purify Vaiśyā.
"I bow, I bow to you, O revealer of the path of Yoga!
O Mother, victorious over the three worlds, may you grant me abundant fruit."

*Klīṃ śūdrāyai namaḥ svāhā*—with this, one should then purify the Śūdra. Alternatively, one may purify all [the castes] with a single mantra. As it is stated in that very same work: *Amṛte amṛtodbhave amṛtavarṣiṇi* (O Immortal One, O Source of Nectar, O Showerer of Nectar).
Then follow the words "ākarṣaya padadvandvam" and "siddhiṃ dehi".
Then he should say to him: "Now,
while reciting the mantra, one should offer [the offering] seven times into the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra),
likewise into the thousand-petaled lotus of the Guru, using the mudrā known as Tattva."
The practitioner, whose mind is intent on accomplishment, should satisfy [the deities] with devotion in three ways;
he should utter the word "aiṃ," then "vadavada," and thereafter the word "vāgvādini."
Then, one should offer oblations into the mouth with the mantra: "O you who are firm on the tip of my tongue, be present in every word; O you who bring beings under control, svāhā!"
If it is asked: "Since no specific qualified persons (*adhikārin*) are mentioned in these statements, how can it be said that they refer to those other than Brāhmaṇas? [The answer is:

"One should avoid all intoxicating substances, such as chickpeas (*caṇaka*) and the like, and the *karañja* tree, because one who commits such a sin is a transgressor (*pātakī*), O best among those who know the Veda."
A Brahmin who gives liquor is indeed deprived of his status as a Brahmin;
by giving the blood from his own body, he incurs the sin of self-slaughter.
Receive [the initiation] according to the statement of the Bhairava Tantra. Then, one should begin the purification of the self through breath control (prāṇāyāma) and other practices.
As it is said in the Kulārṇava: "O Dear One, the purification of the elements along with the ritual bath is accomplished by means of breath control and the rest."
The purification of the self is said to be accomplished through all the ritual depositions (nyāsa), beginning with those of the six limbs.
Now, regarding breath control (*prāṇāyāma*): first, as for breath control, it is stated in the *Sanatkumāra-saṃhitā*:
"Having sat upon a comfortable seat and having indeed performed breath control..."
Then, having performed the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi), one should immediately thereafter perform the ritual placement (nyāsa).
The Sixth Chapter: The Birth from a Jar;
Now, the Offering of the Vessel.

Now, if the hero is one who transcends the Brahmins, then after the dismissal (*visarjana*), if he is such a divine being, then prior to the *brahmārpaṇa* offering, one should first worship the Guru’s vessel with devotion and offer it to the Guru.
For it is said in the Tantra:
Then, having lifted the vessel with both hands, one should offer it to the venerable Guru, who is the manifest form of Paraśiva himself, together with his consort.
Also in the *Bhāvacūḍāmaṇi*, regarding the position of three vessels:
"Having divided the vessel for the *arghya* into three parts, one part is given to the Guru;
having given one to the *Kula*, the propitiation of the Deity is performed with the remaining one."

"To the power of the *kulāya*. Likewise, in the *Kulārṇava* it is said: "But he who consumes the *kula*-substance without having first offered it to Śakti—his worship is fruitless, and the deity does not become pleased."
The libation to the deities (*devatarpaṇa*) consists precisely of the drink. For it is said in the *Kulārṇava*:

"In the Kula, which is the form of consciousness in the shape of Kuṇḍalī and possesses a luster equal to ten million suns rising from the triangle that is the root of the Self, the substance [of worship] is accompanied by mantra."
Also in the *Samayācāra*: "For the purpose of satiating Kuṇḍalinī, one should employ the vessel of enjoyment;
having recollected the internal Power, one should satisfy the deity of the body."

Having constantly given the nectar from the *vīrapātra* to the Kaulikas and from the *yoginīpātra* to the other Śaktis, one should partake of it oneself; this is according to the view regarding the superior vessels. In the *Kulārṇava*:
"One should not drink the substance without the mantra; an expiation is prescribed."
Manu is stated in that very same place: "I drink this purifying, immortal nectar, the medicine for existence, which is the cause for severing the bonds of the bound soul, as proclaimed by Bhairava."
Because the self consisting of bliss has the sovereignty of consciousness as its essence,
and because all entities consist of that [consciousness], all entities are withdrawn into the *rasa*.
For the expansion of one's own sovereignty, the nectar is drunk by him;
therefore, being full, I drink that Goddess, this very wine.
O Goddess of the gods, the knower of mantras, with an undistracted mind, should slowly perform the drinking of the nectar using this root mantra.

He who practices without knowing the characteristics of the types of drinks, their specific effects, their exhilarating qualities, their measurements, and their stability, shall become a vessel for calamities.

Regarding the classification of drinking, it is stated in that very same source: "Drinking is said to be of three kinds, according to the sequence of Divine (divya), Heroic (vīra), and Fettered (paśu).
Divine drinking is [drinking] in the presence of the Goddess; Heroic drinking is performed on the seat of the Mudrā."
Drinking [the wine] like an animal according to one's own whim is called "animal-drinking" (paśupāna).
But as for the fruit: O Pārvatī, by drinking the nectar purified through the consecration of mantra, the state of the deity arises, which liberates one from the bonds of worldly existence.
This and more is stated in that very same [text]. The proof for this is also found there: "Bliss is the nature of Brahman, and that is established in liberation;
considering it to be its manifestor, it is drunk by yogins," and so forth.

The classification of *ullāsa* (ecstatic expansion) is given in that very same [text]: "The initial, the tender, the youthful, the mature, its end, the *unmanā*, and the seventh, called the state beyond stability (*anavasthā*)."
Now, O Mistress of the Kula, their characteristic is that the undertaking consists of the three principles;
O Mother, the youthful effulgence has been described, and youth is bliss.
O beloved, youth is said to be the perfect blossoming of the mind;
when there is stumbling in sight, thought, and speech, it is designated as "mature."
The performance of one's desired actions is proclaimed as the stage of *prauḍha* (mature);
then there is the state of *unmanā* (transcending the mind), falling and rising, and fainting again and again.
The lack of control over the body and the senses is described as instability;
the precedence of mantra for the three principles (tattvas) is the beginning of the drinking of the three handfuls of non-dual nectar, as taught in the Upanishads.

Thus it is; for here, another method for the purification of reality (*tattvaśuddhi*) has been stated. And so, it appears that in another tradition, the commencement consists in the taking [of the substance] three times. "Stability" (*sthiti*) means the established limit (*maryādā*). That is as follows:
"Free from doubt, pure, firm, shameless, and devoid of curiosity."
Having determined the meaning of the Vedas and Shastras, one may drink the Varuni wine that bestows boons.
Having worshipped the gods and the ancestors according to the path taught in the scriptures of the Goddess,
one who drinks wine and eats meat while remembering the gurus incurs no fault.

In this context, the "fathers" (pitaras) are indeed the Guru, the Paramaguru, and so forth. Likewise: "Having lifted the vessel with the left hand and formed the *apasavya* (left-hand) mudrā, one should receive it with the second [hand] according to the rule, while reciting the mantra."
*Mudrā* means purity. In the phrase "by the second," the instrumental case is used in the sense of accompaniment (*sahayoga*).
(256) Drinking without chewing is merely consuming poison;
"chewing" refers to [the crushing of] parched chickpeas and the like.
He who gives the ritual substance of the Śrīcakra to the uninitiated,
whether out of affection, greed, or even fear, shall become a beast for the Yoginīs.
In that regard as well, the union of vessels (pātramelana) should be performed according to one's authority,
[avoiding] those who are uninitiated, of improper conduct, ignorant of the Tantras, and devoid of the deity.
One should not form associations with those who have defiled themselves, who have fallen from their commitments,
who consider themselves possessed of supernatural knowledge, or who practice the vows of conceptual proliferation.
One should not form associations with animals or those engaged in base activities; nor should one offer the substance intended for one's own vessel to Bhairava.
If one should give [it] to anyone else, O Maheśānī, one would incur the curse of the deities;
[it should be given] to the Bhairava practitioner (sādhaka). Likewise:
"Or the Kaulika may perform the union of vessels according to the different currents (srotas)."
The meaning is that, at some point, one might cause a confusion between the current and the tradition due to excessive trust, even when they appear identical;
likewise, there may be a merging of the east and south, as well as the north and west.
In that regard, even by heroes devoted to sequential worship who possess their own respective perspectives—
"And one should perform that [rite] with amorous women and the fourfold stream of currents.
By this, it is implied that there is no figurative identification of the Upper Tradition (ūrdhvāmnāya) with any of these [other traditions]. Likewise:
"One should drink the substance that is the remnant of Śakti, and chew the remnant of Vīra."
One should not give away what remains from one's own meal, nor should one eat what belongs to another.
That which belongs to another is the leavings of another person. Regarding this, there is a specific distinction stated in that very same [text]:
"O Pārvatī, one may eat the leavings of the Guru, the Śakti, and the sons; of the elder and younger brothers of the Guru; and even of one's own elder brother, but not those of anyone else."
One should eat the remnants of women, but one should never give them to them;
O Ambikā, one should give one's own remnants to the younger ones and to one's own disciples.
He who out of affection gives [his food] to others will become a vessel for calamities;
so too is he of deluded intellect who takes the vessel containing the remnants of liquor.
Out of affection, greed, or even fear, one may incur the curse of the deity.

In this matter, the seniority (*jyeṣṭhatā*) and juniority (*kaniṣṭhatā*) among fellow disciples (*satīrthyas*) is determined solely by the sequence of their initiation. For instance, it is stated in the *Rudrayāmala*: "Even a child who was initiated first is senior in the Kula tradition."
Even a twice-born man who is initiated later is inferior to one of the lowest caste who was initiated earlier.
The twice-born who is younger is indeed the elder; such is the settled conclusion of the scriptures.
As long as the gaze does not waver, and as long as the mind does not waver.
One should perform drinking only up to that point; beyond this is the "drinking of the animal" (paśupāna).

Thus, the intended meaning is that drinking should be performed only as far as the height of youthful exuberance (*yauvanollāsa*). This, however, applies to those who have not received the full consecration (*pūrṇābhiṣeka*). For those who have been consecrated, all seven exuberances (*ullāsa*) are prescribed. To explain:
In that very same [text]:
"O Goddess, for those endowed with the full initiation (pūrṇābhiṣeka), drinking is prescribed;
having lifted the vessel with both hands, one should remember the Root Mantra and the Pādukā."
One should drink liquor until the throat is full; he is liberated from this, there is no doubt.
Drinking again and again, drinking repeatedly, until he falls upon the ground.
Having risen and drunk again, rebirth no longer exists;
through bliss the Goddess is satisfied, and through the melodic resonance (mūrcchanā), Bhairava himself is satisfied.
Because of vomiting [the nectar], all the gods [are satisfied]; therefore, one should perform the triad.
In the *Kulāmṛta*: "The knower of Brahman, while practicing the Kula conduct, having drunk the wine, stumbles repeatedly."
If the dust particles falling upon his body dissolve into his limbs,
for as long as that number of dust particles lasts, he is honored in the world of Brahmā.

Likewise: "Having drunk [the nectar] repeatedly and having recited [the mantra], one shall dwell in the world of Brahmā along with ten million kulas, O Goddess; this is the truth, the truth, there is no doubt."
Right there he attains pervasion and shall not fall back into this world again;
having drunk [the nectar] and worshipped the Goddess, he certainly attains lordship.
"In that very state one attains dissolution and never returns again.
This, however, is essential for the Kaulikas. As it is said in the *Haragaurī-saṃvāda*: "That which has been offered to the Goddess must be consumed with careful attention."
If that is not consumed out of delusion, the deities dance to eat it.
Now, regarding the fifth sacrifice, the *Kumārītantra* states: "Then, having offered praise and performed prostration, one should perform the union of enjoyment (*sambhogamelana*).
Indeed, enjoyment in the presence of the deity results in the gratification of the deity."
Likewise: "An actress, a Kāpālinī, a courtesan, a washerwoman, a barber’s wife, a Brāhmaṇa woman, a Śūdra girl, and likewise a cowherd’s daughter."
The daughter of the garland-maker and nine other maidens are proclaimed;
having brought any one of these from there into the circle of her womb—
Having worshipped the Great Goddess, one should then engage in sexual union.
In the *Devīyāmala*: "Now I shall describe the fruit of worship, which becomes increasingly superior;
by worshipping the Supreme Śakti according to one's own capacity, ten thousand times the merit [is obtained]."
Beyond that, the prostitute is to be known as more [wicked], and the washerwoman is even more so than her;
the barber’s wife is superior to the washerwoman, and the leather-worker’s wife is superior to the barber’s wife.
O fair-faced one, it is said that a woman for a specific purpose is more [powerful] than that;
even more so is one born of the lowest caste, and a Cāṇḍālī is even greater than that.
Then Mātaṅginī is the most excellent, and likewise Pukkaśī is superior to Mātaṅgī;
Akṣatā is superior to Pukkaśī, and Atisūdantī is recorded as superior to her.
Sundarī is said to be foremost— affectionate, full of passion, devoted, O Supreme Goddess, intoxicated, and endowed with auspicious marks.
Those who are perfected in the conduct of the samaya, knowledgeable in mantra, free from fear, clever,
and yet unmarried, and who possess both fortitude and independence.
One should worship all women endowed with such qualities—
whether one's own or another's— for they are, O Maheśvarī, nothing but Śakti.
They should be worshipped with all ritual offerings, regarding them as the presiding deities of the mantras,
using various fruits, betel leaves, garments, ornaments, and gold.
Having worshipped according to the rules with devotion, one should cause many offerings to be presented;
he who performs the worship of Śakti while maintaining the latent desire for worldly enjoyment [is not liberated].

He incurs poverty and will certainly become a denizen of hell. Also, in the *Vīracūḍāmaṇi*: "Having brought a beautiful young woman, one who is distinguished by her noble lineage and conduct—a maiden sixteen years of age with full and elevated breasts..."
She was like a female elephant in rut, intoxicated and with eyes rolling from passion;
she had the eyes of a young fawn and the gait of a doe, and possessed a gentle smile.

One who is free from anger, greed, fear, hypocrisy, delusion, and deceit; who is devoted to the duty toward her husband, truthful, and always pure— even if she be a courtesan, an actress, a Caṇḍālī, a procuress, or born of an adulterer.
Women wearing the yogamudrā, as well as a leather-worker and a painter.
Endowed with the four colors, it is excellent when produced from a mountain;
having drawn an excellent circular lotus on the left side. (259)
Adorned with white and red, blue and smeared with vermilion,
the practitioner, facing east, should worship the Goddess who faces west.
According to the procedure for the powers of the seats (pīṭha), one should worship the nine powers:
Rati, Prīti, Priyā, Kānti, Kāminī, and Kāmamālinī.
The nine Śaktis are Kandarpadalani, Durgā, and Bhāvinī;
having uttered "Viyadgaṅgam" (the ether-Ganges), it is endowed with the mantra, the bindu, and the kalā.

Afterwards, having uttered this root mantra ending with "hṛdayāntam" and preceded by the word "mahāpreta," one should then utter the word "Tāriṇī" along with the term of perfect enlightenment (sambuddhi).
"Come, come! he should say repeatedly, and taking his foot with his left hand, he should place it again and again upon the sandals; then he should seat him upon the throne.
O Dear One, one should worship her whose limbs are smeared with red sandalwood paste, who is adorned with red flowers,
endowed with all ornaments, and naked.
And when she is intoxicated by the wine of Varuṇī and enveloped by gestures of amorous allure,
one should cause her to drink until the vessel reaches the level of her throat.
O Maheśānī, one should perform meditation in a cave with a crocodile-like opening,
[visualizing] the form of a cock’s crest and possessing a luster equal to that of the elephant-faced [Gaṇeśa].
One should contemplate the Goddess, the Vidyā who deludes the world, situated there; first the syllable *tāra* (Om), then at the end of the heart, and afterwards the abode of Madana.
O Goddess, one should worship at the end of the fourth [vowel] and cast a flower upon the *bhaga*;
having rinsed it with the *kuladravya*, one should honor it with perfumes and flowers.
Having offered incense, lamps, and so forth, one should thereafter worship the enclosure (āvaraṇa):
Icchā, Jñānā, Kriyā, and then Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, and Raudrikā.
Thereafter, one should worship Rati, Prīti, and Kāma, who bears a flower-arrowed bow, along with Vasanta, accompanied by leaves and sprouts.
O Goddess, one should worship Ciṅkura, accompanied by Alisyanda;
one should worship Virañci at the navel, and Hara and Hari at the heart.
Then, O Maheśānī, one should worship the Trimūrti on the breast and the face:
Kāmeśī, Vajreśī, and Parā Bhagamālinī.
O Maheśānī, one should worship the five arrows at the root of the eyebrows:
Drāviṇī, beginning with *drām*, on the head; and Kṣobhiṇī, beginning with *drīm*, on the feet.
One should place *klīṃ*, the magnetizing power (*vaśīkariṇī*), at the mouth; *blūṃ* preceded by the seed-syllable (*bīja*) at the secret place;
the attracting power (*ākarṣiṇī*) at the heart; and again, [the syllable] joined with *bhṛgu* (ṣ) within all [the others].
Thus, this worship of the arrows, which causes infatuation, has been described in due order.
One should then worship the Sun and the Moon in sequence upon the two wheels of the ears.
Having worshipped Vahni in the rasanā, Nakṣatramālinī in the eyes,
one should worship Prāṇa in the nose, and Tripathagāminī in the ājñā.
One should worship Akṣobhya on the crown of the head with offerings of perfume and flowers;
one should place a garland of flowers around his neck and then the wise practitioner should recite the mantra according to his capacity.
In the Jñānārṇava, however, it is said: "A couch made of elephant tusks and fashioned from gold, silver, and so forth—therein one should place a mattress made of pure linen."
O Goddess, O Daughter of the Mountain, having scattered flowers in the center as well as the powder of camphor, one should place Maṇḍūka and the others there, one above the other.
First, one should worship Maṇḍūka, Rudra who resembles the fire of cosmic destruction,
Ādhāraśakti, Kūrma, Ananta, and Varāha.
Having worshipped the earth, as well as the bulbous root, the stalk, the lotus, the petal,
and the row of filaments, one should then worship the pericarp.
Having thoroughly worshipped the couch,
one should worship Dharma, Jñāna, Vairāgya, and Aiśvarya in sequence upon its four legs.
One should worship these unprecedented [deities] in the vicinity of their feet;
one should worship the Self (Ātman), the Inner Self (Antarātman), and the Supreme Knowledge-Self (Parama-jñānātman).
Having worshipped the three qualities upon the parts of the couch,
one should then honor a messenger (dūtī) who possesses auspicious marks, is beautiful, and is endowed with all the characteristics.
O Supreme Goddess, one should worship her— who is beautiful with various ornaments and under one's own control like the autumnal moon— with the arrows of the five desires.
One should worship Vaṭuka and the others in the four directions for the sake of attaining success;
one should then project the Mātṛkā, endowed with the arrows of Kama, upon her body.
One should place a triangle upon the head and perform worship there in due order;
in the center of the triangle, one should fully worship the goddess named Bālā, who is Kāmeśī.
Having worshipped Gaṇeśa, the presiding lord of the Kula, as well as Lakṣmī and Sarasvatī, and likewise Vāsanta and Madana within the triangles, O beloved; 261)
Afterwards, one should worship Kalādhara on her breasts;
[one should worship] Vāgbhava, Kāmarāja, and the Strībīja which is Kāmarāja upon her face.
Having offered that which consists of laughter, one should utter the *ādhāraśakti*;
then, having offered the *śrīpādukā*, one should say, "I worship."
With this mantra, having specifically drawn a beautiful triangle upon her forehead using vermilion and other substances;
O beautiful one, one should worship Vaṭuka, Yoginī, Kṣetrapāla, Gaṇeśvara, Lakṣmī, and Sarasvatī there.
Having uttered the seed-syllable of desire (KĀM), followed by Kāmarāja, and then having offered the venerable sandals (ŚRĪPĀDUKĀ), one should then say: "I worship."
O Goddess, one should worship on the sole of the right foot with this mantra:
having uttered "Vaṃ Vasantam," followed by Ramā devoid of Nāda.
Saying "I worship the sandals," one should place them in her left hand;
then, having uttered the Śakti-bīja, one should utter the word "Soma-pāda."
Then, having offered the venerable sandals, I worship them upon the two breasts;
thereafter, the wise practitioner should perform the placement of the *kāmakalā* according to the sequence of ascent.
Śraddhā, Prītī, Rati, Dhṛti, Kānti-manoharā,
Manoramā, Manorāmā, and Madanonmādinī.
Mohinī, Dīpinī, Śoṣiṇī, Vaśaṅkarī,
Rañjanī, Subhagā, Devī, Ṣoḍaśī, and Priyadarśanā.
The digits (kalās) of the flower-bowed god (Kusumadhanvan) are to be worshipped with the vowels beginning with 'a':
Pūṣan, Aryaman, Sumanas, Rati, Prīti, and Dhṛti.
Ṛddhi, Saumyā, Marīci, and the tenth, Aṃśumālinī;
Aṅgirā, Śaśinī, Chāyā, and Sampūrṇamaṇḍalā.
Puṣṭi and Amṛtā—these are the sixteen digits (kalās) of the Moon;
they, conjoined with the vowels beginning with 'a', should be worshipped by the wise.
O beautiful one, one should worship all the digits (kalās) of both Kāma and Soma on the right side from the feet to the head, and on the left side from the head to the feet.

In another tantra: "Having duly placed the bow of desire (kāmacāpaka), starting from the spinal column and ending at the head, the practitioner of mantra (mantrī) should worship it upon the crown of the head."
Having uttered the word *dharmātmaka* followed by the phrase *kāmacāpa*,
and having offered the *śrīpādukā* of the feet, one should worship with the words "I worship."
One should worship the five arrows with the five arrows in their respective places— on the head, the feet, the mouth, the secret place, and the heart— in due order.
Having uttered "drāṃ," the word for causing to flee, and then the word for the foot of Bāṇa,
one should thereafter say "śrīpādukām" (the venerable sandals) and worship with the words "I worship."
Having uttered the syllable *hrīm*, one should pronounce the "arrow of madness" (*unmādabāṇa*).
Having offered the *śrīpādukā* of the feet, one should worship with the words, "I worship."
Having uttered the word "seed of desire" (kāmabīja), then the word "arrow of delusion" (mohabāṇa),
and having uttered the word "the venerable sandal of the feet" (pādaśrīpādukā), one should worship with the words "I worship" (pūjayāmi).
Having uttered the syllable *vlām*, which is the word of kindling,
then having given the word for the arrow-foot, one should thereafter utter the *śrīpādukā*.
Having worshipped with the words "I worship," one should utter the remaining *bāṇa* [mantra];
then, having written "drying" (*śoṣaṇam*), one should thereafter write the word-form of *bāṇa*.
Then, having offered the venerable sandals (śrīpādukā), one should worship with the words "I worship.
Thereafter, one should worship the triangle within the circle of the forehead.
One should utter the Vāgbhava syllable, then the auspicious foot, and thereafter say "Śrīpādukām.
Having said "I worship" (pūjayāmi), one should then perform worship upon the lines of the right hand.
Having uttered the syllable *hrīṃ*, followed by the word "bhagapāda," and then having offered the *śrīpādukā*, one worships [it] in the western direction with the words "I worship."
Having uttered the seed-syllable of desire (KĀM), then the words "bhaga" and "sarpiḥ," and having assigned the words "śrīpāda" and "śrīpada," one should then utter the word "pādukā."
Having uttered "I worship" (pūjayāmi), one should perform the worship on the left side;
having written the syllable *hsauḥ*, which consists of the self, followed by the word *bhagāvaha*.
Having offered the Śrīpādukā at the feet, one should worship from the central region;
then, having offered the station of Śrī-Uḍḍīśa, [one worships] the goddess Uḍḍīśvarī.
Having bestowed the title "Nāthadeva," one should then utter "Śrī Raktāmbā.
Then, having written "Śrī Caryānātha," one should thereafter [utter] "Pāda Śrīpādukā."
"I worship"—thus one should worship in Uḍḍiyāna within the heart, O lady of good vows;
having written the word "Śrī" and then the word "Jālandhara."
Having inscribed [the syllable] Ramā, devoid of Nāda, upon the Great Seat (Mahāpīṭha),
one should then place the word Jāleśvarī and inscribe the goddess Jālī.
Having bestowed the title "Nātha Deva," and then the title "Śrī Jālāmbā," and having bestowed the title "Śrī Ṣaṣṭhīśa," and then the title "Nātha Deva."
Having offered the foot-ornament of Śrīpādukā, one should worship with the thought, "I worship.
O Goddess, one should worship in the navel-maṇḍala with this mantra.
Then, having offered the *śrīpada*, one should utter *Pūrṇeśvarī*;
likewise, the words *Devī-śrīpāda-śrī-pūrṇanātha-deva*.
Having uttered the word *Śrīcāmuṇḍā*, one should write the word *Devīśrī*;
then, having written *Uḍḍīśanātha*, one should write the word *Devapāda*.
Then, having offered the venerable sandals (śrīpādukā),
[one recites] the word "Kāmeśvarī," then the word "Devīśrī," and [finally] "Kāmeśvarānandanātha."
Having addressed the venerable *Śrīmahāpada*, one then [addresses] the venerable feet of the Mother (*Ambāśrīpada*);
having addressed the Lord Mitrīśanātha, one then [addresses] the venerable sandals of his feet (*Pādaśrīpādukā*).
Having given [the offerings], one should then worship according to the Kāmaśāsana;
the wise one should worship the lineage of gurus on the left of the domestic seat (gṛhapīṭha).
Then, one should worship Anaṅgakusumā and the others again in the lotus of the heart;
having uttered the Vāgbhava syllable *vlauṃ*, one should then pronounce the mantra consisting of *vlīṃ*.
Having uttered "vloṃ vluṃ vluḥ" with this mantra, the practitioner,
having displayed the *yonimudrā*, should then contemplate agitation within the *yoni*.
The Vāgbhava, the Kāmarāja, and immediately thereafter the Strībīja—this is the Vidyā named Kṣobhaṇī; one should perform the agitation of the breasts with it.
Then, having displayed the *yonimudrā*, the practitioner should slowly utter the *vāgbhava* syllable (*aiṃ*), followed by *sphṛṃ*, and then say *bleṃ blīṃ blūṃ*.
Having uttered that which consists of *klīm*, one should utter that which consists of *hrīm*;
then, having bestowed that which consists of *kṣam*, one should contemplate her agitation.
One should contemplate this vidyā named Drāviṇī within the center of the yoni;
then, becoming filled with supreme bliss and overflowing with joy in one's mind, [one should proceed].
The practitioner should contemplate the seed-syllable of his own vidyā upon a lotus at the crown of the head;
then, with the root mantras, he should [place it] within her womb.
Having offered three handfuls of flowers, one should then contemplate the arousal [of the seed-syllable].
In the *Jñānārṇava*: "One should contemplate the ritual placements (nyāsa) performed upon the body of the messenger (dūtī) as being upon one's own body.
In the *Vīracūḍāmaṇi*: "Now I shall explain the ritual placement; one should meditate upon oneself as having the nature of Śiva."
"Śivātmānam" means "the self that is Śiva. Likewise:
"One should install Mahādeva, who has five faces and is endowed with the kalās, in due order.
'Īśānaḥ sarvavidyānām' (The Lord of all sciences) is the first kalā, Śaśinī."
Īśvaraḥ sarvavidyānām, followed by aṅgadā; then brahmādhipatiḥ at the end of the word śabda, and again brahmaṇo'dhipatiḥ.
"May Śiva, the bestower of the desires of Brahmā, be mine. Having thus uttered "Sadāśivoṃ," one should then place the Aṃśumālinī, which is another [mantra] enclosed within the Marīci-sampuṭa.
We know that Tatpuruṣa; thus is Kalā-śānti proclaimed. We meditate upon Mahādeva; likewise is Kalā-vidyā.
After that, the Rudra-foot is recited, and then the Kalā is declared as the Pratiṣṭhā;
having uttered "pracodayāt," Nivṛtti follows thereafter.
O Goddess, one should then sequentially place the *aghorebhyaḥ* mantra and the *tamaḥkalā* upon the heart, in the east, west, south, and north.
Then, at the end of the *ghora* [mantras] and at the end of *moha*, one should place [the syllables] upon the neck;
thereafter, following the end of *ghora*, the *kriyā* [mantra] should be placed upon the right shoulder.
Then, one should place Nidrā on the left shoulder with the mantra "vai"; thereafter, having uttered "sarvataḥ sarvam," one should place Vyādhi on the navel.
One should place that [portion] from all [of them] as the digit of Death (mṛtyu) in the region of the belly;
then, saying "Salutation to you," one should subsequently place the digit of Hunger (kṣudhā) on the back in due order.
At the end of "to those in the form of Rudras," there should be the syllables *tṛṣāṃ tāra-namaḥ*;
at the end of "salutation to Vāmadeva," there should be *rajā* for the secret region.
Having placed [the seed] in the left scrotum, one should offer protection with "Homage indeed to Jyeṣṭha;
homage to Rudra"; then, one should place this digit, Rati, in the left scrotum.
At the end of "Kālāya namaḥ," Pālinī is on the right thigh;
O Goddess of the gods, Kalakāmā is on the left, and [the mantra] is for Vikaraṇāya.
Having uttered the word "namaḥ" at the right knee, *saṃyamanī* is prescribed;
at the left [knee], *balakriyā* is for the purpose of *vikaraṇa*.
Having uttered "vṛddhi" at the end of the *namaḥ*, one should place it on the right buttock;

O Goddess, [there is success] upon approaching a sacred seat (pīṭha), from seeing heroes or one's own kinsmen,
upon the arrival of a teacher, at a holy pilgrimage site, or from the vision of a deity.

One should perform the worship according to one's strength, according to one's faith, according to the place, and as is appropriate; according to the water available, according to the materials at hand, and according to the manner of worship.
A follower of the Kula path should not act out of delusion, for he would incur the curse of the deity.

As stated in the *Kulacūḍāmaṇi*: "O Īśvarī, [one should perform the rites] on the days of the deity, the guest-star (atithi), the lunar mansions, and during the conjunctions of heroes; likewise during lunar and solar eclipses, at the beginnings of Manvantaras, and at the beginnings of the Yugas."

The word "pūjā" (worship) is to be understood as the remainder [of the sentence]. Here, the deities, guests, and so forth, are indeed those known as the *kula*. These will be described later. In the *Yāmala*: "On the day of one's own birth, as well as that of one's own guru, on the day of receiving the *vidyā*, and likewise on the day of the Lord’s manifestation..."
On the new moon day, at the beginning of the yugas, during the solstices, the equinoxes, and likewise at the sun's passage into a new zodiac sign,
one should perform great worship for the sake of pleasing the deity.
In the *Tantrarāja*: "On the birthday of the Guru, on the days of receiving the Vidyā, on one's own birthday, and on the day of the Lord’s pervasive manifestation."

The remainder [of the instruction] is that worship should be performed on the day of the conjunction of the three syllables (*akṣaratrayasampāta*) as well as on the full moon day (*pūrṇādina*). "Pervasion of the Lord" (*nāthavyāpti*) refers to the death of the Guru. The "conjunction of the three syllables" is the unification of the syllable of the *yuga*, the syllable of the day, and the syllable of the rising [of the breath]. That, however, has been stated specifically with reference to Sundarī.

Therefore, the specific occasion for this is stated in the *Kulacūḍāmaṇi*: "On the day of the Kula-astrologer, on the eighth day of the Kula, and especially on the fourteenth, the worship of the Yoginīs is performed there; therein, the worship of the Kula is paramount."
Just as Viṣṇu, when worshipped on his own lunar day (tithi), grants all desires, so too Durgā, when worshipped on her own lunar day, grants all desires.

The phrase "on a kula lunar day" is an elliptical expression (upalakṣaṇa) for both the day of the week (vāra) and the lunar mansion (nakṣatra). The days of the week that are kula and so forth are stated in the *Yāmala*:
"The Sun, Moon, Jupiter, and Saturn—these four are considered akula;
Mars and Venus are called kula; and Wednesday is both kula and akula."
The second, tenth, and sixth lunar days are declared to be both *kula* and *akula*; the odd-numbered days are said to be *akula*, while the remaining lunar days are *kula*.
Vāruṇa (Śatabhiṣaj), Ārdrā, Abhijit, and Mūla are declared to be Kulākula;
those [asterisms] together with their respective constellations are the Kulas, while the remainder are the Akulas.
In the Trikula, however, worship is mandatory.
On a Kulavāra, on a Kularkṣa, at a Kulalagna, and during a Kulakṣaṇa,
the worship of the Yoginīs is never neglected, even if performed only mentally.
Thus, according to the words of the *Kulacūḍāmaṇi*:
"Likewise, one should worship the Goddess at the family tree (*kulavṛkṣa*) and always bow to the family trees;
one should not sleep beneath a family tree, nor should one ever climb it."
If the practitioner does not crush these [leaves], he should not even touch them with his feet;
one must not eat from their leaves, even if one’s life-breaths have reached the throat.
The *sahakāra*, *karṇikāra*, *kesara*, and likewise the *tilaka*;
the *kadamba*, *sindhuvāra*, *kaṅkeli*, and that called *campaka*.
The śleṣmātaka, kuruvaka, nimba, caladala,
yajñāṅga, jaṭila, and bilva— these are considered family trees (kulavṛkṣas).
In these [places], the Yoginīs who grant all desires are eternally present. Among all sacred seats (pīṭhas), that seat which is Kāmarūpa is the bestower of fruits.
Wherever the Goddess, who grants the fulfillment of desires, is worshipped even once,
the merit at the Kāmākhyā-yonimaṇḍala is a hundred times greater than that.
That is declared to be twofold: the manifest and the unmanifest.
From the manifest comes the unmanifest, O sinless one, which bestows the fruit of great merit.
If, by good fortune, it is obtained by a wise man of noble lineage,
then he should worship the Goddess there with manifold offerings.
When, by good fortune, he is seen, then one should perform worship mentally,
whether on a mountain, in a forest region, or likewise in a secluded pavilion.
276) Whether going to a crossroads or a cremation ground, the best of practitioners,
having meditated upon the Goddess and recited the mantra, should then bow and proceed to his place.
Seeing the power of beasts, the power of birds, and the vulture, one should bow to Śivā:
"O slender-waisted one! O greatly fierce one! O you with disheveled hair! O you who are fond of offerings!"
Salutations to you, whose face is radiant with noble conduct, beloved of Śaṅkara!
Having beheld a corpse in the cremation ground, one should bring it forth accompanied by mantras.
Having circumambulated [her] clockwise, one attains the highest perfection—
O you with terrible fangs, fierce eyes, who resounds with the cry of a wild boar!
Homage to you, O dweller of the funeral pyre, who possess a terrible and fearsome hand-clap!
Having beheld the red garment and likewise the flower, one should bow to Tripurā.
O you who resemble the bandhūka flower, O destroyer of fear in the three cities,
O you born from the dawning of good fortune, salutations to you, O lady of excellent complexion!
A king or a prince, elephants, horses, and chariots; weapons, a heroic man, a buffalo, or the leader of a clan.
Upon seeing a black-colored flower, a wise person should bow to Durgā:
"Victory to you, O Goddess, Mother of the World, whose deity is worshipped by Tripura!"
O Goddess, granter of boons to your devotees, O slayer of Mahiṣa, salutations be to you!
[I praise] the first and the second Kumārikā, who is ever restless in play.
Having observed a group of young women and a single young woman at a solitary tree, one should mutter the root-mantra as if empowered by mantra and bow to Bhairava.
I bow to you, O boon-granting Goddess, adorned with a garland of severed heads;
strewn with a garland of blood, I bow to you, the bestower of boons.
Having seen these, the wise person should prostrate for the sake of attaining all accomplishments;
otherwise, he shall never achieve success in mantra.
In the Matsyasūkta: Worship of the Goddess on the eighth day bestows the fruit of all desires;
[one should offer] a rambhā flower, a citron, and fragrant substances mixed together.
Having mixed these together, one should offer the bali, especially on the eighth day;
one should likewise offer milk along with curd and sugar.
One should diligently offer gifts to the deities for the sake of attaining inexhaustible merit. [The auspicious dates are:

the sixth day of the month of Bhādrapada, the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of Āśvina, the ninth day of the bright fortnight of Kārttika, and the fifth day of the dark fortnight of Mārgaśīrṣa. (277)
O Goddess, the full moon day of Pauṣa, the fourth day of the bright fortnight of Māgha,
the eleventh day of the dark fortnight of Phālguna, and the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight of Caitra;
The third day of Vaiśākha, the Daśaharā in Jyeṣṭha,
the twelfth day of the dark fortnight of Āṣāḍha, and the new moon of Śrāvaṇa—
these are the festivals of the Goddess; a wise man should perform them during the half of the night.
Having performed the worship according to the prescribed rule, one obtains the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice.
Regarding this, the Tantrikas maintain that wherever no specific [time] is heard, the bright fortnight (śukla-pakṣa) alone is to be accepted. In the Yāmala:
"In the month of Vaiśākha, on the first lunar day (pratipad) of the bright fortnight, it is certain."
Having risen during the Brāhma-muhūrta and performed his daily obligatory rites, the wise man—
When the sun has half-risen, one should worship one's chosen deity;
having offered the *arghya*, one should personally drink the remainder along with one's consort according to one's capacity.
The practitioner, being self-restrained, should recite the mantra one thousand and eight times;
having performed this every day until such a day arrives, he should do so again on the new moon day.
The mantra-practitioner, skilled in the conduct of the samaya, should consume the śaktis and worship them according to the prescribed rite; thus he obtains his desired fruit.
One should worship according to the prescribed method at midday or in the evening;
or the mantra-practitioner may recite it during the three junctions of the day and shall attain the desired accomplishment.
In the month of Māgha, during the bright fortnight, on the first lunar day (pratipad), the practitioner,
having performed the evening twilight worship and having abstained from food during the day, [should proceed].
When the moon has risen, as before, the wise practitioner, with undistracted mind, should worship the Goddess;
he should recite the root mantra until the setting of the moon.
In this manner, the wise man should perform [the rite] every day until the fourteenth day;
on the full moon day, the discerning one should complete it as before.
In the same way, one of vast intellect should perform [the rites] during the dark fortnight;
he is liberated from all sins and shall attain his desired success.
Then, on the first day of the bright fortnight of the month of Ūrja, one devoted to the vow [should prepare] an excellent vessel filled with water within a Sarvatobhadra mandala.
Having established the water-pot there, one should place a bronze vessel;
one should kindle a lamp here with an excellent, thick wick.
Having meditated thus, the wise practitioner of worship should honor the Great Goddess with lamps;
he should recite the family mantra more than a thousand times.
Having performed this until such a day, then on the new moon day,
one should carry out the remainder as before and shall attain the desired accomplishment.
On a Friday, having summoned Viśālākṣī— the beautiful woman, exuberant in her youth,
radiant with a profusion of flowers, and lovely in every limb—
Having worshipped her, the practitioner should bathe her according to the procedure for anointing;
she is clothed in beautiful saffron garments and adorned with various ornaments.
Endowed with the state of being the deity, he should seat her upon a divine throne.
Having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) upon her body and having invoked the deity into her nose,
the practitioner, with a mind free from modification, should recite the mantra a thousand times before her.
The practitioner should offer the recitation (japa) to her, and having dismissed the Goddess,
he should spend the night with her in various delightful enjoyments.
Thus, whoever performs worship with devotion on a Friday shall attain all perfections; there is no need for hesitation in this matter.
In the Kulārṇava: "He who, though capable, out of delusion does not construct the Śrīcakra on the special festival days, shall become a beast (paśu) for the Yoginīs."

Thus, even the mention of a fruit in certain instances does not contradict its status as being occasional (*naimittika*). For even though the fruit "Indra becomes one with ten crores of matted locks" is mentioned, the ritual bathing during a planetary eclipse is established as occasional elsewhere as well, since the traditional teaching regarding the sin incurred by non-performance is no different [in those cases]. As stated in the *Nīlatantra*:
On the eighth and fourteenth lunar days, one should worship with diligence;
whatever the practitioner of mantra (mantrī) prays for, that he obtains constantly.
One obtains a charming voice; thus, one should always worship on the eighth day.
Worship of the Goddess on the eighth day bestows the fruit of all desires.
Having mixed together the rambhā flower, the bījapūra fruit, and fragrant substances,
one should offer the bali, especially on the eighth lunar day.

It destroys the sin accumulated by a twice-born man at that very moment. Likewise: "Wherever the goddess Tāriṇī resides in the form of Śivā, one should go there with effort; the measure of its merit is not known."
The mantra-practitioner should recite the mantra two hundred thousand times where Tāriṇī resides;
with a mind that is free from desire and steady, success is attained at that very moment.
And the clay that has been gathered, as well as unbroken grains of rice,
honey, milk-rice, milk, clarified butter, and sugar.
One should offer the bali-oblation with a monitor lizard and wine is highly praised;
the most excellent knower of mantras should offer the flower of the plantain tree and the śāla-fish as oblations.
Having attained all accomplishments in succession, one shall finally attain liberation;
one should offer a thousand oblations of bilva leaves together with unbroken grains of rice.
On the great eighth day (mahāṣṭamī), the practitioner obtains charming speech.
In the *Triśaktiratna*: "On the full moon days of the months beginning with Caitra, the best of practitioners should worship Mahāśivā according to the procedure to be described."
O Śivā, having performed the daily worship, one should worship [the deity] with *damanaka* flowers in the month of Caitra,
using blossoms produced in spring mixed with sandalwood and agallochum.
In the month of Vaiśākha, one should worship the beloved of Śaṅkara with golden lotuses or red sandalwood, and with all cooling offerings.
In the month of Jyeṣṭha, one should worship the Goddess with jackfruit, plantains,
and delightful mangoes for the sake of attaining all desires and goals.
In the month of Āṣāḍha, one should worship the Great Śivā with sandalwood and flowers,
as well as with lovely cardamom, cloves, and kakkola.
In the month of Śrāvaṇa, one should worship the Supreme Goddess with sacred threads;
this is known as the Pavitrāropaṇa, as well as the Damanaka festival.
The best of practitioners should know from my *Tantraśekhara* that in the month of Bhādrapada, the beloved of Śaṅkara is to be worshipped with *ketakī* flowers.
In the month of Āśvina, the wise practitioner should perform the sacrifice beginning from the new moon (darśa) until the full moon.
Day by day, the mantra-reciter should offer oblations in increasing numbers—one hundred each day.
He should celebrate a great festival and shall attain all perfections (siddhis).
In the month of Kārttika, the practitioner should worship with saffron and offer lamps soaked in ghee into the fire at midnight.
The wise one should offer sixteen ghee-lamps before the Goddess with the Vidyā-mantra;
he should also offer one to each member of the retinue.
Alternatively, having established one [liṅga] in the center, the practitioner of mantra should offer nine [more] around it to the Goddess,
preceded by the recitation of the root mantra.
In the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, while reciting the mantra, one should offer camphor mixed with coconut water, accompanied by delightful offerings of black gram cakes.
In the month of Pauṣa, having worshipped Maheśvarī with jaggery and sugar,
the practitioner should offer cow’s milk for the attainment of his own desired success.
In the month of Māgha, having worshipped the Goddess with sesame seeds, one should offer cakes and milk;
in Phālguna, one should worship the Goddess with [offerings] made of gold or silver.
With lotuses, mango blossoms, and likewise with various other offerings;

the sacred thread (*pavitra*) consists of a cord made of silk cloth and the like, provided with knots. Its ritual procedure shall be described. In cases where no specific lunar day (*tithi*) for a month is mentioned, the worship and so forth should commence on the full moon (*paurṇamāsī*) itself, according to the context. This is to be performed every year.
The Damanotsava is mandatory.
As stated in the Jñānārṇava: "If a practitioner of mantra does not worship with damana during the course of a year, his worship for that entire year shall be dedicated to the damana."
Likewise: "I shall now describe the offering of *damanaka* flowers for the benefit of practitioners;
for, O beloved, a worship performed throughout the year would not be complete [without it]."
In the Mahākālasaṃhitā:
"One is called the offering of *damanaka* flowers, and the other is the offering of the sacred thread (*pavitrāropaṇī*).
The practitioner who does not perform these every year [is deficient]."
O beautiful lady, the worship performed for him throughout the year becomes fruitless;
even when it has been performed, the hosts of bhūtas, pretas, and other spirits plunder it.
Therefore, every year the practitioner should diligently perform the rite of offering the *damanaka* flower,
as well as the rite of offering the sacred thread (*pavitrāropaṇa*).
Regarding the time for worship, the *Dakṣiṇāmūrtisaṃhitā* states:
"The three months beginning with Caitra, and the two fortnights— the bright and the dark— among these,
each preceding one is the most excellent of all times."
In the *Mahākālasaṃhitā*:
"The primary time for that [rite] is considered to be the bright fortnight of the month of Madhu;
Mādhava (Vaiśākha) is the middling, Jyeṣṭha is the next, and Śuci (Āṣāḍha) is said to be the lowest."
If one of evil intent performs the Dāmana rite when the Cāturmāsya has commenced, he attains no success; rather, the opposite occurs.
Ghosts and spirits, their bellies tormented by hunger, dance about.
281) If, by the turn of our fortune, some inferior practitioner should perform the rite of offering the *damanaka* flower while Janārdana is asleep, [he would incur great sin].
"Then we would plunder and devour that offering;
therefore, one should perform this rite during spring, winter, or summer,
but never during the rainy season, autumn, or the cold season, O beloved."
Therefore, one who desires to bring about the pleasure of the Goddess should perform the worship with *damanaka* during the three seasons previously mentioned, and not during the other three seasons.
Likewise: the constellation Uttara-phalgunī, the thirteenth lunar day, the bright fortnight, the month of Caitra, and the yoga Vṛddhi.
Likewise: "This lunar day shall be known by the name Anaṅgā after your own name;
those who worship you on this day with an abundance of perfumes, flowers, and other offerings [shall attain their desires]."
With offerings of food, incense, lamps, and the like; with songs, instrumental music, and dances;
with the employment of very graceful words; and with the consumption of intoxicating substances.
With chatter involving words such as "vagina" and "phallus," which provoke laughter,
and with speech concerning various forms accompanied by great festivities;
"You shall grant them their desired boons; remember my words.
On the following day, let the worship of Makaradhvaja be performed extensively by me."
In the Dakṣiṇāmūrtisaṃhitā:
"On the eighth, or the fourteenth, or even on the full moon day,
one should perform the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana) either during the first part of the night or immediately."
In the *Mahākālasaṃhitā*:
"One should perform the formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*) which is a constituent part of the rite of consecration (*adhivāsana*),
having declared the current position of the zodiacal sign, lunar day, and so forth."

Having made the formal resolve (saṅkalpa): "For the sake of concluding the annual worship, I shall perform the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana), which is an auxiliary part of the ritual to be performed tomorrow for the offering of the *damanaka* flower," one should worship the five deities (pañcāyatana).
In the *Dakṣiṇāmūrtisaṃhitā*: "Having first addressed the *damana* [plant] with the four *Kalpalatā* mantras and others...
The mantra of the four *Kalpalatās* is as follows: oṃ hrīṃ hraṃ kheṃ cache kṣastrīṃ hūṃ kṣeṃ hrīṃ phaṭ | oṃ hrīṃ aiṃ hrīṃ oṃ sarasvatyai namaḥ | hrīṃ śrīṃ klīṃ drāṃ drīṃ klīṃ ||
Clūṃ Saḥ!
O you who are born from the eye of Kāma and drenched by the water from the eyes of Rati;
O deluder of the ṛṣis, gandharvas, and siddhas, homage be to you!
"By the command of Śiva, you must be led away after having been severed for the sake of an auspicious rite.
Having thus addressed Kāma, the wise one should worship Śiva there.

Even by a lay practitioner (*upāsaka*), no modification (*ūha*) should be made to the mantra in the place of the word "Śiva," because it is stated specifically in the *Śaktitantra* that one should worship one's own chosen deity (*sveṣṭadevatā*). The mention of "Śiva" is merely illustrative. Now follows the rite of consecration (*adhivāsana*).

In the *Mantramuktāvalī*: "On the preceding day, having become self-restrained, the practitioner of mantra should go to the grove of *damanaka* plants, where the *aśoka* tree is established, accompanied by the sounds of musical instruments."
Having sat there upon an auspicious seat and worshipped with the mantra,
the knower of mantras should bow to his guru, Gaṇeśa, and his own chosen deity.

Having performed the ritual identification of his own self with all the deities (*sakalīkṛtya*), the wise one, the best among those who know the mantras, should establish the water-pot (*kalaśa*) and the *vardhanī* vessel according to the prescribed rite.

Having offered the bali-oblation to the spirits and having caused those [obstacles] to depart, the knower of mantras should worship the Aśoka tree there, or, in its absence, create a substitute for it.
Then, having adorned the mandala with sandalwood paste, fruits, and flowers, one should worship Kāla right there; or, in his absence, having fashioned an image of him.
Then, having adorned the mandala with sandalwood, fruits, and flowers, one should worship Kāla and Vasanta there according to the prescribed ritual.
Afterward, having subdued it with the Aghora-vidyā and sprinkled it with water,
one should protect it with the Astra-mantra and veil it with the Kavaca-mantra.
Then, having formed the trident mudrā, one should whirl it over the *damanaka* plant;
one should properly perform a vigil at night with dancing, singing, and other such activities.

The *vardhanī* is a small water-vessel, that is to say, a *karaka*. Its placement should be done in immediate contact with the *kumbha*, according to the instruction: "One should place it touching the *kumbha* without any interval. The offering of the *bali* to the spirits (*bhūta*) should be performed with this mantra: *hrīṃ trīṃ sarvavighnakṛdbhyaḥ sarvabhūtebhyo hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*.
The mantra for their removal is found in that very same place:
"May those beings who cause heresy, whether they dwell on the earth, in the intermediate space,
or reside in the world of mortals, perish by the command of Śiva."

The protective rite (*rakṣā*) consists of the consecration (*abhiṣeka*) itself with the water from the *vardhanī* vessel. The Aghora mantra is as follows: "Oghore ghore hrīṃ, Oghoraghoratare śrīṃ, to all you who are everywhere, to all those who possess the form of Rudra, obeisance to you! Hrīṃ śrīṃ. Regarding the trident mudrā (*triśūlamudrā*), it is described in the *Śivarahasya*: "Having joined the tip of the little finger with the thumb..."
One should extend the remaining three fingers; this is proclaimed as the mudrā named Triśūla (the Trident).
Then one should uproot the *damana* plant. For it is said in the *Dakṣiṇāmūrtisaṃhitā*:
"O Goddess, having oneself uprooted the *damana* together with its roots and sprouts, or else having had it brought by another, or purchased and brought, [one should use it]."
O Goddess, one should place it to the left in the *sarvatobhadra* lotus;
then, on the eighth petal, one should place the *dāmana* vessel and worship it.
O Bhuvaneśānī, "Praṇavaṃ bhuvaneśāni rataye namaḥ" is the mantra of Rati; O Maheśānī, it is likewise called the mantra of Kāma.
One should worship Madana, situated in the pericarp, there with the mantra: "Oṃ, Kāmabīja, and Kāmāya namaḥ."
Then, one should worship in sequence upon the petals starting from the east of that lotus,
using the eight groups of mantras for the eight directions, accompanied by the eight substances.
Kāma, Bhasmaśarīra, Anaṅga, Manmatha,
as well as he whose name is Vasantasakha, and Smara, who wields a bow made of sugarcane.
