Puṣpabāṇa, Tārā, and the others are proclaimed to end with the seed-syllable *ṅe* and the heart-mantra (*hṛd*).
Then, O Dear One, there is camphor, the two types of *rocanā*, and musk.
O Pārvatī, the eight substances consist of agallochum, saffron, emblic myrobalan, and sandalwood, combined with fragrant flowers.
Having properly worshipped Madana with perfumes, flowers, unbroken grains, and other offerings, one should,
with a tranquil mind, recite the Anaṅga-gāyatrī according to one's ability.
Having said "to Kāmadeva," one should then say "vidmahe";
having said "to Puṣpabāṇa," one should then say the word "dhīmahi."
May there be the Anaṅga-gāyatrī: "May Anaṅga impel us.
Salutations be to the one with flower-arrows, who brings joy to the world.
O Goddess, one should thereafter offer salutation with this mantra: "To Manmatha, the eye of the world, and to him who is dear to Rati and Prīti."
Then, holding the *damana* plant in his hand, he should make this request to the Goddess:
"O Śivā, O Mistress of the Gods, you have been invited by me at this very moment."
And according to your command, the full festival should be performed as resources permit;
one should propitiate Tripurā with the mantra known as the *Vijñāpanā*.
284) Thereafter, one should worship the Goddess with perfumes, flowers, unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), and so forth;
having offered the food oblation (*naivedya*) according to the rules, one should then pray to Śrīvidyā.
O Mother of the World, bestower of the fruits of desired objects,
O Goddess, Sovereign of Kāmeśvara, fulfill my heart’s desires residing within my chest.
With this, one should pray to the Goddess; thereafter, O Sovereign Lady, one should perform the *damanaka* rite.
One should veil it with the left hand and protect it well with the *astra-mantra*.
Then one should perform the vigil (*jāgaraṇa*), provided that a vigil has not already been performed on that very day.
Even in the case of bringing another *damanaka* plant, its uprooting must be performed first;

for the phrase "the site of the *damanaka*" (*damanasthalīm*) and so forth denotes merely the location where the *damanaka* stands. However, if the *damanaka* grove were situated nearby, then the uprooting would take place in that very spot as previously described—this is the distinction.

The grammatical construction is: "in an eight-petaled lotus in the Vasvāra [direction]. One desiring sexual pleasure (*ratikāma*) should worship [there], in accordance with the subsequent text. "A pair of *rocanās*" refers to both *gorocanā* (cow-gallstone) and *vaṃśarocanā* (bamboo-resin). "Tripurā" and "Śrīvidyā"—both of these are *upalakṣaṇas* (metaphorical indications), because this rite is prescribed for all [of them] and thus the requirement [for the mantra] is equal. [This applies to] the sixteen-syllable [mantra].

In such mantras as these, when performing the worship of goddesses distinct from Śrīvidyā, the phrase "consisting of sixteen syllables" (*ṣoḍaśārṇe*) should be replaced by the phrase "in all forms" (*sarvarūpe*). Now follows the ritual duties for the day of worship.
In the Mahākālasaṃhitā:
"Then, having risen at dawn and performed one's own daily rites,
and having prepared the materials for worship, one should enter the pavilion of worship."
O Goddess, one should indeed cause the images, temples, and so forth to be brilliantly illuminated;
thereafter, one should perform the formal resolve (saṅkalpa) in their presence.
One should also write: "I shall perform the rite of offering the *damanaka* flower.
In the *Dakṣiṇāmūrtisaṃhitā*:
"Then, having risen in the morning, one should indeed perform the daily worship."
Then one should perform the ritual of signs and worship Damana well.

The *naimittika* [rite] to be described hereafter consists primarily of the worship of one’s chosen deity (*iṣṭadevatā*). Although the worship of *damanaka* flowers is heard of after that, nevertheless, because the *damanaka* itself is not a deity, its worship is to be undertaken as a consecration (*saṃskāra*) of the *damanaka* intended for use in the primary worship; therefore, it occurs at the very beginning.
Therefore, its practice is appropriate, because it has sequence as its intended meaning. For this very reason, it is stated exactly thus in the *Jñānārṇava*:
"One should perform the subduing (*damana*) in nine ways; thereafter, one should worship."
Then, O beautiful one, with the seed-syllable of Ānandeśvara, which is distinct [from the previous], [one should perform the rite].
One should worship Damana in sequence, ninefold with the seed-syllable of Ānandeśvarī together with the Bindu, differentiated by the nine modes.
Having performed a great and enchanting worship according to the rules in the center, mixed with those flowers, he offered excellent food-oblations (naivedya).
Then, having offered betel-leaf with camphor, one should pray:
"O Mistress of all circles, you who embody all vidyās!"
"O Mother of the Vedas, let this which is desired by me be fulfilled by your command.
Then, having honored his own guru with flowers, garments, perfumes, and other offerings, he [proceeded].
Having given the *damanaka* flower to him, prostrated, and propitiated him,
one should then joyfully engage in water-sports together with the initiates (*samayins*).
Beforehand, one should perform a gift-rite endowed with the six flavors;
thus the wise man performs the planting of the *damanaka* in due order.
His annual worship shall be presided over by Śrīvidyā.

Regarding the two previously mentioned mantras of Ānandeśvara and Ānandeśvarī, they possess nine syllables through the separation of the final vowel [from the preceding consonant]. Herein, the specific feature is the application of the anusvāra to all the syllables. And the worship is first...

It should be performed with the syllables of the Bhairava-mantra and the syllables of the Bhairavī-mantra ending in *namaḥ*; such is the tradition (*sampradāya*). First in the center and then proceeding clockwise starting from the east, because it is seen so in the worship of Kāma. "The center" refers to the eight-petaled lotus previously drawn.

It should be mixed with those flowers and *damanaka* flowers; for it is heard in the subsequent statement that the worship of the chosen deity (*iṣṭadevatā*) consists precisely in such a prayer. This very worship is the primary rite.
As stated in the *Mahākālasaṃhitā*:
And the worship of Śakti must be performed after the offering of the *damanaka* flower;
O beloved, if it is done beforehand, everything becomes fruitless.
Furthermore, if the worship of Śakti is not performed, it likewise becomes fruitless;
therefore, the worship of Śakti should be carried out after the offering of the *damanaka* flower.

Likewise: "Having worshipped with *damana* in the month of Caitra, and having worshipped Kālikā with that [flower], one is liberated from the sins committed in seven lifetimes; there is no doubt in this matter."

On the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, having performed the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana) and having placed the *damana* plant [upon the image], one should worship Durgā according to this rite.
O lady of excellent hips, hear now the fruit of merit from what I have spoken,
which is equal to that of a thousand horse-sacrifices and a hundred Rājasūya sacrifices.
Having fully attained that fruit, he rejoices in heaven like a god.
(286) Likewise: "O beautiful one, for him who performs this worship known as the 'offering of *damanaka*,' no calamities ever arise."
His mantras shall be successful, he shall become beloved by women,
endowed with all prosperity, illustrious, and he rejoices in heaven like a god.
Thus concludes the ritual for the offering of *damanaka* flowers.
Now follows the offering of the *pavitra* (sacred thread);
this is obligatory every year. Regarding this, there is the statement of Īśvara in the *Dakṣiṇāmūrtisaṃhitā*:
Now, O Maheśānī, I shall describe the great Pavitrāropaṇa rite;
when this is performed, everything is accomplished, otherwise it is said to be void.
When a year has passed, if one does not perform the *pavitraka* rite,
the fruit of all their merits is forcibly carried away by evil spirits.
The time [for initiation] is also stated in that very same place:
"O Dear One, the month of Āṣāḍha is the best, Śrāvaṇa is middling, and the month of Bhādrapada is inferior; as for the fortnights, both the bright and the dark are suitable."
The bright fortnight is recommended; in its absence, the other (the dark fortnight) may be used. One should indeed perform sacrifice on the fourteenth, eighth, and full-moon days.
Also in the Mahākālasaṃhitā:
"O Dear One, summer, autumn, and the rainy season—this is the most excellent time.
Some wise ones desire spring as the intermediate time."
Neither the winter nor the cool season are ever recommended for this.
Likewise: "That [garment] should be known as made of cotton, or of hemp, or likewise of silk. And likewise: "The thread is prepared with nine strands; it is declared to have nine strands."
For that, O beautiful one, resides within the parts of the phonemes.
That very same scripture, when multiplied many times over in the throats of the gods,
is called by the name "Pavitra" (the Purifier) in the Vedas and other sacred texts.
Likewise: "O Sovereign of the Gods, the threads and syllables differ according to the different traditions;
in the two eastern halves the thread is white, and in the northern half it is red."
In the west it is yellow, and in the south it is considered to be below;
the thread should never be dyed blue in any of the six Āmnāyas.
Furthermore, in all the traditional scriptures, a thread that is white or even praised as such,
spun by a young maiden, brings about great excellence.
That which is prepared by a woman whose husband is living is of middling quality; that prepared by a widow is inferior.
That which is prepared by the wives of those born of the Brāhmaṇa, Kṣatriya, or Vaiśya castes is pure.
That which is offered by Śūdra women is said to be indeed impure;
for it is especially forbidden for these [women] when they are deprived of their husbands.
Others have declared that thread spun by a Vaiśya woman is pure;
or else [it may be spun] by a washerwoman, or by one who works with mechanical devices, or by one whose garments are dyed saffron.
If it is fashioned by a *gopī*, or by a shaven-headed woman (*muṇḍinī*), or by a garland-maker (*mālinī*),
the practitioner will go to hell because of that thread and the *japa*-purifier.
Therefore, one must especially exert effort in the preparation of the thread.

That which is taken by a woman of middling [status] is said to be the best for men; that which is taken by a eunuch (ṣaṇḍāha) would be of inferior quality. The lunar day (tithi) should be one free from the "empty" (riktā) days;
that too should be taken on an auspicious lunar day (bhūtatithi), as well as the fourth day and when it falls on a Tuesday.
On Sunday, the seventh lunar day (saptamī) should be avoided; on Thursday as well, the Riktā days should be avoided.
No lunar day (tithi) here should be abandoned if it is conjoined with Mars;
indeed, by its conjunction with an auspicious asterism (puṇyanakṣatra), an abundance of fruit is produced.
Tāniṣṭha, Jīva, Dinakṛt, Viṣṇu, and likewise Nirṛti—
among these [nakṣatras], on either the previous day or again on the following day, [the rite should be performed].
In the Dakṣiṇāmūrtisaṃhitā: "The sacred thread (paṭṭasūtra) should be made of silk or likewise of cotton;
having tripled it and then folded it three times, one should wash it with pure water."
Then, one should purify [the area] with mantras originating from the western and southern [faces];
thereafter, one should have beautiful purificatory offerings (pavitra) prepared with mantras.
One hundred and eight is the best, half of that is the middling, O Dear One, and half of that again is the lowest; one should perform it according to one's capacity.
One should cause ten knots to be made with the mantras recited for the northern [face];
O Adrijā, one should decorate them with saffron and other substances in various ways.

O Supreme Goddess, one should perform the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana) on the day before the day of offering the purifiers (pavitra), or one may perform the immediate consecration (sadyo'dhivāsana) after the daily worship and other rites,
together with the initiates (samayins) at night.
288) Having laid out the lines to the left with mantras associated with the upward-facing lion-thrones,
one should perform protection and the veiling [of the site] by means of the weapon and armor mantras.
A tooth-stick, as well as fragrant substances, ashes, sandalwood, clay,
white mustard seeds, and likewise the fruit of the dhātrī and that which comes from the vakula tree.
For the sake of attaining success, one should sequentially place [the substances] from the vessel containing the purifying thread into pipal-leaf bowls in the directions starting with the east.
Kumāra, Soma, Svāhā, Īśa, Brahmā, Nāga, Śikhidhvaja,
Sūrya, Sadāśiva, and Śarva are the nine deities.
In the Sūtras, one should worship Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Īśa on the triple-thread;
[the mantras] Kriyā, Pauruṣī, Vīrā, Gāyatrī, and Aparājitā.
Vijayā and the goddess Jayā, Muktidā and Sadāśivā,
Manonmanī as the ninth, and Sarvatomukhī as the tenth.
One should worship the deities residing in the knots, honoring them with ritual offerings;
O Goddess of gods, one should likewise meditate upon the sixteen Nityās and Śrīvidyā, O beloved.

The passage beginning with "arising from the western face" (*paścimāsyodgataiḥ*) and so forth pertains specifically to the Śrīvidyā. However, in this context, one should perform the cleansing either with the root mantra or silently. Kumāra is Sanatkumāra; Śikhidhvaja is Guha.
Even the worship of the sixteen Nityās pertains specifically to the Śrīvidyā. As stated in the Mahākālasaṃhitā:
As many deities as there are, whether in the permanent or occasional rites,
and those who are the retinues and attendants associated with the five shrines—
For that which is required by all in this sacred rite is as follows:
with palms joined in reverence, one should utter this verse in the form of a mantra.
Because of your excellent counsel regarding the performance of Vedic sacrifices, you have attained the name of "cotton-thread.
Having fashioned many sacred threads from you, I shall offer them to the immortals, purified by the thread of worldly existence.
In the Dakṣiṇāmūrtisaṃhitā: "What is called 'adhivāsa' (preparation) shall follow;
after the daily worship, this occasional rite (naimittika) takes place."
In the Mahākālasaṃhitā:
"Then the wise one should begin the occasional worship.
Likewise: "An abundance of food offerings, incense, and lamps should be provided."
The teachers should diligently ensure that their respective groups are not to be neglected;
furthermore, an archway made of flowers should be constructed both outside and inside the house.
In the Dakṣiṇāmūrtisaṃhitā: "One should give various [gifts] to the *samayins* and food to those who are like gold;
one should worship one’s own guru with devotion by means of garments, ornaments, cows, and wealth."
Having paid homage according to the prescribed rite, one should contemplate [the deity] in the form of the Goddess;
then, free from stinginess regarding wealth, one should fasten the sacred thread (pavitra).
Wherever the Guru is worshipped, that action shall become fruitful;
if he is not worshipped there, that ritual act shall be fruitless.
In the absence of the guru, one should worship his son; in his absence, his wife;
or in the absence of a wife, another person born of the guru’s lineage.
Having performed the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti), one should afterwards offer the purifying thread (pavitraka) into the fire;
one should worship the Siddhā in the center of the Śrīcakra and present it as an offering.
In the Mahākālasaṃhitā:
"O fair-faced one, at whatever time of worship may occur for whichever deity, for that very deity at that very time [the rite should be performed]."
The purifying thread (pavitra) should be given to him preceded by the recitation of its mantra;
likewise, goats must necessarily be offered in the ritual of the bali-oblation.
In the Tantra: "One should perform the daily worship by day; the occasional (naimittika) worship should take place at night.
Thus ends the procedure for the investiture of the sacred thread (pavitrāropaṇa). Now follows the worship of the seat (pīṭhārcana).
In the *Kulacūḍāmaṇi*: "If, by chance, one's path should lead to a mountain, a forest, a deserted place, an empty pavilion, a crossroads, or the midst of a marketplace..."

Having meditated upon the *kula*, recited the mantra, and bowed, one should depart as one pleases—whether in the midst of a *kalā* or among women. Here, *kula* refers to the chosen deity (*iṣṭadevatā*). Furthermore, if during the time of the preparatory rite (*puraścaraṇa*) there should be a vision of a sacred seat (*pīṭha*), [one should act accordingly].
At that time, the worship of the sacred seat (pīṭhapūjā) there is not neglected even in thought.
The highly fortunate Devī at Devīkūṭa, Bhairavī at Oḍḍiyāna,
Yoganidrā at Kāmarūpa, and Mahiṣāsuramardinī [at Jalandhara].
One should worship Kātyāyanī, who is known as Kāmā, the bestower of desires, in Kāmabhūmi; Pūrṇeśī in Jālandhara; Caṇḍikā on Mount Pūrṇa;
and Kāmarūpā, who carries the directions, in Cauhāra.
Or else, if by good fortune there is a sight of one who can assume any form at will;
Then, the worship of the goddesses Bhaga and the others is performed there.
Likewise: "First, the best of practitioners, having drawn the previously mentioned yantra on the summit of Devīkūṭa, should worship it according to the Kula path."
In the first [circle], one should worship the goddess Pīṭhā and others with perfumes and flowers;
then, the highly fortunate Root Goddess (Mūladevī) together with her attendants.
Having recited [the mantra] one hundred thousand times there, one should then enter Oḍḍiyāna;
having worshipped the one called Yoganidrā at that sacred seat (pīṭha), one should then perform sacrifice.
With a concentrated mind, one should recite the mantra of one's chosen deity one hundred thousand times;
then, having gone to Kāmarūpa, one should worship Kātyāyanī.
Having recited [the mantra] one hundred thousand times, one should first worship Kāmākhyā at the navel;
then, having gone to Jālandhara, one should first worship Pūrṇeśī.
There too, having recited the mantra one hundred thousand times with a concentrated mind,
one should then go to Pūrṇagiri, worship Caṇḍī, and thereafter perform the recitation.
O child, within Kāmarūpa one should first worship Kāmākhyā;
and at its edge, O Great Goddess, one should worship Dikkaravāhinī.
Having thus worshipped the Mistress of the Seats (Pīṭheśvarī) and honored one’s chosen deity,
one should, with a concentrated mind, recite [the mantra] seven hundred thousand times at night across the seven seats.
Kāmarūpa is the supreme among sacred seats (pīṭhas), yielding great fruit;
O Maheśvara, whatever worship is performed there, even but once—
Having abandoned all other seats, I dwell within his body;
therefore, the Kāmākhyā-yonimaṇḍala is said to be a hundred times more excellent than that.

Now, regarding the worship of the maiden (*kumārīpūjā*), it is stated in the *Mahākālasaṃhitā*: "The Goddess (*Śivā*) is not so pleased by offerings (*bali*), fire-oblations (*homa*), hymns (*stuti*), or recitations (*araṇa*) as she is by [the worship of] a maiden."
Just as she becomes instantly pleased here through the worship of a maiden.
One should not only worship her, but also feed her with diligence. It is proclaimed that through the non-performance of worship, one suffers from physical deformity;
yet through its performance, one attains completeness of limb, even if other [prescribed rites] have not been performed. (291)

Likewise: "For the Kaulas, worship is prescribed at night; for those following the Smṛtis, it is in the afternoon. However, the daily worship is performed in autumn; that for specific desires is occasional, and any other is for special occasions."
The characteristics of the maiden: she has bathed well, wears garments bright with various colors such as yellow and red,
her body is adorned with all manner of ornaments, and she is unaware of the movements of the god of love.
A girl who has not yet developed attachment to men, aged seven, eight, or nine years,
of non-low birth, fair-limbed, and whose father and mother are still living.
One who has no protruding teeth, whose teeth are not uneven, who lacks no limb,
whose hair is not long, who is radiant, whose face bears a beautiful smile, and who is free from greed.

The characteristics of a censurable maiden: one who is dark-complexioned, has long teeth, eyes like those of a female jackal, and tawny hair; one who is thin, of slow gait, wrathful, humpbacked, lame, or suffering from cramps.
One should carefully avoid a woman who has sparse eyebrows and hair, who has a discharging ulcer, and whose breasts have begun to secrete the menses, for she is like the bodiless god of love.
A maiden other than these, however, is to be chosen in the sequence of worship.
In the *Yāmala*: "The practitioner who worships a maiden at all festivals and at all times—by him the Great Goddess is truly worshipped; this is the truth, the truth, there is no doubt."
Sandhyā is declared to be one year old, Sarasvatī two years,
Tridhāmūrti three years, and Kālikā four years.
This Umā is five years old and is called Subhagā; she becomes six years old and is Mālinī; at seven years she is Mālinī; and at eight years she is considered Kubjikā.
Nine years old she is Kālasaṅkarṣā; ten years old she is Aparājitā;
eleven years old she is Rudrāṇī; and twelve years old she is Bhairavī.
Mahālakṣmī is devoted to that; the Kulanāyikā is devoted to that;
the Kṣetrajñā is said to be devoted to that; and Caṇḍikā is sixteen years of age.
In this manner, the maiden should be understood [as the deity] in sequence, even without flowers.
As stated in the Mahākālasaṃhitā:
"With the sounds of song and musical instruments, preceded by joy and reverence..."
Having led those unmarried maidens to the door of the hall of worship, [he should place them there].
Whether there be five, seven, nine, or even eleven [women],
among them only one should be made the principal, she who is beautiful in all her limbs.
For even in the absence of many, there may be a single maiden;
in rites for desired ends and occasional rites, there is one, but in the autumnal worship, there are many.
Having formed themselves into a row, they stood with their faces bowed;
having first appointed the leader, they were positioned in due order.
Having formed the perception of this [woman] as a goddess, the practitioner, free from haste, intoxicated by the wine he has taken, and having prepared the materials for worship, [should proceed].
Having first performed breath control (prāṇāyāma), one should then perform the expulsion of the elemental beings (bhūtāpasāraṇa).
Then, having bowed to the Guru and Gaṇapati on the left and the right, respectively;
In the center, one should likewise [visualize] the Kumārī, who is the very form of the Root Goddess;
then, by means of finger-snaps and three claps of the hands, one performs the binding of the directions.
Likewise: "Then one should wash the feet of the maiden who is the root;
likewise, one should place that water on the head with the realization that it is the water from the Goddess's feet."
Then, with the upper garment itself, one should offer water for the feet;
thereafter, O beloved, taking up unbroken rice grains (akṣata), one should dispel the obstacles while reciting the mantra,
preceded by three claps of the hands.
First, one should utter the seed-syllable *tāra*, the noose (*pāśa*), the digit (*kalā*), the brush (*kūrca*), and the weapons (*astrāṇi*);
as well as "Drive away the spirits" (*bhūtāny apasāraya*) and "Destroy the obstacles" (*vighnān nāśaya*).
One should place [the mantras] at the heart, the head, and finally [the crown]; this is the twenty-one-syllable mantra.
All [these], together with Kumārī—who is of the very nature of the Goddess—[are to be worshipped].
As many beings as there are of divine origin who come for the sake of seeing [him]—
whether they be pretas, bhūtas, piśācas, gandharvas, or even guhyakas.
Rākṣasas, Dānavas, Yakṣas, and others who perform cruel deeds,
having entered together with the Virgin Goddess into the pavilion for the autumnal worship of Śaradā.
They crush the image of the maiden and destroy the worship;
therefore, O beloved, the expulsion of obstacles must be performed twice.
Then, having taken the maiden’s right hand with his own left hand, preceded by the placing down of his right foot;
Chanting those verses in the form of mantras, he should slowly lead those maidens into the interior of the worship hall, bowing his head.
O primordial one of all the worlds, whose form is the support of the universe,
assume the form of a maiden and enter this house of mine.
"O Mother, I do not know what your true form is;
with my human eyes, I see only this form of a young maiden."
O Śivā, having recognized my devotion to your lotus feet,
you have manifested such a form for the sake of all spiritual perfections.
O Goddess worshipped by the gods, my gaze must not be cast upon sinful things or the path of the wicked; it should be fixed solely upon firm devotion.
Indeed, even Śiva and the others do not know what your true form is;
how then could I, a wretched being with a body composed of the five elements, ever know it?
Thus, O Goddess, reciting these five verses, one should carry [the disciple] across on one's own back,
without even looking at him, preceded by song and instrumental music.
In the *Yāmala*: "Having bathed them with scented oil and adorned them with various ornaments, they should be brought near the deity and installed by the wise practitioner."
In the Mahākālasaṃhitā:
"That worship is declared to be primary, as is its mantra for the primary [deity] alone.
By the worship of that alone, all of them become worshipped; of this there is no doubt."
Likewise: "O Supreme Goddess, having offered the bali-oblation to the divine beings, one should then, free from laziness, begin the supreme Kumārī-nyāsa."
Likewise: "In the beginning, indeed, she is considered Mahācaṇḍayogeśvarī by name;
then Siddhikarālī, and again Siddhivikarālī."
Then Mahantā and Māryathā are to be known as Vajrakāpālinī;
Muṇḍamālinī and Aṭṭahāsinī—these two are thus proclaimed.

One should worship from the first day of the lunar fortnight until the full moon according to the various stages of increase; O Goddess, on the great festival days, one should worship with special offerings and services.
O Goddess of gods, on the Mahānavamī day, one should worship the Kumārīs;
he who is devoted should worship Piṅgalā with sixteen [offerings].
Immediately after [her] is Caṇḍakāpālinī, who is also the sovereign of Kālacakra;
then Guhyakālī, followed by Kātyāyanī together with Kāmākhyā.
294) Cāmuṇḍā, Siddhilakṣmī, and Kubjikā immediately after her; Mātaṅgī is to be known following that, and then Caṇḍeśvarī is proclaimed.
Finally, at the very end of all, Kaumārī; thus these eighteen [deities] have been described.
Likewise: "Next I shall state the limbs—the head, then the face, and after that the two eyes."
The two ears, the nostrils, the two cheeks,
their roots, the lower lip, the rows of teeth, the two shoulders, and the heart as well.
The two arms, the belly, the back, the thighs, the knees,
as well as the shanks, the feet, and every limb— there are just as many spots [for the arrows] as there are parts of the body.

In the *Triśaktiratna*: "The wise practitioner, having seated the maiden upon a divine throne, should worship those [deities] beginning with Kalā and ending with Kalā according to the prescribed rite."
One should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) upon her body according to the procedure to be described hereafter;
the first [syllable] is considered the maiden (kumārikā), and the second is regarded as the heroine (nāyikā).
The third is known as Bhairavī, and the fourth is Vāgīśvarī;
the fifth is declared to be Pālikā. These, beginning with Kula, end in the suffix -buddhi.
Having performed the placement (nyāsa) upon the bodies of the maidens by means of the yoga of five limbs,
one should worship the four faces in succession, following the counter-clockwise order.
Then Siddhā is the first Jayā, another Jayā is Kubjikā, and Kālikā is declared the fifth; these should be understood as awakened.

Conjoined with the eastern face and so forth, ending in the dative case and followed by "namaḥ," they should be deposited in their respective locations according to sequence, using one's own intelligence.
The best of practitioners should perform the previously mentioned network of ritual placements (nyāsa) together with the mantra of consciousness through the union of the five *praṇavas*.
Aiṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Hrīṃ Hūṃ—these are the five praṇavas. Sauḥ is the seed-syllable (bīja) of Caitanyabhairavī. Furthermore, in the Yāmala:
"Bāṇī, Māyā, Lakṣmī, and likewise the two Māyā-kūrca syllables."
And these *praṇavas* are to be known for the worship of the Virgin.
The syllable enriched with the fourteenth vowel [au], followed by Bhṛgu [bha] joined with the bindu and the moon [m],
is declared to be the seed-syllable of consciousness (caitanya-bīja), which brings happiness to practitioners.
In the Mahākālasaṃhitā:
"Then one should perform the placement of the *argha* as prescribed for the daily rite (*nityaka*);
the purification of the articles of worship is also stated to be as previously described."
295) Likewise: "Then one should perform the meditation on the maiden as it will be described below.
Likewise: "Then [one should offer] all the ritual services (*upacāra*), beginning with the water for the feet (*pādya*) and ending with hymns of praise (*stuti*)."

In the *Yāmala*: "Alternatively, they should be worshipped again according to the previously mentioned path or by means of the one that will be described hereafter—using their own names in the dative case, preceded by the three stars (the *Tritārā*) and ending with *namaḥ*."
To the west of the deity, the mantra-practitioner should worship these women endowed with auspicious marks:
the first is Śuddhā Kālikā, and another is remembered as the third, Lalitā.
The fourth is known as Mālinī, the fifth shall be Vasundharā;
Sarasvatī, Ramā, and Gaurī, while Durgā shall be the ninth.
A wise person should worship a child who is five years old or nine years old;
one who is five years old is called Vaṭuka, and one who is nine years old is Gaṇeśvara.
Likewise: one should offer a seat with speech; with modesty, one should present water for the feet;
with *rati*, one should offer the guest-water (*arghya*); and then, with one's wife, one should offer sandalwood paste.
The practitioner of mantra should offer a collection of flowers to the maiden with the seed-syllable of Śakti; he should then place incense, lamps, and other offerings with the Caitanya-mantra.

These are declared to be the Tārās; Bhṛgu accompanied by Bhava, pervaded by Bindu and Nāda, is proclaimed as the Mantra of Consciousness (Caitanya-manu). In some places, however, the fifth is considered to be the seed-syllable of Bhairava, which is the Praṇava.
In the Mahākālasaṃhitā: "Ornaments, fine silken garments, vermilion and lac-dye, as well as collyrium, mirrors, renowned fans made of palm leaves, and a casket."
A grooming cloth, a support-cloth, a small stool, a seat, a hammock,
a doll, a chest, sandals, a rug, and a wooden plank.
The addition of moonlight, as well as a vessel for ointments,
beds, pillows, couches, a casket, and a cosmetic box.
Pratigrāha, Hindolā, and likewise Sīmantavartikā—
[one should meditate upon her] whose lotus-face is serene, whose radiance is like the rising morning sun,
who is clad in red garments, adorned with red garlands, and embellished with various ornaments.
One should meditate upon the youthful maiden, who is smiling, intent on the joy of play with divine maidens, and who grants the fulfillment of the desires of her devotees.
296) Gorocanā, mṛgamada, karpūra, and likewise kuṅkuma.
O Sundarī, other such items as these, as many as possible,
should be given so that the maiden may be satisfied.
Likewise: "Then, the vessel that has been set aside should be presented to the maiden;
she should accept it right there and likewise apply herself with effort."
If that vessel is not accepted, a great fault arises;
therefore, one should exert effort so that it may be accepted in whatever manner possible.
Then, having taken the names of the Kumārī-śaktis along with flowers and unbroken rice grains,
one should worship the fifty Śaktis in their proper sequence upon her body.
I shall now proclaim them; listen with attention:
the first is Jayā, then Vijayā, followed by Ṛddhidā, accompanied by Māyā.
Phalā, Siddhidā, Sūkṣmā, Prabhā, and then Suprabhā;
Vidyutā, Viśuddhi, Nandinī, and Viśuddhiyuk.
Aparājitā, Lalitā, Lakṣmī, and likewise Gaurī;
then Medhā, Gāyatrī, Sāvitrī, and again Svadhā.
Svāhā, Icchā, Kriyā, Vidyā, Prajñā, Dīptā,
Cetanā, Bhadrā, Jyeṣṭhā, Umā, Śivā, Muditā, and Kṣamā.
Then there is Śraddhā, Vimalā, and indeed Viśadā Kaumudī;
then Aśokā, Jñānadā, Baladā, and Rājyadā as well.
Following that are Maitrī, Rudrāṇī, Bhavānī, and also Mṛḍānī;
then Sarvajñā, Caṇḍikā, or Kumārī, who resides at the very end of all.
These fifty maidens are known as the Śaktis;
thereafter, one should worship the eight Bhairavas with unbroken rice (*akṣata*) and other offerings,
and then [worship] the Bhairavīs as well as Vighnas and Vināyakas.
To Vaṭuka and Kṣetrapāla, and likewise to the Yoginīs;
to the Bhūtas, Pretas, Yakṣas, and likewise to the Ḍākinīs.
O Goddess, one should perform worship with flowers, unbroken grains, and sandalwood;
furthermore, O Beloved, at the conclusion of everything, one should worship the eight goddesses ending in the feminine nominative suffix *ṅi*.
Mahāmāyā, Kālarātri, and then indeed Sarvamaṅgalā; thereafter, Ḍamarukā is to be worshipped, and likewise Rājarājeśvarī.
Immediately thereafter is the Goddess Kumārī, the bestower of prosperity.
In the *Yāmala*: "One should worship her within the *kula*; one should worship these [goddesses] in the corners of the *kula*: Kāmeśvarī, Vajreśī, and thirdly, Bhagamālinī."
Above, in the corners of the pair of families, one should worship these:
Anaṅgakusumā, Anaṅgamanmathā, and [Anaṅgamadanā], preceded by Anaṅga.
The fourth [rāgiṇī] begins with the words Madanā and Anaṅgā and ends with Kusumā;
the fifth begins with the words Anaṅgamadanā, Āturā, and Anaṅga.
These powers, numbering six like the [six] tastes, are indeed declared to be cool;
by this method, the Kumārī should be worshipped by the most excellent practitioners.
In the *Mahākālasaṃhitā*:
"Having thus completed the worship of the maiden, one should draw a circular mandala on the ground before her with water, and in its center [place] the beloved of the Kula."
Having drawn [the mandala] with water, flowers, unbroken rice, sandalwood, and nāgakesara,
one should worship that mandala and utter "Homage to Śubhadāyā."
Then, having placed all that food in a vessel,
as well as various kinds of provisions consisting of things to be licked, sucked, and so forth;
Having placed meat, fish, wine, and various kinds of foods and chewables,
along with the right hand of a young maiden, upon the top of the food;
One should offer food with the mantra that will be stated hereafter, spreading it out.
Likewise, one should perform the worship of each of the other maidens individually with perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, and food offerings consisting of cooked rice.
Likewise: "Whatever kinds of food have been prepared for this principal [deity], exactly those same kinds should be given to the others; this is the settled rule."
In this context, the wise man should understand that the primary [result] is the attainment of fruits and non-fruits;
while the young maidens are eating, one should not play the sound of musical instruments.
One should not direct the mind elsewhere nor imagine any obstruction.

The mantra for the casting out of the food offering is as follows: *aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ strīṃ sauṃḥ*, [obeisance] to the Blessed Lady Kumārī, who is the embodiment of all powers and the bestower of all accomplishments.

I offer to you this great sacrificial feast (*naivedya*) of enjoyment, prepared with various kinds of foods and drinks endowed with the six flavors; accept, accept! eat, eat! be gracious, be gracious! grant me all success, grant it! *aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ namaḥ svāhā*.
298) One should suppress clamor and whatever things are inauspicious.
One should carefully avoid the downward-moving wind (apāna-vāyu) that has been stirred by weeping;
one must be vigilant in this matter, for what do those [worms] consume first?
What do they whisper among themselves, or what object do they desire?
Where do they cast their gaze, and what do these frightened women say?
By means of these and other various kinds of movements,
their indications of good or evil fortune should be understood through diligent and careful observation.
While they were thus devouring, he should recite that hymn without haste,
with palms joined and head bowed, casting his gaze upon their mouths.
Hymn to Kumārī: Victory to you, O Kālī, the greatly formidable one, of terrifying roar, the remover of fear;
the flame of the forest fire of worldly existence, the one who carries us across the ocean of misfortune!
O Goddess worshipped by the immortals beginning with Brahmā, Indra, Upendra, and Bhūteśa;
O You who perform the creation, preservation, and destruction [of the world], and who destroy that which is harmful!
O Guhyakālī, whose form is filled with the essence of supreme bliss;
O bestower of the bliss of liberation through the tasting of the essence of the Supreme Brahman!
Though beyond attributes, you possess attributes; O dancer at the end of the great aeon, you assume the form of a maiden, O wise one whose very nature is wisdom.
You have come to my home for the completion of the Śārada rite,
and likewise for the indication of the auspiciousness of the year.
I am blessed, I have accomplished my purpose;
my life is fruitful, since you, having assumed such a supreme youthful form, [have come here].
O Guhyakālī, you have arrived here with the desire to accept the annual worship;
indeed, it was you who were requested by the gods in this very form in the past.
O Goddess of gods, you have bestowed upon me sovereignty and even my desired boons; being well-worshipped today, grant a boon to me as well.
In the past, you bestowed upon Brahmā the power of creation,
and likewise, you alone granted Viṣṇu the capacity for protection.
O Śivā, you bestowed upon Mahārudra the power of universal dissolution,
and also granted the gods proficiency in destroying the Daityas.
299) O Sovereign, you are the inner witness even of those dwelling in the three worlds;
what can I report to you, the sole witness of all actions?
I beg for four boons: the destruction of enemies, the attainment of a kingdom, physical health, and devotion to your lotus feet.
Salutations to you, O Blessed Mother; salutations to you, O you who are affectionate toward your devotees;
salutations to you, whose form is the support of the universe; protect me always.
O Mother, I do not know your form, nor your body, nor your qualities;
with single-minded devotion, I know only your worship through the bhakti residing within my heart.
You are the mother, you are the father, you alone are the kinsman and the Sovereign of the universe;
you are the goal, you are the refuge, you are heaven, and you are indeed liberation itself.
O Mother of the World, having abandoned you, I know no other deity;
salutations to you, salutations to you, salutations to you, salutations again and again.
Thus ends the Kumārīstotra. O fair-faced one, one should perform the praise of the Kumārīs with these verses as the fruit of their worship.
One should indeed offer water for sipping at the conclusion of the meal, acting with promptness.
Then one should offer betel-leaf scented with musk and camphor;
having followed [the recipient] for some distance accompanied by musical instruments and other festivities, one should bid him farewell.
O Pārvatī, I shall now declare to you the fruits of both the auspicious and the inauspicious;
therein, I will first speak of the auspicious, and thereafter its opposite.
Then one should give that remnant to jackals on the ground;
or, O Goddess, having stirred it in water, one should cast it away.
If rice cooked with milk is first placed in the hand, there shall be abundance of food in the realm;
if it is milk-rice (pāyasa), the increase of cattle occurs for the patron.
In ghee there shall be long life and health; for worship, it leads to the increase of sovereignty. Likewise, with sweetmeats and fried cakes, one's progeny shall become abundant.
From fish one gains wealth; from rice-and-sesame porridge, the excellence of vehicles;
from meat, the birth of a son; and from sauce, one shall obtain a beloved woman.
I shall indeed describe the distinct and mixed results of each specific meat:
there is gain of wealth from pork, while victory in battle comes from the flesh of the rhinoceros.
300) By means of buffalo meat, the attainment of a kingdom will certainly occur;
by means of deer meat, health is quickly attained; and by means of black antelope meat, eloquence is gained.
By eating hare-flesh one attains wisdom; by goat-meat, even freedom from old age;
and by eating the flesh of a sheep, O Goddess, one shall obtain every auspicious blessing.
The acquisition of land occurs in the tortoise, and an abundance of food in the deer;
the destruction of enemies in the rhinoceros, and the subjugation of men in the swan.
In the Tittiri there is the attainment of desired goals; in the Vartaka, the destruction of sins;
in the Balakā, satisfaction of the mind; and in the Phalekṣu, mastery over all the world.
Great fame is obtained from curd, and supreme prosperity from milk;
from flour-cakes comes the birth of a son, and from potherbs comes the destruction of enemies.
In *hālā* there shall be an increase in merit; in *coṣya*, prosperity and eloquence;
in *phāṇita*, the arrival of wealth; and in *kūrcikā*, the enhancement of strength.
When a meal is prepared with bottle-gourd, eggplant, pumpkin, bitter melon, snake-gourd,
ghoṣa, śūraṇa, long radish, and turnip;
O Goddess, the attainment of knowledge occurs through *takra* (buttermilk), and eloquence of speech likewise;
moreover, when the substance is prepared from wheat flour, there is inspired intelligence in battle.
Liberation would result from seeing the altar; likewise, there would be elevation [to higher status] from seeing the pavilion, the fly-whisks, the parasol, the palm-leaf fans, and the couches.
Furthermore, when the bell and mirror are presented to the sight, there is the highest attainment;
likewise, when the ornaments and the garland are touched, moved, or seen.
O beloved, various kinds of pleasures arise for the husband;
likewise, there are many such activities and foods.

Listen now to the determination of inauspicious results; from this point on, the opposite of what was previously taught will occur. If the principal maiden vomits two or three times, [the following results arise].
Famine will inevitably arise and the subjects will also be afflicted;
the king meets with destruction when a maiden breaks into tears.
In the case of excrement, there is a great plague; in the case of feces, the burning of the city; from eating nothing, fear of enemies; and from eating too much, calamities.
If one remains silent, there will be ailments; if one speaks too much, there will be calamities;
and through the movement of the hands and feet, various kinds of misfortunes arise.
Excessive modesty leads to ruin, and likewise, shamelessness is inauspicious.
If various portents occur while she is silent, there will be destruction of the arms;
if she is frightened, there is total ruin; and if she is angry, there is indeed death.
Upon possession, the king dies at that very moment; there is no doubt about this.
If she is apprehensive, there is fear of an enemy; if she is exhausted, there is fear of death.
If she is merely thought of, it should be known that the ruin of that very kingdom will follow;
through delusion there shall be loss of wealth, and through dullness worship becomes fruitless.
If there is fickleness, the fortune of the worshipper alone becomes fickle;
furthermore, if the maiden there is possessed by dejection, [the same occurs].
Then, O Pārvatī, the kingdom, along with its ruler and its subjects, falls into decay;
the king dies of disease if the subjects become afflicted by illness.
If there is the terror of famine or pestilence and it sheds tears, then total destruction will occur; but if it shakes its head, [it portends otherwise].
When she is terrified, fear from an enemy is foretold for that king;
when there is trembling, the Supreme Goddess Kālikā becomes averse;
and if she lowers her head, the Mistress is dissatisfied.
If the voice of the Earth-lord becomes faltering, the worshipper shall have a short life;
if she becomes agitated, he shall experience wretchedness.
If she is agitated by delusion, the entire city will be thrown into turmoil;
if she is ashamed, there will be disease; and if there is perspiration, there will be the loss of wife and wealth.
If, by the turn of fate, a maiden releases downward wind,
then that city will be afflicted by a foreign army.
If a maiden there sings a song while devoid of ritual action,
there will be the death of the king, along with his subjects, kingdom, sons, and wife.
If at any time the leader disputes with those who have arrived together,
then a most terrible foreign army will suddenly descend upon him.
Whether with anyone at all or with no one at all,
the maiden shines forth, free from fear and devoid of bashfulness or trepidation.
Then, six calamities arise within his realm if they alter the order of the food by moving their hands. (302)
O beloved, whatever object was offered as a gift to the Goddess in the pavilion, all that which was desired by the mind becomes possessed [by her].
If he touches it with both hands, the king shall become terrified and flee in all directions;
if he extinguishes the lamp with the breath from the mouth of a young maiden, [the same fate awaits him].
In that case, there will be a derangement of the intellect and the lamp of knowledge will perish;
moreover, by the turn of fate, young maidens will dance in a state of intoxication.
The entire kingdom, along with its territory, becomes like a cremation ground if the maidens there cast off their garments and remain naked.
If the king is then held captive by his enemies at the head of the battlefield,
they leap about while hissing and whirl about with their hands clasped.
"An obsession by a spirit will arise in the king; there is no doubt about this.
Thus do the young girls speak when they laugh or utter words.
In that case, at the time of eating, there will be the fear of a great pestilence,
if one looks with a gaze whose pupils are flickering, whether to the left or to the right.
The maiden, fierce with passion, whirls her own head and lets out a loud,
mocking laugh by which men are terrified.
In that case, there would be possession by spirits, or ghosts would be dancing in the city;
he would gnash his teeth against each other and produce a grinding sound.
Accompanied by his wife, sons, and kinsmen, he proceeds to the abode of Death,
having fixed his eyes without blinking and pressing his lips with his teeth.
If a young girl, while preparing [the food], threatens [the practitioner] by striking her head,
that very same result is declared which would occur from the sound of "kaṭakaṭa."
One should maintain silence from beginning to end, not touch the food with the hand, not bend the head too far down, and not scratch the ground with the thumb.
He might draw lines on the ground with his fingernails for no purpose,
or he might scratch his head with both hands joined together.
One might cut grass for no reason,
snap one's fingers, cover the eyes with both hands, or block the two ears.
He may make a "bāhurikā" gesture, rub his heels together, take a mouthful that is too large, or remain with his mouth wide open. (303)
He repeatedly sneezes or yawns over the food,
or having taken the food with his hand, he even throws it in the four directions.
Or, having risen, she moves about, abandoning the food and likewise the worship;
or there may be vomiting for her, as well as horripilation and trembling.
If, upon pus or blood emerging from his body,
he suddenly utters a plaintive cry (kāku) even without an apparent cause, it portends death.
She may utter indecent words, weep for the sake of her own kinsmen,
cast off her ornaments, or say, "I am going home."
Or, standing in that place, she may scold anyone at all,
or she may reproach someone who has approached her together with him.
Whether it be a rift, a cause for conflict, or the loss of one's own hands or strength—
once someone has died, she grieves there for her kinsman.
Whatever a young girl may babble without cause,
all of this should be understood as inauspicious, O you who are worshipped by the thirty gods.
Famine, loss of wealth, disease, and likewise the fear of pestilence;
misfortunes at every step, grief, illness, and the rise of enemies.
There will be the sudden arrival of an enemy army, fire burning the city and the home,
fear of death, poverty, and separation from one's kinsmen.
In every house there will be an obsession with ghosts, spirits, and demons;
and by means of the eight great diseases, the destruction of the people shall occur.
Crows, oppressed by fear, flee hither and thither;
what need of much speaking, O Goddess of gods? A rain-storm shall fall immediately.
But for other kings, there shall be great fear from these [omens];
for good and evil are indeed known through the movements of the maiden.
And the fruit for the king during the rainy season shall be victory or defeat,
death, suffering, fear, happiness, apprehension of enemies, or the increase of power.
The prosperity of the kingdom, the oppression of the subjects, physical deformity, and the destruction of the army—
all this is known from the worship of the Kumārī and even from her meal.
Therefore, O Goddess of the Gods, a king should diligently examine his own welfare and misfortune, especially through worship and by means of food offerings. (304)

When an auspicious birth has occurred, worship for specific desires (kāmyārcā) with abundant materials is appropriate; however, in other cases, it would indeed produce a fault, which one should therefore avoid.
Even if the maiden, having returned to her own home,
departs while afflicted by illness on that very same day, there will still be no auspicious result.
Thus, I have explained in detail the manifold fruits of both the auspicious and the inauspicious; hold this in your heart with diligent effort.
Then, at the hour of midnight, one should again perform the worship according to the rules for both the seat (pīṭha) and the image (mūrti), using incense, lamps, and unguents.
With food offerings, presents, and likewise with songs, instrumental music, and so forth; as stated in the *Yāmala*: "A maiden, when worshipped, destroys the impurity accumulated in the past.
One should know that a young girl is the very embodiment of Prakṛti herself."
If one should offer even a leaf, a flower, a fruit, water, or whatever object is beautiful to a virgin, it is said to yield infinite fruit.
If a maiden is fed, the three worlds are fed;
he who bestows a maiden upon a virtuous Brāhmaṇa has truly fed them all.

He enjoys the merit born from the gift of the earth; of this there is no doubt. He who worships a young maiden attains all perfections (siddhis), for the hosts of Yoginīs dwell constantly within her body.
Therefore, she is to be honored, saluted, and cherished according to her own will.
If he lacks the capacity, the best of practitioners should worship a single maiden;
without the worship of a maiden, he must not let a festival pass by.
He who constantly worships her shall attain the highest accomplishment;
when the nine nights have arrived, he should remain focused until the end of the ninth night at midnight.
Having worshipped a young girl with various offerings according to the ritual for prosperity (*vṛddhi*),
one should perform sacrifice according to the sequence of age and shall attain the desired accomplishment. Alternatively, the practitioner of mantra should worship nine young women.
Hṛllekhā, Gaganā, Raktā, Mahocchuṣmā, and Karālikā.
The practitioner of mantra should worship [the goddess] with the nine names— Ichchhā, Jñānā, Kriyā, and Durgā— as before, and should recite the mantra more than one thousand times.
305) If that playful woman herself becomes agitated, one of sharp intellect should spend the night or the day with her.
One should never touch a maiden with a mind possessed by worldly passion;
otherwise, one meets death, unless the Goddess turns her face away from him.

Thus ends the procedure for the worship of the Kumārī. Now, regarding the Śivā-bali, it is stated in the Kulacūḍāmaṇi: "The practitioner [should perform it] at the root of a bilva tree, in a remote wilderness, or even in a cremation ground."
One should offer an oblation consisting primarily of meat at the time of twilight.
In the Mahākālasaṃhitā: "Outside the city at night, near a great forest,
having taken edible substances as well as the materials for worship..."
Accompanied by two or three trusted attendants, one should offer the bali-oblation to the jackals;
one should present raw and cooked meats according to the prescribed rite.
There, facing the northern direction, free from fear, pure, and vigorous,
having performed the six-limbed breath control (prāṇāyāma) and indeed having offered the water of honor (arghya), he should worship.
Having risen and loosened her hair, Śivā should beckon slowly.
In the *Kulacūḍāmaṇi* it is said: "O Kālī, Kālī!"—thus she should be addressed; there, she who is the very form of Śiva arrives in the form of a beast (paśu) together with her retinue.
O ornament of the family, when it cries out with a clear voice after eating, lifting its face toward the northeast, that alone is auspicious for him; it is not otherwise.
One must certainly and invariably satisfy Śivā with the gift of food;
this daily śrāddha is as obligatory as the twilight worship and the libations to the ancestors.
Likewise, this is the constant rule for the worship of the family deities:
he who does not worship the goddess Śivā in her animal form in a secluded place [is at fault].
By the howling of a jackal, all of that— his recitations, rites of worship, and whatever meritorious deeds he has performed— is certainly and instantly destroyed.
Having received the curse and fallen into this state, Śivā weeps in the solitude;
there, O Deva-Bhairava, she is being devoured by a single Śivā.
In that very state, the supreme delight of all powers is most difficult to attain:
O Bhairava, there is the power of the bound soul (paśu-śakti), the power of man (nara-śakti), and the power of the bird (pakṣi-śakti).
Since worship causes even a flawed action to become virtuous,
one should perform great worship with every possible effort.
Having reflected upon the fear of kings and the like, the dangers of other lands and so forth, and one's auspicious and inauspicious karmas, one should offer the bali-oblation.
Accept it, O Goddess, highly fortunate one, auspicious Śivā, whose form is the fire of time;
declare clearly the fruit of good and evil, and accept this offering for you.
Having uttered this, the *bali* offering should be given, O beloved of the *kula* lineage.
In the *Mahākālasaṃhitā*: "O beloved, one should move a short distance away from this place, so that the jackals may come near the food without fear."
Standing there, one should observe what they are eating;
for if they all come together, they will indeed devour everything that has been given.
One should predict total success, the attainment of sovereignty, and the arrival of wealth;
whatever food those [birds] eat, one shall obtain that very result.
Whatever one does not eat at all, that shall not become fruit;
however, a specific rule regarding this has been described in connection with the worship of the Kumārī and similar rites.
Therefore, O Goddess, I do not speak further here, both for fear of excessive prolixity and because Maheśvarī herself approaches assuming the form of a young maiden.
Having likewise assumed the form of a jackal, Kālikā comes of her own accord;
therefore, practitioners must diligently cultivate devotion toward them.
While the jackals are devouring [the offerings], one should present the bali-offering to all:
first to Saṃhārabhairava, and after that to the Vaṭukas.
To the Vināyakas, to the Mothers, and to the Guardians of the Field (Kṣetrapālas);
to the Yoginīs, to the Ḍākinīs, and to the messengers of Śiva (Śivadūtīs).
The mantra previously mentioned shall bring success; with it, one should offer the bali-oblation.
One attains great sovereignty if they consume [the offering] entirely.
If one consumes half, middling success occurs; but if one does not consume it at all, misfortune will arise.
As stated in the *Kulacūḍāmaṇi*: "O child, if it is not taken, then there will be no auspiciousness whatsoever;
if there is to be auspiciousness, then it must be consumed entirely."

In the Mahākālasaṃhitā: "When the hosts of Śivās have finished eating and are standing there, one should personally prostrate like a staff before them all, regarding each with the thought that she is one's own chosen deity."
307) Taking up a handful of flowers anointed with fragrant sandalwood paste,
rising with disheveled hair, eyes closed, and clad only by the directions as his garment;
Full of devotion, free from fear, and with his neck slightly bowed,
he should offer praise with these hymns, preceded by a prayer for boons.
O Goddess who assumes the form of a jackal, O Guhyakālī, salutations be to you!
O Ulkāmukhī (Fire-mouthed), Lalajjihvā (Lolling-tongued), Ghorarāvā (Terrible-voiced), Śṛgālinī (Jackal-woman)!
O dweller in the cremation ground, O ghost, O you who delight in the flesh of corpses, O sinless one!
O wanderer in the forest, O sinless one, O auspicious one in the form of a jackal!
Homage be to you, O Mahāmāyā, O Kālikā who delivers the world!
O Mātaṅgī, O Kukkūṭī, O Raudrī, O Mahākālī, homage be to you!
O bestower of all accomplishments, O formidable one, O inspirer of fear, O remover of fear! Be gracious, O Goddess of gods, O Caṇḍikā, toward me, your devotee.
Victory to you, who crosses the ocean of saṃsāra, O performer of all auspiciousness! O Caṇḍī with disheveled hair, O Cāmuṇḍā, wearer of a garland of severed heads!
O you who effect destruction, when enraged, grant me all accomplishments!
O Durgā, Kirātī, Śavarī, seated upon a corpse, free from fear!
Always bestow your grace; look upon me with compassion.
O Vikaṭā, grant me a kingdom, wealth, long life, sons, and a wife.
O Goddess, may you be pleased by this offering of the *śivā* oblation;
salutations to you, salutations to you, salutations to you, salutations be unto you!
With these eight verses, one should recite the hymn of praise to Śiva;
thereafter, whatever remains of that food, or even another vessel, [should be offered].
O Pārvatī, one must indeed bury everything in the ground with great care,
lest crows, donkeys, dogs, or other such base-born creatures [should find it].
If they consume that leavings, then an obstacle arises;
he should come from the depths of the forest at night itself, free from fear.
Having returned, one should again worship the Goddess with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings.
In the *Kulacūḍāmaṇi*: "O Mahādeva, having understood this, one should perform rites for peace and well-being.
O you of noble vows, the practice of the Kula known as the Dakṣiṇa has thus been described to you."
It must not be taught to anyone if one desires eternal happiness;
it should be practiced only in solitude and never in the presence of people. (308)
Or else, one should not allow birds, insects, and the like to enter;
this may be done in a subterranean pavilion or in a well-secured cave.
Or it should be performed in a flawless pavilion in your presence.
Now, regarding expiation, the *Triśaktiratna* states: "In the case of men performing prohibited acts, as well as failing to perform prescribed ones..."
There would be the occurrence of a transgression requiring expiation.
For the pacification of the transgression of daily vidyās, one should mutter the vidyā one hundred times;
upon the omission of occasional rites, one should mutter the mantra one thousand times.
In the *Liṅgāgama*: "Listen, O Goddess, I shall declare to you the rule for expiation (*prāyaścitta*):
a disciple who abandons his guru must certainly undergo expiation."
Having recited the *śrīpādukā* mantra one hundred thousand times, one is purified from that sin;
O Dear One, one who abandons the mantra should avoid association with such a person.
Being pure, one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times, followed by fire-offerings (*homa*) and libations (*tarpaṇa*).

Regarding the *śrīpādukā* and the *gurupādukā*: renunciation is prescribed only for a Kaulika Guru; it is forbidden for Kaulikas [to renounce their own], but not even for those who are not Kaulikas. For instance, it is stated in the *Yāmala*:
Just as a bee, out of greed for nectar, goes from flower to another flower,
so too a disciple, greedy for a teacher, goes from one teacher to another teacher.
[This refers to] the teacher and the bound soul (paśu). Another teacher who is of noble lineage (kulīna)—and this is as follows:
"If by chance the knowledge is obtained from a bound soul by men of noble lineage, then, having found a Kaulika twice-born (dvija), one should acquire the knowledge once again."
This is made even more clear by such a statement. In this way, it should be understood that for the bound souls (*paśu*) as well, there is a fault in abandoning their *paśu*-guru.

The recitation (*japa*) of that very mantra must be performed one hundred thousand times; the fire-oblation (*homa*) is one-tenth of the recitation; and the libation (*tarpaṇa*) is one-tenth of the oblation, as is seen elsewhere. Furthermore, a mantra that is not inherently defective must certainly not be abandoned.
One who is wicked must indeed be abandoned— whether he be a Śakala, devoid of seed, doubtful, or likewise censured;
for such persons do not attain success, and the Guru would become a slayer of a Brahmin.

Then, having suddenly recognized that [the mantra is defective], one should abandon the mantra, the deity, and the guru. Defects such as *śakala* and so forth are merely illustrative; others mentioned in their respective scriptures should also be understood.
Regarding the abandonment of a non-defective mantra, [one should pray]: "Forgive that sin, O Mother; O Goddess, remove it and show mercy."
The distinction is that one should receive this very *vidyā* after having asked for forgiveness.

309) Likewise: "Those Kaulikas who consume the food of a sacrificial animal (*paśu*) in many ways should mutter the *Lopāmudrā* three hundred thousand times, or they should mutter the *Ajapā* one hundred thousand times."

One should offer oblations with sacrificial food (havis) and cooked rice (anna); thus, one will certainly become free from sin, even after many years. In this case as well, regarding the fire-oblation (homa), the measure is strictly one-tenth of the recitation (japa), whereas there is no such fixed rule for the libation (tarpaṇa) and other rites.
Likewise: "If a heroic Māheśvara drinks a substance from the same vessel [as another], his drink becomes the leavings of a dog; that Kaulika must perform penance."
Having purified his mind through a thousand recitations of the Gāyatrī or by three days of fasting, he should give gold to his preceptor.
The Gāyatrī [mantra] has itself as its deity; it is indeed the Gāyatrī. In the *Mantrārṇava*:
"Whether by force or spontaneously, he who takes pleasure in the Mother of Mantras should recite the mantra ten lakhs of times and then perform the fire-rite with chaff."
The mother of the mantra is the power of the Guru, or the Guru himself;
likewise are the daughter of the mantra, one’s own daughter, a sister, and women of the same lineage.
Through a hundred thousand recitations of the mantra while engaged in sexual union (*ramaṇa*), the Kaulika becomes purified.

The "Mantra-daughter" (*mantraputrī*) is one who has received instruction as a spiritual son; she is mentioned here because instruction is given for the sake of purification even to one's own wife with whom one has sexual relations. A "Kula-woman" (*kulastrī*) is the wife of a hero (*vīra*); and approaching her must indeed be done with the husband’s permission.
Regarding the phrase "to [atone for] a fault": in the *Brahmayāmala* it is said— "Having committed the murder of a hero, or having drunk liquor in vain, or having enjoyed the Guru’s daughter-in-law,
the mantra-daughter, or the wife of a hero, the practitioner of mantra should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times."
This refers to the case of a hero who has fallen from right conduct (*ācāra*).
And thus: "One should recite thirteen thousand [mantras] for the killing of a divine hero.
This refers to the case of killing committed unintentionally, or it refers merely to an action conducive to killing.
Or regarding the case of an assailant:
likewise—"Having killed a multitude of boneless living beings, one shall go to hell;
having killed all kinds of birds, and having killed a woman, one should recite the Ekādaśa [mantra] eleven times."
A multitude of boneless creatures refers to leeches and the like; "woman" refers to those very same [creatures]. "Eleventh" means one hundred and eleven.
The anusvāra in "ekādaśam" is a technical (tāntrika) usage. Likewise:
the snake, the cat, the mongoose, the rat, the camel, the donkey, and the horse.
And having killed all wild animals, such as elephants and the like, one should recite [the mantra] one hundred and eight times.
One should recite the mantra eight thousand times when the killing of small creatures has been committed.

"Eight thousand" means one thousand and eight. Small creatures (*kṣudrajantu*) are those other than those already mentioned, such as goats and the like. As for the statement in another Tantra that "one should recite three thousand times upon killing a goat and so forth," that refers to cases involving habitual practice.
310) In the *Triśaktiratna*: "Without the offering of bali, the practitioner of mantra (mantrī) must never cause the sacrificial animals (paśu) to fall [into the fire].
Otherwise, an expiation (prāyaścitta) prescribed by the wise according to the Smṛti has been declared."
Likewise: "By ten hundred thousand [recitations], one is released from the ocean of hell for killing a cow;
by twelve hundred thousand, a practitioner of mantra is liberated after killing a bull."
By killing a guru through negligence, one becomes pure by [reciting] five hundred thousand [times];
this refers merely to the act of challenging [the guru]. For regarding actual killing, it has been stated that the penance ends only with death. Likewise:
"A practitioner of mantra is liberated from the murder of a woman by ten crores [of recitations]."
Eating only at night and confessing his sins, he should wander through the sacred seats and fields.
If a Brahmin is caused to fall [from his caste] through negligence, one becomes pure by [giving] twenty hundred thousand [cows];
Kṣatriyas and others are freed from this sin according to what has been stated.
As stated, this is in relation to a Brāhmaṇa, with a progressive increase by doubling and so forth according to the sequence. For it is said in the Tantra:
"In the case of killing a Brāhmaṇa, [the number is] one hundred thousand; for a Kṣatriya, it is recorded as double."
For a Vaiśya, it is declared to be threefold; and for one born from the feet (a Śūdra), it is fourfold.

In this context, both "one hundred thousand" (*lakṣa*) and "killing" (*vadha*) are illustrative examples. For whatever sin a Brahmin must perform expiation for, a member of that same caste must perform an amount exceeding that.
For the killing of an Arhat or a Buddhist, a practitioner of mantra should recite the mantra one million four hundred thousand times.

The followers of the Arhat are Buddhists; the followers of the Buddha are Buddhists. "Khābdhilakṣa" means forty lakhs. Likewise: "In the killing of a brown animal and of pigs, one should recite five thousand [times]";
the word "japet" (should recite) is to be supplied. "Babhru" refers to a mongoose. Likewise:
For killing birds, the practitioner is purified by two thousand [repetitions];
for the killing of snakes, cats, or fish, by one thousand Vedic recitations.
For treachery against a deity or treachery against a guru, one should recite the mantra thirty million times.
The statement regarding expiation for [killing] birds, snakes, and cats refers to cases where the act was committed unintentionally.
"Treachery" (droha) is defined as an action conducive to death. Furthermore, this [penance] pertains to a guru who possesses virtuous qualities. Likewise—

Having consumed the property of a deity or the property of a guru, one should recite the mantra thirty million times; likewise if one has consumed it without permission. In the case of violating that permission, one should perform half that number of recitations.
Disruption means agitation.
In the event of reviling the observances (*samaya*), or the *yoginīs* and *vīras*,
or the scriptures, or the mantra-practitioners, or women, one should perform a thousand recitations (*japa*).
When the Vāma and Dakṣiṇa Siddhāntas have been destroyed by the Śaiva and Vaidika [traditions], the practitioner of mantra, reciting that which measures four koṭis, is purified from sin.
The practitioner of mantra is purified by ten recitations when censuring the first and so forth.
One should first drink the nectar of the *argha* offering and then raise up the Goddess;
otherwise, it becomes the drinking of a bound soul (*paśu*), and its merit would be diminished by a hundred thousandfold.
*Arghāmṛta* is the nectar of the *argha* offering; *viśeṣārghāmṛta* is the nectar of the special *argha* offering.
He who eats without having offered [it] should recite the mantra one hundred and eight times. "Without having offered" means without having received the permission of the Goddess. Likewise:
The mantra-practitioner should perform penance for drinking alcohol in vain, as well as for [the transgressions of] a hero’s wife or a hero’s daughter-in-law,
by means of the worship of divine heroes and other such rites.
In the event of the lamp being extinguished, the vessel being broken, or the vessel being knocked over,
one should worship the Great Goddess and recite the mantra one hundred and eight times.
Thus it has been taught for ignorance; through knowledge, it becomes twofold.
This doubling due to intentional action is to be understood everywhere. As stated in the Bhūtabhairava:
"O Dear One, when a yantra is broken, cracked, or stolen by a thief..."
One should observe the fast for one day without indolence.
One should recite the vidyā one hundred thousand times, preceded by fire offerings and libations;
having gratified the guru with devotion, one should also feed the brahmins.
If a mortal ever causes the marks to be erased, or the ornaments to crack and so forth, or breaks [the image], death will certainly befall him.
Therefore, O Goddess, he should cast it into the king of holy fords, or into another river such as the Gaṅgā, or into the ocean; otherwise, he would incur suffering.
Now, regarding the funeral rite (antyeṣṭi),
it is stated in that very same [text]: "O Mother, whenever a practitioner of mantra (mantrī) who has taken recourse to the dharma of the body passes away,
his funeral rite must be performed by his disciples and others according to the prescribed injunctions."
Having performed the daily rites, the performer should purify the deceased— who has departed for another world— by means of the five jewels through the path of the eyes and other [senses].
Having drawn it forth, one should establish the individual soul (jīvātman) in the deceased through the instruction of the guru,
by means of the conjunction of the five praṇavas with the elements of space, fire, air, and the self.
Having uttered the word "mokṣada" (bestower of liberation), one should recite "cakṣuḥ" and so forth;
then, having recited the name of the deceased, one should say, "I invoke."
With this [mantra], one should invoke the deceased and deposit the vital breaths there;
one should perform the ritual assignment of the limbs by means of the *māyā* [syllable] conjoined with the long [vowel].
Having established the jar, the wise mantra-practitioner should place the deceased there;
having consecrated him with the five products of the cow using the Aghora mantra, he should likewise consecrate him with the vardhanī vessel.
Having established [the body] with pure water, the wise man should then place it with ashes,
laying the deceased upon a bed of *darbha* grass with the head toward the south.
Having adorned [the image] with new garments, garlands, ointments, and ornaments,
the practitioner should worship it with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings using the root mantra.
Having properly constructed a palanquin, one should place the corpse therein;
then, circumambulating the village while accompanied by the sounds of conch shells, kettledrums, and other instruments, [one should proceed].
Having entered the place for the deceased, which extends from south to north,
one should smear the ground level with cow dung and scatter there parched grain, sesame seeds, and unbroken rice.
One should scatter [the ground] with mustard seeds and then install the celestial chariot (vimāna);
having established the funeral fire (cityagni) there, one should strew [sacrificial grass] around it in a counter-clockwise direction.
The practitioner of mantra should place the vessels; on the right, the vessel dedicated to Viṣṇu.
Having placed the praṇītā vessel and worshipped it with saffron and other offerings.
The practitioner of mantras, having covered [the site] with *darbha* grass, should place [the deity] in the southeast corner;
he should worship the god Bhairava on the right side, following the sequence of the mandala.
Having performed the visualization of the tongues of the fire according to the prescribed method,
one should cook an excellent *caru* oblation mixed with sesame seeds and rice.
The wise one, having offered one hundred and eight oblations with clarified butter using the Mṛtyuñjaya mantra, should especially offer the five jewels.
One should offer oblations with the root mantra in sequence up to the end of the enclosure;
thus, by performing the oblations in reverse order, all mantras are offered into the body of the Guru.
Having brought about dissolution in sequence, one should offer oblations with the Vāgbhava mantra;
then, having offered with the root mantra, [one should do so] in reverse order within the body of the preta.
Having brought the principles (tattvas) to dissolution, one should unite everything within the Self;
reciting the mantra, one should offer the merit and demerit of the deceased as an oblation.
Then, having offered the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti), one should unite [the soul] with the supreme state—
pure, consisting of Śiva and Śakti, free from rebirth, composed of existence, consciousness, and bliss, directly transcending all principles, and undisturbed.
Thus the deceased is united by the disciple with the supreme state.
Having abandoned all impurity and turbidity, one becomes fit for the state of Śambhu;
one should offer oblations into the fire with clarified butter, using the root mantra of Aghora Astra.
For the sake of expiation, the practitioner, following the prescribed method,
should prepare a bed according to the measurement of the deceased's body.
On the southern side of the fire, [one should place] stakes produced from the kula-tree with their tips pointing southward,
as well as bilva, javā, and kuśa grass.
Having spread out the bed with a triple-stranded thread,
the practitioner should wrap it around and worship it with offerings such as perfumes and flowers.
Having covered it with a new cloth, the wise man should draw the yantra there:
a lotus with a pericarp, a triangle, a hexagon, and eight petals.
Then, having strewn flowers everywhere upon that [ground] marked with upward lines,
the practitioner should place the deceased there with his head facing south.
Having consecrated it with the protective mantra and ignited it with the Jvālāmālinī-vidyā,
the wise practitioner should burn [the body] from the feet upward with the Aghora-mantra.
With the Aghora weapon mantra or the Pāśupata mantra,
let the practitioner perform oblations here until this [target] is reduced to ashes.
Those who know the rules of conduct, having assembled together, should perform the recitation of hymns and mantras;
once this deceased person has been reduced to ashes, they should properly worship the deities.
On the arrival of the seventh day, the officiant should protect the city-fire;
having extinguished it with milk, he should wrap the bones in a new cloth.
The practitioner of mantra should cast those ashes into some pure body of water,
or the master of mantras should have the heap of bones excavated in a temple of the gods or a mother-goddess shrine.
Or, having buried this in one's own home, one should worship it at the three junctions of the day;
one should likewise perform the festival worship on the anniversary of death every month.
At the completion of the year, one should perform a great festival without indolence;
then, having raised the structural frame, one should cast it into a river or a place touched by ritual injunctions.
One should cast it away or bury it somewhere on the pure surface of the earth;
or else, someone with a bone [of the deceased] should fashion an image of him, or sandals.
Having performed this, the practitioner, devoted to the guru, should worship [the deity]—
whether for those who have died in another land or for those still living.
Having fashioned a body as before out of bundles of *darbha* grass, or *palāśa* leaves, or again with rice flour, the wise practitioner should perform [the rite].
Alternatively, a believer may perform it himself in solitude by means of the mind;
first the Vāgbhava syllable, then the word *Dīpinī*, and thereafter *Jvālāmālinī*.
One should join the syllables *krodha*, *haṃsa*, *indu*, and *heti* as a *saṃpuṭa* (encasement).
These are the seed-syllables (*bījas*) therein; the *praṇava* is for the living being and the corpse.
[One should contemplate] the collection of Haṃsa, Indu, Aṅga, Anta, Kuṭila,
Vahni, Bindu, Bhaga, Āśrita, Śiva, Śakti, Kṣama, Indra, Ambu, Vahni, Vāta, and Arghi.
This is the mantra of Jvālāmālinī as taught by those skilled in mantras:
the seed-syllable of Māyā (Hrīṃ), followed by two *sphura* syllables, and likewise two *prasphura* syllables.
At the end of "ghoraghoratara," one should utter the word "tanu";
