then "caṭa" twice, "pracaṭa" twice, the pair "kaha" twice, and the pair "vama" twice.
Having uttered the two *bandha*s, one should recite the two *ghātaya*s;
ending with *varma* and *astra*, this is declared to be the *aghoramantra*, whose nature consists of the phonemes.
One should utter "Tāra Śrīṃ," followed by the word "paśu," and at the end the two syllables for the armor and weapon (*kavaca* and *astra*).
This is the Pāśupata-weapon mantra, which wards off minor planetary influences.

One should place the five [consonants] ending with *kṣa*, along with the vowels from *i* to *au*, joined with the nasal (*anusvāra*), and preceded by the letter *i*; these should be well-considered as being conjoined with the vowel *u* and the lunar digit (*bindu*) on the left ear.
This is declared to be the Five Jewels (Pañcaratna), which bestows whatever the mind desires.
Thus ends the seventh chapter, on the occasional rites (naimittikavidhi), in the *Tārābhaktisudhārṇava* composed by the Great Professor (Mahāmahopādhyāya) Ṭhakkura Śrī Narasiṃha.
The Eighth Chapter:
Now, regarding *puraścaraṇa* (preliminary rites), it is stated in the *Vāyavīyasaṃhitā*:
The preliminary practice (*puraścaraṇa*) of the root mantra is called the *sādhana*;
because it must be performed first, it precedes the rite known as *viniyoga*.
Or it is stated thus because of the application [of the term] at the beginning.
Just as a body devoid of life is incapable of performing any action,
so too is a mantra declared to be ineffective when it lacks the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa).
In the *Vīracūḍāmaṇi*: "Success in mantra does not arise for one who is devoid of the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*);
therefore, at the outset, one should perform the preparatory service according to rule and in accordance with the prescribed method."
In the Kulacūḍāmaṇi: "O Great Goddess, O Īśvarī, the five limbs are recitation (japa), fire-oblation (homa), libation (tarpaṇa), consecration (abhiṣeka), and the propitiation of Brahmins."
The preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*) is said to consist of one-tenth of each preceding [stage].

In the *Kulamūlāvatāra*: "In this cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*) which abounds in suffering, if one desires one's own welfare, the reciter of the mantra shall proceed to happiness through the worship consisting of the five limbs alone."
O Great Goddess, the five limbs are recitation, fire-oblation, libation, consecration,
and the honoring of Brahmins, O Īśvarī.
The preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*) is said to consist of one-tenth of each preceding [number].
In this regard, for the Kaulikas, the number for recitation (*japa*) is exactly one hundred thousand (*lakṣa*). As it is stated in the *Tārātantra*:
"The practitioner of mantra, intent on acting according to his own will, [should perform it] for the sake of accomplishing the *puraścaraṇa*."

One should always recite the *Rahasyamālā* one hundred thousand times. In the *Surendrasaṃhitā*: "One should recite the mantra exactly one hundred thousand times; one should offer oblations into the consecrated fire with red lotuses from ten fingers [of the hand]; thereafter the mantra becomes perfected."
In the Vīracūḍāmaṇi: "The wise practitioner of mantra should recite it four hundred thousand times and perform oblations amounting to one-tenth of that;
with lotuses smeared with the three sweets, the man becomes a lord of speech."

In the *Ekavīrākalpa*: "For those devoid of meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*), who are base and small-minded, recitation (*japa*) is said to be fourfold for the sake of accomplishment; otherwise it shall not be so."
In the *Tārārṇava*: "Having meditated thus, one who subsists on sacrificial food (*haviṣya*) should recite [the mantra] four hundred thousand times;
or, taking the secret garland (*rahasyamālā*), one should recite it exactly one hundred thousand times. (316)
In the Vaiśampāyana-saṃhitā:
"The number prescribed for the Kṛta age shall be doubled in Tretā;
it is declared to be tripled in Dvāpara, and in Kali, the number is quadrupled."

In this regard, it appears as follows: in the Satya Yuga, the recitation for a Vīra consists of one hundred thousand [mantras], while that for a Paśu consists of four hundred thousand; in the Kali Yuga, the recitation for a Vīra consists of four hundred thousand, while that for a Paśu consists of sixteen hundred thousand. Otherwise, there would be no distinction between the Vīra in the Satya Yuga and the Kali Yuga.

Because it would result in an equality of number. Nor is this an acceptable consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*), because it contradicts the general statement of Vaiśampāyana. As for the claim that in the Kali age alone there is a fourfold method (*caturlakṣavidhi*) for cattle, that is not so; for in the Satya age, cattle and heroes would attain an identical number. In reality, however—
This is because it contradicts the statement in the *Tantracūḍāmaṇi*: "The effort of service in the Age of Perfected Mantras (Siddhamantrayuga) is as follows:
'A bound soul (*paśu*) devoted to his own conduct should always recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times by day;
a celestial being (*divya*) or a hero (*vīra*) should perform the recitation of one hundred thousand times at night.'"
Thus, because the time for the preliminary ritual (*puraścaraṇa*) of the Kālī-mantra as stated in the *Kālīkalpa* is required here as well:
"The wise one, pure and eating sacrificial food (*haviṣya*), should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times during the day;
likewise, being impure, he should repeat it one hundred thousand times at night."

And from the statement in the *Brahmasaṃhitā* concerning the preliminary practice (*puraścaraṇa*) of Tārā: "For a hero, the recitation is one hundred thousand times at night; for a victim (*paśu*), it is always during the day. However, the four-hundred-thousand-fold recitation refers to one who has fallen from the status of a victim. Thus it is stated in the *Matsyasūkta*.
Seated comfortably on a soft cushion, with a rosary of large conch shells,
one should recite the mantra with a concentrated mind for either three months or three fortnights.
Eating only at night and subsisting on sacrificial food (haviṣya), one should recite the vidyā two hundred thousand times.
And the meaning of this statement is that it refers specifically to those who have fallen from their heroic status (*bhraṣṭavīra*). In the *Tantra*:
"At whatever time the initiation (*dīkṣā*) takes place, at that same time this [rite] should take place.
In the *Dakṣiṇāmūrtikalpa*: "A preeminent and learned man, relying upon the first fortnight of the month (*pūrvapakṣa*), should begin [the rite]."
Having bathed according to the prescribed rite at an auspicious moment, under a favorable lunar mansion and on a propitious lunar day,
and having bowed to the Guru, to Gaṇeśāna, and to his mother Durgā;

The *pūrvapakṣa* is the bright fortnight (*śuklapakṣa*). In the *Vaiśampāyanasaṃhitā*: "When the moon and stars are favorable, during the bright fortnight on an auspicious day, one should begin [the practice] at the start of Capricorn; however, one should not recite [the mantra] while Viṣṇu is asleep."

In the Yoginītantra: "Having received the command of the Guru, a person whose inner organ is purified should then perform the preliminary rite (puraskriyā) with the desire for the complete accomplishment of the mantra."
317) Likewise: "Therefore, at the outset, the wise man should perform [the rite] himself, or have a guru perform it;
in the absence of a guru, he should have a brahmin do so, for the sake of the welfare of all living beings."
A friend who is affectionate, learned in the scriptures, and endowed with various virtues;
or a woman who is perfected in character, of good conduct, and devoted to her husband.

Now, regarding the locations, the *Mahākapilapañcarātra* states: "Sacred fields (*kṣetra*), pilgrimage sites (*tīrtha*), forests (*vana*), groves (*ārāma*), temples (*devālaya*), rivers (*nadī*), lakes (*hrada*), huts (*kuṭī*), and those who are dispassionate (*virakta*)— these are the locations that bestow the accomplishment of mantras."

In the *Prapañcasāra*: "Or else, on the shore of the ocean, or on a mountain peak, or on the banks of rivers flowing to the sea, or in a secluded place, or in his own home, or in the temple of Viṣṇu, a wise man should recite [the mantra]."
And a temple of Śiva devoid of a bull is a place for recitation (japa).
This is because of the statement of Agastya (Kumbhasambhava): "In a place of Śiva devoid of a bull, one should face west. In the Yāmala:
In a secluded and pure place, free from the fear and anxiety caused by barbarians, wicked beasts, and predatory animals, and endowed with devotion while remaining free from anxious thought.
One should dwell in a beautiful land, in a righteous kingdom that is well-supplied with food and free from calamity,
in a delightful place inhabited by a community of devotees, and never under the patronage of another.
Now, regarding the places prohibited for the preliminary practice (*puraścaraṇa*):
the knower of reality should not dwell on that path by which kings, ministers, royal officials, and powerful men travel.
One should not dwell in dilapidated temples, gardens, or at the foot of trees near houses; nor on riverbanks, mountain peaks, or in cavities in the earth and similar places.
The state of being "worn out" (jīrṇatva) extends up to trees. However, the prohibition regarding riverbanks refers specifically to banks other than those of rivers flowing into the ocean.
Likewise: "Having gone to a sacred field (puṇyakṣetra) or similar location, one should perform the formal acquisition of the ground (bhūmiparigraha)."
One should say: "For the sake of accomplishing the *puraścaraṇa* of such-and-such a mantra..."
Thinking, "May this ground be taken by me; may my mantra be successful," one performs the enclosure with the *bhīma* [mantra] and determines the dimensions on all sides.
In a village, a space measuring one *krośa* is prescribed; in a city, it is traditionally held to be twice that.
By rivers, mountains, sacred fords (*tīrtha*), and the like, it is exempt from such measurement.
One should drive stakes made of milky trees, consecrated with weapon-mantras,
into the ten directions, and one should worship the Weapon-deity within them.
318) When the field has been secured by means of the *kīlana* rite, the practitioner of mantras is not overcome by obstacles;
there, the knower of the ritual rules should worship the guardians of the field (*kṣetrapāla*) and others according to the prescribed method.

Having offered the *bali* to the lords of the directions, one should then take recourse to the sacred field (*kṣetra*). One should drive stakes (*kīlaka*) into the ground between the East and the Northeast with the thought that they are "above," and between the Southwest and the West with the thought that they are "below. Regarding the mantra "Astra": one should worship the weapons of whichever directional guardian presides over whichever direction.
Some say that one should worship the weapon (*astra*) of the root mantra with its own weapon-mantra as part of the six-limbed (*ṣaḍaṅga*) rite; others hold this view.
Then, one should offer the *bali* to the Kṣetrapāla in the middle of the sacred field (*kṣetra*). As it is stated in the Prathamatantra:
"Having fully worshipped the Kṣetrapāla, one should offer the *bali* according to the prescribed rule."
First there are two [mātrās], then two more; in the wise one (the guru), there should be two moras.
Again, break the pair; then, make the pair dance once more;
thereafter, the pair of feet of Vighna, intent upon Mahābhairava.
"Accept the bali offering of the Kṣetrapāla; O Pāvakasundarī, accept the second! This is declared to be the bali mantra, which bestows the fruit of all accomplishments.

In the *Vīracūḍāmaṇi*, however, it is stated: "Having performed the placement of the seers (*ṛṣi*), meters (*chandas*), and so forth, one should offer the sacrificial oblation (*bali*) to the deities of the directions.
One should write the word 'Brāhmī' ending in the feminine suffix *ṅī* [preceded by] Asitāṅgabhairava."
One should take the offering and divide it into two; the mantra for the offerings to the directions ends with *svāhā* (*dviṭha*).
[The eight Bhairavas are] Asitāṅga, Ruru, Caṇḍa, Krodha, Unmatta, and Bhairava.
Kapālī, Bhīṣaṇa, and Saṃhāra— these are the eight Bhairavas.
Then follow Brāhmī, Māheśvarī, Kaumārī, Vaiṣṇavī,
Vārāhī, Indrāṇī, and Cāmuṇḍā.
Mahālakṣmī is fully described according to the sequence beginning with her own seed-syllable;
having worshipped her with incense and lamps, one should subsequently insert the ritual peg (kīla).
Having first uttered the Praṇava, [one should utter] Māyā, Lakṣmī, and Manmatha;
then, having uttered the word "Indrāṇyai," [one should utter] the word "Cāmuṇḍe" thereafter.
After the word *vicce*, one should then write *idaṃ kṣetraṃ ca kīlaya*.
After that, one should write the words *rakṣa rakṣa* followed by *kālike*.
This mantra, ending with the wife of fire (the *svāhā* syllable), should be worshipped according to the sequence starting from the east.
Having uttered the root mantra, one should pronounce the word "to Āgneyī";
then the word "to Yāmyā," and again the mantra for Nairṛtī.
"O Dear One, having first uttered the mantra of Vāruṇī, Vāyavī, Kauverī, Īśānī, and Bhairavī, one should then speak the word 'Devi'."
One should offer the bali-oblation in due order, presenting the bali to the cardinal and intermediate directions;
having first uttered the Praṇava, one should then utter the Hṛllekhā seed-syllable.
After reciting the word for Vaṭuka, and for the sake of deliverance from calamities,
one should utter the two *kuru*s, then extract *māyā* and *tāra*.
The practitioner, joined with the wife of fire (svāhā), should offer the oblation to Vaṭuka;
having cast the oblation in the southeast, [he should worship] Māyā, Lakṣmī, and Manmatha.
Having extracted the seed-syllable of Vārāhī, and again the seed-syllable of the Destroyer of the Five (Pañcāntaka),
one should then utter the word "Gaṇapataye," followed by "Varavarada."
One should say "sarvajanaṃ" and then "vadeccaiva," followed by "vadenme vaśamānaya";
at the end, one should add "vahnivadhūṃ"—this is the great mantra of Gaṇanātha.
The seed-syllable of Vārāhī is *glauṃ*.
Having extracted the three-fold Raudra, one should likewise extract Nārāyaṇa. Having extracted the seed-syllable of Sūkṣmeśa, one should extract the seed-syllable of Amareśa.
Then, one should offer the bali-oblation to the Kṣetrapāla;
the mantra for the Kṣetrapāla is proclaimed as being joined with the wife of Vahni (the *svāhā* ending).
Having written the seed-syllable of Vāyu in three ways, as well as Ananta and Mādhava,
one should then extract Vartulākṣī from the Yoginīs in the same manner.
The mantra accompanied by the wife of Vahni (the letter *ra*) is for the offering (*bali*) to the Yoginīs in the northwest.
The letter *kṣa* is Raudra. "Triguṇam" means three times. Nārāyaṇa is *āṃ*. Sūkṣmeśa is *īṃ*. Amareśa is *ūṃ*. The seed-syllable of Vāyu is the letter *ya*. Ananta is *ā*. Mādhava is *i*.
The letter *U* is Vartulākṣī.
One should extract the letter *KṢA* mounted upon *KĀLA*, followed at its end by the letter *MĀ* and the letter *ANALA*,
for the sake of all those who create obstacles and for all *bhūtas*.
Having extracted "bhyo varma phaṭ," then the two words "gṛhṇa" [followed by] "dvitāntaḥ" is said to bestow success; with this, one should offer the bali-oblation to all spirits.
The syllable *kāla* is the letter *ma*, and *mā* is the vowel *ī*; by that [is formed] *kṣmīṃ*.
[The offerings are: boiled rice, milk-rice, milk, fish, and likewise meat;
sweetmeats, stuffed cakes, and fried cakes, as well as the three kinds of liquor.

One should always prepare cooked food such as heart-pleasing rice, along with clarified butter, honey, and sugar, according to the prescribed rules; one should perform the ritual offering (utsarga) with milk.
In the *Yāmala*: "Having taken recourse to the center of the field (*kṣetra*), one should contemplate the tortoise-diagram (*kūrmacakra*).
He who performs recitation and sacrifice without knowing the tortoise-diagram [is unsuccessful]."
There is no fruit for one who chants that [mantra]; it leads only to total misfortune.
In the *Sārasaṃgraha*: "That [mantra] exists in the world in four ways; its varieties are thus described:
first is the *para* (supreme), then the *kūrma* (tortoise), and likewise the *deśagata* (local)."
It is established as fourfold: pertaining to the village, the house, and so forth.
In the *Tantrarāja* it is said: "In the *deśakūrma* there are the consonants; likewise, in the *gṛhakūrma* there are the vowels;
in the *grāmakūrma* there is that pair [of both]; in the *parakūrma* neither of those two exists."
In the *Devīyāmala*: "At Kurukṣetra, at Prayāga, at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean, at Mahākāla, and at Kāśī, one should not contemplate the location of the lamp.
In the *Gautamīya*: "On a mountain, on the shore of the ocean, in a sacred forest, or on a riverbank..."
If one should perform the preliminary rite (puraścaryā), one need not contemplate the tortoise (kūrma) therein.
A person should divide a country, a village, or even a house into nine parts;
one should then assign the letters from *ka* to *ma* starting from the east and ending in the west.
Then, one should place the eight syllables beginning with *ya* in the two side-cells;
below those, in the center, one should arrange the vowels starting from the east.
The directions ending with Īśāna (the northeast) shall follow; from the first letter of each name, there shall be the face, then the two sides, the two hands, the two flanks, and then the two feet.
The tail, the one [foreleg], the middle, and the back—thus it possesses six limbs.
Success in all aims occurs at the mouth; minor successes occur at the two hands.
In the belly there is constant fruitlessness; in the two feet, no accomplishments (siddhis); in the tail, death is certain; and on the back, the accomplishment of all aims.
Therefore, having understood this well, one should perform all [rites] such as recitation (*japa*).
In the *Siddheśvarītantra*: "Therefore, relying upon the mouth, one should commence all activities;
in its absence, one may rely upon the hand or the position of the tortoise (*kūrma-sthāna*)."

Regarding the "arising at the [wrong] time": wherever there exists enmity between the name of the place and that of the practitioner, one should know this from the science of syllables (akṣa-śāstra) and abandon that particular place.

In the Gautamīya: "If [the syllable] following the mantra-syllable is *maitra* (the letter 'ma') and belongs to the name of the donor, then why would the practitioner not achieve success, even if it is the name of the reciter?"
The universal form of the Kṣetrapāla consists of fifty letters;
therefore, that field (kṣetra), being endowed with qualities, leads to spiritual accomplishment, and not otherwise.
If it is devoid of its proper qualities, even if it is positioned in the mouth, one will not attain success through it;
therefore, having carefully examined the *cakra* as well as the friend (*mitra*), which bestows all accomplishments.
In whatever land there is a lord of elephants who possesses the qualities of both name and mantra, one should go there with effort; that is considered a rare and sacred seat (pīṭha).
Regarding friendliness and enmity, it is stated in another tantra:
"The mutual state of non-duality is expressed by the letter *ga*;
that of the two *ṛ*s by the letter *ca*; and that of the letter *ma* by the letter *kha*."
The two *ḷ*s [are merged] with the letter *ya*, and the letter *pa* with the two *ḷ*s;
the two *o*s with the letter *ṣa*, and the letter *ṣa* with the pair of *au*s.
The letter *ja* is [substituted] by *ḍha*; the letter *ū* by *kha*;
the letter *u* by *ta*; the letter *pha* by *dha*;
the letter *ma* by *ra*; and the letter *ya* by *sa*.
One should cultivate a sense of friendship toward these castes and others as well, while regarding them as enemies.
Wherever enmity exists between the names of the site and the practitioner,
the practitioner should diligently avoid that place after ascertaining it through the science of syllables (akṣa-śāstra).
Just as Aṭṭahāsa is the great city of Garga’s enemy,
Auḍḍiyāna is that of Ṣaṇmukha, and Cakraka is that of Ṛjubhaṭṭa.
Jayantī is the enemy of ṭaṅkaṇa, and khadhāra is the enemy of ujhaka;
tārā is the enemy of ukadeva, and dhūma is the enemy of phaja.
Bhadrasya’s [residence is] Ramyaka, and Yajñaśarman’s is Somanagara;
having thus understood the locations of his enemies in this sequence, the wise man should abandon them.
In the Merutantra: "If even a single initial syllable of the field-mantras and the practitioner-mantras is present, that mantra is certainly one that bestows the fruit of all accomplishments."
In another tantra: "Once his enmity has been ascertained, one should purify [the syllable] beginning with the second letter of his name.
Having thus prepared the house of the location, the mantra-practitioner should offer an oblation (bali) there."
In the *Gautamīya*: "One should draw the Lord of the Island (Dvīpanātha) in the center, worship him, and meditate upon him.
In the *Tantra*: "One should worship the Lords of the Fields (Kṣetreśas) there in the nine squares starting from the east;
Amṛta is declared in the first, and likewise Vṛṣabha in the second."
Śailarāja is [presided over] in the third, while Vāsuki is recorded in the fourth;
Arthakṛt is declared in the fifth, and Śaktikṛt is said to be in the sixth.
Padmayoni is said to be in the seventh [house], Mahāśaṅkha is considered to be in the eighth,
and the group known as Chāyāchatra is proclaimed by the leaders of practitioners in the ninth.
In the *Puraścaraṇacandrikā*:
"Having taken shelter at its front, [one should construct] a small hut capable of withstanding wind and sun,
four cubits in size, square, and provided with a well-made altar one cubit high."
It was adorned with moonlight-like banners and arches,
yet it was detached and intensely stained, and it was completely surrounded by a wall.
Having performed the rite of emanation (nirmāṇa), one should then observe a single meal on an auspicious day;
having bathed in the morning, one who is self-restrained should recite the Gāyatrī ten thousand times.

For the sake of destroying both known and unknown sins, first [the recitation of] the Vedic Gāyatrī is prescribed by many; however, those who know the secret [teachings] say it is one's own deity’s Gāyatrī. Sanatkumāra says:
"Now I shall describe the excellent *puraścaraṇa* of the mantra."
Having performed the consecration according to the rules and having received the mantra from the mouth of the guru,
Having bathed according to the prescribed rules at an auspicious moment, under a favorable constellation and lunar day,
and having diligently gratified the Brahmins with food, clothing, and other gifts;
Having satisfied one's own guru with gifts of land, wealth, clothing, and ornaments,
one should thereafter commence the recitation (japa), preceded by his permission.
In the Agastyasaṃhitā: "Whether eating sacrificial food (haviṣya), vegetables, or even barley-gruel; or milk, roots, or fruit—whatever is available at any place."
During a vow, one should avoid ciñcā, nālikā greens, peas, lakuca,
kadamba, coconut, and pumpkin.
If one recites [the mantra] while wearing soiled garments, having disheveled hair, and possessing foul breath,
the deity residing in the secret [mantra] will quickly consume him.
During the time of recitation, one should avoid laziness, yawning, sleep, gambling, spitting, fear, contact with low persons, and anger.
In another Tantra: "Sleeping on the ground, observing celibacy, and eating only at night, one should recite the mantra.
In the *Kulārṇava*: "Whatever action a person performs apart from the observances (niyama), not even the slightest fruit of it is accomplished due to the fault of violating the sequence."
323) Deficient or excessive actions never bear fruit;
for it is only those actions performed here according to the prescribed rule that indeed yield results.
May the ritual acts performed according to those injunctions— such as recitation, fire-offerings, and worship—
be pleasing to the deity and grant the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.

In this context, sexual union with one's own wife during the fertile period (*ṛtukāla*) is not prohibited; however, apart from the fertile period, the practitioner (*mantrī*) should not even touch his own wife, according to the statement in the *Gautamīya Tantra*: "The recitation (*japa*) must be performed after having made a formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*). Thus it has been said.
Then, having made a formal resolve, one should perform the *puraścaraṇa* with devotion, as taught by the Pot-born Sage (Agastya).
And the formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*) is stated in the *Sanatkumārasaṃhitā*:

"Having uttered the *praṇava*, then *tat sat*, then *adya* (today), as well as the month, fortnight, and lunar day; [saying] 'I, of such-and-such lineage, named so-and-so,' and thereafter reciting the root mantra..."
One who desires success for this mantra should then perform a recitation (japa) of such-and-such a number;
from that, a fire-oblation (havana) consisting of a tenth part, and from the homa, a libation (tarpaṇa) consisting of a tenth part.
One-tenth of that shall be the cleansing (mārjana), and one-tenth of that shall be the feeding of Brahmins;
thus indeed will I perform the preparatory rite (puraścaraṇa), facing either east or north.

In the *Nāradapañcarātra*: "Having performed worship, one should then perform the recitation (*japa*) for as long as two *praharas*. In the *Tantra*: "One should worship the Lord at the three junctions of the day, twice or once, according to the prescribed rule."
In the *Puraścaraṇacandrikā*:
"One should perform the recitation only after having performed worship; one should not recite the mantra alone.
In another Tantra: "Worship may take place only once [daily], but one should never recite without performing worship."
At the end of the recitation, there should be worship; and at the end of the worship, one should recite the mantra.

In the *Muṇḍamālā*: "O beautiful one, if one is unable to perform worship and so forth due to a lack of materials, the preliminary rite (*puraścaryā*) is prescribed to be accomplished by recitation (*japa*) alone."
Regarding the distinction for women, the *Yāmala* states:
"The observance (*niyama*) is to be understood as applying to men, but never to women.
And in the *Vīratantra*: "In this [practice], there is no ritual placement (*nyāsa*) for women, nor meditation (*dhyāna*), nor worship (*pūjana*)."
For women, mantras are accomplished through mere recitation alone.
Now, regarding the procedure for recitation (*japa*), the *Gautamīya Tantra* states: "Mantras existing in the state of the bound soul (*paśubhāva*) are merely composed of phonemes;
once uttered through the sound of the *suṣumnā*, they attain sovereignty."
One should contemplate the syllables of the mantra as strung upon the thread of consciousness within that very Supreme Sky, which is designated as the Supreme Nectar.
One may manifest the true nature of the Self even without worship, fire-oblations, and so forth.
In the Rudrayāmala it is said: "The recitation of a mantra during the time of sleep does not yield fruit;
the time of sleep is when the breath flows through the left [nāḍī], and the waking state is when it flows through the right."
In the Kulārṇava: "Birth-impurity occurs at the beginning and death-impurity at the end;
a mantra that is joined with these two types of impurity does not succeed."
O Supreme Goddess, having placed the seed-syllable of Brahmā at the beginning and end of the *mantra*,
one should recite the *mantra* seven times for the sake of liberation from the two types of birth-impurity (*sūtaka*).
Having thus performed the recitation previously, one should worship the form of radiant energy with fragrant substances,
flowers, and water for the arghya offering in the right hand of the deity.
Having realized that [the breath] is fruitful, one should perform *prāṇāyāma*;
at the end of the recitation (*japa*) and at the beginning of the recitation, one should perform it three times each.
In another Tantra it is said: "Whoever should recite a hymn with the mind and mutter a mantra with the voice—both become fruitless, like water poured into a broken vessel."
In the Rudrayāmala: "If another hears one's recitation, that mantra is said to be void;
it is abandoned by the Ṛṣi, the meter, and the deity, like a serpent."
One should not converse with women or Śūdras at night, nor while intent on recitation (japa),
nor in water, nor during the twilight hours, nor at dusk, nor when afflicted by illness.
Vaiśampāyana said: Whatever recitation, fire-offering, or gift is performed with dry clothing while in water, or with wet clothing while on land, all of that becomes fruitless.
In the Rudrayāmala: "O Dear One, one should perform japa endowed with trust, faith, compassion, devotion, self-restraint, resolve, contentment, and virtues such as pure action."
Excessive eating, overexertion, idle chatter, obsession with rules, attachment to people, and fickleness— by these six, the mantra is not accomplished.
In the Kulārṇava it is said: "For those desiring spiritual accomplishments (siddhi), mental recitation is prescribed; for those desiring nourishment (puṣṭi), whispered recitation;
and for the purpose of killing (māraṇa), vocal recitation is declared to be excellent.
Whether impure or pure, whether walking, standing, or even sleeping," [the recitation should be performed].
The wise person who takes sole refuge in mantra should always practice with the mind alone;
there is no fault in mental recitation at any time or in any place.
In the *Uttaratantra*: "At the beginning of recitation and other rites, one should carefully worship the rosary after sprinkling it with water;
having placed it within a mandala, or holding it in the left hand."
The sprinkling of the rosary with the chosen mantra is thus proclaimed:
"O Mālā, O Mālā, O Great Illusion (Mahāmāyā), whose nature is all-pervading power!
The fourfold aims of life have been entrusted to you; therefore, grant me success."
Having performed worship, one should then take the rosary in the right hand;
thereafter, one should perform the recitation while remaining established in meditation as before.

One should contemplate the Guru upon the crown of the head according to his color and other attributes; one should meditate on the mantra in the middle of the throat as being yellow in color and golden.
One should contemplate Mahāmāyā in the heart, oneself at the feet of the Guru,
and thereafter the Guru-mantra and one's own mantra at the Ājñā-cakra.
Then, having brought even the Goddess to a state of oneness by way of the *suṣumṇā* path,
one should transcend that single wheel which is the very nature of reality (*tattva*).
Having meditated with effort for a moment upon Mahāmāyā within the six cakras,
one should lower the primary sixteen cakras by means of the root mantra—
the [goddess] who resides in the center of the primary sixteen cakras and bestows bliss upon the practitioner.
The practitioner should contemplate the goddess and perform the rite of recitation.
The sixteen-spoked wheel is described in that very same [text]: "In the heart, there is a unification of all three channels;
that location is the sixteen-spoked [wheel], measuring seven finger-breadths."
That is called the "drunkard" (pīta) by the knowers of yoga, consisting of the sixteen primary wheels (*cakras*).
Likewise: "Having taken the rosary close to the heart with the right hand," the word "should mutter" is to be supplied.
In the Śaiva Āgama: "One should not touch the thread with the index finger; one should not shake it nor swing it about."
One should not touch [the rosary] with the left hand, nor cause it to fall from the hand;
when moving the beads, one should use the thumb and not let another bead touch it.
During the time of recitation, the wise man should never cross over the *meru* bead.
And at the time of turning it over, one must not cause any friction at all.
Kali perceives instability in the sound of a rattling door-bolt and becomes agitated in his mind when things are in motion.
If it moves, there is enmity; if it breaks, the occurrence of disease;
if it falls from the hand, a great obstacle; and if the thread snaps, one perishes.

Likewise: "If a yawn occurs while the hand has slipped [from the mouth], one should abandon one *āvartana*. If, through negligence, there is contact with the index finger (*tarjanī*), one should abandon the *āvartana*."
They say that this constitutes the "revolving" of the mantra. Likewise:
"If an improper touch occurs during the recitation (*japa*), one should wash [the hands] and recite again.
In the *Uttaratantro*: "One should avoid the middle portion of the middle finger, but [use] the index finger..."
With the ring finger and the little finger joined together in a state of humility.
Having placed a garland there, O Bhairava, one should hold it with the tip of the thumb and place each seed-syllable upon it, starting from the bottom upwards.
At each repetition, the practitioner of mantra should recite slowly and move his lips gently.
As stated in the *Mahākapilapañcarātra*:
"With a single-pointed mind, a serene soul, holding the rosary, and being pure..."
With his neck slightly bent and raised, he was tranquil and free from the blinking of his eyes or the scratching of his body.
The wise practitioner should recite the mantra clearly, with the visarga, the mātrās, and the bindu, along with each syllable; neither too fast nor with pauses, following the proper sequence.

Here, the meditation on the mantra is presented by another method. This has been stated in the very section on the daily recitation (*nityajapa*). Other varieties of recitation (*japa*) and the methods for their dedication have also been explained in that same place; therefore, they are not elaborated upon here.
From the *Vāyavīya* [Purāṇa]:
In the *Saṃhitā*: "Meditating with his intellect on the identity of the deity, the guru, and the mantra, he should recite [the mantra] one-pointedly from the morning until midday."
One should perform day and night that which was commenced according to its prescribed number;
if one should do less or more than that, one becomes fallen from the vow.
In the *Muṇḍamālā*: "The time for recitation is proclaimed to last from morning until midday.
One should perform the recitation day after day neither less nor more."
The limit of uninterrupted practice has been declared; one should not let the days pass by.
For men, if the days are exceeded, an obstruction to success arises.

"Food and drink consecrated by the recitation of mantras, as well as bathing, sipping water, and eating—these [acts] performed in the morning and so forth pertain to the daytime *puraścaraṇa*. In the *Puraścaraṇacandrikā*:
'Having meditated upon oneself in the form of one's chosen deity (*iṣṭadevatā*), one should recite the mantra.'"
Upon completing the count, one should again perform the restraint of breath (prāṇāyāma) along with its ancillaries, such as the visualization of the ṛṣis.

"Upon the completion of the count" means upon the completion of the daily count. "Ṛṣi and so forth" refers to the intention of performing the nyāsa of the ṛṣis and others. In the *Siddhasārasvata*: "Having thus performed the recitation (japa), one should perform the ten-part oblation with blue lotuses."
The mantra-practitioner should offer oblations with [substances] smeared with clarified butter, and then satisfy [the deity] with a tenth part of that amount.
With pure fragrant waters mixed with liquid black aloe-wood,
as stated in the *Puraścaraṇacandrikā*:
"Then, one should perform a fire-oblation (*homa*) every day with a tenth part of the number of recitations (*japa*)."
Alternatively, when the number of recitations reaches one hundred thousand, one should perform the fire oblation (homa).
Or rather, one should perform a fire-oblation (homa) equal in number to the recitation (japa) once that [recitation] is completed;
because of the separate mention of "upon the completion of a hundred thousand" (lakṣapūrttau), this refers to cases where the preparatory rite (puraścaraṇa) consists of many hundreds of thousands.
As stated in the *Siddhasārasvata*: "Having thus performed the recitation, one should perform the ten-part oblation with blue lotuses."
The practitioner of mantra should offer oblations with *akoda* fruits and satisfy [the deity] with a tenth part of that amount.
In the *Matsyasūkta*: "The practitioner should perform the fire-oblation (*homa*) with *vilva* leaves as a tenth part [of the recitation].
The consecration of the fire for the purpose of the oblation is to be observed in the section on initiation (*dīkṣātaraṅga*). In the *Sārasaṃgraha*:
Then, having worshipped the deity in water with a tenth part of the oblations (homa),
one should offer libations upon the head with water, reciting "I satisfy" at the end of the mantra.

Then one should perform the ritual sprinkling (*mārjana*). Thus Vaiśampāyana says: "Reciting the mantra ending with 'namas', using a tenth part of the libation (*tarpaṇa*), one should sprinkle one's own head with water by means of the mudrā called *kumbha*."
In this context, they apply the formula: "I consecrate such-and-such [person] upon the head. The *kumbha-mudrā* has already been explained in the section on the daily bath (*nityasnāna*).
However, in the *Vīracūḍāmaṇi*, it is said:
"At the conclusion of the libations (*tarpaṇa*), the master of the great mantra should perform the consecration."
On ground smeared with cow dung, one should draw a lotus petal.
One should place a water-pot (kalaśa) there and worship the Kalā with fragrances, dūrvā sprouts, aśoka flowers, and mango shoots.
Having honored [the deity] with offerings such as perfumes and flowers, one should worship thoroughly;
having uttered the Mātṛkā-mantra, one should recite each individual mantra.

One should sprinkle [the water] upon the head while reciting the words "I consecrate you" (*abhiṣiñcāmi*). Then, with a tenth part of that which was used for the cleansing (*mārjana*), one should feed the devotees of one's chosen deity and the *kaulikas* using the aforementioned substances.
In the Tantra: "For Brahmins who are unable to perform the fire-sacrifice (homa) and other rites, the recitation (japa) is doubled;
for the other castes, however, it is three, four, or five times [the standard number]."
The doubling and so forth [of the recitation] is in relation to the fire oblations (*homa*) and the like. As stated in the *Sanatkumāra-tantra*:
"Whichever limb [of the ritual] may be broken, the recitation (*japa*) for that should be double the number [of oblations].
In the absence of oblations, the recitation should be performed four times the number of the oblations. (328)
For Brahmins and Kshatriyas, the quality is said to be sixfold;
for Vaishyas, it is eightfold. This is the rule regarding their women as well.
Whatever caste a Śūdra relies upon, he should follow the prescribed rules for that [caste].
As stated in the Agastyasaṃhitā: "If one is unable to perform the fire-oblation (homa), or the worship, or even the libation (tarpaṇa)..."
By reciting the mantra that many times and by propitiating a Brāhmaṇa with that same number [of offerings], [the goal is attained].
In this case, the *puraścaraṇa* rite indeed consists of only two components.
For women and *śūdras*, there is only the recitation (*japa*) as prescribed in place of the fire-oblation (*homa*), even if they possess the capacity [to perform it], but no *homa*.
This is because of the scriptural injunction: "Women and *śūdras* must not perform a *homa* preceded by the utterance of mantras."
In the Vārāhī Tantra: "The twice-born have the authority for the tantric rite of homa;
however, if he is desirous, even a Śūdra may perform the rite of homa."
"Having abandoned the wife of Vahni (the *svāhā* mantra), *namaḥ* is prescribed at the end of *svāhā*"; thus it is stated in the Tantra:

"The recitation (*japa*) which has been prescribed by the wise for the twice-born in the absence of fire-offerings (*homa*), that very same [recitation] applies to beautiful-browed women and to Śūdras who are devoted to them."
In general, however, it has already been stated that for Śūdras there is a fivefold [repetition].
In the *Puraścaraṇacandrikā*:
"Having thus performed the *puraścaryā* correctly, the most excellent of practitioners..."
At the conclusion of that, one should perform a great worship and feed the Brāhmaṇas.
One should honor one's own guru with many garments and ornaments;
by satisfying the poor and the helpless, the mantras of practitioners attain accomplishment.
In the determination of the components of the fire-sacrifice (homa): "For one who is self-restrained, mantras grant success through recitation, fire-offerings, and worship;
it is traditionally taught that mantras grant success even through threefold recitation."
In the *Kulamūlāvatāra* and the *Rudrayāmala*:
"O Goddess, without food, without libations,
and even without fire-offerings, one should recite the mantra three times over for the sake of attaining success."
Now, regarding the specific details for the *vīra-puraścaraṇa*:
therein, the time for recitation (*japa*) and other rites is exclusively the night. It has already been stated that the rosary (*mālā*) is made of *mahāśaṅkha* (great conch).
As for another specific detail, it is stated in the *Kulacūḍāmaṇi*:
During the period of *puraścaraṇa*, one should worship the Supreme Śakti with garments,
flowers, and other offerings, as well as with foods consisting of milk-rice (*pāyasa*), for one who has been initiated.
Having brought [the disciple] into an empty house and purified him with arghya water,
one should perform the rite of nectarification (amṛtīkaraṇa) and lead him before the Śaktis.

Having brought together the substances and other items required for the worship of Śakti, one should perform the *amṛtīkaraṇa* (the rite of transformation into nectar) upon them. Thus it is said: "Having consecrated all those [substances] with the water of the *arghya* according to the prescribed rule, one should perform the *amṛtīkaraṇa*, and thereafter the *sakalīkaraṇa*."
Herein [are described] the rites such as the *amṛtīkaraṇa* for the Śaktis. He speaks of the Śaktis to be worshipped:
"Now I shall describe the eight maidens, since they bear the form of the Goddess:
the Brāhmaṇī, the Kṣatriyā, the Vaiśyā, and the Śūdrā, who are the ornaments of the Kula."
A courtesan, the daughter of a barber, a washerwoman, and likewise a female ascetic.
All these auspicious women of noble family, endowed with exceptional skill and discernment,
became filled with indignation upon seeing the eightfold variety of the maiden's forms.
They are designated by the names of the eight powers beginning with Brāhmaṇī;
their forms are white, black, and so forth, and they possess qualities such as gentleness.
The names of the Śaktis are to be stated in the hymn that will be recited later. He describes the manner of worship:
"Having first offered a seat, one should again say 'Welcome';
then [offer] water for the guest-offering (arghya), water for the feet (pādya), water for sipping (pānīya), the honey-mixture (madhuparka), and water."
One should bathe [the image] with water scented with perfumes and flowers, and perform the grooming of the hair;
then, having fumigated the hair, one should offer a silken cloth.
Then, having spread a seat in another place and placed a pair of sandals there,
she sat down, adorned with various ornaments.
Having adorned her with unguents, one should offer perfumes and garlands;
having invoked each respective power, one should bring them together at the head [of the image].
In the center of the dining pavilion, within a beautiful golden vessel,
[he placed] food to be chewed, sucked, licked, drunk, eaten, and even crunched.
When they may be uninitiated, then one should offer [the oblation] to Māyā.

Regarding the phrase "to that and that": the meaning is that one should invoke that specific Śakti upon the head of whichever [deity] has been designated by its name, and then worship her. Furthermore, this invocation, though mentioned in the middle [of the ritual], ought to be performed at the very beginning in every case.
Because it is seen thus:
there, one should perform the hymn of praise upon their left ears;
that is the Śaktistotra.
O Mother Goddess, salutations to you, O sinless one who bears the form of Brahman;
out of compassion, remove my obstacles and grant me the perfection of the mantra.
O Maheśī, O boon-granting Goddess, whose form is supreme bliss!
Out of compassion, remove my obstacles and grant me the perfection of the mantra.
O Kaumāri, sovereign over all obstacles, who delights in the play of Kumāra,
please remove my impediments and grant me the accomplishment of the mantra.
O Goddess who bears the form of Viṣṇu, O rider of the great Garuḍa!
Out of compassion, remove my obstacles and grant me the perfection of the mantra.
O Vārāhī, O boon-granting goddess, you who lifted the earth with your tusk!
Out of compassion, remove my obstacles and grant me the accomplishment of the mantra.
O Goddess who bears the form of Śakra, worshipped by the gods beginning with Śakra,
please remove my obstacles and grant me the accomplishment of the mantra.
O Cāmuṇḍā, adorned with a garland of severed heads and smeared with blood, O destroyer of obstacles!
Out of compassion, remove my obstacle and grant me the perfection of mantra.
O Mahālakṣmī, O destroyer of great delusion, agitation, and torment!
Out of compassion, remove my obstacles and grant me the accomplishment of the mantra.
O Goddess, who consists of father and mother, yet is beyond father and mother;
O Goddess, who are both one and manifold, whose form is the universe—salutations be to you!
Whoever, being well-restrained, recites this hymn at the commencement of an undertaking,
or upon seeing a clever woman, no obstacle shall arise for him.
If they are overcome by modesty regarding the meal, they should stand outside the house and recite the hymn of praise until satiety is produced.
Having sipped water for purification, one should offer mouth-fresheners such as betel-leaf (*tāmbūla*).
Likewise: "Then one should again offer a garland and auspicious, streaked sandalwood paste.
Having bid farewell, performed circumambulation, and requested a boon, one shall become happy."
If no other women go— neither one's own daughter, nor one's younger sister,
nor an elder sister, nor a maternal aunt, nor one's mother or her co-wife.
A female friend, a relative, or even a married woman who is childless—
whichever is available in the absence of the preceding one— should be honored, for women are portions of myself.
O Kulabhairava, if even a single young woman there is honored or beheld,
then all the goddesses are thereby honored.

331) And this [rite] should be performed at the beginning, the middle, and the end of the preliminary practice (*puraścaraṇa*). For it is said in that very same [text]: "If one does not worship one's beloved wife at the beginning, the end, the middle, and especially upon the completion of a hundred thousand [recitations], then one is destroyed by obstacles."
In the *Vīracūḍāmaṇi*: "First, having thoroughly purified the site, one should have a beautiful altar constructed with level lines;
there, in the center, one should place a severed head."
One should perform the smearing with honey and draw an eight-petaled lotus in the center;
one should know that the pairs of vowels are to be written in sequence, starting from the east.
One should write the eight groups [of letters] there, and in the center, one should draw a temple;
likewise, one should place the Sky (ha) joined with the Bindu (m), and similarly Lāṅgalīśa (la).
Then, O beautiful lady, one should write [the syllables] with the visarga upon the filaments;
having worshipped the foundation and so forth there, the wise man should establish the seat.
Having sat down on a seat anywhere— even one without a cushion— the hero should strike the ground three times with his heel and then snap his fingers three times.
The wise one should perform the binding of the directions with the Astra-mantra, starting from the east in due order;
[he should worship] Pinākīśa, adorned with Nāda and Bindu, at the end of the hair-tuft (vakeśānte).
Having uttered the word *paśu* and the supreme weapon-mantra at the end of *ramā*,
this is the Vidyā known as Pāśupata, which destroys all obstacles.

The letter *va* is Vakeśa; the letter *la* is Pinākīśa. Having first performed the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*) preceded by the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) according to the injunctions, one should likewise draw a mandala on ground smeared with cow dung.
One should perform the anointing with either honey or yakṣakardama.
The lotus is delineated with thread, its lines perfectly even and captivating;
it is red, white, or green in color, with black petals and beautiful filaments.
In the center of that [mandala], which is square and richly adorned with beauty, is a pair of yonis;
and in the center of that is a triangle. One should contemplate the void within the void.
One should unite with the radiant woman there and worship the mantra;
having installed the Goddess right there—she who has beautiful eyes and a slight smile.
A sixteen-year-old maiden, who has not yet borne children, who is ascetic, self-controlled,
dressed in pure garments, and laughing with a fearless, loud laugh.
She possesses intense purity and firm conduct; her hair is disheveled and she is naked, or else she wears the yogic gesture (yogamudrā) and is devoted to the practice of yoga.
At the time of sacrifice, one should worship Mātaṅgī and Tantukārī— who destroys the fear of the ocean of worldly existence— endowed with such mantras.
One should approach a maker of beds, a leather-worker, an artisan, a barber’s wife,
or especially a woman of the marketplace, who is tender and adorned with beautiful flowers.
One should place within them the general offering (sāmānyārghya), the special offering (viśeṣārghya), one’s own vessel, and the vessel of the Śakti,
along with the substance produced from the nectar of equanimity (sāmarasya).
The wise one should purify each [element] with the mantra of the five principles (tattva-pañcaka):
the fire-sun digit, the moon-digit, and finally the heart-mantra.

One should draw a triangle in the center, with another triangle beginning with the letter A; likewise, [the letters] from Kha to Ṣa, from Na to Ya, and from Dha to Śa, along with their respective enemies.
Joined with the left ear [the letter *v*] and adorned with the *bindu* and *nāda*,
this mantra known as Ratneśvarī consists of the five jewels.
Having worshipped with the sixfold ritual alone, one should consecrate [the offering] with the root mantra;
then, O Mahogratārī, one should personally perform the inner sacrifice, the internal worship.
Having raised Kuṇḍalinī within the three-footed one who flows along the triple path,
and having filled the vital breath into the channel, [one perceives] there the arising of the sound (nāda).
One should contemplate there the smoke-colored [light] arising from *nāda* and *bindu*,
shaped like a *kadamba* bud, situated within the cavity, and consisting of dissolution.
The universe consists of Śiva and Śakti, whose nature is a stream of nectar;
it arises from their bliss as the supreme Śiva, both manifest and unmanifest.
In that regard, one should display the mudrā of Mahābauddha, which has arisen or emerged as the supreme refuge; therein, one should show the mudrās of Mṛgī, Haṃsī, and Vajriṇī.
O Goddess, one should satisfy each [deity] here on the crown of the head three times;
one should contemplate them on the crown at the three periods of the day, proceeding in order from the south to the north.
One should worship Vyomakeśa and Ūrdhvakeśa, and then again Nīlakaṇṭha; afterwards, one should worship Nādānta, preceded by Vyomāmbā.
One should likewise worship Ūrdhvakeśa, Nīla, and the divine streams (divyaughas),
as well as Matsya, Kūrma, Vasiṣṭha, and Maheśvarānanda.
One should worship Tārā, Bhānumatī, Jayā, Vidyā, Mahodarī, and Ambāntā in the center, and with devotion, Ekajaṭā Śivā.
Thus is to be known the flood of Siddhas, the lineage of the gurus of the tradition:
Sukhānanda, Parānanda, Pārijāta, and Kuleśvara.
Likewise, Virūpākṣa is formidable and terrifying to the multitude of men;
he beholds Suṣumṇā, the supreme intellect, as well as Paśyantī and Vaikharī.
One should meditate upon Nīlasarasvatī, the speech-lordess of the Pārijāta tree;
having first joined the three Tārās, one should recite the mantra ending with "namas."
Having worshipped the row [of letters] on the head, and having gratified one's own name at the *mūlādhāra*, one should satisfy the power Kuṇḍalinī according to the procedure of the five mudrās.
Meat, fish, mudrā, sexual union, and the fifth beginning with the letter *ma*—wherever these are present, there is the Goddess; of this there is no doubt.
Wine is not the *mādhavī* wine; wine is that which arises from the power of *śakti*. Suṣumṇā and Śaṅkhinī are the fish; the supreme *unmanī* is the *mudrā*.
That sexual union, which is the manifestation of the nectar of aesthetic oneness, is Sadāśiva.
The divine, the heroic, and the animal, as well as the threefold drink—
the hero who delights in the animal and the drink is to be consumed by the hosts of yoginīs.
The hero who delights in divine drink attains union with the Goddess; the teacher, through the drinking of the hero's drink, goes to the world of the Goddess;
but the practitioner, by drinking the drink of the bound soul (paśu), shall go to the Raurava hell.
Having unified the prāṇa and apāna breaths, with the mind steady in pratyāhāra,
one pierces the solar orb and enters this center of the mandala.
Constantly raining down streams of nectar through the path of the Suṣumṇā,
this is declared to be the supreme divine drink that bestows all spiritual accomplishments.
Having abandoned the entire accumulation of the roots of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) and the substratum (*āśaya*),
one should offer libations by means of the five principles (*pañcatattva*) through the yoga of the Kaulika conduct.
One should offer the substance accompanied by mantras according to the sequence of the six cakras;
this is meditation, worship, the state beyond [ordinary] states, and the unsurpassed heroic drink (vīrapāna).
One who is attached and greedy for gain through deceit, without engaging in the purpose of the mantra, is a hypocrite;
one who is lustful regarding the assignment of tasks is called a "drinker of cattle" (paśupāna). 334)
Also in the Siddheśvara Tantra: "The power which resides in the root-tubers, having the form of a serpent—this [universe] is born from its whirling motion; therefore it is so described by the wise."
Moving, clearly sweet, and warbling, she likewise arises;
going through the aperture of Brahmā, she enters her own abode.
One should effect the dissolution of the mind there through the very process of going and returning;
by that, the crest-jewel of mantra is born, which illuminates all accomplishments.
Likewise, in a house possessed by darkness, nothing is perceived;
similarly, in a mantra devoid of its crest-syllable (śikhā), there is no accomplishment even in ten million eons.
This internal sacrifice (antaryāga) must be performed even during the daily worship (nityapūjā) by the initiate (paśu), prior to the placement of the arghya water.

In the *Svatantratantra*: "Having worshipped the Goddess at night according to the rule with meat and wine, the initiate, naked and even if possessed by the flow [of sexual fluids], should then take pleasure with a naked woman."
Then, having recited [the mantra] one hundred thousand times, one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) for the Goddess in a blazing fire.
The practitioner should offer clarified butter, fish, meat, and likewise fruit situated in the vulva-shaped sacrificial pit;
he should satisfy [the deity] with liquor mixed with meat in the tenth part [of the offering].
Having consecrated the tenth part of the libation (tarpaṇa) with [the mantra] consisting of the universe,
one should feed a virtuous practitioner who is dear to Kālikā as the tenth part.
One should cause wine, meat, fish, and chewed food to be offered;
then, O beloved, one should gratify the Guru with devotion by means of gold and other gifts.

And although this was stated with reference to the Kālikā-mantra, nevertheless, because of such statements as "As is Kālī, so is Tārā," they practice it here as well. For this very reason, it is also said in the Vīracūḍāmaṇi:
"One should perform the libation according to rule with a stream of blood, [observing] the prescribed number."
Or with honey, clarified butter, wine, milk-rice, or even water.
In this regard, the distinction is that [the means may be] a hero, a deity such as Surā, an animal, water, and so forth. As stated in the Agastyasaṃhitā:
"O Maheśvarī, by the perfect accomplishment of a single mantra and through the worship of its five limbs, all mantras become effective through Your grace."
In the *Tantraśekhara*: "For one who acts in this manner, during the first three years, many inauspicious obstacles arise, such as the loss of faith and so forth."
In this matter, if the practitioner (mantrin) remains with an undisturbed mind and is confident that "it will succeed," then he shall attain accomplishment (siddhi).

335) On the day of commencing the initiation (*dīkṣā*) and the preparatory rites (*puraścaraṇa*), or on the day of their completion, one should pray for a dream at night. The method for doing so has been explained in the *Dīkṣāyāga* itself. Now, the signs of success (*siddhi-cihna*).
In the *Vakratuṇḍakalpa*: clarity of mind, contentment of the intellect, moderation in eating, aversion to sleep,
and the perception of vehicles and other such things in dreams— these are the immediate signs of one who has attained perfection.
In the Bhairavītantra: "One sees light everywhere, or the body endowed with radiance;
or indeed one's own body as consisting of the deity."
In the *Nāradapañcarātra*: "O Nārada, for one who is capable of propitiating the mantra and remains steadfast in his observances, many obstacles arise during the first three years."
If the practitioner does not experience agitation through either action or mind,
then from the third year onwards, even kings and sovereigns [will be subdued].
Even those who are proud and full of self-respect entreat others out of consideration;
O Lord, please grant your grace for the sake of my deliverance.
And seeing her blazing with splendor and majesty,
O tiger among sages, they were unable to speak harshly to her.
From the ninth year onwards, the king of mantras becomes self-perfected;
indeed, various wonders consisting of mantra-siddhi arise within the heart.

O Brahmin, these [means] quickly bestow extreme bliss both externally through direct perception and internally; yet one of dull intellect remains delighted for only a moment, and then for another moment [is despondent].
For a moment he hears the sound of drums resounding in the sky,
and for a moment he hears sweet music accompanied by various songs.
For a moment he smells fragrances produced from camphor and musk;
for a moment, moreover, he sees himself by means of his own self as if leaping upward.
For a moment, the twice-born man should gaze at the sky filled with the rays of the moon and sun,
and for a moment he should listen to the roars of elephants, cows, and bulls.
For a moment, the yogin even draws toward himself the various stars situated in the sky, along with the agitation of the overflowing clouds.
He always sees those possessing mantras either grasping [the teachings] for a moment,
or for a moment making shouts of joy (*kilikilārāva*), as well as sounds like those of swans or peacocks.
For a moment one may see the rising of clouds, and for a moment, while night and day exist, one sees the light of day with the sun even during the night. (336)
He was filled with strength and like the sun in splendor;
he resembled the full moon in beauty and was like a bird in his gait.
Endowed with mature tranquility, profound depth, and ease,
he does not become emaciated by eating very little, nor does he suffer even when eating much.
Indeed, there is a reduction in excrement and urine, as well as victory over sleep;
the practitioner of mantra engaged in recitation and meditation does not experience fatigue.
O Sage, for periods such as a fortnight or a month without food or drink—
by such signs that cause great wonder.
"Those engaged [in the practice] should fully understand that the King of Mantras has become propitious.
Baudhāyana says: "There are three signs of success: the giver, the enjoyer, and the non-beggar. In the *Prapañcasāra*: "Then, as he recites the mantra, these signs of conviction arise for him."
A house blessed by a lamp at night becomes free from darkness.
By his splendor, he becomes like the sun; O Lotus-born One, she shall be his constant servant;
diseases perish instantly at his sight, and he becomes surrounded by wealth and grain.
The gods always offer salutations to him, and serpents do not bite his children.
Having protected his grandsons, friends, and elders during times of calamity, he departs for the supreme abode of Viṣṇu.
In the *Phetkāriṇītantra*: "If one does not attain success due to a powerful karma that is non-obstructive, one should perform the rite again two or three times.
This refers to another preliminary practice (*puraścaraṇa*).
An alternative *puraścaraṇa* has also been prescribed for one who is unable to perform the previously mentioned *puraścaraṇa*.
In the *Muṇḍamālā*:
"Starting from the eighth day of the dark fortnight until the next eighth day of the dark fortnight..."
When it has been recited one thousand times, the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) is considered complete.
In the seat of Candra— beginning from Mahālakṣmī up to Amahānavamīśvarī—
it is recorded in the Śākta-mantra that [the period] from Kṛṣṇāṣṭamī to Navamī occurs in the month of Madhu.

The bright fortnight (śuklapakṣa) occurs in the months of Ūrja, Tapas, or Rādha during the Vaiṣṇava year; however, in the Īśa year, it is traditionally held to end on the eleventh lunar day (ekādaśī), while in Phālguna, it ends on the fourteenth (bhūta).
In the month of Bhādrapada, however, it is for the King of Obstructors (Gaṇeśa); but for Māgha and Bhādrapada, it begins from one's own day of birth.
For other mantras as well, the previously mentioned Navarātra applies.
The recitation (japa) should be performed with the Mātṛkā-mantra from the morning until midday;
at night, it should be carried out for the duration of one watch (yāma), subsisting on water, roots, and fruits.
In the fourth watch of the night, the oblation for the *mālāmantra* should be performed as a tenth part [of the recitation];
for other mantras, the oblation is considered to be either a twentieth part or a tenth part.
And the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) should be given here as prescribed; one should not practice stinginess regarding wealth.
In this way, the mantra indeed becomes fit for application; of this there is no doubt.

In the Muṇḍamālā: "Having reached the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight during a great festival, one should perform worship especially on the night of the eighth and ninth days while [the deity] is engaged in ascetic practice."
On the tenth day, one should perform the breaking of the fast with fish, meat, and other such foods;
devoted to a spirit of faith, one should daily recite the mantra six thousand times.
Likewise: "Alternatively, the *puraścaraṇa* is described in another manner:
beginning from the fourteenth day [of the lunar fortnight] until the next fourteenth day."
O Maheśānī, when that many recitations have been performed, the *puraścaraṇa* is considered complete;
indeed, by mere recitation alone, the mantras become perfected.
Especially through the offering of bali-homa and other gifts during the worship of the sacred seats (pīṭha), one attains the Yonipīṭha,
the Mahāpīṭha, and likewise the supreme Kāmarūpa.
One of these two is to be worshipped, while the other is like the body of Rudra.
In the Kālītantra: "Alternatively, the *puraścaraṇa* is desired by another method:
on a Tuesday or a Saturday, a human skull is procured."
Having mixed it with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and especially with sandalwood and other ingredients,
one should deposit it in the ground within a forest, measuring half a cubit in depth.
If, on that day, during the night, the practitioner recites the mantra alone a thousand times, he shall become a wish-fulfilling tree.
In that very same [text]: "Alternatively, the *puraścaraṇa* is described in another manner:
having brought a corpse, it is buried right there at its door by means of that very [corpse]."
From that day until the end of the day, for as long as one hundred and eight [times], he shall become the lord of all siddhis; no doubt should be entertained in this matter.
"On those days" means on Saturdays and Tuesdays. "In that same manner" means up to the measurement of half a cubit (*hastārddha*).
The ellipsis (*anuṣaṅga*) is that one should recite [the mantra] one hundred and eight times every day. In that very [text]:
"Alternatively, the preparatory rite (*puraścaraṇa*) is described by another method."
On the eighth or the fourteenth day of both fortnights.
338) Beginning from sunrise until the next sunrise,
by reciting [the mantra] during that interval, one shall become free from all affliction and a master of all accomplishments.
In this context, even the fire-oblation (homa) and other rites must be performed, because of the scriptural injunction regarding the *puraścaraṇa* (preliminary observance).
As stated in the *Kālītantra*: "Alternatively, the *puraścaraṇa* is described by another method:
during an eclipse of the moon or sun, from the moment of first contact until liberation [from the eclipse]."
Having recited the mantra as many times as the number [prescribed], one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) and other rites that many times.
In the *Sanatkumāra-saṃhitā*:
"Alternatively, there is another method for the procedure of the purificatory rite (puraścaraṇa)."
And having bathed during an eclipse of the moon or the sun, with a restrained mind, one should [perform the rites].
With undistracted mind, one should recite the mantra beginning with contact (saṃsparśa) and ending with liberation (vimokṣa).
Having seen [the deity], bathed, and made the formal resolve (saṅkalpa), one should perform the recitation (japa) until liberation.
A pure man should perform the fire-oblation and other rites until the end of the eclipse;
by reciting the mantra in this manner, the accomplishment of the mantra will surely occur—of this there is no doubt.

The word "tāvat" (so many) means as many recitations as have been performed. And this [practice] pertains to the subject of Gopāla; they say this because the statement originates from Sanatkumāra. By the word "pumān" (a man), the prohibition of *homa* for women is permitted [as an exception].
In another tantra: "At the eclipse of the moon or the sun, being pure and having previously fasted, one should stand in water reaching to the navel in a river that flows to the ocean."
Alternatively, having bathed in pure water, being composed and in a clean place,
one should perform the recitation with undistracted mind from the moment of touch until liberation.
Immediately thereafter, one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) and other rites in sequence, using a tenth part [of the total count];
at its conclusion, one should perform a grand worship and feed the Brahmins.
Then, for the sake of accomplishing the mantra, one should worship and satisfy the guru;
thereafter, the knower of mantras should perform the ritual applications (prayoga) as set forth in the Kalpa texts.
In the *Ratnābali* and other texts, it is stated regarding the *Candrapīṭha* and the revelation of the mantra-deities:

"Having performed three days of fasting, or likewise according to one's capacity; or, in the case of an eclipse, the *śrāddha* and other rites may be performed in extreme brevity, merely upon the first contact."
Standing in water reaching up to the neck in a river flowing to the ocean,
one should perform the recitation (japa) until its completion, followed by the fire oblation (homa) and other rites consisting of a tenth part of that number.
Having given the complete sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), one shall attain the perfection of the mantra;
thereafter, the knower of mantras should perform the ritual applications (prayogas) as set forth in the ritual manuals.

339) Here, the term "contact" (sparśa) refers to the cognition of contact; otherwise, because that moment is subtle, there would be invalidity characterized by the absence of performance [of the ritual].
That which is the seeing of Rāhu with the eye is called "grasping" (grahaṇa).
In that regard, one should perform the ritual actions; for they are not [determined] merely by counting.
Thus, from the Smṛti statement:
"Likewise, no other time is praised for [performing rites] than the time of a solar eclipse and so forth;
yet, one who, out of regard for the Śrāddha, [performs it] during an eclipse of the moon or sun..."
He who does not perform the preliminary practice (puraścaryā) will undergo maturation in hell.
According to this statement, the preliminary practice (*puraścaraṇa*) for the recitation of mantras is indeed mandatory for practitioners.
And thus: "The *śrāddha* ceremony must certainly be performed even at the cost of one's entire wealth during the appearance of Rāhu;
he who does not perform it out of atheism sinks like a cow in the mud."

Thus, in the context of the *śrāddha* ritual, this explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) expressing censure according to the *smṛtis* refers to those other than the initiated (*dīkṣita*). However, some authorities prescribe the *śrāddha* by means of Brāhmaṇas and others; while others state:
"In the absence of food, in the absence of twice-born men, during travel abroad, or upon the birth of a son..."
A Śūdra himself should indeed perform the Hemaśrāddha during a planetary eclipse.
According to this statement, some desire to perform the *puraścaraṇa* after having given some gold dedicated to the ancestors (*pitṛ*).
Alternatively, the *puraścaraṇa* is desired in another manner:
specifically during the autumn season, from the fourth to the ninth lunar day.
Having worshipped with devotion, one should then recite the mantra a thousand times alone at night in a solitary place, a dwelling of total darkness.
One should be intent on fasting from the eighth day until the ninth;
such a person shall become a lord of all accomplishments—of this there is no doubt to be made.

In the autumn season, during the fortnight of the goddess, one should recite [the mantra] six thousand times; that is, from the fourth day until the ninth, one should recite six thousand times every night, and observe a fast on the eighth and ninth days—this is the meaning. As stated in the *Muṇḍamālā*:
Alternatively, the *puraścaraṇa* is described in another manner:
the great annual worship (*mahāpūjā*) which is performed during the autumn season.
In that case, being especially intent on the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa),
one should be devoted to fasting from the eighth day until the ninth.

One should worship with devotion at night and perform six thousand recitations (*japa*). Here, it appears that the *japa* begins on the first lunar day (*pratipadā*) and continues until the ninth day (*navamī*).
In the *Kālītantra*: "Alternatively, the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*) is described by another method."
At the junction of time on the eighth day, there was a bower of one hundred and eight creepers.
Having entered and diligently worshipped them according to the prescribed rite, the minister,
having followed the previously mentioned ritual manual, should perform the worship and other rites.
This Kāmadeva alone should mutter [the mantra] one hundred and eight times;
having muttered it at the base of their leaves, he should collect [the essence] and place it upon his head.

Great accomplishment (mahāsiddhi) occurs immediately from the sight and worship of the creeper at the junction of the eighth [tithi], that is, at the junction of the eighth and ninth [tithis]. The "house of the eight-and-a-half creepers" is the temple of passion (madanamaṇḍira), the abode of the Śaktis up to the eighth, as far as they may be found.

The previously mentioned ritual procedure is called the *dūtīyāga*. Having recited the seed-syllable (*bīja*) upon the "three roots" (*trimūla*), that is, the excellent organ (*varāṅga*), one should cast it away;

then, having taken that very same seed-syllable and applied it to the head—that is, having made a forehead mark (*tilaka*)—this [rite] is intended for the hero (*vīra*). This should be understood as applying to what follows as well. Likewise:
Alternatively, another method for the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) is described:
having drawn [the deity] into the house of a kula woman and having written the mantra itself [there].
Having worshipped there, performed the consecration, and offered it to her,
and having muttered the mantra a few times, he should lead [the disciple] forth, intent upon the state of the deity.
Having dismissed her and paid homage, one should sleep oneself while well-restrained.
In the morning, having offered the *bali* to the women, there is no doubt that the mantra will be perfected.
The *saṃskāra* is as stated in the *Pañcamayāga*; here, however, there is only worship and not [the other rites].
It should also be noted that there is communal enjoyment (*saṃbhoga*).
Having brought the Guru and established him, one should perform the worship of the Lord as if he were a deity,
and likewise satisfy the Guru with garments, ornaments, gold, and other such offerings.
Having honored his son, his daughter, and his wife,
and having worshipped them and recited the mantra, one shall himself become a master of supernatural powers (siddhīśvara).
Thus ends the eighth wave in the *Tārābhaktisudhārṇava* composed by the Great Professor, the illustrious Ṭhakkura Narasiṃha.
The Ninth Wave:
Now, the Vīrasādhana from the Yoginīhṛdaya.
The Goddess said: O Blessed One, knower of all dharmas (and mantras), expert in all scriptures!
Previously, you have indicated that the preliminary rite (*puraścaryā*) is to be performed in a cremation ground.
"Tell me now, if you have affection for me. The Lord said:

all the Bhairavas, the Gandharvas, and the Yogins.

Likewise: having wrapped the cloth used for binding the jar with the root mantra, one should again wrap another cloth over it, and anoint the limbs with the root mantra.

Having brought [the body] to the cremation ground himself, the practitioner, free from fear, should be accompanied by friends who hold weapons in their hands and are endowed with qualities equal to his own.

if the practitioner there is afraid, the practitioner should likewise [look] toward the four directions.
For the sake of protection, he should station his own guru, his circle of brothers, or even Brahmins of firm vows, as well as his friends, at some distance away.
If he is not proclaimed as Bhairava alone,
then the best of practitioners, having gone to a cremation ground that has not been washed clean, [should proceed].
If one generally causes the collection of bones to be washed, [it is done] with the root mantra ending in the weapon-mantra (*astra*).
In the *Vīratantra*: "In the sacrificial grounds, there is sprinkling with the root mantra ending in the weapon-mantra."
Having meditated upon the pair of the Guru’s feet, as well as Gaṇeśa,
Vaṭuka, the Yoginī, and the Mātṛkās, beginning with the left foot.
And those gods who are stationed here, as well as the terrifying rākṣasas, piśācas, siddhas, yakṣas, gandharvas, and hosts of water-spirits;
May the yoginīs, the mothers, the bhūtas, and all the women who move through the sky be the bestowers of siddhis here, and likewise be my protectors.
Having prostrated with this mantra, one should cast three handfuls of flowers toward the Lord of the Cremation Ground,
Bhairava Kālabhairava.
The knower of mantras should diligently worship Mahākāla in the four directions beginning with the east using water for the feet and other offerings, and thereafter present the bali offering.

"Seize, seize the yoke that wards off obstacles;
then, having said 'Accomplish my success,' grant it accompanied by svāhā."

Having first extracted the offering for Bali on the east, one should bring forth the offering for Bali on the south;
and after [the offering] for Mahākāla ending with *hūṃ*, one should extract it on the west as before.
In the western direction, one should assign [the mantra] to Kāladeva, beginning with the *praṇava* (oṃ);

One should cause the supreme bali offering to be given with a mantra beginning with the Praṇava;
at the end of "hūṃ sarvagaṇanāthān," one should likewise place the word "adhipati."
Having placed it on the head in a cremation ground, one should extract it as before;
O beautiful one, having offered the *bali* with the syllable *Tāra* (Oṃ) and so forth, and with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*).
Having performed the sprinkling of the bones, one should again install the seat-mantra;
one should install that seat-mantra there upon either birch bark or a banyan leaf.
In another tantra: "Then, having gathered the heap of bones from the west into one, [one should worship] again with the mantra:
*oṃ hrīṃ ādhāraśaktaye namaḥ*."
Having sprinkled it with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), one should write the mantra "Hsauḥ" on birch bark or a banyan leaf, and then install that [mantra] there once again.

Having placed a seat made of wool cloth and so forth there, one should worship the foundational power (Ādhāraśakti) with the mantra "Oṃ Namaḥ" and likewise worship [the seat] beginning with the syllable Hrīṃ.

In the Vīra-tantra: "Having spread out a seat upon that [ground] and having assumed the vīrāsana posture there, O Goddess of gods, one should cast clods of earth in all directions with the 'Vīrārdana' [mantra]. (344)
O Goddess, [the mantra consists of] the two seed-syllables of Kūrca, followed by a pair of Māyās; then:
Kālike, Ghoradaṃṣṭre, Pracaṇḍe, Caṇḍanāyike.
Having said "dāraya" (tear asunder) for the Dānavas, he then said "hana" (slay) twice;
thereafter, he said "chedaya" (cut down) twice for the great hero, the enemy of heroes.
This mantra for the subduing of Virādha consists of the armor (*varma*), the weapon (*astra*), and ends with *dviṭha* (svāhā).

In the midst of that, the god Bhairava is not overcome by obstacles;

Protected by all those various friends, one is not overcome;
[using] a wick made from the fibers of the arka, indu, sita, vātyāla, and tūla plants.

If it be a single-syllable mantra, one should then recite it a thousand times;
for a two-syllable mantra, eight thousand times; and for a three-syllable mantra, fifty thousand times.
