beginning from midnight until sunrise.
One thousand and eight [recitations] are like a thousand elephants-destroyers;
if there is unbearable fear, one should bind the ears and eyes with a cloth.
Then, until midnight, if nothing whatsoever is perceived, [success is attained].
One should offer the *arghya* with the *Jayadurgā* mantra and scatter mustard seeds with that same mantra:
"Oṃ, you are sesame, whose deity is Soma; you are the essence of the cow-sacrifice (*gosava*), the cause of satisfaction."
You are the bestower of the creation of the ancestors, the protector of mortals,
and the bringer of peace amidst obstacles caused by bhūtas, pretas, and piśācas.
Having thus scattered sesame seeds there in four portions, beginning with Śiva,
one should then walk seven steps and return once more to that very spot. Having performed worship there in this manner, one should worship the supreme mantra.
"One should recite the mantra fearlessly until success is attained;
however, fear should be understood as being like a dream, and on the following day one should perform the remaining rites. Thus it is said.
In the Vāmakeśvaratantra: "At the conclusion of the recitation, one should offer a bali-oblation to the deity according to the prescribed rite, having taken a buffalo, a goat, or even a boar."
With a joyful mind, he should go home together with his circle of friends.
Thus concludes the ritual procedure for preparing the funeral pyre.

Now follows the ritual procedure for using a corpse as the means of accomplishment (*śavasādhana*), as stated in the *Bhūtaḍāmara*: "That which has been declared in the *Bhāvasarvasva* and kept secret in all tantras..."
For this is the procedure for the accomplishment of the Hero, taught by Śambhu, the God of gods.
By the mere knowledge of which even one of dull fortune attains success;

In the *Vīratantra*: "Having taken up the previously mentioned offerings and so forth, the practitioner should accomplish the success (siddhi) beneficial to himself and resort to a place for practice."
The wise person should rely upon everything previously mentioned, beginning with meditation on the Guru;
in the earth-element at the end of the piercing of the hero, neither illusion nor delusion exists.
With the mantra beginning with "ye cātra," one should offer three handfuls of flowers upon the ground;

One should scatter mustard seeds in all directions while reciting the mantra known as Jayadurgā.

One should also scatter sesame seeds with the mantra "tilo 'si.
[The victim may be] pierced by a spear, pierced by a trident, pierced by a sword, or restored to life by water.
One pierced by a rope, one bitten by a snake, or one overcome by outcasts;
a youth, handsome, heroic, radiant, and lost in battle.
One who is devoid of flight, one who is most skilled in facing the enemy in battle,
one who has died by his own will, a two-year-old child, an old woman, and likewise a twice-born man.

Having abandoned one of the previously mentioned corpses— whether it be one that died from lack of food, one who died of leprosy, or likewise one who has been dead for more than seven nights— one of these eight types.

even if it has been seized by outcastes or the like, it quickly bestows the fruit of accomplishment.

and sacrificial wood pieces, measuring twelve finger-breadths, should be placed in the cardinal directions.
Accept this offering; cause a pair [of attendants] to accept it.
Having dispelled all obstacles, bestow success—*ṭha* twice.
With this mantra, one should first offer a bali-oblation containing meat;

Having prepared the seat and worshipped it,

Having placed kusha grass beneath his feet and having smoothed back the hair of the corpse,

The wife is seized and led away by the Pālakas; one should abandon fear of them.
If one is not agitated there, then what indeed cannot be obtained?

The goddess, assuming the form of a woman, and the man, assuming the form of a brahmin, shall indeed say the words "Choose a boon" three times; at the end of those three times, one shall obtain a boon.
If a woman, whether virtuous or even unvirtuous, grants her boon,
then what on this earth cannot be accomplished for that heroic lord?
A man who is sinless and well-refined within his family,
while a queen who is unrefined, will undoubtedly be joined with sin.
Whether in his presence or even in his absence, whoever speaks another [word] in Sanskrit is that very Goddess; of this there is no doubt—that is Bhairava himself.
If it were not thus, then because the body is enveloped by illusion,
one would not choose a boon there, nor would one ever declare "this is a boon."
If he speaks in refined Sanskrit, such should be said;
otherwise, one should accept the excellent and unconfused teaching according to the oral tradition of the Kaulikas.
Alternatively, one may obtain some intense benefit for oneself;
or a true reputation arises, or even the nectar of immortality is attained.
Having investigated everything, one should accept it; thus has the direction been proclaimed.
The forms of the Goddess are manifold, appearing sometimes in human and other such forms.
One must certainly be afraid there; one should never have confidence in that place, for the Bhairavas and Vaṭukas are devoted to the Kula scriptures.
In connection with this treatise, one should describe the magical rites (*kṛtyā*) of crooked form:
having become a son, one should choose [him as a husband], and having become a woman, one should delude him.
Therefore, a hero devoted to reality should exert effort in his conduct.
Once truth has been realized and the boon obtained, he should abandon recitation and the like;
knowing that the fruit has been attained, he should then release the *juṭikā* (the topknot).
Having thoroughly washed and arranged [the area], one should release the *juṭikā* at the feet;
having cleansed the circle of the feet (*padacakra*), one should cast the materials of worship into the water.
350) Having cast the corpse into water or into a pit, one should perform a ritual bath;
then, having gone to one's own home and offered a bali-oblation, on the following day—
On this final night, whatever deities I am sacrificing to,
may they accept this offering of food along with meat given by me.
Then, having given horses, men, elephants, and boars as requested—
though made only of flour— one should observe a fast.
In another tantra it is also said: "Whether made of barley flour or of rice flour, one should cause it to fall according to the rule with the sword Candrahāsa and its respective mantra."
On the following day, having performed the daily rites, one should then drink the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and feed twenty-five Brahmins there.
Or having taken five or five [verses] up to ten in succession,
one should then bathe, eat, and dwell in an excellent place.
If there were no food to be offered to the Brahmins, then one would fall into poverty;
and if, because of that, poverty should occur, then the God becomes enraged.
One should guard the Kula practice for three nights or six nights;
if one should engage in sexual intercourse on the bed, then disease will arise.
Having heard a song, the deaf man [regains his hearing], and from seeing a dance, the blind man [regains his sight]; yet if he speaks a word during the day, then he shall fall back into muteness.
For the residence of the Lord within the body lasts for fifteen days;
one should never, under any circumstances, utter disparagement against cows, Brahmins, or the gods.
Being pure, one should touch deities, cows, Brahmins, and others every day;
moreover, at the conclusion of the daily morning rites, one should drink water from bilva leaves.
Then, when the sixteenth day has arrived, one should bathe at a sacred ford or similar site;
having recited the root mantra ending with "svāhā," one should utter the words "I satiate, obeisance."
In this manner, after three steps, the libation for the gods is performed with water;
however, for one who omits the libation for the sages (munis), there can be no libation for the gods.
*Tarpaṇa* means satisfaction. By this procedure, one certainly attains perfection; having enjoyed excellent divine pleasures here, one goes at the end to the abode of Hari.
Having performed this very sādhana, one shall become most beloved by Śakti.
The practice of Vīrasādhana should be performed either in the absence of a corpse or in a cremation ground;
for if one does not worship with those very elements that have been prescribed for it, [the rite will fail].
By such a sequence of practice, the practitioner becomes fallen;
one should not teach the internal state therein, nor should one prescribe worship therein.
"Having reached the edge of the cremation ground, purification is thereby produced.
Thus ends the ninth chapter, the procedure for the *vīrasādhana*, in the *Tārābhaktisudhārṇava* composed by the Great Mahopādhyāya, the illustrious Ṭhakkura Narasiṃha.
The Tenth Chapter:
Now follows the description of the six rites for specific desires.
In the Kālītantra: "First, one should perform the preliminary service (puraskriyā) according to rule and according to the prescribed method;
thereafter, the practitioner whose mantra has been perfected is fit for ritual application (prayoga), and not otherwise."

In the *Phetkāriṇītantra*: "The rites of pacification and so forth should be commenced according to the rules based on the conjunction of the day of the week and the lunar date; that [system] is now being fully explained."

The wise proclaim the six rites (ṣatkarma) to consist of pacification (śānti), subjugation (vaśya), immobilization (stambhana), then inciting enmity (dveṣaṇa), expulsion (uccāṭana), and finally killing (māraṇa).
The fifth, second, third, and likewise the seventh lunar days,
when conjoined with the weekdays of Mercury and Jupiter, are highly esteemed for rites of pacification.
The sixth, when joined with Jupiter and the Moon, as well as the fourth,
thirteenth, seventh, eighth, and ninth lunar days, are recommended for rites of nourishment (pauṣṭika).
The tenth and eleventh lunar days, when conjoined with Sunday or Friday;
for the purpose of attraction (ākarṣaṇa), the new moon day, the ninth, and likewise the first lunar day.
The full moon day conjoined with Saturn is for the rite of inciting enmity;
likewise, the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight and the eighth day on a Saturday are auspicious lunar days for the rite of eradication,
especially during the evening watches.
The fourteenth and eighth days of the dark fortnight, as well as the new moon day,
when joined with the days of Saturn or Mars, are recommended for rites of killing.
The fifth lunar day joined with Wednesday or Monday, as well as the tenth and the full moon,
should be known as the appropriate dates for the rite of immobilization (stambhana).
One should perform auspicious acts when the moon is rising in an auspicious sign, and inauspicious acts when it rises in an inauspicious one;
one should perform fierce deeds on a Riktā tithi when the sun is there, and the act of killing during the Mṛtyu yoga.

*Ījya* is Jupiter. *Manda* is Saturn. *Kārṣṇī* refers to that which pertains to the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*). *Āra* is Mars. According to the *Piṅgalāmata*: "Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim the presiding deities of the days of the week, the lunar dates, and the asterisms:
for Sunday it is Sūrya; for Monday, O Goddess, it is Śiva and Antaka (Yama); thereafter [for Tuesday]..."
353) On Tuesday, Maṅgala and Guha; thereafter Budha and Viṣṇu;
on Thursday, Guru and Caturvaktra (Brahmā); on Friday, Bhṛgu and Purandara (Indra); and on Saturday, Śanaiścara and Kāla—these, O Goddess, are proclaimed as the lords of the days.
Regarding the enumeration of the lords of the lunar days (tithis):
Brahmā, Vidhātṛ, Viṣṇu, Yama, Śītakara (the Moon), Guha, Indra, the Vasus, the Nāgas, Dharma, Śiva, and Divākara (the Sun).
O Goddess, on the new moon day (darśa), Manmatha, Kali, the Viśvedevas, the lords of the lunar days (tithīśvaras), and the ancestors (pitaraḥ) are to be worshipped with all ritual offerings.
The enumeration of the lords of the lunar mansions:
the two Aśvins, the two Yamas, Vahni (Agni), Brahmā, Indu (Soma), Śiva, Aditi, Guru (Bṛhaspati),
Kadrūja (Tvaṣṭṛ), the Pitṛs, Bhaga, Aryaman, and the Sun.
Tvaṣṭṛ, Vāyu, then Indra and Agni, Mitra, and Indra are dear to you;
likewise Nirṛti, Water, the Viśvedevas, and Prajāpati.
O Goddess, Viṣṇu, the Vasus, Varuṇa, Ajapādaka,
Ahirbudhnya, and Pūṣan are declared to be the deities of the lunar mansions.
O Goddess, on those days one should worship these [deities] with all ritual offerings,
using their names preceded by the Praṇava and ending in the dative case.
In the Brahmayāmala: "In rites of killing, one should avoid Brahmins and others who are very righteous;
one should employ [such rites] against enemies of the king, excluding women."
One should perform that [rite] either out of one's own anger or for the sake of protecting the worlds;
however, a practitioner of mantra should never perform a rite of killing out of greed or fear.
O Goddess, an expiation must be performed for the pacification of that fault;
the practitioner of mantra should recite [the mantra] ten thousand times and offer oblations that many times, O Īśvarī.
O Goddess, honored by heroes, the wise should always perform self-protection at the time of ritual action using ghee, milk-rice, or sesame seeds.

In the *Pañcamīśvarītantra*: "O Goddess, having performed the rites for cruel actions according to the prescribed rule, the wise one, having been anointed with oil and bathed again, [should worship] the Goddess together with her limbs and her retinue."
O Daughter of the Mountain, having worshipped and offered oblations to the deity for the sake of self-protection,
O Beloved, one should recite the mantra with a tranquil mind one thousand and eight times.
Having said, "Protect me, protect me," and having prostrated before Śivā, one should dismiss her;
however, one should have one's protection ensured by other very affectionate friends.
O Goddess, by means of that mantra, such as the Mṛtyuñjaya and others,
one should perform practice through recitation, fire-offerings, worship, and the like, as well as through the propitiation of Brahmins and other such rites.
The Necessity of Cakra-pūjā:
In the Kulārṇava it is said— "At the conclusion of the ritual application, the practitioner of mantra should likewise perform the worship of the cakra;
endowed with meditation and ritual placement (nyāsa), the practitioner should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times."
For the sake of pacifying defects in the ritual application and for the sake of self-protection,
if one does not do so, one will not obtain the fruit due to the curse of the deity.
And this refers to an even more cruel object. Thus:
"For those who perform rites for the sake of desired results, there is no world beyond;
the attainment of the rite itself is their fruit, and nothing else exists."
For a single injunction, O Goddess of the Gods, no two fruits are ever seen anywhere; therefore, one should worship the deity without desire for rewards.

In another tantra: "Having recited the Gāyatrī ten thousand times, having performed the rite that destroys obstacles to success, and having performed the *abhyudaya-śrāddha*, one should observe the rule of eating only sacrificial food (*haviṣya*)."

Having ascertained the planetary positions and other factors of the enemy, a wise person should commence the ritual application for killing and so forth; otherwise, undesirable consequences will ensue.
If the time for the enemy is auspicious, one should certainly not act;
when Mars, Rāhu, Ketu, and the Moon are in his eighth house.
If Tvaṣṭā or Nabhas is in a quadrant (kendraka) and the lord of the ascendant has set,
or if it is situated in the eighth or sixth house, or is situated between malefic planets;
Likewise, when the lord of the twelfth house is situated among malefics, and the *āpa* (water) planet is located in the *klima* (the eighth house),
being combust and having set, then one should commence the rite of killing (*māraṇa*).
Others, however, say that if there should be astrological configurations (yogas) indicating an undesirable outcome,
one should first ascertain this from the science of astrology (jyotiḥśāstra) and then commence rites such as killing.
Having thus understood the allotted lifespan and the ripening of the periods (daśās),
an application made by men when the life span is real will be fruitless.
If the planetary period (daśā) of Mars, Saturn, or Rāhu occurs,
then the most excellent of mantra-practitioners should perform the rite of killing.

355) When the enemy is under an inauspicious asterism, or when the moon, the day of the week, and the lunar date are likewise unfavorable, yet one's own ascendant and the time for the respective ritual application and so forth are auspicious; [then one should act].
A practitioner of mantras, adhering to the prescribed ritual, may commence cruel rites when the lord of the ninth house,
the lord of the third house, and the lord of the ascendant belong to the enemy [sign].
If the Moon and the aspect should be together in one place, or if they aspect each other, then one should perform the rite of eradication; otherwise, misfortune will befall.
If the apprehension of the goal is defective, then the month and likewise the year are also defective;
it is certain that one should not perform any auspicious rite for such a person.
Having performed a great worship of the deity with diligence at the commencement,
and having carefully honored the preceptor, one should also feed the Brahmins.

In the Kulārṇava: "Having understood the lunar days, weekdays, asterisms, karaṇas, yogas, months, seasons, and fortnights, as well as the diagrams of the Lord of Lamps and the Tortoise, one should accomplish the ritual acts."
The *kūrmacakra* has been described previously. Likewise:

"Having understood the five purifications, the postures (*āsana*), breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), ritual assignments (*nyāsa*), the rosary (*akṣamālikā*), the defects, the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*), the aggregates (*rāśi*), and so forth, one should accomplish the rites."
The defects are cutting and so forth; the refinements are birth and so forth.
As for the wheel of the zodiac signs (*rāśicakra*), it is as follows: among the signs, [the mantras] are *bāla*, *gaura*, *khura*, *śoṇa*, *śamī*, and *śobhā*.
The letters beginning with 'śa' are traditionally held to be the differentiated forms of vowels within the maiden.

The twelve zodiac signs (rāśis) are: the Ascendant (lagna), wealth (dhana), siblings (bhrātṛ), friends (bandhu), children (putra), enemies (śatru), wife (kalatra), death (maraṇa), dharma, action (karma), income (āya), and expenditure (vyaya).
Likewise, by means of the mantra belonging to one's own second sign, [one seeks] wealth; by means of that belonging to the fifth sign, [one seeks] children.
One should perform the ritual application for the sake of a wife using the seventh zodiac sign; in this manner, other matters should also be inferred.

Here, on the wheel of the zodiac signs and lunar mansions (*rāśi-nakṣatra*), whichever sign or mansion the first letter of the name falls upon—just like the mantra—that alone is the zodiac sign and lunar mansion of the practitioner, and not his birth sign or birth mansion.

If that were the case, the drawing of this wheel would be purposeless, as there would be no determining factor for its being intended for the mantra alone. With reference to the zodiacal wheel (*rāśicakra*), it is said:
"By means of that first letter of the mantra and the first syllable of the name..."
One should count that which is the sixth, or the eighth, or the twelfth.
356) "The mantra of an enemy would have unfavorable syllables; that would not be beneficial for him.
This is because of the statement in the *Tantrarāja*. In reality, however:
"For one whose birth asterism (*janmarkṣa*) is manifest, [the calculation] should be made from that birth asterism."
One should declare that the birth asterism has been lost for him whose name-asterism is missing from the calculation.

Thus is the established rule according to the statement of Piṅgalāmata. Likewise: "Having understood the compatibility with the letters of the zodiac signs known as Koṣṭha, Bāndhava, and Tārā, as well as the friendship of the elements and the Yantra, one should accomplish the mantras."
The grid-wheel beginning with *makatha* and so forth. As stated in the *Tantrarāja*:
"By means of five threads extending east, west, south, and north, there shall be sixteen squares here; one should write the letters in them in sequence."
One should indeed arrange those [deities] in four groups of four in successive order:
the first [deity] in the first of the first [group], and likewise in the first of the second [group].
One should arrange a second [syllable] from another [source], and likewise imagine yet another;
one should write each respective fifth syllable in its corresponding squares.
In this manner, one should write up to the stage of *kṣānti* within the four squares,
such that the first letter of one's own name is clearly visible in whichever square it falls.
Regarding the counting of the *siddha* and other classes: one should count the *siddha* and others until the first syllable of the mantra is seen.
Through recitation, a *siddha-siddha* mantra is perfected; a *siddha-sādhya* is perfected by double that amount.
The *siddha-susiddha* is attained; the *siddhāri* destroys one's kin;
the *sādhya-siddha* results from extreme affliction; and the *sādhya-sādhya* causes great suffering.
A *sādhyasusiddha* [mantra] grants success through worship; a *sādhyāri* [mantra] takes away one's own fortune;
and a *susiddhasiddha* [mantra] bestows the desired fruit simply through study.
Through recitation and other practices, the *susiddha-siddha* becomes successful; otherwise, it is not.
However, the *susiddha* [mantra] is perfected for one who has exerted effort in a previous birth.
Therefore, one should employ that mantra for the accomplishment of all siddhis;
otherwise, if it is not properly mastered, it will certainly destroy one's own lineage entirely.

A mantra that is *ari-siddha* (conquered by the enemy) kills one's son; one that is *ari-sādhya* (to be mastered by the enemy) destroys one's own wife; but a mantra that is *ari-su-siddha* (well-mastered by the enemy) brings about the destruction of one's entire lineage.
The mantra that destroys one's own self is certainly an enemy as soon as it is attained.
However, in the *Piṅgalāmata*, it is said: "A *siddha-siddha* [mantra] is accomplished from what has been prescribed; a *sādhya* [mantra] by twice the number of recitations (*japa*);
a *susiddha* [mantra] by half that number of recitations; but its enemy [the *ari*] destroys one's kinsmen."
If the recitation is successful despite obstacles, that which is to be accomplished is achieved; however, if it is obstructed, it is useless.
A *susiddha* [mantra] is perfected by half a recitation; it destroys enemies born in one's own lineage.
A *susiddhasiddha* is perfected by a quarter-recitation, and a *sādhyasusiddha* by double that number of recitations.
If that [planet] is well-accomplished (susiddha), it destroys the enemy and the class of one's kinsmen;
if it is accomplished by the enemy (arisiddha), it kills the son; but if it is to be accomplished by the enemy (arisādhya), it kills the daughter.

"If that [name] is well-established, it is a killer of one's wife; if it is an enemy [of the mantra], it destroys the practitioner. Thus, in the *Piṅgalāmata*: "Whether it be a name that is already well-known, or his birth-name, or that which was given by the Guru through the casting of flowers for ascetics (*yati*)."
One should cause the letters of that very name to be divided [into syllables].
Elsewhere it is said: "The name well-known in the world, or one given by the mother or likewise by the father.
Elsewhere also: "That by which one who is asleep wakes up, and one who is far away speaks."
Even if one is distracted by another thought, the name [of the deity] should be uttered here;
for it is said elsewhere: "The name given by the mother or father must be purified with great effort."
And as for that which is stated: "Having observed [the first letter] from the syllable of the birth-star, there the first syllable of the mantra [is to be determined]."

Thus it has been said. That which is well-known by the very name given at birth is the primary one; for that alone is the enumeration of the *siddha* and other classes stated for each syllable. Furthermore, there is the name given by the mother and father, as well as that bestowed by kinsmen.
Having indeed separated its phonemes according to the distinction between vowels and consonants.
In that very manner, one should then begin the purification of the mantra-syllables arising from the bindu,
the double-bindu, the upadhmānīya, and the tongue and feet.

Having abandoned the four neuter vowels, as well as syllables resulting from combined pronunciation, those with extra syllables, and corrupt (apabhraṃśa) syllables, [one should recite] one hundred thousand [times].
One should purify each letter of the name together with the syllables of the mantra:
the consonants with the consonants alone, and likewise the vowels with the vowels.
Having purified the first [syllable] with the first [mantra-syllable] and the second with the second,
when the syllables in either the mantra or the name are unequal [in number], [the following procedure applies].
Then, having commenced the mantra, one should employ it evenly;
O fair-faced one, in whichever mantra there are two accomplished syllables at the beginning and the end.
358) In a very short time, he shall become the bestower of all accomplishments;
however, one who possesses [the mantra] joined with the end and beginning of the sādhya is accomplished only with great difficulty.
That which is well-established at both the beginning and the end bestows the power of all desires;
however, that mantra whose beginning and end are hostile must be abandoned.
That which is accomplished at the beginning but difficult to accomplish at the end is mastered by doubling [the recitation];
that which is accomplished at the beginning and easily accomplished at the end is mastered through the recitation as prescribed.
If the final syllable is a *siddha* [letter] and the last enemy [of the mantra], it should be abandoned by the best of ministers;
however, even if it begins with a *sādhya* [letter], it is accomplished through recitation once it has been multiplied three times by the final *siddha* [syllable].
One who is initially *sādhya* and finally *susiddha* attains success through the prescribed method;
however, one who is initially *sādhya* and finally an enemy (*antyaśatru*) should be avoided with great effort.

One who is well-accomplished (susiddha) or superior to that is accomplished from the very moment it is stated; however, one who is well-accomplished or superior to that, ending with the "to-be-accomplished" (sādhya), requires four times [the effort].
One whose beginning is well-accomplished (susiddha) and whose end is an enemy (ari) is proclaimed as mediocre;
likewise, one whose beginning is an enemy (ādyāri) and whose end is accomplished (siddha) is also to be avoided in this ritual action.
Established at the beginning, middle, and likewise at the end, it bestows auspicious results;
it is declared by Svayambhū in the Tantra that such a [mantra] is effective for all purposes and remains indifferent [to obstacles].
One who has successfully mastered the three positions shall accomplish all goals;
however, a mantra whose enemy occupies the three positions is death, without a doubt.
A mantra beginning with a *siddha* and ending with a pair of *sādhya*s is declared by the wise to be useless.
The *siddha* group, beginning with *siddha* and ending with *dvisusiddha*, is the accomplisher of all purposes and effects.
The *siddha* group, beginning with *siddha* and ending with *ariyugma*, is proclaimed as the destroyer.
When [the planet] is an enemy at the beginning, a Siddha in the middle, and a Sādhya at the end,
there is accomplishment of the task with difficulty, and its fruit becomes very small indeed.
If there is an enemy at the beginning, and a pair of neutral planets in the middle, the task will be delayed;
however, it will perish very quickly at the end.
When that which is to be accomplished [sādhya] occurs at the beginning and end, that which is already established [siddha] arises in the middle;
when that which is already established occurs at the beginning and end, that which is to be accomplished arises in the middle.
Indeed, both of these—the *sādhya* and the *siddha*—are accomplished through an abundance of recitation (*japa*). Likewise, the *susiddha* becomes effective when it is encapsulated by the *ari*.
It should be known that this brings about the total destruction of the practitioner; of this there is no doubt.
(359) The object to be accomplished should be separated by a *siddha*, and it should be further separated by a *susiddha*.
"This mantra is accomplished quickly; so the Lord himself has declared.
Even if an enemy is shielded by one who is accomplished, or even by one who is highly accomplished, [this mantra overcomes him]."

That mantra would not be an enemy; however, it is accomplished with difficulty. But if even a *susiddha* (well-accomplished) mantra is intercepted by a *sādhya* (to-be-accomplished) one, it likewise [requires effort].
"Having observed such characteristics, one should avoid [the mantra] from afar.
A mantra corrupted by an enemy must never be given.
Thus it is also stated in the *Nārāyaṇīya*: "A mantra that abounds in corrupt syllables is censured."
The meaning is that one should accomplish one's own desired aim by means of a mantra that is favorable, and the undesirable aim of others by means of one that is unfavorable.
As stated in the Piṅgalā: "In all these defects, [one should employ] either Māyā or Kāma."
And first, having cast [the obstacles], one should bestow prosperity for the sake of liberation from the defects.
Regarding the phrase "the circle of stars, called Tārā": as for the circle of stars— for example, Ruru gave to Rudra a mountain as a hand-gift out of greed for wealth.
The local, the upapada, the suffixes, and the particles are distinguished among the [eight] categories beginning with nouns.
The letters, in their respective order, always occupy the portions of Revatī;
these are: birth, prosperity, adversity, security, enmity, accomplishment, and death.

"Mitra" and "paramamitra," as well as birth and so forth, occur again and again; here too, it should be understood as previously explained. In the *Vārāhītantra*: "The purification of the womb occurs in Varāha, and the *kulākula* [principle] belongs to Mahālakṣmī."
The wheel of names and so forth belongs to all, and likewise the wheel of the elements.
For the Vaiṣṇavas, there is purity of the stars; for Śiva, purity of the square (koṣṭha);
for the Traipura, there is purity of the zodiac signs (rāśi); and for Gopāla, the akaḍama is prescribed.
Regarding the "uncompleted wheel" (*akaḍamacakra*):
one should write the letters beginning with *ṇa*, *ṣa*, *ṇḍha*, *ka*, *na*, and so forth, in the sequence of the signs starting from Aries (*meṣa*).
Therein, one should determine the status as "accomplished" (*siddha*) and so on, starting from the first letter of one's own name.
"Bhūtamaitrī" means the wheel of the *kulākula*.
Now, the method for the examination of the *kulākula* wheel is being described.
360) Wind, fire, earth, water, and space are the fifty letters in their respective order.
There are five short vowels and five long vowels, ending with the bindu and arising from combinations;
the consonants beginning with *ka* and ending with *la*, *sa*, and *ha* are likewise proclaimed in groups of five.
If one should know that the first syllable of the practitioner and likewise the first syllable of the mantra have the same deity, then that indeed is his own family (kula).
The earthly, the watery, the friendly, and even the fiery and the windy [elements]—
among the earthly syllables, the windy is considered their enemy.
The element of fire is the enemy of water, and likewise, the element of fire is the enemy of water;
however, the element of space is not in conflict with any of these.
A wise person should not bring together things that are mutually contradictory. Regarding the *khadyotacakra* machine, as it is said in the *Kulamūlāvatāra*:

Having drawn a wheel with edible offerings, one should write the letters beginning with 'A' (arka) and so forth, one by one, in the petals starting from the east, excluding the neuter (*niṣpaṇḍha*) and compound (*kūṭa*) vowels.
One should investigate starting from the first letter of one's own name;
when that letter arises, prosperity is indicated, while in the second, there is the destruction of prosperity.
In the third, however, one should know there is wealth; in the fourth, conflict with kinsmen;
in the fifth, one will be of a doubting nature; and the sixth is the destroyer of everything.
This is an illustration; one should also examine whether it is favorable to the *gaṇa*, *yoni*, *phaṇi* (serpent), *varga*, *cakra*, and *ṛṇadhana-cakra*.
[The *gaṇa-cakra*:]
As for the *gaṇacakra*: the asterisms Hasta, Āśvinī, Śravaṇa, Mṛgaśiras, Puṣya, Anurādhā, Aśvinī, Revatī, Punarvasu, and Jupiter are considered auspicious by the practitioners of mantras.
The three [asterisms] preceding and following [Punarvasu], as well as Ārdrā, Bharaṇī, and Rohiṇī,
are declared by the learned to be the group of asterisms dear to mortals.
Citrā, Āśleṣā, Mūla, Maghā, Dhaniṣṭhā, and Jyeṣṭhā are likewise [assigned to Varuṇa];
Varuṇa, Kṛttikā, Indra, and Agni are declared to belong to the host of Rākṣasas.
The highest affection exists between two women, while that between two men is middling;
it is said that the enmity between gods and humans, as well as between humans and great rākṣasas, is likewise intense.
Thus, the awakened one should apply the mantra to himself according to the ritual.
(161) Now, regarding the *yonicakra*: horse, elephant, goat, snake-pair, dog, bull, crow, ram, seasons, and mouse—

The female donkey, the cow, and then the buffalo; the tigress, the female buffalo, the tiger, the deer, the spotted antelope, the monkey, then the two types of brown bears, the ape, the lion, the horse, the king of beasts (the lion), and the elephant— such is the order of the origins of these animals.

The cat is the eater of bulls; the female buffalo is the *sairibhī*; the dog is the *maṇḍala*; the mongoose is the *vabhru*. The elephant is the *karaṭī*. As for enmity: the cow and the tiger, the elephant and the lion, the horse and the buffalo, the hawk and the mongoose, and the snake and the mongoose [are natural enemies].

"Having understood through worldly custom these great enmities— the monkey and the ram, as well as the cat and the mouse— and others too, those who seek auspiciousness should always diligently avoid this [conflict] between husband and wife, or even between a king and his servant. Thus it is said.
Then, having drawn the serpent-wheel (phaṇicakra) in sequence, one should place the twenty-seven lunar mansions there,
assigning numbers three by three from top to bottom.
The wheel should take the form of a serpent; this is what they call the *nāḍīcakra*.
Also in the *Yāmala*: "One should draw the wheel beginning with Aśvinī in the shape of a serpent consisting of three channels (*nāḍī*);
the asterisms for piercing the three channels are Aśvinī, Ārdrā, and the pair of Uttarās."
The Hastendra (Jyeṣṭhā), Mūla, Vāruṇī (Śatabhiṣaj), and likewise Pūrvabhādrapadā;
Yāmya (Bharaṇī), Saumya (Mṛgaśiras), Guru (Puṣya), Yoni (Pūrvaphalgunī), Citrā, Mitra (Anurādhā), and the two Phaṇis (Āśleṣā and Svāti).
Dhaniṣṭhā and Uttarā are auspicious when situated in the middle channel (nāḍī);
likewise are Kṛttikā, Rohiṇī, Āśleṣā, Maghā, Svātī, and Viśākhā.
Uttarā, Śravaṇa, and Revatī (Pauṣṇa) are situated in the *pṛṣṭhanāḍī*. Pūrvaphalgunī is the *yoni*. The two *paṇis* are Pūrvāṣāḍhā. And the result is as follows:
"He whose Guru, mantra, and personal deity are situated within a single *nāḍī*..."
In that case, one should predict the results as hatred, debt, and death, respectively.
Then, having determined the purity of the groups (varga-śuddhi) within the wheel of the eight groups, the most excellent guru should bestow the mantra.
The 'a'-group is to be known as belonging to birds, and the 'ka'-group belongs to the cat.
The *ca*-group is the lion, the *ṭa*-group is the dog;
the *ta*-group is said to be the elephant, and the *pa*-group is the mouse.
The *ya*-group is to be known as the elephant, and the *śa*-group as the goat and the ram.
(362) There is enmity between the Garuḍa and the serpent, and likewise between the elephant and the lion.
There is enmity between the cat and the mouse, as well as between the dog and the ram;
yet there is friendship between the serpent and the lion, and likewise between the ram and the mouse.

And that which is to be known as other than worldly [law] is derived from the application of legal practice (*vyavahāra*). Thus, in the *Manu-kaumudī* regarding debts, wealth, and interest: "Having ascertained the wealth and so forth, whether in the case of a *siddha* (a perfected one) or others, according to the *Manu* [code]."
The wise should proceed [in this way], for otherwise it would be fruitless.
One should draw nine excellent lines extending from south to north;
likewise, one should fashion solar lines extending from east to west.
The wise man should write two vowels each in five squares, and likewise others;
having written one letter each in six squares, he should then write the letters from *ka* to *ha*,
one by one, in eleven groups of three.
One should multiply the letters of the practitioner, distinguished by vowels and consonants, by the numbers ten, one, seven, eight, four, eight, seven, and six, respectively.
O Indra, the duration of a Manu is measured by the stars, the eyes, the sun, the fifteen seasons,
the Vedas, the fires, the weapons, the lord of serpents, and the nine [tattvas].
Then, one should place the numerical value of the letters of the name, starting from the first and ending with the last, in sequence;
this is multiplied by the value of the other [first] square, just as the fifth [square] is multiplied by five.
Thus, those who desire qualities are briefly concluded:
they consist of the states of the ruru-deer, fish, man, and garden, within the syllable of the practitioner.
Among the syllables of the mantra, however, the wise [should understand] mountains, lands, suns, and rivers; this is more than eight times the number of names, waters, and the like.
Having understood the debt of both, the knower of numbers should know the remainder to be greater;
and it is said that one should divide both by eight.
Where a preponderance [of the mantra] is observed, that is proclaimed as the debtor (adhamarṇa).
One should indeed take up those very mantras by which [the mantra] is held;
in their absence, one should never [take up] the creditor (dhanika) who possesses equal wealth.
In the Vārāhī Tantra: "If the mantra has an extra syllable, then the wise practitioner should recite it;
even if it is equal [in length], the practitioner of mantra should recite it, but he should not recite it if it is deficient."
One should recognize death in the void; therefore, one should abandon the void.
(363) The method for clearing debts according to the Kādima-tantra is as follows: starting from the first letter of the name up to the letters of the mantra and so forth.
"Having divided [the number] threefold and differentiated it by the vowels, the other is the reverse.

By "vowels," [it means] the seven vowels. Regarding "the reverse": Rāghavabhaṭṭa says that this refers to multiplying by seven and dividing by three; however, that is to be reconsidered, because when the practitioner's number is divided by three...
Because a number exceeding three digits is not possible;
therefore, its meaning is that the reversal occurs only in the calculation of the *ka*-syllables. In another tantra:
"The mantra to be accomplished, doubled and joined with the practitioner..."
One should divide by eight and take the remainder; the other [calculation] is the reverse of this. Thus it is said.

The meaning of this is as follows: one should double the syllables of the mantra, having separated them individually according to their nature as vowels (*svara*) and consonants (*vyañjana*). One should likewise double the syllables of the practitioner’s name, having separated them individually according to their nature as vowels and consonants, [and then join them] with the syllables of the mantra, each separately according to their nature as vowels and consonants.

One should divide [the total] by eight when they are combined. Thus is the heap of the practitioner (*sādhaka*). The meaning is that one should accomplish that which is undesirable for him who is the creditor (*uttamarṇa*)—that is, the mantra—and that which is desirable for him who is the debtor (*adhamarṇa*). Regarding the division of the wheels: "The wheel of Hara, the six-petaled wheel, and likewise the wheel beginning with Siddha."
And in the wheel of the zodiac signs and lunar mansions, as well as one's own family and non-family [lineages].
The Akaḍava, the Ākaṭhava, and likewise the Vargacakra—
these nine cakras have been described as those which bring about the accomplishment of mantras.
The mantra whose nature is purified by the nine wheels (navacakra) is effective for one's desired goal;
O Dear One, even the deliberation on the circle of the Gaṇas (gaṇacakra) is approved by some.
Now, the Wheel of Hara:
henceforth I shall fully explain the Wheel of Hara, which brings great prosperity;
by knowing which, one becomes a possessor of knowledge in this world and the best among those who know mantras.
"Otherwise, one should avoid the mantra," so said the Blessed Lord Śiva.
Therefore, with every effort, that wise person should deliberate upon this.
One should prepare the field for the deities, resembling a grid of stars;
in its center, one should divide it into four squares using diagonal lines.

The "star-square" (tārākoṣṭha) refers to the square of the zodiac signs. By this, there are four squares in the cardinal directions, four squares in the intermediate directions, and one square in the center. Regarding the phrase "four squares": since there is no laying down of a thread in the center, the state of being fourfold is established otherwise; for while the diagonal thread (*karṇasūtra*) would otherwise be merely the second [thread], when the four threads are laid out, [the configuration is complete].
The meaning is that the square becomes composed of four parts (*rāśi*).
One should place Durgā, Bāṇī, Tārā, and Bharavī in the cardinal directions;
on both sides of the diagonal line (*karṇasūtra*), one should join them starting from Īśāna and the other [directions].
364) Tripurā, Bhuvaneśā, Pīṭheśī, and Tryambaka;
Vāsudeva and Śrī, as well as Chinnamastā and Caṇḍikā.
[I worship] Vivasvat beginning with Īśāna, then Tvaritā in sequence,
as well as Indrākṣī, Heramba, and immediately thereafter Pitāmaha.

"Mahāmāyā, Kālī, and whatever other gentle deity [there may be]"—this refers to beginning with Īśāna. The meaning is "having made the northeast corner (īśānakoṇa) the first. This is because of the statement: "One should write the fifty letters in order, starting from the square of Īśa. Here, by the word "order" (krama),...
The inclusion of names derived from the directions is also intended.
A name bestowed by one's mother or father, refined by Vedic mantras,
and suitable for all ritual acts— such a name is praised when examining a mantra.
This, however, refers specifically to the wheel of Hara.
Beginning from the first letter of the name up to the range of the letters of the deity,
one should perform the grasping for the sake of purification, but never when it is impure.

One should contemplate wealth, a son, gain, and indeed loss in a state of agitation; liberation, happiness, and dharma, as well as even the fulfillment of desires; and the terrifying—this is declared to be the Wheel of Hara within the body.
In this regard, the sequence of circumambulation is as follows. Thus ends the wheel of Hara. In the *Vijayamālinītantra*:
"Mantras that have few defects and many qualities should be bestowed by the wise.
Thus, even in the case of mantras such as those beginning with Tārā, there is a requirement for consideration regarding their status as *siddha* (accomplished) and so forth.

Now, one might object: "Since there is no requirement for [attaining] the *siddha* state and so forth here, nor any concern regarding [the suitability of] friends and the like, according to the statements in the *Nīlatantra* and other texts concerning mantras such as the *tārā-dakṣiṇā*, why is there a need to consider those [factors] even in optional (*kāmya*) ritual applications? Thus:

One need not investigate the success (siddhi) and other stages regarding the mantras of Nṛsiṃha, Arka, and Varāha, nor the Praṇava temple-mantra, nor those mantras consisting of syllables together with their seed-syllables (piṇḍākṣara).
If it is asked: "How is this [system of] investigation applicable even to the applications of mantras compiled in other tantras?"—[the answer is:
"For the Nityās and the Traipuras, the [astrological] divisions such as the *aṃśakas* and so forth are not required.
Nevertheless, something is stated here for the sake of accomplishing rites such as *abhicāra* (sorcery)."

Accept this according to the statement from the *Tantrarāja*. And thus, for those seeking the practical application [of the rites], even when taking up mantras such as Tārā and others, the purification of the *koṣṭha*s and so forth follows as a necessity. Furthermore, it appears that the prohibition of such purification applies solely to those whose aim is liberation (*mokṣa*).
In the Tantra: beginning from sunrise, ten *ghaṭikās* in succession constitute the seasons, starting with spring, day after day throughout the day and night.
Spring, summer, the rains, autumn, winter, and the cool season—
winter is prescribed for rites of pacification, and spring for rites of subjugation.

The cool season (śiśira) is to be known for immobilizing (stambhana); the summer (grīṣma) is declared for creating enmity (vidveṣa); the rainy season (prāvṛṣ) is to be known for eradication (uccāṭana); and autumn (śarat) for the rite of killing (māraṇa).
In the *Phetkāriṇītantra*: "One should perform the rite of immobilization (*stambhana*) in the pitcher when Leo or Scorpio is rising;
rites such as inciting hatred (*dveṣa*) and expulsion (*uccāṭana*) [should be performed] when Capricorn, Cancer, or Libra is rising."
In Gemini, Virgo, Sagittarius, and Pisces, one performs rites of subjugation (vaśya), pacification (śāntika), and nourishment (pauṣṭika);
in the eighth sign from the enemy's [ascendant], one performs killing (māraṇa) and suppression such as cutting (cheda).

Haryakṣa is the lion; nakra is the crocodile; kulīra is the crab; aja is the ram; yama is the twins. Likewise: one should write for subjugation on the previous day at midday; for inciting enmity and eradication, one should write at the end of the day; for peace and nourishment, however, at the time of twilight; and for killing, at the same time.
One should draw the pillar for paralyzing at midnight, and for attracting before sunrise;
whatever other auspicious task there may be, the wise man should draw that at dawn.
In the northeast (Indra) is immobilization and eradication; in the southeast (Agni), all malevolent rites;
in the south (Yama) and the southwest (Rākṣasa), inciting enmity; and in the west (Varuṇa) and the northwest (Soma), pacification.
In the portion of the Maruts, one brings about the destruction of a family; in that of the Yakṣas, strife and conflict;
and in the station of Brahmā, one should not perform any auspicious rite.
One should write for subjugation and attraction on birch bark; one should write for eradication on a flag;
one should write for inciting enmity on the skin of a donkey; and for immobilization on elephant hide.
On a garment made of rags from a corpse, one should draw [the deity] for the purpose of killing those afflicted by fever, heat, and the like;
likewise, on a stone slab, one may draw it for the subduing of disputes, the immobilization of armies, and the bewitching of others.
One should draw [the diagram] for subjugation (*vaśya*) with saffron, camphor, *rocanā*, and turmeric;

for paralyzing (*stambhana*) and attracting (*ākarṣaṇa*), with barley-ash; for causing enmity (*vidveṣa*), with the blood of a jackal; and for killing (*māraṇa*), with the blood of a crow. One should also draw it with the blood from the ring finger.
Delusion [is achieved] with the blood of a wolf, and eradication with the blood of a camel.

Lac (alaktaka) [is used for writing]. With the blood of the ring finger—that is, with the blood from the ring finger. A jackal (pheru) is a wild dog (śṛgāla). Likewise: "For subjugation and the like, the pen is made of dūrvā grass; for attracting, a peacock feather;
for causing enmity and expulsion, a crow's wing; and for killing, likewise."
One should visualize [the deity] as red in color for subjugation, attraction, and immobilization;
and as white for neutralizing poison, pacification, nourishment, and replenishment.
One should visualize [the deity] as yellow for rites of immobilization, as smoke-colored for rites of eradication;
as resembling an indragopa insect for rites of insanity, and as black for the rite of killing. (366)
A seat that is white in form is declared to be *sāttvika*;
one situated on a path of travel and yellow in color is proclaimed to be *rājasa*.
The fierce and black [form] established upon the staff is said to be tāmasa;
it is sāttvika for those desiring liberation, and rājasa for those desiring sovereignty.
One should meditate upon the Tāmasa [form] for the purpose of destroying enemies, warding off all diseases,
and pacifying all calamities.

In the Kulaprakāśatantra: "One should worship with white substances for pacification (śānti), with reddish ones for the rite of subjugation (vaśya); one should worship with yellow-colored substances for paralyzing (stambhana) and with smoky-colored ones for creating enmity (vidveṣaṇa)."
For the rites of eradication and killing, one should worship with black substances;
at that time, one should likewise adorn oneself with such garments and other items.
Rati, Vāṇī, Ramā, Jyeṣṭhā, Durgā, and Kālī are declared to be the deities of the six rites (ṣaṭkarman) respectively; one should worship them at the beginning of each rite.
In the case of Kātyāyanī’s transgression, the earth was submerged by the southern ocean;
red clothing is prescribed, and a red turban is traditionally enjoined.
For the Saumya [planet], a sacrificial thread (yajñasūtra) made of gold or silver is prescribed;
for Stambhana and Vidveṣa, it is said to be made from the entrails of a cat.
The wise have declared that a sacrificial thread made from the entrails of a cock is used for rites of eradication,
while one made from the entrails of a dog is prescribed as the sacred thread (upavīta) for such purposes.
For the rite of killing, the sacrificial thread should be made from the entrails of an owl;
for subjugation and pacification, it should be made of *haviṣya* grain; and for paralyzing, it is considered to be made of milk-rice (*pāyasa*).

In rites for causing enmity, there should be food made of black gram or green gram; in rites dedicated to Vāyu, wheat; and in rites for Śāli rice or goat’s milk and rice-pudding, food made of śyāmāka grain or lentils.
Regarding the act of killing, it has been stated that this [victim] shall be the food; thus is described the restraint of eating.

For the performance of the six rites, the suitable postures are the lotus posture (padmāsana), the auspicious posture (svastika), the wide-legged posture (vikaṭa), and likewise the cock posture (kukkuṭa).
The wise call the *vajra* "auspicious" (*bhadraka*);
its characteristics are stated in another tantra:
having placed the right foot upon the left thigh, and likewise the left [foot upon the right].
Having firmly grasped the thighs with both hands according to the western method,
placing the two thumbs at the heart, and gazing at the tip of the nose while holding the chin [near it],
this is called *padmāsana*, which destroys various diseases for those who practice self-restraint.
Having properly placed both soles of the feet between the knees and the thighs,
sitting with the body straight— this is declared to be the Svastika posture.
Placing one foot upon one thigh while the other thigh is likewise positioned [upon the other foot],
this is declared to be the vikaṭāsana posture.
Having assumed the lotus posture (padmāsana) by placing the hands between the knees and the thighs,
and having established them on the ground, one performs the cock posture (kukkuṭāsana), which is situated in the void.
Having placed the left ankle above the penis and likewise above the other,
and having set the space between the ankles [below], this is called the vajrāsana posture.
One should place [the feet] at the ankle, below the testicles, and on both sides of the perineum;
having firmly bound the sides and feet with the hands, one should remain perfectly motionless.
This Bhadrasana shall be the destroyer of all diseases. Now, following the Tantras, I shall describe the support for the posture (āsana) and the determination of that support for the posture.
The skin of a leopard is for all accomplishments; the deerskin is for the accomplishment of knowledge.
A seat made of cloth removes disease; one made of cane increases prosperity;
that of silk is said to be nourishing; and one made of wool alone liberates from suffering.
In rites of sorcery, the color is black; in rites such as subjugation, it is red;
for pacification, white is prescribed; and for all rites, it is said to be variegated.
For the rite of immobilization, there should be an elephant hide; likewise, for killing, a buffalo hide;
for expulsion, a sheepskin; and for the rite of subjugation, a tiger skin.
For inciting enmity, a jackal skin is prescribed; for rites of pacification, it should be a cowhide;
and for the rite of subjugation, it should be at an auspicious temple.
Peaceful rites should be performed in the home, and fierce rites in the cremation ground;
alternatively, all rites may be performed in the temple of the deity.
The six mudrās suitable for the six rites should be known in their proper order as those called the lotus, the noose, and the mace;
one should display the ones named the pestle, the thunderbolt, and the sword during rites such as pacification and the others.
Having brought the two hands together facing each other,
with the fingers slightly bent and the thumbs joined at the palms— this is the mudrā known as Padma.
Having joined the index finger held in the left fist with the index finger held in the right fist,
one should strike the tips of one's own index fingers with the tips of the thumbs.
This mudrā, called the noose (pāśa), is proclaimed by the learned:
having placed the two hands facing each other with the fingers interlaced.
Furthermore, when the two middle fingers are joined and well-extended,
this is declared to be the *gadā-mudrā* (mace-gesture) of Viṣṇu, which increases his satisfaction.
Having formed fists with both hands, placing the right over the left—
this is the mace mudrā (muśalamudrā), which destroys all obstacles.
From the joining of the little finger and the thumb, it is known as the "Triangle Thunderbolt" (trikoṇāśani);
having bound the little finger and the ring finger with one's own thumb from the right side.
When the remaining fingers are extended and joined together, it is the *khaḍgamudrā*.
The fire-pits suitable for the six rites are square, semi-circular, triangular, and hexagonal.
And they are circular, with the shapes of the mandalas of earth and the other elements in sequence;
their colors are yellow, white, red, black, and smoky, respectively.
One should meditate on the mandala of air at the navel, conjoined with its seed-syllable;
one should contemplate the triangular, tawny-colored mandala of fire in the heart.
One should visualize a yellow square earth-maṇḍala at the throat,
and a white half-moon marked with two lotuses on the forehead.

One should contemplate consciousness within these [elements], which are joined with their respective seed-syllables, as a circular sphere of space (vyomamaṇḍala) of smoky hue located at the crown of the head.
Water is recommended for rites of pacification; fire is declared for subjugation;
earth is praised for immobilization; and space is celebrated for inciting enmity.
Vāyu is traditionally prescribed for the rite of eradication (uccāṭana), while Agni is considered superior for the rite of killing (māraṇa);
these should be correctly performed during the rising of their respective elements, conjoined with their corresponding maṇḍalas.
The mantra-practitioner, with a sharpened mind, should perform the respective ritual action;
the movement of the earth is rod-like beneath both the two cavities.
The movement of water is upward; that of fire is upward; that of the wind is horizontal;
and the movement of space is in the midst [of all]; this is known as the origin of the elements.

369) When the element of earth arises, the knower of the self should perform the rites of immobilization (stambhana) and subjugation (vaśya); when the element of water arises, he should perform the rites of pacification (śāntika) and nourishment (pauṣṭika). When the element of fire arises, [he should perform the rites of] attraction (ākṛṣṭi). When the element of wind arises, he should perform the rites of expulsion (uccāṭana) and killing (māraṇa). When the element of space arises, he should perform the rites of piercing (vedha), summoning (āhvāna), and the rest. One who knows the sequence of the elements should perform these rites according to the specific time of each element. Thus ends the thirty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Sequence of the Elements. The thirty-seventh chapter follows. The venerable one said: "O Mañjuśrī, listen now to the supreme method for the accomplishment of the mantra. I shall explain it in its entirety; listen with a focused mind. The wise one should first perform the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) for the sake of the accomplishment of the mantra. He should perform it for six months, or else for twelve months. Having completed the preliminary rite, he should then proceed to the stage of the 'attainment of power' (siddhi). He should worship the deity day and night with flowers, incense, and the like. He should offer food offerings (naivedya) and lamps, and likewise offer water for the feet (pādya) and water for sipping (arghya). He should offer various kinds of food and drink, as well as betel leaves and other such items. He should always offer fragrant flowers and incense. He should offer various kinds of fruit and likewise various kinds of grain. He should offer various kinds of meat and likewise various kinds of liquor. He should offer various kinds of garments and likewise various kinds of ornaments. He should offer various kinds of musical instruments and likewise various kinds of dance. He should offer various kinds of songs and likewise various kinds of praise. He should offer various kinds of prostrations and likewise various kinds of circumambulations. He should offer various kinds of offerings and likewise various kinds of service. He should offer various kinds of vows and likewise various kinds of observances. He should offer various kinds of fasts and likewise various kinds of penance. He should offer various kinds of gifts and likewise various kinds of charity. He should offer various kinds of mantras and likewise various kinds of mudrās. He should offer various kinds of meditations and likewise various kinds of concentrations. He should offer various kinds of recitations and likewise various kinds of contemplations. He should offer various kinds of rituals and likewise various kinds of ceremonies. He should offer various kinds of initiations and likewise various kinds of empowerments. He should offer various kinds of blessings and likewise various kinds of protections. He should offer various kinds of seals and likewise various kinds of knots. He should offer various kinds of diagrams and likewise various kinds of yantras. He should offer various kinds of mandalas and likewise various kinds of maṇḍalas. He should offer various kinds of seats and likewise various kinds of thrones. He should offer various kinds of vehicles and likewise various kinds of mounts. He should offer various kinds of weapons and likewise various kinds of implements. He should offer various kinds of armor and likewise various kinds of shields. He should offer various kinds of banners and likewise various kinds of standards. He should offer various kinds of umbrellas and likewise various kinds of canopies. He should offer various kinds of mirrors and likewise various kinds of jewels. He should offer various kinds of gems and likewise various kinds of pearls. He should offer various kinds of gold and likewise various kinds of silver. He should offer various kinds of copper and likewise various kinds of iron. He should offer various kinds of bronze and likewise various kinds of bell-metal. He should offer various kinds of crystal and likewise various kinds of lapis lazuli. He should offer various kinds of coral and likewise various kinds of amber. He should offer various kinds of agate and likewise various kinds of topaz. He should offer various kinds of emerald and likewise various kinds of sapphire. He should offer various kinds of ruby and likewise various kinds of diamond. He should offer various kinds of pearls and likewise various kinds of conch shells. He should offer various kinds of shells and likewise various kinds of cowries. He should offer various kinds of seeds and likewise various kinds of grains. He should offer various kinds of herbs and likewise various kinds of roots. He should offer various kinds of fruits and likewise various kinds of flowers. He should offer various kinds of leaves and likewise various kinds of bark. He should offer various kinds of wood and likewise various kinds of grass. The Maruts are prescribed for rites such as killing, as well as for the expulsion of adversaries and the destruction of poison and the like; they are also auspicious at the rising of the sky [the planet Jupiter].
The five elements, beginning with earth, are known as the kalās starting with Nivṛtti.
Nivṛtti is accompanied by Pratiṣṭhā; then come Vidyā and Śānti immediately after.
They are to be known as "Beyond Peace" (śāntyatītā), and they are to be worshipped in their respective places;
the addition of the name at the end of the mantra is called the "sprout" (pallava).
For killing, the neutralization of poison, the subduing of planets and spirits,
as well as for expulsion and inciting enmity, the sprout (pallava) is praised.
The placement of the mantra at the end of the name is designated as "yoga";
[it is used] in rites for pacification, nourishment, subjugation, expiation, and purification.
Wise men employ the yoga of *mohana* (enchantment) and *dīpana* (illumination);
it is also said to be used for *stambhana* (paralysis), *uccāṭana* (eradication), *udbheda* (separation), and *vidveṣa* (enmity).
The mantra should be placed at the beginning, end, and middle of the name;
this is desired as a "blocking" [seal] for bringing the mantra face-to-face and for warding off all diseases.

For the pacification of afflictions such as fever, planetary seizures, and poison, the *rodha* (obstruction) rite is prescribed; for the purpose of enchantment (*sammohana*), that same rite is used, as well as the syllables of the name of the mantra.
That which is knotted with a single interval between each is proclaimed as "grathana";
it should be employed for rites of pacification (śāntika), and likewise, the mantra should be placed at the beginning and end of the name.
That indeed is the *sampuṭa* (encasement), which is defined for the purpose of *kīlana* (nailing);
it is the *sampuṭa* used in *stambhana* (paralyzing), in the divine *mṛtyuñjaya* (conquest of death), and in divine protection.

The process by which each syllable of the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*) is sequentially interlaced with two syllables of the mantra is called *vidarbha*; it is employed for the rites of subjugation (*vaśya*), attraction (*ākarṣaṇa*), and nourishment (*pauṣṭika*).
Thus has the sequence of yoga been proclaimed by the wise for all undertakings.
One should employ *huṃ* in cases of binding, eradication, hatred, and mixed rites;
*phaṭ* in cutting; and *hūṃ phaṭ* for warding off obstacles and malevolent planets.
One should utter *vauṣaṭ* during nourishment and replenishment; *svāhā* during obstruction and defilement; *agnikārye* (at the fire-rite); and *namaḥ* everywhere during worship.

For pacification (śānti), nourishment (puṣṭi), subjugation (vaśa), hatred (dveṣa), attraction (ākṛṣṭi), eradication (uccāṭana), and killing (māraṇa), one should employ, in sequence: *svadhā*, *svāhā*, *vaṣaṭ*, *hūṃ*, *vauṣaṭ*, and *phaṭ*.
For subjugation, attraction, torment, and fever, one should employ *svāhā*.
The wise should employ "namas" for the pacification of anger, for tranquility, and for the cultivation of love.
Vauṣaṭ is used for enchantment, illumination, nourishment, and the Mṛtyuñjaya rite;
likewise, Hūṃ is used for the destruction of affection, as well as for cutting and killing.

*Vaṣaṭ* is prescribed for rites of eradication (*uccāṭana*) and inciting enmity (*vidveṣa*), as well as for causing lameness; it is also remembered for the purpose of kindling mantras and for matters concerning gain and loss.
Regarding the six rites, there are distinctions among mantras;
the classes of mantras are twofold according to the division into *mantra* and *vidyā*. Mantras are to be known as having male deities, while *vidyās* have female deities.
All mantras are declared to consist of female, male, and neuter natures.
Male mantras end with *hūṃ* and *phaṭ*, while those considered female end with *svāhā*.
The neuter [mantras] end in "namaḥ"; the *manus* are divided into three types.
These three kinds of mantras are for the rites of subjugation (*vaśya*), pacification (*śānti*), and malevolent magic (*abhicārika*).

The mantras for the cruel and gentle rites should be understood as being of the nature of Agni and Soma; they are said to end with the syllables *vahni* (ra) and *tārā* (oṃ), and to consist primarily of the element of space (*viyat*).

The *mantras* are of two types: fiery (*āgneya*) and lunar (*saumya*). Those that consist predominantly of syllables representing the nectar of the moon are lunar; those that awaken when the vital breath (*prāṇa*) moves through the right [nostril] are fiery.
When the vital breath (prāṇa) abides in another portion, the gentle ones attain awakening;
and when the vital breath has entered both channels, all attain awakening.
All these— the moon, water, the earth, the sky, wind, and fire— always bestow their fruits upon awakened practitioners who employ mantras.
The phonemes (varṇas) are the seed-syllables (bījas) of the mantras, corresponding respectively to the six rites (ṣatkarmasu).
Regarding the six rites, there are different types of recitation (japabheda); recitation is the repetition of its own syllables, and I shall now declare its various classifications.
Recitation is said to be of two kinds: vocal as well as mental.
The first is proclaimed to be of two kinds: whispered (upāṃśu) and loud (uccais);
the second is also said to be twofold, distinguished by the tongue and the mind.
When one recites the mantra with speech using high, low, and circumflex tones, with clear words and syllables,
that is called vocal recitation (vācika-japa).
One should recite the mantra slowly, moving the lips slightly;
that recitation which is audible to some extent is known as *upāṃśu*.
That which is performed by the wise using only the tongue is to be known as *jihvājapa* (tongue-recitation);
that which one should utter with the intellect while reciting the mantra is called *mānasajapa* (mental recitation).
Whispered recitation is ten times superior to loud recitation;
mental recitation is a hundred times superior to lip-movement recitation, and a thousand times superior to whispered recitation.
For those desiring spiritual accomplishments (siddhi), mental recitation is prescribed; for those desiring nourishment (puṣṭi), whispered recitation;
and for the purpose of killing (māraṇa), vocal recitation is said to be recommended.
Likewise: "One beginning with the *praṇava* (Oṃ) brings liberation; one beginning with the *śrībīja* (Śrīṃ) leads to the acquisition of wealth;
one beginning with *hṛllekhā* (Hrīṃ) bestows great supernatural powers (*mahāsiddhi*) and subjugates all."
One should practice the Vidyā beginning with *Vāgbhava* for [attaining] knowledge, and that beginning with *Kāma* for pleasing people.
In the Rudrayāmala: "For pacification, one should recite with the gaze directed upward; for enchantment, with the gaze directed downward;
for immobilization, with the gaze level; and by the sequence of looking to the sides."
In cases of conflict, for the purpose of eradication or killing, one should gaze at the sun;
for the sake of acquiring knowledge, while standing in the midst of water, one should gaze at the solar disc.
O Goddess, by beholding the center of the earth, there is auspicious liberation and peace in its entirety;
O Goddess, by beholding the tip of the nose, there is auspiciousness in every virtuous action.
In Tantra, one should always perform the recitation (japa) with the hands and never with a rosary;
a rosary is prescribed for ritual application (prayoga) according to the specific nature of each rite.

Regarding the different types of rosaries for the six rites, the *Tantraśekhara* states: "For subjugation (*vaśya*), there should be a rosary of lotus seeds; for pacification (*śānti*), it should be made of conch-shell;
for immobilization (*stambha*), it consists of *nivāriṣṭa* seeds; and for inciting enmity (*dveṣaṇa*), it is made from the teeth of a corpse."
A tooth from a horse is for causing expulsion; one produced from a donkey's tooth is for killing.
In the Tantra: A rosary fashioned from rudrākṣas accomplishes all rites;
one made from conch shells bestows wealth and fame.
With lotus seeds, it bestows the fortune of nourishment and likewise destroys enemies;
produced from the Putrañjīva tree, it grants abundance of sons, cattle, and grain.
A garland fashioned from pearls bestows abundant good fortune, prosperity,
and success that is directly manifest through mantra, as well as peace and nourishment.
Likewise, even a rosary made of crystal bestows liberation. According to the *Sārasvata*: "A rosary made of rubies grants abundant gain, while one made of gold or silver bestows all desires. (372)

A rosary made of *sārasvata* wood brings eloquence; one made of sprouts (*prabāla*) leads to subjugation; one made of *adhikadhana* wood brings the arrival of great wealth; and one made of *kauśī* grass, beginning with *rudrākṣa* and ending with *kuśa*, effects the destruction of sins.
A garland fashioned from all of these leads to liberation for men;
for the purpose of eradication, a garland of horse-teeth and horse-tails is prescribed.
A garland fashioned from the lower tusks of wild asses, strung together with threads of human sinew, is considered a destroyer of enemies.
A rosary for recitation should be made from the lower teeth of a preta;
it should be strung with hair from the body of the person against whom the rite of hatred is directed.
Regarding the rule for the number of recitations in the sixfold ritual (*ṣaṭkarman*):
in the case of general recitation, it is either one hundred or half of that;
the accomplishment of desired rites (*kāmyakarman*) occurs with fifty [recitations], or with those increased by four.
It is said that with one hundred and eight [beads] made into a garland, all accomplishments (*siddhi*) are attained;
for one seeking liberation (*mokṣa*), twenty-five [beads] are used, and fifteen for malevolent rites (*abhicārika*).
For daily invocation, one should recite with the middle finger and the thumb;
for inciting hatred and expulsion, one should recite with the thumb and the index finger.
For the rite of slaying an enemy, one should recite with the thumb and the little finger;
for other rites, however, one should recite with the thumb and the ring finger.
Regarding the rule for stringing the rosary during the six rites:
the wise one should prepare the thread for the purpose of stringing the rosary;
white, red, yellow, mixed, black, and smoke-colored threads are prescribed.
The mantras are declared according to their color, and the deities are assigned to the six types of ritual actions;
in certain specific rites, the visualization for the practice is described.
Having thoroughly examined all of that, one should perform the ritual procedure:
attraction is like subjugation, while auspicious [rites] are said to be like pacification.
The fierce rite of killing is to be known by practitioners everywhere as a specific result of the particular fire-pit used among the six rites;
regarding the application of the fire-oblation, the fire-pits are according to the requirements of each respective rite.
These have been correctly shown by the wise; now they are being uttered by me according to the prescribed rule.
The quadrangular sacrificial pit is declared to be the bringer of all accomplishments.
The Yonikuṇḍa, shaped like a half-moon, bestows sons and grants auspiciousness;
the triangular kuṇḍa destroys enemies; and the circular one is for rites of pacification (śāntika).
For acts of cutting and killing, the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) should be hexagonal and resemble a lotus;
for bestowing rain and pacifying diseases, the pit is said to be octagonal.
Other sages have declared the fruit of piercing the pit to be otherwise:
in the eastern direction it is square for paralyzing, and in the southern quarter it is shaped like a vulva.
A half-moon [shape] is for killing in the south; a triangle is for hatred in the southwest;
a circle is for pacification in the west; and a hexagon is for expulsion in the northwest.
In the north, for rites of nourishment, a lotus-shaped pit; in the northeast, an eight-cornered pit that grants liberation;
and in the northwest, a five-cornered pit for the suppression of spirits, planets, and the like.
One should place the seven-pointed [weapon] upon the Lord for the purpose of pacifying malevolent magic;
that earth which is white and fragrant is proclaimed as Brāhmī.
The earth is declared by the wise to be red clay for a Kṣatriya, yellow for a Vaiśya,
and likewise black in color for a Śūdra.
The Brāhmī [lineage] brings success in all aims; the Kṣatriyā is considered to bestow sovereignty;
the Vaiśyā produces wealth and grain; but the Śūdrā is censured by the wise.

Within the triangle in the center of the *kuṇḍa*, the wise one should draw the pericarp; he should write the seed-syllable of Śakti and, all around it, the letters corresponding to each of those elements.

The mantra practitioner should [employ] the root mantra by means of its syllables, either as a *grathita* (strung together), a *vidarbha* (interwoven), or a *sampuṭa* (encased), according to the specific requirements of each respective rite.
The practitioner of mantra, with a concentrated mind, should write the syllables of the name of the person for whom the rite is intended;
likewise, the tongues of Agni are described according to the distinctions of the qualities (guṇas) in various rites.

Regarding the six rites, the different tongues of the fire are considered to be Hiraṇyā, Gaganā, Raktā, Kṛṣṇā, Suprabhā, Bahurūpā, and Atiraktā; these are the Sāttvikī tongues used for auspicious rites.
Padmarāgā, Suvarṇā, and thirdly Bhadralohitā; then Lohitā, Śvetā, Dhūminī, and Karālikā.
The tongue of fire, which is rājasya, is ordained for rites of subjugation;
it has a universal form, is full of sparks, is smoke-colored, and possesses the speed of thought.
Lohitā, she called Karālā, and Kālī are said to belong to Tamas;
these seven are employed by practitioners of mantra in cruel rites.
With eight oblations of clarified butter, each accompanied by the syllable Om,
one performs the rites of conception (garbhādhāna), the rite for a male child (puṃsavana), and likewise the parting of the hair (sīmantonnayana).
Immediately thereafter, the birth-rite (jātakarma) should take place, as well as the naming ceremony (nāmakaraṇa);
after that, the rite of going outside (bahirniṣkramaṇa), and then the first feeding of solid food (annaprāśana) is prescribed.
The tonsure ceremony (cūḍā) and the initiation (upanayana), followed by the Mahānāmnī rites and the Great Vow (mahāvrata);
then the Upaniṣad study, and finally the Godāna, marriage, and death.
Those rites ending with marriage are prescribed for auspicious acts; those ending with death are designated for cruel deeds by those who know the Agamas of fire.
The vessels for sprinkling and so forth should be made of gold or silver;
those for rites such as pacification (śāntika) should be copper, while for rites such as inciting hatred (dveṣaṇa) and expulsion (uccāṭana), other materials are used.
The assignment of the senses, such as hearing, to the *bahuvāraka*, the *akṣa*, the *śobhāñjana*, and others has been declared by those who know the Tantras to belong to fire.
The face [of the altar] is in the center, the head in the south, and the two feet in the northern direction;
for rites of pacification (śānti), the face is between Indra (east) and Īśa (north), while for rites of desire (kāmyakarman), it is in the direction of Agni (southeast).
Regarding the slaying of a *rakṣasa*, the summoning of Vāyu,
and other such [rites], the *rudrayāmala* states that the *homīya-mudrā* consists of three mudrās prescribed for the fire-oblation (*homa*): the *mṛgī*, the *haṃsī*, and the *śūkarī*.

The Haṃsī mudrā is formed by extending the index fingers; this mudrā is proclaimed to be threefold, for use in rites of pacification (śāntika), enrichment (pauṣṭika), as well as in killing (māraṇa) and expulsion (uccāṭana).
O Supreme Goddess, in rites of inciting enmity, paralyzing, and subjugation, as well as in rites for peace, she is to be known as Mṛgī; in rites for nourishment, she is Haṃsī.
In rites of sorcery (*abhicāra*), one should employ the *śūkarī* [mudrā]; likewise in rites of inciting enmity (*vidveṣa*) and eradication (*uccāṭana*).
Regarding the determination of the limbs of the fire-oblation (*homāṅga*): "The gods do not accept an oblation that is devoid of mudrā.
That dull-witted person who, out of delusion, desires to offer an oblation lacking mudrā..."
It certainly causes both the sacrificer and oneself to fall;
therefore, having ascertained the stability of the fire, the ritual action must be performed with certainty.
Now I shall describe the fire-wheel (*agnicakra*), O Great Goddess, which grants success in the rites of *homa*;
