Now I shall describe the excellent yantra, by wearing which one becomes armored.
First, one should draw a hexagon and place the root mantra in its center.

One should place the *tāra* (OM) within, together with the object of accomplishment (*sādhya*) and accompanied by *lajjā* (HRĪM); and one should place the sixfold mantra in the hexagon and the *kulluka* in the interior of the corners.
On the filaments (kesara) there should be the eight Tārās, and on the petals the groups of consonants along with the vowels;
one should string these letters together with the Praṇava and seal them on the exterior with that very same [syllable].
One should form a chain with *praṇavas* at the ends of the ten directions, and then place the seed-syllables;
the remaining letters should be situated in the corners, and Tāriṇī at the ends of the chains.
One should join a sixteen-petalled lotus outside of that;
at its end, one should surround the filaments with the syllables of the Kāmabāṇa mantra.
One should encircle the middle of the petals with the syllables *nṛ*, *siṃha*, *kroḍa*, *tā*, and *rṇa*;
outside of that, a chain should be formed, and there, the goddess Tāriṇī should be placed along with the *lajjā* (the seed-syllable of shame).
One eager for victory should apply [the mantra] with the divisions of each syllable and the *kalās*;
one should fashion an outer lotus with inner petals and leaves endowed with the vital breaths (*prāṇa*).
The three-syllable seed-mantra joined with "Tārā" and the word "Jaya" should have the Tārā-seed at its core;
this is the flawless seed-mantra of victory.

One should perform the encirclement with the excellent *kālimālā* mantra, the *kūrca* chain, and the three earth-mandalas; then, at the beginning, one should place the deities starting with Padmāntaka.
In the corner sections, one should place tufts of grass marked with the syllable *kṣā* accompanied by the *tāra* (oṃ) and belonging to their respective families;
outside of that, the syllables of the weapons (*astra*) accompanied by the *tāra* are declared to be the perfected mantra.
One should place the seed-syllables (*manu*) of Indra and the other deities on the exterior, each infused with the syllable *phaṭ*.
Outside of that, the wise practitioner should apply the armor (*kavaca*) mantra and write it using the eight fragrant substances.
It must certainly be written on birch bark with a golden stylus.
One should wrap it with yellow silk cloth or red cloth;
having inscribed it with the eight perfumes, one should again enclose it with lac.
One should place that [image] within gold, endowed with its sevenfold enclosure;
it is to be worshipped according to the specific deity, preceded by the ritual placement of the vital breath (jīvanyāsa).
One should perform a fire sacrifice (homa) one thousand and eight times with oblations smeared with the three sweets;
there, one should also recite the root mantra one thousand times, accompanied by the name of the person to be accomplished (sādhya).
Having worshipped the Guru according to the rules with cows, land, gold, garments, and other offerings,
and having satisfied him, one should receive [the mantra] from his hand and wear it with a restrained mind.
One will certainly become invincible to all gods and asuras;
this highly powerful yantra, when placed upon the head, destroys the fear of death.
Situated on the arms, it grants victory in battle; situated on the throat, it is the deluder of the universe;
situated in the heart, it fulfills desires; situated at the navel, it causes paralysis and destroys disease.
Held in the fist during a dispute at dice, it grants victory;
worn on the crest of the hair, it wards off the multitude of weapons—of this there is no doubt.
O mighty-armed one, no weapons whatsoever can pierce the body of him upon whose head is the armor equal to that of Brahmā in battle.
O child, even weapons such as the Brahmāstra, upon seeing him, turn away and become powerless; I tell you this in truth, I speak the truth.
Bhairavas, Yātudhānas, Rākṣasas, and Brahmarākṣasas do not even step upon his shadow, let alone his physical body.
Fanged and horned creatures, as well as cruel lions, tigers, and the like,
fled upon seeing him, oppressed by fear of his splendor.
The planets, nāgas, gods, and others— including the siddhas, gandharvas, yakṣas, and so forth, as well as the vidyādharas and mahoragas— inflict that suffering upon him.
Those who, by themselves or through others, commit acts of malice against him—
them he indeed devours by the power of Ugratārā.
Those fools situated in the cardinal and intermediate directions who harbor enmity toward him are consumed by the fire of their own anger and perish along with their kinsmen.
404) Through the sight of this practitioner, malevolent spells and acts of malice are pacified;
the sick are freed from their diseases, and even poison turns into nectar.
Seeing him who bears upon his head this armor joined with a discus,
all the gods, together with the Siddhas, bow down in reverence.
Whosoever among the fierce ones who consider themselves Rākṣasas fall at the feet of Śatruvasta, their minds being forcibly drawn by his majesty.
The oceans turn into dry land, fire attains coolness,
mountains become level ground, and darkness turns into light.
Even the most fierce beings attain gentleness by the sight of this practitioner who recites this auspicious,
divine armor (kavaca) of Mahogrā.
For him, the perfection of mantras shall quickly occur even without prior ritual service (puraścaryā);
the eight supernatural powers (siddhis) will be within his grasp, and he is declared to be a son of the Goddess.
He who, while wandering the earth clad in armor, beholds the smoke of a funeral pyre— he is undoubtedly a vessel for dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa.
Even he attains liberation; what need is there to mention those who have already attained perfection?
For in that sacrifice where he goes, adorned with the armor of Brahman, [all obstacles vanish].
Upon seeing [it], the ancestors together with the fire-gods and the deities attain satisfaction;
there is no misfortune or famine there, nor any transgression of dharma.
Wherein dwells the pure and wise one, ever devoted to recitation and wearing the armor;
he who, having recited the armor-mantra, indeed offers a handful of flowers.
Homage to Mahogratārā! By what means does one obtain the fruit of ten thousand years of worship? How is she—the auspicious one who delivers from fierce transgressions—pleased?
Those who are practitioners of the Great Vidyā and recite it with a desire for virtue,
and others who maintain it with devotion— they too obtain that fruit.
Those women who, having obtained this great armor through good fortune,
wear it, shall obtain divine sons by its power.
Those intent on victory obtain abundant fortune, enjoyments, health, and all prosperity; thus she is called the Goddess manifest.
Thus, my child, this armor has been told to you out of devotion;
for it is dearer to me than life itself, and it must be guarded with great effort.
405) The kingdom may be given, the head may be given, but this wondrous armor must not be given to anyone; this is the truth, the absolute truth, O Śikhidhvaja!
"Since you are dearer to me than my own life and are the protector even of the gods, therefore, my child, I have told this to you; practice it with full attention."
"By means of this [missile], I formerly conquered Tripura while wearing armor;
with it, I slew the fierce one named Tāraka who was arrogant with pride—destroy him with this!"
The illustrious Bhairava said: Having obtained this divine armor consisting of Brahman, as proclaimed by Śaṅkara,
Kārtikeya indeed slew the demon Tāraka.
O Goddess, O Bhairavī, this secret armor has been revealed by me; it must be guarded with great effort, like one's own private parts.
Thousands of horse-sacrifices, hundreds of Rājasūya sacrifices,
and even other millions of rituals are not equal to this armor.
The murder of a Brahmin, the drinking of liquor, and likewise sexual intercourse with those who should not be approached—
this [mantra], when remembered even once, quickly burns these away, just as fire consumes heaps of cotton.
Whosoever may be a practitioner of Tāriṇī or Kālikā,
if they do not know this armor (kavaca), they shall certainly not attain success.
Even by ten million recitations alone, the deity becomes well-pleased;
as is Tārā, so is Kālī—for she who is Tārā is that very Kālikā.
Indeed, there is no difference between the two regarding the wearing of this armor;
it is a divine armor consisting of three chains, equal to Brahman itself.
Whoever should preserve [this] according to the prescribed rule, preceded by the worship of the Guru,
for him Tāriṇī shall be pleased and the supernatural powers (siddhis) will remain in his hand.
Having satisfied his own guru with gifts such as cows, land, gold, and garments,
and having received the divine armor (kavaca), he should perform the consecration with the mantras proclaimed by Śiva.
The deities should consecrate the pill with the great mantras beginning with Aghora, with the root mantra, and with those mantras that rescue one from calamity.

Having placed [the deity] within a vessel made of gold or other precious materials, filled with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) and the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), the wise one should worship it with the aforementioned ritual offerings.
The preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) for this [mantra] is accomplished with fifty [oblations];
having established the sacrificial fire in a prepared pit as previously described, [one should proceed].
One should perform oblations with eight hundred and eight bilva leaves mixed with honey and sesamum seeds; then, one should sprinkle this [object] with the resulting drops.
Having worshipped with peace-mantras, one who maintains a restrained mind should wear it;
whatever one desires, all that one obtains here—of this there is no doubt.
Thus has been declared this primordial, divine armor of Tāriṇī;
whoever wears this well-guarded kavaca with devotion shall become identical with Śiva, the Lord of the North, through the grace of Brahmatārā.
The fortune of victory over the three worlds remained as if already held in his hand.

Thus ends the armor named *Trailokyavijaya* from the *Tārākalpa* in the *Uttaragandharvatantra*. Now, regarding the general method of drawing the yantra, as stated in the *Kālikā*: "The life-force of the solar yantra shall be placed below the central seed-syllable."
One should write "hasaḥ so'haṃ" along with the vital breath (prāṇa) in the sequence beginning from the northeast (aiśānī).
One should place *i* and *īṃ* on the eyes, and likewise *u* and *ūṃ* on the ears;
however, in the case of the eight-petalled lotus and others, the writing of the Gāyatrī is prescribed as the specific distinction.
One should write the syllables of the Yantra-Gāyatrī three times on each leaf;
one should write the *Pratiṣṭhā* [mantra], which bestows life-force, within the spaces between the lines of the fire-altar. Thus it is said.
In another Tantra it is also stated: "The heart of the Yantra is traditionally taught to be written together with the Bindu;
'Haṃsaḥ' and 'So'ham', representing the vital breath and the individual soul, should be inscribed in the Yantra with great care."
"The wise one should inscribe [the mantra] joined with the *visarga* within the yantra.
Thus, the *yantragāyatrī* is as follows: "We know the King of Yantras; we meditate upon the Bestower of Boons; may that Yantra impel us."
Now, regarding the consecration of the yantra,
in the Vāmakeśvaratantra, Bhairavī said:
O Great God, through your grace I have heard about the schism of the Wheel;
now I wish to hear the determination of the ritual for consecration.
Śrī Śaṅkara said:
Listen, O Goddess, O Kaulinī, savior of the world; I shall explain the determination of all castes as part of the concluding rite (udyāpana) for that [observance].
Having bathed, the practitioner of mantras should form a formal resolve (saṅkalpa) and perform the worship of the Guru;
with the mantra of the Guru, he should draw the yantra using a golden stylus.
Then, having prepared the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) consecrated with the Śiva-mantra,
the practitioner should cast the wheel there, accompanied by the syllable Om (praṇava).
Having extracted that wheel from there, one should place it upon a golden pedestal,
[anointing it] with the five nectars, milk, and cool water.
O Goddess, one should bathe [the deity] with sandalwood paste, musk, and saffron,
using eight golden jars filled with water.
One should bathe [the deity] while reciting the mantra, using water infused with astringent decoctions;
then, having lifted that yantra, one should place it in a golden vessel.
May we know the King of Yantras; may we meditate upon the Great Yantra;
at the end of this, one should utter: "May that Yantra inspire us."

Having touched the yantra with the tip of a blade of kusha grass, one should consecrate it with the Gāyatrī mantra one hundred and eight times, O Goddess, for the sake of attaining the state of identity with the deity.
Then, having performed the purification of oneself, one should worship the deity with the six limbs;
having invoked the Great Goddess there, one should perform the ritual placement of the vital breath (jīvanyāsa).
There, one should worship the Goddess with fruits, betel, and food offerings;
one should present silk thread and the like, along with garments, ornaments, and so forth.
O Maheśvarī, one who is intent on his own welfare should diligently offer a mirror, a fly-whisk, and a bell, as appropriate for each.
Then one should recite [the mantra] one thousand times for the sake of accomplishing all desired goals;
having then performed the offering of the bali-oblation, one should prostrate before the King of Yantras.
Having offered one hundred and eight oblations, he should pour the residual clarified butter [into the fire];
the Guru should perform everything according to the procedure for the residual drops of the weapons.

Having given the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the preceptor, one should dismiss him according to one's ability. Now, regarding the optional offering (kāmyabali), Dakṣiṇāmūrti says: "One should perform the offering of the bali in the forenoon for the pacification of obstacles."
The wise have declared that the bali offering is of two kinds: rājasa and sāttvika.
The rājasa [offering] consists of meat and blood, adorned with the three fruits,
combined with honey and milk-rice (pāyasa), and sprinkled with the three sweets.
The *sāttvika* [offering] is devoid of meat; the rest is as previously stated.
(408) A Brahmin, being self-controlled and pure, should present the *sāttvika* bali.
For the performance of the bali-homa rite, it cannot be accomplished without a vessel;
one should place the bali offering in the center of a vessel filled with food and water.
In the *Narasiṃha Purāṇa*: "One should prepare the oblations for the *homa* and the *bali* using the measure of a fresh *āmalaka* fruit.
In the *Tryambakapaddhati*: "O Goddess of the Gods, at the conclusion of the *bali*, one should likewise offer a goat-bali and a ram at all times for the attainment of all desires and goals."
In rites that are obligatory, occasional, or performed for specific desires, one should offer an oblation of buffalo meat for victory,
for the fulfillment of all wishes, and for the attainment of the world of the Goddess.
Having bathed the animal, which is endowed with all auspicious marks, according to the mantra,
and having placed it before the Goddess, one should then sprinkle it with the arghya water.
Having protected it with the Astra-mantra and veiled it with the Kavaca-mantra,
one should recite the Mūla-mantra and consecrate it as nectar by means of the Dhenu-mudrā.
Having properly worshipped with perfumes, flowers, unbroken grains, and ritual offerings,
one should recite the mantra that liberates from the bonds of the fettered (paśu) into his ear.
Oṃ, let us know Paśu-pāśa; let us meditate upon Vipra-karṇa; may Jīva inspire us. This is declared to be the Gāyatrī that liberates from the bonds of the bound (paśu-pāśa).
One should recite this into the right ear for the sake of attaining liberation for that person.
The Sword Mantra:
Then the practitioner should worship the sword on the right side with this mantra:
one should write the Praṇava (Oṃ), Bhuvaneśvarī, and the pair of Kālīs.

The mantra is considered to consist of nine syllables: first the word *vajreśvarī*, then *lohadaṃṣṭrām* ending in the feminine nominative suffix *ṅe*, followed by the heart-mantra (*hṛt*). This is regarded as the mantra.
With these [substances], such as perfumes and flowers, the wise one should worship the sword;
then, at its hilt, middle, and tip, in due order.
With perfumes, flowers, and unbroken grains (akṣata), the mantrin should worship the triad of couples:
Brahmā together with Vāgīśī, and likewise Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa.
And Umā-Maheśvara—thus is the triad of couples proclaimed.
Then, with this mantra, one should consecrate that sword.

O Lord of the Sword, you who are intent on the destruction of the asuras with your sword and devoted to the task of the spear, may the sacrificial animal be swiftly cut by that [spear]; salutations be unto you!

409) Then, having taken the kuśa grass, unbroken rice, water, and other items contained in the copper vessel, and having recited the root mantra and made the formal resolve (saṅkalpa), one should release the sacrificial animal.
Having taken the unbroken rice, water, and other items, he should cast them upon the head of the sacrificial animal;
then, with that very sword and the root mantra, the practitioner [should proceed].
One should perform the severance of the sacrificial animal while personally recollecting the Goddess.
Regarding the result of the falling of the head of the sacrificial offering (*bali*):
if it falls to the right, there is prosperity; if on the left side, it is censured.
If it falls or is severed on the left, the wise man should recollect the mantra of the Goddess.
Then, having offered fifteen oblations into the sacrificial pit and other vessels,
one should pacify the fault arising from the *huṃ*-utterance, as characterized by the signs of the *bali* offering.
In the Śrīkramasaṃhitā: One should offer that *bali* with effort, but one should not kill it oneself;
one should not harm any living beings, nor should one harm those honored by heroes.
One should not offer a bali-oblation with one's own hands; therefore, one should avoid violence.
If one should kill [an animal] through negligence, one will go to the Raurava hell.

As for this expiation: having consumed everything and having shaken the world, one is liberated by bowing to Durgā. Regarding the offering of the sacrificial oblation (*bali*) to all the gods, the *Kālikā Purāṇa* states: "In the offerings of oblations by practitioners, [the portion] of every deity is to be accepted."
Birds, tortoises, fish, and nine kinds of wild animals are to be caught.
The buffalo, the gayal, the cow, the goat, the brown bear, the boar,
the rhinoceros, the black antelope, the monitor lizard, the sarabha,
the lion, the tiger, and the man— likewise their own bodily blood.
The offerings for Caṇḍikā, Bhairava, and the others have been fully described. Through these offerings, liberation is accomplished; through these offerings, heaven is attained.
By means of the offering of a sacrifice, a king shall constantly conquer his enemies;
likewise, Śivā is always [propitiated] by the blood of fish and tortoises.
The Goddess attains satisfaction for one month with the blood of crocodiles, for three months with that of deer, and especially with that of human beings.
She who bestows auspiciousness attains satisfaction for eight months;
with the blood of cows and iguanas, one obtains satisfaction for a year.
With the blood of the black antelope and the blood of the boar,
the Goddess constantly attains satisfaction for twelve years.
By means of the blood of goats and sheep, [the rite lasts] for twenty-five years;
and by means of the blood of buffaloes and goats, it lasts for a hundred years.
He attains supreme satisfaction likewise by the blood of a tiger,
a lion, a sarabha, or even from the blood of his own body.
The Goddess obtains satisfaction for a thousand years from the flesh and likewise from the blood of anyone, to whatever extent their satisfaction may be.
With the flesh of the black antelope as well as that of the rhinoceros,
Caṇḍikā certainly attains satisfaction for exactly five hundred years.
With the flesh of the rohita fish and the vārdhrīṇasa crane,
Caṇḍikā attains satisfaction for three hundred years.
With a blue neck, a red head, black feet, and white wings, this crane—
the lord of birds— is dear to both the Goddess and Śambhu.
O Goddess, when a powerful man offers [oblations] for a thousand years,
Kāmākhyā Bhairava, who bears my own form, attains satisfaction.
The blood, purified by mantras, always becomes nectar;
and Śivā always eats both his head and his flesh.
Therefore, in its worship, one should offer the head and blood of Bali;
for that which is given without being purified by mantras brings total destruction upon the giver.
A wise person should employ meats in feasts and burnt offerings;
however, a practitioner should never offer meats during ritual worship.
Except for the blood from the head, which is indeed nectar;
likewise, the *kuṣmāṇḍa* fruit, the sugarcane stalk, liquor, and fermented spirits [are permitted].
These offerings are said to be equal to goats for the purpose of satisfaction;
cutting [the victim] with a crescent-shaped sword (candrahāsa) or a knife (kartarī) is declared to be the primary method.
The middle [type of weapon] is described as the *dātra* (sickle), the *asi-dhenu* (small knife), the *krakaca* (saw), and the *śaṅkulā* (curved sickle);

the lowest is proclaimed to consist of the *kṣura* (razor), the *kṣurapra* (razor-headed arrow), and the *bhalla* (broad-headed arrow). (Note: *Asi-dhenu* is a small sword; *śaṅkulā* is a curved sickle.)
The offering (bali) must never be cut by anyone other than these [deities] using weapons such as spears or arrows.
There is no deity who would accept that offering; rather, the practitioner who cuts the consecrated animal with his hand shall meet his death. (411)
Or he incurs the most unbearable sin of killing a Brahmin by slaying a bird;
therefore, a wise man should not employ a sacrificial offering of a rhinoceros without first consecrating it with a mantra.
Whatever mantras were previously taught for the invocation of Khaḍga, those indeed,
along with the Mahāmāyā and Bala mantras, should be employed there by the wise as prescribed.
The mantra of Khaḍga is as follows:
first "Kālī" twice, then the word "Vajreśvarī" for the Goddess;
thereafter, one should append "namo lohadaṇḍāyai" at the end.
Having worshipped with this mantra and taken the sword in his hand,
he should consecrate that sword with the mantra of Kālarātri.
One should employ the center of the seed-syllable of Netra by repeating it twice;
thereafter, [one recites] "Kālī Kālī, O you with formidable fangs, O Terrifying One!"
The letters beginning with ha and ending with na [are joined] with the third vowel, which is indeed the eleventh.
Having joined [the mantra] with *nāda* and *bindu*, one should thereafter join two [syllables].
Then follows the word *phetkāriṇī*, and then *khādaya chedaya*.
After that, [one says] "all evil ones" (*sarvaduṣṭān*), and then twice "slay the buffalo-demon" (*māraya lulāpakam*).
"Cut! Cut! with a sword; then indeed "Kila! Kila!"; then "Ciki! Ciki!"; and then "Drink! Drink!"—thus it was said.
Then, "ruṃ rudhiram," "sphauṃ sphauṃ," and "kirikirī," followed by "kālikāyai namaḥ"— this is the mantra of Kālarātri.
When a sword has been consecrated with this mantra,
Kālarātri herself becomes gracious toward it for the purpose of destroying enemies.
Then, intent upon the deity and upon his own desire,
he should cut that sacrificial offering with that sword while it faces the east.
Then, being himself facing east,
he should likewise apply the previously mentioned substances such as rock salt to his northern face, which is red in color.
Facing north, the practitioner should likewise look at the bali offering facing east,
and then recite this mantra:
You are a beast who has appeared before me by the power of my fortune in the form of Bali;
therefore, I bow down to you, who possess all forms, appearing now in the form of Bali.
By the gift that pleases Caṇḍikā, the misfortunes of the donor are destroyed;
salutations be to you, O Bala, who take the form of the offering to Cāmuṇḍā.
"Beasts were created by the Self-born One himself for the sake of sacrifice;
therefore, I cause you to be slain today. Thus, in a sacrifice, killing is no killing."
Having abandoned this body and assumed a divine form,
rejoice together with the Pramathas for as long as the fourteen Indras endure.
O Bhairava, having meditated upon that offering (bali) in the form of liquor with the mantra "Aiṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ," one should place a flower upon its head.
Then, having consecrated [the sword] with effort for the sake of the Goddess and for the sake of his desire,
he should thereafter worship the sword.

As for meditation: [one should meditate on him] as dark-complexioned, holding a bow (pināka) in his hand, having the form of the Night of Destruction (kālarātri), with red eyes, wearing red garments, holding a noose, and dripping yellow blood.
Oṃ! You are the sword, the slayer, the blade, with a sharp edge and difficult to approach;
you are the essence of prosperity, victory itself, and the protector of Dharma—homage be to you!
Then, having worshipped the sword with the mantras "Āṃ Hūṃ Phaṭ," and having taken up that stainless sword, one should cut the supreme sacrificial offering (bali).
"Oṃ hrīṃ aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ, O Kauśikī, may you be satiated with blood!
Thus one should place the blood in the vessel and a lamp upon the head.
By offering the *bali* in this manner, the practitioner attains the full fruit.
If [the offering] is inferior, it will lead to inferiority; conversely, if it is the opposite, it will be fruitless.
This is the settled rule everywhere regarding the offering of bali to Durgā.
Regarding the determination of the vessel for the offering (balipātra):
it may be made of gold, silver, copper, bell-metal, or likewise a leaf-cup;
or it may be made of clay, bronze, or even of sacrificial wood.
A vessel for the giving of blood should be prepared according to one's means;
it must not be made of iron, nor of bark-fiber, nor of tin, nor of lead.
One should offer blood to the *valis* either on the ground, or in the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles;
not in a jar, nor on the bare earth, nor in a small drinking vessel.
A supreme man desiring prosperity should indeed offer blood;
however, except for the horse-sacrifice, he should never offer a horse as a sacrificial oblation.
413) Likewise, a lord of men may give an elephant during sacrifices to the guardians of the quarters;
however, he should never give either a horse or an elephant to the Goddess.
A Brahmin should never, under any circumstances, give a lion, a tiger, or even a human being, nor his own body's blood, nor liquor to the Goddess.
By giving lions, tigers, or human beings, a Brāhmaṇa shall go to hell;
even in this world, he shall have a short lifespan and be deprived of happiness and comfort.
By giving the blood from his own body, one incurs the sin of suicide;
by giving liquor, however, a Brāhmaṇa falls away from his very status as a Brāhmaṇa.
Kṣatriyas and others, however, should not offer a black antelope as a sacrificial fee;
for one who gives a black antelope would incur the sin of killing a Brahmin.
But when there is an abundant offering of oblations, the practitioner, having placed two or three at his own head as the foremost,
should worship them all by means of the ritual manual (tantra).
And one should offer a buffalo to the Goddess Bhairavī and to Bhairava;
with this very mantra, one should likewise worship that sacrificial offering (bali).
Just as you hate me and just as you carry Caṇḍikā, so indeed do you destroy my enemies; bear auspiciousness, O buffalo!
You are the vehicle of Yama, O imperishable one who assumes many forms.
Bestow longevity, wealth, and fame; salutations be to you, O Kāsarā.
Whatever is offered to the Goddess by others, even to other deities,
one should offer that very thing after it has been worshipped to the deity who has indeed been honored.
One should avoid an animal that has been offered as a sacrificial victim, one that is one-eyed, maimed, excessively old, diseased, or has a sore on the throat;
likewise, one that is impotent, deficient in limbs, possesses the characteristics of an old animal, or has a discharge of phlegm from a wound on the throat.
Likewise, one who has leprosy, one who is exceedingly short, and a perpetrator of a great sin;
as well as those among beasts, birds, and especially among men.
One should not give a woman as a sacrificial offering; by giving such an offering, one would fall into hell. Nor indeed should one offer a bird for less than three fortnights.
One should certainly not [offer] an animal or a bird that is defective— such as being one-eyed or deformed—
nor one whose tail, claws, or ears are severed, nor likewise one whose horns are broken.
One should never offer anything such as a broken tooth;
one should place a lion on the right and present a buffalo in front.
One should offer a bird to the left and the blood from one’s own body in front;
likewise, the heads and blood of carnivorous animals and birds [should be offered].
One should offer on the left side all kinds of aquatic creatures,
as well as the black antelope, the tortoise, the rhinoceros, and the hare.
One should first offer the heads of crocodiles and fish;
however, one should not give the back or the head of the *bali* snake.
In the Mahākālasaṃhitā: "The black antelope, as well as the goat, the deer, and even the wild boar;
the ram, the buffalo, the rhinoceros, and likewise those with five claws."
The pigeon, the ṭiṭṭibha, the swan, the ruddy goose,
the quail, the śarāli, the partridge, fish, the sparrow, and the jackal.
One should never give anything that has not been specifically stated to the class of twice-borns;
likewise, a Kṣatriya should regard himself as a lion, a tiger, or a man.
Having abandoned the black antelope (*kṛṣṇasāra*), the sacrificial offering (*bali*) may belong to a Kṣatriya or others;
however, by giving a lion, a tiger, or a human, a Brāhmaṇa becomes a slayer of a Brāhmaṇa (*brahmahā*). By giving a mouse, a cat, or a blue jay (*cāṣa*), a Śūdra falls downward.
One should strike with the Candrahāsa sword in a single blow;
one should strike while standing and never while seated.
Having killed an animal with one's own hand, one shall attain birth in the womb of that animal;
furthermore, [the same applies to] buffaloes and the like if they are less than three fortnights old, or less than three years old.
One should never give anyone younger than three months;
nor should one include the elderly or those with deformed limbs in the performance of the bali offering.
The ritual for a Kṣatriya or others may involve giving the blood from one's own body;
however, one characterized by sattva should never, under any circumstances, commit the taking of life.
Having fashioned an animal out of stalks of sugarcane, pumpkin, wild fruits and the like,
along with balls of milk and rice flour, one should perform the bali offering.
One should offer each particular sacrificial animal according to its specific fruit:
a pumpkin gourd as a buffalo, and a karkaṭī melon as a goat.
Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "The Ritual for Desired Objects," in the *Tārābhaktisudhārṇava* composed by the Great Mahopādhyāya, the illustrious Ṭhakkura Narasiṃha.
The Eleventh Wave:
Now, regarding the different forms of Tārā, it is said in the *Brahmasaṃhitā*: "O Sage, listen with a one-pointed mind; I shall describe the many kinds of Vidyās."
On a mountain, or in a thicket, or in a desolate place, or at a crossroads.
In a whirlpool, when fear of fanged beasts arises, or when danger from kings and the like has come;
likewise in a city or marketplace, or at the foot of great trees.
On a riverbank, in fear of predatory beasts, and in fears of scorpions and the like—
one should recite these various [mantras], and they will quickly destroy all danger.
One attains freedom from fear on a mountain by reciting this mantra: having first uttered the syllable *oṃ*, [one should say] "in danger, in great danger."
Having first recited the root-vidyā— the supreme ten-syllable mantra consisting of the seed-syllable of Ramā (Śrī) and the wife of Fire (Svāhā)— one should thereafter recite this mantra.
By the grace of Ugratārā, one may dwell joyfully on the mountain;
and when fear arises in the dense forest, one should recite this mantra a hundred times.
Having extracted the seed-syllable Oṃ, then [the word] Vikaṭe,
then Śīghraṃ Vighnaṃ, and after that the pair Nāśaya twice.
Then, after saying "svāhā," one should recite the mantra ten times;
one should recite this vidyā ten times, and at the end, the root-mantra ten times.
By the grace of Ekajaṭā, one may dwell joyfully in the forest;
and when danger arises in a desolate place, one should recite the ten-syllable vidyā.
Having first uttered "Kālī," and then "Mahākālī," followed by "Oṃ Oṃ Svāhā"— this mantra bestows all spiritual accomplishments (siddhis).
I shall proclaim the Great Vidyā, which is unsurpassed and peerless;
by the mere accomplishment of which another person becomes submissive.
The seer is Vākstambhaka, the deity is Deva, and the metre is Nivṛt;
the deity is declared to be Anuttara, and it is proclaimed as "I am Śiva."
Having first performed worship there, one should recite the mantra seven hundred thousand times;
by the mere sight of him, he becomes like a second Indra among his enemies.

If one recites [the mantra] ten times for each of ten repetitions (one hundred times) and applies a forehead mark (*tilaka*) made of *rocanā*, even kings will become servants; how much more so, then, common men?
If an obstacle arises on a mountain, in a forest, or in a difficult pass,
a person should meditate for a moment and recite the mantra, and then proceed at ease.
Listen, O Brahmin, to this supreme, great secret, more secret than the secret itself,
by the mere knowledge of which one quickly attains that which bestows happiness.
Through the union of passion, it should always be recited; it destroys even the greatest sins.
When pleased through the yoga of the Kula alone, she bestows liberation.
One desiring wealth should recite the mantra when approaching another's wife;
one desiring knowledge should recite the mantra while taking refuge with a person of noble family.
And he should be intent upon inverted sexual union above the heart;
the sacrificial substances for worship should always be held raised up in her hand.
One should offer [the oblation] especially with the goddesses, conjoined with the five "ma" syllables;
without the five substances, one will never attain success.
The mantra of Tārā is not accomplished by one who is devoid of the kula-yoga;
this incomparable secret has been spoken by me in brief.
The wise person who recites this mantra for Tārā ten times in this manner shall become happy in solitude through the grace of Ugratārā.
In the event of fear at a crossroads, one should recite the eighteen-syllable mantra;
having first extracted the Praṇava (Oṃ), followed by the pair "matha" twice.
Having uttered "Sphoṭa Sphoṭa" and then "Mahāmaheśvarī," the wise practitioner should append the *praṇava* at the end of "Svāhā" and recite it ten times.
She who dwells at the crossroads in the form of Ugratārā—
by the grace of Ugratārā, there is indeed no fear at the crossroads.
One should recite Tārā, the pacifier of beings, the protectress who bestows all accomplishments:
having first extracted the Praṇava (Oṃ), followed by Tāre Tutāre Ture.
Therefore, this ten-syllable mantra "svāhā" has been proclaimed by me;
merely by remembering it at that moment, it shall swiftly destroy all fear.
Through the grace of Ugratārā, there shall be no fear of water at all;
when fear of fanged creatures arises, one should recite the mantra with firm resolve.
Having first extracted the *praṇava* (oṃ), followed by "Ugratāre," then "māṃ tāraya tāraya svāhā," one should recite this mantra ten times.
Having emerged from the fear of fanged beasts through the grace of Ugratārā,
if the danger of fear of a king should arise, then the wise one should recite the mantra.
Having first extracted the Praṇava, then the seed-syllable of Ramā,
followed by "sarvavaśaṅkari svāhā," and finally the beginning of the Vedas (Om) tripled.
One should recite "sarvasammohinī svāhā" exactly twenty-one times twelve times; then the king there will indeed be brought under control.
If one should encounter danger in the city, one should recite this mantra:
having uttered the seed-syllable of desire (KĀM), joined with the Praṇava and Svāhā.
One should recite the vidyā ten times; at that moment, fear is destroyed.
At the marketplace, one goes beyond [worldly] existence; then one should recite the seed-syllable of desire (Kāma-bīja).
One should recite it ten times; it will swiftly destroy fear.
If, through negligence, there is fear of kinsmen beneath a great tree, [one should do the same].
The wise one should recite the syllable *ma* joined with the *bindu* five times;
it destroys all fear there, and one becomes a son of the Goddess.
And on the bank of a river, being pure, one should recite the *kugati* mantra and likewise the *vidyā*;
as well as the *praṇava*, the seed-syllable of Vāyu, the seed-syllable of Kāma, and that which consists of *trapā*.
One should offer oblations to the fire and recite the mantra ten times;
if fear arises upon seeing a serpent, one should recite the mantra with a proud gaze.
Having uttered "vyālavyālam," followed by "garuḍāya," one should then say "svāhā svāhā"; thus, no fear of serpents arises.
If one is terrified by the sight of a scorpion, one should recite the mantra with undistracted mind;
having constantly recited the syllable *oṃ*, one should then rub one's hand in that place.
All that [evil] becomes distant through the grace of the Sovereign of All;
one should recite all these mantras to the extent of ten thousand repetitions.
Therefore, the powerful vidyā is ineffective without its recitation;
likewise, mantras that bring kings under control, as well as those that bring elephants under control, [are ineffective].
The mantras for subjugating the buffalo, the donkey, and the tiger have been revealed;
however, the mantra of Tārā that grants accomplishment is said to be difficult to find on this earth.
418) The science of subduing archery, likewise the science of subduing swords,
the science that wards off weapons, and likewise the science that wards off arrows;
the immobilization of fire, the immobilization of enemies, and the immobilization of water according to the prescribed ritual.
The glorious goddess Ekajaṭā is the bestower of all accomplishments.
If one recites [the mantra] into the ear-cavity of a mad elephant,
it becomes submissive at that very moment and becomes like a jar of powder.
One should say "Kaṅkālī," and then one should utter "Guhyakālī";
likewise, the mantra is "Oṃ Kāli Svāhā" up to ten syllables.
Because Vatsalohikarī, having placed her hand upon the head [of the practitioner] and performed ten thousand recitations, one becomes endowed with all virtues.
The end of the five [syllables] joined with the Bindu, followed by "to Gaṇeśvara";
having thus stabilized the performer, [the mantra is] "Oṃ Oṃ Svāhā," which is twofold.
This is the mantra for subduing elephants, which brings joy to princes;
upon seeing a very large buffalo, one should form the goad-mudrā.
Having placed [the mantra] at the beginning and recited it as a *japa*, one attains subjugation day by day;
having extracted the seed-syllable *Oṃ*, the word *Śivāya* follows thereafter.
After that, the mantra "durge durge" followed by the word ending in "agnijāyā" (svāhā) should be recited six times; there is no doubt that success will surely follow.
And by merely looking at Khara while muttering the mantra "svāhā," Svara comes under one's control;
success shall not be otherwise.
Upon merely seeing a tiger, one should recite the great mantra of Kālī ten times; by reciting this vidyā ten times, one will quickly destroy all fear.
The Method for Accomplishing the Bow:
Now, therefore, I shall explain specifically the mantra of the bow.
One should then write the seed-syllable of desire (Kāma-bīja) in the middle of the bow.
One should worship the Kāmabīja with fine perfumes, flowers, and incenses.
The Praṇava should be written at the tip of the arrow, and then one should write the Māyā in the middle.
One should first offer the Vahnivadhū [mantra] and worship according to the prescribed rule;
having thus performed worship for one month in this very sequence of rites.

And at the end of the month, having offered the bali-oblation and grasping a bow in his hand, he should discharge it toward whichever [direction]; indeed, upon whichever limb it falls, [that is the sign].

Having become equal to the Brahmāstra, the arrow should remain fixed upon the bow. As for the method of attaining mastery over the sword: having procured the eight metals, one should certainly fashion a sword.
And in the center of that, one should draw a beautiful eight-petaled lotus wheel.
One should draw a hexagon in the center and write the seed-syllable there;
joined with the *kāmakalā*, one should recite the mantra for only half a lunar fortnight.
At the conclusion of the recitation, one should bury it in the middle of a cremation ground;
having performed ten thousand recitations there, the accomplishment of the sword will then arise.
Having grasped the sword, one should say: "Cut the enemy's shoulder in two!
Having spoken thus, one should indeed release the sword toward the region of the foe.
Having cut, having cut again, and having cut yet again, it returns to the *kaulika* [thread].
O Great Sage, I shall now declare the mantra that wards off weapons, the *vidyā* that wards off weapons.
Hṛllekhā, the final Śakti, Kāma, and likewise Vahnivadhū.
The three letters ending in *ṭha*, joined with the nasal drop (*bindu*) and preceded by the *praṇava* (oṃ),
consecrated with the dust from a crossroads, and used as an ornament for the body.
Having acted thus and become firm, one is not afflicted by the weapons of others;
for when this vidyā has been recited, it occurs at the beginning of the seed-syllable of Śrī.
Having likewise written the mantra on her hand with red powder upon her pale body, she should then form a fist with the *kāṇḍanivāraṇī* [staff-warder] mudrā.
It quickly paralyzes all things as long as one does not release the fist;
this is the supreme method for paralyzing fire, water, and enemies.
Through the grace of Ekajaṭā, one becomes a lord of great accomplishments;
through the grace of Ugratārā, indeed, the eight siddhis are attained.
Through the grace of Mahānīla, one's speech shall flow forth;
through the grace of Haṃsatārā, she brings about the destruction of the enemy faction.
Through the grace of Bījakhaṇḍā, one shall attain the favor of the king;
through the grace of Ugrajaṭā, joy and nourishment are produced.
420) By the grace of Śrīvajriṇī, one will possess a vajra-body;
by the grace of Mahākālī, the medicinal pill (guṭikā) itself is accomplished.
Through the grace of Mahāghorā, various vidyās are accomplished;
however, if one recites this vidyā after having first recited the root-vidyā (mūlavidyā).
Having attained all accomplishments, one shall dwell upon the earth like a god.
Now, regarding the great mantras in the Māyātantra:
The Blessed Lord said: Now I shall declare the Tārā mantras, which bestow the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
by the mere remembrance of which the entire world will certainly become submissive.
Tārā, Cogā, Mahogrā, Vajrā, Nīlā, Sarasvatī, Kāmeśvarī, and Bhadrakālī— these eight are known as the Tāriṇīs.

The living soul, having entered the letter of heat (u), is joined with the tone of the Vedic recitation (nigama-svara); it is pervaded by the resonance (nāda) and the point (bindu), and endowed with the rays of reality (tatva).

The letter *ka* (Kapila), the left ear (*va*), the first sound (*na*) topped with a dot (*bindu*), the final letter of the side (*pa*), and likewise the final letter of the vowels (*a*)— this is proclaimed as the syllable of the corpse (*śava*).

The letter *ha* is the individual soul (*jīva*). The sibilant *ra* is situated therein. The Vedic vowel *ī* is the sound of the scripture. By these [letters], the seed-syllable of Bhuvaneśvarī is formed. By the term "ray of the principle" (*tattvaraśmi*), the seed-syllable of Vadhū is expressed. *Ha* is Kapilā. The left ear is the long vowel *ū*. By these, the seed-syllable of Kūrca is formed. *Pa* is the side. Its final [letter]...
The letter *pha*; the letter *ṭa* at the end. By that, *phaṭ* is established.
The second supreme mantra is the armor (*kavaca*) preceded by *māyā* (the letter *h*), with its middle [part] inverted;
it should be known as threefold, and the fourth begins with *kūrca* (the syllable *hūm*).
The fifth is proclaimed as beginning with *māyā* (the syllable *hrīṃ*) and ending with *kavaca* (the syllable *hūṃ*).
The sixth is situated in the middle of *māyā*, and the seventh is the final letter of the second [vowel].
The eighth [syllable] shall be in the middle of the armor; thus there will be eight variations.
This is the specific rule for the three-syllable [mantra]: where there is *phaṭ*, it is certainly not there.
In recitation (*japa*), however, it should be known as three-syllabled; in ritual placement (*nyāsa*), everything is established.
"Threefold" means the third [case-ending].
The seer (*ṛṣi*) is Aṣṭaka, the meter (*chandas*) is indeed Anuṣṭubh, and likewise the deity (*devatā*).
O Maheśānī, consort of Śambhu, whoever should recite [this] among the four aims of life (caturvarga), [shall attain them].
One should recite the mantra for as long as it takes to count a thousand [units] of time according to the path thus described;
one should perform all activities such as meditation and worship as previously instructed.
The characteristic of the time is six hundred thousand [recitations]. In the Bhairavatantra:
"The first of the Vedas (OM), the syllable of modesty (HRĪM), the 'tushkara' of the bride (STRĪM), followed by 'namas';
this is the six-syllabled mantra of Tārā, hidden in all tantras."
The *kūrca* (hūṃ), the *māyā* (hrīṃ), the *vadhū* (strīṃ), again the *kūrca* (hūṃ) joined with *phaṭ*—
this is the Great Vidyā, proclaimed as Bījatārā.
*Kāmaṃ*, *lajjāṃ*, *strībījaṃ*, *kūrcabījaṃ*, and likewise *phaṭ*—
this indeed is the supreme vidyā, the bestower of all desires.
The Praṇava, Lañjā, the pair of Kūrca-s, followed by "Namaḥ"—
this is the six-syllabled Vidyā, hidden in all Tantras.
O Goddess, the first [syllable] of Vāgbhava and the third of Bālā;
O Goddess, the first of the Vedas, which is Vāgbhava, joined with Kāma and Svāhā.
This eight-syllabled lore is proclaimed as the knowledge of Brahman;
these seed-mantras of Tāriṇī are independent and bestow all accomplishments.
These divisions of Mahogrā are impetuous promoters of human goals; they bestow longevity, prosperity, beauty, poetic talent, knowledge, and good fortune.
At the beginning are the stainless Brahman and those [mantras] which bestow liberation while living.
In the *Svacchanda-saṃgraha*: "O Maheśānī, one should recite the seed-syllable of Śiva, followed by the seed-syllable of Śakti;
joined with the Bindu and Sarga, one should recite that which begins with the Vedas (the syllable Om) below it."
The syllable *māyā* (hrīṃ) followed by the three seed-syllables of armor (*huṃ phaṭ*) and ending with the seed-syllable of the *haṃsa* (*so 'haṃ*)—
this eight-syllabled vidyā has been proclaimed, which is difficult to obtain on earth.
One attains the perfection of command and brings the three worlds under one's control;
the fourteen branches of Vedic knowledge come swiftly under one's power.
This great vidyā of Haṃsatārā has been revealed out of affection for you;
it brings poetic talent to men, and one who seeks wealth shall obtain wealth.
One who seeks liberation attains liberation; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
In the *Mātṛkā-arṇava*: "O sinless one, listen attentively as I declare another Vidyā:
[the syllable] Vāgbhava, then Kuladevī, then Tāraka, and likewise Vāgbhava."
The mantra ending with the weapon-mantra (astra) and culminating in the wife of fire (svāhā), preceded by Hṛllekhā,
is declared to be the supreme eight-syllabled mantra of the Mother of the Vedas, unsurpassed.
One should fashion the five limbs of this mantra by means of the five seed-syllables;
having assigned the weapon-mantra with the remaining syllables, the person becomes one who has accomplished his purpose.
One should perform all the meditations, offerings, and so forth as previously described.
This Great Vidyā, Ugratārā, is declared by me to be my own manly power.
The five-syllabled great vidyā, beginning and ending with *haṃsa*, which brings about great prosperity,
has been revealed to you through my affection and solely by means of effort.
One should perform the recitation, worship, and other rites for these two as one does for the five-syllabled mantra;
likewise, the seed-mantras, the mantra-sections, and the great vidyās beginning with Tārā are each distinct.
These [mantras] alone bestow the perfection of poetic skill and grant prosperity to one's lineage;
one should perform the six-limbed ritual (ṣaḍaṅga) by means of the six long vowels.
The worship is prescribed as before, and the ritual applications are likewise the same.
In the *Ekavīrākalpa*: "Then Śiva, Śakti, Māyā, and the syllable *phaṭ* are proclaimed;
this mantra of three and a half syllables is the lamp of knowledge (*jñānadīpa*) that bestows poetic skill."
Śiva-śakti is *hrīṃ*; Māyā is *hūṃ*.
Tāra, Māyā, and Śiva-śakti, ending with the syllable *phaṭ*, is remembered as Parā. Of these two, the ritual procedure (*kalpa*) taught for Mahogrā is the most excellent.
Likewise, one should write the syllable Khaṃ joined with the Kūrca (Hūṃ), which is Raudra and possesses the three qualities (guṇas),
according to the sequential application of the respective Śaktis of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara.
This is considered the Great Vidyā, which bestows all accomplishments upon the virtuous.
Khaṃ is the Bindu; Raudra is the Prāsāda; Tryaiguṇya is the Praṇava;
Vidhi-śakti is the Vāgbhava; Viṣṇu-śakti is the Śrībīja.
The seed-syllable of Bhuvaneśvarī is the power (śakti) of Maheśa.
The meditations, worship, and ritual applications for Tāriṇī should be understood as they were previously described.
In the Gandharva Tantra: "I shall now describe another Tārā who pacifies the afflictions of water; listen to her according to the truth."
By the mere remembrance of whom, fear is swiftly destroyed.
Having first extracted the Praṇava, then "Tāre," then "Tattāre," and likewise "Ture Svāhā"—
this mantra is said to consist of ten syllables.
I shall describe meditation, O wise one; listen, for it wards off all calamities, since no harm occurs anywhere in the waters when it is remembered.
Dark-complexioned, with two eyes and two arms, she holds a boon-granting lotus and is surrounded by [attendants] of many colors and many forms.
One should meditate upon her whose face is like that of Smara, adorned with shimmering pearl ornaments,
and whose pair of lotus-feet rest upon jeweled sandals.
The practitioner, having gained mastery through disciplined practice, should recite the vidyā one hundred thousand times according to the prescribed rule;
the mantra-master should then perform a fire oblation with red flowers smeared with ghee, numbering one-tenth of the recitation.
Thus, the Mahāvidyā is established; she shall grant all heart’s desires.
In the Bhairavatantra: Tāra (Om), Māyā (Hrīṃ), Vadhū (Śrīṃ), Kūrca (Phreṃ), Kālī, Kāmakalā, then Ugratārā, Bhaga, Kāma, Parā, Lakṣmī, Śivā, and Aṅkuśa.

This Great Ṣoḍaśī has now been declared by me as the Goddess Tārā. *Tāram* is the Praṇava (Oṃ). *Māyābīja* is Bhuvaneśvarī (Hrīṃ). *Vadhūbīja* is the seed-syllable of women (Auṃ). *Kūrcabīja* is the seed-syllable of armor (Hūṃ). *Kālībīja* is Krīṃ. *Kāmakalā* is the letter *Ī* with the bindu (*Īṃ*).

The essential form of Ugratārā is as follows: *bhaga* is the letter *e* joined with the nasal drop (*bindu*); *kāma* is the seed-syllable of desire (*kāmabīja*); *parābīja* is Bhuvaneśvarī; *lakṣmībīja* is the seed-syllable of Śrī; *śivabīja* is the seed-syllable of Prāsāda;
and *aṅkuśabīja* is *krom*.
Thus, O Goddess, I have told you that which is more secret than the secret;
it must never be given to just anyone, nor ever to one who is not a disciple.
One should perform all [rites] such as meditation and worship as previously described.
Now, regarding the Guptasodaśī mantra, it is stated in the Matsyasūkta: "Having first uttered the Praṇava (Oṃ), one should likewise utter the pair of 'Padme' (Padme Padme)."
One should utter the word "Mahāpadme," and then the word "Padmāvati."
This mantra, "māye svāhā," consisting of seventeen syllables, has been proclaimed;
having performed the worship as before at midnight at a crossroads.
Whoever performs the recitation (*japa*) of this [mantra] shall indeed become a swift poet.
Likewise: "Now I shall proclaim another Tārā, the savior of the world;
by her mere remembrance, she instantly destroys the fear of all living beings."
Having first extracted the Praṇava, one should extract the Hṛllekhā seed-syllable;
then Gaganam joined with Śeṣa, adorned with Bindu and Nāda.
One should extract the seed-syllable of the *kūrca*, the heart-mantra, and [the name] "to Tārā.
Then, one should utter: "Save me, save me from all that is difficult to cross! and likewise again.
This mantra, consisting of the pair of *tāra*s (om) and the wife of fire (svāhā), is the celestial wish-fulfilling tree;
it bestows speech composed of both prose and verse, which I shall now proclaim.
Whoever recites it four hundred thousand times shall indeed attain the eight siddhis;
one should perform all rites such as meditation and worship as previously described.
In the Siddhasārasvata: the seed-syllables of Vāc, Māyā, and Kamalā; the Lord (H) prescribed by Bhṛgu (M);
joined with the fourteenth moon (AU); and Parā, Bhṛgu, and Maheśvara.

Abounding in fourteen *visargas*, followed by the pair "vadat" and the word "vāk," then the word "vādinī," and thereafter the three *trīṃ* syllables; then the word "nīlasarasvatī" with a triple repetition of "vāk" and "manas."
After that, the two syllables "kaha," followed by "kalarī" and "vahnivallabhā."
The mantra of Nīlasārasvata consists of thirty-four syllables;
it is to be understood as having six sheaths, being composed of six mantras.
Listen, O Pārvatī, to the classification of the sages, meters, and deities:
the sage of the Gaṅgāpravāha [mantra] is Janārdana in the form of a fish.
Nīlasarasvatī possesses extraordinary speech and poetic talent; she is the embodiment of sovereignty over all forms of expression and the bestower of every desired object.
The seed-syllable *hūṃ* is to be known as the wedge (*kīlaka*), and *hsauḥ* is declared to be the power (*śakti*).
Its color is to be understood as blue, and its fruit is the attainment of poetic skill.
The mudrās are proclaimed as the mudrās of the faces of all the lords of speech;
one should perform the six-limbed ritual (ṣaḍaṅga) with the *hṛllekhā* mantra joined with the six long vowels.
She is in a state of meditative absorption, wearing blue garments and made of jewels, holding in her hands a lute,
a mudrā, and a vessel filled with nectar.
I worship with my heart that dark-hued Sarasvatī, who carries the flowing stream of poetry emerging from her four faces.
One should recite the vidyā one hundred thousand times and offer oblations with white lotuses ten thousand times;
the worship and the preparatory rite (puraścaryā) shall all be identical to that for Nīlā.

In another tantra: "The seed-syllable of modesty (hrīṃ), the seed-syllable of the bride (strīṃ), then the long 't' (t) and the 'armour' (h), followed by Sārasvata (aiṃ)—this is declared to be the four-syllabled mantra."

If at its end there is the syllable *phaṭ*, the mantra becomes five-syllabled. Likewise: *tāra* (oṃ), *śakti* (hrīṃ), and the seed-syllable of the *vadhū* (strīṃ), followed at the end by the long *tanucchada* (huṃ) and the *astra* (phaṭ) with the *vadhū* (strīṃ) at the end; this mantra becomes seven-syllabled.
In the mantra scriptures, it is proclaimed that the seed-syllable of the bride (Vadhū-bīja) is likewise encapsulated by the long armor (Dīrgha-varman); this is another syllable of qualities.

In the *Tantraśekhara*: "The third [syllable] is Bhuvaneśānī; the armor and power are the two syllables for the body-protector (*tanutraka*); ending with the weapon-syllable and beginning with the *praṇava*, this is the Vidyā worshipped by Dhātṛ."
The third is *trīm*. Likewise: "The third is Bhuvaneśānī; Kamala and Mīnaketana; Bhṛgu joined with Manu; Sargī; and Śiva joined with Karṇendu."
Furthermore, Ugratārā has armor ending in *phaṭ* and is worshipped by Viṣṇu;
*praṇava*, armor, *hṛllekhā*, and the two *smara*s are for the third armor.
This second weapon, worshipped by Viṣṇu, has been prescribed;
it consists of the syllables *hṛllekhā* (hrīṃ) and *smara* (klīṃ).
Likewise, if the third [weapon], the *tryai-pura*, is joined with these preceding ones:
Then those beautiful goddesses would become worthy of worship by the Four-faced One.
The construction is: "If [the third] is at the beginning first. The previously mentioned Ekajaṭā is considered to be the Vidyā devoid of the third [syllable].
Furthermore, that same [Vidyā], when deprived of Māyā and the Praṇava, is [Ekajaṭā] again.
The previously mentioned five-syllable vidyā, when deprived of its third syllable, becomes the Ekajaṭā;

thus, this [mantra] consists of four syllables. That same five-syllable vidyā, when deprived of both Māyā and Praṇava, would likewise become the Ekajaṭā; thus, this [mantra] consists of three syllables.
The third armor and weapons are Ratīśa and the final [syllable] of Vāgbhava;
this is the vidyā worshipped by Nārāyaṇa, which bestows all prosperity.

The third [set] consists of the armor (*kavaca*) and weapons (*astra*), which take the forms of three *hūṃ* and *phaṭ*. *Ratīśa* is *klīṃ*. The term *vāgbhava* refers to the letter *ai*; that which has this as its final [element] is an epithet of *ratīśa*. Thus, this [mantra] consists of five syllables. Likewise: "For these kings of mantras, Śakti is declared to be the seer (*ṛṣi*)."
The Gāyatrī meter is prescribed, and the supreme deity is Tārā.
The arrangement of the ritual placement (nyāsa) should be performed as before; then one should meditate upon the Goddess:

she who is like camphor and the moon, white in complexion, possessing two excellent hands, adorned with glittering jewel ornaments, her forehead marked by the crescent moon, three-eyed, and graced with strings of pearl necklaces.
I take refuge in the supreme Goddess Tārā, who bears a garland fashioned from human skulls, whose lotus-face is resplendent, and who is surrounded by her handmaidens.
One should worship the Supreme Goddess on the previously mentioned pedestal as before;
one desiring knowledge should perform the fire-oblation with auspicious offerings of sugar and milk-rice.
426) One should meditate on this [goddess] as red for subjugation; for paralyzing, one should remember her as resembling gold;
for expulsion, one should meditate on her as smoke-colored; and for the rite of killing, as black.
The mantra is said to begin with *Tārā*, followed by *aparā* and *namas*, and end with *bhagavati ekajaṭe mama vajrapuṣpaṃ pratīccha svāhā*.
The sage is declared to be Patañjali; the meter is the Gāyatrī, which has been purified;
the deity is declared to be Ekajaṭā, the supreme one who accomplishes the corpse.
One should perform the assignment of the limbs using the seed-syllable called Māyā, which possesses six long vowels;
one should carry out all [rites] such as meditation and worship according to the previously mentioned path.
*Tāraḥ* (Oṃ), *śrīśaktitārtīye* (Śrī Śakti Tārtīye), *hūṃ phaṭ*—this is the mantra of Nīlasarasvatī ending in *ṅe*; it is declared as the supreme *manulipi*.
The sage is declared to be Brahmā, the meter is the revered Gāyatrī,
and the deity is said by the virtuous to be the goddess Nīlasarasvatī.

May Sarasvatī bestow auspicious blessings upon us— she who, with her sprout-like hands, holds a sword, a trident, and a severed head adorned with a bell, while she tramples a sacrificial animal under her feet; she whose limbs are fashioned from the syllables of the mantra, arranged as two, one, two, two, six, and two.
The wise one should worship on the previously mentioned pedestal according to the previously mentioned procedure.
Now, O Goddess, I shall proclaim the rite of placement (nyāsa) for this Vidyā which is very difficult to obtain.
Speech, Power, Kamalā, Kāma, Bhṛgu adorned with the nasal drop (bindu),
Pañcabāṇa, Parāvāc, Kuṭilā, and joined with Indra.
The left ear is the support for the *lava*; from that comes the mantra consisting of the female principle (*strīmātmaka*).
After the word *nīlatāre*, one should utter the word *sarasvati*.
The two Atris are joined with the letter *ra* and adorned by the long vowel, the left eye, and the moon;
they are the seed-syllable of Kāma (*klīm*), adorned by the sixth vowel and the earring.
Then the Moon (ca), the Creator (sa), the five seeds beginning with the Five-Arrowed One (pa),
Sauḥ, Parā, and the wife of Fire (svāhā)— this is the thirty-two-syllable mantra.

Speech is the syllable *aiṃ*; Śakti is the syllable *hrīṃ*; Kamalā is the syllable *śrīṃ*; Kāma is *klīṃ*; Bhṛgu is the letter *sa*. Adorned with the *au* vowel, the nasal dot (*anusvāra*), and the circle (*bindu*), it is the syllable *auṃ*. The Five Arrows is the syllable *klīṃ*. The two supreme Speeches are *hrīṃ* and *aiṃ*, which are their forms. The letter *ba* ends in *kuṭilā* (the letter *ṭa*) and ends in *pha* (the letter *pa*).
The letter *la* is Indra. The long *ū* is the left ear. The *lava* is the bindu. By these, [the seed-syllable] is *blūṃ*.

That which consists of the feminine (*strīmātmaka*) is *strīṃ*. *Nīlatārā* is its own form; *Sarasvatī* is also its own form. *Atrī* refers to the two *da*s joined with the letter *ra*. The long *ā* is [the vowel].

The left eye is the letter *ī*; the moon is the *anusvāra*. Joined with these, [one obtains] *drāṃ* and *drīṃ*. The seed-syllable of desire (*kāmabīja*) is *klīṃ*. *Valoṃ* consists of the letters *ba* and *la*. The sixth vowel is *ū*; the earring is the *anusvāra*. The moon is the letter *sa*; the one possessing emission (*sargī*) is the *visarga*. The five arrows are the letter *ai*. That which begins with this [is the mantra].

The five seed-syllables (*bījapañcaka*) consist of *aiṃ*, *klīṃ*, *blūṃ*, *strīṃ*, and *saḥ*. *Sauri* is its essential form (*svarūpa*). *Parā* is the syllable *hrīṃ*. *Vahnijāyā* is *svāhā*. Likewise, the sages (*ṛṣi*) and other [limbs] have been mentioned previously; the arrangement of the ritual placement (*nyāsakalpana*) is as before.
Mounted upon a boat, the three-eyed goddess, whose body is embraced by [Her Consort], whose nature is consciousness and bliss,
holding in her own hands a skull-cup, a trident, a saw, and a cleaver; she is endowed with a loud,
boisterous laughter and is made beautiful by the ever-shimmering garlands of severed heads.
She shines, with small bells tinkling gracefully upon her broad hips that rise up like the ocean.

Having meditated thus, one should recite the mantra four hundred thousand times with a concentrated mind. One should perform oblations with blossoming *kiṃśuka* flowers soaked in the three sweets (*madhuratra*) in a square [mandala] at the corners of fire, wind, Maheśa (northeast), and the moon (northwest).
Vighneśa, named Vaṭu, as well as Kṣetreśa and Bhairava.
Then, having worshipped the Yoginī, one should worship the Guru in the northeast;
on the first line of the subterranean chamber (bhūgṛha), one should worship Aṇimā and the other [siddhis].
Aṇimā is declared the first, and likewise laghimā is the second;
mahimā is declared the third, and the fourth is known by the name īśitva.
The fifth is known as Vaśitā; the sixth is named Prākāmya. The seventh is called Bhukti, and then the eighth is Icchā.
On the second day, one should worship Asitāṅga, Ruru, Caṇḍa, Krodha, Unmattakapālin, Bhīṣaṇa, and Saṃhāra.
On the third day, the practitioner of mantra should worship Brāhmī and the others, who possess the previously described characteristics;
in the first enclosure, the practitioner of mantra should display the yoni-mudrā.
Kuleśī, Kulanandā, Vāgīśī, Bhairavī, Umā,
Śrīśāntā, Caṇḍā, Dhūmrā, Kālī, and Karālinī.
Mahālakṣmī, Kaṅkālī, Rudrakālī, Sarasvatī, Vāgvādinī, Nakulī, Bhadrakālī, Śivā, and Prabhā.
Pratyaṅgirā, Siddhalakṣmī, Amṛteśī, Caṇḍikā,
Khecarī, Bhūcarī, Siddhā, Kāmākhyā, Hiṅgulā, and Balā.
Jayā, Vijayā, Ajitā, Nityāyuktā, Aparājitā, Vilāsinī, Ghorā, Citrā, Mugdhā, and Kuleśvarī.
Someśvarī, Mahācandrā, Vidyā, Haṃsā, Vināyakī, Vedagā, as well as Bhīmā, Ugrā, Vaidyā, Satī, and Gati.
Ugreshvari, Chandragarbha, Jyotsna, Satya, Yashovati, Kulika, Kamini, Jnana, Dakini, and then Kakini.
Lākinī, Kākinī, then Sākinī, and likewise Hākinī—
these are to be worshipped in the sixty-four petals of the second enclosure.
One should demonstrate the Khecarī mudrā, which brings about the state of moving through the sky;
[it is guarded by] Kirātā, Yoginī, Vīrā, Vetālā, Yakṣiṇī, and Harā.
Ūrdhvakeśī, Mātaṅgī, Mohinī, Vaṃśavardhinī,
Mālinī, Lalitā, Dūtī, Manojñā, Padminī, and Parā.
Varvarī with a parasol in her hand, Raktanetrā, Vicarcikā, Mātṛkā, Dūradarśā, Kṣetreśī, Raṅgiṇī, and Naṭī.
The practitioner of mantra should worship these— Śāntā, Dīptā, Vajrahastā, Dhūmrā, Śvetā, and Sumaṅgalā— who reside within the midst of the thirty-two petals.
In the third enclosure, one should display the mudrā called Bījāhvā;
[the goddesses] are Mugdhā, Śrīkurukullā, Tripurā, Trotanā, and Kriyā.
Rati, Prīti, as well as Vālī, Sumukhī, Śyāmalā,
Vilā, Piśācī, Vidārī, Śītalā, and Vajrayoginī.
O Maheśvarī, one should worship these [deities] endowed with power in the fourth enclosure; one should display the mudrā called the goad (aṅkuśa).
On an eight-petaled [lotus], the auspicious mantra-practitioner should worship the eight Sarasvatīs;
beginning with the Praṇava, the heart-mantra, and "on the lotus-seat," followed again by the word "sound" (śabda).
*Rūpe*, *vāk śambhuvanitā*, *kāmaḥ*, *vadavadeti*—
this twenty-four-syllable mantra is the beloved of Vahni (Agni), known as Vāgvādinī.
By means of this, one should conquer the Goddess Vāgīśī, who possesses auspicious characteristics;
she is adorned by Śambhu, Jīva, Kala, Īśa, and Agni, and is garlanded with the Bindu.
Then, O wise one, one should worship the goddess Citreśvarī with this mantra: "Vada-yugmam, then Citreśvari, Vāgvahni-sundarī, Citreśvarīm.
One should worship the goddess Citreśvarī with this mantra.
Śambhu is the syllable *ha*; Jīva is the syllable *sa*. *Kala* is its own form. Īśa is the syllable *ha*; Agni is the letter *ra*.
Following the word *maṇḍitā*, there is an elision (*praśleṣa*) of the vowel *a*; by this, the form of the *bindu* (dot) is indicated.
Bindumālinī is the syllable *ī*. Thus, [the mantra] is *hasakalahrīṃ*. Vāk is *aiṃ*; Vahnisundarī is *svāhā*. The remainder...
The essential form: "Vāgruddhaḥ kulaje śabdaḥ sarasvati śiro namaḥ.
By means of this mantra, the practitioner should worship the goddess Kulajā.
Vāk Aiṃ; Śiras Svāhā;
Parāvāk Kamalā Ruddhā, followed by the pair of words "vada" and "śabda";
Kīrtīśvarī Priyā Vahne—by means of this mantra, one should worship the Heart.
The practitioner of mantra should then worship Kīrtīśvarī, followed by Vāk Śambhusundarī;
before her, at the word "Antarikṣa," [he worships] Sarasvatī, the beloved of purity.

By means of this mantra, the practitioner should worship the goddess Sarasvatī, who dwells in the intermediate space, using the syllables *ha sa kha preṃ* with the vowels of the human scale (*manusvara*).
Joined with the fires of Śiva and Jīva, adorned with Bindu and Nāda,
and united with Varāha, Haṃsa, Kuṭila, Vali, and Pradyumna.
"O left-eyed one! O supreme speech! O Lakṣmī! O destroyer of arrows! From the sound of the word 'ghaṭa'—O Sarasvatī, from the sound of the word 'ghaṭa,' speak the two descents!"
The third case-ending Rudrājñā should state my desire;
one should worship the beloved of Fire with this mantra preceded by "kuru."
The practitioner [should worship] the Goddess Ghaṭasarasvatī, renowned throughout the three worlds.

"Manusvara" is an epithet for this [mantra]; the two [terms] beginning with "Śiva" are its qualifiers: Śiva is *ha*, Jīva is *sa*, and Agni is *ra*. "Varāhī" is an epithet for "Vāmākṣī": Varāha is *ha*, and Haṃsa is...
The letter *sa* [is the seed-syllable]. The curved one is the letter *pha*. The powerful one is the letter *ra*. Pradyumna is the *anusvāra*. The left eye is the letter *ī*.

Thus, [the mantra is] *hasaphrīṃ*. Speech is *aiṃ*. Parā is *hrīṃ*. Lakṣmī is *śrīṃ*. The arrows are *drāṃ drīṃ klīṃ blūṃ saḥ*. "Ghnī" is its essential form (*svarūpa*). "In the third case" is an adjective qualifying the command of Rudra (*rudrājñā*).
By that command of Rudra; the rest is easy to understand.
Bhūdhara is declared to be Bhūdhara, possessing the crescent moon on the left ear;
the third [syllable] is the pair of waters (va-va), like the moon of the Blessed One.
With that mantra ending in *phaṭ*, the practitioner of mantras should worship Nīlā.
*Bhūdhara* is the syllable *va*; *bhūdhara* is the bearer of the syllable *la*. The left ear is the syllable *ū*;
the "moon-segment" is the half-moon (*ardhacandra*). Thus, [the seed-syllable is] *blūṃ*. *Bhaga* is the syllable *e*; likewise, it is joined with that.
Candra is the half-moon; "tadvat" means joined with that. Nīra is the syllable *va*; thus, *veṃ*. The third is the syllable *trīṃ*. Krodha is the syllable *hūṃ*.
Vāgbhava is Śambhu joined with speech, namely *hrīṃ*; again, the pair of *kili*s.
430) One should worship this nine-syllabled mantra, known by the name Kilinā.
"Vāgyuta" means joined with the letter *e*. "Śambhu" is the letter *ha*; thus, [the seed-syllable] is *haiṃ*. The remainder is its own form.
In the fifth enclosure, the wise one should display the Kṣobhamudrā.
The best of mantra-knowers should worship the limbs, beginning with Ḍākinī, in the corners.
One should display the Drāviṇī mudrā; this is considered the sixth enclosure (āvaraṇa).
One should worship Parā, Bālā, and Bhairavī within the triangle.
One should display the Karṣaṇī mudrā; this is known as the seventh enclosure.
Furthermore, one should worship the Goddess again with enchanting offerings;
then the mantra-practitioner should present the *bali* offering daily at a crossroads.
To Gaṇapa and Kṣetrapāla, to the Yoginī and to Bhairava,
one should offer blood, meat, food, black gram, lamps, and curd for the Goddess.
That which is known as the sacrificial offering (bali-dravya) bestows the fulfillment of one's desires;
meditation is declared to be threefold, according to the sequence of creation, maintenance, and dissolution.
For each specific rite, however, one should perform the corresponding meditation:
[meditate on her] as four-faced and eight-armed, adorned with ornaments of pearl.
[He is] white-clad, holding in his hands the akṣamudrā, the śakti, the noose,
the water-pot, the lotus, the flower-garland, and the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
One should visualize her seated upon a swan-vehicle in the midst of an ocean of sound,
wearing red garments and adorned with various ornaments of gold and jewels.
In the great grove on Ratnadvīpa, she is surrounded by her retinue;
she is seated upon a jeweled lion-throne, displaying the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, and holding a rosary.
One should visualize her in a standing posture, holding a jeweled cup;
one should further visualize her mounted upon a boat in the midst of a sea of red water.
She has nine faces and an eye in her forehead; she is terrifying with her black garments, and she holds the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, as well as an axe and a ladle.
In his left hand he holds the Saṃhāra weapon, and likewise the Pāśupata in his right;
with his left hand he holds a three-headed trident, and a sword and a chisel.
With her arms she holds a lotus, a noose, a plow, a spear, a triple-form [trident], a drum, a skull-topped staff, and a pestle; her mind is intent on devouring her enemies.
Bestowing boons upon devotees and protecting the practitioner—
one should perform each respective rite through this yoga of meditation.
Thus, the practitioner who has accomplished the mantra shall become the foremost among poets;
he should write the mantra upon the tongue of a child whose umbilical cord has not yet been severed.
In the eighth year, the child shall transcend all desires; having consecrated ten thousand and eight hundred stalks of *vacā* grass with mantras.
Having offered the oblation as before, one should perform that rite which reaches the throats of children;
when the twelfth year has arrived, what is consumed therein produces poetic talent.
During an eclipse of the moon or sun, one should consume one karṣa of oil derived from *jyotiṣmatī* that has been consecrated with this mantra.
Standing in the midst of water, the mute child becomes Vācaspati;
and at the cremation ground, at the crossroads, the practitioner, having mounted a corpse, [attains the same].
Freed from fear and shame, one should recite the vidyā with undistracted mind;
at midnight, a sound will arise, and one will become a master who has reached the further shore of existence, knowledge, and purpose.
Having established a pair of eight-year-old children born of his own lineage who have been well-bathed,
the practitioner should place both hands upon their heads.
In a secluded forest, in a wilderness adorned with a pavilion of plantain trees, he engaged in a great and tumultuous debate on Nyāya and Vedānta;
having prepared an altar there, he sat comfortably upon it, smiling.
In a forest adorned with *campaka*, *aśoka*, *punnāga*, and plantain trees,
she was seated upon a swing, her face serene, a beautiful woman sent there by her maidservants.
Meditating thus, one should recite the mantra with a concentrated mind for twelve hundred thousand times;
at the conclusion of the recitation, one should offer an oblation to the Goddess together with her retinue.
By this procedure, O Goddess, one attains one's well-desired goal. Now follows the ritual manual of Tāriṇī from the Tāriṇītantra:
Īśvara said:
Listen, O Daughter of the Mountain, to this supreme knowledge which destroys dullness,
which yields the fruits of the four aims of life, and bestows the perfection of mantras.
The first letter of the class [ka], joined with fire (ra), adorned with the left eye (ī),
and endowed with nāda and bindu, bestows the eight siddhis.
Furthermore, O Goddess, it has four faces adorned with the letter *ta*, along with the fourth vowel and a crescent moon, O Beloved. (432)
The great seed-syllable (Mahābīja), marked with the *lāñchana*, bestows the fruits of the four aims of life;
thereafter, having uttered the word "Kṛṣṇa," the word "Devī" is then remembered.
Then one should give the syllable *hrīṃ*, and thereafter extract the letter *va*;
it is adorned with the letter *ī*, the letter *ra*, and the letter *ma*.
Then, having uttered the Vāgbhava [seed-syllable], one should extract this mantra;
O Goddess, this nine-syllabled Mantra is proclaimed as that of Tāriṇī.
This very Mahāvidyā is extremely difficult to obtain in heaven or among mortals;
O Goddess, she bestows the eight supernatural powers and grants the fruits of the four aims of human life.
There is no knowledge equal to this, no mantra equal to this;
there has never been, nor will there ever be, an accomplishment equal to this.
O Goddess, what is there that does not happen for one who attains this knowledge?
Before long, he obtains speech that bestows both prose and verse.
O Pārvatī, by the mere knowledge of this science, one shall quickly become a swift poet,
even without prosody, without phonetics, and without practice.
Even for a poet, without knowledge, without effort, and without discourse,
poetic skill born of aesthetic relish arises upon the tongue.
In that regard, the sequence of worship is as follows:
first, having brought water, the washing of the feet is prescribed;
having sipped water twice and tied the topknot, one then performs the purification of the ground.
Having performed the expulsion of obstacles, one should then purify the flowers;
O Goddess of Gods, being intent on that, one should thoroughly purify both hands with the Astra-mantra.
Having bowed to the gurus and Gaṇapati, one should perform the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi).
The seed-syllable Vāgbhava, which bestows all accomplishments, resides in the Svādhiṣṭhāna;
with the flames of the fires of those respective elements, the wise burn the body.
Having cleared away that heap of ashes with the wind produced by the syllable *hrīṃ*,
and having flooded those bones with the nectar produced from the *kāmabīja* on the forehead,
one should then perform the rite once they have become solidified.
The practitioner, having meditated upon the self as stainless, devoid of qualities, pure, consisting of the deity,
and completely liberated from all sins, [should contemplate] the body.
433) Then, having purified the body, one should perform breath control (prāṇāyāma).
One should contemplate three rounds of prāṇāyāma with the root-bīja of Aghora.
Then, O Goddess, hear the mantra-installation (mantranyāsa) which bestows the perfection of mantras.
Śakti is declared to be its seer (ṛṣi), and the Bṛhatī meter is said to be its metre (chandas).
The deity is declared to be Tāriṇī, the seed-syllable (bīja) is said to be Hrīṃ, and Vāgbhava is called the power (śakti); thus one should perform the ritual beginning with the seer (ṛṣi).
One should perform the six-limbed assignment using the seed-syllable and the six limbs;
the practitioner of mantra should then place dharma and the others, and subsequently place adharma and the others.
Then, one should place these in sequence above, above, and in the middle;
having uttered "Kalpavṛkṣa" (the wish-fulfilling tree), one should utter "Maṇipīṭha" (the jeweled pedestal).
Having held a corpse-skull and then a red skull-cup,
O Goddess, one should place them in the four directions together with the fire of the funeral pyre.
Then, one should place eight powers there upon the eight petals of the heart-lotus:
Durgā, Jayā, Medhā, Vijayā, and Suprabhā are considered [the first five].
Kālī, Gaurī, and Śivā—these are remembered as the eight Śaktis.
Therefore, the wise man should install the five wombs (pañcayoni) within his own body in this manner.
Then, one should place the Yoni-vīrā at the right side of the hair-parting;
subsequently, one should place the Yoni-vidyā at the left side of the hair-parting.
