O Goddess of gods, one should place the form of the *yoni* at the root of the nose according to its divisions;
the *yoni*-desire and the *yoni*-necklace on the right and left eyes;
and the form of the *yoni* on the lip for the sake of accomplishing all desires and goals.
O Goddess of gods, [this is done] in the mouth and the ear, according to the distinction between right, left, and so forth.

And then, O Great Goddess, the most excellent practitioner should place [the seed-syllable] on the chin; thereafter, [he should place] the one whose necklace is the womb, whose body is the womb, and whose form is the womb upon the region of the womb.
Then, O fair-faced one, one should meditate upon her at the base of the left arm and in the heart as the womb-mind, established in the womb, and having the form of the womb.
One should always remember the locus of the *yoni* in the breasts and the region of the navel;
then, one should install [the goddess] who is perfected by the *yoni*, pierced by the *yoni*, and whose form is the *yoni*.
These [mantras] are remembered by the wise as ending in the dative case and concluding with "namas";
then, with a steady mind, one should meditate upon the Goddess within the seat of the body.
She is black, pot-bellied, and formidable, adorned with serpent earrings;
her face is red, her tongue lolls out, and she wears a red garment around her waist.
O Goddess of gods, she is fierce, with full and elevated breasts, encircled by a great serpent;
she stands upon a corpse, and above that, upon a skull-cup.
She is intent on meditation upon the tip of the nose, most formidable, and the bestower of boons;
she has four arms and long hair, with her upper right arm raised.
Bearing a single lotus in her left half and a drinking vessel,
the Goddess holds the gestures of boon-granting and fearlessness below, in her right and left hands respectively.
[He beheld] the Goddess who dwells on the mountain, the eternal one who bestows all accomplishments, drinking a stream of blood from her drinking-vessel in the presence of Sadāśiva.
She was endowed with three eyes, wearing a serpent as a sacred thread;
she had a long nose, long shanks, long limbs, and a long tongue.
She who possesses three eyes through the divisions of the moon, sun, and fire;
the goddess who destroys enemies, is most formidable, and bestows boons.
With her head bound by a tiger skin, she is renowned throughout the three worlds;
she brings happiness to practitioners while causing terror to all the world.
I bow down to the Great Goddess Tāriṇī who has become thus.
Having meditated in this way and worshipped her mentally, one should perform the ritual installation of the *argha* vessel as in the case of Tārā.
Her worship diagram (*pūjāyantra*) is likewise as follows:
O Goddess of the gods, having fashioned the yantra, one should place it in the center of the [diagram];
then, with red sandalwood paste, one should draw an eight-petaled lotus.
Outside of that, the best of practitioners should draw sixteen petals;
then, he should draw a pair of fire-maṇḍalas in the center of the yantra.
O Goddess of gods, one should then write the first seed-syllable on the eastern petal,
the second on the southern petal, and the third on the western petal.
O Goddess of gods, one should then write "phaṭ" on the northern petal and likewise write the syllable Vāṇī;
[the mandala] should be provided with four gates and endowed with eight vajras.
Then, having worshipped the pedestal on all sides according to the previously mentioned sequence,
one should invoke the Great Goddess there and worship her while reciting the mantra.
O Goddess of the gods, having worshipped Pārvatī with the sixfold ritual (ṣaḍaṅga), one should worship these four—
the Kṣetrapāla, Bhairava, Gaṇanātha, and Mahāntaka—
at the four gateways, O Goddess. (435)
O Goddess, having worshipped these on the eight petals starting from the east, the practitioner [should proceed].
O Goddess, Aṇimā is Anaṅgamadanā, Laghimā is Madanāturā, and then Anaṅgakusumā; thus are the eight Karṇikās.
O Goddess of gods, one should likewise worship Kapālikā and then the eight Yoginīs; furthermore, one should worship the attendants upon the sixteen petals.
There, she bestows happiness, liberation, devotion, and likewise enjoyment;
she grants emancipation, spiritual perfection, the fulfillment of desires, and the prosperity of the lineage.

O Goddess, you who bestow security, or indeed auspiciousness, the giver of boons, and likewise the giver of the Self; you who grant passion, the giver of enjoyment, the giver of liberation, and the giver of all perfections.
Then, O Goddess, one should worship the eight siddhis beginning with aṇimā at the eastern gate,
and likewise the ten kalās of Fire at the southern gate.
One should worship the digits of the Moon at the western doorway as well;
and likewise, O Goddess, one should then worship a digit of the Sun in the north.
One should worship the Goddess with the six-limbed rite, and thereafter worship the weapons;
O Goddess of the lords of gods, these [mantras] are prescribed with the dative case ending.
O Great Goddess, those [mantras] ending in *namaḥ* are said to bestow all accomplishments (*siddhi*),
when worshipped with various kinds of flowers smeared with red sandalwood paste.
O Great Goddess, with red flowers endowed with various fragrances,
as well as bilva leaves, perfumes, and especially with javā flowers.
With white and red powders, as well as campaka and ketaka flowers—
one should worship the Great Goddess Nityatāriṇī with these blossoms.
At that time, one should not worship with *mālatī* or *vakapuṣpa* flowers,
nor with *dūrvā*, *kadamba*, white blossoms, saffron, or *kāñcana*.
O Maheśvarī, having thus performed the worship with these materials,
one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times, subsisting on sacrificial food (haviṣya) and with senses subdued.
Thus ends the Tāriṇī-kalpa.
Thus concludes the eleventh chapter in the *Tārābhaktisudhārṇava* composed by the Great Professor, the illustrious Ṭhakkura Narasiṃha. || 11 ||
